STRAP Experimental Procedures. Polymer recovery using STRAP broadly consists of polymer dissolution, filtration, precipitation, and recovery. STRAP was carried out using two experimental protocols with different heating setups and feed size: (1) a simple setup for a smaller amount of feed (1 -20 g) and (2) a jacketed dissolution vessel for a larger amount of feed (150 -200 g). 19 Silicone oil was used as heat-transfer fluid to achieve a desired temperature during dissolution. 19

Small-Scale STRAP Setup. Figure 2a shows the overall experimental process for the recovery of PE and EVOH. The setup shown in Figure 2b involves five steps to recover the PE and residual film components. In step 1, 5 g of shredded films is dissolved in 100 g of dodecane (feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:20) at 110 °C. The solution is stirred in a silicone oil bath with a magnetic stirrer for 90 min to maximize PE dissolution. In step 2, the hot solution is filtered out to separate dissolved PE from other components using a stainless-steel wire mesh filter with an opening size of 0.0277 in. and an open area of 44.2%. In step 3, the dodecane -PE solution is cooled at room temperature for 30 min, allowing the PE to precipitate. In step 4, the cooled solution is mechanically filtered under vacuum to recover the precipitated PE. Finally, in step 5, the recovered PE and undissolved residual flakes are dried in a vacuum oven at 100 °C for 2 h. This process yielded 4 g of PE and 1 g of residual flakes for further analysis.

The residual flakes recovered after the dodecane wash were found to be rich in EVOH. The small-scale STRAP setup was applied to 1 g of the residual flakes, and all steps were repeated with 20 g of DMSO as a solvent. After drying in the vacuum oven, this process yielded 0.3 g of EVOH which was 6% of the films by weight. However, some fractions remained undissolved even after the DMSO wash, and there were some material transfer losses as well. The undissolved fraction (residue) was found to be 0.2 g (4% of the films), with the rest of the film mass lost in material transfer.

Jacketed Dissolution Vessel STRAP Setup. A 4 L jacketed dissolution vessel was used to perform experiments at larger scale and produce resins for mechanical testing. The vessel is heated by a continuous flow of silicone oil through the jacket. The undissolved fractions were collected in a filter mesh made up of steel with a 1000 μ m pore size. A total volume of 3.1 L ( ∼ 2120 g) of heptane was preheated to 95 °C in the vessel before 155 g of shredded film was added, maintaining a feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:13.6. This feed-tosolvent ratio was achieved after averaging 7 -8 runs. A feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:12 resulted in a low PE yield (70%) and undissolved flakes (20%) that were contaminated with PE. Undissolved flakes, presumed to be EVOH, were separated using an internal filter mesh and retained for subsequent analysis, as detailed later in this study. To generate sufficient STRAP PE for a cast film, the experiment was performed in ten iterations, with the average batch material balance illustrated in Figure 3.

Characterization. FTIR. Attenuated total reflectance Fouriertransform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectra were acquired with a Bruker Vertex 70 FTIR spectrometer equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium -telluride (MCT) detector (Bruker Corporation, Billerica, Massachusetts, USA). An average of 16 scans was collected in the range of 4000 -600 cm -1 with a resolution of 4 cm -1 . Each spectrum was scanned with an air background.

TGA. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted on a TGA Q500 analyzer (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA) from 40 to 550 °C for PE with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 under a nitrogen flow rate of 50.0 mL min -1 . For EVOH, TGA was conducted on the same machine from 40 to 220 °C with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 and held at 220 °C for 10 min.

DSC. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was used to estimate the melting temperature ( T m) and crystallization temperature ( T c) on a DSC Q100 calorimeter equipped with a Refrigerated Cooling System 90 (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA). Samples were encapsulated in standard aluminum pans, heated from -20 to 220 °C with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 and cooled from 220 to -20 °C at the same ramping rate. The heating/cooling process was looped twice at a 50.0 mL min -1 nitrogen flow rate.

GC -MS. Gas chromatography -mass spectrometry (GC -MS) was used to analyze the solvents on a Shimadzu GCMS-QP2010 mass spectrometer with an RTX-VMS column and quadrupole MS (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan).

Figure 3. Schematic of the jacketed dissolution vessel for large-scale STRAP experiments.

Hot Press for Compressed Films. Small films for EVOH testing were produced by placing 0.75 g of polymer between two 6 in. × 6 in. PTFE-coated fiberglass sheets followed by two 6 in. × 6 in. aluminum sheets on the outside. The Carver Press 3970 was used to heat the sample at 190 °C without pressure for 1 min, followed by 3 mt of pressure for 1 min.

Extrusion of Recovered Polyethylene and Cast Film Production. The PE recovered from the jacketed vessel STRAP method was cryoground with liquid nitrogen in a Thomas Model 4 Wiley Mill to 3 mm granules before extrusion. The PE powder was extruded to 3 mm pellets using a Leistritz twin-screw extruder with a temperature profile of 170 -190 °C and a 19 rpm screw speed. After this, the PE pellets were extruded into a cast film at an average barrel temperature of 177 °C and a die temperature of 193 °C with a Labtech Engineering cast film extruder.

Characterization of the PE Cast Film. Tensile properties of the films were measured using an Instron testing machine following ASTM Standard D882-1. 36 The thermal properties of the films were analyzed with a NETZSCH TGA 209F1Libra. The analysis compared the dynamic cooling and the second heating of the films, from -20 to 250 °C, at rate of 10 K/min. Final color of the cast films was quantified with a spectrophotometer and measurements were converted to CIELAB color space values, L * (lightness), a * (redgreen color component) and b * (blue-yellow color component), and YI (yellowness index). 37 Optical properties were analyzed following the ASTM standard D1003-21 for haze and luminous transmittance of transparent plastics. 38 The defect analysis for determining the number of impurities in the cast films was performed with an Amcor internal method.

Technoeconomic Analysis (TEA) and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The process model was developed in BioSTEAM, an opensource platform in Python for the design, simulation, and evaluation (via TEA and LCA) of chemical processes. 39,40 The model is based on data from laboratory experiments, the construction of a 25 kg/h STRAP pilot plant at Michigan Technological University, 41 and builds upon past TEA/LCA studies on STRAP. 13,17

The plastic feedstock is fed into a dissolution vessel and is mixed with the solvent to dissolve the target polymer (Figure 4). The effluent is sent through a series of filters to separate the solids (i.e., insoluble plastics and biogenic material) from the solution. A vacuum twin-screw drier recovers >99.9% of the solvent retained on the undissolved plastic. The undissolved plastic can be landfilled or further processed to remove another resin layer. The dissolved resin is then precipitated by cooling within a jacketed precipitation and filtration module. After precipitation, a melt devolatilizer removes the solvent down to <1 wt %, and an outgassing extruder recovers the last solvent fraction, leaving low concentrations (<10 ppm) in the resin. Plastic additives, inks, and any soluble biogenic material which may accumulate in the solvent are removed by adsorption with granulated activated carbon. The design of the adsorption module follows the procedure outlined by Gabelman. 42 The solute capacity was estimated using the fitted Freundlich isotherm of Yellow 12 dye (commonly found in plastics) with activated carbon. 43 The length of the unused bed was estimated through numerical mass transfer modeling. After adsorption, the cold solvent is reheated and returned to the dissolution tank. To improve energy efficiency and economics, a heat exchanger was added between the hot and cold solvent streams.

Techno-Economic Analysis. Cost estimates for solvent removal equipment were provided by Amcor. Cost estimates for specialized STRAP equipment (e.g., dissolution and precipitation vessels) were provided by industry vendors. The 6/10th rule for economies of scale was used to formulate capital cost correlations for the specialized modules in STRAP. 44 The cost of the adsorption columns was estimated as pressure vessels using ASME guidelines to vessel thickness. 44 All other equipment cost correlations originate from various public sources, 44,45 as detailed by Cortes-Pena and coworkers. 39 The chemical engineering plant cost index (used to account for the increasing cost of equipment due to inflation) was assumed to be 816.0. All parameters used in the discounted cash flow analysis follow the assumptions made in NREL's cellulosic ethanol report. 46

Life Cycle Assessment. The system boundary extends from the cradle to facility gate for the operational phase and does not include the construction phase. None of the environmental impact was allocated to plastic sent to landfill, in agreement with past LCA studies. 14 The environmental impact of multiple coproduct resins was allocated by mass. All operational inventory data (i.e., life cycle inventory) originated from the model leveraged in this study. The life cycle impact assessment methodology used was the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 2013, 47 with a focus on GWP100 as the primary indicator. Life cycle inventory data for virgin resins, raw materials, and ancillary inputs were adapted from the Environmental Footprint 2.0 database.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Development of STRAP Processing Steps. The general steps for the development and assessment of a new STRAP process for a multilayer film include identifying the polymer components of the film, choosing solvents and operating temperatures suitable for selectively dissolving each polymer component, performing STRAP at a small scale to assess recovered resin yields and properties, and then repeating STRAP at a larger scale to evaluate the properties, of films created from STRAP resins. We first acquired the FTIR spectra of the shredded films to verify the composition of polymers in the film. The FTIR spectra of the Cytiva film and virgin LDPE (Figure S2) were compared and display identical spectral bands with no bands belonging to other resins. This comparison confirmed that the films mainly consisted of PE, with EVOH expected as a minority component, as will be discussed later in the paper.

To choose STRAP solvents and operating temperatures, we leveraged our computational modeling approach to identify solvents with high predicted solubility for the target polymer (PE or EVOH) at an elevated temperature and negligible solubility for the other polymer. Additionally, ideal solvents have a low solubility for both polymers at room temperature, allowing for temperature-based precipitation. Figure S1c lists example solvents that are selective for each polymer, along with predicted solubilities. Based on these criteria, xylene, dodecane, toluene, and heptane were identified as potential selective solvents for LDPE dissolution. Similarly, DMSO, ethylene glycol, and propylene glycol were identified as potential selective solvents for EVOH dissolution. These solvents are commonly available and were selected from a larger database of 1000+ solvents. For initial small-scale experiments, we selected dodecane as the selective solvent for PE because of its low volatility, thereby decreasing unintentional solvent loss in this laboratory setup, and DMSO as a selective solvent for EVOH because it is easy to work with due to its low viscosity and has been used to dissolve EVOH in previous work. 13 -15

The recovered fractions were analyzed with FTIR to confirm polymer identity and assess purity after each step, as shown in Table 1. Figure 5 shows the FTIR scan of the Cytiva film, the extracted PE (referred to as STRAP PE), the extracted EVOH (referred to as STRAP EVOH), and the remaining DMSO undissolved fraction as well as comparisons to virgin resins. The FTIR results (Figure 5a) show that STRAP PE is comparable to virgin LDPE. Spectra of STRAP EVOH and virgin EVOH (Figure 5b) displayed identical spectral bands without traces of other resins, confirming that the purity of STRAP EVOH is comparable to virgin EVOH. The DMSO undissolved fraction (Figure 5c), after PE dissolution and before EVOH dissolution, showed the presence of PE and EVOH, which will be discussed in later sections.

Further characterization of STRAP PE and STRAP EVOH was done by using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to thoroughly analyze the purity of recovered polymers. Comparative TGA, shown in Figure 6, revealed that STRAP PE and virgin LDPE exhibit comparable thermal stability and decomposition behavior. The main decomposition ranges were similar, from 400 to 520 °C.

The DSC curves in Figure 7a and 7b reveal two melting point peaks for Cytiva film around 95 and 113 °C, corresponding to melting points of mLLDPE (98 °C) and virgin LDPE (113 °C), respectively. This indicates that Cytiva films are made up of two different types of polyethylene. The DSC results of the STRAP PE align with those of mLLDPE/ LDPE blends (Liu et al. 48 ), indicating that STRAP PE is a blend of mLLDPE and LDPE originating from the Cytiva film. Figure S3 and the heat of fusion values in Table S1 estimate the composition of STRAP PE as approximately 20/80 wt % LDPE/mLLDPE. Virgin LDPE exhibits the highest crystallinity, evidenced by its elevated fusion ( Δ H f ), while the lower Δ H f values for STRAP PE and Cytiva film are attributed to mLLDPE. mLLDPE is classified as plastomers with inherently lower heat of fusion. 49 The STRAP PE melting point range lies between the melting point ranges of Cytiva film component peaks (95 and 113 °C). This suggests that the extracted material is morphologically different from that of the film. The peak at 193 °C represents the melting peak of EVOH in the film, with a detailed discussion provided in later sections.

Large-Scale Polymer Extraction and Cast Film Production. We prepared cast films of STRAP PE and virgin LDPE for comparison to validate the practical uses of STRAP PE in film manufacturing. Approximately 0.8 -1 kg of STRAP PE was required, which was extracted using a jacketed dissolution vessel shown in Figure 3 that can process 150 -

400 g of feed per batch, depending upon the bulk density of the feed. For these large-scale STRAP experiments, heptane was chosen as the selective solvent for dissolving PE because its low flash point allowed for easier drying of the recovered polymer.

STRAP PE cast film production involves extrusion and pelletization after drying in a vacuum oven, as shown in Figure 8. The STRAP process was also applied to virgin LDPE pellets (STRAP virgin LDPE) which involved dissolving virgin LDPE pellets in the solvent and recovering the PE after precipitation and drying. This was done to understand the effect of STRAP on the polymer. The pellets were extruded into a cast film, and a third cast film of virgin LDPE (Westlake EG412) resins was also extruded on the same equipment for comparison. Figure 8 shows that the large-scale experiments produce STRAP PE pellets that lead to visually clear, optically transparent, and nonvisible yellow color.

The DSC results of the STRAP PE cast film and virgin LDPE cast film are shown in Figure S4 and Table S1. Table S1 shows that the STRAP PE cast film has low heat of fusion ( Δ H f ) which is similar to STRAP PE. This shows the cast film is likely made up of mainly mLLDPE (plastomers) and making cast film did not change thermal properties. Table 2 shows tensile properties of the three films made from STRAP PE, STRAP virgin LDPE, and virgin LDPE. The LDPE control and STRAP virgin LDPE cast films have similar mechanical properties. The STRAP PE film was more flexible than the other two cast films due to its lower Young's modulus, which is likely caused by the presence of mLLDPE in the original feedstock (Figure 7). 50,51 The low heat of fusion, i.e., low crystallinity, is a characteristic of a plastomer and is responsible for the higher elongation at break and lower Young's Modulus. 49 It is also possible that some PE oligomers (C10 -C15) were permanently removed during STRAP.

Optimized Route for EVOH Recovery. Following the positive results with STRAP PE, we aimed to study EVOH recovery. The large-scale jacketed dissolution vessel (Figure 3) method was used to obtain residual flakes after PE dissolution. The aim was to recover high-quality (high EVOH content and low PE content) residual flakes with a single PE-selective solvent. However, the residual flakes recovered from heptane (Figure 10a) during cast film production with a feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:13.6 were found to have visible PE contamination based on comparison with the FTIR spectrum of virgin EVOH (Figure 10b) and the spectrum of the residual flakes recovered from the heptane wash (Figure 10a). We tested four solvents, heptane, dodecane, toluene, and xylenes, to get high-quality residual flakes comparable to virgin EVOH by dissolving only the PE. Dissolution with heptane was performed at 95 °C, whereas dissolution with dodecane, toluene, and xylenes was performed at 110 °C, all with a consistent feed-to-solvent ratio equal to 1:20. Heptane was heated to 95 °C, slightly below its boiling point ( ∼ 100 °C), to minimize vapor pressure buildup and to remain within safe operating limits, considering its low flash point ( -7 °C). Higher temperatures could impair solvent recovery and require design modifications to handle increased pressure in the STRAP systems. Table 3 summarizes these experiments and residual flake recoveries, while Figure 11 compares the FTIR spectra of the residual flakes to virgin EVOH for each of these solvents. Based on FTIR results, there was no noticeable difference in the quality of the EVOH recovered by each solvent. All solvents tested yielded EVOH with minimal contamination visible on FTIR. Additionally, Figure S5 shows the FTIR spectra of residual flakes recovered from varied feedto-solvent ratios. In the cases where less solvent was used, the FTIR spectra also indicated higher PE contamination. These findings provide evidence that the feed-to-solvent ratio can greatly impact the quality of the remaining undissolved polymer, and solvent amount may be more impactful than the type of solvent used.

text: The variability in the residual flakes after single-solvent washing was assessed by using FTIR, as shown in Figure 12. Each spectrum represents the analysis of 10 -15 residual flake samples. Table S2 shows characteristic peaks for PE and EVOH for a better understanding of FTIR spectra of residual flakes. However, variability in the OH stretching intensity ( ∼ 3300 cm -1 ) suggests the potential presence of PE adhering to residual flakes, which the solvents failed to remove during the previous step. This may be due to the presence of a coextruded adhesive layer positioned adjacent to the EVOH layer, typically PE grafted with maleic anhydride. The maleic anhydride reacts with EVOH hydroxyl groups to form interfacial covalent bonds. 54 The maleic anhydride content of a polyolefin tie layer can be 0.15 -0.30 wt.% for EVOH adhesion. 55 However, the maleic anhydride or any other grafting material was not detected with the characterization method used, but it is possible that the quality of residual flakes is affected by it and it is rigorous to detect the anhydride content. 54

For further characterization, compressed films of xyleneresidual flakes were prepared using a hot press at 190 °C. DSC curves of EVOH compressed film and virgin EVOH are shown in Figure 13. The DSC results indicate the relative purity of residual flakes, as their thermal properties align with those of STRAP EVOH, which was the high-quality EVOH recovered after a DMSO wash at a small scale (Figure 5). However, additional testing is necessary to confirm their suitability for commercial use as recycled EVOH.

Techno-Economic Analysis (TEA). The following analysis compares three commercial-scale scenarios for a STRAP plant that processes SUT film waste composed of PE and EVOH as depicted in Figure 14. Additional results are included in workbooks Supporting Information W1, W2, and W3. The SUT waste is received as whole films or bags, and shredding and preprocessing are included in the model. In scenario 1, only PE is recovered and all undissolved components are landfilled after drying. Scenario 2 is similar but assumes that the undissolved fraction is purified EVOH that can be sold. It uses a single PE-selective solvent, with increased solvent volume compared to scenario 1 to improve residual flake quality, and is best suited for minimally contaminated postindustrial waste. In scenario 3, the undissolved fraction is further processed with an EVOH-selective solvent to purify EVOH. Any remaining solid waste in scenarios 1 or 3 is landfilled at the average California tipping fee of $72/ton. 56 Base case parameters for each scenario are listed in Table S3.

The three scenarios are compared in Figure 15, which was created by calculating the product unit operating cost (UOC) per kilogram of given plant capacity. The product is defined as the annual operating costs divided by the annual recycled resin production in kilograms. Also shown is the total capital investment (TCI) for each scenario, which includes all costs required before operation and is further defined in the CAPEX tab of Supporting Information W1, W2, and W3.

Table 4 further compares the 3 scenarios. All values were calculated for a 5 kton/year plant using the base case assumptions from Table S3. The sale prices of the resins were set to match the average prices of virgin PE and EVOH resins, which are $1.20/kg and $8.00/kg, respectively. A scale of 5 kton/year was selected for analysis as a representative estimate of collectable SUT film waste in California. Not all scenarios provide a return on investment at 5 kton, so Table 4 also shows the minimum scale required for each process to achieve NPV = 0 with a 15% IRR.

Scenario 1 has the lowest capital cost but without the added revenue from EVOH, it is the least profitable option. Scenario 2 requires more capital due to increased solvent volume and equipment size but has the lowest UOC. The recovered EVOH contributes over 40% of scenario 2's revenue, making it the most profitable at 5 kton/year. This scenario depends on a clean, two-polymer feed  likely a well-sorted postindustrial waste  to ensure high-quality EVOH residue. Scenario 3 is the most capital-intensive option and has the highest UOC. However, the purified EVOH product makes this scenario more profitable than scenario 1. Scenario 3 has the potential to produce the highest-quality EVOH, but the economics may suffer if the feedstock regularly contains less than 8% EVOH.

Single-point sensitivity analysis was performed on selected variables to identify the key drivers of economics and environmental impact. All variables, along with their bounds and justifications, can be found in Table S3. Figure 16 displays the most impactful variables on minimum selling price (MSP), for scenarios 1 -3. MSP is defined as the minimum product sale price for a plant to be economically viable, covering all costs and the required return on investment over the plant lifetime. MSP was chosen for the sensitivity analysis because it reflects changes in both capital and operating expenses.

Figure 16. Single-point sensitivity of the most impactful variables on STRAP resin MSP. Variables are defined as the variable name (lower bound, base case, upper bound).

The most important economic driver is processing scale because plant capacity directly affects capital expenses which see benefits from economies of scale. Similarly, dissolved polymer concentration (dissolved solvent capacity) affects required solvent volume and equipment size, directly influencing capital expenses. In scenarios 1 and 3, the target polymer mass fraction in the feedstock strongly influences the economic performance, highlighting the need for careful feedstock selection. In contrast, scenario 2 benefits from a lower target polymer fraction  when two products are recovered with one solvent, less dissolved polymer reduces solvent and equipment requirements. This advantage, however, depends on sourcing clean feedstock that can be separated into two useable products; otherwise, contaminants will be mixed with the undissolved stream. Clean SUT waste and other twocomponent postindustrial streams are ideal candidates for this scenario.

Additionally, if solvent loss can be limited to 1% or less, it is only the fourth or fifth most impactful variable considered. The plant design includes solvent recovery from the waste and product streams as well as solvent cleaning/regeneration with adsorbents before each recycling step; therefore, maintaining solvent losses below 1% is reasonable.

Ultimately, the commercial design of a STRAP plant that processes SUT waste should be based on the quantity and quality of feedstock available. If sufficiently clean, twocomponent feed is available, then scenario 2 is a good design. However, further studies are needed to verify if there is a difference in EVOH quality between scenarios 2 and 3 and how that difference may impact the economics. In contrast, scenarios 1 and 3 are more robust options for varied feedstock and are also economically viable above 9 and 4 kton/year, respectively.

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Scenarios 1 -3 were also subjected to a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment to directly compare the environmental impacts of the STRAP process to virgin resin production. Workbook Supporting Information W4 includes key assumptions and parameters used to perform the following calculations. Figure 17 shows the global warming potential (GWP) to produce resins in each of the three STRAP scenarios for a plant processing 5 kton/year of SUT waste. STRAP reduces GWP by 58% compared to virgin PE production, and STRAP EVOH emissions are 85% lower in scenario 2 and 73% lower in scenario 3 compared to virgin. Electricity use is, by far, the main contributor to STRAP's environmental impact, accounting for at least 77% in every impact category analyzed. This study used a representative US grid energy mix, but the STRAP process impacts could be greatly reduced if it was powered by renewable energy sources.

The GWP impacts were also analyzed with a single-point sensitivity analysis (Figure S8). The top four most sensitive variables are in descending order: target polymer mass fraction, feedstock distance, solvent loss, and dissolved polymer concentration. While GWP is not a comprehensive indicator, it effectively highlights relative environmental impact and trends. In all cases, scenario 3 EVOH produces higher impacts than scenario 2, due to the high processing requirements for relatively little product. This, again, emphasizes the importance of scale and feedstock selection.

■ CONCLUSIONS

STRAP successfully extracted high-quality polyethylene (PE) and ethylene-vinyl alcohol (EVOH) from single-use technology (SUT) biocontainer films. The resulting STRAP PE cast film exhibited comparable color and mechanical properties to those of a virgin low-density polyethylene (LDPE) cast film. However, the STRAP PE cast film displayed a lower Young's modulus, mainly attributed to the presence of mLLDPE plastomer in the Cytiva films. The STRAP PE was mainly composed of mLLDPE. STRAP also yielded high-quality residual EVOH flakes in a single PE-solvent wash. The quality of the residual EVOH flakes increased with increasing solvent amounts.

The techno-economic analysis shows that capital expenses and feedstock composition and quality are major drivers of the profitability of a commercial STRAP plant that processes SUT waste. Recovering EVOH can increase the revenue of a plant by nearly 40%. However, the capital cost of a plant that recovers EVOH is higher, which introduces risk if a consistent feedstock is not available. Additionally, life cycle analysis shows that most configurations of a STRAP plant processing SUT waste have similar environmental impacts while reducing GHG emissions and fossil fuel consumption by 50%. Electricity and heat are the main contributors to STRAP environmental impacts, and these are most influenced by variables such as feedstock composition and solvent loss. Future studies such as oxygen barrier tests on STRAP EVOH and extractable and leachable tests on STRAP resins could provide clearer insights into the value of STRAP-recovered resins. More bioprocess SUTs should be investigated as well to develop a clearer understanding of potential feedstock types and scales.

Our results show that STRAP is a viable recycling method for SUTs that balances economic and ecological sustainability while producing high-quality recovered materials with mechanical, optical, and thermal properties similar to those of virgin resins. However, complex waste streams can contain more than two polymers, requiring further analysis to determine feasible scales for systems with three or more solvents. 57 As waste complexity increases, a combined approach of mechanical and solvent-based recycling can be a more effective approach to increase recycling rates. 58 Additionally, pretreatment and sorting require further investigation, as their importance varies with the SUT compositional complexity. Future work will involve comparing thermograms of STRAP solvent blends and melt blends of LDPE and mLLDPE to better interpret the DSC profile of STRAP PE. Further investigation will also determine if the initial application of STRAP to SUTs can facilitate the recovery of additional polymers and valuable materials, like neodymium magnets, PP fittings, filters, and silicone tubing, from other SUT components. While this study focused on postindustrial biopharma plastic waste, future research should assess postconsumer biopharma waste, evaluating its recyclability, quality, and pretreatment requirements compared to postindustrial waste.

Polystyrene recycling processes by dissolution in ethyl acetate

ABSTRACT: This study evaluated the thermal, morphological, chemical, and mechanical properties of virgin and recycled polystyrene. The recycling process was carried out by dissolution of polystyrene (extruded and crystal) in ethyl acetate, followed by two processes for solvent removal: vaporization by direct contact with water at 85 8 C in a tubular evaporator and vaporization during the extrusion process. For the samples produced by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator, there was practically no degradation on polymer chain, neither reduction in glass transition temperature. For the samples produced by solvent evaporation during the extrusion, a polymer chain degradation was noted by reduction in molar weight and in glass transition temperature. The FTIR evaluation suggests that polymer oxidative degradation, in both samples, was more pronounced in the extruded sample. The removal of plasticizing additives could be evidenced by the glass transition temperature increase in the recycled samples produced in the tubular evaporator. V C 2018 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. INTRODUCTION

Polystyrene (PS) is a versatile polymer and it is used in rigid and foamed materials. The disposal of this material creates environmental problems because of its long degradation time in nature (hundreds of years). 1 Increasing landfill costs and decreasing landfill space are forcing consideration of alternative options for the disposal of PS materials. These problems are worse for the expanded form, because the low density of PS foams, which increases costs in transportation and disposal. Nowadays, there are four main approaches for polymer recycling: direct recovery without polymer modification (primary and secondary recycling), tertiary, or chemical recycling which plastic returns into a petrochemical product or monomer and energy recovery (also known as quaternary recycling). Environmental argumentations such as toxic emissions are building up a public resistance against incineration. Dissolution processes include different stages to manage plastic waste with solvents. Initially, the polymeric materials are dissolved, and then different processes are applied to recover the polymer and the solvent. The use of solvents as a method to recycle foamed polymers offers some advantages. Any

insoluble contaminants can be removed by filtration leaving the polymer clean for further reprocessing. The dissolution process also allows separating plastics from other types of waste and polymers nonsoluble depending on their chemical nature, in a recycling process known as selective dissolution. For the expanded material, the foam dissolution in a suitable solvent will cause considerable volume reduction (volume reduction of more than 100 times), reducing transport costs. 2,3

There are studies of PS dissolution in different solvents, such as toluene, xylene, benzene, chloroform, acetone, cyclohexane, butyl acetate, ethyl acetate, methyl ethyl ketone, D-limonene, terpinene, terpinolene, p -cymene, and phellandrene. 2-15 Among the processes proposed for solvent/polymer separating on PS recycling, are dissolution-precipitation, 4-7 separation by supercritical extraction, 8,9 and solvent evaporation. Among the studies related to solvent vaporization, there are reports on the use of steam distillation, 10-12 vacuum evaporation, 13 vacuum distillation, 2 and drying in a drum dryer. 14

In this study, two techniques for PS recycling by dissolution in ethyl acetate were used that are different in the way solvent evaporates. The reasons for choosing this solvent were its low toxicity compared to most organic solvents that also dissolve PS (benzene, toluene, chloroform, among others), its significantly lower saturation temperature in relation to other low toxicity solvents (77 8 C vs 176 8 C for D-limonene) and also its lower cost (1/10 of the price of D-limonene). The first process was based on the solvent vaporization by direct contact with water at 85 8 C in a tubular evaporator, and the second process was based on the solvent evaporation during the extrusion process of the polymer (which uses temperature up to 200 8 C). The aim of this study was to determinate the effect of the proposed recycling processes on thermal, morphological, chemical, and mechanical properties of virgin and recycled PS.

EXPERIMENTAL

Materials

The solvent used for dissolution was ethyl acetate, supplied by Butilamil (S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil), and had a purity higher than 99%. Ethyl acetate has a vaporization temperature of 77 8 C.

Extruded polystyrene (XPS) was obtained from food packages, supplied by Fibraform (S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil), and a weight-average molecular weight ( Mw ) of 244 kDa and a polydispersity index (PI) of 2.0.

Crystal polystyrene (CPS) was a virgin material, in form of pellets, supplied by Videolar-Innova S.A (Triunfo, Brazil), and Mw of 180 kDa and a PI of 2.3.

Recycling Processes

The samples were dissolved in the solvent at concentrations of 27 and 35 wt % in a closed glass vessel, to avoid solvent evaporation. The solutions were used only after at least 24 h, to ensure complete dissolution. The polymeric solution was stirred by mechanical stirrer (300 rpm) for 3 min before the start of each solvent evaporation process. Relatively close concentrations of dissolved sample were used because of the pumping capacity and it is expected that the solution will contain a concentration of polymer to require less ethyl acetate, so reducing the concentration of polymer is not interest to the process.

Solvent Evaporation in the Tubular Evaporator. The vertical tubular evaporator has an internal diameter of 95 mm and height of 700 mm and has no stirring system. The evaporator has a vessel, filled with 5 L of water at 85 8 C, maintained through a temperature monitoring and control system, performed with an Arduino microcontroller, with temperature measurement via thermocouple (type J) and 600 W electrical resistance controlled by an electronic dimmer. The electrical resistance is located at the bottom, near the place where the solution is fed. At 100 mm above the electrical resistance is located the thermocouple that makes the temperature measurement for the controller. A peristaltic pump (Watson-Marlow brand, model 323E, Barueri, S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil) drains the polymer solution to the bottom of the evaporator, with feed rate of 400 mL h 2 1 of polymeric solution. The feed in the tubular evaporator is upward, entering the evaporator through a circular orifice with 2 mm diameter. The samples were taken at the top of the evaporator into form of wires. The recycled samples were then dried in a forced convection oven at 60 8 C. Figure 1

Solvent Evaporation During the Extrusion Process. The extruder was operated with a feed rate of 1600 mL h 2 1 of the polymer solution (35 wt %). XPS samples were recycled once and CPS samples were recycled for three times. The twin screw extruder (NZ Philpolymer Termopl  asticos de Engenharia, S ~ ao Roque, S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil, model SJSL-20) used has the following characteristics: double corotating thread, L / D ratio 5 32, six heating zones plus cooling and ventilation head, 10 HP direct current motor. Table I shows the temperature parameters for the extrusion process used in this work, with thread rotation of 150 rpm. Working temperatures were determined based on the ability of the extruder to process the dissolved material at the lowest temperature combination possible, to minimize sample degradation. Figure 2 shows the schematic diagram of the process. Solvent evaporation occurs in the feed hopper of the extruder.

Samples that were recycled in the tubular evaporator had a volatile compounds content. The volatile compound content and the solids content were evaluated by gravimetric. Samples conditioned in Petri dishes were submitted to oven drying and weighed in an analytical digital scale, with an accuracy of 0.1 mg supplied by Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Maryland, USA. The weighing to evaluate the mass loss was carried out at different instants of time in two drying conditions: 40 and 60 8 C.

Molecular Weight Measurement

text:
The Mw and PI were performed by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) on a Shimadzu High Performance Liquid Chromatograph (HPLC model LC 20-A, supplied by Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Japan) equipped with three Shim Pack GPC 800 Series columns (GPC 801, GPC 804, and GPC 807). The mobile phase was tetrahydrofuran (THF, Merck, Germany) at a flow rate of 1 mL min 2 1 at 40 8 C. Polymer was dissolved in THF at concentration of 5 mg mL 2 1 and filtered through 0.45 l m filter before analysis. The system was calibrated with narrow disperse PS standards and molecular weights are reported as PS equivalents supplied by Merck, Germany. The molecular weight ( Mw ) averages and the distribution of molecular weights are determined in accordance with ASTM D5296 standard. 16

Differential Scanning Calorimetry

A Perkin-Elmer model Jade differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Waltham, MA, USA) calorimeter was used to obtain thermograms of the virgin material and the recycled samples. The measurements were carried out between 20 and 150 8 C in a nitrogen atmosphere and using an empty capsule as reference. Sample weights varied from 2.0 to 12.5 mg and the heating rate was fixed at 10 8 C min 2 1 .The glass transition temperature was measured by the half-extrapolated heat capacity temperature, in accordance with ASTM D3418 and ASTM E1356 standards. 17,18

Dynamic Mechanical Properties

Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is useful for the evaluation of viscoelastic properties of a polymer. When an oscillating sinusoidal load is applied to a specimen at a particular frequency, the strain will lag somewhat behind the stress because of the viscoelastic nature. The data of the storage modulus, loss modulus, and loss tangent are obtained through DMA. 19

A Netzsch model DMA 242-E Artemis (Selb, Germany) was used in this work. The mode chosen was single cantilever and the sample size was about 36 3 12 3 3 mm. The samples were produced by thermal press (5 min at 180 8 C and 65 MPa). Measurement was performed from 40 to 130 8 C, heating rate of 3 8 C min 2 1 and frequency of 1 Hz. DMA standard data analysis software was used to evaluate viscoelastic properties of the samples. The glass transition temperature was determined as the loss peak observed in dynamic mechanical test (tan( d ) has an accuracy of 0.00005 N/N), in accordance with ASTM D4065 and ASTM D4092 standards. 20,21

Fourier Transform Infrared Analysis

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analysis was performed on CPS, before and after the recycling, with a FTIR Shimadzu model IR Prestige 21 (Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Maryland, USA). The samples were films produced in a thermal press (1 min at 180 8 C and 5 MPa). The IR spectra (4000-400 cm 2 1 ) were measured with an average of 20 and a resolution of 4 cm 2 1 .

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Volatile Compounds Content

The results for the drying processes of the samples produced by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator are summarized in Table II.

The results show that there was no uniformity in the initial volatile compounds content. This is due to that the samples are removed from the tubular evaporator in the form of wires of different sizes. The high content of initial volatile compounds is largely due to the presence of water in the samples, caused by the characteristic of the proposed solvent evaporation method, which happens by direct contact of the polymer solution with hot water. The water is removed from the samples at the initial instants, while the solvent remains solubilized in the PS, and will be evaporated at a lower drying rate, controlled by diffusion.

A higher drying rate was observed in the samples with a concentration of 27 mass % when compared to samples with a concentration of 35 mass %. However, no relationship was found between the solution concentrations and the equilibrium volatile compounds content, for each drying condition. In the comparison between the drying temperature, an increase in the drying rate and a reduction in the equilibrium volatile compounds content were observed in the samples dried at 60 8 C, when compared to the samples dried at 40 8 C.

Dynamic Mechanical Properties

The DMA results are presented in Figure 5 and Table V. As reported in comparative studies, the value of Tg determined by DMA is higher than the value determined by DSC. 23 It was observed an increase in Tg of 3.4 8 C for the sample produced in tubular evaporator, and a reduction of 2.4 8 C in Tg for the extruded sample. The results corroborate the degradation observed in the extruded sample and the removal of plasticizing additives from CPS in the sample produced in the tubular evaporator.

For the extruded sample, the storage modulus measured at 40 and 80 8 C shows a reduction of about 13% in comparison with the control sample, in both temperatures. For the sample produced in the tubular evaporator, the reduction observed is about 15% at 40 8 C and about 11% at 80 8 C. The graph analysis shows the same value of the elastic modulus (884 MPa) for the recycled samples at the temperature of 71 8 C. This change in viscoelastic behavior for the sample produced in the tubular evaporator can be explained by the vaporization of residual ethyl acetate.

CONCLUSIONS

For the samples produced by solvent evaporation by direct contact with hot water in the tubular evaporator, there was practically no degradation of the polymer chain, neither significant change in the glass transition temperature of the polymer. In the evaluation of three consecutive recycling processes by this method, no changes were observed. However, the samples recycled by this method showed a volatile compound content, with values between 26.7 and 43.9 wt % for the samples before drying, values between 0.9 and 1.9 wt % for the dried samples for 60 h at 60 8 C, and between 0, 3, and 0.5 wt % for the dried samples for 200 h at the same temperature. In the initial measurements, the most part of the volatile compound content is water, due to the method of evaporation by direct contact with water.

The increase in the glass transition temperature observed in the CPS recycled sample by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator, in comparison to the virgin PS, indicates the removal of plasticizing additives from the CPS.

For the samples produced by solvent evaporation during the polymer extrusion process was noted a degradation of the polymer chain, measured by Mw reduction. Degradation can also be observed in the reduction of the glass transition temperature, both in DSC and DMA. For the three times recycled sample, a higher degradation was observed in the molar weight, but without additional change in the glass transition temperature. The evaluation of the FTIR spectra in the region that indicates the polymer degradation suggests that thermal and oxidative degradation was more pronounced in the samples produced by this method compared to the samples produced in the tubular evaporator. A negative point observed in the process for this recycling method was the significant reduction in the processing capacity of the extruder. Under similar operating conditions, but using virgin PS pellets, the same extruder should operate with a production about three times higher.

1. Introduction

Achieving  a  circular  economy  is  key  to  preventing  depleting  re sources  and  environmental  degradation  (Khan & Haleem,  2021).  A circular economy aims to achieve this through recycling and upcycling materials and energy at the consumer, producer, urban, regional, and national levels (Prieto-Sandoval et al., 2018). To achieve high degrees of circularity,  it  is  necessary  to  develop  strategies  and  technologies  to recover  and  generate  value  from  waste(Lase  et  al.,  2023;  PrietoSandoval  et  al.,  2018).  In  doing  so,  Material  Recovery  Facilities (MRFs) play a pivotal role (Cimpan et al., 2015) because they separate waste  (recyclable  waste  and/or  municipal  solid  waste),  which  is  a complex waste mixture, into various streams that have varying levels of economic value. Furthermore, MRFs are key players in reducing waste

A B S T R A C T

Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs) are crucial players in achieving a circular economy. MRFs receive complex waste  streams  and  separate  valuable  recyclables  from  these  mixtures.  This  study  conducts  techno-economic analysis (TEA) to estimate the net present value (NPV) and life cycle assessment (LCA) to estimate different environmental impacts of a commercial scale standalone, single-stream MRF to assess the economic feasibility and environmental impacts of recovering valuable recyclables from an MRF processing 120,000 tonnes per year (t/y). The TEA employs a discounted cash flow rate of return (DCFROR) analysis over a 20-year facility lifetime, along with a sensitivity analysis on the impact of different operating and economic parameters. Results show that the total fixed cost of building the MRF facility is $23 MM, and the operating cost is $45.48/tonne. The NPV of the MRF can vary from $3.57 MM to $60 MM, while 100-year global warming potential can range from 5.98 to 8.53 kg carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-eq) per tonne of MSW. We have also found that MSW composition (arising from regional effects) significantly impacts costs, 100-year global warming potential, and other impact categories such as acidification potential, eutrophication potential, ecotoxicity, ozone depletion, photochemical oxidation, carcinogenic effects, and non-carcinogenic effects. Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis indicate that waste composition and market prices significantly impact the profitability of the MRF, and the waste composition mostly impacts global warming potential. Our analysis also indicates that facility capacity, fixed capital cost, and waste tipping fees are vital parameters that affect the economic viability of MRF operations.

MRFs are sophisticated industrial facilities that separate marketable recyclables from different waste streams and resell the recovered ma terials  to  secondary  recyclers.  MRFs  are  classified  into  four  primary types based on the input waste streams they process (Combs, 2011): single-stream, dual-stream, mixed-stream, and presorted MRFs. Mixedstream  MRFs  receive  and  process  all  kinds  of  MSW.  Single-stream MRFs  only  process  recyclable  materials  collected  in  dedicated  bins from households, and commercial organizations. Dual-stream and pre sorted MRFs receive and process waste streams that have been presorted and are almost ready to be repurposed. Mixed-stream MRFs operated in the early 1990 s in the U.S. achieved poor material recovery rates due to the presence of a significant amount of organics and other non-valuable

In  recent  years,  singlestream MRFs have become more prevalent than other kinds of MRFs in  the  U.S.  because  of  its  increased  recovery  rate  and  community participation  in  storing  all  accepted  recyclable  materials  in  one  bin (Fitzgerald et al., 2012). These facilities allow consumers to dispose of all  their  recyclable  waste  in  one ' recyclable ' container.  However, existing single-stream MRFs still face critical technical and economic challenges such as waste collection and transportation, uncertainty in waste  stream  compositions,  tipping  fees,  sorting  efficiencies,  sorting cost, low-quality recyclable materials, and volatility of post-consumer recovered  material  market  prices  (Chaudhari  et  al.,  2021;  Cimpan et al., 2016; Milios et al., 2018).

Few studies have modeled the operations of MRFs, and even fewer studies have investigated the economic feasibility and environmental impacts of recovering value from waste in MRFs. Chang et al. (2005) studied  the  optimal  design  for  the  sustainable  development  of  an average MRF in the U.S. in 2004. Franchetti (2009) conducted a study on the economic and operational feasibility of an MRF for municipal waste recycling in Ohio, U.S. These MRFs relied heavily on manual sorting, which is outdated compared to recent MRFs ' state-of-the-art technology, which sorts with automated machines.

Recent studies  have  modeled the operations of  MRFs considering more  automated  separation  and  recovery  equipment  (Combs,  2011; Pressley et al., 2015). Combs (2011) analyzed material recovery pro cesses to characterize the relationship between crucial MRF parameters, processing cost, and resulting emission. Combs (2011) reported costs of $15.16, $9.72, $11.06, and $7.77 to process 1 tonne (t) of waste in single-stream,  dual-stream,  mixed-stream,  and  presorted  recyclables MRFs, respectively.  The  author  highlighted  that  a ± 25% change in equipment efficiencies and diesel cost could result in a 10% to 5% change in total cost. This same paper also reported a global warming potential (GWP) of 14.94, 14.94, 11.40, and 3.62 kg CO2-eq /t for singlestream,  dual-stream,  mixed-stream,  and  presorted  recyclables  MRFs, respectively. Moreover, this study also showed through sensitivity and uncertainty analysis that a ± 25% change in diesel combustion from rolling stock used to haul materials around the MRF results in a ± 20% change in CO2  emissions.  In  addition,  the  study  reported  that  waste composition is the most influential factor in the profitability of MRFs (Combs, 2011). Pressley et al. (2015) built on Comb ' s (2011) work and developed a process model to evaluate the MRFs ' cost and energy use. Their model allows for estimating the labor and energy requirements, cost, and mass transfers, given the MRF configuration and the type of waste to be processed. For example, this study reported that the elec tricity needs of MRFs can range from 4.7 to 7.8. kWh/t of waste pro cessed, and the amortized cost can vary from $19.8 to $24.9/t of waste processed (Pressley et al., 2015). The model developed by the authors is flexible and can be modified to analyze the four primary types of MRFs (Pressley et al., 2015). Although the study presented models to estimate the cost and emissions associated with a specific MRF configuration, the study did not consider market prices of recyclables to evaluate their return on investment (Pressley et al., 2015).

Cimpan et al.(2016) conducted a detailed techno-economic assess ment (TEA) of central sorting at an MRF in Germany using lightweight packaging waste as a feedstock. The analysis considered four different plants ranging from 25,000 to 100,000 t/y and reported that capital investment could range between $7.55 to $22.64 MM. The operating costs increased by 240% when the scale increased by 300% (25,000 to 100,000 t/y). The study identified the feedstock ' s complex nature and the MRF ' s challenging processing conditions as significant factors that affect the recovery efficiencies and economic feasibilities of these plants (Cimpan et al., 2016).

Other  studies  have  conducted  life  cycle  assessments  (LCA)  on standalone MRFs to estimate the environmental impacts associated with such  facilities.  Fitzgerald  (2012)  analyzed  and  compared  the  GHG emissions of dual-stream and single-stream MRFs. The study assessed the GHG emissions benefit or penalty associated with transitioning from dual-stream  to  single-stream  MRFs.  The  author  reported  that  singlestream  MRFs  could  recover  50%  more  recyclables  than  dual-stream MRFs.  Single-stream  MRFs  have  significantly  lower  emissions  than dual-stream  MRFs,  and  for  both  MRF  types,  avoided  emissions  from recyclables are significantly higher than emissions of MRF operations. However, this study did not report the impact of waste composition on emissions. Smith et al. (2022) evaluated the total emissions associated with an MRF as part of an analysis focusing on recycling polyethylene terephthalate (PET). The study reported that MRFs emit 8.58 kg CO2-eq /t of waste processed in the MRF. The study allocated 0.429 kg CO2-eq of the total GHG emissions to separate PET from the waste stream (Smith et al., 2022). Based on the literature review, no study has conducted TEA and LCA of a standalone single-stream MRF that considers the impacts of waste composition and market prices on net revenues while including multiple mid-point environmental impact categories. By addressing this gap, we aim to identify opportunities to improve the profitability and environmental sustainability of material recovery in MRFs.

This study investigates the economic feasibility and environmental impacts of a standalone MRF. We build upon the Pressley et al. (2015) process model that simulates a single-stream MRF and utilizes the mass and energy balance from the process model to conduct a TEA and LCA. This  study  also  investigates  the  effect  of  waste  composition  sampled from four U.S. regions on the economics and environmental impacts associated with the single-stream MRF.

2. Methodology

The TEA and LCA performance of a single-stream MRF that processes 120,000 t/y of waste obtained from four different U.S. locations are investigated. The analysis employs a process model that provides mass and energy flow data of a commercial-scale MRF. The MRF receives waste streams of various compositions and separates them into various post-consumer recovered materials (PCRM). Based on the waste stream, the  net  present  value  (NPV)  and  mid-point  category  environmental impacts of recovering recyclables are estimated. The analysis employs sensitivity  and  uncertainty  analysis  to  evaluate  the  effect  of  critical parameters, such as the waste stream ' s composition, capital cost, and tipping fees, on the economic and environmental impacts of recovering the recyclables.

2.1. Waste composition

The  baseline  analysis  employs  the  U.S.  national  average  waste composition reported in the U.S. EPA Waste Characterization Report (US EPA, 2010). The U.S. EPA waste composition was selected because it includes all the materials that can be recovered in the MRF. The mate rials  include  various  grades  of  plastics  (high-density  polyethylene (HDPE), PET, plastic film, and mixed plastics), iron, aluminum, glass, old-corrugated containers (OCC), and non-OCC. OCC is used in boxes, containers,  or  other  packaging  materials  consisting  of  three  or  more layers of kraft paper. Non-OCC materials are all other fiber materials that are not classified as OCC materials. PET is typically used in pack aging food and beverages, while HDPE is used in packaging bottles, milk jugs, bags, containers, and toys. Plastic films include trash bags, plastic labels, videotape, grocery bags, storage bags, sheet film plastic, etc. Most MRFs do not accept plastic films because it clogs process equipment. Our analysis  assumes  that  the  MRF  we  model  has  sufficient  capacity  to accept the plastic film. Mixed plastics consist of all other plastic grades that are not PET, HDPE, and plastic films.

The U.S. EPA waste stream recorded 40% of the recyclable waste stream as OCC. The TEA and LCA results might be overestimated by the amount of OCC present in the waste stream as OCCs are mostly baled in commercial locations, i.e., most of the OCC may not make it to an MRF that receives recyclables from curbsides (Pressley et al., 2015). To ac count for the large amount of OCC in the U.S. EPA stream and waste O. Olafasakin et al.

stream composition variation regionally and over time, the study as sesses three additional scenarios based on waste stream compositions that represent the spectrum of conditions observed in the U.S. The other waste compositions include Pennsylvania (with information from the Pennsylvania  Recovered  Composition  Study  (Beck,  2005),  Oregon (comingled  recyclables  before  and  after  processing  with  information from the Solid Waste Policy, and Program Development Section Land Quality Division Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (Spen delow, 2011)), and Seattle (with information from the Seattle Public Utilities Residential Waste Stream Composition Study (Cascadia, 2007)). Going forward, the Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Seattle waste stream will be referred to as Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Seattle, respectively. The waste  stream  composition  from  different  locations  has  been  widely studied and confirmed to vary from state to state and municipality to municipality (Jhun et al., 2021; US EPA, 2010). The variation is due to the  point  the  waste  was  characterized,  type  of  community,  level  of industrialization, lifestyle, and waste management regulations (AbdelShafy & Mansour, 2018; Jhun et al., 2021; US EPA, 2010). Pennsylva nia ' s waste stream recorded a low amount of OCC because the waste stream was characterized at the MRF (Beck, 2005). As stated earlier, we believe most OCCs in Pennsylvania could have been baled before the stream arrived at the MRF. Fig. 1 shows the percentage composition of each recyclable material in the various waste streams. The small or zero amount of plastic films in Seattle, Oregon, and Pennsylvania could be because the waste streams were characterized at recovery facility gates. Most  recovery  facilities  do  not  accept  plastic  films  in  single-stream waste.

2.2. MRF process model

This study assumes that garbage trucks collect waste from curbside recycling bins and transport it to the MRF. The trucks deliver the waste to the MRF tipping area, which can accommodate up to three days of stock, ensuring a steady supply of waste.

Fig. 2 shows the process flow of the MRF. The recovery process be gins with floor sorting, where sorters remove large materials from the waste stream. Rolling stock pushes the material to a drum feeder that distributes the commodities to a belt conveyor at a constant rate. The belt  conveyor  moves  the  waste  to  a  presort  location  where  sorters identify and remove large and bulky recyclables that can clog, jam, or damage the recovery equipment. Sorters remove the plastic films in the stream and direct the plastic films to vacuum, and recovered plastic films  are  sent  to  the  two-way  baler,  where  it  is  packaged.  The  pre liminary results of a national-level MRF survey show that approximately 8 out of 58 respondent MRFs keep track of the plastic films they sort in their  facility,  with  most  MRFs  sending  the  plastic  films  to  landfills (Personal communication with survey team, 2022). The rest of the waste stream go through a series of screens,  where  OCC and non-OCC are recovered. The rest of the materials in the stream (mostly packaging containers) fall through and go to the glass breaker screen, where the glass in the stream is broken into cutlets and recovered with other fines in the stream. The mix of broken glass and fines goes through an air knife which separates the fines and other light materials from the glass. The glass  is  further  separated  based  on  color  by  an  optical  sorter.  The separated glass is subjected to manual sorting to remove ceramics in the mix. The rest of the waste is then sent to optical sorters that recover the PET and another optical sorter that separates high-density polyethylene (HDPE) based on color. The remaining materials in the stream are sent to a  magnet  and  eddy  current  separator  to  recover  the  ferrous  and aluminum  materials,  respectively.  The  remaining  stream  is  sent  for manual sorting, where pickers recover other valuable commodities in the stream. The residuals, which represent a mix of all the materials that cannot be separated, are sent to a landfill.

The material and energy balance of the MRF is modeled based on the design described in Pressley et al.(2015). The mass of the recovered material is calculated by multiplying the mass of the waste material by the recovery equipment ' s  accuracy, shown in table S1 in the SI. The model estimates the electricity consumption of each piece of equipment based on its motor rating and maximum throughput using Eq (1).

Ej = e MaxMotor j * f MC j m MTP j * f MTP j (1)

The electricity model assumes a linear relationship between the mass of the waste stream processed through each piece of equipment and the electricity  consumption.  The  limitation  of  this  assumption  is  that  it generalizes that all equipment ' s efficiency is constant across all loads; electricity consumption is directly proportional to load. However, some studies have shown that motor efficiencies vary with load (Burt et al., 2008; Li et al., 2015). Therefore, some equipment ' s  electricity  usage does  not  have  a  linear  relationship  with  the  mass  of  materials  they process.

2.3. Techno-economic analysis

In this work, we use NPV as our primary economic indicator, which is estimated based on discounted cash flows of the MRF throughout its lifetime. We derive NPV as the difference between the present value of cash inflow and the facility ' s cash outflow over its lifetime ( ˇ Zi ˇ zlavský, 2014). NPV is a common metric used in evaluating the profitability of an investment. This study employs NPV because it facilitates comparisons across  multiple  products,  unlike  the  minimum  product  selling  price (MPSP), and over a broader range of profitability measures than the return on investment (ROI), which is challenging to interpret when the NPV is negative.

2.3.1. Financial assumptions

The TEA employs n th plant assumptions (Meyer et al., 2020; Olafa sakin et al., 2021). The n th plant assumption assumes that the technology is mature, well-understood, and similar facilities have been built and are operating. It also implies that all technological breakthroughs needed for reliable and seamless facility operations have been accomplished. This is a realistic assumption as more than 335 MRFs are operating in the U.S. with similar equipment used in this analysis (Partnership, 2022). The study assumes that the cost of the MRF is financed through 40% equity and a 60% loan with a ten-year debt financing term at a 10% interest rate. The TEA estimates the NPV of the MRF, assuming a 10% internal rate of return (IRR) over 20-year plant life. The planning and construction period is assumed to be three years, and the start-up time is six months. All the financial assumptions we made for conducting the TEA are shown in Table 1.

The total fixed capital investment (TFCI) is the sum of the total direct and indirect costs. Total direct costs include investment and land costs, while indirect costs include engineering design, construction, project contingency, and legal and contractor fees. The construction cost was estimated by multiplying the MRF floor space by the construction cost rate of $97.7 per square foot (Pressley et al., 2015). The MRF floor space required for processing 120,000 t/y is obtained from Combs (2011). The engineering design and contingency costs were assumed to be 32% and 37% of the investment cost, respectively (Pressley et al., 2015).

Operating costs are divided into fixed and variable costs. The fixed operating  cost  includes  the  maintenance  of  the  equipment,  labor, overhead,  insurance,  and  depreciation,  which  are  evaluated  as  per centages of total capital investment. Meanwhile, the overhead cost is estimated as a fraction of the labor cost. The detailed cost parameters are cited from Combs (2011) and are presented in Table S1 in SI. Informa tion on the labor requirement of the MRF is supplied in section 2.1.2 of the SI.

Variable  operating  costs  include  the  cost  of  waste  collection  and transportation, diesel for operating forklifts and rolling stock, electricity for  offices,  floor  spaces,  and  running  equipment,  residue  and  waste disposal cost, income tax, and baling recyclables. Both electricity con sumption  and  baling  wire  usage  depend  on  the  waste  composition. Table S3 in the supporting information (SI) shows the summary of the operating cost assumptions.

To evaluate the facility ' s revenue, we use the PCRM market data for Chicago (Midwest/Central America) from recyclingmarkets.net (Recy clingMarkets,  2020).  Figure  S1  in  the  SI  shows  the  market  prices  of PCRMs as of Dec. 28, 2021. The prices of PCRMs are very volatile (RBAC,

2019). They vary over time because of factors like oil prices, commodity demand, and market supply. The variation in prices over time does not follow a particular trend, and materials that cost more in the past can cost  less  in  the  future.  To  account  for  the  high  variation  of  postconsumer recovered material prices over time, a set of sensitivity ana lyses is conducted to evaluate the impacts of the variable market prices of products on the NPV.

2.4. Life cycle assessment

LCA is a practical and widely accepted methodology for estimating the  health  and  environmental  impact  of  a  product  system  from  raw material  extraction  through  production,  consumption,  and  disposal/ recycling of the final product(s) (Finkbeiner et al., 2006). This study uses the LCA method, following the ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 framework (Finkbeiner et al., 2006), to assess the health and environmental impacts of processing one t of waste as delivered to the MRF, which is defined as the functional unit. The system boundaries are from cradle-to-gate. The system includes all activities within the MRF, and impacts related to upstream  energy  production  and  material  inputs  used  at  the  MRF (Fig.  3).  The  study  assumed  a  zero-burden  approach  for  the  waste received at the MRF, meaning that the environmental burdens associ ated with the production and use of the recovered waste materials before collection and transportation to the MRF are excluded. The zero-burden approach is a standard practice in solid waste management LCA (Voss et al., 2021). The cradle-to-gate scope covers all processes such as waste collection  and  transportation,  equipment  and  office  electricity  con sumption, rolling stock and conveyor diesel consumption, and waste residue disposal.

For the inventory analysis, four major hierarchy groups are modeled: waste collection and transportation to the MRF, recyclables separation, recovery,  and  packaging  at  the  MRF,  residue  disposal,  and  avoided emissions.  The  energy  and  material  balance  from  the  process  model serves as input data for the LCA. Residue disposal involves transporting residues to landfills. The study assumes that recovered materials in the

MRF will be repurposed and used in place of virgin materials. Avoided emissions  account  for  the  impacts  of  displacing  materials  by  MRF products in the market. This LCA approach is also known as the system expansion  or  substitution  method.  The  study  employs  the  OpenLCA (OpenLCA,  2022)  software  to  analyze  the  inventory  data  using  the United States Life Cycle Inventory Database (USLCI) (NREL, 2012). The study did not include the embodied emissions and decommissioning of the facility. McKinsey and Company reported that 24% of emissions of a process come from embodied emissions in the building, while 76% come from energy used for cooling and heating. In an industrial facility, where electricity for heating and cooling represents a small amount of the total energy needed, embodied emissions are significantly smaller than 24%. They can be negligible compared to total emissions. Table S5 in the SI shows the life cycle inventory data as collected from OpenLCA.

Environmental and health impacts can be evaluated at the midpoint or  endpoint  level  using  various  life  cycle  impact  assessment  (LCIA) methods. Commonly used LCIA methods include ReCiPe, CML 2002, and eco-indicators (Al-Salem et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2017). This  analysis  employs  the  Tool  for  Reduction  and  Assessment  of Chemicals  and  Other  Environmental  Impacts  (TRACI)  impact  assess ment  method  at  the  midpoint  impact  assessment  level.  The  TRACI method is representative of U.S. conditions, and it groups the impact categories into environmental and human health impacts. The evaluated environmental impacts with TRACI include 100-year global warming potential (GWP) in kg CO2-eq, acidification potential (AP) in H + -eq, eutrophication potential (EP) in kg N, ecotoxicity (ETP) in kg 2,4-D-eq, ozone depletion (ODP) in CFC-11-eq, and photochemical oxidation (PO) in kg NOx-eq. The human health impacts include carcinogenic (Ca) in kg benzene eq and non-carcinogenic (NCa) in kg toluene eq. Table S4 in SI shows the emission factors used in this study.

The study assumed the average U.S. electricity mix in the LCA to highlight the impact of waste stream composition on the environmental impacts. However, it is important to highlight that the electricity mix varies from state to state and can significantly impact the environmental impacts of the MRF. Hence, the study assessed the effects of the varying electricity mix by location on the GWP, assuming the MRF is located in the state where the waste was collected. Emission factors for the indi vidual state are obtained from the U.S. Energy Information Adminis tration (EIA) electricity profiles (U.S. EIA, 2022).

2.5. Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis

Sensitivity analysis is a methodology employed to assess the vari ability of a model ' s output to critical model input parameters when each parameter is altered, and other variables are kept constant. Sensitivity analysis is used in this study to identify the parameters (changed by ± 30%) that most influence NPV and LCA impact assessment categories. For NPV, the changed variables are operating hours, waste tipping fee, total fixed capital investment cost, diesel consumption, residue disposal cost, and electricity consumption. Due to the high variability of waste composition and PCRM market prices, the study evaluates the NPV ' s sensitivity to variation in waste composition and recovered materials selling prices. The critical parameters varied for LCA impact categories include  diesel,  electricity,  baling  wire,  transportation,  and  waste composition. Table S5 in SI shows the sensitivity analysis variables for the base, optimistic, and lower cases.

For the uncertainty analysis, we evaluate the effect given that the uncertainty of crucial parameters varied in the sensitivity analysis and waste composition on NPV and GWP. This study utilizes Monte Carlo simulation to generate 10,000 distinct combinations of waste composi tion  and  key  parameters  in  the  TEA  and  LCA.  The  analysis  uses  a triangular distribution to generate random combinations using the U.S. EPA  waste  stream  and  baseline  parameters  as  the  mean  value.  The triangular distribution was chosen because it is common in Monte Carlo analysis when the actual distribution is unknown (Nanthakumar et al., 2009).

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Techno-economic analysis

The cost  for  a  120,000  t/y  single-stream  MRF  is  estimated  to  be $23.13 MM. This capital cost is in the range of $22.4 MM -$29.4 MM reported  in  the  literature  (Cimpan  et  al.,  2016;  Logan  City  Council, 2018; Pressley et al., 2015). An MRF feasibility report carried out by the Logan city council, Iowa, estimated the capital cost of a 60,000 t MRF which  services  about  93,000  households  as  $29.4  MM  (Logan  City Council, 2018), while Cimpan et al. (2016) estimated the capital cost of building an MRF could range from $7.42 MM for a 25,000 t/y facility to $22.4 MM for a 100,000 t/y MRF (Cimpan et al., 2016). The capital cost recorded in this study is similar to the values recorded by Cimpan et al. (2016). The slight difference could be attributed to the difference in facility size. Logan city MRF and the MRF modeled in this study have similar operating capacities per hour, the main difference being that the Logan city facility only operates one shift daily. However, the significant $6 MM difference in the capital cost is found to be attributed to the disparity in the equipment cost reported in this study and the Logan MRF report (Logan City Council, 2018). The Logan MRF report did not break down the equipment cost to allow for further investigation.

The total equipment investment cost accounted for about 20% of the TFCI. The optical sorters for glass (19%), HDPE (10%), and PET (5%) account for about 34% of the total equipment investment cost. The oneway and two-way balers also contribute about 23% of the total equip ment investment cost. This study assumes a fixed MRF configuration for all waste streams considered. Therefore, the waste composition does not affect the capital cost distribution.

The fixed operating cost for the 120,000 t/y facility is 45.48 $/t of waste processed. The variable operating cost varies with the processed waste stream. Due to some of the assumptions in this study, the diesel price, waste disposal, transportation, and collection cost vary with the quantity of waste processed in the MRF. However, the baling wire and electricity requirements vary with the waste composition. Section 3.1.1 in the SI gives more information on the baling wire and electricity re quirements for all  waste  streams considered in the  study. Recovered aluminum is this study ' s most valuable recoverable material at $1,708 /t, followed by HDPE and plastic film (Figure S1). Fig. 4b shows the total revenue generated from each waste stream and how much each recycled material contributes to the total revenue. The U.S. EPA generated the largest  annual  revenue  because  of  its  high  HDPE,  plastic  films,  and aluminum content. Seattle showed the lowest revenue due to its low aluminum and high OCC and Non-OCC fiber content.

The operating cost, capital cost, and revenue were used in a DCFROR analysis to estimate the NPV of the facility across the 20 years lifetime. Fig. 4a shows the NPV for the four waste streams. The NPV recorded for the U.S. EPA average waste stream showed a net present value of $59 MM. The TEA model resulted in an NPV value of $3.57 MM, $30.54 MM, and $43.39 MM for Seattle, Oregon, and Pennsylvania ' s waste compo sitions. The difference in NPV is because of the revenue generated from the different waste streams. Fig. 4b shows that the U.S. EPA, Oregon, and Pennsylvania  composition  generates  more  revenue  than  the  Seattle waste stream. Seattle generates the lowest revenue because the waste composition has high glass, OCC, and non-OCC fibers, which sell for lower  prices.  Whereas  the  other  waste  streams  have  more  valuable materials like aluminum and plastics. Glass increases the operating cost because of the high electricity required for sorting glass but contributes less  to  the  revenue,  hence,  reducing  the  NPV  of  the  system.  Plastics improve the MRF ' s economic viability but are a small component of the waste  streams  recovered  in  the  MRFs.  However,  the  NPV  (Fig.  4a) showed that the MRF is profitable for the four waste streams considered in this study.
