from an environmental and circular perspective. However, the most currently used recycling processes are mechanical, [4] which do not produce high quality polymers, leading to the downcycling of the pristine polymer. [5] Chemical recycling, on the other hand, converts the polymers to smaller molecules or even monomers. Although this is an interesting option to obtain different materials, it commonly involves complex processes with extreme operating conditions, [5] and its application for closed-loop recycling requires the repolymerization of the monomers. Furthermore, it is still inefficient for various types of polymers, namely polyolefins.

In recent years, dissolution-precipitation has been emerging as an alternative promising strategy to end-of-life plastics. Dissolution-precipitation is a physical recycling strategy that consists in dissolving the polymer in a good solvent and recovering it by the addition of an antisolvent or changing the solution temperature, inducing polymer precipitation. A general scheme of operations involved in a dissolution-precipitation process is presented in Figure 1. Unlike mechanical recycling, this technique produces high-quality polymers, maintaining the pristine polymeric physicochemical characteristics', [6] except for polymer ' s crystallinity. [7] Another major advantage is its high selectivity, allowing to process multilayer plastic films [8,9] as well as removing key impurities such as metal [10] and dyes [11] through the use of adequate solvents. Moreover, as this technique does not involve chemical reactions, the only possible source of polymer degradation is the high temperature usually used in the dissolution process. [12] The fundamentals of the dissolutionprecipitation strategy hinge on the precise design of solvents that afford favorable interactions between solvent-polymer (dissolution) or solvent-antisolvent (precipitation) interactions. [13] The antisolvent interacts directly with the solvent, with no affinity for the polymer, leading to desolvation of the polymer. [13] This set of interactions allows the polymer to be precipitated by itself, with little to no impurities. Temperature based processes are scarce but have the advantage of only using one solvent, lowering the overall process costs.

Figure 1. General scheme of a dissolution-precipitation process.

Possibilities and challenges for the dissolution-precipitation process can be assessed using a S trenghts, W eaknesses, O pportunities and T hreats (SWOT) analysis (Figure 2). This strategic tool provides a clear visualization of the technique ' s position in the market. Currently, recycling rates are clearly insufficient considering the enormous amounts of plastics produced daily. This shortfall is partially due to the inability of mechanical recycling methods to handle the complexity of most plastic waste, particularly multipolymer materials and additivated plastics. With a higher tolerance to feedstock contamination and the ability to separate different plastics from solid mixtures without degrading them, dissolution-precipitation is well-suited to address these complex plastic wastes.

Compared to mechanical methods, this physical recycling process is more expensive, due to the costs associated with solvents usage and with the energy required for their recovery. On the other hand, dissolution-precipitation is much simpler than chemical recycling, has lower energy requirements, and presents the additional advantage that the recovered polymers can be directly used in new applications. Chemical recycling may allow greater versatility in monomeric uses, since they can be transformed into other compounds, but it requires an extra (re)polymerization step to produce new polymers. Thus, even though chemical recycling can be seen as a possible threat to dissolution-precipitation, the two technologies cannot be viewed as mutually exclusive, but rather complementary approaches. Moreover, all recycling technologies, mechanical, physical, and chemical, can become more advantageous if they are combined and each used for different grades of plastic waste streams, taking into account how the impacts and requirements of each relate between them. Lange et al. [14] proposed a cascade of the various recycling technologies would be the optimal strategy to maximize the impacts of plastic recycling. Furthermore, licensing difficulties might be a possible threat, as the dissolution-precipitation technology is relatively recent which may, by itself, delay the legal processes for the use of recovered polymers in certain applications. The conventional solvents typically involved in already implemented processes could become an issue for licensing, namely in food packaging, a sector where legislation is extremely strict regarding recycled materials. [15] One possible bypass to this situation is the engineering of packaging in ways that allow the recovered polymer to be isolated from contact with the product itself. [16] Still, it is likely that the replacement of these solvents with nontoxic alternatives, which is starting to gain more attention, will facilitate these processes.

Figure 2. SWOT analysis of the dissolution-precipitation process.

Current Methodologies for Solvent Selection

The selection of adequate solvents is the foundation of wellperforming dissolution-precipitation processes, as the interactions between polymer, solvent, and antisolvent determine operating conditions, material recovery and quality. Thus, accurate thermodynamic models and computational approaches to predict polymer solubility are of extreme importance, minimizing the need for experimental screenings, that are costly and highly time consuming. These include solubility parameters (Hildebrand, Flory-Huggins, and Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP)), COSMO-RS (Conductor-like screening model for realistic solvents) and machine learning models, which have been emerging as large sets of data become available.

HSP is perhaps the most widely used model to assess the solubility of a polymer in a given solvent. This model represents each compound in a three-dimensional space, as illustrated in Figure 3, according to different interactions: nonpolar ( δ d ), dipole-dipole ( δ p ), and hydrogen bonding ( δ h ). A good solvent is that which HSP lay within a sphere centered on the polymers HSP with radius R0. Although HSP and R0 are tabulated for most common polymers and solvents, they can also be obtained experimentally through inverse gas chromatography, or estimated using group contribution methods, allowing the application of this method to new solvents. This standard approach was implemented for selecting polymer ' s solvents in various works. Hanschmann [17] used HSP to select green solvents for both PP (polypropylene) and PET (polyethylene therephtalate) dissolution with good agreement with experimental results. Hansen parameters can also be a good tool to analyze the selectivity of the solvents screened, by ensuring the

Hansen Solubility Parameters

solvent used is exclusively contained in the solubility sphere of the target polymer or additive. For example, Das et al. [18] aimed to selectively dissolve bromated additives present in ABS (Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene), and Sánchez-Rivera et al. [8] screened solvents that selectively dissolve PE (polyethylene) and EVOH (Ethylene vinyl alcohol) but not PU (polyurethane)based inks, allowing the separation of each of component from a multilayer film. Additionally, antisolvents can also be chosen among the compounds located outside the polymer ' s HSP sphere, as shown by Yu et al., [19] regarding PC (polycarbonate) precipitation.

However, this model sometimes fails to predict solubility in certain scenarios, such as apolar solvent and polar polymer pairs, or vice-versa, [20] and different grades of the same polymer, to which HSP are not sensitive or available6, or the presence of additives that can inhibit polymer dissolution [21] . Some attempts to minimize these inaccuracies have been proposed. For example, Yu et al. [19] constructed the solubility sphere of PC based on experimental dissolution tests, increasing the predictions accuracy for pure solvents. Another limitation of HSP is the significant complexity increase to estimate the parameters at temperatures other than 25 °C. Considerable progress has been made by Karim et al., [22] who developed an iterative MATLAB program to calculate and analyze HSP over a range of temperatures for PET. Despite the mentioned limitations, HSP proved to be a valuable method to predict solubility using relatively low amounts of data, leading to smaller errors than other descriptors, such as molecular descriptors and fingerprints. [23] Recently, Denolf et al. [24] successfully built ternary diagrams for different polymer-solvent-antisolvent systems by combining the Flory-Huggins theory with polymer-solvent and polymer-antisolvent interaction parameters obtained from HSP, and solvent-nonsolvent interactions described by the UNIQUAC model.

COSMO solubility predictions

Figure 3. Application of HSP and COSMO to predict polymer-solvent solubility.

COSMO-RS is another widely used tool to select solvents for polymer dissolution-precipitation processes. This can be achieved either by estimating the activity coefficients and excess enthalpy of polymer in solvents, or by calculating the quantitative polymer solubility at a certain temperature. Zhou et al. [25] quantitively estimated the solubility of EVOH, PE, PET, PP, PS (polystyrene), PVC (polyvinyl chloride), and nylon (PA (polyamide)) in different solvents, by inputting an experimentally measured variable for each polymer. Sánchez-Rivera et al. [8] followed the same procedure for PE, EVOH, and PET. Aparício et al. [6] estimated the solubility of HDPE in several natural solvents, with good agreement with experimental tests. However, the authors highlighted that the quantitative predictions are influenced by parameters such as polymer crystallinity and molecular weight, which input values must be carefully chosen and the results analyzed accordingly. [6] Both Yu et al. [26] and Mohan et al. [27] screened Ionic Liquids through the analysis of activity coefficients and excess enthalpies, for dissolution of lignin and PET, PS, PP, and PVC, respectively. Both works validated the COSMO predictions with experimental results. In particular, Mohan et al. [27] showed that both parameters analyzed were directly correlated with the experimental quantitative solubility of PET. COSMO-RS can also be useful to understand the interactions that govern the dissolution ability of a certain solvent towards a polymer, through the analysis of the σ -profiles and σ -potentials. [18,27]

Although HSP and COSMO-RS present satisfactory results, the development of machine learning models has created the opportunity to increase the screening power of these and other models. For example, Sumer et al. [28] established a model that estimates the activity coefficient of the polymer in the solvent (trained through a dataset of COSMO-RS estimations), using Kamlet-Taft parameters to describe the solvent. Kern et al. [29] trained a model to predict room-temperature solubility, using experimental data for training, and chemical fingerprints as input. Similarly, Aoki et al. [30] estimated Flory-Huggins parameters using as input solely the chemical structures, after training the model with experimental data. However, the quality of the results obtained is still limited by the quality and quantity of the data that is available for training, regarding the dependance on dissolution conditions or polymer properties.

The above-mentioned strategies have proven to be extremely helpful to make preliminary solvent selections, allowing to reduce greatly the number of experimental tests needed to identify good solvents for the target polymers. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that these thermodynamic-based models do not take into account other factors that strongly impact the dissolution process, namely the kinetic behavior and viscosimetric effects. [31] Thus, computational screenings serve as a great tool to aid solvent selection, but do not eliminate the need for careful evaluation of these solvents' experimental performance.

State-of-the-Art Solvents for Polymer Dissolution

Dissolution-precipitation is a very promising technology to address the increasing need for improved modern plastics recycling. Despite the great development in the tools for solvent selection in recent years, few solvents have been used in experimental studies. Table 1 presents a compilation of the solvents reported for common synthetic polymers. There are still very few proven options for non-toxic solvents in polymer dissolution-precipitation strategy. Meanwhile, solvents such as toluene, which are known as being toxic and environmentally problematic, while also being severely restricted by EU regulations appear as options for use with multiple polymers. Regarding the search for safer, greener options, polyolefins is the class of polymers for which more solvents were tested, including a few greener ones (limonene, p-cymene, α -pinene, [6] biodiesel [32] ). On the other hand, PS, reported to be soluble in limonene since 1998, [33,34] is the polymer for which the most natural solvent options, including natural oils, have been studied. Although we consider the above-mentioned options to be preferred to most conventional solvents, which are proven to pose various hazards, we should highlight that some of these recent alternatives still lack some toxicity and safety studies. This is especially the case for the solvent mixtures as well as the natural oils shown in Table 1. Still, those experiments show that dissolution-precipitation is a technology that can and will be adapted to the pursuit of green solvents.

The precipitation, recovery and subsequent characterization of some polymers, namely polyolefins, PET, and polyamides, has been comprehensively studied in several works. Parameters taken into account include the antisolvent used, the amount of antisolvent, and temperature influence on the precipitation. Furthermore, recovered polymers are commonly analyzed regarding the chemical structure through FTIR (Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy), melting and crystallization temperature through DSC (Differential Scanning Calorimetry), crystallinity through DSC or XRD (X-Ray Diffraction), thermal resistance through TGA (Thermogravimetric Analysis), and molecular weight through viscosimetric measurements or GPC (Gel Permeation Chromatography). In some works, the mechanical properties of the recovered polymers, such as tensile stress at maximum load, elasticity, and strain at break, as well as surface structure, using SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) are also analyzed.

Nevertheless, many reported solvents were studied with the aim of using the polymers in other applications, rather than establishing their closed-loop recycling. These include membrane and nanoparticle fabrication, [35,36] where little attention was given to the recovered polymer characterization. Furthermore, certain specific classes of polymers are rarely analyzed regarding the possibility of their recovery and reuse. These are typically cases of polymers that exist in low amounts in complex samples, and thus most authors are interested in their removal rather than their recovery. Examples of these are polyurethane, commonly used as an adhesive or base for ink layers in multilayer films, [8,37] or PVDF (Polyvinyldiene fluoride), a typical binder material for battery cathodes. [38-40] Therefore, this technique is versatile, allowing recovery of different highquality materials when these are associated with plastics. On the other hand, there is a gap in information regarding less common plastics, as well as biopolymers. Still, there is no reason to believe this technique would not yield these polymers in high quality, as long as adequate solvents are used.

text: Even if it is not the main objective of this technique some depolymerization can happen. This is usually due to the removal of substances such as plasticizers and other stabilizers that, when removed, cause some depolymerization. [41] In these cases, to be reused new additives are added to fulfill the conditions needed for market usage, depending on the intended application. On the other hand, there have been studies focused on removal of additives such as brominated flame retardants [18] and phosphorated compounds, [42] the latter which can also be recovered with high purity, allowing the availability of pure polymers for recycling, which increases the process overall circularity. Not many studies do a deep analysis regarding plastic additives, which means there is a general lack of information regarding how these compounds affect the process as in if they are dissolved, their interaction with the solvent/antisolvent pair and their influence in the process repeatability. In fact, additive presence and type is only one of the several understudied factors which impact the performance of these processes. Other examples are initial molecular weight, and characteristics of sample particles, such as thickness.

Poor solvent selection can also lead to depolymerization, since the high temperature in which the process occurs may favor the occurrence of such reactions. Usually this is addressed in literature by characterizing the polymer before and after solvent treatment with techniques such as FTIR and TGA. This is usually enough to address situations in which the depolymerization grade is minimum. Still, careful solvent selection and quantitative depolymerization analyses, namely viscosimetry or GPC, are suggested.

Final Remarks and Sustainability Considerations

The dissolution-precipitation strategy consists of a straightforward recycling process that enables the recovery of clean polymers from complex polymer mixtures, while maintaining the same properties as the pristine material. However, most studies still focus on the use of volatile organic solvents that are traditionally considered environmentally dangerous and/or toxic for humans. On the other hand, no toxicity data exists for some of the tested natural solvents, such as natural oils, while other tested natural solvents, such as turpentine, are known for their toxicity for humans and the environment. Despite the enormous advances in the last decade in the design of solvents, the stringent regulations on air quality enforced by EPA in USA and Green Deal in EU underline the need to assess the toxicity for human health and the environment of the plethora of novel, natural, bio-based, mixed solvents. [73] The recent advancements in solvent screening and selection models will undoubtedly play a crucial role in broadening the range of solvents used in these processes, facilitating a transition towards greener and more sustainable alternatives. Even so, a thorough safety and toxicity analysis of these solvents will be essential to make informed decisions on which would contribute the most to safer and more sustainable plastic dissolution processes.

Another important aspect to be highlighted is the lack of techno-economic analysis and Life Cycle Analysis (LCA) studies of dissolution-precipitation processes. Some studies concluded that the recycled polymers have lower or comparable costs to the virgin materials, [8,46] but only one article reports the critical importance of the solvent reuse and recycle for the economic viability of the process. [6] Conversely, few studies point out the significantly lower environmental impacts of polymer recycled through solubilization-precipitation than those produced from virgin materials, [8,46] and the energetic efficiency of this process. [43] Considering the requisites for a greener, efficient recycling process, the choice of non-toxic, environmentally friendly solvents, as well as further technoeconomical studies regarding the process as a whole are essential to solidify the position of dissolution-precipitation as a prime, green, plastic recycling process.

1. Introduction

The industrial sector ' s quest for ever-increasing growth has led to more  and  more  new  products  being  flushed  onto  the  market  at decreasing intervals. The consequences can be seen in the electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) sector: the ever-shorter product lifetime is leading to an increased volume of waste from electrical and electronic equipment  (WEEE).  In  2022,  62  Mio  tons  of  WEEE  were  generated globally (Baldé et al. 2024). About 2.6 Mio tons of plastic from WEEE are generated annually in Europe (Forti et al. 2020). In contrast, demand for plastics  for  EEE  applications  amounts  to  3.1  million  tons  in  Europe, which means immense value creation for this waste (Plastics Europe 2024). The electronics industry ' s products are very diverse. While metal components  predominate  in  WEEE,  plastics  form  the  second  largest component. There are six different categories of WEEE, of which small WEEE (sWEEE) has the largest share (Nikolic et al. 2024). The compo sition varies and changes increasingly. The study of Maris et al. shows a typical plastic composition of sWEEE (e.g., IT applications like phones and printers, vacuum cleaners, toys). The most commonly used polymer

A B S T R A C T

The significant challenges of recycling plastics from electrical and electronic equipment waste (WEEE) comprise the  mixture  of  different  plastics  and  their  content  of  brominated  flame  retardant  (BFR).  Current  recycling techniques are insufficient in removing BFRs, leading to high rejects and incineration of valuable resources. In this study, it is shown that de-pollution by a dissolution-based recycling technique (DBR) is feasible with pre sorted  flame-retarded  (FR)  acrylonitrile  butadiene  styrene  (ABS-FR)  and  polystyrene  (PS-FR)  fractions  from WEEE. This was demonstrated at a technical scale of five kg/d with shredded samples, originating from different European sources, characterized by a PS share of > 95 % and an ABS share of > 70 %, as well as bromine concentrations  of  12,000  ppm  and  33,000  ppm,  respectively.  Besides  novel  brominated  flame  retardants (NBFRs), tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) and decabromodiphenyl ether (decaBDE) above legal thresholds have been detected. After successive extraction by dissolution-based recycling, restricted BFRs have been effectively eliminated  to < 500  ppm,  ensuring  their  legal  compliance.  This  achievement  underscores  the  regulatory compliance of the DBR process. The DBR process can be part of a cascade for the treatment of WEEE plastics that includes both spectroscopic pre-sorting and chemical recycling of the side streams. With the interconnection of existing techniques, a far-reaching circulation of EEE plastics is possible.

types  are  ABS,  HIPS  (high-impact  PS),  and  PP  (polypropylene). Together, they account for approximately 77 % of plastics in the elec trical and electronics sector. However, the share of polycarbonate (PC) and PC/ABS (8 %) is not negligible (Maris et al. 2015). Because EEE can become  hot  and  catch  fire,  they  are  often  equipped  with  flame  re tardants. There are 140 -200 different substances that can be used for flame  retarding;  half  of  these  are  brominated  (Wolf  et  al.  2017). Currently, the most common BFRs found in WEEE plastics in Europe are i.a.  tetrabromobisphenol  A  (TBBPA),  decabromodiphenylether (DecaBDE), decabromodiphenyl ethane (DBDPE), and 1,2-bis(2,4,6)-tribro mophenoxy ethane (BTBPE) (Chris Slijkhuis 2018). Some of the BFRs used in the past are considered harmful to humans and the environment and have therefore been classified as substances of very high concern (SVHCs) or persistent organic pollutants (POPs) with restrictions in their use,  as  is  the  case  with  polybrominated  diphenylethers  (PBDEs)  and hexabromocyclododecane (HBCD), for example (Wagner und Schlum mer 2020).  If  these  are  contained  in  WEEE  plastic,  they  have  to  be disposed  of  in  such  a  way  that  these  substances  are  destroyed  irre trievably  according  to  European  RoHS  II  and  WEEE  II  Directives

When EEE reaches the end of its service life, it is disposed of. There are various ways of disposing of WEEE, whereby WEEE and its con taining plastics can only be recycled at designated collection points. In Europe, about 50 % of the generated WEEE is actually collected (1.4 Mio t plastics out of 2.6 Mio t plastics) (Haarmann et al. 2023). Due to several challenges, including the high complexity of WEEE plastic mixtures and the current state of plastic sorting technologies, it is estimated that only 50  %  of  the  collected  (1.4  Mio  t  plastics)  and  presorted  (0.4  Mio  t plastics) WEEE plastics are typically effectively recycled (0.2 Mio t of regranules  with  sufficient  quality)  at  European  WEEE  plastic  recyclers (Haarmann et al. 2020; Haarmann et al. 2023). 12 % follow a comple mentary recycling route, i.e., they are disposed of with ferrous and nonferrous metal scrap outside any standards. About 7 % is sent for energy recovery, such as incineration or as a substitute fuel in cement kilns (coprocessing), or ends up in landfills (Cardamone et al. 2021). About 30 % is  undocumented  and  likely  to  be  exported  for  reuse,  recycling,  or disposal (Haarmann et al. 2020). The complex composition of WEEE presents a challenge that requires special treatment processes to recover it. Usually, sWEEE is shredded after decontamination (e.g., Hg switches) and cables have been dismantled. The focus of this shredding process is on recovering metals. Plastics emerge as a secondary fraction, which requires further downstream sorting. Due to economic reasons, manual sorting to remove plastic from housings beforehand is not applied to sWEEE in mid Europe  and  is  limited  to  larger  items  of  electric  and electronic equipment like copiers or TV flat panel displays (Potrykus et al. 2024). In simple terms, the mixed WEEE plastics fractions obtained from  dismantled  and  shredded  WEEE  are  typically  cleaned  of  nonpolymeric  impurities,  such  as  metals  or  minerals.  This  cleaning  is generally achieved through air classification, magnet sorting, or eddy current separation. The plastic fractions obtained in this way are then shredded to a smaller particle size to optimize the efficiency of further sorting technologies. They are further separated via two-step density separation (1.0 g/cm 3 ; 1.1 g/cm 3 ) in a saline solution and subsequently sorted  by  electrostatic  separation  into  the  different  polymers.  The outcome  of  the  process  includes  separate  polymer  fractions  high  in polyethylene (PE), PP, ABS, and PS shares, respectively, and with low bromine content. The bromine-rich and filled polymers ( > 1.1 g/cm 3 ), however, which can vary from 20-70 % of the input, are sent to incin eration, defined by a > 2-second treatment at temperatures > 850 °C with  best  available  techniques  (BAT)  and  efficient  raw  gas  cleaning (Strobl et al. 2021; Potrykus et al. 2024). As this is the only way to ensure that the limit values for dioxins and furans, which derive from burning  BFRs,  are  below  the  legal  limits  and  BFRs  are  irretrievably destroyed (Mukherjee et al. 2016). Because this heavy fraction ( > 1.1 g/ cm 3 ) contains not only plastics with high BFR content but also those with low concentrations, existing sorting technologies cannot achieve the full value creation potential of WEEE plastic recycling. Research is being conducted into effective ways of recycling brominated plastics.

A promising approach for overcoming the obstacles of bromine-rich WEEE plastic  recycling  constitutes  dissolution-based  recycling  (DBR) technologies. In these processes, either the entire polymer matrix can be selectively  dissolved  using  solvents,  or  only  the  components  to  be eliminated, such as BFRs (van Melkebeke et al. 2025). In principle, three extraction principles for BFRs have been reported in scientific literature. Van Melkebeke et al. (2025) report membrane filtration of adsorbed BFR in the dissolved polymer matrix. This approach requires small mesh sizes like 0.45 µ m and may suffer from increasing polymer share in dissolu tion  and  other  non-dissolved  matter  (like  fillers)  usually  present  in WEEE plastics. Xia et al. (2021) describe supercritical CO2  extraction from molten polymer, which requires specific equipment and does not reach > 99 % reduction. This study focuses on the selective dissolution of the target polymers and subsequent precipitation to gradually elim inate the BFR concentration. However, many of the DBR technologies reach their limits when scaled up. For example, membrane filtration requires very thin polymer solutions, and supercritical CO2  extraction requires a complex extruder design to sufficiently separate BFRs, which has a major impact on industrial feasibility. In this study, the target polymers  ABS  and  PS  in  a  bromine-rich  WEEE  plastic  mixture  are separated by different selective solvents and subsequently precipitated to eliminate BFRs below legal limits on a technical scale at 5 kg/d. The DBR approach in this study is evaluated in terms of the recycled quality of PS and ABS, as well as the cleaning performance in removing BFRs using X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy and gas chromatographyIn 2006, the  dissolution  process  was  already  compared  with  other  recycling technologies for WEEE plastics and found to be one of the most sus tainable  recycling  technologies  (Freegard  et  al.  2006).  In  order  to improve the polymer yield and thus the efficiency of the process, the bromine-rich WEEE plastics in this study were subjected to sorting using laser-induced  fluorescence  spectroscopy  before  the  DBR  approach.  A previous study on the LCA of this DBR process indicated already a lower environmental impact, compared to conventional mechanical methods (Ardolino et al. 2021).

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

2.1.1. Solvents

All solvents were polymer-specific CreaSolv ® formulations supplied by CreaCycle GmbH, Grevenbroich. The solvent composition is an un disclosed  property  of  CreaCycle  GmbH.  Thus,  information  on  the chemical structure or polarity may not be disclosed in this context. For analytical purposes, THF, ethanol, and toluene were purchased (all p.a. grade from Merck).

2.1.2. WEEE plastics

We  received  seven  pre-sorted  different  plastic  fractions  from  the WEEE sector with a total weight of 157 kg. These were provided by five European WEEE plastic recycling facilities and include fractions that are currently not recyclable through state-of-the-art techniques and which are normally sent to incineration. The mixed plastic fractions resulted from separation via sink and float ( > 1 g/cm 3 ) and X-ray transmission (XRT) sorting and are bromine-rich. The detailed composition of the samples  has  already  been  investigated  and  reported  by  Strobl  et  al (2021).  The  authors  concluded  that  the  WEEE  plastic  fractions  after density separation, on average, contained the following polymer shares: 60 % halogenated PS/ABS/PC/PC-ABS (1.1 -1.25 g/cm 3 ), 28 % ABS/PS (1.0 -1.1 g/cm 3 ), 7 % PVC/POM/PA ( > 1.25 g/cm 3 ), and 4 % PE/PP ( < 1.0 g/cm 3 ). It was decided to mix the samples to simulate the complexity of a real high-density WEEE plastic fraction. The bromine content of the composite sample is 16,500 ppm. This sample was shredded (16 mm sieve insert) and treated by laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy to produce two target plastics fractions, rich in ABS and PS, respectively. For  the  upfront  determination  of  the  extraction  parameters  of  BFR removal, a bromine-rich WEEE plastic fraction (96,220 ppm Br) from CRT  monitors,  pre-sorted  by  laser-induced  breakdown  spectroscopy (LIBS), and with an ABS share of 71 %, was investigated at laboratory scale.

2.2. Recycling and BFR extraction

2.2.1. Feedstock characterisation

The  polymer  composition  of  the  pre-sorted  (laser-based)  waste polymer  fractions was  analysed using a fractionated dissolution approach described by Strobl et al. (2021). For this, the bromine-rich PSand ABS-fractions from laser-induced sorting have been dissolved at 10 wt% in a selective solvent, and undissolved residues have been filtered S. Wagner et al.

through a büchner funnel under vacuum, respectively. The undissolved residues were dissolved further in ABS-, PS-, and PC-selective solvents and were filtered again. All polymer dissolutions from this procedure have  been  dried  in  a  vacuum  cabinet  dryer  for  a  mass  balance  and analyzed via FTIR for identification and purity assessment.

2.2.2. Dissolution-based polymer separation via fractionated dissolution

After laser-spectroscopy sorting, the dissolution-based recycling of plastics was applied to the pre-sorted polymers (Fig. 1a). Details of this technique  are  described  elsewhere  (Strobl  et  al.  2021;  Wagner  und Schlummer 2020). In brief, the PS fraction was dissolved at elevated temperature and below the flashpoint with a solvent that selectively dissolves PS in a 110 L double-walled stirring vessel. The dissolved PS (approx.  10  wt%  in  solvent)  was  then  separated  from  undissolved foreign  polymers  and  other  impurities  by  coarse  filtration  in  a  sieve basket with a 1 mm mesh size, followed by separation from all smaller particles by fine filtration in a bag filter with a 25 µ m mesh size. After this step, the coarse filter residue from PS separation was mixed together with the ABS fraction, and the mixture was first dissolved through a PS selective solvent in a 110 L double-walled stirring vessel at an elevated temperature. This was done because an unexpectedly high PS share was detected  in  the  pre-sorted  ABS  fraction.  The  dissolved  PS  was  first coarsely filtered (1 mm), then finely filtered (25 µ m) to remove undis solved non-target material, and mixed with the dissolved PS from above. ABS was then dissolved (approx. 10 wt% ABS in solvent) from the coarse filtration residue in an ABS selective solvent at elevated temperature; the undissolved residue was separated by 2-step filtration (coarse 1 mm, fine 25 µ m). The dissolution-based approach for both fractions had to be processed in two batches since the vessel volume of the pilot plant was insufficient.
2.2.3. Extraction of halogenated flame retardants and drying of recyclate

As shown in Fig. 1b, the polymers were precipitated into a gel to purify the dissolved polymers (PS, ABS) and remove brominated flame retardants. The elimination of BFRs is based on the patents WO2024038130A1 and EP1311599B1, which describe the precipitation with polar and non-polar solvents (Wagner et al. 2024; M ¨ aurer et al. 2010). This was done by adding an anti-solvent to the dissolved poly mers  in  the  above-described  vessels.  A  subsequent  separation  of precipitated polymer gel and supernatant extract through a suction unit, which removed the liquid phase (including the dissolved additives), was followed. The polymer gel remaining in the vessel was further purified (post-extraction)  by  adding  a  solvent/anti-solvent  mixture.  Thus,  the precipitated gel is post-extracted, and the BFR-loaded post-extract was removed  from  the  vessel  with  a  suction  unit  while  the  polymer  gel remained in the vessel. This procedure was repeated until an acceptable bromine concentration in the polymer gel was reached and monitored via  X-ray  fluorescence  analysis  (XRF).  Finally,  the  polymer  gel  un dergoes a drying (vacuum melt drying in a 50 L double-walled stirred vessel at boiling conditions of the solvent) and granulation step (in a twin-screw  extruder  with  two  degassing  domes).  In  comparison,  the loaded extractants are submitted to a solvent recovery step (in a 250 L double-walled  stirred  vessel  under  boiling  conditions  of  solvents), leaving a concentrate of halogenated flame retardants for safe disposal.

2.3. Characterisation of input, intermediate, and final products

2.3.1. XRF analysis

To estimate the BFR content, all generated samples were analyzed for their bromine concentration using energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence analysis (XRF) with a Spectrolab 2000 device (Spectro, Germany). For the  input  analysis,  representative  samples  (sampling  of  5  different random subsamples,á 50 g, at different levels of the sample bucket) of S. Wagner et al.

This plastic powder was placed in cuvettes lined on the bottom with a thin PP film  (4 µ m).  Wet  samples  like  the  dissolved  polymers,  precipitated polymer  gel, and  loaded supernatant (solvent/anti-solvent)  were directly placed in such a cuvette. Every sample was analyzed fivefold due to the expected material inhomogeneity. The arithmetic means of these multiple determinations are given.

2.3.2. GC-ECD analysis

BFRs were determined using gas chromatography (GC) combined with electron capture detection (ECD), which combines high sensitivity to halogenated compounds (comparable to GC -MS) and high stability against co-extracted oligomers that may affect the performance of GC/ MS systems. For the analyses, about 1 g of each sample (dry powder < 1 mm) of the plastic mix fractions and the final recyclates were mixed with 9  ml  THF  (p.a.,  Merck)  in  a  glass  vial  until  the  polymer  dissolved. Subsequently, this solution was precipitated with 90 mL of ethanol (p.a., Merck). A 1 ml aliquot of the supernatant was used for the GC-ECD analysis directly with respect to the cleaned output samples, and feed stock samples, which were expected to contain higher BFR levels, were diluted with toluene by another factor of 10 -1000, depending on the feedstock concentration. Before injection, samples were filtered through a 0.20 µ m PTFE syringe filter.

The aliquots were analyzed by gas chromatography coupled to an electron  capture  detector  (ECD,  Shimadzu  GC-2010).  Samples  were injected at 290 °C in splitless mode and separated on a DB-5HT column (15 m x 0.25 mm, 0.1 µ m, Agilent J & W), using a short oven program (170 °C 2 min, 20 K/min to 230 °C, 20 K/min to 340 °C, 4 min). Samples were qualitatively investigated by comparing their chromatograms with those of injections of reference materials, in detail certified mixture of hexa -through  deca-BDEs  (Wellington  Laboratories  BDE-MXE),  TBBPA (Aldrich), and BTBPE (Great Lakes Chemicals). For the identification of DBDPE, a technical reference material was used.

In line with our preliminary study by Strobl et al. (2021), it turned out that TBBPA, BTBPE, DecaBDE, and DBDPE were the most dominant single BFRs. Therefore, it was decided to quantify only these four single BFRs  to  monitor  their  concentrations  along  the  dissolution-based cleaning procedures. Quantification of TBBPA, BTBPE, DecaBDE, and DBDPE was based  on  5-point  calibration  curves  ranging  from  10  to 1,000  ng/ml,  with  the  smallest  standards  providing  stable  signal-tonoise ratios significantly higher than 10. Combined with the minimum dilution  factor  of  100,  detection  limits  of  1 -5 µ g/g  polymer  were calculated.

2.3.3. FTIR analysis

Polymers were identified using an FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared) spectrometer  (Spectrum  One,  Perkin  Elmer).  Samples  (dry  polymer particles of approx. 0,5 diameter) after laser sorting and of the dissolved polymers and their residues were analyzed with the instrument using Golden  Gate  ATR  (attenuated  total  reflectance).  Polymer  types  were determined by comparing the measured FTIR spectra with entries of a spectra library (references Fraunhofer IVV, Perkin Elmer).

2.3.4. Melt flow rate

Mechanical  properties  from  the  recycled  polymers  were  obtained using MFR analysis. Melt flow rate (MFR) and melt volume rate (MVR) were determined according to ISO 1133 using a capillary rheometer. The test temperatures and weights are for PS 200 °C and 5 kg, for ABS 220 °C and  10  kg.  The  melt  flow  rate  was  calculated  using  the  following formula:

MFR = 600*m [ g ] ∗ t [ s ]

2.3.5. Differential Scanning calorimetry (DSC)

Glass transitions or melting peaks in the DSC thermogram can be used to identify impurities, as they are characteristic of specific poly mers (Menczel und Prime 2009). In this study, glass transition temper atures  were  determined  by  a  DSC  device  from  Mettler  Toledo,  and dynamic  differential  calorimetry  was  performed  according  to  ISO 11357. The following program was used: heating I: 50 -200 °C; cooling: 200 -50 °C, iso: 5 min; heating II: 50 -200 °C; heating rate: 10 K/min, Atm.: N2, 50 mL/min..

2.3.6. Gel permeation chromatography (GPC)

GPC was performed with all recyclates. This analysis determines the average  molecular  weight  (Mw)  distribution  of  the  polymers.  By comparing the Mw of the recyclates with the Mw of virgin PS and ABS, it is  possible  to  identify  unusual  Mw  distributions  as  an  indication  of polymer chain degradation upon treatment.

Therefore, a solution containing 5,000 μ g/g dry sample (50 mg) in THF was prepared. The samples were dissolved at room temperature for 12 h. If the polymers were not completely dissolved, they were further tempered  in  a  heating  oven  for  another  two  hours  until  complete dissolution. Before analysis, the solution was filtered through a 0.22 μ m PTFE  syringe  filter.  Distilled  THF  was  used  as  the  chromatography mobile phase. A 600 mm long column with a diameter of 8.0 mm and a particle size of 5 µ m (PSS SDV Linear M, 600 mm, 5 µ m) served as the stationary phase. The measurement occurred at a flow rate of 1 ml/min and a temperature of 40 °C. Polystyrene reference materials dissolved in THF were used as calibration standards. According to the manufacturer of the GPC instruments, the error range of the GPC measurement ac counts for 10 %.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Input characterization of the sorted WEEE plastic fractions

The purity of the bromine-rich WEEE plastic fractions, which were excluded from mechanical recycling and produced after laser-induced sorting, was investigated using FTIR analyses and fractionated dissolu tion  with  polymer-specific  CreaSolv ® solvents.  Only the PS and ABS fractions separated by laser sorting were further processed with DBR to purify and eliminate brominated compounds. Since a preliminary study by (Strobl et al. 2021) showed that the measured concentrations of the BDEs with a lower degree of bromine substitution (Hexa-NonaBDE) in the  examined WEEE samples were much lower than TBBPA, BTBPE, DBDPE, and DecaBDE, only these four BFRs are reported quantitatively in this study.

3.1.1. Analysis of sorted PS fraction

For the first investigation of the composition of the sorted material, 60 FTIR analyses on single particles of the sorted PS fraction were per formed and evaluated. The FTIR analyses showed a PS content of 92 % and an ABS content of 3 %. The remainder consists of non-target poly mers, such as PE. In addition, polymer type identification was performed using the CreaSolv ® solvents as described in 2.2.1 with 100 g of the sorted PS fraction. As shown in Fig. 2, the distribution of the polymers in the  analyzed  fraction  is  similar  for  the  two  methods.  With  the dissolution-based method, it was possible to extract 94 % PS, 2 % ABS, and  1  %  other  polymers  as  residue.  3  %  loss  can  be  explained  by handling the laboratory trials (e.g., residues in the beaker glass). Both methods are equally suitable for determining the different components of the sorted material. However, it can be stated that the dissolutionbased method provides faster results on the one hand and is evaluated as more representative on the other hand since a 100 g sample was used instead of 60 pieces of approx. 0.5 g each. In addition, the FTIR analysis refers to particle numbers and does not reflect particle weights.

The PS content of a typical WEEE plastic mixture varies between 16 -78 % (non-halogenated, PS/ABS mixture) and 8 -44 % (halogenated, > 1.1 g/m 3 fraction) (Strobl et al. 2021). With the laser-induced sorting, it was possible to reduce the share of false polymers in the PS fraction by S. Wagner et al.

GC-ECD  analyzed  the  types  of  brominated  flame  retardants  con tained in the input. Table 3 shows the content in ppm of the different kinds of flame retardants in the input. Nevertheless, it should be noted that only extractable BFRs can be detected by GC-ECD. Thus, reactively bound BFRs are not detected.

DecaBDE is a PBDE already classified as SVHC and restricted under REACH, so it is no longer allowed in articles (European Commission 09.02.2017). Exemptions in recycled plastic products are allowed up to 500 mg/kg (European Parliament 20.06.2019). For DecaBDE and its degradation  products,  adverse  effects,  i.e.,  on  fertility  and  impairing neurodevelopment, have been shown based on experimental studies on animals  and  epidemiological  observations  on  humans  (Linares  et  al. 2015). Novel brominated flame retardants (NBFRs) are replacements of restricted  PBDEs  (tetra-,  penta-,  hexa-,  hepta-,  deca-BDE)  and  are increasingly being detected in the environment (Li et al. 2024). These include, i.a., decabromodiphenyl ethane (DBDPE) as a replacement for deca-BDE  and  1,2-bis(2,4,6-tribromophenoxy)ethane  (BTBPE)  as  a replacement for octa-BDE (Hsu et al. 2018). Although NBFRs show low toxicity levels, recent studies on birds and rodents have demonstrated that NBFRs, like restricted PBDEs, have the potential to cause endocrine disorders and reproductive development toxicity, too (Dong et al. 2021). Since  January  2023,  2,2 ′ ,6,6 ′ -tetrabromo-4,4 ′ -isopropylidenediphenol (Tetrabromobisphenol A, TBBPA) has been listed as an SVHC candidate because of its possibly carcinogenic effects (ECHA European Chemicals Agency). In addition, TBBPA is classified by GHS as H410, ' very toxic to aquatic life ' . Waste containing TBBPA in a concentration ≥ 2,500 ppm is labelled  hazardous  and  cannot  be  recycled  via  current  mechanical recycling techniques (Wagner und Schlummer 2020).

Due to the increased DecaBDE concentration, this PS fraction is un suitable for a conventional recycling route and would end up in incin eration, where valuable resources are wasted.

3.1.2. Analysis and sorting of the ABS fraction

As with the PS fraction before, the composition of the sorted ABS

fraction  was  analyzed  on  60  single  particles  via  FTIR.  The  analyses showed an ABS content of 82 % and a PS content of 8 %. The remainder consists of non-target polymers, such as PP, PC, and PMMA. In addition, polymer  type  identification  was  performed  using  a  solvent-based approach as described in section 2.2.1 with 100 g of input material. As can be seen in Fig. 2, the two methods produced different polymer distributions. In the first extraction step, 20 % PS was extracted, and in the second extraction step, 68 % ABS was extracted via solvent-based dissolution. The residue amounts to 7 %. A 5 % loss can be explained by the handling of the trials. It is assumed that the solvent-based method is  more  accurate,  as  a  larger  amount  of  material  is  homogeneously distributed in a solution.

Typical ABS shares in WEEE vary between 13 -45 % in the heavy fraction > 1.1 g/m 3 (Strobl et al. 2021). Through the laser-induced presorting of these WEEE fractions, the ABS content could be concentrated by a factor of six in the best case, starting from an initial concentration of 13 % in the WEEE fraction. Although the ABS yield after laser-induced sorting is not as good as the PS yield, 45 % ABS could be obtained for further recycling using this method, which would otherwise be sent for incineration. The low purity of ABS was unexpected, even when taking into account that the separation of ABS and PS in automated sorting is a challenge (Greiff et al. 2024). Earlier work has shown the potential of this instrument to achieve purities of 95 -98 % for ABS, PS, and PC/ABS WEEE plastics (Arends 2024). The poorer ABS yield may also be due to inadequate calibration of the fluorescence detector. A further sorting step would have produced a higher yield, but this would have required more time and energy.

GC-ECD  analysis  was  used  for  the  determination  of  halogenated flame retardants in the ABS fraction (Table 3). Here, as already deter mined in the PS fraction, TBBPA, BTBPE, decaBDE, and DBDPE have been  found  (only  extractable  and  non-reactive  flame  retardants).  As described  in  the  previous  paragraph,  there  are  legal  thresholds  for TBBPA and DecaBDE that are exceeded in the case of TBBPA ( > 2,500 ppm), but not for DecaBDE. Consequently, with the subsequent DBR of this fraction, TBBPA has to be eliminated until the legal threshold is reached.

3.2. Polymer separation by solvent-based dissolution process

The process described above was implemented on a technical scale by optimizing feedstock material (through pre-sorting by laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy) to reduce overall efforts. The sorted PS and ABS fractions from WEEE have been further processed in a small tech nical pilot plant (5 kg/d) to recover the pure polymers and eliminate the halogenated flame retardants. Since the PS share in the ABS fraction is quite high, a pre-extraction of the PS has been performed. Before the extraction of FRs, the dissolved PS and ABS were prepared separately according to the scheme in Fig. 1a. After separation and purification of the two recycled polymer types, PS and ABS showed similarities in melt flow rate (MFR), molecular weight (Mw), and glass transition temper ature (Tg) to the corresponding data obtained for virgin PS and ABS. The PS recyclate is expected to be a mixture of GPPS and HIPS since HIPS is widely used for EEE applications. However, this study has not investi gated the share of polybutadiene in PS recyclate. The higher MFR of the PS recyclate produced at the laboratory scale can be explained by the fact that the laboratory recyclate has been dried in a vacuum cabinet dryer and not by the more effective degassing extrusion at the technical scale, and so may have had a higher amount of residual solvent.

The physical properties of the recyclates have been analyzed and compared to those of virgin (HI)PS and ABS (Table 1).

With this trial, we have shown that separating WEEE plastics into the pure polymers ABS and (HI)PS using the DBR technique is feasible in technical stainless steel equipment.

3.3. Removal of BFRs from WEEE polymers

3.3.1. Determination of purification parameters at laboratory scale

The solvent-based cleaning of a polymer fraction can be divided into three main steps (Wagner and Schlummer 2024). The first step involves dissolving the polymer fraction in a solvent with similar polarity. This unknots the polymer chains, and the embedded additives (non-cova lently bound) are distributed in the medium. The second step involves the addition of an anti-solvent to the dissolved polymer, which is partly miscible in the solvent, so the polarity of the medium is changed, and the polymer forms clusters again and precipitates. This results in two pha ses:  an  extract  of  free  solvent  and  anti-solvent,  and  the  precipitated polymer as a polymer gel containing both polymer and extract. The dispersed additives are distributed between the two phases according to their polarity. By separating the polymer gel and the extract, the first extraction of BFRs is achieved. Further removal of BFRs in the polymer is achieved by adding a mixture of solvent and anti-solvent to the polymer gel and extracting these at an appropriate temperature for the needed time while stirring (first post-extraction). Because of the presence of an anti-solvent, the polymer won ' t dissolve. Still, BFRs are diffusing into the solvent/anti-solvent mixture. The  post-extraction  can  be  repeated  until  a  pre defined target, e.g., a legal threshold of BFRs, has been reached (second post-extraction → n  post-extraction).  The  extraction  of  the  BFRs  by solvent/anti-solvent  is  based  on  the  principle  that  the  BFRs  are  codissolved  when  the  polymer  is  brought  into  solution  and  therefore cannot be separated by filtration with a size of 25 µ m. The large and nonpolar molecule DecaBDE (M = 959 g/mol) will be used as an example. This has a solubility limit of 7,600 ppm in an organic solvent such as limonene at 60 °C, which is comparable to the solvent used in this study (Chen et al. 2016). In view of the fact that the concentration of DecaBDE in  today ' s  WEEE  plastics  tends  to  be  below  this  value  and  that  the concentration is per se diluted by the dissolution process itself, it can be assumed  that  the  BFRs  are  completely  dissolved  in  this  process  and under  these  conditions,  not  separable  by  filtration  (Haarmann  et  al. 2023). This is evident in the gradual extractive elimination of BFRs in the polymer exemplified in this study.

We investigated the purification of a dissolved ABS fraction obtained from cathode ray tube monitors. GC-ECD analysis with an LOQ of 10 ppm shows that only TBBPA and BTBPE, as BFRs, have been identified in this WEEE fraction. Other bromine compounds, detectable through XRF, were not part of the standard solution and could be assigned to either NBFRs or BFR decomposition products from high-temperature produc tion processes (Altarawneh et al. 2019).

Furthermore,  after  each  purification  step,  we  determined  the remaining brominated compounds (TBBPA, BTBPE), including the first extraction via precipitation and two post-extractions. Table 2 indicates a substantial > 99 % removal of total bromine and a > 99.7 % removal of the two specific BFRs from the polymer.

The reduction of BFRs in the pre-sorted WEEE fraction after each purification step shows an exponential decrease after the curve fits in Fig.  3.  This  approximation  can  help  to  predict  the  extraction  steps necessary to reach legal thresholds if the initial concentration of Br is known.

In this case, the partition coefficient indicates how much of the bromi nated compounds has been transferred to the extraction agent. If this is significantly higher than one, the BFRs have a higher affinity for the extraction agent and diffuse out of the polymer. Accordingly, a K above one should be aimed for each purification step. In addition to evaluating the extraction efficiency, the liquid -solid ratio should also be consid ered,  which  provides information on the amount of extraction agent required to remove the BFRs from the polymer.

The coefficient K of the first purification step and the second to third purification steps have to be considered separately, as they are different physical processes. In the purification step one, the reduction of BFRs is achieved by precipitation at 90 °C. In particular, the polarity of the antisolvent determines the extent to which the brominated compounds are transferred into the supernatant. In this case, K is in all analyzed Br species (K(Brtotal) = 0.8; K(TBBPA) = 1.0; K(BTBPE) = 1.2) above or near one, meaning that the affinity of the majority of the BFRs to the solvent/anti-solvent is greater than to the polymer. A large proportion of the BFRs could be channeled out of the polymer in this way (~70 % of total bromine), as the liquid -solid ratio here is 3.5.

In purification step two, the BFRs diffuse out of the polymer into the supernatant by adding an extracting mixture of solvent and antisolvent at 100 °C and stirring this mixture for 15 min. Hereby, the degree of extraction is  subject  to  the  laws  of  diffusion.  Accordingly,  a  suitable extraction performance can only be achieved if the concentration dif ference,  extraction  temperature,  and  extraction  time  are  correspond ingly high. If the Ks of the purification step two are considered, these are still above one for the different species but fall below one for total Br (K (Brtotal) = 0.7; K(TBBPA) = 1.9; K(BTBPE) = 3.5) with a liquid -solid ratio of 9.0, which leads to a further removal of 90 % of BFRs from the polymer. The higher K values for TBBPA and BTBPE in this extraction step result from the temperature being raised, and the dry matter of the polymer increases from 18 % to 46 %.

The  last  purification  step  is  characterized  by  a  lower  K  in  all considered species (K(Brtotal) = 0.2; K(TBBPA) = 0.7; K(BTBPE) = 1.2). This observation suggests that the kinetic equilibrium has not yet been reached after 15 min, which decelerates the diffusion rate compared to the two extractions before, but leads to another reduction of Br of a further 70 % in the polymer. Another reason for the low K for total Br is the expected bromine residues that can no longer be extracted. These originate  either  from  reactive  BFRs  or  BFR  decomposition  products, which are bound to the polymer chain. The liquid-to-solid ratio amounts to 14.

The trend of steady decline becomes apparent in the BFR reductions per purification step (Figs. 3, 2nd y-axis). However, the investigation aimed  not  to  optimize  the  K  values  but  to  determine  the  technical feasibility of  the process with the specified parameters, such as tem perature, extraction time, and solvent-to-precipitant ratio. In summary, it  can  be  concluded  from  the  experiments  that  by  adding  the  same quantity ratio of solvent and precipitant per purification step, the BFRs can be significantly reduced, and the polymer can be concentrated in the gel.  With  the  given  conditions,  the  bromine  level  was  reduced  to < 1,000  ppm  with  three  purification  steps,  which  is,  according  to  the CENELEC  standard  EN-50625  (CLC/TS  50625 -3-1), sufficient for further use.

3.3.2. Application of the extraction parameters on a small technical scale

The dissolved PS of both polymer fractions was mixed together and extracted following the scheme presented in Fig. 1b. Several extraction steps  were  necessary  to  reduce  the  bromine  concentration  in  the  PS fractions, as presented in Fig. 5a. The extraction aims to reduce the Br concentration below 2,000 ppm in the polymer fraction to comply with CENELEC  standard  EN-50625  (CLC/TS  50625-3-1).  This  states  the general pollutant removal limit values and target values and describes the corresponding procedures and methods to be applied for measuring the pollutant removal efficiency of the treatment processes for WEEE. When this standard was issued in 2015, the following applied: If the total bromine concentration is below 2,000 ppm, it can be assumed that the fraction  will  also  comply  with  the  POP  threshold  levels  (Stockholm Convention 2021). However, this was still the case when the old limit S. Wagner et al.

values for PBDEs and HBCD were still 1,000 ppm. Since then, the limit values have become stricter, which should lead to revising the CENELEC standard.

As shown in Fig. 5, the total bromine content met the threshold of the CENELEC standard EN-50625 in Batches 1 and 2 after processing with a solvent-based recycling technique. Five steps were necessary to reduce the  total  bromine  content  to < 2,000  ppm  with  Batch  1  and  2.  By extrapolating the data (Batch 1; Batch 2) through curve fitting (Fig. 5a), the  necessary  extraction  steps  for  further  bromine  removal  can  be determined.  If  two  further  purification  steps  are  added,  the  total bromine content can be reduced to below 1000 ppm. This is of relevance when legal thresholds are further lowered. However, a further require ment is the extractability of the brominated substances. To reduce the technical effort, the extraction volume can also be increased to improve extraction  efficiency.  With  the  GC-ECD  analysis,  it  was  possible  to determine the concentration of the remaining critical substances found in the initial polymer fraction (Table 3). The solvent-based recycling technique has reduced TBBPA and DecaBDE below the legal threshold. BTBPE and DBDPE, which are not yet restricted, have been reduced to 99 % and 60 %, respectively. If this result is related to the legal limit values, it is sufficient, but not satisfactory from a technical point of view.

The ABS polymer fraction has undergone the same procedure after removing the PS part. Starting with a total bromine concentration of 33,010 ppm, a concentration below 1,000 ppm total bromine could be achieved through DBR. During the experiment, Batches 1 and 2 were extracted three times to achieve the CENELEC threshold of < 2,000 ppm for total bromine (Fig. 5a). Should the standard be adapted to lower limit values in the future, it could be shown here that bromine can be further eliminated by increasing the extraction steps. A more detailed investigation by GC-ECD revealed that TBBPA has been reduced to < 1,500 ppm. (Table 3). The calculation of the reduction of DecaBDE and DBDPE is limited due to the detection limit reached in the recyclate; BTBPE has been reduced by 99.9 %. However, the data are interpreted in such a way that the reduction was very effective and complete. The obtained  BFR  levels  of  the  GC-ECD  analysis  comply  with  threshold values defined by the European directive on the Restriction of Hazard ous Substances (RoHS) and the European POP regulation. The tests have shown that tetra- and hexabromo-substituted flame retardants (TBBPA, BTBPE) can be reduced by approximately 99 % in the laboratory and on a  technical  scale  in  both  polymer  fractions.  Decabromo-substituted flame retardants (DecaBDE, DBDPE), on the other hand, have shown poorer reduction. This is due to the poor solubility of the latter BFRs

(almost insoluble in aqueous solvents, slightly soluble in organic sol vents). Polar and non-polar precipitations, as mentioned in the method section,  therefore  have  an  effect  on  the  cleaning  efficiency  in  the process.

In summary, it can be said that approximately 50 % of plastics could be  recovered  from  the  original  bromine-rich  heavy  fraction  at  the beginning of the cascade discussed in this study. This is divided into 20 % bromine-free PS and 10 % low-bromine ABS, as well as 20 % PC, PC/ ABS, which has not been further investigated here (Fig. 4).

3.4. Side-stream management

The DBR process ends with a recyclate, coarse filter residue (mix of non-target polymers, c(Br) = 7,876 ppm) and a halogen-loaded super natant from BFR extraction. To close the solvent cycle, the loaded su pernatant  is  regenerated  through  evaporation,  leaving  a  brominecontaining sump (c(Br) = 30,665 ppm) and pure solvent, which can be used again for dissolution.

In addition to BFRs, the bromine sump also contains other additives such as Sb2O3 and chlorinated FRs and oligomers from the EEE plastics separated by precipitation.

Pyrolysis and staged gasification can be used to utilize the compo nents of these two fractions as far as possible. In staged gasification, the high bromine-loaded sump is first subjected to pyrolysis (550 °C, > = 15 min), in which the material decomposes in a tar-rich gas (HCl, HBr) and solid residue as a char-metal mix, which can be used as a feedstock for pyrometallurgical processes. While the gas flows into a hightemperature gasifier ( > 1,230 °C) to break down the tar, the char is removed. Subsequently, the syngas from the gasifier is cleaned by a NaOH scrubber to remove all HBr and HCl and recover the halogens as NaBr and NaCl (Hense et al. 2015). Due to the absence of oxygen in the syngas, it is expected that the concentration of possibly present poly halogenated dibenzo-p-dioxins and furans (PXDD/F) is at least twelve times lower than in the case of combustion of the materials (Pekárek et al. 2001). Further, the bromine solution can be used as a recycled feedstock  to  produce  modern  BFRs.  Former  studies  have  shown  that staged gasification can recover about 96 % bromine out of the total infeed bromine mass (Hense et al. 2015).

The coarse filter residue, which still has a considerable amount of bromine, can, for example, be subjected to one-stage pyrolysis at 500 °C with red mud as a catalyst for dehalogenation during the decomposition of the polymer. Another approach to processing DBR residues is the EU Life project ' PSLoop ' .  The  recovery  of  the  EPS  foams  from  construction  and  de molition (C & D) waste leads to an HBCD additive that stays in the sump. In  this  project,  the  sump  recovery  occurs  in  high-temperature  waste incineration, which enables the recovery of the elemental bromine and reuses it to produce modern polymeric flame retardants. 4. Conclusion

This study shows that DBR is applicable and upscalable to WEEE plastics (ABS, PS) to recover halogen-free polymers with high purity and virgin-like physical properties. However, the efficiency of this recycling method depends heavily on pre-sorting. Actual restricted brominated flame retardants (non-covalently bound) can be eliminated through DBR under a legal threshold or detection limit. The majority of the BFRs examined here were specifically NBFRs that are not currently subject to any restrictions. However, because these substances are also increas ingly  detected  in  the  environment,  they  will  likely  be  regulated.  It cannot be ruled out that legal limits for restricted BFRs will be tightened in the future so that they may only be present in recyclate at levels far below 500 ppm, as is the case with hexabromocyclododecane (HBCD; 100 ppm legal threshold) and PBDEs (gradual reduction to 200 ppm by 2027 at the earliest). Also, assuming that the decrease in the measured BFRs is the same for further extraction steps, it could be shown that this recycling  process  would  be  suitable  for  WEEE  plastics  containing restricted BFRs with lower legal thresholds. One difficulty that arises from this is the lack of a fast and reliable analysis method. Although XRF

analysis provides a fast and reliable indication of the bromine content, it cannot distinguish between the individual BFRs, even those chemically bound. When realizing the DBR on an industrial scale, a reliable online method must be developed to detect individual BFRs during the process to make a reliable statement that the currently valid limit value has been reached.

A  real  material  cycle  for  WEEE  plastics  is  complex  and  requires several technologies to be implemented. Optimizations are necessary in all process steps to convert this into an economical process to increase the yield.

Dissolution/Reprecipitation: A Model Process for PET Bottle Recycling

J. G. POULAKIS, C. D. PAPASPYRIDES

Laboratory of Polymer Technology, Department of Chemical Engineering, National Technical University of Athens, Zographou, Athens 157 80, Greece

Received 1 November 1999; accepted 5 September 2000

Published online 18 April 2001

ABSTRACT: A dissolution/reprecipitation route was followed for the recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET). Model experiments on virgin material, either in the form of pellets or blow-molded bottles, are presented. The process proposed comprises dissolution of the plastic in an appropriate solvent, reprecipitation by using a nonsolvent, thorough washing of the material obtained, and drying. The solvent mixtures involved are separated by fractional distillation for further reuse. N -Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP)/ n -octane 1 n -hexane proved to be a particularly effective solvent/nonsolvent system. Further investigation was focused on the effect of the sample history through successive recycling cycles. The recycled material was evaluated in terms of molecular weight, crystallinity, and grain-size analysis, resulting in an excellent quality, competing with the virgin grade. © 2001 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. J Appl Polym Sci 81: 91-95, 2001

Key words: recycling; poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET); dissolution/reprecipitation; bottles

INTRODUCTION

Based on the concept of ' selective dissolution ,' according to which one polymer could be dissolved at a time, dissolution-based processes can be used for the separation of mixed plastic wastes. 1-3 Especially for poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), relevant recycling efforts can be reviewed as follows:

An integrated chemical process for recycling commingled plastics was developed at the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in cooperation with the M. W. Kellog Co. Two technologies, selective dissolution and flash devolatilization, are basic to this process. A mixture of the six main thermoplastics (PS, LDPE, HDPE, PP, PVC, and PET) are dissolved in xylene to form a homogeneous mixture of concentrations of 5-10 % by weight, followed by controlled temperature-solvent extractions that separate the individual polymers. 1,4,5 Alternatively, a process was described for separating a waste stream of 2-L bottles consisting of PET, an HDPE base cup, paper, or a PP label, and PP or an aluminum cap. The bottles are shredded, air-classified to remove the paper, washed with a detergent/water mixture, then sent to a sink-float tank containing water. Dried chips from the sink-float system are washed with the process solvent at a temperature sufficient to remove soluble impurities, but insufficient to dissolve the target polymer. For example, in the PET case, this washing will remove any adhesive, PS, or PVC which may be present from use in 2-L bottles or from sortation errors. 6,7 Finally, recycling of polyester/cotton blend fabrics can be accomplished by separating the polyester from the cotton fabric. The polyester is dissolved into a sulfone solvent, while maintaining the integrity of the cotton. The dissolved polyester solution is then dispersed into a sulfone/water coagulation solution where the polyester is precipitated out of the solution. The solution is filtered while hot, and the filtrate is filtered repeatedly. The cotton samples are contained within the autoclave. 8,9

In the present article, the possibility of recycling PET by the aforementioned dissolution/reprecipitation technique was investigated, while taking into account that this process can be safely applied in successive cycles, since it is carried out at mild temperatures, in contrast with melt recycling. 10-15 As a model experiment, two successive recycling cycles were applied to virgin PET to assess their influence on the structure of the recycled products. Moreover, blow-molded bottles for edible-oil packaging are recycled for use as a commercial end product, the collection of which, as a single-type plastic waste, is easy. N -Methyl2-pyrrolidone (NMP)/ n -octane 1 n -hexane proved to be a particularly suitable solvent/nonsolvent system, according to the following criteria 3 : (i) precipitation of the polymer in an acceptable form, (ii) total recovery of the polymer, and (iii) limited, as much as possible, quantities of the solvent and nonsolvent employed. The aforementioned solvent/nonsolvent system could be characterized as more effective than were others proposed in the past, 5,8 as it can be separated and almost fully recycled by a conventional distillation process, whereas PET is dissolved at relatively ambient temperatures, high polymer concentration, and using rather simple equipment. Characterization studies on the recycled grades were focused on the molecular weight, crystallinity, as well as grain-size distribution.

EXPERIMENTAL

Materials

Virgin PET pellets under the code name STA-22 (SKC Co., Korea) were used as the starting virgin material for the production of blow-molded bottles (0.5 and 1.5 L), for edible oil and water packaging.

All solvents used were general reagentgrade chemicals.

Polymer Recovery by the Solvent Process

Pellets of virgin PET or PET bottles cut into pieces were dissolved into NMP up to the level of

0.20 kg L 2 1 at 165°C. The upper concentration level was kept at this value, because with further increase of the concentration, the solutions became so viscous that they could not be processed under our experimental conditions. A 2-L reaction vessel, fitted with stirrer, reflux condenser, and thermometer, was employed. Stirring was applied for 90 min to assure quantitative dissolution of the polymer. The polymer solution was then filtered through a Seitz Merkur EF 6/03 device with volume capacity of 300 mL, using as filter paper 5500 Seitz-T-Filter sheets of an exclusion size in the range of 20-70 m m. V1 L of n -octane was then properly added to the hot filtrate and the polymer contained was precipitated. The polymer grains were isolated by filtration under a vacuum. The phase-separated solvents were then replaced by V2 L of n -hexane and stirring was again applied for 40 min. This washing procedure was repeated once more (V3 L n -hexane employed). The reclaimed polymer was dried in a vacuum chamber at 90 o C for 14 h. This once-recycled grade represented by the code name 1stREC was again subjected to the same procedure to produce the twicerecycled grade (2ndREC). Furthermore, the term 'Recycled from Bottles' describes the product derived upon applying this recycling procedure once on the bottles. The ternary solvent/nonsolvent mixture was separated for reuse in a distillation column (0.85 m height) filled with Raching Rings and equipped at the top with a side condenser.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Yield in Polymer and Solvent/Nonsolvent System

Table I shows the operating conditions of a typical example of the recycling procedure. Recovery yields of the polymer, solvent, and nonsolvent represent the mean value of eight iterations for each recycling cycle. The applied solution/nonsolvent ( n -octane) ratio was 1:2, while the additional quantity of n -hexane for each washing step was kept at a ratio of 1:2. Under our experimental conditions, the yield in the polymer nearly attains the theoretical value, while separation and recovery of the solvent (NMP) and both of the nonsolvents ( n -octane, n -hexane), obtained by fractional distillation, stand equally at excellent levels. Obviously, the effect of scaling up will lead to even better values, not deviating from the theoretical limits, that is, to closed-loop solvent recycling.

Crystallinity and Melting Ranges

DSC runs were performed to study the fusion behavior and crystallinity of the PET samples. It is well known that the heat of fusion is the amount of energy necessary to transform a polymer from a crystalline or a partially crystalline state to a completely disordered amorphous state. Valid heat effects of a physicochemical process can be estimated by measuring the area under a well-defined thermogram peak. If the heat of fusion D Hf of perfectly crystalline PET is known, the percentage crystallinity x can be derived as follows:

x 5 ~D H exp / D Hf ! 3 100

text:
where D H exp is the actual heat of fusion of the sample tested. D H exp is calculated by measuring the area under the thermogram peak, while D Hf is taken here equal to 32.5 cal g 2 1 , corresponding to the heat of fusion of the 100% crystalline polymer. 17

The resulting crystallinity values, according to this approach, are listed in Table III. Virgin PET possesses a crystallinity content of 44.8%, whereas the once-recycled polymer, the twice-recycled polymer, and the recycled bottles possess a crystallinity of 25.2, 27.0, and 25.0%, respectively. On the other hand, the melting point remains practically unchanged. Nevertheless, the melting range of the recycled grades is apparently broader than that of virgin PET since the lower is the degree of crystallinity, the broader is the melting range. The rather broad Tm observed for the recycled grades could also be attributed to plasticization of the polymer due to the presence of trace amounts of the solvent that would likely remain in the polymer structure.

In addition, the variation of the crystalline content could be correlated with the dissolving and precipitation procedure itself. The polymer is induced to reprecipitate from its hot solution by adding a cold nonsolvent. This sudden cooling apparently inhibits PET to develop crystallinity. The higher crystallinity seen with the virgin polymer is to be expected, as this polymer was presumably made via solid-phase polymerization, which amounts to a 12-24-h annealing at about 200°C. Without such annealing, or significant mechanical drawing, high crystallinities are not seen in PET.

Finally, the polymer concentration seems to be a critical factor affecting the crystallization ability of PET. Crystallinity measurements of recycled PET at different concentration levels (0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 kg L 2 1 ) revealed that by increasing the concentration crystallinity decreases (Table IV). The levels of crystallinity seen in the solution-crystallized samples are likely due to solvent-induced crystallization of the polymer, again consistent with some level of plasticization by the solvent.

Grain-size Analysis

According to the grain-size analysis (Table V), over 94% of the recycled polymer mass has a grain size smaller than 1 mm, suitable for feeding the PET processing units.

CONCLUSIONS

A model dissolution/reprecipitation process was investigated to recycle virgin PET and PET bottles. Concentrated solutions in NMP were employed (0.20 kg L 2 1 ) and the polymer was precipitated, in the form of small grains, through the addition of n -octane and subsequent washing with n -hexane. Excellent recoveries in the polymer and solvents are achieved. The evaluation of the effect of the previous history on the properties of the recycled product was accomplished by applying two successive recycling cycles on the PET pellets.

CONCLUSIONS

A model dissolution/reprecipitation process was investigated to recycle virgin PET and PET bottles. Concentrated solutions in NMP were employed (0.20 kg L 2 1 ) and the polymer was precipitated, in the form of small grains, through the addition of n -octane and subsequent washing with n -hexane. text:
The dissolution/reprecipitation once or twice applied did not appear to affect the molecular weight characteristics of the final product. The recycled grade, free of any soluble or insoluble additives, can be used in many different applications, competing with the virgin material. Largerscale experiments are expected to result in even higher concentration levels and also in 'closedloop' solvent recycling.

The results quoted do not aim to propose this dissolution-based process as a tool to recycle single-type PET waste, for obvious cost reasons. However, this effort could be very useful in separating PET from other polymers, in applications where different phases coexist.
