A B S T R A C T

The lack of economic dye-polymer and fiber-fiber separations for blended textiles prevents large-scale textile recycling. We focus on a clean, cost-effective, and destruction-minimized fiber-to-fiber recycling, suitable for polyester/cotton blended textiles. Here, dyed polyester was dissolved and separated from the blend, followed by controllable polyester precipitation to retain its dyes separately in the solution. The remaining-colored cotton was swollen to remove its dyes after cleavage of dye-cellulose bonds. Colorless polyester and cotton were re generated  into  fibers  with  similar  and  60  %  higher  tenacity  than  those  before  the  recycling,  respectively. Recycled fibers also had desirable dyeability, including dye exhaustion and colorfastness, after being dyed with the dyes extracted from the polyester/cotton blends, via our newly developed solvent dyeing system. More than 99 % of the solvent used in the recycling was recycled. Our recycling had a cost and energy consumption of less than 20 % of the production of virgin materials.

The circular economy plays a pivotal role in reshaping the textile industry into a more sustainable and socially responsible sector. Beyond its positive impact on environmental challenges, the circular economy brings forth economic advantages and societal benefits, establishing it self  as  the  foundation of textile recycling and a driving force behind sustainability practices within the industry (Jia et al., 2020). Cost-effective and high-quality textile recycling enables resource con servation,  waste  reduction,  energy  and  emissions  reduction,  water saving, and job creation (Kazancoglu et al., 2020).

The current textile recycling mainly contains textile-to-non-textile, fabric-to-fabric,  yarn-to-yarn,  fiber-to-fiber,  and  polymer-to-polymer recycling  (Zhang  et  al.,  2022).  In  recent  years,  several  companies worldwide have initiated textile recycling based on the above recycling technology (Craig Bettenhausen, 2022; Mu  et al., 2023d). The textile-to-non-textile recycling refers to transforming waste textiles into non-textile  products  such  as  rags  and  insulation  materials  (Schmidt, 2016). In fabric-to-fabric  recycling,  sorted  waste  garments  are  trans formed into fabrics that are remade into new  garments in a labor-intensive manner (Johnson et al., 2020). In yarn-to-yarn recycling, waste garments are color sorted or discolored via oxidation/reduction and mechanically disintegrated to make yarns (Biesinger et al., 2011; Esteve-Turrillas and de La Guardia, 2017; Liu et al., 2011). Fiber-to-fiber recycling regenerates waste textiles into new textile fibers via melt or wet spinnings after textile discoloration or color sorting (Kwon et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2019). Polymer-to-polymer recycling refers to a polymer regeneration  process  containing  depolymerization  of  waste  textile polymers, distillation to the separation of impurities, and repolymeri zation (Kurian, 2005; Scott, 2022). However, due to either low-valued end products or unaffordable costs,  achieving  profitable  recycling  of waste  textiles  based  on  the  above  technologies  is  still  very  difficult (Elander and Ljungkvist, 2016; Lu et al., 2022; ¨ Ostlund et al., 2015). Till now, textile reuse has been much more popular than textile recycling. Less than 0.5 % of used clothes were recycled into new clothes in 2021 (Scott, 2022). About 7 -10 % of waste textiles in Europe were reused mainly via export to developing countries. Nevertheless, reuse cannot fully  solve  the  environmental  and  health  issues  waste  textiles  bring (Sandin and Peters, 2018).

Many recycled products from textile-to-non-textile, fabric-to-fabric, and yarn-to-yarn recycling have less-than-expected quality and values. For the textile-to-non-textile recycling, many non-textile products have lower  values  than  original  textile  products.  Apparels  from  fabric-tofabric  recycling  have  poor  quality  due  to  impairment  from  use.  In addition, the recycled garments faced style limitations (Johnson et al., 2020). For yarn-to-yarn recycling, mechanical disintegration of fabrics causes damage to the recycled fibers, mainly fiber breakage, fiber sur face cracking, and loss of strength (Araújo et al., 2017; Wanassi et al., 2016). As a result, those recycled cotton fibers have to be blended with virgin cotton fibers. Even so, the tensile strength of blended yarns was only 75 % of pure virgin cotton yarns (Yilmaz et al., 2017; Zeidman and Sawhney, 2002).

Non-destructive and sustainable separation of polymers, dyes, and other impurities from waste textiles are the most challengeable steps in fiber-to-fiber recycling (Mu et al., 2023a, 2023c). For example, vat dyes and  many  reactive  dyes  substantially  reduced  or  even  eliminate  the spinnability of cellulose solution (Haslinger et al., 2019b). Melt spinning of dyed polyester led to unsatisfactory color quality and serious envi ronmental  and  health  issues(Singha  et  al.,  2021).  To  recycle  textile polymers into fibers, impurities, especially dyes, have to be separated. However,  non-destructive  and  environmentally  responsible  technolo gies for dye-polymer separation have yet to be developed. Bleaching is the most common method to destroy dyes on textile fibers (Haslinger et  al.,  2019a;  Kwon et  al.,  1998; Yousef  et al.,  2019).  However, dye removal  via  time-consuming  bleaching  generates  large  quantities  of wastewater, and deteriorates the properties of recycled polymers (Lu et al., 2022).

Unaffordable polymer-to-polymer recycling cannot be applied to all textile forms and is unable to retain dye structures. Though polymer-topolymer  recycling  was  applied  to  polyester  recycling  in  the  1960s (Kurian, 2005; Scott, 2022), such recycling is still not widely used due to the  unaffordable  costs  of  depolymerization  and  repolymerization. Furthermore, the technology cannot be applied to recycling of synthetic fibers via addition polymerization, natural fibers, such as cotton, wool, and silk, and regenerated fibers from natural polymers, such as rayon and acetates.  Furthermore,  the  conditions  used  for  depolymerization including  high  temperature,  strong  alkali  and  long  processing  time inevitably damage dyes on textiles and thus pollute the environment (Zhang et al., 2022).

Here  we  have  developed  a  cost-effective,  and  destruction-anddischarge-minimized  fiber-to-fiber  recycling  technology  for  blended textiles,  the  dominant  textile  form  in  the  world  (Wang  and  Salmon, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). For the first time, each polymer and dye is completely separated from polyester/cotton blended textiles via poly mer dissolution, polymer swelling, and polymer precipitation without chemical degradation or color destruction. Our recycling can overcome significant  obstacles  of  the  lack  of  cost-effective  and  non-destructive technologies  enabling  efficient  dye  removal  from  textiles.  As  our fiber-to-fiber  recycling  has  affordable  costs,  satisfactory  properties  of recycled products, and minimized discharge of pollutants, the portion of recycled textiles can be substantially improved. The high recyclability retention of chemical structures of textile after wearing and laundering indicates  the  feasibility  of  fiber-to-fiber  recycling.  The  polyester  is highly resistant to various environmental factors(Panowicz et al., 2021). The molecular weight of polyester did not change statistically even after 14,000  h  of  natural  weathering  (Al-Azzawi,  2015).  The  molecular weight of cotton after 50 laundering times was still higher than wood pulp (Palme et al., 2014), indicating that lyocell fibers from recycled cotton still have a high quality. Via the technology, textile fibers from fiber-to-fiber recycling have very high property retention. The regen erated fibers demonstrated similar or even higher mechanical properties and dyeability to those before the recycling. The process, eliminating costly depolymerization and repolymerization processes necessary for polymer-to-polymer recycling, enables profitable recycling of all textile wastes, including but not limited to polyethylene terephthalate (poly ester),  cotton,  and  their  blends  and  their  dyes.  Besides,  minimized discharge with 99.17 % recycling rate of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) has been achieved in the fiber-to-fiber recycling technology.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Preparation

2.1.1. Dyeing of 50/50 polyethylene terephthalate (polyester)/cotton with disperse dyes and reactive dyes, respectively

The 50/50 polyester/cotton fabric was dyed with disperse dyes first. About 2 % owf (on weight of the polyester part in the fabric) of CI Disperse Blue 56 and CI Reactive Blue 19 were dyed to the polyester and cotton portions under a liquor ratio (weight ratio of fabric to aqueous solvent) of 1:10, respectively. For polyester dyeing, the pH of dyeing medium was adjusted to 4.5 by acetic acid. The dyeing took place at 120 °C for  1.5  h.  For  cotton  dyeing,  about  50  g/L  NaCl  and  10  g/L Na2CO3 were added. The dyeing happened at 65 °C for one hour. Sup plementary Figure 1 shows the structures of CI Disperse Blue 56 and CI Reactive Blue 19.

2.2. Recycling polymers and dyes from polyester/cotton fabric via the zero-pollution-discharge recycling

2.2.1. Separation of polyester and cotton

Fig. 1 shows the major steps to recycle polymers and dyes from waste polyester/cotton  fabrics.  The  polyester  part  and  disperse  dyes  were separated from  polyester/cotton blends using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).  Specifically,  three  parts  of  DMSO  were  added  to  1  part  of polyester/cotton at 150 °C. The dissolution occurred within 5 min.

2.2.2. Controllable polyester precipitation for disperse dye-polyester separation

Since DMSO only dissolves polyester at temperatures higher than 150 °C, dissolved polyester can be precipitated to control the polymer morphologies via control of temperatures. As shown in Fig. 1, recycled polyester and disperse dyes in DMSO were cooled down, so that the precipitated polyester was completely amorphous. Dispersed dyes were separated from completely amorphous polyester via rinsing polyester with  a  small  amount  of  hot  DMSO.  After  the  disperse  dye-polyester separation,  colorless  polyester  was  washed  to  remove  DMSO  and dried.  DMSO  was  reused  by  water-DMSO  separation  driven  by distillation.

2.2.3. Substantial swelling of cotton to separate reactive dyes from cotton

After the separation of polyester and disperse dyes, solvents with different ratios of DMSO to water were added to the color-remaining cotton  fabrics  to  swell  cellulose  molecules.  Based  on  our  previous

studies, dyes have little affinity to substantially swelled cotton. Given reactive dyes had covalent bonds with cellulose, 0.07 -0.6 wt % of NaOH was added into the DMSO/water solvent to break the dye-cellulose co valent bonds. The swelling of cotton was repeated three times to achieve complete dye separation from cotton. Each cycle took place at 90 °C for 10 min. Weight ratios of the solution to cotton each cycle were 3. After the separation of reactive dyes, cotton was rinsed to remove organic solvents.  DMSO  was  reused  by  water-DMSO  separation  driven  by distillation.

2.2.4. Recycled polyester fibers via melt spinning

The dried polyester was wet spun into recycled polyester fibers at 270 °C  using  a  laboratory  mixing  extruder  (Dynisco,  Franklin,  MA, USA).  The  diameter  of  the  spinneret  on  the  extruder  was  0.5  mm. Polyester fibers were collected at a roller running at 200 m/min.

2.2.5. Recycled lyocell fibers from colorless cotton via wet spinning

A solution containing 5 % of color-removed cellulose, 87 wt% NMethylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO), and 13 wt% water was prepared via stirring at 110 °C for 2 h. About 1 % of propyl gallate, the stabilizer, was added to the cellulose solution. The cellulose solution was extruded into fibers via a dry-jet wet spinning, modified based on a laboratory mixing extruder (Dynisco, Franklin, MA, USA). Specifically, the cellu lose solution at 110 °C was spun into a 250 mm air gap and subsequently into a water bath. The drawing ratio was up to 40.

2.2.6. Dyeing recycled polyester fibers using recycled disperse dyes

Different amounts of water were added to dye-stripping DMSO so lutions to adjust the solubilities and chemical potential of dyes in the solutions.  Recycled  polyester  fibers  were  added  to  the  above  dyecontaining solutions for dyeing, which took place at 90 -120 °C for 1 h. For the control, virgin Disperse Blue 56 was added to water to dye recycled polyester fibers at 115 °C for 1 h. The dye concentration for all dyeings was 2 % based on the weight of polyester fibers. Dyed polyester fibers were washed and dried.

2.2.7. Recycling of reactive dyes

Since recycled reactive dyes had their functional groups hydrolyzed, the reactive dyes cannot be reused to dye cotton. However, according to the previous research, such dyes can be used as acid dyes to dye poly mers such as nylon and wool (Yang and Xu, 1996). Here, we used the recycled Reactive Blue 19 to dye nylon 66 fabrics. About 2 % owf (on the weight of fibers) of recycled Reactive Blue 19 was used to dye nylon fabric. Different amount of water was added to the reactive-dye-stripping solutions to adjust solubility and charged groups of recycled dyes. The dyeing took place at 90 °C for 1 h. The pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3 using acetic acid. To compare the dyeability of recycled Reactive Blue 19, Acid Blue 25, with the same chromogenic structure as Reactive Blue 19, was used to dye nylon under an aqueous dyeing system. The dyeing temperature was 90 °C while the pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3 using acetic acid.

2.2.8. Conversion of spent dye bath into dye-stripping solutions for zeropollutant-discharge

After  dyeings,  water  was  removed  from  the  spent  dye  bath  via distillation to produce pure DMSO solvent. The recovered DMSO can be used to recycle polymers and dyes from waste polyester/cotton blends again.

2.3. Characterizations
2.3.1. Determination of dye concentration on polymers, change in dye structures after discoloration, analysis of secondary structures of fibers and mechanical properties of fibers

To determine dye concentrations in polymers, polyester and cotton textiles were dissolved in phenol/tetrachloroethane (1:1 w/w) solution and  70  %  sulfuric  acid,  respectively.  The  dye  concentrations  were determined by the absorbance of the solution. Detailed procedures are in the Supplementary Information. Wavelength scan was to determine the changes in the dye structures. Detailed procedures are in the Supple mentary Information. FTIR coupled with viscosity measurement were used  to  determine  the  structures  of  polyester  and  cellulose.  Detailed procedures are in the Supplementary Information. 1 H NMR on a Bruker AVANCE DRX 700 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA) was used to determine the solvent structures. The solvent used was D2O. Morphologies of regenerated polyester and cellulose fibers were char acterized using a field-emission scanning electron microscope (Hitachi S4700  Field-Emission  SEM).  The  secondary  structures  of  fibers  were determined  by  X-ray  diffraction.  Detailed  procedures  are  in  Supple mentary  Information.  Mechanical  properties  of  fibers  were  obtained according to ASTM standard D-3822. Detailed procedures are in Sup plementary Information.

2.3.2. Colorfastness

The colorfastness to washing, rubbing, and light of dyed fibers were measured according to ISO 105-C10:2006(E), ISO 105-X12:2016, and ISO  105-B02:2013,  respectively.  For  colorfastness  to  washing,  test number B2 was used. For staining measurement, multifiber MFF #10 was used.

2.3.3. Determination of polymer density

Polymer densities under different temperatures were determined by BIOVIA  Materials  Studio  2018  (18.1.0.2017).  The  software  module utilized the Amorphous Cell Calculation to generate an amorphous unit cell. This cell consisted of a unit volume containing 5 polyester mole cules with 15 repeating units and 200 DMSO molecules. The energy of the cells was minimized until convergence, with a convergence criterion set at a 0.001 kJ/mol difference between successive minimizations. To accomplish this, the Smart algorithm was employed with a maximum of 5000 iterations. The temperature range for the calculations was set be tween 313 K and 403 K. Following the construction of the amorphous cell, a Forcite calculation was applied to optimize the polymer-solvent interactions through a geometry optimization process. Multiple simu lations were conducted to ensure that the simulated structures ' confor mations were energy minimized to the extent that the energy differences between them did not change by more than 5 % after repeated simula tions. Finally, after the energy minimization, the densities of the poly mers were determined.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Complete separation of polymers from blended textiles with minimized destruction

Fig.  2  shows  that  a  complete  polymer-polymer  separation  and polymer-dye separation in polyester/cotton blended textiles were ach ieved in a destruction-minimized manner. The polymer-polymer sepa ration  and  polymer-dye  separation,  included  in  the  fiber-to-fiber recycling, achieved zero-destruction to polyester and minimized dam ages to cellulose. Polyester and disperse dyes were first separated from the  textile  blends  followed  by  temperature-controlled  dye  separation from amorphous polyester gels. Colorless polyester was obtained. The remaining-colored  cotton  were  through  cleavages  of  reactive-dyecellulose bonds and substantial swelling to obtain colorless cellulose.

Figs. 2a-c discuss how to obtain colorless polyester from the blends. DMSO was found to fast dissolve polyester at 150 °C while precipitate polyester below 150 °C. According to Fig. 2a, the density of polyester can be adjusted by controlling the temperatures of DMSO in polyester precipitation. Previous study showed the decrease in polymer density led to a sharp decline in the van der Waals interactions between dyes and polymers and, thus, a substantial increase in the chemical potentials of dyes on polymers (Mu and Yang, 2022). When the chemical potential of the disperse dye at any position in the polymer was greater than the chemical  potential  of  the  dye  in  the  solvent,  the  disperse  dye  was completely separated from the polymer. Fig. 2a shows that as the tem perature increased, the density of the polyester decreased from nearly 0.8 g/cm 3 at 40 °C to less than 0.2 g/cm 3 at 130 °C. The sharp drop in the density of polyester substantially eliminated physical interactions be tween disperse dyes and polyester. Fig. 2b shows the separation ratios of disperse dyes from polyester at different temperatures in the process of polyester precipitation. The results show that almost all disperse dyes were separated from polyester polymer when controllable precipitation of polyester occurred at temperatures between 120 and 150 °C. As the temperature  continued  to  decrease,  the  proportion  of  disperse  dyes separated from polyester amorphous gels, resulting from controllable precipitation,  gradually  reduced  due  to  the  increase  in  the  polymer density (Mu et al., 2023b). The chemical potential of disperse dyes on polyester gels decreased with the increased in polymer density in the gel. The difference in chemical potential of the disperse dye between poly mer gel and polyester dissolution solvents determined the separation ratios  of  disperse  dyes  from  the  polymer. Fig. 2c compares the FTIR and molecular weights of virgin and dye-recycled polyester. The results show that the whole polyester-cotton and  polyester-disperse-dye  separation  had  no  effect  on  the  chemical structures and molecular weights of the polyester. The FTIRs of poly ester before and after the separation process were overlapped entirely. There was no statistical difference in molecular weights between the virgin polyester and the one after the separation process.

The remaining-colored cotton was swollen to remove the reactive dyes as shown in Figs. 2d-f. Fig. 2d shows that reactive dyes bonded with cotton  in  polyester/cotton  blends  can  be  completely  separated  by eliminating  dye-polymer  interactions  via  substantial  cotton  swelling. The  separation  process  maximized  retention  of  the  degrees  of  poly merization (DP) of cellulose. Before completely separating reactive dyes from cotton, the covalent bonds between reactive dyes and cellulose have to be cleaved without substantial damage to the dyes and cellulose. Reactive dyes are the dominant cotton-used dyes. An alkaline treatment was used to cleave the dye-cellulose bonds since alkalinity can retain the chemical  structures  of  cellulose  and  chromogenic  structures  of  dyes. Fig. 2d shows that only a low concentration of NaOH in a dye-stripping solvent, as low as 0.3 %, was strong enough to break all dye-cellulose bonds.  Without  covalent  bonds  with  cellulose,  reactive  dyes  were completely separated from cellulose under solvents with solubility pa rameters close to cellulose, as shown in Fig. 2e. When the solubility parameter of dye-stripping solutions is close to cellulose, the solution maximizes the swelling degrees of cotton. In Fig. 2e, by adjusting the parameters of the dye-stripping solution, two rinsing cycles realized a 99.9 % separation of the Reactive Blue 19 from cotton at 90 °C. The DMSO/water solvent, reactive-dye-stripping solvent, also greatly simplified  the  process  of  recycling  polyester/cotton  blended  textiles because the DMSO, used to separate polymers and recycle polyester as well  as  disperse  dyes,  was  not  necessary  to  be  removed  from  cotton before recycling of cellulose and reactive dyes. Fig. 2f shows that the process of separating polyester, disperse dyes, and reactive dyes did not change the chemical structure of cellulose except for a 6 % reduction in the molecular weight of cellulose. The FTIR of the cellulose before and after the separation process was the same. The DP of cellulose decreased from 2368, before the separation process, to 2223. Such a reduction resulted from the alkaline treatment for cleavage of dye-cellulose bonds. With such a decrease in the DP of cellulose, fibers from cotton recycling should have a desirable property. As shown in Fig. 1, colorless polyester and cotton were separated from 50/50 polyester/cotton blends. About 99.8 % of polyester was recovered after the recycling process while 99.9 % of disperse dyes were separated from polyester. Also, 99.2 % of cotton was also recovered. Up to 99.9 % of reactive dyes were separated from the  remaining-colored  cotton.  Next,  processibility  of  converting  the recycled polymers into textile fibers will be studied.

3.2. Desirable properties of recycled fibers

Fig. 3 demonstrates the properties of recycled polyester and lyocell fibers from waste polyester/cotton blended textiles. Results show that recycled  polyester  fibers  had  similar  properties  compared  to  virgin polyester fibers while cotton-derived lyocell fibers had higher tenacity than wood-pulp-derived lyocell fibers.

Figs. 3a and b compare the properties of recycled polyester fibers to virgin polyester fibers from perspectives of morphology, crystallinity, and  mechanical  properties  of  fibers.  The  results  show  no  significant differences in the morphologies, degrees of crystallinity and mechanical properties between recycled and virgin polyester fibers. The degrees of crystallinity of virgin and recycled polyester fibers were 59.13 ± 4.17 % and 60.12 ± 4.76 %, respectively. Complete recycling of polyester has been  achieved  via  the  non-destructive  dye-polymer  separation  tech nology. To evaluate the spinnability of the recycled polyester polymer, a high ratio of drawing was performed during the melt-spinning process. Fig. 3a demonstrates the separation process did not affect the polymer spinnability since the final diameter of regenerated fibers, 12 µ m, was

even slightly lower than that of virgin polyester fibers, 16 µ m. Fig. 3a also  shows  that  the  recycled  and  virgin  polyester  fibers  had  similar crystallization behavior. The degree of crystallinity of recycled polyester fibers  was  slightly  higher  than,  but  not  statistically,  that  of  virgin polyester fiber, possibly  due to the higher drawing ratios during the extrusion  of  regenerated  fibers.  A  high  drawing  ratio  promoted  the linearity of polymer in fibers, resulting in more crystallized structures. Fig.  3b  compares  the  mechanical  properties  of  recycled  and  virgin polyester fibers. The results show that the tenacity and breaking elon gation of regenerated polyester fibers were higher and lower than that of virgin  fibers,  respectively.  Overall,  recycled  polyester  fibers  had  a desirable mechanical property.

Figs.  3c  and  d  compare  the  morphology,  XRD  and  mechanical properties of lyocell fibers from recycled cotton to those of cotton fibers. The results indicated that complete cellulose recycling was realized by non-destructive dye-cellulose separation technology. Fig. 3c shows that the crystal structures of cellulose changed after regeneration in ionic liquid, from the original Cellulose I to Cellulose II. For example, new crystals formed at 2 θ = 20.1 (110) and 2 θ = 21.53 (200). Cellulose, found in its natural state, is referred to as cellulose I. In cellulose I, the individual cellulose strands are oriented in a parallel manner, and there is no hydrogen bonding between the strands. On the other hand, cellu lose  II  is  thermodynamically  more  stable  and  consists  of  cellulose strands  arranged  in  an  antiparallel  fashion,  with  hydrogen  bonding occurring between adjacent strands (Jacob John and Thomas, 2010). Even with changes in crystal structures, the degree of crystallinity of lyocell  fibers  was  not  significantly  different  from that  of  cotton.  The degrees of crystallinity of virgin cotton fibers and recycled lyocell fibers were 65.49 ± 4.65 % and 63.83 ± 4.23 %, respectively. Compared to the traditional wood-pulp-derived lyocell with a DP of about 1000, the DP of recycled cotton was higher than 2000. The higher DP did not affect the spinnability of cellulose in N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO). As shown in Fig. 3c, lyocell fiber had a desirable fineness. The diameter of  lyocell  fiber,  regenerated  from  recycled cotton, was about 11 µ m, much lower than that of regular cotton fibers, 20 -25 µ m. Fig. 3d com pares the mechanical properties of cotton-derived lyocell fiber and other cellulosic fibers. The results show that, like wood-pulp-derived lyocell fibers, cotton-derived lyocell fibers had higher tenacity than cotton and viscose fibers in both dry and wet states. The tenacity resulted from stronger  interactions  between  cellulose  molecules  in  lyocell  fibers. Compared to wood pulp, the cotton-derived lyocell fibers had an even higher tenacity due to the higher DP of cotton. In addition, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers not only reserves a lot of resources, including wood, but also eliminates various wood pre-treatment processes such as de-barking, chipping, defibration, bleaching, and washing. Therefore, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers is a green, sustainable, and environ mentally responsible process. Next, we will study recycling of dyes and dyeability of recycled fibers.

3.3. Recycling of textile dyes and dyeability of recycled fibers

Fig. 4 demonstrates that dyes from waste polyester/cotton blended textiles  can  be  easily  recycled  due  to  the  undamaged  chromogenic structures  and  desirable  dyeability  of  recycled  polymer  fibers.  Dye stripping solvent system can be easily turned into dyeing solvent system via easy modifications. Via the recycling of textile polymers, dyes and Recycling of disperse dyes solvents,  the  overall  fiber-to-fiber  recycling  technology  realized  zero discharge.

Fig. 4. Recycling of disperse dyes and reactive dyes from waste polyester/cotton blended textiles. (a) The comparison of chromogenic structures of Disperse Blue 56 before and after dye separations using visible wavelength scan. (b) Structures of stripping solvents before and after separating polyester-cotton and polyester-disperse dyes (Solvent for 1 H NMR was deuterium oxide). (c) Dye uptake on recycled polyester fibers (R. polyester) using recycled dyes. 2 % owf (on the weight of fibers) of recycled Disperse Blue 56 (R. dyes in the figure) was used. (d) Comparison in chromogenic structures of Reactive Blue 19 before and after dye separations. (e) Structures of DMSO before and after separations of cellulose-polyester and cellulose-reactive dyes. (f) Dye uptake of recycled Reactive Blue 19 on nylon66 fabric.

Figs. 4a -c show the recycling of disperse dyes via dyeing the recycled disperse  dyes  onto  recycled  polyester  fibers.  Fig.  4a  shows  that  the chromogenic structure of the Disperse Blue 56 remained intact after the dissolution  of  polyester,  formation  of  amorphous  polyester  gels,  and dye-polymer separation. Via visible wavelength scanning, there were no changes for Disperse Blue 56 before and after the separation process. Fig. 4b shows structures of the DMSO solvent, determined by 1 H NMR, involved in the separation process. The results showed that the structure of DMSO did not change after the separation process, given the stable structures of DMSO and short separation durations. In the separation, polyester and disperse dyes were fully dissolved in DMSO within 5 min at 150 °C and dye-polymer separation completed for another 5 min at 120 °C.  DMSO  is  highly  stable  at  temperatures  below  150 °C.  For example, DMSO was expected to lose 0.1 to 1 % of its weight at 150 °C for 24 h (Tudino et al., 2020). In 1 H NMR, no new impurity peaks except methyl hydrogen atoms attributed to DMSO appeared. The undamaged DMSO can be used to develop a new dyeing system to recycle dyes so that  recycled  dyes  in  the  dye-stripping  solutions  did  not  need  to  be extracted before the recycling. Fig. 4c shows that adding an appropriate proportion of water to the DMSO to adjust the solubility and chemical potentials of disperse dyes achieved similar dyeing results on polyester fibers compared to that in traditional aqueous dyeings. The dyeing result also indicated recycled polyester fibers had good dyeability. In addition, because of the better swelling properties of DMSO on polyester mole cules, the dyeing temperature could be 20 °C lower than that of tradi tional  aqueous  dyeing  to  achieve  a  similar  dye  uptake.  Dyeing temperatures for DMSO-involved dyeing and traditional aqueous dyeing were 95 °C and 115 °C, respectively. Reduced dyeing temperature saved substantial energy in the dyeing process.

Figs. 4d-f show the recycling of reactive dyes via dyeing the recycled reactive  dyes  onto  nylon  fabrics.  For  reactive  dyes,  their  functional groups  after  dye-cellulose  separation  were  hydrolyzed.  Therefore, recycled reactive dyes can no longer be used as reactive dyes to dye recycled cellulose fibers. However, given the undamaged chromogenic structures after dye-cellulose separation, recycled reactive dyes can be used as acid dyes for ionic fibers such as nylon, wool, and silk according to previous research (Yang and Xu, 1996). Fig. 4d compares the chro mogenic  structures  of  reactive  dyes  before  and  after  the  separation process. The results show separation process did not change the chro mogenic structures of reactive dyes given the same scanning curve in the visible wavelength range. For a fair comparison, functional groups of Reactive Blue 19 before recycling reacted with water before the visible wavelength scan. The solvent was 70 %DMSO/30 %water. Fig. 4e shows that DMSO was very stable during the dye-cellulose separation. 1 H NMR did not show any additional impurity peaks. Fig. 4f shows that slight increase in the water portion in reactive-dye-stripping solution trans formed the dye-stripping system into dyeing system, which provided the similar dye uptake as traditional aqueous system. The increase in water portion  helped  recycled  reactive  dyes  negatively  charged.  Therefore, dyes can be easily sorbed by nylon. The recycled reactive dyes, with hydrolyzed functional groups, were used as acid dyes to dye nylon. To compare the properties of recycled dyes, Acid Blue 25, with the same chromogenic structure as Reactive Blue 19, was used to dye nylon under an aqueous dyeing system. The dyeing temperature was 90 °C while the pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3. 2 % owf (on the weight of fibers) of recycled Reactive Blue 19 was used. Via water distillation, the solvent dyeing systems for disperse dyeing and reactive dyeing can be turned into fiber-to-fiber recycling system again.

The use of recycled disperse dyes also provided a desirable color fastness on recycled polyester fibers. As shown in Table 1, the color fastness of recycled disperse dyes on recycled polyester fibers was the same as that of virgin disperse dyes on virgin polyester fibers. Table 1 shows that under a similar dye uptake on polyester, there was no dif ference in colorfastness to light, dry crocking, wet crocking, laundering color change, and staining.

The use of recycled reactive dyes also provided a similar colorfast ness on nylon to virgin acid dyes with the same chromogenic structure. As shown in Table 2, the colorfastness of recycled reactive dyes on nylon fabrics was the same as that of acid dyes on nylon fabrics. Table 2 shows that under a similar dye uptake on nylon, there was no difference in colorfastness  to  light,  dry  crocking,  wet  crocking,  laundering  color change,  and  staining.  The  above  results  demonstrate  the  complete Colorfastness of recycled polyester dyed with recycled dyes and virgin polyester dyed with virgin dyes.

text: 3.4. Cost-effective fiber-to-fiber recycling

Supplementary Table 1 shows that fiber-to-fiber recycling is not only cost-effective but also energy-conservative. The fiber-to-fiber recycling only  needs  two  major  steps,  polymer  dissolution,  and  controllable polymer  precipitation,  to  obtain  colorless  polymer  materials  in  a destruction-minimized manner. The cost of the two steps is much less than that of depolymerization and polymerization, used in polymer-topolymer recycling to separate impurities. The recycled dyes can also be redyed onto recycled fibers. In addition, the fiber-to-fiber recycling realizes the recycling of not only synthetic fibers but also natural fibers and  recycled  fibers  from  natural  polymers.  Since  the  fiber-to-fiber recycling technology used the same spinning method to produce poly mer fibers as the other polymer-to-polymer recycling and traditional virgin fiber production, the cost calculation only covers the process of conversion of waste textiles to recycled polymers and dye recycling. For polyester, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste polyester fabrics to polyester pellets while for cellulose, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste cotton fabrics to cotton linter pulp. Based on calculations, recycling 1 ton of textile fibers, including polyester  and  cellulose,  potentially  adds  at  least  $  1600  values.  The added  values  were  calculated  based  on  the  difference  between  the market prices and the total production costs of materials and energy. The energy consumed by the recycling technology are also calculated. The recycling of 1 ton of polyester consumed about 830 kwh of energy while recycling of 1 ton of cotton consumed about 330 kwh of energy. The energy consumed by the recycling was substantially lower than that by producing virgin polymer materials.

3.5. Environmental viable fiber-to-fiber recycling

The process of producing recycled polymers was compared to that of producing  virgin  polymers.  The  comparison  demonstrated  that  our fiber-to-fiber recycling has substantial environmental viability since it conserves more resources, consumes much less energy, and discharges much less waste. As shown in Table 3, the production of 1 ton of recycled polyester only consumed less than 20 % of the energy needed for pro ducing 1 ton of virgin polyester and eliminated various emissions such as CO2, CH4, and other hydrocarbon chemicals. Besides, recycling 1 ton of polyester saved 0.65 tons of natural gas, 1.28 tons of crude oil, 0.51 tons Comparison in resource consumption and emission between the production of 1 ton of virgin and recycled polyester.

4. Conclusions

text: This novel, clean, and cost-effective fiber-to-fiber recycling, regen erating waste textiles into new textile fibers via spinning, completely separated dyes from polymers and retained the chemical structures of polymers  and  chromogenic  structures  of  dyes.  The  recycling  process maximized the retention of chemical structures of polymers. The recy cled  polyester  fibers  from  waste  polyester  had  similar  fineness  and mechanical properties compared to virgin fibers. The lyocell fibers from recycled cotton had much better fineness and strength than virgin cotton fibers. The recycled fibers also demonstrated desirable dyeabilities. The chromogenic structures of recycled dyes have not been damaged and can be further used as textile dyes without discharge. 99.17 % of DMSO used in  the  recycling  was  recycled.  The  recycling  is  techno-economically viable and energy conservative given that the cost, including material and  energy,  and  energy  consumption  for  the  recycling  process  were 6 -12% of the sale prices of raw polymers and 5 -20 % of the production of virgin materials, respectively. The fiber-to-fiber recycling promotes the establishment of a large-scale recycling industry with an emphasis on  environmental  sustainability,  resource  conservation,  waste  reduc tion, and fashion industry transformation. Besides, the technology can be fit for future regulatory changes, which mandate the textile recycling.

Abstract: Polyvinyl(butyral) (PVB) post-production waste collected from the windshields of endof-life vehicles and post-consumer building laminated glass are valuable polymeric materials that can be reused. Every year, large amounts of PVB waste are still being buried in landfills owing to a lack of appropriate recycling techniques. Before reuse, PVB should be thoroughly cleaned of solid contaminants such as glass dust, fused heating wires, and other waste polymers, metals, and ceramics. This can be done by polymer dissolution and filtration. In this study, we propose the purification of PVB from contamination by dissolving the post-consumer polymeric materials into single and binary organic solvents. As part of the experimental work, measurements and optimization of the dissolution time of PVB were performed. PVB dissolves faster when a binary solvent (2-propanol + ethyl acetate) than pure 2-propanol is used. From the point of view of the practical application of PVB solutions, measurements of density and dynamic viscosity as a function of PVB concentration and temperature were performed. The PVB solutions obtained in this work can be widely used as glues for glass, ceramics, metal, impregnating, and insulating materials or as paint additives that are entirely transparent for visible light and to block UV rays.

Keywords: polyvinyl(butyral); recycling PVB; waste PVB; laminated glass; solution of PVB

1. Introduction

Environmental aspects, increasing growth of virgin polymer prices, and still growing landfill fees bring about the increasing interest encountered in plastic waste recycling [1]. The problem has been solved at a global level for common plastics such as polyethylene, polypropylene, poly(ethylene terephthalate), and poly(styrene) [2-4]. However, poly(vinyl butyral) PVB does not belong to this group, although it is commonly used in the glass lamination process, especially as an interlayer in car windshields, architecture (facades and construction), and security glass [5-8]. PVB is also used as an interlayer in the construction and encapsulation of solar cells [9-11]. PVB is a polymer material with excellent properties, including excellent optical clarity, high adhesion strength to glass, metals, and ceramics, high mechanical strength, and high deformation. PVB for laminated glass is currently manufactured and commercialized by companies worldwide, among which should be mentioned: Eastman Chemical Company (US), Kuraray (Germany), Sekisui Chemicals (Japan), Everlam (Belgium), Genau Manufacturing Company (India), KB PVB (China), Chang Chun Group (China), DuLite (China), and Tiantai Kanglai Industrial (China) [12].

Currently, the major source of waste PVB is the windshields of end-of-life vehicles and also side windows because, by 2018, a third of car models had laminated side windows instead of tempered windows. The total number of end-of-life vehicles reported in the European Union reached 6.1 million in 2018, sharply rising from the 4.8 million recorded in 2016 and 5.3 million in the year 2017, and was the highest since 2010 [13]. This shows that more and more waste PVB will be collected in landfills each year. Most countries limit the recycling of automotive windshields, architecture windows, and solar panels to aluminum and glass, and PVB interlayer is a less important waste.

Current researchers and recycling companies are focused on the recycling of interlayer PVB of laminated glass, mainly from the automotive sector [14-17]. To the best of our knowledge, so far, only two manufacturers offer 100% recycled PVB films or powder [18,19]. The interlayers are manufactured from collected postindustrial PVB trimmings. By carefully sorting and reprocessing PVB trimmings generated during the production of laminated glass, the Butacite ® G sheeting is a clean, reliable raw material for use with new safety glass laminates.

Miloš Mat ú š et al., in publication [15] and patent [20], proposed an economically efficient process. The decomposition of laminated glass is based on the principle of retaining the integrity of the PVB film and is carried out on the process line made up of modules: the breaking module in which the glass is broken in both transverse and longitudinal directions, the vibration module in which a broken but compact car windshield can be shaken, and the stripper module in which mechanical cleaning of the PVB film is carried out. At the end of the process line, an additional washing module can be used. This is a typical approach where the PVB is mechanically separated from glass, and the final product is film or flakes of PVB. It is probably the best solution to recycle PVB, but this would not remove the impurities embedded in it, such as resistance wire, which is used to heat the windshield. Another module in a process line should be added, where the PVB can be dissolved and the solid contaminants filtered out.

The PVB polymer chain has both hydrophobic groups (butyral or acetyl group) and hydrophilic groups (hydroxyl residues). This composition allows the PVB to dissolve in polar and a mixture of polar and nonpolar organic solvents. PVB should be soluble or partially soluble in the following solvents: acetic acid, acetone, methanol, ethanol, 2-propanol, butanol, 2-butoxyethanol, cyclohexanone, benzyl alcohol, 1-methoxy-propanol-2, butyl glycol, n-butyl acetate, ethyl acetate, N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), N,N-dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and tetrahydrofurane (THF), but solubility is strongly dependent on the average molecular mass, composition and the vinyl acetate content [21]. In the literature, various solvents or a mixture of binary solvents to dissolve the PVB were used. Daniela Lubasova and Lenka Martinova dissolved PVB in different types and quantities of solvents and their mixtures (methanol, ethanol, THF, DMSO) [22]. Wenwen Luan et al. measured the intrinsic viscosities of PVB in ethanol/water solutions in the temperature range of 293.15-313.15 K [23]. Ryoichi Furushima et al. used a mixed organic solvent consisting of xylene and 2-propanol [24]. However, some of these solvents are not environmentally friendly; for example, THF, NMP, and xylenes are toxic, as is methanol. In the literature, the dissolution time in the proposed solvents, the effect of temperature on dissolution, and physicochemical parameters: density, dynamic viscosity, and refractive index of the PVB solutions are not presented.

In this work, the PVB polymer into the pure solvent, 2-propanol, and binary solvent mixture {{2-propanol + ethyl acetate, V / V = 1/1} were dissolved. In the solubility measurements, two sizes of polymer flakes: 30.0 × 30.0 × 0.82 mm and 10.0 × 10.0 × 0.82 mm, were assumed. Similarly, sized polymer flakes are obtained in the processes of mechanical shredding of car windshields and laminated glass. As part of the experimental work, measurements and optimization of the dissolution time of PVB were performed. From the point of view of the practical application of PVB solutions, measurements of density and dynamic viscosity as a function of PVB concentration and temperature were performed.

The prepared PVB-based solutions can be used as impregnates, varnishes, and glue for glass, metal, wood, paper, leather, cloth, and other materials. The reuse of PVB, which is currently landfilled, is of environmental importance. It allows for the management of waste material, the storage of which currently has to be paid for. The costs for the preparation of solutions are as follows: solvent, IPA, and ethyl acetate amounting to 1300 /t [25], the energy of purifying PVB from the glass, and the costs of the dissolution process: heating the solvent, stirring, or ultrasound.

text:
The Fourier transform-infrared spectrum analyses of the polymer were carried out using Nicolet iS5, a Thermo Scientific Mid Infrared FT -IR spectrometer equipped with iD7 ATR Optical Base. After washing the ATR crystal with ethanol, the samples of PVB were directly placed on the surface of the ATR. The wavenumber ranged from 3900 to 400 cm -1 . The solution of PVB was characterized by UV -VIS spectroscopy using Genesys 180, Thermo Scientific ranging from 190 to 1100 nm.

Differential Scanning Calorimetry

Glass transition temperature ( Tg ) and heat capacity change at the glass transition temperature ( D Cp ( g )) have been determined using differential scanning calorimetry, DSC technique. The experiments were performed with DSC 1 STARe System (Mettler Toledo) calorimeter equipped with a liquid nitrogen cooling system and operating in a heat-flux mode. The sample cell was constantly fluxed with high purity nitrogen at a constant flow rate of 20 mL · min -1 . The apparatus was calibrated with the 99.9999 mol% purity indium sample and with high purity ethylbenzene, n -octane, n -decane, n -octadecane, n -eicosane, cyclohexane, biphenyl, and water. The calibration experiment was carried out with a 5 K · min -1 heating rate in the temperature range from 180 to 450 K. The sample was sealed in hermetic aluminum pans. An empty pan was used as a reference. Measurements were taken three times, each time for a new PVB sample. The average sample mass was 9.9 mg throughout this study. The experiments were performed at a heating rate of 5 K · min -1 . Measurements were performed and ranged from 240 to 360 K.

Solubility of PVB

For the measurement of PVB solubility, polymer samples with dimensions of 30.0 ( ± 0.1) × 30.0 ( ± 0.1) mm or 10.0 ( ± 0.1) × 10.0 ( ± 0.1) mm and a thickness of 0.82 ( ± 0.02) mm were prepared. Each of the samples was weighed on AB204-S, Mettler Toledo analytical balance with an uncertainty of 1 × 10 -4 g. 10, 15, and 30 mL of pure 2-propanol or binary solvent mixtures {2-propanol + ethyl acetate, V / V = 1/1} were used to dissolve PVB. Knowing the PVB mass, volume, and density of the solvent, the final solution concentration could be calculated. PVB dissolution processes were prepared in a jacketed and thermostatted glass vessel with a volume of 50 mL. The jackets were connected to the thermostatic water bath, Julabo CORIO CD-BC6, to maintain a constant temperature with an accuracy of T = 0.05 K. The heterogeneous mixtures of dissolving PVB and solvent were vigorously stirred with a coated magnetic bar. Magnetic stirrer IKA RCT basic was used. The rotation speed of the stirrer was constant and equal to 500 rpm, which was enough to provide perfect contact between the PVB and the solvent. In the next part of the experiment, an ultrasonic bath, PROCLEAN 2.0M ECO with a capacity of 2 dm 3 , and ultrasound power of 60 W were used instead of a mechanical stirrer. Samples of the solution were taken at specified intervals using 1 mL syringes with a steel needle. The refractive index of the PVB solution was measured. The concentration of PVB was determined using the calibration curve of the refractive index. Solubility measurements were performed in the range from 0 to 20% wt PVB. Above this range, the polymer flakes do not dissolve, and a gel-like swollen layer on PVB is formed.

Density

The temperature-dependent density of liquid PVB solution was determined under ambient pressure using a vibrating tube densimeter-DMA 4500 M, Anton Paar. The densimeter has an automatic correction of the viscosity of the liquid sample. Doubly distilled and degassed water and dried air was used for calibration. Two integrated Pt 100 platinum thermometers allow for precision temperature control within 0.05 K. Density was measured with resolution 1 · 10 -5 g · cm -3 , but considering the impurities of the samples and solvents, the measurement uncertainty was estimated to be better than 5 · 10 -4 g · cm -3 . The density of PVB solutions was measured in the range from 0.7494 to 0.8542 g · cm -3 .

Dynamic viscosity

The dynamic viscosity of dissolved PVB was determined using an AMVn, Anton Paar rheometer based on the 'falling ball' principle. Before the experiment, a liquid standard provided by the supplier was used for the apparatus calibration. The temperature was controlled with a precision of 0.05 K. The relative standard uncertainty of the measured viscosity was estimated to be 5%. Over the measured viscosity range, capillaries of varying diameters were used depending on the viscosities of the fluid. The diameter of the capillary was 1.6 mm (ball diameter 1.5 mm) for viscosity in the range from 0.3 to 10 mPa · s, 1.8 mm (ball diameter 1.5 mm) for viscosity in the range from 2.5 to 70 mPa · s, and 3.0 mm (ball diameter 2.5 mm) for viscosity in the range from 20 to 230 mPa · s, and 4.0 mm (ball diameter 2.5 mm) for viscosity in the range from 200 to 2500 mPa · s. The dynamic viscosity of PVB solutions was measured in the range from 0.639 to 940 mPa · s.

Refractive index

The refractive index of the liquid PVB solution was determined by a precision Carl Zeiss Abbe Refractometer Type G with an accuracy of 5 · 10 -5 at T = 298.15 ± 0.05 K. A calibration curve was made for each mixture, and the accuracy of the composition determination was better than 0.05% wt PVB. The refractive index of PVB solutions was measured in the range from 1.37083 to 1.38521.

3. Data Modeling

The experimental data of PVB dissolution in a pure or binary mixture of solvents were fitted to a quadratic equation:

% wt = A 1 · t 2 + A 2 · t (1)

where % wt and t (h) are the PVB weight percent in a solvent and time, respectively. The adjustable parameters of the equation, A 1 and A 2, along with the average absolute relative deviation ( AARD ), are listed in Tables S8 and S9 in Supplementary Materials. The AARD is defined as:

AARD ( % wt ) = 1 n n i = 1 ∣ ∣ ∣ ∣ ∣ % wt exp -% wt cal % wt exp ∣ ∣ ∣ ∣ ∣ (2)

where % wt exp and % wt cal are the experimental and calculated values of PVB weight percent and n is the total number of data points.

The concentration and temperature dependence of density, d , and dynamic viscosity, h , for each system under study was described using the following equations [26]:

d / ( g · cm -3 ) = B 1 · % wt + B 2 (3)

where parameters B 1 and B 2 are linear functions of temperature:

B 1 = b 11 · T / K + b 12 (4)

B 2 = b 21 · T / K + b 22 (5)

where b 11 , b 12 , b 21 , and b 22 are regressed parameters.

h / ( mPa · s ) = exp ( C 1 + C 2 T / K ) (6)

where parameters C 1 and C 2 are linear functions of concentration:

C 1 = c 11 · % wt + c 12 (7)

C 2 = c 21 · % wt + c 22 (8)

where c 11 , c 12 , c 21 and c 22 are calculated parameters. A simple linear equation has been successfully used to describe the refractive index:

nD = D 1 · % wt + D 2 (9)

The quality of the data fit was determined using the root mean square error ( RMSE ):

s ( X ) = √ √ √ √ N i = 1 ( X exp -X cal ) 2 N -k (10)

where X exp and X cal are the experimental and calculated values of a density, dynamic viscosity, and refractive index. N and k are the total numbers of data points and parameters, respectively. The adjustable parameters with RMSE are presented in Tables S10-S12 in Supplementary Materials. The useful uses of the correlations are to provide an expression for interpolating the experimental information.

4. Results and Discussion

4.1. Analysis of PVB

The structure of PVB was confirmed by infrared spectroscopy. The FT -IR spectrum of PVB is presented in Figure 1. The PVB molecule contains a CH2 backbone and different functional groups, which all have their typical vibrations. The IR bands at 2957, 2935, and 2870 cm -1 were the valence vibrations of CH2-groups of the polymer backbone. Corresponding deformation modes appeared in 1458, 1434, and 1380 cm -1 . Free hydroxyl groups showed characteristic broadband between 3500 and 3200 cm -1 as well as the deformation mode at 1342 cm -1 . Adistinctive peak of the spectra appeared at 1731 cm -1 . This band and also the peak at 1240 cm -1 are caused by the carbonyl group of ester. The strong vibration between 1200 and 1000 cm -1 is derived from the acetal groups. This FT -IR spectrum is consistent with the literature spectra [9,27].

The DSC thermogram of the analyzed PVB is presented in Figure S2 in the Supplementary Materials. As reported in the literature, un -plasticized PVB had a glass transition temperature, T g, as measured by DSC and corrected for a thermal lag of 347 ± 2 K [28]. All commercial PVB used in glass lamination exhibited T g = 289 ± 2 K. The addition of 25% wt plasticizers, such as dibutyl sebacate and butyl phenyl phthalate, lowered the glass transition temperature. The PVB tested in this work showed the glass transition temperature, T g = 289.8 K, and the heat capacity change at glass transition, D Cp ( g } = 0.39 J · g -1 · K -1 . The T g is consistent with the PVB used in automotive windshields and reported in the literature [29].

In Figure 4, the effect of temperature on dissolution time was presented. Fixed parameters for the process were established: the stirrer speed of 500 rpm, an initial solvent volume equal to 10 mL, and polymer size 30.0 × 30.0 × 0.82 mm. It can be seen that as the temperature increases, the dissolution time decreases. At higher temperatures, solvent penetration into the polymer matrix is simplified. The mobility of the polymer segments in the solvent phase increases appreciably. PVB swells much more efficiently, and the chains disengage easily from the swollen surface. The increase in dissolution rate can be explained on a thermodynamics basis, as presented by M. T. Garc í a et al. for the polystyrene/organic solvent systems [33]. The dissolution of an amorphous polymer in a solvent is determined by the free energy of mixing:

D G m = D H m -T D S m (11)

where D Gm is the Gibbs free energy change on mixing, D Hm is the enthalpy change of mixing, T is the temperature, and D Sm is the entropy change of mixing. A negative value of D Gm means that the mixing process will occur spontaneously. According to the FloryHuggins theory that describes the thermodynamic equilibrium at constant pressure for polymer/solvent systems, the Gibbs free energy change of solution can be calculated as:

D G m / RT = ( f 1 / V 1ln f 1 + f 2 / V 2ln f 2 + c 12 f 1 f 2 ) (12)

where R is the ideal gas constant, f and V are the volume fraction and the molar volume of components in the mixture, respectively. c 12 is an empirical parameter expressing the interaction enthalpy between two different molecules. The first two terms on the right side of Equation (12) denote the entropy of mixing, which quantitatively is negative since, in solution, the molecules display a more chaotic arrangement than in the solid state [34]. The PVB polymer chain contains hydroxyl groups, which form hydrogen bonds with each other as well as with the hydroxyl group of the solvent, IPA. Hydrogen bonds break at higher temperatures, leading to lower solution viscosities. AcOEt does not form hydrogen bonds; thus, intermolecular interactions in the system with binary solvents are weaker, and the viscosity is lower. To describe the dynamic viscosity as a function of temperature, the Andrade-type equation was used; Equation (6). Furthermore, the dependence of the equation parameters on the PVB concentration has been applied (Equations (7) and (8)). Thus, for a given temperature and concentration of the PVB solution, determining the viscosity of the solution is possible and vice versa. The calculated parameters are shown with the RMSE in Table S11 in Supplementary Materials. A better agreement of calculated values compared to experimental data and a lower RMSE, σ = 2.5 mPa · s, was obtained for the system with pure IPA than for the system with binary solvent {IPA + AcOEt}; σ = 7.5 mPa · s.

The refractive index as a function of PVB concentration in IPA and binary solvent {IPA + AcOEt} are depicted in Figures 9c and 10c and further detailed in Table 4. The refractive index of pure PVB is 1.4850 [51] and is significantly higher than for an IPA, nD = 1.37522 or {IPA + AcOEt} system, nD = 1.37083. Therefore, a linear refractive index increase with increasing PVB concentration was observed in the measured range. The determined linear dependence of the refractive index can be successfully used as a correlation curve to determine the concentration of PVB polymer in the test solution.

Figure 11 exhibits the UV-VIS absorption spectra of 10% wt PVB solution in IPA and {IPA + AcOEt, V / V = 1/1} at room temperature. Both spectra are similar, showing full transmittance of radiation in the visible range and absorption of UV radiation. The obtained spectrum is comparable to the ones PVB/ethanol solution presented in the literature [52]. The absorption bands observed in the UV range are a result of the hydroxyl groups present in the polymer chain. The n to π * electron transitions are characteristic of the lone pair of oxygen electrons of the OH group or the cyclic acetyl electrons C=O and C-O-C present in the polymer chain; all functional groups involved in intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonding [53]. From an application point of view, the PVB solution can be used as a clear varnish, which will form a transparent film once the solvent has evaporated. Moreover, the PVB protective coating provides a barrier to UV rays, which is a major advantage. 16  of  19

5. Conclusions The present study investigated the effects of temperature, polymer size, and solvent volume on the dissolution time of polyvinyl butyral used in laminated glass. The following solvents were used: 2-propanol and a binary mixture of 2-propanol and ethyl acetate. PVB dissolves much faster in binary solvents than in pure alcohol under the same conditions. Moreover, a positive effect on reducing dissolution time using ultrasound was observed. Experimental and calculated data of the density, dynamic viscosity, and refractive index of PVB liquid solutions as a function of concentration and temperature can be used to design a system of filtration. Complete removal of solid contaminants, especially heating wires and glass dust, will only be possible after polymer dissolution, filtration or decantation. The results obtained are of great importance in the design of a PVB recycling process line, as well as in the preparation of PVB polymer-based solutions that can be used as impregnates, varnishes, and structural adhesives for bonding glass, metal, wood, paper, leather, cloth, and other materials. In subsequent studies, other binary mixtures, e.g., alcohol with acetone, 2-butanone, butyl acetate, acetic acid, toluene, or xylene, should be the research aim. The appropriate solvents for the above-mentioned applications should be selected. Moreover, using these binary mixtures can reduce the dissolution time of the PVB and design the physicochemical parameters of the PVB solution: a lower dynamic viscosity with a higher polymer concentration and different evaporation rates, which is important, e.g., the adhesive cure time and impregnation.

1. Introduction

Advances in the food packaging industry have brought many environmental and societal benefits; for instance, packaging is essential for enabling long shelf-lives, which helps to mitigate food waste and fosters food accessibility (facilitates transport over long distances). 1 ML plastic films are an essential component of packaging applications. These films represent approximately 20% of food packaging in Europe, with projections showing an increase over the following years based on the current demand and trends ( e.g. , convenience products, single-serve meals, and small packaging). 2 ML films are built View Article Online View Journal | View Issue

Quantifying the environmental bene fi ts of a solvent-based separation process for multilayer plastic fi lms †
Aurora del Carmen Munguía-López, ‡ a Dilara Göreke, ‡ a Kevin L. Sánchez-Rivera, a Horacio A. Aguirre-Villegas, b Styliani Avraamidou, a George W. Huber a and Victor M. Zavala* a

Food packaging often appears in the form of multilayer (ML) plastic fi lms, which leverage the functional properties of di ff erent polymers to achieve speci fi c food protection goals ( e.g. , oxygen, water, and temperature barriers). These properties are essential to enable long shelf lives, reduce refrigeration usage, mitigate food waste, and increase food accessibility. However, ML fi lm production processes generate large amounts of plastic waste that cannot be mechanically recycled. Recently, we have proposed a process, called solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP), that enables the separation and recycling of the constituent polymers of ML fi lms. This technology uses a series of solvent washes that selectively dissolve and precipitate target polymers. Quantifying the environmental bene fi ts of STRAP over virgin resin production is essential for the commercial deployment of this technology. This work uses life cycle assessment (LCA) methods to evaluate these impacts in terms of carbon footprint, energy use, water use, and toxicity. We analyze three STRAP process variants that use antisolvent and temperature-driven precipitation to treat di ff erent ML fi lms. Our analysis reveals that the STRAP-A and STRAP-B process variants can provide environmental bene fi ts over virgin fi lm production. Furthermore, it gives valuable insight into the critical components of ML fi lms (speci fi c polymers) and of the STRAP processes (equipment) that are responsible for the highest impacts. Ultimately, we believe that the proposed analysis framework can lead to the design of more environmentally-friendly ML fi lms and recycling processes.

using several layers of di ff erent polymers 3 that are combined to achieve unique properties ( e.g. , oxygen, water, and temperature barriers) and help preserve food products and reduce energy use. 4 Moreover, ML films help reduce packaging costs, as they reduce the amount of plastic material needed to attain these properties (compared to single layer packaging materials). 5 Films with up to 17 layers of di ff erent polymers can be found in some applications 6,7 and more specialized applications might require hundreds of layers. 8

The production of ML films generates large amounts of waste known as post-industrial waste (PIW), which is the result of manufacturing ine ffi ciencies that are di ffi cult to avoid. It is estimated that up to 20% of all ML films produced are discarded as PIW. 9 Compared to post-consumer waste (PCW), PIW has the advantage that is relatively clean, because it is not contaminated with food or other impurities. 10 Unfortunately, PIW of ML films is not currently recycled 11 due to a lack of commercially available technologies. Conventional technologies, such as mechanical recycling, cannot be used to recycle ML films; 12 -14 therefore, ML films end up in landfills or combusted. 15 -17 The improper management of ML films can also lead to plastic leakage into the natural environment, with plastic entering the waterways and consequently, the food chain. 18,19

Solvent-based separation has been recently proposed as a paradigm that enables the recovery of polymers from ML films. A specific process, known as solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP), 9 uses sequential solvent washes to separate the constituent polymers. The design of these processes has been facilitated via the use of molecular simulations, which enable the identification of selective solvents for targeted polymer layers. Previous work has reported di ff erent configurations for the process, called STRAP-A, STRAP-B, and STRAP-C. 20 STRAP-A precipitates dissolved polymers via the addition of antisolvents and requires subsequent separation of solvent and antisolvents via distillation (which can be energy intensive). STRAP-B aims to reduce or eliminate the use of antisolvents via using temperature-driven polymer precipitation. Both approaches have been shown to deconstruct an industrial ML film composed of PE, EVOH, and PET (film A1). STRAP-C is a process that combines the two precipitation techniques (antisolvent addition and solvent temperature reduction) and has been designed to separate a more complex ML film (film A2), composed of PE, EVOH, PET, and PETG.

The economic viability of the STRAP processes has been previously studied using detailed techno-economic analysis (TEA). 20 This work has found that the minimum selling price of the resins recovered via STRAP is comparable to the average market values of virgin resins. The analysis has also found that the economic benefits increase when precipitation can be achieved via temperature-driven approaches ( e.g. , STRAP-B and STRAP-C); this is due to the avoidance of distillation, which is expensive from a capital and operation standpoint. Other applications of solvent-based polymer recycling processes, including solid mixtures and electronic waste, have shown economic and environmental benefits when compared to virgin plastics. 21 However, the environmental impact of the STRAP process has not been reported in the literature; this is essential to foster the adoption of this technology and to identify more environmentally-friendly designs of processes ( e.g. , solvent selection) and of ML films ( e.g. , polymer layer selection), as well as to understand the interplay between ML film design and recycling.

Life cycle assessment (LCA) is an established methodology used for quantifying the environmental impacts of consumer products and associated production processes. 22 One of the main objectives of LCA is to provide information to industries, policy-makers, and society regarding the environmental impacts and feasibility of emerging processes and technologies. Regarding plastic waste, multiple LCA studies have compared di ff erent recycling alternatives such as pyrolysis, mechanical recycling, and energy recovery. 23,24 Jeswani et al. 23 found that pyrolysis and mechanical recycling have a lower contribution to climate change than producing energy products from waste plastics. However, the energy recovery alternative performs better for other impact categories ( e.g. , acidification, eutrophication, photochemical ozone formation,

|

and human toxicity). An innovative scheme to treat plastics from the waste of electrical and electronic equipment has been studied from an LCA perspective. The environmental benefits of this process were reported under ' ideal ' and ' real ' scenarios. 25 These studies leverage the LCA methodology to analyze the environmental feasibility of new waste management and production processes. The LCA methodology has also been used as a metric to evaluate the environmental sustainability of some circular economy strategies, including narrowing, slowing, and closing resource flows. 26 The goals of a circular economy involve the reduction of waste, use of natural resources, and emission levels. Other key characteristics of circularity are increasing the share of renewable resources by limiting the use of virgin materials and increasing the durability of products through high-quality recycling. 27

In this work, we conduct a detailed LCA study of STRAP processes; our goal is to identify if recycling ML films via STRAP can bring benefits over virgin resin products (thus enabling more circular economies). To do so, we evaluate diverse environmental impacts (carbon footprint, energy use, water use, and toxicity) of STRAP and compare them to those of virgin resin production. We analyze STRAP-A, -B, and -C process variants in order to identify the specific components of the STRAP process and of the ML films that are responsible for the highest impacts.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the methodology, which includes key assumptions of the study, the description of the STRAP process, as well as details about the LCA approach. Section 3 presents the findings for the di ff erent STRAP processes and impact categories. The final section presents conclusions and final remarks of the study.

2. Methodology

The principles of the LCA methodology used in this study are in compliance with the ISO-14040 and 14044-LCA series of standards. 28,29

2.1. Scope of the study

This LCA study aims to quantify the environmental benefits (climate change, energy use, water use, and process toxicity) of the STRAP technology and of the production of ML plastic film from virgin resins. This comparison is essential for assessing the environmental feasibility of the STRAP process and identifying key bottlenecks. The study evaluates the impacts of a potential commercial plant of 3000 tonnes per year, which has been found to be economically viable (the minimum selling price of the recovered resins is comparable to their market values). We consider the inputs and outputs for three di ff erent STRAP processes (STRAP-A, STRAP-B, and STRAP-C) presented in Sánchez-Rivera et al. ; 20 we refer the reader to this study for a detailed description of the process.

The LCA study is performed by taking a product perspective; 23 from this perspective, the STRAP process is seen as an alternative process that produces virgin-grade polymers (raw materials of ML films). Therefore, we compare the environmental impacts of producing ML films from virgin resins (from fossil sources) against producing ML films using STRAP (which avoids using fossil sources). We disaggregate the total impacts into contributions of each polymer layer ( e.g. , PET, PE, EVOH, PETG), which provides important insight that can enable more sustainable packaging design. Furthermore, we disaggregate the impacts into di ff erent components of the STRAP processes, which provides insight that can enable more sustainable process designs.

2.2. System boundaries

The system boundaries for the material production from virgin resins (from fossil sources) and of STRAP (from ML film PIW) are presented in Fig. 1. Following a product perspective, we treat STRAP as another method to produce ML films of virginresin quality. 20,23 In the virgin resins alternative, the system boundaries include the extraction and transportation of raw materials (fossil sources), material processing (production of monomers, polymerization, and ML film extrusion), and consumption of process utilities (energy and water inputs). Any additives such as fillers (fibers), reinforcements, colorants ( pigments), or functional additives (stabilizers, flame retardants, lubricants, foaming agents, flame retardants) 30 are not considered within the scope of the system boundaries. In the STRAP alternative, the ML film PIW is treated through the recycling technology to isolate the constituent polymer layers. The resins are then extruded to produce an equivalent amount of ML film. Thus, the STRAP system boundaries include the collection and transportation of ML film waste (considering a distance of 1000 km), the material inputs (solvents and utilities), the transportation of the process solvents, and the ML film extrusion to produce the new film from recovered polymers. The film treated in the STRAP process is assumed to be clean PIW; therefore, product use, and treatment (such as screening, sorting, grinding, and cleaning) are not within the scope of the system boundaries. The ability to use PIW is a key benefit compared to PCW.

2.3. Functional unit

LCA studies can be conducted for systems composed of multiple processes. Defining a functional unit is essential to provide a fair comparison basis, allowing relevant quantitative evaluation and comparison between di ff erent strategies serving the same function. 31 This study defines the functional unit as the production of 1 kg of ML film; therefore, we compare the environmental impacts of producing 1 kg of film from virgin resins with producing 1 kg of film from the recovered resins through the STRAP processes.

2.4. STRAP process description

The STRAP technology aims to recover the polymer components of post-industrial waste of ML films. 9,20 Particularly, it has been used for a couple of ML films manufactured by the company Amcor (films A1 and A2). The main building polymers of film A1 are PE, PET, EVOH, and ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA). Film A2 is a more complex film composed of PE, PET, EVOH, and PETG. Three di ff erent STRAP processes were previously designed based on the type of film and on the use of di ff erent precipitation strategies: precipitation by antisolvent addition or solvent temperature reduction (to 35 °C).

The first variation of the STRAP approach, STRAP-A, was developed for recovering PE (with minor EVA component), PET, and EVOH from ML film A1, following the solvent/antisolvent strategy. In this method, the target polymer is selectively dissolved in a solvent, while the remaining polymers are left insoluble. Then, the polymer -solvent solution is separated from the residual polymers, and an antisolvent is added to precipitate and isolate the targeted polymer.

The STRAP-B process was developed for the same ML film A1. In this process, all the constituent polymers were separated (PE, PET, and EVOH). Additionally, the EVA component from the PE resin was isolated. Regarding the precipitation strategy, instead of adding an antisolvent, the temperature of the polymer -solvent solution (95 -110 °C) is lowered to the point that the target polymer becomes insoluble (35 °C). It is worth highlighting that this temperature reduction is done using cooling water. After this, the polymer is precipitated and isolated. The process flow diagrams and a detailed explanation of these processes are reported in the ESI. †

The process flow diagram of the STRAP-C approach is presented in Fig. 2. This approach is used to recover a more complex material, ML film A2, which consists of PE, PET, EVOH, EVA, and PETG. The process combines a couple of solvent precipitation techniques (antisolvent addition and solvent temperature reduction), as we describe next.

Fig. 1 System boundaries for the LCA study. (a) Multilayer fi lm production from virgin resins (from fossil sources). (b) Multilayer fi lm production via STRAP technology (from ML fi lm PIW).

Fig. 2 STRAP-C process for recycling ML fi lm A2 composed of PE (4 wt%), EVOH (2.2 wt%), PET (71.8 wt%), EVA (1 wt%), and PETG (21 wt%).

PETG is the first component to be separated, using a 60% DMF/40% THF (v/v) solution (4 hours, 87 °C), which only solubilizes the targeted resin while leaving the other polymers in the solid phase. These polymers are separated from the solution by mechanical filtration. Then, 1-propanol is added as an antisolvent to facilitate the precipitation of the PETG in the solution. The PETG is then filtered and dried. After this, this recovered polymer is sent to the extruder, and, finally, it is sent to the storage tank in pellet form. The DMF/THF/1-propanol mixture is recycled back into the process after a series of distillation operations. The remaining polymer constituents in the film are recovered following the same steps as STRAP-B. PE and EVA components are selectively dissolved in toluene (4 hours, 110 °C) and separated from EVOH and PET via mechanical filtration. The temperature of the toluene mixture, containing the dissolved polymers PE and EVA, is reduced from 110 °C to 35 °C to enable PE precipitation while the remaining EVA component is recovered by adding acetone which acts as an antisolvent. After filtration and drying, both polymers are sent to the extruder and then to the storage tank. The acetone/toluene mixture is separated by distillation and then recycled back into the process. For the EVOH and PET layers, EVOH is selectively dissolved in a 60% DMSO/40% water (v/v) solution (30 min, 95 °C) and then cooled down to 35 °C to achieve precipitation. The precipitated EVOH is stored following its filtration, drying, and extrusion processes while the solvent mixture is directly recycled back into the process. After the EVOH separation, the remaining PET component in the dissolution vessel is extruded and stored after filtration and drying. Finally, after the polymers are recovered in pellet form, they are sent to the film extruder to produce virgin-grade ML film. Since the STRAP process recovers the polymers in pellet form, they can be used in several applications. However, in this study, we consider the STRAP process as an alternative method to produce ML films (product perspective); therefore, the film extrusion step needs to be included in the analysis.
