The factors to estimate the environmental impacts of the processes are obtained from the Ecoinvent and the Environmental Footprint databases. The Ecoinvent 3.6 cut-o ff by classification database 32 is used for the solvent impacts since it has all the necessary factors for the solvents utilized in STRAP processes. Similarly, the impacts related to the production of polymers are modeled based on the Environmental Footprint database. 33 The software openLCA v1.10.3 34 is used to perform the LCA calculations with the Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0) 35 impact assessment method, providing fair evaluation and comparison for all products within the system boundaries. We observed high regional sensitivity (U.S. and Europe) for some impact categories regarding energy obtained from natural gas (see ESI † for more details). Because of this and the lack of data availability, we present our case study based on European data (materials production, energy carriers, and transportation), which we found to be consistent.

2.5.1. Impact categories

The impact categories considered in this study are climate change (kg CO2 eq.), energy use (MJ), water use (m 3 ), freshwater ecotoxicity (CTUe), and human toxicity (cancer/noncancer, CTUh). Climate change impact is an indicator of the global warming potential of the di ff erent greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of a system and takes into account gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O). Energy use or energy demand are indicators of fossil fuel depletion and are thus key factors for assessing emissions related to fossil-based energy consumption. Water use is a measure of water consumption of the processes weighted by regional water scarcity (depending on the case study). This factor assesses the potential of water deprivation and pollution based on freshwater use and water quality loss at a spatial scale, accounting for water-stressed regions. Process water inputs are multiplied by location-specific waterstress indicators, ranging from 0.1 to 100, to assign higher impacts for water-stressed regions. 36,37 Regarding toxicity impact factors, we consider freshwater ecotoxicity, a measure of impact on freshwater organisms exposed to toxic chemicals released into the aqueous environment, this measure is expressed as a comparative toxicology unit (CTUe). Also, we consider the human toxicity (cancer/non-cancer), estimated as the increase in human population disease rates based on a unit mass emission of chemicals, this category is expressed as a comparative toxicology unit (CTUh). 38

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Climate change impacts: product perspective

This section compares the climate change impacts of producing an ML film via the STRAP process against ML film production from virgin resins by process utilities. The impacts are expressed per functional unit: the production of 1 kg of an ML film. The STRAP-A and STRAP-B processes are used to treat the ML film A1. Thus, we compare their impacts with the CO2 eq. emissions related to the production of the same film from virgin resins. Also, we compare the climate change impact of STRAP-C and the CO2 eq. emissions related to the production of film A2. We present the climate change impact of each method in Fig. 3. The impacts related to the production, transportation, and extrusion of producing the virgin ML film are also shown in Fig. 3. For the STRAP processes, we present the impacts related to the process utilities (steam, electricity, and cooling water), solvents (including their transportation), extrusion of the film, and collection and transportation of ML film waste.

Fig. 3 Impact on climate change of the production of 1 kg of A1 and A2 ML fi lms through STRAP technology and through the production of virgin material (from virgin resins).

We can see that the STRAP-B and STRAP-C processes generate less CO2 eq. emissions per kg of film than the virgin production of films A1 and A2. However, the STRAP-A process has a higher climate change impact, mainly due to the CO2 eq. emissions associated with the required amount of steam used.

This occurs because the precipitation method used in this approach (antisolvent addition) has high steam requirements (due to the use of distillation units). On the other hand, STRAP-B generates 54% fewer emissions than producing film A1 from virgin resins. These avoided impacts highlight the environmental benefits of the STRAP approach and the feasibility of using this process as an alternative for producing virgin-grade ML films. Since both STRAP-A and STRAP-B are used for the ML film A1, we observe that the STRAP-B process is more promising to replace the production of this film from virgin resins.

Regarding climate change impacts of producing the ML film A2, we can see that the STRAP-C process had a lower GHG emission (by 18%) than the material virgin production. These environmental benefits show that STRAP-C is a suitable alternative to produce the ML film A2 instead of producing it from virgin resins.

3.1.1. Climate change impact and energy use per layer. STRAP-A impact and energy use by each constituent polymer of film A1 are presented in Fig. 4. The impacts are estimated based on the process inputs and utilities required to separate the corresponding polymer layer and produce (film extrusion) the ML film A1 via the STRAP-A process. We also compare these impacts to the ones related to the material processing to produce the di ff erent polymers required for the ML film A1 using virgin manufacturing. Fig. 4(b) shows the energy requirement comparison of the STRAP-A process (outer circle) with virgin film production (inner circle).

As expected, the climate change impacts have the same trend as the energy requirement of the process. For instance, although the EVOH only consists of 3.6 wt% of the film, the EVOH separation step in the STRAP-A approach is the main contributor to energy use and climate change, requiring 76 MJ of energy input with a climate change impact of 5.15 kg CO2 eq. per kg of film A1. We can see that EVOH production demands less energy in the virgin film production approach. It only requires 6 MJ with a climate change impact of 0.27 kg CO2 eq. The PE and EVOH separation steps require less energy than virgin film production and have a minor climate change impact. Overall, the STRAP-B process has 57% less climate change impact and 73.2% less energy demand than virgin film production. 3.1.2. Climate change impact per processing step. We also evaluated the climate change impacts associated with each piece of equipment of the STRAP process, in order to identify areas for improvement. The energy requirement is not discussed since the trends of this factor are the same as the climate change impact (as shown in the previous section). Fig. 8 shows the GHG emissions of each piece of equipment in the STRAP-A approach. Here, the total impact of isolating each polymer and the impact related to the extrusion of the polymers to produce the recycled film (film extrusion) are presented. The sum of these two impacts (considering the film composition) results in the total impact per polymer.

Regarding the climate change impact per equipment, we can see that the distillation column, extruders, solvent tanks, and dryers have the highest impacts. The impacts from solvent inputs are related to the production of the fresh solvents fed to the process and estimated by considering the individual solvent impacts multiplied by the make-up solvent used. We can see that these impacts are moderate due to the high solvent recycling rates in the process (around 99.9%). The distillation columns are required to separate the toluene and acetone, as well as for the DMSO and water separation. A higher climate change impact from the destillation columns (10 times higher than the next in line, the extruder) is a result of a higher energy requirement. The high utility demands of the distillation columns make STRAP-A generate a higher amount of GHG than the virgin production method. The high energy demand of distillation columns might be due to factors such as the properties of the solvent/antisolvent solution to be separated and the distillation column inlet conditions (flow rate, temperature, pressure, etc .), as well as the high solvent recycling rate criteria set (99.88%) at the process design stage of STRAP. 20 In this regard, improvements in the energy demand of the distillation unit could be achieved by selecting solvents with a low boiling point or reducing the amount of antisolvent used. 40

Similarly, the climate change impact of each piece of equipment for the STRAP-B approach is presented in Fig. 9. In this process, most of the precipitation of the polymers is done by lowering the solvent temperature, which results in considerably fewer GHG emissions for the STRAP-B equipment.

However, the solvent/antisolvent precipitation strategy is also used to recover the minor component EVA. Here, a distillation column is required, which represents the highest climate change impact of the process. This result suggests that identifying solvents that allow the precipitation of EVA by temperature reduction or recovering PE and EVA together can be more environmentally benign. The other pieces of equipment that have high environmental impacts are the extruders and dryers.

3.2. Water use: product perspective

For the water use analysis, we factor in the direct and indirect water consumption of the processes. We consider the direct water consumption related to cooling water and to the use of water as a solvent. Also, we consider the indirect water consumption associated with the use of water for the extraction of raw materials, production of solvents, and the generation of process utilities ( e.g. , electricity and steam).

The water use results show that the STRAP-B and STRAP-C approaches require less water than virgin film production (Fig. 10). Manufacturing virgin film A1 results in water usage of 0.70 m 3 kg -1 film A1. Of this amount, 90.2% is required for PET production, followed by 7.0% for EVOH production, 1.5% for EVA production, and 1.3% for PE production. Alternatively, recovering the constituent resins of film A1 via the STRAP-A process increases water usage due to the high cooling water requirements by the distillation units. On the other hand, STRAP-B requires 74.5% less water than STRAP-A and 45.7% less water than the virgin production method. For STRAP-C, the water usage is estimated as 0.58 m 3 kg -1 of film A2, performing 29.3% better than the virgin film A2 production (0.82 m 3 kg -1 of film A2). In all STRAP processes, the main source of water usage is the cooling water (mainly used in distillation operations) followed by water used in heat exchangers. 3.3. Toxicity impacts: product perspective

We now present the environmental impacts related to the toxicity of virgin film production and the STRAP technology evaluating their freshwater ecotoxicity and human toxicity (cancer/ non-cancer) impacts. The freshwater ecotoxicity is expressed as a comparative toxicology unit (CTUe) and is a measure of the impact on freshwater organisms exposed to toxic chemicals released into the aqueous environment. Human toxicity (cancer/non-cancer) is expressed as a comparative toxicology unit (CTUh) as well and is estimated as the increase in human population disease rates based on a unit mass emission of chemicals.

Fig. 11(a) shows the freshwater ecotoxicity expressed in the comparative toxicology unit CTUe per kg of film (A1 and A2). For the virgin films, the ecotoxicity values are estimated based on the impacts of the individual polymer production, their transportation, and extrusion. The freshwater ecotoxicity of the STRAP processes is estimated by considering the utility inputs (steam, electricity, and cooling water) and raw materials (solvents) used in the process, as well as the extrusion to make the new ML film and transportation of ML film waste. The results reveal that the STRAP-A and STRAP-B approaches are 63% and 89% less toxic than the virgin film A1 production. Similarly, STRAP-C is 86% less toxic than virgin film A2 production, suggesting that the STRAP technology is an environmentally safer alternative than virgin ML film production. In the STRAP process, steam is the main source of process ecotoxicity followed by cooling water. We performed a sensitivity analysis for the regional data variability on the toxicity values (see ESI † ). This analysis reveals that the production method and fuel type used to generate the utilities can a ff ect the process ecotoxicity values. Thus, the ecotoxicity impact can improve by switching to less toxic fuel sources for utility production. Similarly, process ecotoxicity can be reduced by using less toxic solvents. Solvent production impacts reveal that the STRAP-A and STRAP-C have the highest impacts due to the precipitation strategy.

The human toxicity impacts are presented as cancer and non-cancer (see Fig. 11(b) and (c)) and they are expressed using the comparative toxicology unit CTUh. We find that human toxicity results have the same trends as the ecotoxicity impacts. Therefore, the STRAP processes are considerably less toxic to humans than the corresponding film production from fossil-based virgin resins. Human toxicity analysis shows that, on average, STRAP-A is 44% and STRAP-B is 85% less toxic than virgin film A1 production, whereas STRAP-C is 78% less toxic compared to virgin film A2 production. Cancer-related human toxicity impacts show that the main source of toxicity for the STRAP approach is the process utilities (cooling water and steam). The significant contribution of cooling water to human toxicity (cancer) is due to the toxicity impact related to Chromium VI. We can see higher toxicity in STRAP-A and STRAP-C processes because of their higher steam and cooling water requirements. Also, we find that these approaches have higher solvent-related toxicity than STRAP-B. This behavior occurs due to the precipitation technique and the solvents used (mainly DMF and THF).

3.4. Sensitivity analysis on process fuel sources

We conducted a sensitivity analysis for the climate change impact of the process utilities by changing the energy source for producing steam and electricity. For this analysis, we assume that process energy can come from only one type of energy source. We evaluate di ff erent fossil and non-fossil energy sources. The potential of using various non-fossil energy sources to produce steam and electricity has been studied. For instance, Saygin et al. 41 reported that the production of steam from biomass can be cost-e ff ective and lead to a significant reduction of emissions. Furthermore, the economic and environmental advantages of meeting energy demands via the deployment of large-scale concentrating solar power systems have been widely studied. 42 -44 Similarly, the wind energy development for suitable regions has grown in the last years due to its low costs and emissions. 45,46 Using nuclear energy and hydropower can also lead to low climate change impacts and are economically feasible alternatives. 47 -49 Therefore, we compare the impacts of the di ff erent energy sources with our base case scenario, which considers European data (due to data availability). For steam, the base case mix includes 75% natural gas, 12.5% hard coal, and 12.5% biomass. Fig. 12 shows the impacts of changing the energy source to produce steam using only biomass, natural gas, or coal.

As mentioned in the previous sections, STRAP-A has the highest steam requirements due to the use of distillation units. Therefore, when we change the energy source for steam production, the STRAP-A approach achieves the highest environmental benefits. 4. Conclusions and future work

This study presented an LCA methodology using a product perspective for assessing the environmental impacts of the STRAP technology. Previous work has shown that the STRAP technology is economically feasible for recovering the constituent polymers of ML film with nearly 100% material e ffi ciency. In this approach, we evaluated the environmental benefits of producing two ML plastic films A1 and A2 (manufactured by Amcor) via the STRAP process. We compared the climate change, energy use, water usage, and toxicity (ecotoxicity and human toxicity) impacts of producing 1 kg of ML film via virgin resin production or the STRAP approach. We presented the impact of recovering each layer or polymer ( e.g. , PET, PE, EVOH) to provide information for a more sustainable packaging design. Furthermore, we estimated the climate change impacts related to each piece of equipment of the STRAP process to identify areas for improvement.

For the ML film A1 (composed of resins PE, EVOH, EVA, and PET), we found that the STRAP-B process performs better than STRAP-A in all the impact factors due to the precipitation method (temperature reduction). Furthermore, the STRAP-B approach provides environmental benefits over virgin film production. Producing ML film via the STRAP-B technology requires 73% less energy and generates 57% fewer GHG emissions. We found that the polymer with the highest impact and lowest composition is EVA which suggests that this polymer should be recovered along with the PE since this is a widely used copolymer blend. The equipment with the highest impact was the distillation columns due to the energy requirements. Similarly, we found environmental benefits for the STRAP-C process over virgin resin production (film A2). This STRAP approach uses 52% less energy and generates 23% fewer CO2 eq. emissions. Here, PETG is the polymer with the highest impact followed by the impact of the minor component EVA. We found that these impacts are related to the polymer precipitation strategy (antisolvent addition). Therefore, we conclude that temperature-driven precipitation is essential to achieve high environmental benefits.

For the STRAP-B modified process, we illustrated how, by separating two layers together (PE and EVA), the climate change impact can be decreased significantly due to the high energy requirements to separate EVA. For future work, we are interested in developing an optimization framework to identify the optimal process design including which layers to separate. We aim to identify optimal processes for di ff erent types of ML films and provide insights for sustainable packaging. Additionally, we are interested in comparing the STRAP processes with other end-of-life disposal methods, such as incineration, and landfilling.

In this work, we presented the environmental benefits of using the STRAP process to recycle PIW. Therefore, the environmental burdens of waste sorting and cleaning were not considered. For future work, we are interested in studying the environmental benefits of using solvent-based processes to recycle PCW and evaluating the impacts of sorting and cleaning.

ABSTRACT: This study compares two types of methods used for the valorization of multilayer films, namely, mechanical recycling (MR) through thermomechanical reprocessing and the selective dissolution -precipitation (SDP) method, which lead to products of different nature. Both approaches were evaluated on a five-layer coextruded film composed of polypropylene (PP) (88 wt %) used as the outer layer, maleic anhydride-grafted polypropylene (PPg -MA) (5 wt %) serving as the tie layer, and ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) (7 wt %) used as the barrier layer. The comparison of the two processes was primarily based on their applicability. However, two additional criteria, namely, environmental impact and economic aspects, were also briefly addressed based on literature data. MR consisted of thermomechanical reprocessing applied over

five cycles to the multilayer film by using a twin-screw extruder. The results show that MR is a promising route up to the third recycling cycle; beyond this point, the rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate. This degradation is attributed to the competition between different reaction mechanisms, namely, PP β -scission, EVOH cross-linking, and the esterification reaction generated by the interaction between EVOH and PPg -MA. Nevertheless, according to the literature, the MR process presents a low environmental impact and a relatively affordable cost. In contrast, the SDP process consisted of a layer separation system based on the use of a solvent system. Although the SDP process successfully separated PP from EVOH, the thermal and rheological properties of the recovered materials were altered due to incomplete recovery or recovery of the interface/interphase material during dissolution, resulting from strong physicochemical interactions between the constituents (PPg -MA/EVOH), as well as the use of solvents at elevated temperatures. Compared with MR, the SDP method is more energy-intensive and has a higher environmental impact, notably because it requires solvents and antisolvents, involving additional distillation steps for their separation. It is also more expensive due to the cost of solvents and antisolvents, as well as the equipment required for layer separation. Finally, in terms of processing time, layer separation by dissolution requires approximately 60 h, compared with 6 h for thermomechanical reprocessing.

■ INTRODUCTION

Each year, more than 100 million tons of multilayer thermoplastics are produced worldwide. The production and accumulation of these multilayer packages increase annually due to consumers' growing reliance on packaged products, posing a significant recycling challenge. 1 To date, plastic packaging accounts for 44% of global plastic production. 2 From this production, 17% is dedicated to multilayer flexible polymer films (MFPFs), with food packaging being the primary application. 3 The configurations of multilayer food packaging generally consist of two outer layers of polyolefins, mainly polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE), and a central gas barrier layer, usually made of ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) or polyamide (PA). Tie layers are used to bond and create a solid structure. 3 MFPF is a material composed of multiple layers combined to form a single structure with synergistic properties, including mechanical, thermal, and gas and water barrier properties. Due to their lightweight nature, versatility, ease of processing, and printability, MFPFs are attracting increasing attention, and their demand continues to grow. 4 -8

In general, the heterogeneity of the layers forming multilayer films makes their recyclability particularly complex. As a result, multilayer films are often considered nonrecyclable. Postconsumer waste management options are generally limited to energy recovery or landfill disposal. 9 -11 According to a study conducted in Europe by Plastics Europe in 2022, 41% of

postconsumer plastic packaging waste was recycled, 35% was used for energy recovery, and 24% was landfilled. 2 Certain multilayer systems, such as LDPE-EVOH or PP-EVOH, can be recycled in municipal streams if the EVOH content is below 6% by weight. However, even in this case, the barrier material is not recovered due to the inherent difficulty of its extraction and reprocessing. 8,12

The proposed European PPWR regulation (2022), which aims to enhance the recyclability of packaging in Europe, sets out specific rules for multilayer packaging. It introduces strict recyclability criteria: a multilayer package containing less than 10% impurities may be exempt from certain recycling obligations for composite materials, provided that it is primarily composed of a single recyclable material. 13,14

With the increasing demand for MFPF, the growing amount of postconsumer multilayer films and manufacturing waste highlights the need to develop sustainable management and recycling strategies. 3

According to our previous work by Adam et al., 9 various methods have been employed to improve the recyclability of postconsumer and postindustrial multilayer films, generally classified into: physical recycling, including both mechanical recycling and solvent-based dissolution precipitation, and chemical recycling, including pyrolysis, gasification, and depolymerization.

Among these, mechanical recycling is considered the predominant approach due to its cost-effectiveness, industrial viability, low energy consumption, operational simplicity, and limited environmental impact. 9 However, this method generally leads to irreversible modifications of the physicochemical properties of the polymers present in these films. These alterations are attributed to high-temperature conditions, pressure, and shear forces, which cause polymer degradation by chain scission or polymer cross-linking. 15 -18 Furthermore, exposure of these recycled polymers to oxygen, moisture, and residual contaminants leads to thermo-oxidative degradation. 19 -21

Mechanical recycling remains limited, especially in closed loops, as it does not allow for the efficient separation of the different polymers that make up multilayer structures. As a result, a significant portion of these plastic wastes ends up in landfills or is incinerated, thereby contributing to environmental pollution. To address this issue, innovative strategies based on selective dissolution have been developed to decompose these materials into basic constituents and enable more efficient recycling.

́

A promising approach is the solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) strategy, developed by Walker et al. 22 This process relies on the use of specific solvents and cosolvents that selectively dissolve and precipitate each polymer present in multilayer structures. The application of this method to industrial waste has made it possible to recover PE, EVOH, and PET with high purities, thus ensuring their reuse. Moreover, a techno-economic assessment demonstrated that this process could be viable on an industrial scale, with a processing capacity of approximately 8000 tons per year. 22 Similarly, the Newcycling technology developed by APK, which uses a solvent-based process to separate and purify multilayer plastic films (PE and PA) in order to produce highquality recyclate reusable for packaging, also has a capacity of 8000 tons per year. 23,24 Sa nchez-Rivera et al. 25 further refined this approach by applying it to printed plastic films containing polyurethane (PU)-based inks. These inks present an additional challenge, as they must be removed without altering the properties of the recovered polymers. The study showed that the use of gamma-valerolactone (GVL), a bioderived solvent, effectively removed the inks while preserving the quality of the recycled PET. By adjusting the STRAP process parameters, particularly the film particle size (1 -3 mm), the researchers were able to reduce processing time and improve the overall efficiency of the process.

In the case of multilayer structures based on polyolefins and EVOH, several studies 3,26,27 emphasize the need to separate EVOH from polyolefins (PP, PE) prior to mechanical recycling. The interfacial reaction between compatibilizers and EVOH inevitably leads to the formation of an interfacial copolymer, which may induce EVOH cross-linking during thermomechanical recycling and, consequently, alter the properties of the recovered polyolefins. Nevertheless, the valorization of EVOH through its prior recovery, followed by mechanical recycling, may represent a more suitable approach.

A recent study conducted by Meadows et al. 8 demonstrated the potential of selective dissolution to recover high-quality EVOH from K-cup coffee capsules. In this work, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was used to extract EVOH from polyolefins, which are not soluble in DMSO, even at a high dissolution temperature (100 °C). The recovered EVOH exhibited thermal properties comparable to those of virgin EVOH, although its rheological properties were slightly affected. Despite the growing number of research articles and patents dedicated to this topic, only a few studies have focused on the structure -rheology -properties relationship of polymers after selective dissolution precipitation processes.

In this context, selective precipitation by dissolution is presented in the literature as a promising method for recovering EVOH and an external polyolefin layer from multilayer films. Although several studies 9,10 have pointed out certain limitations of this technique, particularly related to the use of solvent and antisolvent systems and the complexity of their implementation.

The objective of this work is to compare two technologies used for the valorization of multilayer films, namely, mechanical recycling and the selective dissolution -precipitation process, applied to a barrier multilayer film based on PP, PPg -MA, and EVOH. These technologies lead to products of a different nature and potentially target distinct markets. Mechanical recycling consists of thermomechanical reprocessing carried out over five cycles on a multilayer film with the configuration PP/PPg -MA/EVOH/PPg -MA/PP. The dissolution -precipitation process is applied to two systems: the same multilayer film and a multilayer film recycled three times (Multilayer-R3). The two technologies are compared in terms of their applicability. In addition, environmental impact and economic aspects are also discussed based on data available in the literature.

Coextrusion Process

The multilayer films used in this study were produced by using a laboratory-scale coextrusion process illustrated in Figure 1, with the

Figure 1. Laboratory-scale coextrusion process used in this study.

text: main processing parameters summarized in Table S1 (see the Supporting Information). The process consists of three extruders, each dedicated to a different material. PP is processed in extruder C and forms the outer layer; EVOH, acting as the barrier layer, is processed in extruder A; and PP-g-MA, serving as the tie layer, is processed in extruder B. The three extruders deliver the molten material streams to a feedblock, whose specific geometry enables a controlled multilayer architecture. Layer formation occurs in two successive stages: first, the tie layer merges with the fluid barrier layer to form a three-layer film: tie layer/barrier layer/tie layer. Subsequently, the outer PP layer is added on both sides to produce a five-layer film. The final multilayer structure is therefore PP/PP-gMA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP. Based on calibration curves obtained during processing, PP constitutes the major phase, representing 88 wt % of the total composition, while EVOH accounts for 7 wt % and PPg-MA for 5 wt %. During coextrusion, two interphases are formed: a diffuse interphase between PP and PP-g-MA, and a reactive interphase between the hydroxyl groups of EVOH and the maleic anhydride groups of PP-g-MA. 29 Extruder A was operated at 210 °C with a screw speed of 4 rpm, while extruders B and C were operated at 200 °C with screw speeds of 6 and 40 rpm, respectively. The feedblock and die were maintained at 210 °C, where layer assembly and interfacial reactions occur. After coextrusion, the multilayer films were ground prior to thermomechanical processing.

Thermomechanical Reprocessing (Mechanical Recycling through a Twin-Screw Extruder)

The individual materials, namely, PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH, as well as the multilayer film, were subjected to five thermomechanical processing cycles. The thermomechanical recycling process was carried out using a corotating twin-screw extruder (PolyLab System Rheocord RC400P, Thermo Electron, Germany) with a screw diameter of 16 mm and an L/D ratio of 40, coupled to a filament extrusion die. All materials were processed at 210 °C in all heating zones with a screw rotation speed of 150 rpm. The filament of the processed materials was conveyed, cooled by ambient air, and then pelletized. These pellets were subsequently reintroduced into the same extruder to undergo the same process, thus enabling multiple recycling cycles. The sample codes used are listed in Table 2.

■ CHARACTERIZATION METHODS

Thermal properties

Differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) experiments were carried out using a TA Instruments Q20 instrument under a nitrogen purge of 50 mL/min to evaluate thermal properties and degree of crystallinity of neat PP, EVOH in the multilayer film, and their recovered materials after recycling cycles. Approximately 5 mg of polymer was weighed and sealed in a low-mass aluminum pan. The temperature program consisted of heating the samples from -30 to 230 °C, cooling to -30 °C, and then performing a second heating scan up to 230 °C at a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C/min. The glass transition and melting temperature ( T m) were determined from the second heating scan as the maximum of the melting peak. The first heating scan was chosen to eliminate the thermal history and allow comparison under identical conditions. The crystallization temperature ( T c) was taken from the maximum of the exothermal peak in the cooling scan. Polymer crystallinity was calculated from the second heating cycle according to the following equation.

where X c is the percentage of crystallinity of the samples.

Here, Δ H m is the melting enthalpy of PP or EVOH, Δ H m 0 corresponds to the melting enthalpy for a 100% crystalline polymer, and ϕ represents the weight fraction of the individual component in the blend. The Δ H m 0 values of PP and EVOH are 209 30 -32 and 202.4 J/g, 33,34 respectively.

Shear Rheological Experiments

Small Amplitude Oscillatory Shear measurements (SAOS) were performed at the molten state using a stress-controlled rheometer DHR-2 (Discovery Hybrid Rheometer, TA Instruments) with a parallel plate geometry ( Φ = 25 mm). The analyses were conducted under a nitrogen flow to prevent polymer degradation. Prior to testing, polymers were dried under a vacuum in an oven at 80 °C overnight.

Disks were compression-molded for 2 min at 210 °C to reduce any residual stress with a pressure of 200 bar between two Teflon films to obtain a smooth surface. Dynamic frequency sweep tests were performed over a frequency range from 628 to 0.01 rad/s at a fixed strain amplitude of 1% at 210 °C. Dynamic time sweep tests were also conducted at 210 °C at a constant angular frequency of 1 rad/s. The strain value was fixed at 1% to ensure the linear viscoelastic domain was primarily validated through dynamic strain sweep tests.

Mechanical Properties

Tensile tests were carried out on a 5-kN tensile testing machine. The specimens were injected at 210 °C according to ISO 527 type 5A and dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight before testing at a displacement speed of 50 mm/min. An extensometer was also used during the tests. To validate the repeatability of the results, each test was carried out on 5 specimens, and an average was calculated.

Morphology Analyses

A morphological characterization of multilayer films and their recycled materials was carried out using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, QUANTA 250) at a voltage of 10 kV and a working distance of 10 mm. The samples were cryofractured after immersion in liquid nitrogen and then coated with a 15 nm thick carbon layer for enhanced conductivity prior to the observation.

Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC)

SEC analysis for EVOH was performed in a Waters APC Acquity system equipped with a p -isocratic solvent Manager pump, an autosampler manager -pFTN, Waters refractive index detector (35 °C), WYATT viscosimeter at 35 °C (micro ViscoStar), coupled to a MALS WYATT (microDawn), using 1,1,1,3,3,3 hexafluoro-2propanol (HFIP) as eluent at a flow rate of 0.3 mLmin -1 . The device was equipped with a four-column Manager-S: one precolumn Acquity APC XT450 (2.5 μ m 4.6 × 30 mm) in series with three columns, an Acquity APC XT450 (2.5 μ m 4.6 × 75 mm), an Acquity APC XT125 (2.5 μ m 4.6 × 75 mm), and an Acquity APC XT45 (1.7 μ m 4.6 × 150 mm). Samples at a concentration around 5 g/L were prepared on HFIP and were filtered with a CHROMAFIL Xtra PTFE45/13, pore size 0.45 μ m. The molecular weights were determined with a calibration curve relative to those of methyl methacrylate (PMMA) standards.

For the PP, the instrument used was a PolymerChar GPC-IR system (PolymerChar, Valencia, Spain). Detection relied on a filterbased, multiple-band infrared detector (IR5-MTC model, PolymerChar, Valencia, Spain). As the stationary phase, three PLgel Olexis analytical columns (7.5 × 300 mm, PolymerChar, Valencia, Spain) were used. The molecular mass distribution (MMD) was determined by calibration with polystyrene standards (EasiCal PS-1, Agilent, Waldbronn, Germany). Data acquisition was performed using WinGPC version 8 (PolymerChar, Valencia, Spain). The instrument was equipped with a 200 μ L sample loop, corresponding to the injection volume. The mobile phase consisted of 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene (TCB), containing 0.4 g · L -1 of butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), and its flow rate was set at 1 mL · min -1 . For each measurement, about 6 mg of polymer was automatically dissolved in 8 mL of the eluent. During dissolution, the vials were flushed with nitrogen. Each sample was dissolved under shaking in the autosampler for 1 h at 150 °C before injection. The molar masses obtained from polystyrene (PS) standards were converted to polyethylene equivalents using the following Mark -Houwink coefficients: K PP = 1.7 × 10 -4 dL · g -1 , a PP = 0.725, K Ps = 1.6 × 10 -4 dL · g -1 , a Ps = 0.702. Samples from batches 1 to 7 were measured with a Tosoh instrument, while those from batches 8 to 17 were analyzed with a PolymerChar instrument.

Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy

Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used to analyze the evolution of the chemical structure. Attenuated total reflectance (ATR) analyses were performed on the exposed side using a Nicolet spectrometer (Nicolet IS10, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Massachusetts, USA) with a diamond crystal. 32 scans were realized between 4000 and 650 cm -1 with a resolution of ± 4 cm -1 .

Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR)

NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker Avance 400 spectrometer (Billerica, MA, USA). The experimental parameters were as follows: 1 H NMR: 400 MHz, 298 K, 512 scans; 13 C NMR: 100 MHz, 298 K, 6144 scans; HSQC and HMBC: 400 MHz, 298 K, 32 scans. DMSOd 6 was used as the solvent.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Mechanical Recycling (MR)

Thermomechanical Recycling of Multilayer Films via a Twin-Screw Extruder. The multilayer film with a PP/PP-gMA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP configuration, produced by coextrusion, was subjected to thermomechanical treatment for five successive cycles by using a twin-screw extruder. The main objective was to highlight the structural evolution of this material throughout the recycling cycles. Rheological and mechanical properties were therefore analyzed as a function of the recycling cycle.

The rheological properties reveal an initial decrease in viscosity after the first recycling cycle (Multilayer-R1), followed by an increase in viscosity in the third cycle (Multilayer-R3) compared with the first cycle, and then a second decrease observed in the fifth cycle (Multilayer-R5), as shown in Figure 2a. The complex viscosity of the virgin multilayer film remains higher than that of all recycled materials. These variations can be attributed to three competing reaction mechanisms. The initial drop in viscosity during the first cycle (Multilayer-R1) is likely associated with β -scission of macromolecular chains in the PP phase induced by thermo-oxidative degradation. This chain scission is supported by the decrease in zero-shear viscosity and PP molar mass with increasing recycling cycle number (Figure 2b,c and Tables S2 and S3 in the Supporting Information). In our previous work published in Rheologica Acta, 35 we similarly reported a reduction in the complex viscosity of PP with increasing recycling cycles (Figure S1 in the Supporting Information).

The increase in viscosity in the third cycle (Multilayer-R3) can be attributed to cross-linking reactions involving EVOH macromolecular chains. This behavior is illustrated in Figure 2d, where EVOH viscosity increases with recycling cycle number (data in Table S4 and in the Supporting Information). The evolution of the EVOH complex viscosity as a function of the recycling cycle number is presented in the Supporting Information (Figure S2). In addition, interactions between EVOH hydroxyl groups and anhydride groups of PP-g-MA may lead to copolymer formation, which could also influence the rheological behavior of this material. The second decrease in viscosity observed at the fifth cycle reflects competition between β -scission in PP, cross-linking in EVOH, and esterification reaction between EVOH and PP-g-MA. These mechanisms were thoroughly described in our rheological study previously conducted and published on these materials in Rheologica Acta. 35

The mechanical properties show that the multilayer film exhibits ductile behavior, characterized by high elongation at break (Figure 2e). This response is primarily governed by the PP phase (Supporting Information, Table S5). However, repeated recycling cycles reduced this ductility and led the materials to gain in yield strength and Young's modulus. Elongation at break decreased progressively with increasing recycling cycle number. Consequently, the mechanical behavior of recycled materials becomes increasingly dominated by EVOH, resulting in a more rigid and brittle response (Supporting Information, Table S5).

For each layer, a solvent must be specifically selected. In this study, solvents were chosen based on calculations of Hansen solubility parameters (HSP), 36 which are described in detail in Section 1 of the Supporting Information.

The HSP values of both the solvents and EVOH are summarized in Table 3. In this work, DMSO was selected as the solvent for EVOH because of its strong solubilizing ability and relatively low toxicity.

EVOH and PP Recovery from Multilayer Film and Multilayer-R3

In order to promote the dissolution of the materials (multilayer films and Multilayer-R3) and optimize solvent -polymer interactions, the films were first cryogenically ground using liquid nitrogen in a Pulverisette 11 grinder (Fritsch, Germany). This technique allowed the transformation of the samples, initially in film form, into a fine powder. The grinding was carried out at temperatures below the glass transition temperatures of the constituent polymers (Tg ≈ -10 °C for PP and Tg ≈ 62 °C for EVOH32), ensuring the preservation of the material integrity. The samples were then dried at 80 °C for 9 h to remove water condensed during cooling with nitrogen.

The multilayer film and the reference Multilayer-R3 were thus reduced to a powder. In the present work, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was selected as the solvent due to its good affinity with EVOH, whereas it is ineffective for PP (RED = 2.35). In this study, the mass ratio of the sample to DMSO was set at 0.1:1. Twenty grams of powder were dissolved in 200 mL of DMSO at 100 °C for 12 h to recover the maximum possible amount of EVOH (Figure 3). The objective of this work was to investigate the effects of prolonged exposure to hot DMSO (100 °C) on the thermal and rheological properties of the extracted EVOH and PP, as well as to ensure complete extraction of EVOH. For this reason, an extraction time of 12 h was selected, which is longer than the minimum extraction time reported in the literature. 22,25,37

̈

The setup was equipped with a silicone oil bath heated to 100 °C and maintained under agitation, along with a flask in which the material -solvent mixture was homogenized using a magnetic stir bar (Figure S4a, see the Supporting Information). After cooling of the homogeneous solution, a phase separation occurred, leading to the formation of a white gel floating on the surface of a yellowish liquid (Figure S4b, see the Supporting Information). The mixture was mechanically filtered under vacuum using a Bu chner filter (4 -5.5 μ m), allowing isolation of the gel from the yellowish filtrate. Addition of water as an antisolvent to the filtrate induced the precipitation of a white solid, which was collected by vacuum filtration. Both the gel and the precipitated solid were subsequently washed with water, filtered again on Bu chner, and dried under a vacuum at 80 °C for 24 h in order to remove residual solvent as completely as possible. The resulting samples were then characterized.

Regarding EVOH, an extraction rate exceeding 100% is observed, suggesting a partial coextraction of PPg -MA, which reflects a stronger compatibilization at the interface.

FTIR and NMR Analyses

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analyses (Figure 4) were carried out to determine whether the recovered materials indeed corresponded to EVOH. This technique also allowed verification of the possible presence of residual DMSO in the samples. The NMR spectra led to the identification of several characteristic peaks: peak 'a' was assigned to the main ethylene backbone of the polymer, a typical signature of EVOH; peaks 'b' corresponded to the carbons of the vinyl alcohol units; and peaks 'c' were associated with the hydroxyl groups of EVOH.

To support these findings, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy analyses were also performed (Figure 5). Table S7 (Supporting Information) summarizes the assignment of the bands to the characteristic vibrations of the different chemical entities of EVOH, as reported in the literature. 38 -45 The bands centered at 3300 cm -1 were attributed to the presence of the O -H stretching vibrations involving hydrogen bonding. The extracted EVOH, particularly from the virgin multilayer (rEVOH-from-multilayer) and from the Multilayer-R3 (rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3), exhibited bands centered at 1726 and 1742 cm -1 , respectively, slightly shifted compared to the band observed for virgin EVOH at 1764 cm -1 . These bands can be assigned to C  O stretching modes, probably resulting from the oxidation of the hydroxyl groups.

Figure 5. FTIR analyses were performed on the virgin and recovered EVOH.

The bands at 1636 (EVOH), 1654 (rEVOH-from-multilayer), and 1658 cm -1 (rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3) are most likely associated with C  C stretching vibrations. In contrast, the band at 1566 cm -1 , observed in virgin EVOH and attributed to O -H deformation of the -H involved in hydrogen bonding ( δ OH), was absent in the recycled EVOH samples. Furthermore, the results revealed an increase in the relative band intensities in the recycled EVOH compared with the virgin EVOH. This increase may be attributed to enhanced chain mobility, most likely induced by the solvent during the dissolution process. Moreover, a comparison between EVOH subjected to five thermomechanical recycling cycles (EVOHR5) and rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3 (Figure S5, Supporting Information) shows that the majority of absorption bands of EVOH-R5 exhibit higher intensities than those of the recovered rEVOH. This increase in intensity is attributed to the thermomechanical treatment undergone by EVOH.

FTIR analyses performed on the recovered PP samples (Figure 6) show that the recycled polymers, particularly those originating from the multilayer film (rPP-from-multilayer) and multilayer-R3 (rPP-from-Multilayer-R3), exhibit a band centered at 3400 cm -1 , assigned to hydroxyl ( -OH) groups, indicating the presence of EVOH traces in the recycled PP. In addition, a weak band appears around 1740 cm -1 in these samples, which can be associated with C  Ostretching modes. Comparison between PP subjected to five thermomechanical recycling cycles (PP-R5) and recovery rPP (Figure S6, Supporting Information) shows that PP-R5 exhibits a band centered at 1646 cm -1 , most likely corresponding to C  C

Figure 6. FTIR analyses were performed on the virgin and recovered PP from multilayer and Multilayer-R3.

stretching vibrations. Both materials present a band at 1744 cm -1 , which can be assigned to C  Ostretching modes. These bands may indicate the formation of carbonyl-containing species, likely resulting from thermo-oxidative degradation in the presence of air. 3,38 The recovered rPP also shows a band centered at 3400 cm -1 assigned to hydroxyl ( -OH) groups, likely arising from enhanced interaction between PPg -MA and EVOH. 46 This observation suggests that the interface/ interphase region was not completely dissolved by EVOH extraction.

Thermal Properties. Thermal analyses of recovered EVOH (Figure 7) provide further insight into its thermomechanical history. Table 4 summarizes the glass transition ( T g ), melting ( T m), and crystallization ( T c ) temperatures, as well as the corresponding melting and crystallization enthalpies of both virgin and recovered EVOH determined from the second heating cycle. The results indicate that the recovered EVOH samples exhibit T g values of 35 °C (rEVOH-frommultilayer) and 42 °C (rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3), both significantly lower than that of virgin EVOH (57 °C). The observed decrease in T g can be attributed to residual DMSO, which acts as a plasticizer, 47 enhancing chain mobility and promoting structural reorganization. 48 -51 A similar behavior was reported by Cecon et al. 48 for PET recovered from PE/ EVOH/PET multilayer packaging films via a solvent-targeted dissolution -precipitation approach, where the reduction in T g was attributed to the presence of solvent within the polymer matrix. According to these authors, DMSO entrapped within the PET matrix contributes to the lowering of the glass transition temperature. To mitigate this effect, the samples were dried at 180 °C for 8 h prior to DSC measurements, using a hermetically sealed aluminum DSC pan. In the present work, the samples were dried at 80 °C for 48 h prior to analysis, and hermetically sealed aluminum DSC pans were also employed. Therefore, heating to 230 °C will not necessarily lead to volatilization of DMSO.

This behavior may be attributed to strong polymer -solvent interactions, whereby the solvent promotes chain rearrangement and swelling, ultimately facilitating crystallization. 48 -51

Rheological Properties

The rheological behavior of virgin and recovered EVOH was investigated by monitoring the evolution of complex viscosity as a function of the angular frequency at 210 °C (Figure 9a). The results reveal a clear decrease in complex viscosity for the recovered EVOH samples compared to the virgin material. This reduction is particularly pronounced for the rEVOHfrom-Multilayer-R3, derived from a multilayer film subjected to three successive thermomechanical recycling cycles. The observed decrease in viscosity can be attributed to reduced molar mass resulting from polymer dissolution and, in the case of rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3, additional thermo-oxidative degradation.

Thermal stability analysis (Figure 9b) further shows that neither virgin nor recycled EVOH exhibits significant stability at 210 °C, as evidenced by the progressive increase in complex viscosity over time. When comparing the rheological behavior of the three times thermomechanically reprocessed EVOH (EVOH-R3) with that of rEVOH-from-multilayer-R3, the former displays a high complex viscosity (Figure S7 and Supporting Information), suggesting less severe degradation.

Similar trends are observed for polypropylene (PP). A marked decrease in complex viscosity is detected for recovered PP obtained via dissolution -precipitation compared to virgin PP (Figure 9c). This pronounced reduction can be attributed to the partial dissolution of the interface/interphase region along with EVOH. As the region may include PP chains, its removal likely leads to a decrease in the molar mass of PP, and consequently, a reduction in viscosity. Thermal stability analysis (Figure 9d) corroborates this significant drop in complex viscosity. However, recovered PP samples exhibit improved thermal stability compared to virgin PP, as evidenced by the more stable evolution of complex viscosity over time at 210 °C. When comparing the rheological behavior of the three times thermomechanically reprocessed PP (PP-R3) with rPPfrom-multilayer-R3, PP-R3 exhibits a higher complex viscosity (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The presence of PPg -MA acting as a compatibilizer plays a key role in the behavior: maleic anhydride groups can react with hydroxyl groups of EVOH, resulting in the chemically bonded and morphologically cohesive PP/EVOH interfacial region. Consequently, separation is more challenging than that in simple immiscible polymer systems. During the selective dissolution, a part of this interface/interphase region could be dissolved with EVOH, which explains the lower viscosity of the recovery rPP. These findings are supported by SEC results, which show that the number-average molar masses of recovered rPP are lower than those of virgin PP.

Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC)

Figure 10 illustrates the molecular weight distribution of virgin PP and EVOH, as well as their recycled counterparts. The number-average and weight-average molar masses, along with the polydispersity index, are presented in Table 7. Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) analyses show that virgin PP has a weight-average molar mass nearly twice as high as that of the recycled PP samples, as well as a slightly higher numberaverage molecular weight (results confirmed by morphological analysis). The polydispersity index of virgin PP is also higher than that of recycled PP samples. Regarding EVOH, the number-average and weight-average molecular weights of rEVOH-from-multilayer are slightly higher than those of virgin EVOH, suggesting the possible coprecipitation of a fraction of the copolymer present at the interphase (EVOH/PP-g-MA) with EVOH. In contrast, rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3 exhibits a lower weight-average molecular weight than both virgin EVOH and rEVOH-from-multilayer, which may be attributed to its history of thermomechanical processing.

The multiple thermomechanical processing cycles undergone by rPP-fromMultilayer-R3 prior to the dissolution -precipitation process promoted the formation of an interfacial copolymer, induced by an esterification reaction between the hydroxyl groups of EVOH and the maleic anhydride groups of PPg -MA. As a result, rPP-from-Multilayer-R3 was likely coprecipitated with a fraction of this copolymer, which may explain the observed increase in elongation at break.

Discussions: Comparative Analysis of Mechanical Recycling versus Selective Dissolution Precipitation

This section compares MR by thermomechanical reprocessing with the SDP process. Both technologies are used for the valorization of the multilayer films. This study focuses on the applicability of the two processes, although they lead to products of a different nature and are generally intended for different markets. Two additional criteria, namely, environmental impact and economic aspects, are also addressed; however, the comparison for these criteria relies mainly on data from the literature. These aspects are currently being studied within the framework of this project.

MR is currently the most widely implemented industrial route due to its operational simplicity, low cost, and relatively low energy consumption. However, its main limitation lies in the immiscibility of most base polymers, which results in phase separation and poor interfacial adhesion in mixed plastic streams. Consequently, recycled materials often exhibit reduced mechanical performance, mainly due to thermal and mechanical degradation during processing. For instance, thermomechanical treatment of a multilayer film based on PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH over several recycling cycles leads to multiple reaction mechanisms, including PP β -scission, EVOH cross-linking, and copolymer formation resulting from interactions between EVOH and PP-g-MA. These mechanisms affect the mechanical and rheological properties of the material. As a result, mechanical recycling of the PP/PP-gMA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP multilayer film remains promising up to the third cycle; beyond this point, rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate. 9,54,55 In terms of environmental impact, despite differing opinions in the literature, most studies consider MR to have a lower environmental impact than other methods (physical recycling and chemical recycling). 9,54,55 Furthermore, Faraca et al. 56 quantified the costs associated with mechanical and chemical recycling in Denmark and demonstrated that advanced MR is the only scenario generating net financial savings. Other studies also support the economic viability of mechanical recycling. 57,58

In contrast, the SDP process relies on differences in the polymer solubility to achieve separation and purification. This approach enables the recovery of high-purity polymers while preserving their molecular structure, thereby maintaining properties close to those of virgin materials. It is particularly advantageous for processing complex or multilayer plastic waste that cannot be efficiently treated by mechanical routes. In this study, the method was applied to two systems: a PP/ PP-g-MA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP multilayer film and the same multilayer film after three thermomechanical recycling cycles. The results show that the PP and EVOH fractions are well separated. However, their thermal and rheological properties are modified, likely due to solvent use at an elevated temperature.

Moreover, this process is more complex than MR because it involves several steps, namely, shredding, solvent selection, temperature adjustment, filtration, followed by washing and drying. Solvent selection is critical since a specific solvent must be used for each layer. The choice of the temperature and dissolution time is also important to ensure effective dissolution. Washing and drying are essential to separate the recovered products from the solvent. Within the scope of this project, the total time required to separate PP and EVOH is 60 h, including 12 h for dissolution and 48 h for washing and drying. In contrast, applying five recycling cycles to the multilayer film by MR required only 6 h.

From an environmental perspective, this process is more energy-intensive than MR due to heating and solvent evaporation steps. It also uses antisolvents, which require additional distillation stages to separate solvents from antisolvents, thereby increasing environmental impact. 59 Several studies emphasize the need to reduce antisolvent use and optimize solvent recovery loops. 25,37,60 Finally, the process is costly due to the use of solvents and antisolvents, as well as the required equipment, notably reactors and distillation/ evaporation units. 22,61

■ CONCLUSIONS

This work presents a comparative assessment of two recycling technologies, MR and the SDP process, based on process robustness and product quality, as well as environmental and economic considerations. These approaches yield materials of a different nature and are therefore likely to target distinct market applications. The study focuses on multilayer films composed of PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH.

MR was performed through thermomechanical processing over five successive recycling cycles. The results indicate that this approach remains effective up to the third cycle; beyond this point, both rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate due to reaction mechanisms occurring during processing. These include β -scission of PP chains, cross-linking of EVOH, and esterification reactions between EVOH and PP. According to literature data, MR exhibits a relatively low environmental impact and remains economically favorable.

In contrast, the SDP approach relies on differences in the polymer solubility to achieve selective separation and purification. In the present study, SDP was applied to separate EVOH from PP in both a multilayer film and a Multilayer-R3 material composed of PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH. The results demonstrate separation between PP and EVOH; however, alterations in thermal and rheological properties were observed. These changes may be attributed to residual solvent retained within the samples as well as to partial dissolution of interfacial regions. From an environmental perspective, the SDP process is more energy-intensive and exhibits a higher environmental footprint than that of mechanical recycling. The use of solvents and antisolvents necessitates additional processing steps, such as distillation, for their separation and recovery. Economically, beyond the capital investment required for reactors, heating, and evaporation systems, the cost of solvents and antisolvents may further increase the overall process cost.

So fi a C. Aparício, a Pedro M. Castro, b Bernardo D. Ribeiro c and Isabel M. Marrucho * a

Polyole fi ns comprise some of the most abundant plastics, but their recycling faces several di ffi culties. This work focuses on the recycling of high-density polyethylene (HDPE) through the dissolution -precipitation method. Although few works have been published on this topic, this is an extremely promising plastic recycling strategy. However, for this kind of process to become a viable alternative, the replacement of conventional solvents by green solvents and the minimization of energy usage need to be implemented. In this work, several natural terpenes were screened based on COSMO-SAC predictions for HDPE solubility, and three were tested: limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene. These solvents showed a good capability of dissolving HDPE, con fi rming the computational predictions. The dissolution and precipitation conditions were optimized based on the results for limonene, with the optimal values being 3 wt% initial concentration of the polymer in the solvent, a dissolution period of 10 min at a temperature of 110 °C, and an antisolvent/solvent ratio of 2/1. Comparing both HDPE and solvent recoveries for the three selected solvents, the best results were obtained for α -pinene as the solvent and ethanol as the antisolvent. The recovered HDPE samples were analyzed by TGA, FTIR, and DSC, showing little modi fi cation between the recycled and pristine materials. Scaling up of the process and solvent reuse were also investigated. Through process simulation, it was concluded that solvent recovery and reuse is a crucial step for economic viability. HDPE dissolution -precipitation with α -pinene was found to be a sustainable process from preliminary sustainability analysis, and the separation of HDPE and PET (polyethylene terephthalate) was successfully carried out.

In 2019, polyolefins (PP, HDPE (high-density polyethylene), LDPE (low-density polyethylene) and LLDPE (linear low-density polyethylene)) accounted for nearly 40% of the global plastic use. 4 These polymers are commonly used in packaging applications. In particular, HDPE can be found in beverage bottles, sti ff bottles and as flexible films, but it is also typically used in rigid toys and outdoor products. 5,6 Polyolefins are also ideal constituents of multilayer films, commonly in combination with di ff erent polyolefins or PET, 7 where they can have sealing and structural functions. 8 Although these plastics can be individually recycled, they are often present in complex waste streams that cannot be e ffi ciently sorted, as is the case of multilayer films, or contain various additives that preclude the use of mechanical recycling processes. 7 -10 It is estimated that the total percentage of HDPE that followed recycling pathways between 1950 and 2016, in Europe, was 12%, while more than half ended up in landfills, 11 as shown in Fig. 1. This low recycling rate is clear evidence that the recycling processes implemented so far still lack e ffi ciency for post-consumer products. Although landfilling and incineration reduce the existing volume of plastic waste and minimize water and soil contamination, they come with few other benefits, as they do not reduce the need for primary polymer production. This is very important because polyolefins are usually obtained from the steam cracking of naphtha, a product of crude oil refining, 12,13 a fossil fuel whose consumption needs to be minimized.

Fig. 1 Fate of HDPE in Europe between 1950 and 2016 (data from Kawecki et al. 11 ).

The recycling routes for plastic materials include mechanical, chemical, and physical recycling. In spite of being most widely implemented, mechanical recycling faces various challenges regarding the quality of the recycled plastics, whose properties greatly depend on the uniformity of the input materials. 14 -19 Chemical recycling is also a limited approach in the case of HDPE, as its complete depolymerization to monomers has not been achieved so far. Instead, pyrolysis and gasification are the common approaches converting plastics to hydrocarbons that can be used as chemical feedstock, after further purification and separation treatments. 13,14,16,20 -23 On the other hand, physical recycling is better suited for complex plastic mixtures than mechanical recycling, yielding simpler processes. 14,24

Physical recycling, and dissolution -precipitation in particular, makes use of solvents to recover the polymers without degradation or structural modifications, resulting in a recycled plastic with similar properties to the pristine material. 14,24 Dissolution -precipitation processes rely on the selective dissolution of a target polymer from a mixture of plastics. When this polymer is dissolved, the solution can be filtered, thus separating it from the other polymers. The dissolved polymer can then be recovered by precipitation, converting it back to a solid plastic, through the addition of an antisolvent or by lowering the temperature of the system.
