ization of the polymer (the additives and other polymers remain solid and are removed by filtration), or through the solubilization of both the polymer and the additive, and the use of an antisolvent causes the precipitation of the pure polymer. 13,14,25 The possibility of tuning the solvents to selectively dissolve a targeted polymer in a mixture opens up the way for the treatment of mixed plastic streams, such as multilayer films, where typical sorting is not possible. 8 This technology has already been successfully employed to separate mixtures of plastics at the laboratory scale: Kannan et al. 26 separated LDPE, HDPE, PS (polystyrene) and PET, Walker et al. 27 used dissolution -precipitation to separate a mixture of HDPE, EVOH (ethylene vinyl alcohol) and PET, and Cécon et al. and Sánchez-Rivera et al. 28,29 separated HDPE, EVOH, EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate), PET and PETG (polyethylene terephthalate glycol). It was also implemented in some pilot-scale plants, using the CreaSolv process by Creacycle GmbH, namely for separating PE, PP, PA (polyamide) and PET, 30 and PE and PP. 31 HDPE, the focus of the present study, was the subject of various physical recycling studies using dissolution and precipitation, mostly using toluene, 27,29,32 -35 xylene 26,33,34 or petroleum ether-based solvents. 36 -38 Only in 2022, Ferreira et al. 39 proposed the use of D-limonene, a biobased solvent, for the dissolution of HDPE. However, the objective of that work was the recovery of dyes from the plastic, and plastic recovery itself was not considered in detail. In another study, p -cymene was found to be a good solvent for LDPE and PP, but HDPE dissolution was not studied. 40 Acetone, 26 -29,32,40 2-propanol 26 or n -hexane 33,34,36 -38 are the usual choices for antisolvents.

Although the dissolution -precipitation technology seems to be a promising option for recycling polyolefins, there are some bottlenecks that need to be addressed to guarantee its future applicability. First, the most commonly used solvents, toluene and xylene, are dangerous air pollutants 41 and pose serious hazards to aquatic and human life. 44,45 Toluene is even suspected to be a carcinogenic agent and harmful for the reproductive system. 42,43 The environmental, health and social impacts associated with the production and use of these solvents are extremely concerning, and current solvent selection metrics identify them as problematic. 44 Several legal measures have restricted their usage, both in Europe and the U.S.A. 45 -47 Thus, it is urgent to replace them by greener, natural, and less hazardous solvents in the dissolution of HDPE. Acetone, one of the most common antisolvents, should also be replaced by other less problematic compounds, such as alcohols. 44 Furthermore, from the economic point of view, this technology is currently limited, since the high amounts of energy required for the separation of the solvent and antisolvent drive the minimum selling price to a higher value than that of the virgin polymer. 48 Greenhouse gas emissions are also mostly related to the recovery of the solvent. 30,48 Thus, the present work aims to develop a novel circular approach for the dissolution -precipitation of HDPE using natural solvents and finding antisolvent combinations that allow a simple, coste ffi cient recovery of the solvent while recovering the polymer with its pristine quality.

2. Materials and methods

2.1 Materials

HDPE was used in the form of commercial clear fruit bags, obtained from Continente supermarkets. PET was used in the form of clear water bottles from Luso.

Limonene rich extract was graciously provided by SumolCompal, as a subproduct of mechanical processing of orange peels. It was then purified through steam distillation, followed by fractioned distillation. The remaining solvents and antisolvents used were purchased in the desired grade, according to the respective purities and suppliers described in Table S1 in the ESI. † For the separation of HDPE and PET, PET was dissolved with a thymol : carvacrol natural deep eutectic solvent (NaDES), whose characteristics are also presented in Table S1. † Bi-distilled water was used for solvent recovery, from the BioSan Labaqua Trace purification system, with a conductivity of 0.055 μ S cm -1 .

2.2 Experimental methods

2.2.1 HDPE dissolution, precipitation and solvent recovery.

HDPE dissolution was carried out by heating the polymer and solvent mixture in an oil bath at a controlled temperature, and a stirring speed of 400 rpm. After complete dissolution, the antisolvent was added, promoting the precipitation of the polymer. The obtained mixture was then filtered under vacuum, and the resulting polymer flakes were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 48 hours. The dry HDPE was then ground using liquid nitrogen, washed with ethanol, and dried for another 48 hours. The percentage recovery of HDPE was determined through gravimetric measurements.

For the solvent ' s recovery, water was added to promote phase separation between the solvent and the antisolvent, according to the liquid -liquid equilibrium diagrams calculated using COSMO-SAC. The resulting mixtures were centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 20 minutes, using a VWR CompactStar CS 4 centrifuge, and solvent recovery was evaluated by gravimetry.

2.2.2 HDPE and PET selective dissolution and recovery. The separation of HDPE and PET was performed from a solid mixture containing equal masses of both polymers shredded. HDPE was selectively dissolved first, at the optimized conditions studied in this work, following the procedure described above in section 2.2.1. The mixture was then filtered using a 2 mm mesh filter, retaining the solid PET, and allowing the solubilized HDPE to pass. Afterwards, the anti-solvent was used to precipitate and recover HDPE.

After filtration, PET was washed and dried at 40 °C and then dissolved and recovered following the procedure described by Pestana et al. 49 The solvent, a natural deep eutectic solvent (NaDES) composed of thymol and carvacrol (1 : 1), was prepared by heating the mixture of the two compounds up to 80 °C for around 1 hour, after which the obtained clear solution was slowly cooled. The PET dissolution, in the polymer to solvent ratio of 1/10, was carried out at 150 °C for 7 minutes, and a mixture of ethanol (60 v/v%) and water was used as the antisolvent to precipitate it, in the proportion of 50 mL of antisolvent for 1 g of PET.

2.2.3 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. Attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy was used to evaluate the integrity of the recovered polymer and solvents, in comparison with the virgin materials. A PerkinElmer UATR Two spectrometer with a diamond crystal was used, and the analysis was carried out in the range between 4000 and 400 cm -1 , based on the accumulation of 8 scans with a resolution of 4 cm -1 .

2.2.4 Di ff erential scanning calorimetry. Samples of the recovered HDPE were analyzed by di ff erential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess the changes in the main thermal properties of the polymer due to the dissolution and precipitation process. The equipment used was a DSC 200 F3 from NETZSCH, in which two sequential heating -cooling cycles were performed, between 20 and 250 °C, at a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C min -1 , and with a nitrogen flow rate of 50 mL min -1 . The melting and crystallization temperatures and the enthalpy of fusion were determined based on the second cycle. This value was used to estimate the percentage of crystallinity of the polymers, taken as the quotient of the enthalpies of fusion calculated from DSC data and that of the completely crystalline polymer. The values were 293 J g -1 for PE and 140 J g -1 for PET. 50

2.2.5 Thermogravimetric analysis. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was carried out to quantify eventual solvent residues in the recovered HDPE. The weight loss of the samples was analyzed in a HITACHI STA7200 model thermal analysis system, between 35 and 600 °C, at a heating rate of 10 °C min -1 , under a nitrogen atmosphere (with a flow rate of 200 mL min -1 ).

2.2.6 Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy was performed to infer the recovered solvent ' s integrity and purity. The 1 H and 13 C APT spectra were recorded in an AMX 400 MHz spectrometer, from Bruker, at 25 °C, using deuterated chloroform as the solvent.

2.3 Computational methods

2.3.1 Thermodynamic estimations: COSMO-SAC solvent screening. HDPE molecules were simulated based on the charge density screening of the representative monomer, taken as the most central monomer of a trimer, thus minimizing the end groups ' influence on the density functional-theory (DFT) calculations, performed in an AMSinput 2023.101 interface, with the parameterization GGA:BP86/TZP86, using a pre-optimized molecular geometry with the Universal Force Field (UFF) package. The same parametrization was used to optimize the molecules of the solvents not included in the COSMO-SAC database, such as 3-carene and β -caryophyllene. After geometry optimization, the compounds were added to the COSMO-SAC calculation environment.

All calculations were performed with the activity coe ffi cient model COSMO-SAC, particularly with the parameter package DHB, determined as the most adequate for the systems under study. To improve the accuracy of the calculations, some properties, such as melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, and density at 25 °C, were manually introduced. Table S2 in the ESI † summarizes all the properties for the pure compounds used in this work. For HDPE, the properties of the completely crystalline polymer were used: T m = 141.4 °C, Δ H f = 293 J g -1 , 50 and ρ C = 1.00 g cm -3 . 51 The considered molecular weight was the COSMO-SAC default.

2.3.2 Process simulation: economic and sustainability evaluation. The proposed dissolution -precipitation process was simulated with the Aspen Plus V11 software to estimate energy requirements and the cost associated with each step.

The HDPE polymer was defined as an oligomer using C2H4R as the repeating segment. The polymer molecular weight is a required input parameter, which was fixed at a value of 100 kg mol -1 . The necessary phase equilibrium properties for the process simulation were estimated using the POLYUF method, which is a modification of the activity coe ffi cient ' s group contribution method UNIFAC, specifically improved for polymers. The distillation column used to separate water and ethanol, with residual amounts of α -pinene was also simulated using the UNIFAC method. Group contribution methods were used due to the lack of adequate data in the available Aspen databases for α -pinene.

The required utilities were defined according to the Aspen templates and attributed to each equipment so that the minimum temperature di ff erence of 10 °C between streams is respected. 52 Considering a pessimistic estimation of the process costs, no heat integration was performed. The utilities used were heated air, low pressure steam, cooling water and refrigerated water. Table S3 in the ESI † shows the properties of each utility.

The prices associated with the raw materials were taken from the Sigma Aldrich website. 53 In the case of water, a price of 1.24 € per 1000 kg was considered. 54 For estimating the costs associated with utilities, the cost per unit was used as tabulated, 54 and the values were actualized to the year of 2023 according to inflation 55 (Table S3 in the ESI † ). The conversion between U.S. dollars and euros is for July 8, 2023.

The sustainability assessment was performed according to the EcoScale methodology, developed by Aken et al. : 56 starting from 100 points, tabulated penalties were assigned based on yield, price, safety, technical setup, temperature, and purification.

3. Results and discussion

3.1 Thermodynamic estimations: solvent screening using COSMO-SAC

The representative oligomer of HDPE (Fig. S1 in the ESI † ) was modeled and optimized as described in section 2.3.1. Based on these DFT calculations, the σ -profile ( p ( σ )) (Fig. 2) and σ -potential ( μ ( σ )) (Fig. S2 in the ESI † ) of the HDPE molecules were drawn. From the analysis of HDPE ' s σ -profile and σ -potential, it is clear that no polar interactions are favored by the polymer ' s completely apolar structure. Thus, and in line with the solubility rule of thumb ' like dissolves like ' , apolar compounds were considered to be potential solvents. Several natural and widely available terpenes that are commercialized at prices below 100 € per kg, according to the values available in the Sigma Aldrich website, 53 were screened. The COSMO-SAC model was used to estimate the solubility of HDPE in the selected solvents, at di ff erent temperatures, as shown in Fig. 3, and described in Table S4 in the ESI. † The σ -profiles of these solvents are also presented in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2 σ -Pro fi le of HDPE and screened solvents, drawn in COSMO-SAC.

Although it has already been reported that HDPE is soluble in toluene, 27 -29,32 -34 xylene, 33,34,57,58 and D-limonene 39 at 110 °C, no dissolution is predicted by the COSMO-SAC model.

Fig. 3 Solubility of crystalline HDPE in di ff erent solvents, as calculated through COSMO-SAC.

At this temperature, the experimental solubility limit has only been reported in toluene being between 14.56 wt% 28,35 and 23.1 wt%. 59 The di ff erence between the experimental and the COSMO-SAC predicted solubility can possibly be explained by the use of the properties of completely crystalline HDPE in the COSMO-SAC calculations, while commonly available samples have lower degrees of crystallinity. At 120 °C, the solubility predicted for HDPE in toluene and xylene is of 12 wt% and 1 wt%, respectively. The only green solvent studied that shows some HDPE solubility at this temperature is α -pinene (1 wt%). Nevertheless, at 130 °C, COSMO-SAC predicts that HDPE is soluble in all the screened solvents: β -caryophyllene is estimated to dissolve HDPE up to 32 wt%, while the predictions for all the other terpenes lay between 50 and 60 wt%.

The solvents D-limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene were selected to proceed with the experimental study based on their promising predicted capability to dissolve HDPE and on their wide availability, namely as waste byproducts of existing industries, such as paper pulping and fruit processing. 60,61 It was also taken into account that these compounds have similar properties to those of toluene and p -xylene, such as melting and boiling points, density and viscosity. 62

3.2 Limonene as HDPE solvent

3.2.1 Optimization of the dissolution conditions. The dissolution of HDPE in limonene has been reported by Ferreira et al. , 39 with HDPE solubility values up to 2 wt%, but only at 110 °C and a minimum dissolution time of 30 minutes. Consequently, the dissolution conditions regarding limonene ought to be optimized. Thus, in this work, the dissolution time and the recovery yields of both HDPE and limonene were studied at temperatures between 100 °C and 120 °C, starting from di ff erent initial HDPE solid contents, up to 5 wt%. The precipitation of the polymer was carried out using ethanol as the antisolvent, in an antisolvent/solvent mass ratio of 2/1.

Regarding the required dissolution time, corresponding to the moment when a completely clear homogeneous solution was attained, it was observed that it does not depend on the initial solid polymer content within the range studied, implying that the solutions are not close to saturation. No experiments were conducted with larger HDPE initial solid contents due to the enormous increase in the viscosity of the polymer solutions, which causes di ffi culties in the subsequent recovery operations, ultimately compromising the reliability of the obtained results. The dissolution time decreases for high temperatures, although in all samples, HDPE was dissolved in less than 10 minutes (around 7 min at 100 °C, 4 min at 110 °C and 3 min at 120 °C). These dissolution times are significantly smaller than those commonly found in the literature for similar HDPE processes using the same polymer initial concentration range. 26 -29,33,34,36,39,57,59

Fig. 4 (and Table S5 in the ESI † ) shows the recovery of HDPE and limonene at di ff erent temperatures and initial solid polymer contents. It was observed that conducting the HDPE dissolution at the temperature of 110 °C yielded the best solvent recoveries, when solutions of 2 -5 wt% HDPE content are used. Up to 3 wt%, this is also the temperature at which most polymer was recovered. Above this polymer content, the HDPE recovery increased at 120 °C but yielded a significantly lower amount of recovered limonene. Taking this into consideration and also the increased handling di ffi culty of the samples containing 4 and 5 wt% HDPE, 3 wt% was established as the higher limit of the HDPE initial concentration. Polymer recovery is significantly reduced below 3 wt%, therefore this content was chosen for further experiments, together with the temperature of 110 °C, due to the increased solvent recovery. Under these conditions, 80.5 wt% HDPE and 47.3 wt% limonene are recovered.

3.2.2 Antisolvent study. The influence of the antisolvent used and the antisolvent/solvent ratio was studied at the aforementioned HDPE dissolution conditions: 110 °C, 3 wt% HDPE in limonene and dissolution time of 10 min. Several alcohols were selected for this antisolvent study, with varying alkyl chain length, number of OH groups and position of these groups in the molecule. Water was also added to the antisolvent screening.

Fig. 4 Recovery yield (wt%) of HDPE (A) and limonene (B) as a function of the concentration of HDPE in limonene solution.

The recovery of the solvent was achieved by adding water to the solvent -antisolvent mixture, which in most cases allows for the nearly complete recovery of limonene with high purity, with the antisolvent rich phase containing less than 2 wt% limonene, according to the ternary liquid -liquid diagrams calculated by COSMO-SAC and provided in the ESI (Fig. S3 -S11 † ). Two exceptions are the systems composed of 2-propanol and 1-butanol, in which the limonene-rich phase is not of high purity. Limonene is not soluble in water, so no further purification step was needed for its recovery.

The experimental recovery yields for both the polymer and the solvent for the considered antisolvents are shown in Fig. 5 (and Table S6 in the ESI † ). Overall, it is clear that the mass ratio between the antisolvent and the solvent does not have a considerable impact on polymer recovery. Conversely, the solvent ' s recovery is much more influenced by this parameter, although for most antisolvents no significant improvement was observed for ratios above 2/1, with the exception of diethylene glycol.

However, di ff erent antisolvents lead to significantly di ff erent results, which can be further understood by analyzing the solubility of limonene in each one of these compounds, estimated at 25 °C using COSMO-SAC and listed in Table 1. In fact, the highest limonene recovery, above 50 wt%, was obtained using ethanol as the antisolvent, in which limonene is very soluble. However, in this case, the HDPE recovery is slightly lower than for other systems, possibly due to its higher a ffi nity for the limonene -ethanol mixture than for other systems, limiting the amount that actually precipitates. On the other extreme, HDPE recoveries above 100 wt% were obtained for water and glycerol, leading to the conclusion that the solvent was not e ffi ciently removed from the polymer, due to its low a ffi nity towards the antisolvent. Coherently, limonene recovery for these systems is low or even almost null. Following the mono-alcohols (ethanol, 2-propanol and 1-butanol), 1,2propanediol is the compound in which limonene is the most soluble,16 wt%. This antisolvent is an example where intermediate results are obtained, with HDPE recoveries above 80 wt% but solvent recoveries as low as 20 wt%.

3.4 Solvent selection for HDPE dissolution and precipitation

A comparison of the results obtained for the three di ff erent solvents is given in Table 2, fixing the dissolution conditions at 3 wt% HDPE, 110 °C, 10 minutes, and an ethanol/solvent ratio of 2/1. 3.5 Recovered HDPE characterization

The integrity, purity and quality of the recovered HDPE, after being dissolved in α -pinene and precipitated using ethanol, was assessed by thermogravimetric analysis, di ff erential scanning calorimetry and FTIR.

TGA was used to infer about the presence of solvent residues in the recovered polymer. The sample showed no weight loss before 400 °C, and the polymer content was determined to be 99.8%, according to the thermogram in Fig. S18 in the ESI. † This behavior follows the normal thermal degradation behavior of virgin HDPE, 63 and the absence of degradation peaks other than that corresponding to the polymer implies that there are no traces of solvent in the HDPE matrix, and thus its removal and drying were e ffi cient.

Although TGA showed no traces of solvent residues, FTIR spectroscopy was performed to assess if the process had led to any modifications in the structure of the polymer. The FTIR spectra of both pristine and recovered HDPE, in Fig. 6, show the characteristic bands of PE (listed in Table S11 † ). For the α -pinene/ethanol system, the recovered polymer ' s spectrum di ff ers from that of the pristine only in the region between 800 and 1200 cm -1 , although these additional bands do not show clear correspondence with either the solvents or the antisolvents, and are not associated with any weight loss, as TGA had confirmed.

Furthermore, DSC allows comparison of the thermal properties of the pristine and recovered polymer, in particular the melting and crystallization temperatures and enthalpy of fusion, which are directly correlated with the crystallinity of the polymer. No significant changes were observed in any of the aforementioned properties, as shown in Table 3.

It can, thus, be concluded that the polymer was not degraded nor did it undergo significant modifications throughout the dissolution process, and that the removal of the solvent and drying step were e ffi cient, as no traces of α -pinene nor ethanol were identified in the recovered polymer.

3.7 Scaling up and solvent reuse

text:
The viability of scaling up the process of HDPE recovery using the α -pinene/ethanol solvent/antisolvent system was assessed by increasing the initial amount of polymer to be dissolved by 5 times, from 50 to 250 mg. All the ratios between the components were maintained at the optimal values, as well as the temperature (110 °C) and dissolution time (10 min). The results obtained are shown in Fig. 7, and in Table S13 in the ESI. † The possibility of improving the total solvent recovery was also assessed, by adding water and centrifuging the washing solution.

The recovery of HDPE increased nearly 10 wt% by scalingup the process. The most probable cause is that eventual losses related to the experimental procedure become less significant. On the other hand, the increase in scale did not lead to significant changes in the recovery of the solvent. From the washing step mixture, it was possible to recover roughly an additional 17 wt% α -pinene in both cases, resulting a total α -pinene recovery of 73 wt% at the larger scale, similarly to the small scale.

Fig. 8 HDPE and α -pinene recovery considering three consecutive solvent reuses.

In conclusion, scaling up of the process did not lead to any decrease in the final yields, but rather to some improvement regarding the polymer recovery, thus pointing towards the viability of a more intensive scale increase.

Solvent reutilization is another essential requirement for a feasible implementation of a large-scale process. This possibility was tested in the larger scale process, and the same solvent was used 3 consecutive times, leading to the results shown in Fig. 8, and described in Table S14 in the ESI. † No pure solvent was added between each cycle, and thus the scale of the experiments was adapted accordingly (250 mg of HDPE in the first cycle, 125 mg in the second, and 50 mg in the third).

The polymer recovery only varied around 3 wt% throughout the three cycles, reaching the lowest value in the last, with a value of 90 wt%. This value was obtained at the original scale of 50 mg of HDPE, but after using the same solvent twice, meaning that the recovery increased around 6 wt% by reusing the solvent, with no other modifications to the experimental conditions. The solvent ' s recovery, on the other hand, decreases about 3 wt% in each cycle. One possible cause for this is the presence of water in the recovered α -pinene, as proved by NMR analysis (section 3.6), meaning that the amount of solvent considered in the subsequent cycles slightly deviated from the actual quantity. Also, small residues of unprecipitated HDPE might exist in the solvent, below the detection levels of NMR, which could play an important role in facilitating the precipitation of the polymer, thus increasing its recovery.

The integrity of the solvent recovered at the end of the third cycle was investigated by FTIR analysis (Fig. S24 † ), and NMR (Fig. S25 and S26 † ). Again, the only identified contamination was water, at less than 1 wt%, identical to what was observed after only one dissolution -precipitation cycle.

3.8 Process simulation: economic and sustainability analysis

The dissolution -precipitation process of HDPE was simulated as a continuous process, in order to assess the relative impact of each step in its economic performance. For this purpose, a calculation base of 1 kg HDPE per h was used, and the flowsheet representing the simulated process is shown in Fig. 9.

The simulation was performed based on the assumption that the polymer was completely dissolved and precipitated. Mimicking the experimental results attained for α -pinene, a 70% recovery and recycling percentage was considered, and ethanol and water were recycled through distillation and recycled back to the respective operations. Further information on the simulation details can be found in section 2.9 in the ESI. †

The required make-up of each solvent was determined as shown in Table 4, as well as the respective costs. It is clear that the cost associated with ethanol and water is negligible in comparison with that of α -pinene. On the one hand, the unitary cost of this last compound is one order of magnitude above the remaining compounds, but on the other hand, its cost is mostly caused by the incomplete e ffi ciency of its recovery.

A more detailed economic evaluation would require further optimization of the energy expenditure, namely by performing heat integration where possible. Nevertheless, even with the suboptimal implemented configuration, the total estimated cost of utilities is 6.9 € per h, compared to 628.3 € per h for raw materials, which represents 99% of the operating costs estimated. Thus, it is evident that α -pinene is the major driver for the economic performance of the process, and therefore solvent recovery is the step of the process that will need the most profound improvements to make this process attractive for industrial implementation. Possible influential factors that could not be optimized at the laboratory scale are the agitation parameters during the precipitation step, the control of the particle dimensions after this step, and the possibility of recovering the solvent evaporated during the drying step.

Fig. 10 Schematic representation of the selective dissolution of HDPE and PET (illustration designed in BioRender).

In addition, the process was evaluated from the sustainability perspective, through the EcoScale methodology. 56 α -Pinene recovery is the step with the lowest yield, and thus its value, 70 wt%, was considered representative, corresponding to 15 penalty points. The solvents used do not correspond to any penalty from the price and safety criteria. The unitary operations are conventional, thus not requiring any penalty for the technical setup. The dissolution temperature is associated to 2 penalty points, and the separation and purification operations (filtration, distillation, and washing) account for 6 penalty points. The combined total is 77%, a value that results in a score ' excellent ' of the EcoScale. In spite of the great result, the greatest share of penalty points is associated with the solvent ' s recovery yield, thus reinforcing the need for improvement in this sense.

Both preliminary economic and sustainability analysis reached the conclusion that α -pinene recovery is the main bottleneck of the HDPE dissolution -precipitation process. Despite α -pinene current price, which limits the economic attractiveness of the process, its use should be preferred to that of conventional solvents since it is associated with much less safety and health hazards. 65 The health safety shall also be an important driver to facilitate the licensing of recovered polymers for use in consumer goods such as food packaging. Furthermore, the demand for this solvent has been growing for multiple applications, and its global market size is expected to continue increasing in the next years. 66 This trend has also been a driving force for the search for novel extraction and production methods, which may play an important role in the future price decrease of this compound. 61

text: Starting from a mixture with equal masses of HDPE and PET, HDPE (3 wt%) was dissolved first in α -pinene, at 110 °C, and the solution was filtered to remove the undissolved PET particles. These showed no modifications in comparison with the pristine material, and the process did not lead to any PET weight loss. The remaining procedure was carried out as usual, with HDPE being recovered as described in section 2.2.1, using ethanol as the antisolvent in the antisolvent/solvent ratio of 2/1, while PET was dissolved and recovered as described in section 2.2.2, dissolved in NaDES at 150 °C and precipitated with a mixture of ethanol and water. The attained results for polymer and solvent recovery yields are shown in Fig. 11 (and listed in Table S15 † ).

80 wt% HDPE was recovered, a value which agrees with the previous results obtained for the single polymer. The average recovery of α -pinene was 55 wt%, although the replicates are less coherent than in previous studies. This value is significantly lower than that observed for the individual studies, suggesting that the additional intermediate filtration step may lead to di ffi culties in the solvent removal during the precipitation step. In fact, it was observed that in general, HDPE solutions start to solidify as soon as the heat source is removed, and the intermediate filtration step to recover solid PET implies a larger amount of time spent between the end of the dissolution step and the addition of the antisolvent, which was not possible to mitigate with the laboratorial set-up used. In this way, it is possible that more solvent was entrapped in the polymer during precipitation, but the drying steps before and after grinding were still e ffi cient, as the FTIR analysis showed similar results to that of the individually dissolved samples (Fig. S27 † ).

Regarding PET, it was possible to recover 84 wt% from the initial amount of polymer, as well as 68 wt% DES. TGA analysis showed a weight loss of PET around 1%, peaking at 150 °C, and the polymer content was 98.4 wt%, according to the thermogram in Fig. S28. † Both the recovered PET and thymol : carvacrol NaDES were evaluated by FTIR analysis (in Fig. S29 and S30, † respectively), showing a complete correspondence with the spectra of the pristine materials.

The melting point of PET, evaluated by DSC, showed a small deviation between the virgin and the recovered samples. The crystallization point, on the other hand, increased around 10 °C. The estimated crystallinity was reduced around 7% with the recovery process, which might be caused by the quick crystallization during precipitation. These values are described in Table 6.

In conclusion, it was possible to selectively dissolve each polymer, e ffi ciently separate and recover both of them while maintaining their integrity and without causing significant changes to the pristine materials.

4. Conclusions

In this work, several natural solvents were screened for the dissolution of HDPE using the COSMO-SAC calculation model. The experiments performed on a selection of these solvents, limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene, showed good qualitative agreement with the predictions for dissolving HDPE. The influence of the experimental dissolution conditions (temperature and polymer content) was observed to influence the quantitative recovery of both the polymer and limonene, the solvent for which these were optimized. The a ffi nity between the antisolvent and the solvent was also determined to be an important factor for the adequate recovery of the system ' s constituents.

The solvent/antisolvent system α -pinene/ethanol was considered to be the most promising, as it allows simultaneously high polymer and solvent recovery with high purity while maintaining their integrity in comparison with the pristine materials. Besides the fact that α -pinene is, by itself, a better option than most common solvents used for these processes, regarding its greener origin and low hazard, the studies conducted also point to the suitability of this system for largescale implementation, as scale-up and solvent reuse experiments were successful. Within the presented sustainability metrics, the proposed process scores as ' excellent ' , but from an economic point of view, the critical aspect of process feasibility will be the recovery of the solvent, which still needs improvement.

The same system was successfully applied to selectively dissolve HDPE from a mixture containing PET, and both polymers and solvents were recovered with good yield and quality, thus indicating the suitability of this dissolution -precipitation process to handle complex waste streams that most recycling processes fail to address.

Recycling of polypropylene by the

dissolution/reprecipitation technique: I. A model study

J.G. Poulakis, C.D. Papaspyrides *

Received 26 August 1996; received in revised form 16 December 1996; accepted 27 December 1996

Abstract

The dissolution/reprecipitation technique is proposed here for the recycling of polypropylene (PP). It comprises dissolution of the plastic in an appropriate solvent, reprecipitation by using a non-solvent, thorough washing of the material obtained and drying. Furthermore, the solvent mixtures involved are separated by fractional distillation for reuse. In this paper model experiments on virgin material, either in the form of pellets or of commercial pipes for hot water piping applications, are presented. Xylene/acetone proved to be a particularly effective solvent/non-solvent system. Further investigation was focused on the effect of sample history through successive recycling cycles. The recycled grades were evaluated in terms of the following properties: melt flow index (MFI), crystallinity, mechanical performance in tensile and impact mode and grain size analysis. The properties of the recycled grades proved to have no substantial difference from the starting material. © 1997 Elsevier Science B.V.

Keywords: Recycling; Polypropylene; Dissolution/precipitation technique; Evaluation; Physical properties

* Corresponding author.

1. Introduction

Before dealing with the future of plastic waste, it is useful to remember that plastics play an important role in reducing the environmental impact in many current applications, as packaging, automotive and building industry [1].

It is time to consider how the efficiency of plastics can be incorporated in a comprehensive strategy for a future ecological' economy and the only way out is to find effective ways of disposal the plastic wastes. Unfortunately, current recovery rates for all materials in the municipal solid  waste stream, with the exception of food wastes, exceed that of plastics. Paper is estimated at a 26% recovery rate, aluminium at 32% and glass at 12%. Plastic is just now reaching an approximate rate of 1% [2]. This low rate has been a major concern to the plastic industry since it reinforces the belief that plastics are not recyclable.

Approaches to plastics recycling mainly include [3,4]: (i) incinerated' plastic behaves as a fuel — 1 ton of plastic gives off as much energy as 1 ton of oil (energy recycling' quaternary recycling); (ii) cracked' or depolymerized', plastic returns into a petrochemical product or monomer, which will be transformed again into plastic (chemical conversion or chemical recycling'— tertiary -wes  o o wor  or  ( oor ondary recycling).

2. Recycling methods

2.1. Quaternary recycling

According to the first option, the recovery of the locked-in' energy (Quaternary Recycling) is aimed by direct incineration and combustion or conversion to the so called Refuse Derived Fuel [5,6]. This recycling option is currently the most effective way to reduce the volume of organic material which, due to a lack of other recycling possibilities, may then be ended in landfilling disposal. Quaternary recycling has been widely accused as ecologically unacceptable due to the health risk from airborne toxics. Nevertheless, especially polypropylene is an easily burning hydrocarbon product, free from chlorine, sulphur, heavy metals. Combustion by-products are only water, CO2 and negligible quantities of ashes. So when compared to the usual sulphur-containing fuel oils, PP can be considered a pollution-free white coal' [7].

2.2. Tertiary recycling

Chemical recycling (Tertiary Recycling) includes pyrolysis, glycolysis, alcoholysis and hydrolysis. In principle, cleavage of the polymer chains results in chemical products of lower molecular weight distribution or even in the original intermediates (monomers) which can be used for another complete cycle of polymerization. In the literature results are referred on the glycolysis of poly(ethylene terephthalate), alcoholysis of polyurethanes, hydrolysis of nylon 6 and pyrolysis of polypropylene [2,8-10]. However, both incineration and chemical recycling are characterized by the fact that the value added during polymerization is lost. At current polymer prices this comprises a major disadvantage [11].

2.3. Primary recycling

In terms of direct recovery (Primary Recycling), reprocessing in the melt phase remains the most popular recycling technique. It ensures simplicity and low cost, especially when done in-plant' and feeding with clean, uncontaminated, single-type plastic scrap of controlled history [12]. Nevertheless, this route often leads to degraded products, because during processing or in-service use a plastic may undergo chemical reactions that can affect its physical properties. If these properties are affected to any marked extent the plastic may become unsuitable for its original use. Screw extrusion is the most damaging procedure that polymers could be subjected to. It involves the mechanical scission of the polymer chain in its viscous environment in the polymer melt. This produces highly reactive macroradicals at the ends of the chain which, in the presence of the small amounts of oxygen dissolved in the polymer, cannot recombine but form peroxyl radicals and hydroperoxides [13].

In particular, the thermodynamic incompatibility of chemically different polymers leads to poor mechanical performance of the resultant mixtures, usually inferior to that of the original components [14].

In particular:

Solubility based processes, as an alternative route of secondary recycling by type, include stages of treating plastic waste with solvents so that the polymeric materials are dissolved and then recovered by several ways:

— PP moldings were dissolved in toluene or xylene at 100–110°C and the polymer was obtained by cooling while stirring in the form of powder [17]. Recycling of PP can also be achieved by the dissolution/reprecipitation technique according to which the polymer waste is dissolved in a typical solvent, such as tetrachloroethylene and reprecipitated by methyl cellusolve acting as non-solvent

[18]. Similar is the process proposed by Drain et al. [19] concerning PP. The process comprises dissolution of polypropylene in tetrachloroethylene, subsequent slow cooling, centrifugation, complete drying and solvent recovery by bed drying in a hot gas stream. On the other hand, PS foam was recovered by being dissolved in p-xylene at room temperature, filtered and the filtrate was stirred with methanol to precipitate 100% polystyrene powder which was recovered by filtration [20]. Another process uses tetrahydrofuran or cyclohexanone as solvent and methanol or eh on stn n oi n n s   n  otin materials [21]. Nylon 6 fiber waste was dissolved in a mixture of methanol and water in an autoclave at 135-143°C and cooled at 80-85°C to give fine powder [22].

In our laboratory a dissolution/reprecipitation technique has been studied, aiming to obtain recycled thermoplastics of the highest possible quality. The technique proposed consists of the following stages: (a) cutting the wastes into smaller pieces and washing with water if necessary; (b) dissolution to the highest possible concentration; (c) filtration of the solution under pressure to separate any insoluble ingredients, (d) precipitation of the polymer still in solution by means of non-solvents and (e) filtration, washing the polymer obtained and drying. Furthermore, the solvent/non-solvent mixtures involved are separated by fractional distillation for reuse.

Results published so far include recycling of rigid poly(vinyl chloride) bottles [23,24], polystyrene waste foam [25,26], poly(methyl methacrylate) decorative sheets [27,28], low density polyethylene film for greenhouses [29,30] and high density polyethylene bottles for agrochemicals packaging [31].

Technologies that impart above-average heat deflection temperature, stiffness, hardness, clarity, gloss and barrier to grades establish polypropylene into uses held by higher-priced plastics and traditional materials [32]. Moreover, recycling of polypropylene has a profound environmental impact since it is one major component of the municipal solid waste plastic frame. In 1994 polypropylene constituted about 20% (5 m tonnes) of the total plastics consumption in Western Europe (25.5 m tonnes) [33].

In this paper, the dissolution/reprecipitation technique is applied for the recycling of PP and the combination of xylene/acetone is evaluated under the following criteria: (i) precipitation of the polymer in an acceptable form (granules), (ii) total recovery of the polymer, (iii) total recovery of the solvents employed, (iv) limited quantities, as much as possible, of the solvent and non-solvent employed. Xylene is an effective solvent of PP [17] while acetone is very successful as a non-solvent because the polymer can be precipitated in the form of powder without the formation of gelling lumps. This quenching/precipitating role of acetone to yield a flaky brittle product has been dealt in detail when the dissolution/reprecipitation of polyolefins was studied [29].

Pre   ru l  r  r  Arlir pipes are recycled as an example of a widely used end-product. Furthermore, it seemed worthwhile to prove that the dissolution/reprecipitation process can be safely applied in successive cycles, since it is carried out at very mild temperatures, in contrast with melt recycling. As a model experiment, two successive recycling cycles were applied to virgin PP to detect any variation in the structure of the end-products. Characterization studies on the recycled grades were focused on melt flow rate, crystallinity, mechanical properties retention (tensile and impact tests) as well as grain size distribution. The data collected can be safely applied in a selective dissolution/reprecipitation cycle in which different grades of plastic waste are separated by means of differences in solubility [16].

3.1. Materials

3.2. Polymer recovery by the solvent process

Pellets of virgin PP or PP pipes cut into pieces were dissolved into xylene up to the level of 0.15 kg·1- at 135°C. The upper concentration level was kept at this value, because when increasing further the concentration, the so-uo  md escccod o o    sos os n onr imental conditions. A 2 1 reaction vessel, fitted with stirrer, reflux condenser and thermometer was employed. The solution obtained was filtered under pressure through a Seitz Merkur EF 6/03 device, using 5500 Seitz-T-filter sheets of exclusion size in the range of 20-70 μm. V, 1 of acetone was then properly added to the filtrate and the polymer contained was precipitated. The polymer grains were isolated by filtration under vacuum. The phase -separated solvents were then replaced by V2 l of acetone and stirring was again applied for 30 min. This washing procedure was repeated once more (V3 l acetone employed). Finally, the polymer grains were dried in a vacuum chamber at 90°C for 10 h. This once recycled grade represented by the code name 1st REC, was again subjected to the same procedure to produce the twice recycled grade (2nd REC). The solvent/non-solvent mixture collected was separated for reuse in a distillation column (0.85 m height) filled with Raching rings and equipped at the top with a side condenser.

3.5. Tensile tests

Tensile tests were carried out using an Instron tensile machine in standard laboratory atmosphere. The specimens were tested according to the D638-76 ASTM method with a rate of extension equal to 50 mm/min for the determination of the tensile strength at yield and break and elongation at break and 1 mm/min for the modulus of elasticity.

Specimens were prepared by compression moulding and subsequent cutting. A hydraulic thermopress was employed under the following conditions: temperature, 270–290°C; pressure, 8.85 MPa; time of heating, 10 min. The same exactly cooling rate was always followed to exclude interference with processing history effects.

4.2. Melt flow index (MFI)

With regard to the melt flow index of virgin and recycled materials (Table 2), increased values for the recycled grades are observed. This behavior could be possibly related with some degradation occurring during the MFI measurement itself because of not adding any antioxidant in the recycled polymer mass. It should be pointed out that in polypropylene degradation is manifested either by reaction with oxygen at elevated temperatures or by chain scission, causing an increase in melt flow (thermal/oxidative degradation) [13,34].

It is worthwhile to mention here that a direct comparison between virgin material and its recycled grades is undoubtedly meaningful, but this is not necessarily the case between the latter and the material recycled from waste pipes. This is because the pipes manufacture process implies completely different history of the material in terms of both processing and additives employed.

The data also suggest that sample history has no practical effect on the mechanical properties of the recycled grades.

4.5. Grain size analysis

According to the grain size analysis (Table 5), over 87% of the recycled polymer mass has a grain size smaller than 1 mm, suitable for feeding polypropylene processing units.

5. Conclusions

The dissolution/reprecipitation technique is studied to recycle polypropylene based waste. Model experiments were run first on virgin pellets and then on polypropylene pipes for hot water piping applications. Concentrated solutions in xylene were employed (0.15 kg·1– ') and the polymer was precipitated, in the form of small grains, through the addition of acetone. Excellent recoveries in polymer and solvents are achieved, while all properties tested remained practically intact. An evaluation of the effect of the sample history on the properties of the recycled product has been also accomplished, but no considerable differences were monitored. Larger scale experiments are expected to result in even higher concentration levels and better recovery values for the solvents used. In accordance with previous studies, the information established provide fundamental input for the development of a selective dissolution process dealing with mixtures of waste plastics.

Although this original packaging was initially made of waxed  paper,  today  multilayer  Tetra  Pak ® packaging  is  a  result  of laminated stiff paper (75 wt%), LDPE (20 wt%) and aluminium foil (5 wt %) (Rausing, 1969; Tetra Pak International, 2020b). According to Tetra Pak Company -part of Tetra Laval Group -in 2019 over 160 countries around the world were supplied with more than 190 billion Tetra Pak ® packages while post-consumer Tetra Pak ® car tons were recycled by Tetra Pak itself with a rate of 26% (Tetra Pak International, 2020d).

The technologies generally applied to PCBCs are divided into those that reprocess them as a mixture and those that include a prior step for removing the cellulosic fibers.

Tetra  Pak  cartons,  i.e.  multilayer  packaging  consisting  of  paper,  low  density  polyethylene  (LDPE)  and aluminium, are widely used as aseptic packages in the food and beverage industry. Paper can be easily recovered from this type of post-consumer beverage cartons (PCBCs) by the pulp industry. The remaining LDPE/aluminium by-product, however, cannot be easily separated to its constituents so currently it is mostly downcycled or used for energy recovery. The aim of this work is to develop an effective process that separates and recovers LDPE and aluminium of high purity and good quality from Tetra Pak cartons. To this purpose, following paper recovery by hydropulping, LDPE and aluminium are separated using a selective dissolution-precipitation (SDP) process. The recovered LDPE is characterized by FTIR spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning (DSC) and melt flow rate (MFR) measurements. The findings reveal that the SDP separation process is an effective method to recover LDPE and aluminium from PCBCs.

Such a treatment, however, is not efficient due to the low heating value and other characteristics of paper (moisture content, high ash value) which constitutes the main material of beverage cartons. Alternatively, PCBCs are downcycled and used for the produc tion of laminated boards or various products of different shapes by hot pressing shreds of PCBCs (Zawadiak et al., 2017).

In the second case, removal of paper is carried out through hydro pulping: in the presence of water, cellulosic fibers are separated from plastic and aluminium layers by centrifugal forces (Selke, 2016). Re siduals  of  paper  recovery,  i.e.  outer  LDPE  layer  and  Al-PE  laminate, usually contain up to 5% paper fibers. They are mostly used in thermal processes for energy recovery due to their high heating value. A typical application is their use in cement industry, since the Al2O3 that is formed is  useful  for  cement  production (Zawadiak et al., 2017). Gasification applications also exist, such as Alcoa Aluminio, Klabin and TSL Ambi ental plant in Brazil which uses plasma gasification to transform plastic into  paraffin  and  recover  aluminium  in  its  pure  form  (BusinessWire, 2005).  Also,  pyrolysis  is  applied  in  Stora  Enso ' s  facilities  in  Spain exposing the Al-PE residue from the hydropulping process to 400 °C in an  oxygen  free  chamber. On the other hand, Al and PE can be also recovered from the Al-PE laminates  by  breaking  the  mechanical  bonds  that  keep  the  layers together.  Zhang  et  al.  (2009)  achieved  Al-PE  delamination  using aqueous solutions of organic acids. Al partially dissolved in the solution, so  both  Al  and  acid  were  consumed  to  some  extent.  Reaction  time, temperature, solid size and the type of acid affected separation time and Al loss, which for the optimum conditions was 4.7%. Delamination using mixed  organic  solvents  has  been  also  investigated  by  Zhang  et  al. (2014). In this case delamination occurred due to the swelling of PE. Some  material  loss  was  observed,  lower  that  the  one  obtained  with separation with organic acids. Concerning the efficiency of the separa tion, SEM images of the PE and Al surfaces indicated molecular structure consisting of C, O and Al (Zhang et al., 2015). Al-PE delamination has also found industrial application in China. (Zawadiak et al., 2017).

Finally, solvent-based PE extraction methods have been studied for the  separation  of  Al-PE  laminates  coming  from  PCBCs,  where  PE  is dissolved in an organic solvent and separated from the undissolved Al (Kaiser et al., 2018; Lindner, 2011; APK AG). This type of processes, referred to as Selective Dissolution-Precipitation (SDP), is grounded on controlling  and  adjusting  polymer ' s  solubility  by  changing  solvent and/or dissolution conditions and can be effective either for separating mixtures of plastics or for removing impurities/additives from post used plastics. The basic steps of SDP for recovering a certain polymer with high purity involve dissolution of the polymer of interest in properly selected solvent (S) and conditions, removal of the non-dissolved ma terial through filtration and addition of a non-solvent or anti-solvent (AS) so that the polymer precipitates again (Zhao et al., 2018). Start ing from four decades ago, SDP has been extensively studied and suc cessful experimental work has been carried out for recycling a variety of high quality polymers from post-used plastics, such as PVC (Achilias et  al.,  2009b;  Kampouris  et  al.,  1986;  Papaspyrides  and  Diakoulaki, 1986), PS (Achilias et al., 2009a, 2009b; Kampouris et al., 1987;1988; Schlummer et al., 2017), LDPE (Achilias et al., 2009b; Achilias et al., 2007; Papaspyrides et al., 1994), HDPE (Achilias et al., 2007; Poulakis

text: Interest on SDP has gradually faded, mainly because of the low cost of polymers, but lately it has boosted again, since the need to obtain high purity  recyclates  from  plastic  waste  is  recognized  (Sherwood,  2019; Ügdüler et al., 2020). Introduction of a variety of chemical additives into polymers to improve their performance depending on the application, as well as development of composite materials with specific characteristics have resulted to plastic waste of complex composition, which cannot be effectively sorted by mechanical methods and still end up in landfill or are recycled into poor quality plastics (Wagner and Schlummer, 2020). SDP  offers  the  ability  to  remove  additives  (Schlummer  and  M ¨ aurer, 2006) and reinforcements from polymers (Cousins et al., 2019; Knap pich et al., 2019; Tapper et al., 2019) and recycle polymers with quality that meets that of their virgin counterparts, broadening the closed-loop recycling options.

This work aims to the effective separation of PCBCs to their con stituents.  To  this  purpose  hydropulping is  applied for  paper  removal followed  by  SDP  to  separate  the  Al-PE  laminate.  Hydropulping  is  a simple,  well-known  and  widely  applied  technique,  also  for  paper removal from PCBCs, so in this study it is used to provide the Al-PE input material  for  SDP  and  is  examined  only  in  terms  of  the  recoveries  it yields. On the other hand, with regards to SDP, this paper aims to prove its technological feasibility for the separation of Al-PE to recyclates of high quality with high recovery ratios. In this context, the purity of the separated Al and LDPE are examined while for LDPE several properties related to its quality and reprocessability are also investigated.

2. Experimental

2.1. Chemicals and materials

For hydropulping, deionized tap water was used. For SDP, analytical grade xylene and isopropanol obtained from Fisher Scientific were used. Regarding the Tetra Pak ® packages, typical post-used milk and juice containers  were  utilized.  The  lids  were  removed  and  packages  were washed, dried, flattened and stored.

2.2. Separation processes

2.2.1. Hydropulping process

PCBCs were cut and mixed with water at a ratio of 1:25 (g/L). The mixture was stirred at 400 rpm for 2 h at ambient temperature until paper swelled and PCBC was split to outer LDPE/paper and inner LDPE/ Al/paper parts. Stirring continued for 3 more hours at 700 rpm to further remove paper fibers from the plastic surfaces. During stirring, water was absorbed by cellulosic fibers forming paper pulp, while the centrifugal forces of stirring contributed to the separation of the pulp from LDPE and aluminium. When hydropulping was completed, the mixture was filtered in order to remove paper pulp from the Al-PE laminate and outer LDPE layer, which were then subjected to an additional hydropulping cycle for 1 h at 700 rpm, in order to remove as much residual paper as possible. Finally, the obtained pulp was filtered for water removal and then  compressed and dried in a Gallenkamp OVA031.XX1.5 vacuum oven at 100 mbar and 40 °C until weight stabilization was observed, resulting to stiff paper. The process flowsheet is shown in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2. Hydropulping process.

Fig. 3. Selective Dissolution - Precipitation process.

2.2.2. Selective dissolution - Precipitation process

Selective  Dissolution  -  Precipitation  (SDP)  method  was  applied separately to the Al-PE laminates and the outer PE layers so as to be able to compare the quality of the two recyclates. Based on previous work (Pappa et al., 2001) xylene is utilized as solvent (S) for LDPE dissolution and isopropanol as antisolvent (AS) to precipitate it.

In the first case, Al-PE laminate pieces and xylene, were fed at a ratio of 1:15 (g/mL) into a jacketed, vessel. The mixture was heated to 85 °C and stirred at 300 rpm for 2 h. A condenser was connected to the top of the vessel to minimize solvent losses. The hot solution was filtered to remove insoluble materials (aluminium and paper fibre residuals). The filtrate  was  led  to  another  jacketed  and  stirred  vessel,  where  roomtemperature isopropanol was added drop by drop up to a final ratio of 1.8 AS/S, causing precipitation of the plastic in fine granules, stirring conditions  similar  to  those  of  dissolution.  During  precipitation,  the temperature of the solution was kept at 85 °C by hot-oil circulation in the vessel ' s jacket. Then, heating was interrupted and the mixture was stirred until it reached ambient temperature, then filtered through filter paper and finally compressed to further reduce the remaining S/AS. In order  to  increase  LDPE  recovery  as  well  as  to  further  purify  Al,  the insoluble  material  of  the  first  filtration  was  subjected  to  two  more similar SDP cycles. After the 3rd dissolution the hot solution was first coarse-filtered for Al recovery and then fine-filtered for paper removal. The process flowsheet is shown in Fig. 3.

In the second case, outer LDPE layer was dissolved in xylene at a ratio of 1:20 (g/mL), filtered to remove residual paper, precipitated by means of  AS  addition  (1.9  AS/S  ratio),  filtered  for  AS/S  removal  and  com pressed.  The  recycled  inner  and  outer  LDPE  were  finally  dried  in  a Gallenkamp OVA031.XX1.5 vacuum oven at 100 mbar and 40 °C until their weight stabilized, which typically occurred in less than 3 h.

Fig. 4. Hydropulping products from PCBCs: (a) paper, (b) Al-PE laminates (c) outer LDPE.

2.2.3. Effect of solvent purity on dissolution

A  closed-loop  SDP  process  requires  that  the  resulting  xylene/iso propanol  mixture  is  separated  and  reused.  The  higher  the  solvent tolerance in antisolvent presence, keeping at the same time its dissolu tion capability, the lower the corresponding separation cost.

The limit of isopropanol content in xylene that ensures total disso lution of PE at the process conditions applied in this work was experi mentally  determined.  To  this  purpose,  fine  white  powder  of  LDPE, obtained from the SDP process, was dissolved in pure xylene at a con centration equal to 80 g/L, as described in the previous section. After dissolution, isopropanol was gradually added to the solution, up to the point where precipitation was visually observed.

Furthermore, the effect of isopropanol presence on polymer disso lution time at 85 °C was examined. To this purpose quantities of filmgrade  LDPE  pellets  were  added  into  pure  xylene  and  a  mixture  of xylene/isopropanol (85/15 v/v), which were heated at 85 °C and stirred at 250 rpm, in such amounts so as to obtain final concentrations of 80 g/ L for each solvent. The time needed for total dissolution was measured in each case.

2.3. Characterization

2.3.1. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted on samples of 4 -5 mg in a Mettler Toledo TGA/SDTA851e thermobalance with heating rate equal to 10 °C min 1 from 25 to 800 °C under nitrogen flow (10 mL min 1 ). The onset decomposition temperature was defined as the tem perature at 5% weight loss ( T d,  5%), the degradation temperature ( T d) was determined at the maximum rate of weight loss, and the char yield as the% residue at 800 °C.

2.3.2. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)

Differential  scanning  calorimetry  (DSC)  measurements  were  per formed on samples of 8 -10 mg in a Perkin Elmer DSC 6 differential scanning calorimeter with a heating rate of 10 °C min 1 from 25 to 200 °C under nitrogen flow (10 mL min 1 ). All samples were submitted to  heating-cooling-heating  cycles  in  order  to  eliminate  their  thermal history. Melt crystallization temperature ( T c) was determined from the cooling curves and melting temperature ( T m) was determined from the 2nd heating curves along with the mass fraction crystallinity ( XC .,%) using the equation:

XC % = Δ Hf Δ H 0 ⋅100 (1)

where, Δ Hf is the heat of fusion of the sample (J g 1 ) and Δ H 0 is the heat of  fusion  of  100%  crystalline  polymer  (J g 1 ).  For  LDPE, Δ H 0 is considered equal to 70 cal g 1 (293.76 J g 1 ) (Fischer and Hinrichsen, 1966).

2.3.3. Melt flow rate (MFR)

In order to check the melt reprocessability of the recovered material the  MFR  of  LDPE  was  measured  according  to  procedure  A  of  ASTM D1238, 2013. The temperature was fixed at 190 °C and a capillary die, with length of 8 mm and diameter of 2.095 mm along with a driving weight  of  2.16  kg  were  used  for  the  measurements.  The  procedure involved cutting off the extrudate at specific time intervals as it exited the rheometer, weighing the pieces to determine the average mass and extrapolating to the mass extruded in 10 min by using the equation:

MFR = 600 t ⋅ w (2)

where, t ( sec ) is the time interval and w (g) is the weight of the extrudate material.

2.3.4. Fourier transform infrared spectrometers (FTIR)

FTIR analysis was conducted using a JASCO FT/IR-4200 spectrom eter, performing a total of 32 scans in the range 4000 -400 cm 1 at room temperature, displayed as absorbence vs. wavenumber. A background spectrum was subtracted before sample analysis. Sample was in the form of powder dispersion in a KBr tablet. The spectrum of the examined PE was compared with literature data (Asensio et al., 2009; Gardette et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2018; Noda et al., 2007) for material identification and observation of degradation signs.

The carbonyl index ( CI ) was calculated as the ratio of the maximum absorption of the carbonyl, C = O , band around 1650 -1800 cm 1 to the methylene, (CH2), scissoring band absorption around 1420 -1480 cm 1 , using the following equation (Wang et al., 2017):

CI = Absorption 1650 1800 cm 1 Absorption 1420 1480 cm 1 (3)

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Separation processes

A  number  of  batches  were  performed  to  study  the  separation  of PCBCs to their constituents, i.e. paper, LDPE and Al. In this section the results of a typical batch are presented.

3.1.1. Hydropulping process

The hydropulping process was conducted in a 30 L stirring vessel where 502.5 g of PCBCs (8 × 8 cm pieces) and 20 L of water were stirred for 5 h in total. The additional step for residual paper removal of the secondary products lasted 1 hour.

The process resulted to paper, free of aluminium and plastic (Fig. 4 (a)), Al-PE laminates, consisted of an Al layer between two LDPE layers (Fig. 4 (b)) and the outer LDPE layers which were coloured (Fig. 4 (c)).

It is concluded that the experimental composition of the PCBCs is in good agreement with the theoretical composition of Tetra Pak ® and that high paper recovery (96.9% of the typical paper content) is achieved with hydropulping.

3.1.2. Selective dissolution -precipitation process

SDP was applied to 10.02 g of Al-PE laminate (1 × 1 cm pieces) using xylene as S and isopropanol as AS. For the 1st, 2nd and 3rd SDP cycle, 145, 121 and 110 mL of S were used and 262, 220 and 193 mL of AS, respectively. Heating (85 °C) and stirring (300 rpm) were applied for 2 h for the 1st dissolution cycle, to ensure high-extent LDPE dissolution, and 1 hour for the 2nd and 3rd ones. SDP resulted in fine LDPE white powder (Fig. 5 (a)) and aluminium layers (Fig. 5 (b)). After each SDP cycle the products ' mass was measured (Table 3). Application of three successive cycles was necessary in order to remove practically all plastic from the aluminium foil and reach high LDPE recovery.

Concerning the outer LDPE layer, 7.09 g were dissolved for 2 h in 141 mL S and LDPE precipitated with the addition of 263 mL AS. In this case, recycled LDPE was received as light-coloured agglomerates (Fig. 5 (c)) which indicates the presence of impurities.

3.1.3. Effect of solvent purity on dissolution

4.1 g of recycled LDPE powder were dissolved in 50 mL xylene (S). When dissolution was completed AS was gradually added at a rate of 1 mL/min.  After  the  addition  of  each  mL,  the  mixture  was  left  under stirring for 1 min, and then to rest for another 2 min. At the addition of 13 mL of AS, precipitation was observed and the procedure ended. The final concentration of LDPE in the xylene/isopropanol was calculated equal to 65.1 g/L. Based on the above, it was concluded that presence of isopropanol  up  to  20.6%  v/v  does  not  affect  dissolution  of  LDPE  in xylene, at least not at concentrations like those employed in this work for Al-PE. This suggests that it is not necessary to separate the S/AS mixture to high purity streams for reuse, since recycled xylene with less than ~20% v/v isopropanol is acceptable for mixture concentration up to 65.1 g/L. This is expected to have a positive effect on the distillation

cost especially for large scale application.

Regarding the effect of solvent purity on dissolution time, 8 g of filmgrade LDPE pellets were added in 100 mL of each solvent, which was already heated. It was found that, for solutions of 80 g/L the presence of 15%  v/v  isopropanol  prolongs  dissolution  time  from  35  to  43  min (approximately 23%). This should be taken into account in a future step for the optimization and economic evaluation of the process.

3.1.4. Discussion on the sdp solvent requirements

The advantage of SDP to produce recycled plastics of high quality and in proper form for further processing is somewhat countervailed by the large solvent requirements. The dissolved plastic concentration that can be achieved is usually bounded by the solution viscosity, which affects stirring, filtration, etc., especially in a lab-scale apparatus. In this work, polymer solutions up to 50 g/L were obtained, so that they could be  easily  manageable  with  the  available  lab-scale  equipment.  This resulted to a ratio of 133 kg solvents per kg recycled LDPE, which is high both from a technological and an economic point of view and needs to be optimized for scale-up. There is, however, the possibility to use more concentrated solutions as pointed out by Papaspyrides et al., (1994) who applied SDP for LDPE recycling, using LDPE solutions up to 300 g/L in toluene and up to 200 g/L in xylene. Reducing the amount of solvent leads also to the reduction of antisolvent quantities. This suggests that there  is  a  large  margin  for  solvents  saving  and  consequently  lower distillation cost by using more effective equipment.

3.2.3. Chemical structure

FTIR spectrum (Fig. 8 (a)) of the recovered inner LDPE showed the characteristic IR bands of polyethylene (Asensio et al., 2009; Gardette

0,7

et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2018; Noda et al., 2007): the stretching vibration of  carbon-hydrogen  (C -H)  group  of  the  main  polymeric  chain  at 2850 -2918 cm 1 , the wagging vibration of the methylene group (CH2) at 1466 cm 1 and the rocking vibration of CH2 at 719 cm 1 . These two last  bands  present  shoulders  at  1444  cm 1 and at  around 729 cm 1 respectively, which are attributed to the branched character of LDPE, and cannot be found in linear  structures  like  HDPE  (Martínez-Romo et al., 2015). The bending vibration of the methyl group (CH3) at 1377 cm 1 can also be seen and its intensity is proportional to branched chain ends (Jung et al., 2018).

Specific regions of the spectrum were observed to investigate any degradation of the material attributed to the herein applied separation process. The main degradation products of the polyolefins are hydroxyl (-OH)  (3200  -  3650  cm 1 ),  carbonyl  (C = O )  (1630  -  1850  cm 1 ), methylene ( = CH2) (1620 - 1680 cm 1 )  and vinyl (-CH --CH2) (800 1000 cm 1 )  groups  (Moldovan  et  al.,  2012).  Zero  absorbence  in  the region of 900 cm 1 (Fig. 8 (b)) proved the absence of -CH --CH2 groups. However, the appearance of a weak peak at 1701 cm 1 (Fig.  8  (c)) indicated the presence of C = O and the carbonyl index of the recycled LDPE was calculated 0.17. This value is considered low compared to aged LDPE samples after 500 h UV exposure (Luyt et al., 2020) and after 800  h  UV  exposure  (Gulmine  et  al.,  (2003)  that  present  CI > 1. Comparing the results with infrared spectrums of pure LDPE and Al/PE composite obtained from post-consumer aseptic packaging (Lopes and Felisberti,  2006),  it  was  concluded  that  the  polymer  degradation possibly takes place due to processing of LDPE films (Andersson and Wesslén, 2003), production of the multilayer composite or even envi ronmental factors, rather than SDP itself.

4. Conclusions

In  the  present  study,  post-consumer  Tetra  Pak ® PCBCs,  were processed by hydropulping followed by Selective DissolutionPrecipitation (SDP), leading to high recovery of paper, aluminium and LDPE.  The  identified  losses  are  related  to  paper  fibers  and  can  be managed with proper design and technical improvement of the process. LDPE coming from the inner layers was recovered as white powder of high  purity  with  thermal  properties  similar  to  those  of  pure  LDPE. Thermal  analysis  showed  only  some  restricted  degradation,  possibly originated from the virgin LDPE processing rather than the laminate recycling with SDP. On the other hand, LDPE from the outer plastic layer still contained impurities, such as printing inks, suggesting that further purification may be needed depending on the application it is destined for. It was also shown that the presence of AS in the S up to a certain content  does  not  affect  its  dissolution  ability  and  consequently  the effectiveness of the process. This can lead to a reduction of the energy requirements of the process coming from the Solvent/Antisolvent (S/ AS) separation for large scale applications. It, however, increases the time needed for dissolution. In conclusion, the combination of hydro pulping for paper recovery with Selective Dissolution-Precipitation for Al-PE separation is a very promising approach which recovers all the valuable materials that compose Tetra Pak ® cartons.

ABSTRACT: Direct mechanical recycling of multilayer plastic packaging (MPP) leads to downcycling, as the costly barrier layer loses economic value and often degrades the quality of the recycled blend. In this study, a five-layer MPP film consisting of low-density polyethylene (LDPE) structural layers, maleic anhydride-grafted linear LDPE (MAg -LLDPE) tie layers, and an ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) barrier layer was treated with formic acid to selectively extract the EVOH. The effects of the solvent concentration, temperature, sample size, and solvent-to-sample ratio on dissolution efficiency were evaluated, and optimal conditions were identified and scaled in a pilot setup. The polyolefins reclaimed after EVOH extraction were reprocessed into a blend through a conventional mechanical recycling process.

Article Recommendations

Mechanical testing showed that the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited enhanced performance compared to the MPP film blend obtained via direct mechanical recycling and demonstrated properties comparable to those of virgin LDPE. Analysis of the chemical structure and rheological behavior revealed that chemical changes of the MAg -LLDPE tie layer via hydrolysis and ring-opening reactions played a key role in affecting intermolecular interactions and consequently the mechanical performance of the reclaimed polyolefin blend. Moreover, the thermal properties of the reclaimed polyolefin blend remained largely consistent with those of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend without dissolution treatment. These findings demonstrate that solvent-based selective dissolution is a practical and scalable method for extracting EVOH and reclaiming polyolefins, enabling subsequent mechanical recycling with satisfactory results.

KEYWORDS: recycling, multilayer food packaging, oxygen barrier layer, tie layer, selective dissolution, polyethylene

1. INTRODUCTION

As plastic production continues to rise and less than 10% of plastic waste is recycled globally, the environmental and health concerns associated with plastic pollution have driven longstanding efforts to develop effective recycling strategies. 1,2 Among all plastic applications, packaging is the most prevalent, accounting for 40%, with a considerable portion being multilayer plastic packaging (MPP), widely used for food packaging. 3 -6 MPP refers to packaging materials composed of multiple layers of different polymers, each designed to provide specific functional properties and laminated together using tie layers between the polymer layers. 7,8 In MPP used in the food industry, polyolefins such as polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) are commonly used as structural layers to provide the functions of mechanical strength, moisture resistance, and sealability, while ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) or nylon serves as the oxygen barrier layer, and maleic anhydride (MA)-grafted PP or PE is employed as the tie layer. 3,9 -11

Compared to single-layer plastic packaging, MPP has garnered increasing attention due to its enhanced functionality and superior ability to extend the shelf life of food products, leading to rapid growth in both its annual production and market share. 12,13 However, the complex composition of MPP poses significant challenges for recycling, as current commercial techniques struggle to identify, sort, and separate its individual layers. 14 -16 Consequently, MPP is typically
