categorized as mixed plastic waste under resin identification code # 7 and often ends up being incinerated or landfilled, resulting in environmental pollution and resource waste. 9,17 Developing cost-effective and scalable recycling methods for MPP has attracted significant attention from stakeholders in both the industrial and academic communities. 18,19

A range of strategies has been explored to recycle MPP, generally classified into: (1) physical recycling, including both mechanical recycling and solvent-based dissolution -precipitation; (2) chemical recycling, including pyrolysis, gasification, and depolymerization; and (3) delamination, which can be either physical or chemical depending on the method used. 18,20 Among these, mechanical recycling, which commonly involves direct reprocessing of plastic waste through well-established techniques such as thermal compounding, injection molding, or extrusion, is considered the most cost-effective and industrially viable option due to its low energy requirements, technical feasibility, minimal environmental impact, and operational simplicity. 18,21,22 However, direct mechanical recycling of MPP containing barrier materials such as EVOH, one of the most widely used oxygen barriers, leads to significant economic loss. Specifically, EVOH is considerably more expensive than polyolefins and, when combined with them in low-value applications, its original high value is lost. 23,24

Moreover, the presence of EVOH generally has a negative impact on the mechanical properties of the blend because it is incompatible with polyolefins and highly prone to thermooxidative degradation under high temperatures and oxygen atmosphere resulting in cross-linked structures, which are typically encountered during mechanical recycling processes. 18,25 For example, Briassoulis et al. 10 investigated the effect of EVOH on the mechanical properties of an MPP composed of low-density PE (LDPE) and linear LDPE (LLDPE) structural layers, along with a MA-grafted LLDPE (MAg -LLDPE) tie layer. They found that the presence of an EVOH barrier layer resulted in lower tensile strength and elongation at break compared to MPP without EVOH. A systematic study on the changes in the mechanical performance of MPP blends during mechanical recycling was also reported in our previous work. 26 It was observed that the mechanical performance of the MPP blend increased at the initial stage, as the MAg -LLDPE tie layer acted as a coupling agent providing good compatibility between LDPE and EVOH. However, the performance declined significantly after several recycling cycles due to EVOH gelation, which led to severe phase separation between the constituent polymers. Additionally, the color of the MPP blend progressively darkened with increasing cycles due to thermo-oxidative degradation which affects its aesthetics in other applications. Therefore, both economic and performance considerations establish the necessity of extracting the EVOH prior to mechanical recycling. Effective extraction of EVOH for potential reutilization not only saves the economic cost of producing virgin EVOH but also avoids the detrimental effect of the degraded EVOH on the properties of the mechanically recycled MPP.

Solvent-based dissolution -precipitation has recently emerged as one of the most widely studied strategies for MPP recycling, with several studies focusing on EVOHcontaining MPP and reporting that EVOH can be successfully extracted using solvents, and that the recovered EVOH obtained through precipitation exhibited chemical character-

́

istics and thermal properties comparable to those of virgin EVOH. 27 -30 Notably, Walker et al. 27 developed a solventtargeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process to deconstruct MPP into its constituent polymers. This method employed a series of solvent washes to selectively dissolve individual polymer layers, such as PE and EVOH, from MPP. The STRAP process enables the recovery of these polymers with high purity and efficiency, yielding materials that are chemically comparable to their virgin counterparts. Furthermore, Sa nchez-Rivera et al. 29 introduced a temperaturecontrolled polymer dissolution and precipitation approach to improve the STRAP process. By achieving polymer precipitation through controlled cooling, the modified process reduces reliance on antisolvents, thereby lowering operation costs and improving the potential for scalability.

Solvent-based dissolution -precipitation is promising in terms of recycling rate and the quality of recovered materials, and efforts have been made to reduce costs by optimizing the precipitation process. However, as highlighted in recent studies, 18,31,32 there are still significant concerns regarding solvent costs and process complexity, which limit its scalability for commercial applications. Most reported approaches are designed to dissolve MPP layer by layer, starting from the outer structural layers and progressing to the inner ones. Each layer requires a specific solvent, a defined dissolution time, and a corresponding antisolvent to recover the dissolved polymers, which increases the complexity of the recycling process, energy consumption, and overall cost. For relatively inexpensive polyolefin layers, mechanical recycling may be the most widely adopted method, offering advantages such as cost-effectiveness, extensive existing infrastructure, and mature technology. 18,33,34 Additionally, many solvents and antisolvents used in the process are flammable, toxic, or volatile, raising operational safety and environmental concerns. 32 Simplifying or reducing the number of dissolution and precipitation steps could enhance the overall feasibility of the operation.

In a recently published work by Tushar et al., 35 both PE and EVOH components were recycled via the STRAP process, which employs cooling for the precipitation steps to eliminate the use of antisolvents. However, two separate dissolution steps were still required to sequentially dissolve the outer PE layer and inner EVOH layer. A combined strategy that applies only a single solvent-based dissolution to selectively extract the EVOH oxygen barrier layer, rather than dissolving each layer sequentially, followed by mechanical recycling of the remaining polyolefins, may provide a more practical, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly solution. This approach avoids handling large quantities of polyolefins, through solvent treatment and reduces the precipitation steps required for their recovery. It enables the recovery of high-value EVOH through dissolution -precipitation for reuse, preserving its high economic value, while allowing polyolefins to be mechanically recycled without the negative impact of EVOH on blend properties. Meadows et al. 30 recently demonstrated the potential of using selective dissolution to remove EVOH from coffee K-cups. However, the potential impact of the selective dissolution process on the structural and mechanical properties of the remaining polyolefin layers remains underexplored. Although the solvent is not intended to dissolve polyolefins, exposure to elevated temperatures and solvent contact may still cause property changes or degradation. Herein this work, we seek to explore this gap in this aspect of this approach.

In this study, the selective dissolution of the oxygen barrier material of EVOH from a five-layer MPP film in formic acid was investigated. This five-layer MPP film consists of two LDPE structural layers, two MAg -LLDPE tie layers, and one EVOH barrier layer. The postdissolution MPP film was then processed into a blend through conventional mechanical recycling processes, including thermal compounding, grinding, and injection molding. The objective was to explore the feasibility of recycling MPP by extracting the EVOH layer through selective dissolution and subsequently mechanically recycling the remaining polyolefin layers, with a focus on clarifying the effect of the dissolution process on the properties of the reclaimed polyolefin blend.

2. MATERIALS AND METHODS

2.1. Materials

LDPE (density: 0.925 g/cm 3 , melt index: 0.8 g/min at 190 °C/2.16 kg), MAg -LLDPE (density: 0.930 g/cm 3 , melt index: 2.5 g/min at 190 °C/2.16 kg) and EVOH (density: 1.190 g/cm 3 , melt index: 3.2 g/min at 190 °C/2.16 kg, ethylene content: 32 mol %) pellets, and MPP film were supplied by Berry Global, Inc. The MPP film was manufactured by the supplier using these pellets in a five-layer structure of LDPE/MAg -LLDPE/EVOH/MAg -LLDPE/LDPE, with a thickness ratio of 35/10/10/10/35% and a total thickness of 60 μ m. The EVOH content in the multilayer film is estimated to be approximately 13 wt % based on its density and thickness ratio within the structure. A simplified structure of the MPP film is presented in Figure 1. All pellets were dried in a forced-air oven overnight at 80 °C

Figure 1. Simplified structure of the five-layer MPP film.

to remove moisture prior to use. Formic acid (assay: 88%, Aqua Solutions, Inc.) was purchased from VWR International.

2.2. Solvent-Based Selective Dissolution

2.2.1. Lab-Scale Experiment. The lab-scale dissolution experiments were conducted in a 250 mL three-neck flask equipped with a condenser, with nitrogen continuously flowing through the flask to a bubbler to maintain an inert atmosphere. A magnetic hot plate stirrer was used to control both temperature and stirring speed. Formic acid served as the solvent to dissolve the EVOH from the MPP film, while deionized water was used to adjust the solvent concentration as needed. The stirring speed was maintained at 300 rpm, and the solvent volume was fixed at 50 mL for all experiments. The temperature of the dissolution system was controlled in a water bath with the hot plate supplying the heat. The effects of solvent concentration and temperature were investigated by monitoring the mass change of the MPP film samples over time, with formic acid concentrations of 88, 50, and 20% and temperatures of 75, 50, and 25 °C. Five circular samples (25.4 mm in diameter) were cut from the multilayer film and used for each experiment. After the solvent was heated and stabilized at the target temperature, the samples were introduced into the flask containing excess solvent at a ratio of approximately 200 mL/g. Samples were taken out every 30 min to record mass changes until no further change was observed, indicating complete EVOH dissolution. When the film samples were taken out of the reactor at various times, consistent cleaning and drying procedures were applied to each sample. All the samples were cleaned using Kim-wipes and dried at room temperature under the hood.

The effect of sample size was evaluated by measuring the mass change of square samples with an original dimension of 50 mm × 50 mm, as well as samples cut into four segments of 25 mm × 25 mm and eight segments of 25 mm × 12.5 mm, corresponding to solventexposed EVOH surface areas of 12, 24, and 36 mm 2 , respectively. For these experiments regarding the sample size effect, the solvent concentration and temperature were fixed at 88% and 75 °C, and the total mass of samples added to the flask was kept constant across different sample sizes to investigate the surface area effect. Mass measurements were taken every 10 min until a constant value was reached. At least three replicates were conducted for each sample size, and results were reported as average values. The effect of solvent-tosample ratio was evaluated by measuring the mass change at four different ratios (15, 25, 35, and 45 mL/g), with the solvent concentration (88%), temperature (75 °C), and sample size (25 mm × 12.5 mm) held constant. For each condition, the sample mass was recorded after 20 min of dissolution. At least three replicates were performed for each ratio, and the results were reported as average values.

2.2.2. Pilot-Scale Experiment. The pilot-scale dissolution was carried out under the optimized conditions identified from the labscale experiments, using a 5 L single-jacketed glass reactor (Model JR5L, USA Lab) equipped with a heating circulation bath with silicone oil as the heat transfer fluid. The MPP film was cut into circular samples with a diameter of 16 mm. A total of 120 g of film samples in circular shape was placed into the 5 L glass reactor along with 4.2 L of 88% formic acid, achieving a solvent-to-sample ratio of 35 mL/g. The dissolution was carried out at 75 °C for 1 h with continuous stirring provided by a Teflon mechanical agitator operating at 200 rpm. After dissolution, the formic acid solution containing the dissolved EVOH was collected from the draining port and stored separately. Subsequently, 4.2 L of deionized water was added to the reactor to wash the remaining polyolefins with stirring at 200 rpm for 2 min. This washing step was repeated twice to thoroughly remove any residual solvent. The remaining polyolefins were then collected and dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight. The pilot-scale dissolution experiment was performed twice to collect an adequate amount of LDPE for further mechanical recycling studies.

2.3. Mechanical Recycling of Reclaimed Polyolefins

2.3.1. Thermal Compounding. A 200 g sample of reclaimed polyolefins from the pilot-scale experiment was compounded into a blend using an internal bowl mixer (Model 2128, C.W. Brabender Instruments, Inc.) equipped with two counter-rotating roller blades. Compounding was performed at 200 °C for 5 min at a speed of 60 rpm. After compounding, the molten polyolefin blend was scraped from the mixer using a scraper and allowed to solidify at room temperature.

2.3.2. Grinding. After solidification, the reclaimed polyolefin blend was ground into particles using a low-speed granulator (Model SG-2042NH, Shini Plastic Technologies, Inc.) equipped with a 3 mm sieve. The particles were then dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight to remove moisture prior to injection molding.

2.3.3. Injection Molding. Particles of the reclaimed polyolefin blend were manufactured into test samples using a benchtop injection molding machine (Proto-Ject 150 HP, Manning Innovations, Inc.) and three customized aluminum molds. Tensile testing samples were processed using a preheated mold (180 °C, 10 min) with dimensions of 102 mm × 20 mm × 0.98 mm at 235 °C under a pressure of 57 MPa. Samples for the essential work of fracture (EWF) test and rheological measurement were produced using molds with dimensions of 64 mm × 13 mm × 3.2 mm and 102 mm × 20 mm × 1.5 mm, respectively, at 200 °C under a pressure of 51 MPa.

Virgin LDPE, a blend of virgin LDPE and MAg -LLDPE with the same weight ratio as the reclaimed polyolefin blend, and MPP film were subjected to identical thermal compounding, grinding, and injection molding processes for comparison purposes. These samples are referred to as virgin LDPE, LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, and multilayer film blend throughout the context. All samples were stored in Ziploc bags to prevent moisture intrusion prior to characterization.

2.4. Characterizations

Tensile Test. Tensile properties were evaluated according to ASTM D882 using a universal testing machine (Model ESM750S, Mark-10) with a 500 N load cell. Specimens with dimensions of 102 mm × 15 mm × 0.98 mm were cut from injection-molded samples using a razor blade. The testing speed was 50 mm/min, corresponding to an initial strain rate of 1 min -1 . Five replicates were tested per sample. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) in Origin software at a significance level of 0.05, followed by Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test to identify significant differences among group means.

Essential Work of Fracture (EWF) Test. The EWF is proportional to the ligament area, and the non-EWF is proportional to the volume of the plastic zone. The relationships among W f , W e , and W p are described in eq 1: 43

By dividing the W f by the tL , the specific total work of fracture ( w f) is obtained, as shown in eq 2: 44

The EWF test was performed using the same universal testing machine and load cell as the tensile test. Double-edge notched tension (DENT) specimens were prepared using a notching machine (CEAST Manual Notchvis, Instron) equipped with a blade (angle: 45 ± 1 ° , radius: 0.5 ± 0.05 mm). Ultraviolet -Visible (UV -Vis) Spectrophotometry. Optical properties were analyzed using a UV -vis spectrophotometer

(GENESYS 150, Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a Xenon flash lamp light source. Measurements were conducted over a wavelength range of 200 -800 nm at a slow scanning speed and a data interval of 1 nm. Solid film samples with a thickness of 0.98 mm were placed directly in the light path without further treatment. Transmittance spectra were recorded to evaluate optical clarity.

Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy. Chemical changes were analyzed using an FTIR spectrometer (Nicolet iS10, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode with diamond/ZnSe crystals as the internal reflection element. Spectra were recorded from 650 to 4000 cm -1 with 128 scans per sample. Each sample was measured in triplicate, and the average spectrum was used for analysis.

Rheology. Rheological properties were measured using a rheometer (HAAKE MARS 60, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a 25 mm parallel plate geometry and a gap of 1.3 mm. Circular specimens with a diameter of 22 mm and a thickness of 1.5 mm were obtained from injection-molded samples using a Gasket punch. All measurements were collected at 200 °C. An initial amplitude strain sweep at 10 rad/s was performed to determine the linear viscoelastic region, and a strain amplitude of 1% was selected for all subsequent oscillatory tests. Frequency sweeps were carried out over an angular frequency range of 0.1 -100 rad/s. Time sweeps were performed at a constant angular frequency of 10 rad/s for 60 min. All measurements were conducted in triplicate, and results are presented as average values with error bars indicating standard errors.

Approximately 7 mg of each sample was sealed in an aluminum pan and tested under a nitrogen flow of 50 mL/min. A second heating from 30 to 220 °C at 10 °C/min was conducted to capture melting behavior. Three replicates were collected per sample. 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1. Solvent-Based Selective Dissolution

Solvent Concentration and Temperature. A simplified flow diagram of the solvent-based selective dissolution process is illustrated in Figure 3a. Unlike most reported solvent-based dissolution methods, where the solvent is designed to dissolve the MPP sequentially from the outer

Figure 3. (a) Simplified flow diagram of the solvent-based selective dissolution process. (b) Dissolution kinetics of the MPP film at 75 °C in 50% formic acid. (c) Dissolution kinetics of MPP with different sample sizes at 75 °C in 88% formic acid. (d) Film sample weight changes at various solvent-to-sample ratios at 75 °C in 88% formic acid. Different letters (A-C) in figure 3d indicate statistically different groups.

layer, this study directly targeted the dissolution of the inner oxygen barrier layer. Formic acid was used to selectively dissolve the EVOH barrier layer under specific solvent concentrations and temperatures with continuous stirring. The polyolefin layers, including the inner and outer LDPE layers and the MAg -LLDPE tie layer, were separated and reclaimed through a simple filtration process.

The dissolution kinetics of the MPP film at 50% concentration and 75 °C are shown in Figure 3b. Initially, the weight of the MPP film increased as the film was swollen by solvent penetration in the EVOH layer, which was also found by a measurable increase in film thickness. As the dissolution time progressed, the weight of the film sample began to decrease, reaching approximately 85 wt % of the initial sample weight after 2 h. The weight of the samples remained unchanged thereafter, indicating the complete EVOH dissolution and no more film mass change occurred. Notably, delamination of the outer layers was observed after the inner layer was completely dissolved. However, some of the delaminated films adhered together again after drying due to the presence of tie layers. The dissolution kinetics of the films at different solvent concentrations and temperatures were recorded and summarized in Table 1. Both solvent concentration and temperature significantly influenced dissolution efficiency. A notable improvement in dissolution efficiency was observed with increasing solvent concentration and temperature. Under the condition of 88% concentration and 75 °C, nearly complete EVOH dissolution was achieved within 0.5 h. The complete dissolution was also confirmed using FTIR and DSC in this study, as discussed in later sections.

3.1.2. Sample Size and Solvent-to-Sample Ratio. The EVOH layer was targeted to be dissolved by the solvent, and the effect of sample size on dissolution efficiency was associated with the EVOH layer's surface area exposed to the solvent. The dissolution kinetics of the MPP film for different sample sizes under fixed conditions of 88% solvent concentration and 75 °C are shown in Figure 3c. A surface area of 3.6 mm 2 exhibited significantly higher dissolution efficiency (achieving complete EVOH extraction within 20 min) compared to surface areas of 1.2 and 2.4 mm 2 (30 min for complete dissolution). The dissolution efficiency benefited from the decreasing sample size, namely the increasing EVOH surface area, highlighting the necessity of sample fragmentation in practical solvent-based selective dissolution of MPP.

3.2. Mechanical Properties

3.2.1. Tensile Properties. The tensile stress -strain curves of the polyolefin samples from the pilot-scale experiment after one-time mechanical recycling operation are shown in Figure 4a. Virgin LDPE exhibited typical yielding behavior, which was attributed to its inherent high flexibility that allowed easy chain slippage once the critical stress was reached at 10 MPa. A similar yielding behavior was observed for the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, however, the blend displayed a greater strain at break, likely due to improved intermolecular interactions introduced by the MA groups, which enhanced the blend's ductility. In contrast, the multilayer film blend showed no yielding behavior and a smaller strain at break, which was caused by the presence of EVOH. EVOH is inherently rigid and prone to gelling during the thermal compounding process. 10,26 The rigidity and gelling of EVOH restricted chain mobility and prevented easy chain slippage, making the blend stiffer and more brittle, and causing it to deform less and fracture earlier.

After EVOH extraction, the stress -strain curve of the reclaimed blend overlapped with those of virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend at the early stage (before the virgin LDPE's yielding point). The reclaimed polyolefin blend also exhibited increased ductility compared to the multilayer film blend, as indicated by the greater strain at break, although it remained lower than that of both virgin LDPE and LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. However, unlike virgin LDPE and the LDPE/ MAg -LLDPE blend, no distinct yielding behavior was observed, and the reclaimed blend maintained a higher stress than them across the strain range until fracture. These observations were due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding formed as a result of chemical changes in the MAg -LLDPE tie

Furthermore, the reclaimed polyolefin blend sample exhibited significantly higher transmittance than the multilayer film blend in the visible light range (400 -700 nm), indicating better optical clarity (Figure 4b). Its transmittance was also close to that of virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. A pronounced yellowish appearance was visually observed in the multilayer film blend sample, likely caused by the thermo-oxidative degradation of EVOH during exposure to elevated temperatures and oxygen in the thermal compounding process. 49

Statistical comparison results of tensile strength, secant modulus, strain at break, and energy to break are shown in Figures 4c,d. The tensile strength of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was comparable to both the multilayer film blend and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, and significantly higher than that of virgin LDPE. The secant modulus of the multilayer film blend was significantly greater than those of all other samples, owing to the presence of rigid EVOH. The strain at break of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was lower than that of virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, but still significantly higher than that of the multilayer film blend. The energy to break of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was higher than that of the multilayer film blend and comparable to that of virgin LDPE. Overall, the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited better mechanical performance than the multilayer film blend in tensile testing, highlighting the substantial benefit of EVOH extraction in the mechanical recycling of MPP.

3.2.2. EWF. The EWF measurement results are presented in Figure 5, with insets displaying the corresponding load displacement curves. All samples exhibited similar load -displacement curve shapes across different ligament lengths, indicating that variations in ligament length had no significant influence on the fracture behavior. This consistency is a necessary condition to validate the applicability of the EWF concept. 50 Good linear relationships were obtained for the plots of specific total work of fracture against ligament length for all samples, with R 2 values greater than 0.96.

The EWF value represents the toughness, while the nonEWF value is associated with the capability to dissipate energy through plastic deformation. 45 The virgin LDPE exhibited an EWF value of 15.3 kJ/m 2 , which increased to 23.2 kJ/m 2 in the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. The reclaimed polyolefin blend showed an EWF value of 22.5 kJ/m 2 , slightly lower than that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend but distinctly higher than those of both virgin LDPE and the multilayer film blend. Moreover, the non-EWF value of the reclaimed polyolefin blend (12.8 MJ/m 3 ) was greater than that of the multilayer film blend (11.4 MJ/m 3 ) and comparable to that of virgin LDPE, although it remained significantly lower than that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend (15.3 MJ/m 3 ). These results indicate that EVOH extraction through selective dissolution contributed to enhanced toughness and increased energy dissipation capability of the reclaimed polyolefin blend compared to direct mechanical recycling of the MPP and suggest that the reclaimed polyolefin blend could outperform virgin LDPE in applications where improved toughness is required.

3.2.3. FTIR Analysis. The FTIR spectra of virgin EVOH and all the samples subjected to mechanical recycling are shown in Figure 6a. The absorption peaks at 2916, 2849, 1469,

1377, and 718 cm -1 were associated with the CH2 asymmetric stretching, CH2 symmetric stretching, CH2 bending, CH3 bending, and CH2 rocking vibrations of LDPE, respectively. 51 -53 The spectrum of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend closely resembled that of virgin LDPE, without the MA group being clearly detected, which could be due to its low content. In contrast, distinct absorption peaks at approximately 3300, 1087, and 833 cm -1 were observed in the spectrum of the multilayer film blend, corresponding to the O -H stretching, C -O stretching, and C -C skeletal vibrations of EVOH, respectively, as confirmed by comparison with the virgin EVOH spectrum. 25,54,55 Furthermore, a cluster of weak peaks between 1620 and 1750 cm -1 was detected, likely originating from oxygen products generated by the thermo-oxidative degradation of EVOH during mechanical recycling. 56 Notably, the EVOH absorption peaks disappeared from the spectrum of the reclaimed polyolefin blend, confirming the complete extraction of EVOH after selective dissolution. However, two new absorption peaks emerged at 1724 and 1190 cm -1 , which were absent in both virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, suggesting that they likely originated from degradation or chemical reactions during the selective dissolution process rather than the mechanical recycling process.

To further investigate, FTIR analysis was conducted on samples after selective dissolution but before mechanical recycling as well, with the corresponding spectra shown in Figure 6b. The FTIR spectrum of the LDPE layer surface was identical to that of virgin LDPE, except for a minor peak at 1730 cm -1 , which may be stemmed from to the C=O stretching of carboxylic acid groups from a small amount of residual formic acid solvent. However, the spectrum of the MAg -LLDPE layer surface exhibited the same absorption peaks at 1724 and 1190 cm -1 as those observed in the reclaimed polyolefin blend shown in Figure 6a, indicating that these peaks were related to reactions involving the MAg -LLDPE layer. The proposed chemical reactions are illustrated in Figure 6c,d. Under elevated temperatures, the MA underwent hydrolysis to form maleic acid containing carboxylic groups. 57 during the dissolution process, contributing to the C=O stretching observed at 1724 cm -1 . Additionally, the MA reacted with formic acid via a nucleophilic ring-opening reaction, 58 in which formic acid acted as a nucleophile by donating a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of its

This reaction led to the formation of monoformyl maleic acid containing formate ester groups, which were responsible for the C -O stretching observed at 1190 cm -1 . These new functional groups, formed through chemical changes of the MAg -LLDPE tie layer during the dissolution process, likely altered the intermolecular interactions within the reclaimed polyolefin blend, resulting in changes in mechanical performance observed in the tensile and EWF tests compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. 3.2.4. Rheological Properties. 3.2.4.1. Frequency Sweeps. The complex viscosity data for all the samples are shown in Figure 7a. The MPP film blend exhibited a higher complex viscosity than the other samples across the entire testing range, due to the presence of EVOH, which enhanced interfacial interactions through reactions with MAg -LLDPE and simultaneously contributed to a cross-linked structure via degradation during thermal compounding. 25,59 The LDPE/

MAg -LLDPE blend exhibited a complex viscosity largely close to that of virgin LDPE across the entire frequency range. At frequencies below 1 rad/s, the reclaimed polyolefin blend showed a higher complex viscosity than both virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. This increase in viscosity could be caused by chemical changes of the MAg -LLDPE tie layer during the dissolution process, as revealed by FTIR analysis. These changes led to the generation of carboxylic acid and ester groups, which facilitated intermolecular hydrogen bonding between polymer chains in the tie resin, with carboxylic acids acting as both donors and acceptors and esters serving as acceptors, 60 as illustrated in the inset of Figure 7a. Hydrogen bonding in the reclaimed polyolefin blend formed dynamic physical cross-links, suppressing the chain mobility and increasing its complex viscosity. 61

However, at higher frequencies above 10 rad/s, the complex viscosity of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was slightly lower than that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. This difference can be attributed to the reactive MA groups in the virgin LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, which likely formed strong covalent bonds with LDPE radicals generated during hightemperature compounding. In contrast, the MA groups in the reclaimed blend were chemically modified during the dissolution process, diminishing their ability to establish covalent interactions with LDPE. Although hydrogen bonds may still be present, rheological testing at higher frequencies probes smaller structural scales and shorter time scales, which may not be sensitive enough to detect the contribution of the transient hydrogen-bonded network. Interestingly, despite differences in complex viscosity across frequencies, both the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend and the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited good compatibility, as evidenced by the near-ideal semicircular arcs in the Cole -Cole plots (Figure 7b). 62 The reclaimed blend displayed a larger arc radius, suggesting a longer relaxation process, while the slight upward tendency observed at the low-frequency region is likely associated with the hydrogen-bonding network. Phase separation was also not observed in the multilayer film blend between LDPE and EVOH, as the MAg -LLDPE tie layer functioned as an effective coupling agent.

Similarly, the storage modulus (Figure 7c) and loss modulus (Figure 7d) of the reclaimed polyolefin blend were higher at low frequencies compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. The elevated moduli at low frequencies are attributed to the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which enhanced the capability to store and dissipate energy over long time scales. At the crossover point ( G ′ = G ″ ), the frequency for the reclaimed blend (10 rad/s) was lower than that of the virgin blend (25 rad/s), indicating a longer relaxation time resulting from increased intermolecular interactions via hydrogen bonding. This observation is consistent with the larger arc diameter observed for the reclaimed polyolefin blend in the Cole -Cole plot (Figure 7b). The crossover storage modulus of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was around 21,000 Pa, lower than that of the virgin LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend (around 37,000 Pa). This can be interpreted as the result of chemical modifications of MA, which likely disrupted interfacial bonding and uniform chain interactions in the reclaimed blend, leading to increased polydispersity. Notably, compared to the powerlaw dependencies observed in the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend ( G ′ ∼ ω 1.21 and G ″ ∼ ω 0.78 ) in the terminal region, the reclaimed blend ( G ′ ∼ ω 0.81 and G ″ ∼ ω 0.61 ) exhibited greater deviations from the ideal terminal behavior of a viscoelastic polymer melt ( G ′ ∼ ω 2 , G ″ ∼ ω 1 ). 63 These deviations confirm that hydrogen bonding disrupted the reptation process and hindered complete chain relaxation in the reclaimed blend.

text: 3.2.4.2. Time Sweep. Time sweeps were conducted to assess thermal stability, as shown in Figure 7f. Both the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend and virgin LDPE maintained relatively stable storage moduli during the first 25 min, after which the moduli began to increase due to radical-induced cross-linking during thermal aging under high-temperature conditions. 64 The storage modulus of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was comparable to that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend during the initial 15 min but gradually increased thereafter. Although the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited lower thermal stability than virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, it was significantly more stable than the multilayer film blend, which showed a rapid and continuous increase in storage modulus from the beginning of the test. This behavior was ascribed to the presence of highly susceptible EVOH, which readily underwent cross-linking reactions under thermal conditions, as reported in our previous studies. 25,26

3.2.5. Thermal Properties. 3.2.5.1. DSC. The melting and crystallization behaviors are presented in Figure 8a,b, respectively. The multilayer film blend exhibited two melting peak temperatures at 112.2 and 180.4 °C, and two crystallization peak temperatures at 102.5 and 159.8 °C, corresponding to LDPE and EVOH, respectively. However, in the reclaimed polyolefin blend, both the EVOH melting and crystallization peaks disappeared, indicating that EVOH was completely extracted after the selective dissolution process. The melting and crystallization peak temperatures of the reclaimed polyolefin blend (112.6 and 101.8 °C) were comparable to those of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend (112.7 and 101.5 °C), suggesting that the selective dissolution process had no significant effect on the melting and crystallization peak temperatures of the reclaimed polyolefin blend. Additionally, the melting and crystallization onset temperatures, as well as the degree of crystallinity, remained largely unchanged in the reclaimed polyolefin blend compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, as shown in Table 2.

3.2.5.2. TGA. The TGA and DTA curves are shown in Figure 8c,d. EVOH exhibited a two-step thermal degradation behavior, with the first mass loss starting around 290 °C, attributed to the dehydration of vinyl alcohol units, and the second beginning near 430 °C, corresponding to the thermal degradation of ethylene segments. 65 LDPE and the LDPE/ MAg -LLDPE blend exhibited a single-step degradation profile, where thermal decomposition was primarily governed by random chain scission of their PE backbone, with the LDPE/ MAg -LLDPE blend showing a higher decomposition onset temperature around 410 °C. 66 The slightly lower decomposition onset temperature of the reclaimed polyolefin blend, compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, was likely originated from chemical changes of MAg -LLDPE during the dissolution process, which introduced polar groups and reduced its compatibilization effect, thereby weakening the structural stability of the reclaimed blend. However, it remained more thermally stable than the virgin LDPE and the multilayer film blend. DTG results showed that all samples exhibited similar thermal stability in terms of their decomposition temperatures at maximum weight loss rates, except for the multilayer film blend, which displayed an earlier decomposition peak at 390 °C due to the presence of EVOH.

4. ENVIRONMENTAL AND ECONOMIC IMPLICATIONS

Against the backdrop of the increasingly stringent environmental policies around the world that aim to address plastic pollution (e.g., China's and other developing countries' waste import ban or restriction since 2018), the technology presented in the current study regarding MPP recycling has profound environmental and economic implications.

Due to existing technical barriers of recycling, only 9% of plastic waste is recycled annually, while the majority is landfilled (50%), incinerated for energy recovery (19%), or discarded as litter in the environment (22%). 67 Landfilling occupies valuable land resources and generates microplastics, while incineration releases greenhouse gases and toxic pollutants, such as carbon dioxide, methane, and aromatic hydrocarbons, both posing significant threats to the environment and human health. 68 -70 More than 100 million tons of MPP are produced globally each year, representing a substantial portion of the plastic waste that is landfilled or incinerated. 27 The presented recycling technology has the potential to significantly reduce the quantity of MPP landfilled, incinerated, or littered, thereby reshaping the landscape of MPP waste management and delivering notable environmental benefits.

Furthermore, from an economic perspective, the solventbased dissolution process has been reported to be cost-effective for recycling MPP via layer-by-layer recovery. 28,71 Meanwhile, mechanical recycling is one of the most economical methods for LDPE, with an estimated processing cost of approximately $0.38/kg compared to $1.00/kg for virgin LDPE produced from crude oil. 72,73 The presented recycling method involves applying solvent-based dissolution to remove the EVOH layer, while using mechanical recycling for the remaining LDPE. This combined approach may offer economic potential if the removed EVOH is also recovered. However, further investigation is required to perform a practical economic analysis to provide solid evidence. In future work, a comprehensive assessment could be conducted considering greenhouse gas emissions, toxic pollutants, recovered material selling price, solvent and equipment costs, labor, and other operational factors.

5. CONCLUSIONS

A solvent-based selective dissolution approach was applied to a five-layer MPP film for the extraction of the EVOH barrier layer and the separation of the remaining polyolefin layers. Key processing parameters, including solvent concentration, temperature, sample size, and solvent-to-sample ratio, were evaluated for their effects on dissolution efficiency. A condition of 88% formic acid at 75 °C, with a 3.6 mm 2 EVOH exposure area and a solvent-to-sample ratio of 35 mL/g, was identified as an effective condition for dissolving EVOH and reclaiming polyolefins at a 5L reactor. The reclaimed polyolefins, consisting of the LDPE layer and the MAg -LLDPE tie layer, were mechanically recycled through thermal compounding, grinding, and injection molding. The resulting polyolefin blend exhibited higher tensile strain at break and toughness compared to the MPP film blend produced via direct mechanical recycling and demonstrated mechanical properties mostly comparable to those of virgin LDPE, although with reduced tensile strain at break. FTIR analysis revealed that the MAg -LLDPE tie layer underwent chemical reactions, primarily through hydrolysis and nucleophilic ring-opening reactions with the existence of water and formic acid, contributing to the observed changes in material properties. Rheological data indicated that the resulting carboxylic acid and ester groups facilitated hydrogen bonding, enhancing intermolecular interactions within the blend. The thermal behavior of the reclaimed polyolefin blend closely resembled that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend.

Overall, this study demonstrates the effectiveness and scalability of solvent-based selective dissolution for EVOH extraction and polyolefin reclamation from MPP. The reclaimed polyolefins can be mechanically recycled into a polyolefin blend with satisfactory performance and may serve as a potential replacement for virgin LDPE in similar applications, as it exhibits comparable properties and, in some cases, such as tensile strength and fracture toughness, even better performance. Future research can focus on EVOH recovery and property characterization, as well as a more comprehensive evaluation of this method's practical environmental and economic feasibility.

1. Introduction

Annually, the world generates ca. 2.24 billion tonnes of solid waste with about 20% attributed to plastic materials, of which polypropylene (PP) represents a major fraction. Despite the urgent need for improved waste management, global plastic recycling rates remain low; less than 10% of the 7 billion tonnes of plastic produced have been recycled, with PP recycling rates estimated to be as low as 1%. [1,2] Such low recycling rates contribute to environmental degradation and pose severe risks to ecosystems. Moreover,  plastic production relies heavily on nonrenewable fossil fuels and accounts for 4.5% of the global carbon foot print, further intensifying its environmental impact. [3]

A significant proportion of polypropylene waste arises from singleuse products and non-woven polymer materials. Disposable face masks

A B S T R A C T

Efficient recycling of polypropylene (PP) from complex waste streams remains a significant challenge, particu larly for multilayer non-woven materials. Here, we report a rapid dissolution -reprecipitation process for poly propylene recovery using a tailored ionic liquid formed from tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine and 3,3-dimethylbutyric acid.  The  process  operates  at  160 °C under ambient pressure, achieving up to 99% polymer recovery, with complete dissolution occurring in less than one minute. An integrated hot filtration step simultaneously removes pigments and additives, eliminating the need for additional purification stages. The recovered polymer exhibits thermal, structural, and mechanical properties comparable to virgin polypropylene, confirming preservation of polymer integrity. Quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) provides molecular-level insight into the dissolution mechanism, revealing enhanced polymer mobility and plasticisation induced by the ionic liquid. Complementary spectroscopic and chromatographic analyses confirm the chemical stability of the solvent across the investigated temperature range, supporting its potential for reuse. This work establishes a mechanistically informed, solventbased strategy for polypropylene recycling, offering a scalable pathway for recovering polyolefins from complex waste streams.

[4] Most  disposable masks  are composed  primarily  of  multilayer  non-woven  polypropylene  fibres designed to provide filtration, mechanical strength, and moisture man agement. [5]

Improper disposal of such materials contributes to environmental pollution through landfill accumulation, incineration, and fragmenta tion into microplastics. Non-woven polypropylene materials are partic ularly challenging to recycle due to their fibrous structure, additives, and  colourants  introduced  during  manufacturing.  As  these  materials undergo environmental weathering, they can fragment into microplastic particles that contaminate aquatic ecosystems and may enter the food chain, posing risks to marine organisms and potentially human health.

[6 -8] Considering that disposable face masks are primarily composed of polypropylene-based fibres, the development of effective strategies for recovering and recycling such materials is essential to reduce plastic pollution and support a circular economy. [9]

Conventional plastic recycling generally follows two main routes: mechanical  recycling  and  chemical  recycling.  [10] Mechanical  recy cling,  the  most  widely  implemented  approach,  involves  collecting, sorting,  cleaning,  shredding,  and  reprocessing  plastic  waste  through melting and re-moulding or re-extrusion. While this method is relatively straightforward and economically viable, repeated thermal -mechanical processing  often  leads  to  polymer  degradation,  resulting  in  reduced molecular weight, deterioration of mechanical properties, and limited applications for the recycled material. The presence of additives, dyes, and contaminants in the polypropylene waste further complicates me chanical  recycling,  affecting  the  quality  and  consistency  of  the  final product.

Chemical recycling offers several advantages over mechanical recy cling,  particularly  the  potential  to  recover  higher-purity,  virgin-like polymers,  through  the  removal  of  impurities.  [10] Various  chemical recycling approaches have been explored, including pyrolysis, super critical fluid extraction, and dissolution -reprecipitation processes. Py rolysis  and  supercritical  fluid  extraction  are  attractive  due  to  their ability to generate high-value chemicals from plastic waste; however, they typically require high operating temperatures (~400 °C) and spe cialised  equipment,  which  increases  process  complexity  and  cost.  In contrast, dissolution -reprecipitation methods generally operate at lower temperatures  and  require  less  complex  equipment,  making  them promising strategies for the selective recovery of polymers from mixed waste streams. [2]

Most approaches to polypropylene dissolution rely on aromatic hy drocarbons such as benzene and its derivatives, including toluene and xylene, which have demonstrated the ability to dissolve PP at concen trations of ~10% wt/v. [11,12] However, these conventional solvents present drawbacks including high volatility, toxicity, flammability, and their derivation from non-renewable fossil resources.

Ionic liquids (ILs) represent a promising yet underexplored alterna tive for PP dissolution and recovery. ILs are salts with melting points below  100 °C,  that  often  exist  as  liquids  at  room  temperature,  and consist of organic cations paired with various anions. [13,14] Unlike conventional  molecular  solvents,  ILs  exhibit  unique  physicochemical properties including negligible vapour pressure, high thermal stability, non-flammability,  and  tunable  chemical  structures.  [15,16] These distinctive characteristics have led to increasing interest in ionic liquids across  diverse  applications,  [17] including  polymer  processing  and separation, e.g. the recycling of carpet waste, [2] energy storage elec trolytes, [18,19] designer solvents for chemical reactions, [20] and CO2 separation and capture. [21,22] However, despite increasing interest in solvent-based polymer recycling, the molecular-level mechanisms gov erning polymer dissolution remain insufficiently understood, particu larly the dynamics of polymer -solvent interactions during dissolution. Advanced analytical techniques are therefore required to probe poly mer -solvent interactions and elucidate the dissolution process.

Herein, we propose a novel and facile process for recovering poly propylene from non-woven waste streams, demonstrated using dispos able face masks, through the use of an ionic liquid composed of tris(2ethylhexyl)  amine  (TEHA)  and  3,3-dimethylbutyric  acid  (DMBA),  in 1:1  M  ratio.  The  ionic  liquid  forms  via  proton  transfer  between  the tertiary  amine  and  the  carboxylic  acid,  producing  an  ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid. The selection of these components was guided by physicochemical compatibility with polypropylene and builds upon our previous work on solvent-driven polymer recycling systems. [2]

Polypropylene is a highly non-polar polymer composed of saturated hydrocarbon chains, and its dissolution is therefore governed primarily by  dispersion  interactions.  The  long-branched  alkyl  chains  of  TEHA promote favourable hydrophobic interactions  with polyolefin chains, improving solvent compatibility with the polymer. In combination with DMBA, proton transfer generates an ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid containing  both  ionic  character  and  hydrophobic  alkyl  domains.  [2] Such solvent systems can promote polyolefin swelling and plasticisation, enabling solvent penetration into the polymer matrix and facilitating dissolution. In  addition, both  precursors exhibit low vapour pressure and high thermal stability, making them suitable for operation at the elevated temperatures required for polypropylene processing.

Using this solvent system, polypropylene was rapidly dissolved and recovered from non-woven materials, yielding a polymer with proper ties comparable to virgin polypropylene. The recovered polymer was characterised using FT-IR, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differen tial  scanning  calorimetry  (DSC),  high-temperature  gel  permeation chromatography (HT-GPC), and nanoindentation. Proton nuclear mag netic resonance ( 1 H NMR) spectroscopy was used to confirm the for mation  and  stability  of  the  ionic  liquid,  while  quasi-elastic  neutron scattering (QENS) was employed to probe the molecular dynamics of the polymer -ionic liquid system and provide mechanistic insight into the dissolution process. These results demonstrate the potential of tailored ionic liquids as sustainable solvent systems for efficient polypropylene recycling.

2. Experimental

2.1. Materials

The hybrid ionic liquid (TA-DA)  was  prepared  using tris(2ethylhexyl)amine  (97.0%,  Sigma-Aldrich,  UK)  (TEHA)  and  3,3-dime thylbutyric acid (DMBA) (98%, Fisher Scientific, UK). The precursors were used as received. Both solvents have high boiling points and low vapour pressures (TEHA boiling point = 335 °C at atmospheric pressure with a vapour pressure of 0.001 Pa at 20 °C, and DMBA boiling point = 185 °C, at atmospheric pressure with a vapour pressure of 0.07 Pa at 10 °C). [23]

The antisolvent used was 98% industrial grade isopropanol (IPA) (Romil  Ltd.,  Cambridge,  UK).  Virgin  isotactic  polypropylene  (PP) (Sigma-Aldrich, UK; CAS 9003-07-0) had a density of 0.9 g cm 3 at 25 °C, a number-average molecular weight (M ₙ ) of ~67,000 Da and a weight-average molecular weight (Mw) of ~250,000 Da. The melt flow index was 12 g/10 min (230 °C, 2.16 kg), and the melting temperature ranged from 160 to 165 °C, as specified by the manufacturer. Dispos able,  commercially  available  non-woven  face  masks  (Model  YX-001) were  manufactured  from  Jiangsu  Yongxu  Construction  Development Co. Ltd.

2.2. Methodology

2.2.1. Ionic liquid preparation

TA-DA  was  prepared  by  slowly  adding  3,3-dimethylbutyric  acid (DMBA)  to  tris(2-ethylhexyl)  amine  (TEHA)  (1:1  M  ratio)  under continuous stirring at room temperature in a glass reactor. The reaction schematic is shown in Fig. 1. The mixture is kept under stirring for 30 min under air, and it is transferred into a brown glass bottle and stored at room temperature. Due to the toxicity of TEHA, and by association TADA, all handling and PP recovery studies using the ionic liquid were carried out in a fume hood.

2.2.2. Dissolution experiments

The  objective  of  the  experiments  was  to  determine  the  optimal dissolution temperature for virgin PP in ionic liquid TA-DA. This was achieved by conducting tests at three selected temperatures below the boiling  point  of  DMBA:  140,  150,  and  160 °C.  The  samples  were correspondingly labelled as TA-DA 140 p-PP, TA-DA 150 p-PP, and TADA 160 p-PP. In a typical experiment, TA-DA was added to a three-neck reaction  vessel,  fitted  with  a  stirring  bar,  a  reflux  condenser,  and  a thermometer. To ensure an inert environment throughout the experi ment, the flask was purged with nitrogen, maintaining a continuous H. Salazar et al.

The mixture was stirred at 900 rpm and main tained at constant temperature until the PP had fully dissolved ( t < 1 min). 2.3. Equipment

A Thermo Fisher Nicolet iS50 Fourier-transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectrometer was used to characterise PP samples as well as the ionic liquid between 4000 and 400 cm 1 . A Shimadzu UV-1800 instrument was employed to record UV -Vis spectra of diluted TEHA, DMBA, and TA-DA  in  IPA  from  200  to  850  nm. The sample was placed into a 70 μ L alumina crucible and heated to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min 1 while being exposed to a 50 mL min 1 flow of nitrogen. Utilising the STARe and Origin software, respectively, the weight loss and tempera ture  were  recorded  and  processed.  An  Agilent  Infinity  II  HightTemperature  Gel  Permeation  Chromatography  (HT-GPC)  equipment was used for analysis. The HT-GPC device was equipped with differen tial refractive index (DRI), viscometry (VS), and dual angle light scatter (LS 90 + 15) detectors. Two 300 × 7.5 mm PLgel Olexis columns and a 10 μ m guard column were equipped with the instrument. 1,2,4-trichlor obenzene with 250 ppm butylated hydroxytoluene additive served as the  mobile  phase.  The  operating  conditions  were  160 °C  and  1  mL min 1 .  A  third-order  calibration  was  performed  using  Agilent  Poly styrene EasiVials standards. To determine the degradation of TA-DA after the dissolution process, a Thermo Surveyor High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) system was used. This system consisted of a pump, an autosampler, and a  photodiode  array  (PDA)  detector,  all  coupled  to  a  Thermo  TSQ Quantum  mass  spectrometer.  A  range  of  sample  dilutions  were attempted to optimise peak shape and establish a linear range. Specif ically, dilutions ranged between 25 μ L mL 1 and 223 fL mL 1 . The in jection volume spanned from 5 to 25 μ L. Ultimately, an injection volume of 5.0 μ L was set, and the concentrations were between 22.7 nL mL 1 and 2.5 μ L mL 1 for acid precursor, and between 227 fL mL 1 and 2.27 nL mL 1 for the base precursor (note that the mass spectrometer is more sensitive to the base). For quantification, the peak area from a selected ion chromatogram at 354 m / z was used to assess the base. Additionally, the PDA peak area at a wavelength of 218 nm was used to quantify the acid. The samples were diluted in varying v /v proportions of IPA and H2O, ranging from 5:95 to 28:72 H2O:IPA. The chromatographic method for the base involved an ACE SuperC18 analytical column, measuring 150 mm in length and 3 mm in diameter, with 3 μ m particle size. The mobile phase was an isocratic mixture of 8:92 H2O:IPA, with a retention time of approximately 8 min. As for the acid, an ACE HILIC-B column of the same dimensions was used, with an isocratic mobile phase of 5:95 H2O:IPA and a retention time of about 11 min.

3. Results and discussion

In this study, we explored a chemical recycling approach for poly propylene  (PP)  recovery  from  disposable  face  masks  using  an  ionic liquid (TA-DA) composed of tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine (TEHA) and 3,3dimethylbutyric  acid  (DMBA).  Proton  transfer  between  the  tertiary amine  (TEHA)  and  the  carboxylic  acid  (DMBA)  produces  a  tri alkylammonium carboxylate ionic liquid. The resulting solvent contains hydrophobic  alkyl  domains  arising  from  the  branched  TEHA  chains, which interact  favourably  with  the  polypropylene  backbone  through dispersion  interactions,  while  the  ionic  character  facilitates  solvent penetration and plasticisation of the polymer matrix. These combined features  facilitate  efficient  dissolution  of  polypropylene  in  the  ionic liquid. The following sections discuss the characterisation of the nonwoven face masks, the dissolution and reprecipitation of PP, and the characterisation and stability of the ionic liquid used in this study.

3.1. Dissolution and reprecipitation of polypropylene

Dissolution of non-polar polymers such as polypropylene typically requires elevated temperatures, and is conventionally achieved using aromatic hydrocarbons solvents, [28,29] which suffer from volatility, toxicity and suistainability profiles. Here, a low-volatility ionic liquid (TA-DA) is introduced as a viable alternative for selective polypropylene recovery from non-woven face masks materials. Temperaturedependent  studies  identified  160 °C  as  the  optimal  operating  condi tion, enabling rapid and efficient dissolution with high selectivity to wards PP.

To evaluate the performance of the proposed solvent system, a pre determined amount of the face mask material, cut into small sections, was introduced into the pre-heated solvent, resulting in rapid dissolu tion of polypropylene, with complete dissolution occurring in less than 1 min. The polymer was subsequently recovered by antisolvent induced reprecipitation using isopropanol (IPA) followed by membrane filtra tion. A schematic of the overall process is illustrated in Fig. 2 .

Using  this  approach,  a  recovery  rate  of  approximately  99%  was achieved for both the polypropylene introduced into the reactor and the ionic liquid solvent.

A solubility study was conducted to better understand the dissolution behaviour of polypropylene from face mask materials and to evaluate the effectiveness of the ionic liquid in the recovery process. Experiments were performed at three different temperatures: 140 °C, 150 °C, and 160 °C.

As shown in Fig. 3a, no measurable dissolution of PP was observed at 140 °C, indicating that significant dissolution occurs only at tempera tures above this threshold. At 150 °C, the maximum concentration of PP in TA-DA reached 9.12 wt/v%, while at 160 °C it increased to 14.28 wt/ v%,  corresponding  to  approximately  a  1.6-fold  increase  in  polymer solubility.  These  results  indicate  that  both  temperatures  can  support polymer  dissolution,  with  higher  temperatures  promoting  increased solubility and improved dissolution efficiency. The observed tempera ture  dependence  is  consistent  with  enhanced  polymer  mobility  and plasticisation effects, as later confirmed by the QENS analysis.

The  solubility  rate  results  shown  in  Fig.  3b  further  highlight  the strong influence of temperature on dissolution kinetics. Increasing the temperature from 150 °C to 160 °C resulted in an approximately 2.7-fold increase in the mean solubility rate and a nearly 3.8-fold increase in the maximum dissolution rate. The overall recovery of PP exceeded 98% at both temperatures. These findings indicate that elevated temperatures significantly enhance both the solubility and dissolution kinetics of PP in TA-DA. Consequently,  160 °C  was  selected  as  the  optimal  operating temperature for subsequent face mask recycling experiments.

3.2. Quasi-elastic neutron scattering

Molecular dynamics during the dissolution of PP in TA-DA has been studied utilising quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS). Figs. 4a-c show the QENS spectra of PP, TA-DA, and PP + TA-DA mixture respectively, with Fig. 4d showing the integration of the spectra around 0.0175 to 0.0175 meV, normalised against each sample at 125 °C.

The  integration  window  of ± 0.0175  meV  corresponds  to  the instrumental resolution of the spectrometer. Any dynamics occurring within this resolution window are too slow to be measured and represent elastic scattering, which can be approximated as atoms remaining static on the timescale probed by the instrument ( ≈ 40 ps). Consequently, the integrated elastic intensity provides a direct measure of the fraction of hydrogen atoms that appear immobile on the QENS timescale.

The TA-DA ionic liquid exhibits a single-stage process, showing a gradual and continuous decrease in normalised elastic intensity with increasing temperature. This monotonic decline is expected as the ionic liquid components (cations and anions) gain thermal energy, leading to increased molecular mobility and faster dynamics. The smooth transi tion reflects the intrinsic viscosity decrease and enhanced cation -anion motions with heating.

Pure PP exhibits a distinct two-stage behaviour. The first stage shows a gradual decrease in elastic intensity up to 160 °C, corresponding to increasing  segmental  motions  within  the  amorphous  regions  and  at H. Salazar et al.

crystallite  boundaries  while  the  bulk  crystalline  structure  remains intact. The second stage manifests as a sharp drop in elastic intensity above 160 °C, corresponding to the melting of crystalline polypropylene domains. This abrupt transition indicates that the polymer undergoes a rapid transformation from a semi-crystalline solid to a molten state. The persistence  of  high  elastic  intensity  up  to  160 °C  confirms  that  the polymer remains predominantly rigid in the absence of the ionic liquid. This melting is further confirmed by an endothermic peak, centred at 167 °C, in the heat flow thermograms, shown in Fig. 5.

In contrast, the PP + TA-DA mixture exhibits a more complex threestage  process  that  reveals  the  dissolution  mechanism.  The  first  stage shows  a  gradual  decline  similar  to  the  individual  components  up  to approximately 140 °C. The second stage is characterised by a sharp drop centred at 140 °C, which indicates a substantial transfer of scattering weight from the elastic component into the quasi-elastic wings, signi fying that polymer segments become dynamically mobile on picosecond timescales. As this pronounced feature is absent in either component alone, it is attributed to polymer -ionic-liquid interactions leading to the onset of polypropylene dissolution at ≈ 140 °C. The sudden mobility increase corresponds to polymer chains or segments gaining sufficient freedom to move independently within the ionic-liquid matrix, marking the  dissolution  of  amorphous  PP  regions  and  the  penetration  of  IL molecules between polymer chains. This transition is further confirmed by  the  shifted  endothermic  peak  in  the  heat  flow  thermogram  from 167 °C for PP, to 137 °C.

The third stage occurs around 155 °C and is attributed to the melting of  the  solvated  PP.  In  contrast  to  the  sharp  drop  observed  to  the increased drop in neat PP, this stage involves a more gradual decline in elastic intensity. The decrease of the melting point and the attenuated transition indicate that TA-DA acts as a plasticiser, lowering the effective melting  temperature  of  the  crystalline  PP  domains.  [30,31] The  IL molecules that have already penetrated the polymer matrix disrupt the crystalline structure and reduce intermolecular forces between polymer chains.  [32] Consequently,  when  the  crystalline  regions  melt,  they transition  into  an  already-solvated,  mobile  environment  rather  than undergoing a distinct solid-to-melt transition as observed in neat PP. This plasticisation effect facilitates more  efficient dissolution  by reducing the energy barrier for melting and dissolution of crystalline domains.

This three-stage dissolution mechanism observed at the molecular level supports the solubility studies (Fig. 3), which showed that no PP was recovered at 140 °C as it only started to solvate at this temperature. Whilst the sharp increase in rate between 150 and 160 °C is attributed to the solvation, and plasticisation of the PP at 160 °C.

Additionally,  thermogravimetric  analysis (Fig.  5b)  confirmed  that the TA-DA ionic liquid remains thermally stable under the operating conditions used in this study, with no significant degradation observed up to 180 °C. A minor mass loss (~6%) is observed over three hea ting -cooling cycles.

3.3. Characterisation of non-woven face masks

Disposable face masks typically consist of multilayers of non-woven fabric (see Fig. 6a). Although the exact composition can vary depending on the manufacturer, polypropylene (PP) is the dominant polymer due to its hydrophobic properties and suitability for filtration and protective applications. [33] ATR-FTIR was used to characterise the inner, middle, and  outer  layers  of  the  face  masks  used  in  this  study.  The  spectra exhibited characteristic PP absorption bands, including CH2  and CH3 bending  vibrations  at  1375  cm 1 (symmetric  CH3  deformation)  and 1456 cm 1 (CH2  deformation), as well as C -H stretching vibrations between 2839 and 2953 cm 1 . These spectral features were consistent with those observed for virgin PP, indicating that polypropylene is the primary polymer present in all layers (Fig. 6b). [34]

The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) results for the different face mask layers and virgin PP are presented in Fig. 6c. All samples exhibit a major weight loss between 350 and 550 °C, corresponding to the ther mal degradation of polypropylene. The degradation profiles of the mask materials  closely  resemble  that  of  virgin  PP,  confirming  that  poly propylene is the dominant polymer in the non-woven fabric layers.

A slightly higher residual mass was observed for the mask materials compared with virgin PP. This residue is likely associated with inorganic additives such as pigments, dyes, or fillers incorporated during mask fabrication. The derivative thermogravimetric (DTG) curves (Fig. 6d) show a single dominant degradation peak occurring between 452.5 and 457.3 °C, which is consistent with the degradation temperature of virgin PP (457.7 °C). The similarity of the degradation temperatures further confirms that the polymer composition of the mask layers is predomi nantly polypropylene.

The  recovered  PP  obtained  from  the  dissolution -reprecipitation process initially exhibited a bluish colour, originating from pigments present in the outer mask layer (Fig. 7). To remove these colourants, an additional hot filtration step was introduced. After dissolution of PP in the  ionic  liquid,  the  solution  was  filtered  at  elevated  temperature through a membrane filter to remove insoluble additives. The filtered solution  was  subsequently  reprecipitated  using  isopropanol  (IPA), yielding colourless PP after a second filtration step, as shown in Fig. 7.

The FTIR spectra (Fig. 8a) of the recovered PP samples, both before and  after  filtration,  show  absorption  bands  consistent  with  those  of virgin polypropylene, indicating that the TA-DA recovery process does not alter the chemical structure of the polymer.

The DSC thermograms (Fig. 8b) show melting and crystallisation temperatures  in  the  ranges  of  158.8 -163.7 °C  and  119.1 -123.9 °C, respectively.  The  enthalpies  associated  with  these  phase  transitions were also comparable to those of virgin PP (Table 1), confirming that the dissolution -reprecipitation process preserves the thermal behaviour and crystallinity of the recovered polymer.

3.4. Ionic liquid characterisation and stability

Having established the successful recovery of high-quality PP from face masks, we next examined the chemical stability of the ionic liquid under the applied processing conditions, an important factor in deter mining  the  overall  sustainability  of  our  process.  TA-DA  used  in  this study, along with its precursors (DMBA and TEHA), was analysed using UV -Vis  and  FTIR  spectroscopy  to  evaluate  any  changes  in  optical properties before and after ionic liquid formation (Fig. 9). [37] Addi tionally, solvent samples recovered after polypropylene dissolution at different  temperatures  were  analysed  to  assess  possible  chemical changes  during  recycling.  The  relative  concentrations  of  DMBA  and TEHA were further quantified using HPLC-MS, as shown in Fig. 10 .

The UV -Vis spectra (Fig. 9a -b) show that TEHA exhibits relatively weak absorption in the 275 -400 nm region compared to DMBA. The stronger absorption observed for DMBA arises from the C --O functional group of the carboxylic acid. The TA-DA ionic liquid displays increased absorption  intensity  within  this  region  due  to  the  presence  of  both components in the solvent mixture. Slight increases in absorbance were observed for the used TA-DA samples, which can be attributed to small variations in the acid concentration. This observation is supported by the HPLC-MS analysis described below.

Fig. 10. Molar ratios of DMBA compared to TEHA, for new and used TA-DA at various temperatures, as measured by HPLC-MS. Error bars shown are associ ated with the 97% purity of both reactants.

[38] Upon mixing DMBA with TEHA to form TA-DA, a shift of approximately 6 cm 1 and a reduction in band in tensity  are  observed,  indicating  proton  transfer  and  formation  of  an ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid. Additional peaks in the 1010 -1290 cm 1 region correspond to C -N stretching vibrations of the tertiary amine. The relative concentrations of DMBA and TEHA were further ana lysed using HPLC-MS. The measured molar ratios of DMBA to TEHA were 1.25 at room temperature, 1.22 at 140 °C, 1.16 at 150 °C, and 1.14 at 160 °C, with an experimental uncertainty of approximately 3%. These results indicate only minor variations in composition across the inves tigated  temperature  range. Mass spectrometry identified four major signals at m / z 354( + ), 370 ( + ), 242( + ), and 116( ). The m/z 354( + ) signal corresponds to TEHA, while m/z 116( ) is associated with the DMBA anion. The additional peaks at m/z 370( + ) and 242( + ) correspond to minor impurities orig inating from the commercial amine precursor, namely tris(2-ethylhexyl) amine  N-oxide  and  bis(2-ethylhexyl)ammonium  ions,  respectively. These impurities arise from the 97% purity of the starting amine and were found to be negligible. Overall, the combined UV -Vis, FTIR, and HPLC-MS  analyses  confirm  that  the  TA-DA  ionic  liquid  maintains chemical stability  and consistent composition across the investigated temperature range, indicating its potential suitability for repeated reuse in polypropylene dissolution and recovery processes.

To further evaluate the thermal stability of the solvent after poly propylene dissolution at 160 °C, 1 H NMR spectroscopy was performed on TEHA, DMBA, and the recovered ionic liquid following PP dissolution and isopropanol removal (denoted TA-DA (160 p-PP)).

To perform 1 H NMR analysis, solutions were mixed in 10% CDCl3: CHCl3, with recorded spectra shown in Fig. 11, with integrated values of shifts shown in Table 3. The 1 H NMR spectrum of TEHA in CDCl3  ex hibits the expected aliphatic resonances for its three branched 2-ethyl hexyl substituents. Two terminal methyl groups appear as triplets at 0.86 and 0.92 ppm, corresponding to the -CH3 groups at the ends of the alkyl chains. The methylene protons adjacent to the tertiary amine ni trogen  resonate  at  2.06  ppm,  while  the  remaining  methylene  and methine protons give rise to a broad multiplet centred at 1.29 ppm. [39] The integration ratios are consistent with the expected proton distri bution of TEHA (9:9:6:27 respectively).

The spectrum of DMBA displays a singlet at 2.24 ppm corresponding to the methylene group adjacent to the carboxylic acid and a singlet at 1.07 ppm assigned to the tert-butyl methyl groups (9H). A broad singlet at 10.7 ppm is observed for the carboxylic acid proton, characteristic of hydrogen-bonded carboxylic acid species in CDCl3.

The 1 H NMR spectrum of the recovered solvent (TA-DA 160 p-PP) retains the characteristic aliphatic resonances associated with the TEHA alkyl chains and the DMBA tert-butyl and methylene groups, confirming that  the  molecular  backbones  of  both  components  remain  intact following  high-temperature  polypropylene  dissolution.  Notably,  the resonance corresponding to the carboxylic acid proton (~10 -11 ppm) is absent in the recycled sample. Instead, a new broad signal appears at 6.37  ppm,  which  is  assigned  to  the  proton  of  a  trialkylammonium species (R3NH + ). [40] The disappearance of the -COOH signal together with  the  emergence  of  the  ammonium  resonance  is  consistent  with proton transfer and formation of a stable ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid.

4. Conclusions

text:
In this study, an efficient chemical recycling approach was developed for the recovery of polypropylene from non-woven waste using a hybrid ionic liquid composed of tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine (TEHA) and 3,3-dime thylbutyric  acid  (DMBA).  The  optimised  process  operates  at  160 °C under ambient pressure, achieving recovery rates of up to 99%, with complete dissolution occurring in less than one minute.

Quasi-elastic  neutron  scattering  (QENS)  provided  molecular-level insight  into  the  dissolution  process,  demonstrating  that  the  ionic liquid enhances polymer segmental mobility and plasticisation, thereby enabling rapid dissolution under the applied conditions. Coupled with an  integrated  hot  filtration  step,  the  process  enables  simultaneous polymer recovery and selective removal of additives within a simplified separation method.

The recovered polypropylene exhibits thermal, structural, and me chanical properties within the same order of magnitude as virgin ma terial, indicating preservation of polymer integrity. Spectroscopic and chromatographic analyses (UV -Vis, FTIR, HPLC-MS, and NMR) confirm that the ionic liquid remains chemically stable across the investigated temperature range while maintaining a consistent  DMBA -TEHA composition ratio, indicating its potential suitability for reuse.

Overall, this work establishes a rapid and selective dis solution -reprecipitation strategy for polypropylene recovery enabled by a hybrid ionic liquid. The results show that solvent -polymer interactions govern polymer mobility and phase separation during dis solution -reprecipitation, providing a mechanistic basis for solvent se lection and process optimisation. This study defines a viable solventbased route for recovering polypropylene from complex waste streams and establishes  a  framework for extending such approaches to other polyolefin systems.

1. Introduction

Ever since fast fashion has attempted to satisfy the demands of a rapidly growing population(Hämmerle,2011), theglobal waste pollution has increased tremendously. Europe disposes 75% (4.3 million tons) of textiles waste annually due to the absence of viable recycling strategies. (Briga-Sá et al., 2013) Interwoven cotton polyester blendsrepresentoneofthemostprominentmixturesonthemarket, which are difficult to recycle because of their heterogeneity. Conventional fiber spinning processes can partly reuse pure cellulose waste (Shen and Patel, 2010), but they are unable to handle blended waste garments. Therefore, the recycling of cotton polyester blends has yet demanded either the depolymerization or dissolution of either component. The dissolution of polyester usually involves toxic solvents and elevated temperatures (DMSO), which can influence the properties of the cellulose component (Serad, 1993). Accordingly, polyester is preferably subjected to alcoholysis, hydrolysis, or glycolysis reactions ( 1992; Palme et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2013).

Similar approaches have also been used to degrade cellulose under acidic conditions (Cowan, 1981; Gruntfest and Turner, 1974; Ouchi et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2013). An example is the

The creation of a circular economy for cellulose based textile waste is supported by the development of an upcycling method for cotton polyester blended waste garments. We present a separation procedure for cotton and polyester using [DBNH] [OAc], a superbase based ionic liquid, which allows the selective dissolution of the cellulose component. After the removal of PET, the resulting solution could be employed to dry-jet wet spin textile grade cellulose fibers down to the microfiber range (0.75-2.95 dtex) with breaking tenacities (27-48 cN/tex) and elongations (7-9%) comparable to commercial Lyocell fibers made from high-purity dissolving pulp. The treatment time in [DBNH] [OAc] was found to reduce the tensile properties (<52%) and the molar mass distribution (<51%) of PET under certain processing conditions. Ó 2019 The Author(s). hydrolysis of cotton employing hydrochloric acid to generate a microcrystalline cellulose powder, which can be separated from the remaining polyester fabric. The recovered polyester is re-spun to PET yarns that can then be used to manufacture new textiles (Sun et al., 2018a, 2018b).

Less destructive methods utilize ionic liquids (ILs) or NMMO to dissolve the cotton component. Negulescu et al. prepared a 1-2% cellulose solution from cotton polyester blends, and removed the polyester residue by filtration. Afterwards, the cellulose solution was further concentrated up to 15-17% using cotton material from an alternative feedstock (Negulescu et al., 1998). A recent patent further elaborates this approach. An amine oxide solvent such as NMMO is supposed to dissolve the cellulose component of various blended textile products to yield cellulose solutions of up to 35% (Brinks et al., 2013). Similarly, 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM] [Cl]) and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([BMIM] [OAc]) have been described to foster the recycling of blended textile waste. The process steps are comparable to NMMO. The ionic liquid dissolves the cellulose component, while filtration removes the polyester residue, and subsequent coagulation recovers the cellulose (de Silva et al., 2014). Although both NMMO and IL based approaches highlight the potential of the generated cellulose solutions to be used in a film or fiber spinning process, neither of them provides any relevant data that could serve as a proof of concept.
