HSPs for a wide range of polymers and solvents have been tabulated in the HSP handbook. [29] However, there are multiple sets of HSP values for PE. Table 2 shows seven sets of room-temperature HSP values that are listed for PE in the handbook as well as values for EVOH. The different HSP values for PE resins reflect differences in properties such as crystallinities and molecular weight distributions. Unfortunately, little information is provided in this literature regarding the most appropriate set of parameters.

Table 3 shows R a /R 0 values for the nine solvents tested experimentally for PE and for EVOH. Each value is formatted based on comparison to the experimental solubility data: values of R a /R 0 < 1 are bold if the experimental solubility is greater than 1 wt% and normal if the experimental solubility is less than 1 wt%, whereas values of R a /R 0 > 1 are bold if the experimental solubility is less than 1 wt% and normal if the experimental solubility is greater than 1 wt%. Excluding DMSO, the HSP values for EVOH generally were good predictors of experimental solubility data. The room-temperature DMSO value is also near the threshold and would likely be identified as a good solvent if temperature effects were included. However, different sets of HSPs for PE lead to different solvent screening results. Surprisingly, the HSPs of high-density (HD)PE resulted in a perfect match with the experiments, even though the polymer used experimentally was actually LDPE. The data for PE (1) and LDPE (2) correctly classify 8/9 solvents, but PE (2), LDPE (1), and LDPE (3) perform worse with only 5-6 correct classifications each. Moreover, the errors are generally due to HSP values identifying poor solvents as good (i.e., R a /R 0 values are erroneously low), which cannot be attributed to temperature effects. Since it can be unclear which of these values to select in advance, there are clear deficiencies with using HSP values for screening solvents for these polymers. Similarly, the solubilities of EVOH in DMSO and DMF are substantially higher than that of PE in toluene even though the ratio R a /R 0 for PE in toluene tends to be much lower, highlighting that HSPs cannot provide quantitative information on solubility predictions. These observations motivate the need for alternative methods for solubility predictions.

PE solubility predictions

text:
We sought to develop a quantitative solubility prediction workflow using COSMO-RS to improve upon the deficiencies of HSPs noted above. We first systematically compared the impact of several parameters by predicting solubilities for PE as a simple homopolymer for which HSPs were shown to be inaccurate. Since the computational modeling of a full-length polymer molecule is formidable, the polymers were modeled as oligomers. The oligomer chain length was thus the first parameter we considered: increasing the chain length will increase the computational cost of the DFT calculations (the most time-consuming step in the COMSO-RS workflow) but could increase prediction accuracy. Consequently, there is a potential tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational time that must be quantified to guide the solubility prediction workflow.

To select a reasonable chain length, PE oligomers with 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 carbon atoms were selected. MD simulations were performed of each oligomer and 3 conformers of each length were randomly selected. Each conformer was then input separately to DFT and COSMO-RS solubility calculations, with the latter using literature values for the melting point and heat of fusion of PE. The CPU time of the DFT calculation was used to quantify computational cost because the MD simulation time is not substantially affected by the chain length and the COSMO-RS calculation time is minimal. Figure 4 shows the mean prediction error and DFT calculation CPU time as a function of oligomer chain length. As the PE oligomer length increases, the mean solubility prediction error decreases and DFT CPU time increases, illustrating the hypothesized tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost. This result also confirms that the COSMORS prediction accuracy can be systematically improved. We selected the PE oligomer with 12 carbon atoms (corresponding to 5 ethylene units and 2 methyl end groups) for further workflow development because it has an acceptable prediction error with relatively short computational time.

With the oligomer chain length determined, we next studied the impact of the number of conformers on the tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational cost. Different chain conformations have different screening charge density profiles that can influence the solubility prediction results, with substantial differences possible given conformational flexibility of the oligomers. From the MD trajectory, we selected a set of 30 representative conformations that span a range of R g and SASA values for the 12-carbon PE oligomer using the grid sampling method. A series of subsets of different sizes (1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 conformers) were then generated by randomly selecting each number of conformers from the 30. 10 subsets were generated for each chosen subset size. Figure 5 shows the mean prediction error and DFT calculation CPU time as a function of the number of conformers (defined following the approach of Figure 4), with each point representing the average over all 10 subsets. The computational time required to generate a conformer set linearly scales with the set size. The mean prediction error decreases as more conformers are used and the error values tend to plateau as the number of conformers increases, again indicating that the COSMO-RS predictions can be systematically improved. Based on this comparison, the conformer number was selected to be 10 for the final solubility predictions.

Figure 5. Variation in the solubility prediction error and computational cost with the number of PE conformers used. All points represent an average over 10 subsets of conformers for a PE oligomer with a 12-carbon chain length.

The 10-conformer set of the 12-carbon PE oligomer was used for final solubility predictions to compare to the experimental data. The solubility predictions in Figures 4 and 5 used the melting temperature and heat of fusion data of PE from literature sources, which leads to a relatively large error (Supporting Information). [45] However, the properties of PE resins could vary substantially between different samples, particularly since the heat of fusion will depend on polymer crystallinity. Therefore, we instead utilized the experimental solubility of PE in toluene at 110 °C as a reference value for the solid-liquid equilibrium calculation for all solvents. Table 4 shows corresponding predicted and experimental solubilities. As expected, the COSMO-RS protocol predicts near-zero solubilities for all solvents other than toluene in good agreement with the experimental measurements. Notably, several of these solvents are predicted by some sets of HSPs to be good solvents (e. g., hexane, THF, and ethyl acetate; see Table 3), indicating that the COSMO-RS approach qualitatively outperforms the HSP approach as well as providing quantitative solubility estimates. The COSMO-RS approach does slightly overestimate solubilities in nonsolvents, but these results are highly consistent with the experimental benchmarks if 2 wt% is used as a threshold to distinguish solvents and nonsolvents.

EVOH solubility predictions

text:
We performed a similar process to compare the influence of oligomer length and the number of conformers on solubility predictions for EVOH. Since EVOH is a copolymer, we utilized the block copolymer oligomer structure for predictions when varying these parameters (to ensure a consistent monomer sequence), then compared predictions using the block, alternating and random copolymer structures (Figure 2). Figure 6 shows the mean prediction error and computational cost as a function of oligomer chain lengths between 8 to 32 carbon atoms in increments of 6 carbon atoms. This increment corresponds to 3 monomer units to maintain the 1:2 ethylene/vinyl alcohol ratio. For each oligomer length there are 3 conformers randomly selected from the MD trajectories. Based on the tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational cost shown in this figure, the 14-carbon EVOH oligomer was selected because of the relatively low error values in a short computational time. This oligomer has 2 ethylene units, 4 vinyl alcohol units, and 2 methyl end groups.

Figure 6. Variation in the solubility prediction error and computational cost with EVOH oligomer length. Three conformers in the block copolymer structure are used for the solubility predictions for each data point.

Figure 7. Variation in the solubility prediction error and computational cost with the number of EVOH conformers used. All points represent an average over 10 subsets of conformers for a EVOH oligomer with a 14-carbon chain length and block copolymer structure.

The number of conformers was then investigated for EVOH. A set of 40 representative conformations with various R g and SASA values were selected using the grid sampling method and split into subsets of 1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 conformers. 10 distinct subsets were generated for each number of conformers. Figure 7 shows the mean prediction error and computational cost as a function of the number of conformers with each point representing the average over all 10 subsets. The scale of the vertical axis for mean prediction error is larger than that in Figure 5, indicating that the effect of the number of conformers is more significant for EVOH than for PE, but still plateaus as expected. Based on this comparison, the conformer number for EVOH was selected to be 20.

To further illustrate the effect of conformers on solubility predictions, Figure 8 shows the predicted EVOH solubility in DMSO as a function of temperature. Experimental data at four temperatures are included for reference. Predictions were based on either 1, 5, or 20 EVOH conformers, with 10 separate subsets of conformers used for predictions. Predicted solubilities with only a single conformer varied substantially and lie with the region indicated by the light blue color. The region bounding the solubility predictions decreased substantially for the 5conformer sets (light green region). For the 20-conformer sets, the solubility calculations are highly consistent leading to a deep blue region that nearly converges to a solid line such that variations are difficult to discern by eye. These results indicate that increasing the number of conformers both leads to a decrease in prediction accuracy (Figure 7) and decreases the variation between different subsets of conformers, suggesting more robust results. Moreover, all conformer sets exhibit reasonable agreement with experiments, with the final results (for 20 conformers) slightly overestimating the measured solubilities but exhibiting similar trends.

Unlike PE, EVOH is a copolymer that has two different monomer units. The arrangement of these units leads to different types of structures. As shown in Figure 2, three types of structures were compared using oligomers with 14-carbon chain lengths and 20 conformers per oligomer. For this comparison, the experimental solubility of EVOH in DMSO at 95 °C was used as the reference for the solid-liquid equilibrium calculation. Table 5 compares solubility predictions to the experimental data. Clearly, DMF was recognized as a good solvent in all three cases, but only the block structure result correctly identifies it as the best solvent in the list. Solubilities are somewhat overpredicted for experimentally identified nonsolvents, with ethanol being the most notable deviation. However, the values clearly differentiate solvents and nonsolvents, with a slightly higher threshold (3 wt%) required to distinguish these categories than is necessary for PE. With respect to quantitative predictions, the random structure has the lowest overall mean prediction error, which is consistent with the fact that EVOH is a random copolymer. [46]

Figure 8. Temperature-dependent solubility prediction for EVOH in DMSO with different conformer sets. The light blue, light green, and deep blue regions show the range of predicted solubilities obtained from 10 predictions using subsets of 1, 5, or 20 conformers, respectively. Red dots are experimental data. All predictions used an EVOH oligomer with a 14carbon chain length and block copolymer structure. Results for each set of conformers are shown separately in Figure S4.

Computational screening of selective solvents

To demonstrate the power of the proposed computational solubility prediction method, we applied the COSMO-RS protocol to identify selective solvents for PE and EVOH from a large library of 524 solvents. We note that the results in Tables 4 and 5 (and corresponding experiments) indicate that DMSO and DMF are selective solvents for EVOH (by promoting high EVOH solubility and low PE solubility) whereas toluene is a selective solvent for PE; the screening procedure thus seeks to identify additional selective solvents beyond these examples. As above, a 10-conformer set of 12-carbon PE oligomers and a 20conformer set of 14-carbon EVOH oligomers were used. The solubilities were computed at room temperature and 1 °C below the boiling points of the respective solvents. For this screening procedure, we define selective solvents as solvents with a solubility greater than 10 wt% for one polymer and lower than 1 wt% for the other. Table 6 shows some selected examples of identified selective solvents; full solubility prediction results are available in the Supporting Information. At room temperature, the PE solubility was < 1 wt% in all solvents considered, so no PE-selective solvents were found in this condition. PE-selective solvents were identified when temperatures were increased near the solvents' boiling points. EVOH-selective solvents were found at both room temperature and elevated temperatures. The calculations for this large-scale solvent screening were completed within 2 h since no new MD or DFT calculations were required, demonstrating the efficiency of this computational approach.

The computational efficiency of this solvent screening approach enables its application to the selection of solvents for solvent-mediated plastic recycling processes, such as the STRAP process described in our previous work. In our first STRAP process, pure DMSO was used to dissolve EVOH from a multilayer plastic film, and then water was added as an antisolvent to precipitate the polymer. [8] The computational approach presented in this work is more accurate than the prior approach due to the newly developed methods for conformational screening and oligomer length selection, suggesting that it can be applied to improve the recovery of polymers in revised STRAP processes. For example, our prior work selected solvents for STRAP based primarily on solubility considerations; technoeconomic analysis was then performed to evaluate the minimum selling price of the recovered materials necessary for economic feasibility. The computational screening approach could instead be applied to identify solvents that both selectively dissolve target polymers and reduce downstream costs associated with polymer recovery and solvent recycling, leveraging the computational efficiency and improved accuracy described in this work. The computational approach could also be utilized to identify temperature-controlled polymer dissolution and precipitation at fixed solvent compositions to reduce the use of antisolvent and improve process economics. [21] Another example application would be to search for green solvents (quantified by metrics such as energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions in solvent production or environmental health and safety rankings [47,48] ) as potential replacements for common industrial solvents, permitting quantification of tradeoffs between greenness and solubility behavior of the solvents. There are thus multiple opportunities to apply the computational protocol developed in this work to efficiently identify solvent systems that improve selective dissolution processes for plastic recycling.

Conclusions

In this work, we present a computational approach to quantitatively predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in various solvents. Our approach employs molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) calculations. The MD simulation models a polymer as an oligomer and simulates its motion in a dilute solution to generate various chain conformations. Representative oligomer conformers that span a range of radius of gyration ( R g ) and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) values are then used as input structures to COSMO-RS solubility calculations. We note that while this work uses COSMO-RS, we expect that alternative COSMO-based models (e. g., COSMOSAC) may also be suitable for this approach. [49] We studied the effects of oligomer length, conformer numbers, and copolymer structures on the accuracy of solubility predictions. We show that increasing the oligomer length and number of conformers can systematically improve prediction accuracy, albeit with increased computational cost. By selecting a reasonable oligomer length and number of conformers, the proposed approach leads to solubility predictions in good agreement with experimental measurements for polyethylene (PE) and ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) in DMSO, water, THF, hexane, ethyl acetate, ethanol, acetone, toluene and DMF. These predictions outperform qualitative Hansen solubility parameter (HSP)-based solubility predictions while also enabling predictions of temperature-dependent behavior, and lead to more accurate predictions than the protocol employed in our past work. [8] We demonstrated the applicability and efficiency of the new computational approach by screening 524 solvents to identify selective solvents for the dissolution of PE and EVOH at two temperatures. Future work will apply this protocol to additional polymers, including both industrially relevant polymers and biopolymers (e. g., lignin) that must be solubilized prior to depolymerization. A current limitation of the method is the need for a single experimental solubility measurement in a good solvent as input to account for sample-specific parameter. While a suitable reference good solvent could be identified by initial qualitative screening using HSP values, future work will aim to reduce the amount of needed experimental input by incorporating explicit consideration of polymer molecular weight and crystallinity.

1. Introduction

Plastics  are  widely  produced  and  used  across  various  industries, including construction, food packaging, and automotive manufacturing. In  2022,  global  plastic  production  reached  400.2  million  tons,  with polyvinyl chloride (PVC) ranking second after polyolefins, accounting for 50.84 million tons [1]. Since the 1970s, PVC production has grown steadily, leading to significant challenges in waste management. Recy cling has emerged as a key solution following prior sorting steps [2,3], with two primary approaches: mechanical recycling and physico-chemical recycling.

Mechanical recycling, the most common approach, involves washing and shredding waste with similar formulations. However, it is not well suited for complex materials like PVC, which often contain high levels of

A B S T R A C T

Plastics are widely used materials composed of polymers and various additives to achieve specific properties. Their composition is often highly complex, particularly in post-consumer plastic waste. As mechanical recycling faces increasing limitations, chemistry-driven strategies are attracting growing interest to improve plastic re covery. Among these, dissolution recycling offers the possibility of selectively recovering pure polymers free from additives and contaminants. However, the absence of efficient methods to separate and analyze the different components of plastics remains a major bottleneck to evaluate recycling processes effiency. Here, we report the first application of Centrifugal Partition Chromatography (CPC) to address this challenge using polyvinyl chlo ride (PVC) as a model material. A biphasic solvent system based on heptane, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and 3pentanone (DEK) (25/45/30 w/w/w) was developed, guided by Hansen solubility parameters. CPC enabled the separation of the polymer from organic additives and contaminants, as well as the fractionation of additives into distinct groups, facilitating their subsequent identification and potential quantification. Moreover, CPC allows the recovery of sufficient amounts of purified polymer, enabling detailed spectroscopic characterization to assess its  structural integrity and purity. After fractionation, additives were identified by reverse phase liquid chro matography coupled with tandem high resolution mass spectrometry (RPLC -HRMS/MS), while the recovered polymer was analyzed using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Overall, these results demonstrate that CPC is a promising tool to fractionate complex plastic matrices, offering  new  opportunities  for  advanced  material  characterization  and  supporting  the  development  of  more efficient recycling processes.

Solvent-based recycling, an advanced physico-chemical recycling method, has been gaining interest as a complementary solution. This approach employs solvent systems to selectively dissolve and separate polymers from ad ditives, contaminants, and impurities. It not only enables the recovery of high-purity polymers but also facilitates the identification and potential reuse of extracted additives, making it particularly well suited for PVC and  other  complex  plastics.  PVC  is  highly  versatile,  encompassing  a broad range of formulations for various applications. As a composite material, it combines a polymer base with additives, which can account for up to 70 % of the weight in soft PVCs. For example, di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), a commonly used plasticizer in PVC, has been regulated since 2011 and must not exceed 0.1 % by weight of the plastic.

The  development  of  efficient  recycling  processes,  particularly  for complex  materials  like  PVC,  relies  heavily  on  advanced  analytical methodologies. Analytical techniques enable the precise characteriza tion of waste streams, ensuring the identification and quantification of additives and contaminants. This information is essential for optimizing recycling  processes,  such  as  solvent-based  approaches.  Moreover, analytical  monitoring  supports  compliance  with  evolving  regulations and  guarantees  the  quality  of  recycled  materials,  making  it  a  key element in advancing sustainable solutions for plastic waste management.

Today, methods to characterize plastic waste, including their aging, are limited due to the complexity of the matrix. The two parts of plastics (polymer  and  additives)  are  characterized  differently  and  by  conse quence, their separation is required. In literature, different solid/liquid extraction methods exist, as microwave assisted extraction, accelerated solvent extraction, ultrasonic assisted extraction, soxhlet, etc [6]. The dissolution-precipitation method is also well known as a purification method and continue to be developed [7]. However, this method pre sents limits as capture of additives during reprecipitation or degradation of polymer with high temperature involved [8]. In particular, multiple steps are required to fully recover additives with dissolution-precipitation and obtain a purified polymer. For instance, one  study  demonstrated  that  at  least  seven  purification  steps  are necessary to separate DEHP from PVC resin [9]. The difficulty in sepa rating PVC resin from its additives arises from their high chemical af finity, which is reflected in their very close Hansen solubility parameters [10]. These parameters -describing dispersive, polar, and hydrogen-bonding interactions -are widely used to predict solubility and miscibility between polymers and additives. The closer the Hansen parameters, the stronger the interaction, and the more challenging the separation.

In general, all methods described in literature are useful to extract one additive or  additive  families.  However  they  are  not  associate  to exhaustive extraction methods of additives [11]. The literature lacks fractionation  methods  to  recover  both  the  purified  polymer  and  the additives to characterize or quantify them. In one hand, the polymer is characterized  chemically  by  size  exclusion  chromatography  (SEC) [12 -14] or by Fourier transform infra-red spectroscopy (FTIR) [15,16]. In  the  other  hand,  organic  additives  and  their  respective  potential degradation products are often characterized by gas chromatography coupled  with  mass  spectrometry  (GC -MS)  for  volatiles  [17 -19]  and liquid  chromatography  coupled  with  mass  spectrometry  (LC-MS)  for semi-volatiles and non-volatiles [20 -23].

Centrifugal  partition  chromatography  (CPC)  is  a  well-established method for purifying natural materials. It can also be used to purify macromolecules such as proteins or to fractionate some complex mix tures such as lignocellulosic hydrolysates [24 -27]. This type of chro matography involves two immiscible liquid phases, similar to liquid-liquid  extraction:  one  serves  as  the  stationary  phase  and  the other as the mobile phase. The compounds in the sample are distributed between the two phases according to their affinity for each. Their sep aration depends on their partition coefficients, defined as the ratio of solute concentrations in the stationary and mobile phases. A low parti tion  coefficient  indicates  a  high  affinity  of  the  solute  for  the  mobile phase. During CPC, the mobile phase flows through the stationary phase, which is retained in the CPC cells by centrifugal force. Compounds with higher affinity for the mobile phase elute more quickly, corresponding to higher partition coefficients. One major advantage of CPC is its versa tility:  a  tailored  biphasic  solvent  system  can  be  designed  to  match  a specific  sample  matrix,  provided  the  two  phases  remain  immiscible. Moreover,  both  the  mobile  and  stationary  phases  can  be  recovered, enabling complete recovery of the sample without loss.

This study presents the first application of CPC on plastic materials. It purposes a methodology to separate additives and polymers from plastic without degrading them, focusing on PVC -based materials. Inspired by the  use  of  CPC  as  a  purification  technique  for  natural  products,  the methodology aims to extract and purify molecules of interest -specif ically  additives  such  as  phthalates -and  the  polymer  itself  from  a complex matrix. The main advantages of CPC, as previously discussed, include  its  versatility,  complete  sample  recovery,  and  suitability  for preparative-scale applications. In the context of plastic characterization, separating additives from the polymer is essential to facilitate accurate analysis. CPC is therefore employed to recover all organic additives in one phase while the polymer remains in the other, enabling its total purification  and  recovery.  The  initial  step  consisted  of  identifying  a biphasic solvent system adapted to the PVC matrix, using Hansen solu bility parameters and refining it through the UNIFAC method to ensure stability. The CPC method was then developed using a model feedstock containing a plasticizer from a regulated family (phthalates), and the additive fractions were characterized by liquid chromatography coupled with electrospray ionization high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-ESIHRMS) to confirm complete additive removal. The polymer resin was finally characterized by SEC and FTIR to assess its purity and potential degradation.

CPC experiments were performed on a SCPC100 associated to a Spot Prep II (Gilson Purification, USA). The column used has a volume of 131 mL and the apparatus had a total dead volume of 20 mL. The system was equipped with a quaternary pump, an automatic sample injection valve with a 5 mL sample loop and a fraction collector. Experiments were conducted at room temperature (20 ± 2 °C). The solvent system con sisted  of  heptane/DMSO/DEK  (0.25/0.45/0.30  w/w/w).  Ascending elution mode was used, allowing the use of the DMSO-enriched phase as the  stationary  phase  and  the  heptane-enriched  phase  as  the  mobile phase. The stationary phase (A) is a ratio of heptane/DMSO/DEK (7.7/ 61.4/30.9 w/w/w) and the mobile phase (B) a ratio of heptane/DMSO/ DEK  (62/7.8/30.2  w/w/w).  Each  phase  was  prepared  in  a  separate bottle.

The  Table  2 shows  the  different  parameters  used  to  prepare  the column and carry out the separation. The stationary phase ratio was measured at 50 %. It corresponds to the ratio of stationary phase and mobile phase present in CPC cells after equilibration. Fractions were collected  every  10  mL  during  the  70  min  of  the  elution  part  and numbered consequently from 1 to 49.

Then they are collected every 55 mL for 10 min during the extrusion part, ie the recovery of the stationary phase.

The  partition  coefficient  K  corresponds  to  the  ratio  of  the  solute concentrations [S] in the upper and in the lower phases (Eq. (1)):

K D = [ S ] lower [ S ] upper (1)

KD  was measured on model molecules in the heptane/DMSO/DEK system. The biphasic system was prepared as described in part 2.4. 5 mL of  each  phase  and  approximately  100  mg  of  analytical  standard (phthalates  or  pure  PVC  resin)  were  added  to  a  20  mL  flask. 2.6. Data processing for RPLC-ESI-HRMS data

An automatic  mass  calibration  using  sodium  formate  clusters  be tween 90 -1200 m/z is ensured by the high-precision calibration algo rithm (HPC) during the 0.5 first minutes of each run. The analytical sequence comprises 49 fractions from the CPC fractionation of the model PVC and 49 fractions from the CPC fractionation of a sample containing only the solvent system in order to have a CPC extraction blank.

Data processing was performed on DataAnalysis ® (Bruker Daltonics, Germany). For each fraction, the signal of the correspondent blank was subtracted. It provided to deduce the ions of interest. For each feature, an  extracted  ion  chromatogram  (EICs)  was  built  based  on  the  most intense adduct ([ M + H] + , [ M + Na] + or [ M + NH4] + ). It gives a certain number of compounds of interest for each fraction. EICs were added with  a  home-made  software  and  a ' remastered  chromatogram ' was obtained for each elution fraction (Figure S1).

2.7. SEC analysis

Two  different  SEC  systems  were  used  to  fulfill  complementary analytical objectives. A UV-RI SEC system was employed to determine the partition coefficients of the polymer and associated additives (1), while a multi-detection SEC setup enabled in-depth characterization of the polymer fractions collected after CPC extrusion, including molecular weight distribution and intrinsic viscosity (2).

SEC analysis was performed on an Agilent 1260 system composed of a pump, an autosampler (15 °C), a column over (50 °C), a UV detector and a refractive index (RI) detector. The mobile phase was THF. The injection volume was 5 µ L. Seperation was achieve on 3 columns Waters Acquity APC XT 150 × 4,6 mm (45 Å, 125 Å and  450  Å).  The  flow  was  set  at  0.6  mL/min.  The  signal  of polymer was measured with the RI detection, while the phtha lates  signal  was  measured  at  226  nm  using  UV  detection.  A calibration curve of DBP, DEHP, DIDP and PVC K75 was associ ated to determine the exact concentration of the samples.

 SEC analyses were carried out using a Viscotek TDA 305 system equipped  with  an  autosampler,  a  column  oven,  and  a  triple detection system (RALS-LALS, refractive index, and viscometer detectors), all thermostatted at 40 °C. Injections of 100 µ L were performed  on  a  set  of  three  Mixed-C  columns  from  Agilent operated at 40 °C. The mobile phase was tetrahydrofuran (THF), delivered in isocratic mode at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min. The system was calibrated using a universal calibration method based on PS standards, and a refractive index increment (dn/dc) value of 0.105 was applied [28].

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Optimization of CPC operational parameters

This study presents a method for separating a polymer from additives using a model formulation. The objective is to identify a solvent system that retains the polymer in one phase while extracting and recovering the additives in the other. To achieve this, the system must satisfy four key criteria:

 both the polymer and the additives must be soluble in the solvent system  without  any  precipitation,  to  avoid  damaging  the  CPC equipment and to enable their separation.

 the solvent system must form two immiscible liquid phases.

 effective  separation  in  CPC  requires  the  additives  to  partition between the two phases, while the polymer remains exclusively in one (Figure S2). This behavior is reflected in the polymer ' s partition  coefficient,  which  should  ideally  approach  infinity, indicating  complete  retention  in  a  single  phase -unlike  the additives.

lastly, the two phases must separate (demix) within 30 s to ensure stable operation of the CPC system.

3.1.1. Selection of biphasic solvent systems

The key to selecting an effective solvent system lies in its ability to solubilize compounds and separate them without causing precipitation.

In  CPC,  three  commonly  used  biphasic  solvent  systems  are:  the ARIZONA system (heptane, ethyl acetate, methanol, water), the OKA system (hexane, ethyl acetate, n-butanol, methanol and water) and the acetone  scale  (heptane,  toluene,  acetone  and  water)  which  together cover most cases in natural product purification [24]. When these sol vents are incompatible with the samples -resulting in precipitation -alternative approaches using ' good ' solvents can be considered [29]. This is referred to as the good solvent approach for CPC solvent system selection,  which  has  been  described  in  the  literature  when  standard systems  are  ineffective  [25,30,31].  In  this  study,  the ' good ' solvent approach is applied using HSPs as a guiding tool.

HSPs are used to characterize the solubility of a polymer in a solvent. They are three parameters: δ D  (quantify the strength of dispersion in teractions), δ P (quantify the dipole-dipole interactions) and δ H (quantify the hydrogen bonding interactions). Theses parameters are determined theoretically  or  experimentally  for  a  solvent  or  a  solute  and  can  be represented on a 3D diagram with the three parameters as coordinates.

For polymers, an additional parameter is introduced, represented by a sphere centered at the point corresponding to the polymer ' s Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSPs) in the three-dimensional HSP space. The radius of this sphere (R ₀ ) defines the boundary for ' good ' solvents. The geometric distance (Ra) between a solvent and the polymer in the 3D HSP space indicates how compatible they are. If the ratio R ₀ /Ra is greater than  one  -  meaning  the  solvent  lies  within  the  polymer ' s  solubility sphere - the solvent is considered ' good ' [10].

The same goes for additives, the geometric distance Ra can be used to determine which solvent is the most likely compatible with them. The smaller Ra is, the more compatible they are:

Ra² = 4 ( δ D 1 δ D 2 ) ² + ( δ P 1 δ P 2 ) ² + ( δ H 1 δ H 2 ) ²

If a solvent blend is considered, to estimate solubilities, parameters of each solvent ( δ D, δ P, δ H) are added relatively to their percentage φ in the blend:

( δ D , δ P , δ H ) blend = ∑ φ n , comp ( δ D , δ P , δ H ) n , comp

HSPs offer  insights  into  the  solubility  behavior  of  components  in various solvents. A model PVC formulation was selected as a reference matrix, primarily composed of PVC and DIDP, a widely used plasticizer.

DIDP is part of the phthalate family, a group of additives often pre sent in high concentrations in soft PVC formulations, some of which are subject  to  strict  regulatory  oversight.  Therefore,  the  selected  solvent system will also be evaluated with regulated phthalates to validate its broader applicability.

3.1.1.1. Solvent system selection using Hansen parameters. The selection of solvents is based on their affinity for model plastic using HSPs [32]. More generally, all the solubility parameters were founded in the liter ature, Vebber et al. quote HSPs for 100 common solvents and Hansen gives  HSP  for  phthalates  [32,33].  Then,  Table  3 gives  HSPs  of  the various compounds studied (polymer, DIDP, the selected solvents), as well as the associated Ra values, and the representation of these data in a 3D diagram is also available in Fig. 1. The criteria for the selection of each solvent are detailed below.

The first step involves selecting the most suitable solvent for dis solving PVC. DEK was chosen for this purpose, with Ra values (distance in  Hansen space) of 2.4 MPa 1/2 from PVC and 3 MPa 1/2 from DIDP, indicating it is likely a good solvent for both the polymer and the plas ticizer. Next, heptane was selected for its ability to dissolve the phthalate (Ra = 7.2 MPa 1/2 ) while being a poorer solvent for PVC. This is reflected by its location at the edge of the PVC solubility sphere in the HSP dia gram, suggesting limited compatibility with the polymer. Finally, DMSO was chosen as a third solvent to establish a biphasic system. In the HSP space, it is positioned opposite to heptane, promoting phase separation. However, DMSO still lies within the PVC solubility sphere (Ra = 9.6 MPa 1/2 ),  ensuring  that  the  polymer  remains  dissolved  and  does  not precipitate. (Table 2)

To create a stable bi-phasic system for CPC separation, the ratio of solvent was determined with a ternary diagram (Fig. 2). This diagram was built with the software ASPEN V11 and based on UNIFAC theory [34].

The solvent ratios were selected to ensure compatibility with both the polymer and the additive. PVC should not be exposed to excessive amounts of heptane (e.g., 50 %), as this may lead to precipitation of the resin. Conversely, the phthalate additive (DIDP) should not be in contact with high concentrations of DMSO (e.g., 50 %) to avoid immiscibility issues. As previously mentioned DEK is not considered a limiting sol vent, due to its good compatibility with both components. In this study, a heptane/DMSO/DEK (w/w/w) ratio of 0.25/0.45/0.30 was used. This solvent system proved to be stable, with a phase separation time (also called demixing) of less than 30 s after shaking. The upper phase con sisted of 62.0 % (w) heptane, 7.8 % (w) DMSO, and 30.2 % (w) DEK, while  the  lower  phase  consisted  of  7.7  %  (w)  heptane,  61.4  %  (w) DMSO, and 30.9 % (w) DEK.

The sharing of components between phases is represented by parti tion coefficients, as compiled in Table 4. These partition coefficients are initially  estimated using HSPs and then confirmed experimentally by SEC analysis of each phase. For the HSP estimation, the lower the Ra value, the higher the affinity of the solute for the phase. This estimation helps  determine  whether  the  CPC  method,  along  with  the  identified solvent  system,  can  effectively  separate  plasticizers  from  the  PVC polymer.

Additionally, partition  coefficients  for  two  other  phthalates,  DEHP  and  DBP,  were estimated and included in the analysis. Theses two phthalates are here presented to demonstrate that the solvent system is not only applicable to DIDP, but also to other REACH regulated phthalates. HSP affinities indicate that the phthalates will be distributed between the two phases, while PVC will predominantly prefer the lower phase. Experimentally, the phthalates are effectively split between the two phases, with the PVC resin remaining in the lower phase. The experimental results confirm the potential for CPC separation of each phthalate tested.

The partition coefficient (KD) governs the CPC separation process: the higher the KD value, the faster the solute will be eluted from the CPC column, as shown in Fig. 3.

Consequently, the study predicts the following elution order for the phthalates in  CPC:  DIDP,  followed  by  DEHP and  DBP.  The polymer, however, does not partition between the two phases.

In the end, the four prerequisites for developing a suitable solvent system were validated: the organic fraction of the plastic (polymer and organic additives) is totally soluble, the system is biphasic and stable, the polymer remains in the lower phase and the additives of interest are shared between the 2 phases.

3.2. CPC method development: elution-extrusion

The CPC method is divided in two parts: the elution and the extru sion. After the equilibration of the two phases in the CPC cells at a given flow, the solute is injected. The mobile phase flows through the sta tionary phase and is recovered during the elution part. The stationary phase  is  then  extruded  (pushed  out)  from  cells,  it  corresponds  to extrusion part.

The choice of the solvent system leads to the polymer being present in the lower phase, while the additives are distributed between both phases. The mobile and stationary phases are then selected to promote the partitioning of the different sample components according to the separation objectives. To enable the separation of the additives from each other and from the polymer, the upper phase is selected as the mobile phase. Since the polymer is expected to elute with the extrusion fractions, it should preferentially remain in the stationary phase.

This choice determines the direction of flow (ascending or descending). In this case, the upper phase (used as the mobile phase) must pass through the lower phase. Therefore, an ascending mode is selected.

In practice, the sample is dissolved in the stationary phase and can be concentrated until 12 % of polymer weight in solvent. Above this con centration, the solubility ' s limit of the sample leads to an increase in viscosity, making the solution incompatible with CPC conditions. At 12 % of weight, the concentration of the sample in the solution does not disturb the equilibrium of the bi-phasic system.

3.3. Elution fractions: recovery of PVC additives

The CPC was then applied to a plastic from a model feedstock. This part will purpose method to ensure total recovery of PVC resin and the different  additives  after  CPC  fractionation.  The  solvent  system  was developed using phthalates as a model, given their high concentration in PVC formulations. However, this approach also ensures the complete recovery of other organic compounds present in the plastic. To rule out the presence of residual polymer in the elution fractions, these were characterized by size exclusion chromatography prior to this analysis.

To  characterize  the  elution  fractions  with  potential  additives,  a RPLC -HRMS method is used. The RPLC provides another dimension of separation while HRMS enables a supervised screening. The Fig. 4 shows the two-dimensional separation obtained, with the CPC separation as a function  of  the  LC  separation.  This  cartography  was  built  from  the Extract Ion Chromatograms ( ± 0.005 Da). Principal organic components present in the PVC model sample were annotated according to mass accuracy  ( < 2  ppm)  and  isotopic  pattern  accuracy.  Specifically,  the phthalate DIDP and its isomers were found in the fractions 11 and 13 between 17.4 and 18 min. ESO, chemically corresponding to epoxidized triglycerides, was found in different fractions (10 to 40) and the wax, identified as oxidized polyethylene, was found in fractions 10, 11, 12, 16, 17 and 18.

This cartography allows for conclusions about the recovery of each soluble organic additive from soft PVC in the CPC elution fractions, with these  additives  being  separated  into  distinct  elution  fractions.  This separation is driven by the interactions of each component with the two phases, governed by HSPs, including dipole-dipole interactions, hydrogen bonding, and dispersion forces. In this study, the objective was to separate the polymer from its organic additives, and CPC successfully facilitated this separation.

3.4. Extrusion fractions: recovery of PVC resin

At  the  end  of  the  previous  additive  separation  and  their  total recovering,  the  extrusion  step  is  done.  The  extrusion  fractions  are combined. They contained the polymer dissolved in a solvent incom patible with subsequent analyses. Then to recover polymer, 500 mL of MeOH are added to  the  300  mL  collected  during  CPC  extrusion  for polymer  precipitation.  The  solution  was  filtered  on  Büchner  with cellulose filter. The powder was recovered and dried at 70 °C in oven for 4 h. SEC analysis was then performed to characterize the resin fraction recovered after CPC separation. This analysis yields multiple pieces of information: the refractive index (RI) signal allows quantification of the PVC resin  using  the  appropriate dn/dc value,  while  molar  mass  and intrinsic  viscosity  measurements,  obtained  via  universal  calibration, provide insights into potential polymer degradation [36]. A quantitative analysis by weight confirms the total recovery of the resin.

The  PVC  resin  purified  with  the  CPC  has  been  compared  to  the original resin PVC K75 used to formulate the model compound of this study. On Table 5, SEC results for each resin are shown. They show similar size distributions for both, and a quantification analysis confirms the recovery of all the polymer injected in CPC. In addition, the polymer was not degraded by CPC. Indeed, molar masses are the same before and after  CPC  as  previously  shown.  If  the  polymer  was  degraded,  chains scissions  should  happen and lower molar mass average compared to resin before CPC should be measured [37]. The Mark-Houwink coeffi cient can also help to determine if some branching occur. During its oxidation, PVC polymer can create branches by which increase its vis cosity [38,39]. In fact, this coefficient is given by the Mark-Houwink formula which link the molar mass with the viscosity. Here the two Mark-Houwink coefficients are similar before and after CPC analysis: according to SEC results, PVC polymer was not modified by the CPC extraction process [40].

To  compare  results  with  current  literature:  S.  Wagner  and  M. Schlummer employed the dissolution-precipitation method -currently considered  the  reference  technique  for  PVC  resin  purification -to remove phthalate-type plasticizers from post-consumer flooring mate rials [9]. The authors report a reduction in DEHP concentration from 100,000 ppm to 60 ppm. However, the dissolution-precipitation process, as currently described in the literature, focuses primarily on the removal of  phthalate  plasticizers,  with  a  particular  emphasis  on  DEHP,  while other additives such as stabilizers are not addressed. In contrast, the CPC-based  approach  enables  the  removal  of  all  organic  additives regardless of their chemical nature or functional role. Furthermore, CPC allows for the recovery of pure PVC resin in a single step, compared to the seven purification steps required for dissolution-precipitation.

4. Conclusion

The lack of techniques for separating polymers from all additives and recovering them for characterization remains a major obstacle to the development of physical  recycling  processes.  CPC,  typically  used  for purifying natural products, is applied here for the first time to plastics fractionation. The selection of the two-phase solvent system is critical to the performance of this technique and often requires numerous labo ratory tests. In this study, a more theoretical approach based on HSPs is proposed. This approach facilitates solvent selection with fewer exper imental tests by providing insights into the parameters governing the solubility  of  both  the  polymer  and  representative  additives,  such  as phthalates.

For  a  soft  PVC  the  DMSO/heptane/DEK  system  proved  effective, enabling the complete recovery of the polymer while removing all sol uble organic additives and offering a first dimension of additive sepa ration. These results were validated using RPLC -HRMS analysis of the additive fractions, and FTIR and SEC analyses of the polymer fractions. Importantly, the recovered polymer was pure and remained structurally unaffected by the CPC fractionation process. This method demonstrates its  effectiveness  in  simplifying  complex  plastic  formulations  by  fully isolating soluble organic additives, making it a valuable tool for char acterizing materials such as PVC.

CPC can also be used as a quality assessment method during recy cling, allowing the characterization of plastics through the detection of polymer degradation and the quantification of regulated additives (such as phthalates) and impurities prior to processing. The flexibility of the technique supports its application across a wide range of thermoplastics and polymer-based materials. Moreover, by adjusting the solvent system ratios, CPC can be adapted to achieve tailored separations according to specific objectives -whether focused on time efficiency, solvent usage, or targeting compounds for removal. This adaptability highlights CPC ' s strong potential for broad applications in plastic analysis and recycling.

Removal of undissolved substances in the dissolution-based recycling of polystyrene waste by applying filtration and centrifugation

Rita Kol a,b , Elisabetta Carrieri a , Sergei Gusev a , Michiel Verswyvel c , Norbert Niessner d , Angeliki Lemonidou e , Dimitris S. Achilias b , Steven De Meester a,*

a Laboratory for Circular Process Engineering (LCPE), Department of Green Chemistry and Technology, Ghent University, Sint-Martens-Latemlaan 2B, 8500 Kortrijk, Belgium

b Laboratory of Polymer Chemistry and Technology, Department of Chemistry, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, 54124 Thessaloniki, Greece

c INEOS Styrolution Belgium N.V., Scheldelaan 600, 2040 Antwerpen, Belgium

d INEOS Styrolution GmbH, Mainzer Landstra ß e 50, 60325 Frankfurt am Main, Germany

e Laboratory of Petrochemical Technology, Department of Chemical Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, 54124 Thessaloniki, Greece

A R T I C L E  I N F O

Keywords: Dissolution recycling Plastic waste High-impact polystyrene Polystyrene Filtration Centrifugation

1. Introduction

Plastics are an essential part of the world economy and are used in different market sectors. In 2021, 390.7 Mt of plastics were produced globally, of which 90.2% were fossil-based, 8.3% were produced from post-consumer recycled plastics and 1.5% were bio-based plastics. The biggest annual producer in 2021 was China (32% of the total produc tion),  followed  by  the  free  trade  zone  of  'United  States,  Canada  and Mexico ' and Europe, accounting respectively for 18% and 15% of the total  amount [1].  Within the wide range of polymers in the market, polystyrene (PS) represents 5.3% (~21 Mt) of the total plastic produc tion worldwide and 6% (3.5 Mt) of the total production in Europe [1].

* Corresponding author. E-mail address: Steven.DeMeester@UGent.be (S. De Meester).

A B S T R A C T

Polystyrene (PS) is a versatile polymer typically used in applications such as yogurt cups, packaging trays, disk cases and toys. To increase recycling rates of PS, dissolution recycling is being investigated, which involves the liquefication of the polymer in a suitable solvent, allowing deep cleaning of the polymer from impurities. Quite specific to PS is that polystyrene waste contains both general-purpose polystyrene and high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), which is composed of free PS and polystyrene-grafted polybutadiene particles. In this work the potential of filtration and centrifugation is analyzed with the aim of cleaning the polymer from both, insoluble PB-PS particles and pigments (TiO2, Cr/Sb/Ti oxide and carbon black). The dead-end lab scale filtration were per formed at room temperature and at pressures between 1.5 and 30 bar. The pigments were successfully removed, yet, filtration of HIPS solutions results in low fluxes due to extreme membrane fouling caused by the PB-PS particles, which was confirmed by the application of pore-blockage filtration models. Alternatively, centrifu gation at 14,052 G-force has shown to be a promising alternative to separate the particles from HIPS, resulting in 100% turbidity reduction. Equally, the separation of pigments was successful, highlighting that TiO2 and Cr/Sb/ Ti oxide have shorter sedimentation times compared to carbon black. Finally, the two separation processes are tested on a PS rigid packaging waste sample coming from a sorting line and the results show that centrifugation allows a high turbidity reduction and that a two-step separation process starting with centrifugation for PB-PS particles removal can facilitate further downstream cleaning.

Polystyrene has versatile and tunable properties, making it suitable for applications in several sectors, such as packaging (e.g. yogurt cups, fish boxes),  electric  and  electronics  (e.g.  refrigerator),  building  and  con struction  (e.g.  insulation  foams),  and  automotive  (e.g.  bumper),  and many other applications (e.g. toys, disk and cosmetic cases) [1]. Current installed recycling input capacity for polystyrene is of approx. 0.10 Mt in Europe [2]. Thus, there are still quite some milestones to be achieved towards closing the loop for polystyrene.

Recycling options for polystyrene-based materials include mechan ical  recycling,  chemical  and  dissolution-based  (also  called  solventbased)  recycling  [3].  Yet,  polystyrene-based  materials  differ  in  their composition  and  physical  structures,  resulting  in  challenges  for  the different recycling techniques (Table 1). General-purpose polystyrene (GPPS) is a resin of atactic PS with transparent properties and good ri gidity, moldability and processability but low impact resistance, being mostly used as blend component together with high-impact polystyrene (HIPS)  for  food  packaging  or  as  pure  GPPS  in  disk  and  jewel  cases. Mechanical  recycling  of  GPPS  is  limited  by  the  quality  of  the  input material  and  presence  of  contaminants  that  reduce  the  quality  and properties of the recycled plastic [4]. HIPS is reinforced with grafted polybutadiene (PB) rubber particles that increase the impact resistance properties of PS, making it suitable for applications such as household appliances or more resistant food packaging. Next, acryloni trile -butadiene -styrene  (ABS)  is  a  copolymer  containing  rubber  in different  amounts  compared  to  HIPS  as  well  as  acrylonitrile,  which makes this polymer suitable for applications that require high impact, chemical and heat resistance. These rubber-containing polymers can be subject to some thermo-oxidative degradation during processing, with the double bond of polybutadiene being the main site of oxidation of HIPS and ABS [5 -7]. Multiple recycling loops with high thermal stress therefore might affect the quality of the recycled HIPS and ABS conse quently the types of applications it can be used for [5].

Collected rigid PS-based waste contains both HIPS and GPPS, which have the same recycling code number 6. HIPS is composed of 12 -30 wt % PB-PS particles (or 6 -12 wt% PB), which are formed by PB rubber dispersed in the form of particles into a polystyrene matrix (Fig. 1) [7,8]. The dispersed rubber particles are grafted by PS chains and contain PS inclusions (Fig. 1). The higher the degree of grafting, i.e. the higher the number of grafted chains, the better the dispersion of the rubber parti cles  in  the  matrix  [9].  Choi  et  al.  (2000)  [9]  observed  that  with increasing degree of grafting, PS occlusion in the particles increases in size and is not enclosed well by the rubber layers. The size of the par ticles can vary between 0.5 and 9 μ m [10].

Apart from the rubber particles, PS-based waste typically contain colorants that are added during the manufacturing processes in plastics mostly for aesthetic purposes. These can lower the market price of the recyclate when not removed, since it limits the recoloration options of the  recyclate  [18,19].  Within  colorants,  dyes  and  pigments  can  be distinguished [20]. Dyes are organic molecules that are soluble and are retained in the polymer matrix as a result of an affinity between indi vidual dye molecules and the polymer molecules [21]. On the other hand, pigments are not soluble and are incorporated in the polymer while  it  is  in  a  liquid  phase  and  after  solidification,  the  dispersed pigment particles are retained physically in the polymer matrix [21]. Pigments can be subdivided into organic (e.g. Cu-phthalocyanine, azosalts) and  inorganic pigments  (e.g. TiO2, Cr2O3,  Fe2O3) [3,18]. Compared  to  dyes,  pigments  have  better  migration  resistance  and inorganic pigments can be preferred over organic pigments since these can offer better heat, light, and weathering resistance [21]. Inorganic pigments are added as a colorant to the plastic in a concentration range between 0.01 to 5 wt% and particle sizes varies in general between 0.1 to 1 μ m [3]. Pigments present in the polymer waste will result in greyish polymer recyclates which also poses a limitation towards closed-loop recycling of plastics. Recycling techniques, being able to remove rub ber  particles  and  pigments  (together  with  other  impurities),  should allow a wider use of post-consumer waste in closed loop recycling.

Dissolution  recycling  (or  solvent-based  recycling)  is  a  promising complementary route to conventional mechanical and chemical recy cling, as it avoids the energy costs typically involved in thermal based recycling methods where the polymer chains are broken down, like in thermal depolymerization or pyrolysis (including subsequent purifica tion of co-boiling by-products), but still allows the removal of contam inants and additives [3]. The so-called dissolution-precipitation technique follows 4 steps: (1) dissolution of the polymer with a suitable solvent; (2) solid -liquid separation process for the removal of undis solved contaminants; (3) precipitation of the polymer by the addition of an antisolvent to the solution; (4) recovery of the polymer by filtration and drying steps [3]. When in contact with solvents, HIPS forms turbid suspensions with undissolved PB-PS particles [22], which are in a gel phase whilst free dissolved PS in the liquid phase [23]. Thus, the par ticles  can  be  removed  with  a  solid -liquid  separation  step.  To  our knowledge,  few  publications  can  be  found  on  the  removal  of  PB-PS particles from HIPS. Da ǧ li et al. (1995) [23] have made an attempt to separate PB-PS from HIPS with microfiltration as sample preparation for particle size analysis with different membrane pore sizes between 10 and  1 μ m.  Whilst  reporting  clogging  issues,  the  effect  of  different filtration conditions such as pressure and stirring are not mentioned or tested. Da ǧ li et al. (1995) [23] has then used centrifugation (300 rpm, 2 h, toluene) to separate the particles (gel phase) from the free PS and redispersed the gel phase in toluene to obtain a specimen for the particle size analysis. Keskkula and Turley (1969) [24] used a mixture of MEK and acetone (50/50 by volume) and centrifuged (47000 g, 19500 rpm, 10 °C) to separate the PB-PS particles from free PS as sample preparation for particle size analysis.

Related to dyes and pigments, Mu and Yang (2022) [25] successfully removed dyes from textiles, i.e. CI Disperse Blue 56 from poly(ethylene terephthalate), CI Acid Blue 40 from nylon 6,6 and CI Direct RED 72 from cotton. The removal of dyes was achieved by minimization of fiber density using solvents and temperatures, which results in disruption of dye-polymer interactions and leaching of dyes from the fiber, without dissolving the polymer. Ferreira et al. (2021) [26] successfully removed the organic pigments Cu-phthalocyanine (PB15) and Cromophtal ® Or ange (PO64, benzimidazolone pigment family) from high density poly ethylene (HDPE) by solvent extraction with biosolvents (T > 110 °C, S/L ratio  of  0.02).  In  their  process,  HDPE  is  dissolved  and  antisolvent  is added to precipitate the polymer. The organic pigments remain in liquid phase,  i.e.  antisolvent/solvent  mixture.  Dissolution  in  limonene  has shown the best results for the removal of both PB15 (~90% removal with 1,4 -butanediol as antisolvent) and PO64 (100% removal with 1,2,3- propanetriol and 1,2,4- butanediol as antisolvent). Arends et al. (2012) [19] removed inorganic pigments (TiO2, Cr2O3 and Fe2O3) from ABS by filtration and centrifugation after preparing an ABS solutions in acetone  and  CreaSolv ® solutions.  However,  a  systematic  study  of filtration and centrifugation engineering and solvent effects on free PS recovery and pigment/grafted particles removal is currently lacking.

This  paper  evaluates  filtration  and  centrifugation  parameters  to wards optimizing the cleaning of undissolved particles, with focus on PB-PS  particles  and  pigments,  in  the  dissolution-based  recycling  of polystyrene-based waste. For this, solutions of 5 wt% polymer in xylene and limonene were prepared for filtration and centrifugation. Two HIPS samples with different PB-PS particles  concentrations  were  used  and three common inorganic pigments with different particle size distribu tions were chosen: TiO2 (white color), Cr/Sb/Ti oxide (yellow color) and carbon black (black color). Lastly, the most promising process for the recycling of PS is proposed and tested on a real PS rigid waste sample.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

Polystyrene  (PS)  pellets  (Styron TM  634 -71)  were  purchased  from Resinex ( Mw = 265 000 g ⋅ mol 1 , ρ = 1040 kg ⋅ m 3 ) and two HIPS pellet types  with  different  rubber  content  were  kindly  provided  by  INEOS. Henceforth, the HIPS polymers will be designated as ' HIPS R ' and ' HIPS E ' and the differences between them are summarized in Section 3.1. Titanium dioxide R-350 ( ρ relative = 4.1)  was kindly provided by Che mours, pigment Sicotan ® Yellow K 2001 (Cr/Sb/Ti oxide, ρ = 4700 kg ⋅ m 3 ) was kindly provided by Sun Chemical and Black Pearls ® 4750 carbon black ( ρ relative = 1.7 -1.9) was kindly provided by Cabot. Xylene (isomers mixture) and (R)-( + )-limonene were used as solvents. These two solvents have shown to be good solvents for polystyrene [27].

The  compounding  of  pure  PS  (Styron TM 634 -71)  with  TiO2  and Sicotan ® Yellow  K  2001  (henceforth  designated  as ' white  PS ' and ' yellow  PS ' ,  respectively)  was  done  by  using  a  ZSK  18  MEGALAB Coperion corotating twin screw extruder L/D 40. Polystyrene with car bon  black  was  compounded  by  Centexbel  (henceforth  designated  as ' black  PS ' ).  The  concentration  of  the  pigments  in  the  polymer  was chosen based on the typical concentration range used in plastics, which ranges from 0.01 to 5 wt% [28]. The final concentration of the pigments in polystyrene are: 0.28 wt% TiO2, 0.18 wt% Sicotan ® Yellow and 0.30 wt% for carbon black.

The waste sample ( ' waste PS ' ) consists of PS rigid packaging and comes from the P + MD (kerbside collected packaging) sorting line from Vanheede  in  Rumbeke  (Belgium).  The  waste  PS  was  inserted  in  the shredder (Piovan type RSP15/30) as real-size items without any sample preparation and was shredded first using a sieve diameter of 8.0 mm. Next, a sieve shaker (Endecotts LTD) was used to obtain particles with a narrower size distribution between 2.0 and 5.6 mm. The sample was further  pulverized  (Fritsch,  pulverisette  19)  into  particles  with  size smaller than 1.0 mm to ensure homogeneity upon preparation of solu tions (Fig. S1). To help the pulverization, liquid nitrogen was added to the 2.0 -5.6 mm pieces. Polymer solutions of 5 wt% concentration were prepared in the different solvents in closed vials, with stirring and at room temperature. In a 5 wt% polymer solution, this corresponds to a polymer content of 4.99 wt% for the compounded polymer solution and for the waste sample (Fig. S1).

2.2. Characterization of the solids

The particle size distribution (PSD) of the PB-PS particles in HIPS and of the pigments dispersed in the compounded polystyrene were deter mined using a Malvern static  laser  diffraction  particle  size  analyzer, Mastersizer S. Solutions of 5 wt% polymer in the two solvents, xylene and limonene, were prepared. Three measurements were performed to ensure reproducibility.

A microscope setup was also built to analyze the PB-PS particles in the HIPS samples and calculate their sizes based on captured video re cords (Fig. 2). The optical axis of the setup is horizontally oriented, the holder is designed to support a test tube or a calibration slide, and is attached to a vertically oriented linear table with a positioning accuracy of 0.01 mm. Another linear table is used to adjust the position of the microscope in two perpendicular horizontal directions: for focusing and transversal alignment with an object. A 50X metallurgical microscope objective with a working distance (WD) of 7 mm was chosen (Fig. S2). To  record  videos,  a  camera  module,  12.3-megapixel  Sony  IMX477 sensor, connected to the Raspberry PI 4 model B through an I 2 C interface was  used.  The  video  was  captured  with  Raspivid,  a  command  line capturing application from RaspiCam package written for Raspberry PI single board computers. The resulting files with a 1080p resolution at 30 frames per second (FPS) were further processed on a personal computer with an open-source software: Python V3.9 [29] and OpenCV computer vision and machine learning library [30]. To define the relative scale of the  image,  a  calibration  slide  was  used.  Details  can  be  found  in  the Supporting Information.

A  dynamic  light  scattering  (DLS)  equipment,  Zetasizer  ZS  from Malvern (T = 20 °C, angle of measurement = 173) was used to qualify the presence of smaller carbon black particles ( < 0.1 μ m) in the permeate and supernatant of black PS.

The mass concentration of the PB-PS particles in HIPS, cparticles,HIPS , was calculated using equation (1). The mass fraction of free PS in HIPS was obtained by measuring the mass fraction of polymer in the clear supernatant with TGA, which is free of PB-PS particles [23]. To know if the supernatant was clear, its turbidity was compared with the turbidity of a reference, which was a 5 wt% pure PS solution in the respective solvent  (see  Section  2.3.  and  Eq.  (3)).  For  HIPS  E/xylene,  HIPS  R/ limonene, HIPS E/limonene, a clear supernatant was obtained with a 1hour centrifugation. For HIPS R in xylene, 100% turbidity reduction was not achieved after 2-hour centrifugation time, and therefore a 6-hour duration centrifugation was performed to ensure that all PB-PS parti cles have sedimented. The centrifugations were performed at 20 °C and with a G-force of 14052, see Section 2.5.

The PB-PS particle density was calculated based on the equation of density for mixtures (Eq. S1), which rearranged results in equation (2) [31]. 2.3. Characterization of suspensions

The  turbidity  of  suspensions  was  measured  with  a  turbidimeter

For the cases where turbidity  was  out  of  range,  the  suspension  was  diluted,  and  a  linear relationship was assumed. For the waste, the turbidity reduction was calculated assuming no reference turbidity since polymer concentration varies, and concentration of particles and pigments is unknown.

The viscosity and density of solvents and solutions were measured with an Anton Paar SVM 3001 viscometer at 20 °C. Three measurements were performed to ensure reproducibility.

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted to quantify con centration of polymer in the permeate and supernatant [27]. The mea surements were carried out in a Netsch TG 209 F3 Tarsus thermogravimeter under a constant flow of dry nitrogen at a rate of 20 mL ⋅ min 1 . The temperature profile was as follows: dynamic step from 35 to 250 °C at 15 °C ⋅ min 1 , followed by an isothermal at 250 °C for 15 min, dynamic step up to 600 °C at 100 °C ⋅ min 1 , followed by a dynamic step at 20 °C ⋅ min 1 until 700 °C. The mean absolute error associated with TGA measurement is of 0.09 wt% and the standard deviation of 0.08 wt%, which were obtained by performing five measurements of a solution with a known concentration of 5 wt%.

The  supernatant  of  waste  PS  was  analyzed  with  a  UV -Vis  spec trometer (Hach Lange, DR 6000) to check for the presence of dissolved organic colorants.

Dispersion of particles in suspensions prior to measurements were ensured  by  immersion  of  the  solutions  in  an  ultrasonic  bath  (Ultra schallprozessor UP 400 s, Hielsher GmbH) with an amplitude of 60 % and 0.5 cycles for a minimum of 2 min.

2.4. Filtration

Filtration  experiments  were  performed  using  a  high-pressure  cell (HP4750X Stirred Cell) from Sterlichtech (membrane diameter of 47 mm) with a dead-end filtration configuration and magnetic stirring (500 rpm). The experiments were conducted under constant pressure at room temperature. Different pressures between 1.5 and 30 bar were applied and three microfiltration commercial membranes with different pore sizes  were  tested:  0.1 μ m (Durapore ® ,  PVDF),  0.45 μ m (Durapore ® , Gridded PVDF), 1 μ m (Whatman TM , PTFE supported). The volumetric flux was calculated by measuring the volume collected over time with a graduated cylinder. The retained mass on the membrane was left to dry in the oven at 60 °C for 1 week. A successful microfiltration would be achieved when the pigments and PB-PS particles are retained on the membrane  whilst  clean  dissolved  polystyrene  passes  through  the membrane and can be recovered with further downstream processes [3].

The turbidity reduction was calculated using equation (3) [33,34]. The level of retention of particles is called the sieving coefficient, S , and was calculated using equation (4), which is equal to ratio of the particles concentration in the permeate compared with the concentration of the particles in the feed [35,36]. In this work the particles that are retained are the PB-PS particles in case of HIPS filtration, pigments for colored PS filtration and both particles and pigments in case of waste PS. The value of the sieving coefficient varies between 0 and 1, where 0 represents complete retention of the particle and 1 complete passage of the particle through the membrane [35]. The rejection coefficient of the particles, σ , is given by equation (5) [35,36].

Turbidity reduction ( % )= Turbfeed Turbref ) Turbpermeate Turbref ) Turbfeed Turbref ) × 100 (3)

S = cpermeate cfeed (4)

σ ( % ) = ( 1 cpermeate cfeed ) × 100 (5)

where Turb is the turbidity (NTU), cpermeate is the mass concentration of the particles in the permeate (wt%) and cfeed is the mass concentration of the particle in the feed (wt%) and the subscript ref is the solution of pure PS (5 wt%) in the respective solvent.

For the mass balance, weight fractions of polymer and solvent were obtained with TGA, and weight fractions of pigments (individually) in the  supernatants  were  obtained  with  the  turbidity  calibration  curve. More details on the mass balance equations and results can be found in the supporting information. The experiments were repeated to ensure the reproducibility of the results and the average relative standard de viation for the flux over time is of 8% (Supporting Information - Section 6.1.).

2.4.1. Filtration models

Membrane fouling is a main obstacle to the industrial application of membrane technology, since it causes flux declines, reduction of the membrane service life and thus increase of the operational costs [37]. Recent research has been performed on the development of membranes with antifouling performance [38,39]. Han et al. (2023) [40] has used three-dimensional printing technology to develop and acryloni trile -butadiene -styrene membrane  which  has  showed  antifouling properties for oil/water separation. Kong et al. (2022) [41] developed a Fe3O4@MoS2  polyether sulfone composite membrane for wastewater treatment that showed also antifouling performance. Artificial intelli gence has also been used to optimize the fabrication of membranes for wastewater treatment [42].

In literature, several models have been proposed to predict mem brane fouling behavior and underlying mechanism based on individual cake filtration, complete blocking, intermediate blocking and standard blocking,  or  by  assuming  a  combination  of  different  mechanisms [37,43].  Cake  filtration  means  that  the  particles  accumulate  on  the membrane and form a cake layer. In intermediate blocking the particle settles on previously deposited particles, which means that not every particle that arrives to the membrane surface blocks the membrane pore, and thus there is no cake layer formation [44]. In standard blocking (also called pore constriction) the particle settle inside the membrane pores. In complete blocking it is assumed that each membrane pore is completely blocked by an individual particle and that no cake deposits are  on  the  membrane  [45]. Thus,  the  combined models assume that blocking occurs at the first stages of filtration and is followed by cake build-up  [43].  Finally,  a  more  complex  combined  model  (CF-CB-CF) assumes that the fouling mechanism has a transition point from com bined complete blocking and cake filtration into individual cake filtra tion. In this work, the proposed models from literature were applied to the experimental data with the aim of having an approximate indication of the underlying fouling mechanism (Table 2). For the deduction of the models the reader is referred to the works of Hou et al. (2017) [37] and Heidari et al. (2021) [43]. The model parameters were regressed by minimizing the sum of squares (SSE) and the hybrid fractional error function (HYBRID) which has into account the number of parameters (Eq. (6) and (7), respectively). The modelling was performed using an in-house-made script in R programming software based on the Flexible Modelling Environment (FME) package.

SSE = ∑ n i = 1 Vexp , i Vcalc ) 2 (6)

HYBRID = 100 n p ∑ n i = 1 Vexp , i Vcalc , i ) 2 Vexp , i (7)

where Vexp is the experimental volume and Vcalc is the calculated value, n is the number of data points, p is the number of parameters in the model and the subscripts i corresponds to the i th component.

2.5. Centrifugation

Centrifugation  experiments  were  performed  using  an  Eppendorf Centrifuge, model 5804 R, rotor F-34 -6-38, with an angle of 35 ° , at a Gforce of 14,052 (10500 rpm, Rmax = 11.4 cm, Rmin = 2.5 cm, 20 °C, acceleration and deacceleration = 2). Different times were set between 7 min and 2-hour. After the centrifugal run, 3 regions were distinguished (Fig. 3), where I corresponds to the 1st supernatant, II corresponds to 2nd supernatant and region III to the wet sediment. The two superna tants were carefully pipetted out to separate vials and the sediment was left  to  dry  in  the  oven  at  60 °C for  1  week.  With  centrifugation  the pigments and PB-PS particles are sedimented whilst the clean polymer is dissolved in the supernatant and can be recovered with further down stream processes [3].

The sedimentation time, t*, which is the time required for complete sedimentation of particles with dp size, is given by equation (8) for a fixed-angle rotor. The cutting-off particle size, d* , for a fixed centrifu gation  time, t, is  given  by  equation  (9). 3. Results and discussion

3.1. Characterization of solids & solutions

The results of the characterization of HIPS samples are summarized in  Table  3.  HIPS  E  has  a  higher  concentration  of  PB-PS  particles compared to HIPS R. The calculated mass concentration of PB-PS par ticles for HIPS E is approximated to be around 17 wt% in xylene and 18 wt% in limonene. For HIPS R the concentration of PB-PS particles in xylene gives 12 wt% and in limonene 13 wt%. In both cases the differ ence is  within  the  standard  deviation  of  the  TGA  measurement.  The viscosity of the polymer suspensions shows that limonene leads to lower viscosity than xylene. Pure limonene has a higher viscosity (0.870 ± 0.002 mPa.s at 20 °C)  than  pure  xylene  (0.6100 ± 0.0001 mPa.s at 20 °C). Thus these results may indicate that limonene has a higher sol vation capacity than xylene and consequently the polymer chains are more dispersed in the solution compared to xylene, leading to lower viscosities [27].

Figure 4 and Table S3 show that the particle size distribution slightly differs between HIPS: HIPS R shows a slight bimodal distribution of PBPS particles in xylene with particle sizes ranging between 1 and 100 μ m. HIPS E has unimodal distribution with particle sizes in the range of 1 to 10 μ m. The solvent influence on the PSD of the PB-PS particles is not pronounced. The PSD curves of the pigments dispersed in polystyrene (Fig.  4c  and  d),  show  that  TiO2  and Cr/Sb/Ti oxide have a bimodal distribution in both solvents with particle sizes between 0.1 and 100 μ m, while carbon black has a volumetric size distribution with one peak at 12.2 μ m. This may be related with the low dispersion ability of carbon black in non-aqueous media [48]. The solvent slightly influences the PSD of the pigments, especially for carbon black for which the mean diameter shifts from 12.2 μ m in xylene to 4.9 μ m in limonene, with long tail of the distribution to smaller particle sizes. The microscope results confirm the presence of particles in the range of 1 -4 μ m for both HIPS (Fig. S7).
