3.2. Filtration

3.2.1. PB-PS Particles

For the separation of PB-PS particles from the free PS matrix of HIPS, filtration experiments using three membranes with different pore sizes were tested and different pressures were applied between 1.5 and 30 bar. In all cases, 5 % HIPS solutions in the two solvents, xylene and limonene, were used. An example of the flux over time for HIPS E/xylene solution at 20 bar is given in Figure 5a. The results show that higher fluxes are obtained with the 1 μ m membrane compared to the other two membranes, but the turbidity reductions are lower than 65% for both HIPS samples (Fig. 5b) which means that the retention of PB-PS particles on the membrane is not 100 %. With membranes with lower pore size (0.1 and 0.45 μ m), higher turbidity reductions are obtained, especially for HIPS E/X with 100% turbidity reduction obtained with both mem branes. However, the flux is very low; for the 0.45 μ m membrane the flux rapidly declines with time towards a steady low state, whereas with the  0.1 μ m membrane the flux is steadily  low  since  the  start  of  the filtration (Fig. 5a). In fact, these filtrations were stopped once at least 10 mL (1/4 of the feed volume) of permeate was collected (the minimum required for the turbidimeter) which in all cases resulted in a filtration of approximately  1-hour  duration.  These  results  indicate  that  heavy membrane fouling occurs with the 0.1 and 0.45 μ m membrane, which can be caused by pore blocking induced by the deposition of particles on the surface of the pores or pore constriction due to the adsorption of particles with smaller size than the pores onto the pore walls [49,50]. The PB-PS particles are in a gel phase when in suspension, which can possibly form a gel layer on the membrane surface with low perme ability resulting in the very low flux, as it has been observed by Meng et al. (2021) [50] for starch grains during ultrafiltration. The underlying fouling mechanism is further studied in section 3.2.3.

Figure 5b also shows that the mass concentration of polymer in the permeate with the 0.1 and 0.45 μ m is lower than 2 wt%. This means that part of the free PS stays retained after approximately 1-hour filtration, since the concentration of free PS in the feed is approximately 4.1 wt% for HIPS E, possibly also due to the low permeable PB-PS particles layer. With the 1 μ m, the concentration of polymer (free PS + PB-PS particles) in the permeate is close to the feed concentration (5 wt%), which means that the PB-PS particles were mostly not retained (as indicated by the turbidity results as well). Similar flux curves, turbidity reductions and polymer concentration in the permeate were obtained for HIPS R in xylene and for HIPS E and HIPS R in limonene (Fig. S14-S17, Supporting Information).

The flux vs pressure was analyzed to better understand the mecha nism  causing  the  membrane  fouling  (Fig.  6).  For  HIPS  the  0.45 μ m membrane was chosen because the flux was slightly higher than with the 0.1 μ m. The results show that for HIPS E/xylene the flux increases with pressure until it reaches a plateau independently of pressure, which can indicate that the gelatinous PB-PS particles not only block the pores but also  form  a  cake  on  the  surface  of  the  membrane  that  is  highly compressible [51]. For HIPS R in xylene and HIPS E in limonene, at higher pressures (20 -30 bar), the flux is also constant with pressure (Table S4, Supporting Information). An exception is shown for HIPS R in limonene  where  the  flux  slightly  decreases  with  pressure.  A  similar result was observed by Defrance and Jaffrin (1999) [52] with activated sludge. This can indicate that for HIPS R in limonene a higher pressure leads to a highly compressible cake that increases the resistance for the flux. The flux over time graph at the different pressures presented in Figure  6  and  Table  S4  can  be  found  in  the  Supporting  Information (Fig. S18-S21).

3.2.2. Pigments

The filtration of the pigments was performed at 1.5, 3 and 5 bar with the 0.1 μ m membrane, given the particle sizes of the pigments and the intention to keep them in the retentate. Polymer solutions of 5 wt% were prepared. Figure 6 shows that the flux increases more or less propor tionally  with  the  pressure  for  the  pigments.  For  TiO2 turbidity  re ductions higher than 97% were achieved both in xylene and limonene (Fig. 7). The sieving coefficient is close to 0 at all three pressures in xylene and 0 in limonene, which means that in limonene the pigment 100 % retention was obtained. For Cr/Sb/Ti oxide (Fig. S22) turbidity reductions higher than 98% were obtained in both solvents and sieving coefficients were equal or very close to zero (rejection coefficients = 100 %). For both white and yellow PS, the polymer mass concentration in the permeate was higher than 4.8 wt% for xylene and 4.9 wt% for limonene (Fig.7, Fig. S22). This result is coherent with the values obtained for the filtration of pure PS solutions, namely a concentration of 4.8 wt% in the permeate in xylene and 4.9 wt% in the permeate in limonene. For carbon black, higher turbidity reductions were obtained in limonene (Fig. 7b) than in xylene. Especially at a pressure of 5 bar in xylene, a sieving coefficient  of  0.2  was  obtained.  For  black  PS  filtration,  low  polymer mass concentration in the permeate was obtained (between 3.5 and 4.0 wt% in xylene and 2.6 and 3.4 wt% in limonene, Fig. 7), which indicates that part of polystyrene stays retained in the retentate.

When comparing all filtration curves, the flux of white PS and yellow PS filtration are higher in both solvents compared to the flux obtained with black PS and HIPS (Fig. 8), which means that the overall flow resistance is higher for black PS and HIPS. In the case of the pigments, the flow curve decreases over time, which is different than HIPS. Indeed, for HIPS, the flux is almost constant since the start of the experiment and is very low when compared to the pure PS/xylene filtration, which is indicative  of  membrane  blocking  caused  by  the  PB-PS  particles  (see section  3.2.3)  [53]. 3.2.3. Model based understanding of filtration curves

The filtration models were applied to the filtration results presented in Figure 8b as an example. The results are summarized in Figure 9 and Table  4.  For  the  pigments,  TiO2 and  Cr/Sb/Ti  oxide,  the  complete blockage model (CB) leads to the lowest SSE and HYBRID value, which indicates that the dominant mechanism for the overall flow resistance is the blocking of the membrane by the pigments. This happens because the pigments have a bigger particle size than the membrane pore size. A significant  cake  layer  is  possibly  not  formed  due  to  the  effect  of  the stirring and the low mass fraction of pigment in the feed. For carbon black, the combined cake filtration and complete blocking (CF-CB) leads to the lowest SSE value. This indicates that for carbon black a cake forms on top of the blocking layer. For carbon black the lowest HYBRID value is  obtained  for  the  cake  filtration  model,  whilst  the  SSE  values  are similar  between  the  cake  filtration  model  CF  and  the  model  CF-CB (5.0995 ⋅ 10 -7 for  CF  and  5.0989 ⋅ 10 -7 for  CF-CB-CF),  Table  S5).  This shows that for carbon black the cake build up has an important effect on the flux, which has been observed experimentally and can also be seen when comparing the obtained parameters. Namely, the cake constant Kc is  of  4 ⋅ 10 8 s ⋅ m 2 ,  which  is  much  higher  than  the  complete  blocking constant Kb = 7 ⋅ 10 -10 s 1 ,  suggesting  that  the  main  contributor  the overall flow resistance is the cake formation. This is coherent with the observed low fluxes (Fig. 8b). Thus, for carbon black, complete blocking at  the  initial  stage  of  the  filtration  seems  to  occur  followed  by  cake filtration (Fig. 10).

3.3. Centrifugation

3.3.1. PB-PS Particles

The centrifugation time of the two HIPS samples in both solvents, xylene and limonene, was 10, 30 and 60 min. The centrifugations were performed at 20 °C and with a G-force of 14,052 (see Section 2.5). The results indicate that with HIPS E high turbidity reductions ( > 96 %) were obtained in both solvents at 30 min centrifugation time (Fig. 11). The sedimentation time for HIPS E of the D(v,10%) particles is 12 min in xylene and 14 min in limonene, Table 5. For HIPS R, the sedimentation of the PB-PS particles takes more time (68 min in xylene and 15 min in limonene) and after 1-hour centrifugation the turbidity reduction is of 96% in xylene. In limonene, already after 30 min, the turbidity reduc tion obtained for HIPS R was of 100% For HIPS R, the Δρ in limonene is higher than in xylene, which decreases the sedimentation time and can be related with the density of the solution since pure limonene has a lower density (842.0 ± 0.01 kg ⋅ m 3 at 20 °C) than xylene (868.30 ± 0.01 kg ⋅ m 3 at 20 °C). HIPS R in xylene also has a higher mass fraction of free PS in the supernatant (Table S8), which increases the density of the solution. The viscosity results (Table 3) show that the suspension of HIPS R  in  xylene  has  the  highest  viscosity,  which  also  increases  the  sedi mentation time [31].

3.3.2. Pigments

The centrifugation of pigments was performed at 20 °C, with a Gforce of 14,052 (see Section 2.5) and different times between 7 and 120 min were applied. The results show that TiO2 and Cr/Sb/Ti oxide were 100% removed after 30 min in xylene and limonene (Fig. 12). For car bon  black  higher  centrifugation  times  are  required  for  complete removal. As it can be seen in Figure 12, after 120 min 99.8% turbidity reduction was obtained in limonene but in xylene the turbidity reduc tion is 91.2%. This result can be compared with the calculated sedi mentation times (Table 5) that show that carbon black has the highest sedimentation  time  of  2.50 ⋅ 10 4 min,  which  is  the  time  required  for complete  sedimentation  of  the  particles  with  the  smallest  diameter. Similar as observed during filtration, smaller particles (~1.1 nm) were observed in the supernatant of carbon black in xylene (Fig. S29), which can explain the lower turbidity reduction. Carbon black also has a lower density (1800 kg ⋅ m 3 )  than  TiO2  (4100 kg ⋅ m 3 )  and  Cr/Sb/Ti oxide (4700 kg ⋅ m 3 ), resulting in a smaller Δρ , which is inversely proportional to the sedimentation time. The sedimentation time for TiO2 and Cr/Sb/ Ti oxide are > 3000 times lower than carbon black (Table 5). For TiO2 the sedimentation time is of 8 min in xylene (D(v,10%) = 0.18 μ m) and 6 min  in  limonene  (D(v,10%) = 0.21 μ m).  For  Cr/Sb/Ti  oxide  the  D (v,10%) is of 0.40 μ m in xylene and limonene and the sedimentation times are approximately 2 min in both solvents (Table 5). The separation is overall better in limonene due to the lower viscosity of the solution compared to xylene [3,31]. Thus, whilst TiO2 and Cr/Sb/Ti oxide have low  sedimentation  times,  for  carbon  black  more  research  should  be performed on how to also remove the smaller particle sizes [31].

The mass balance for white and yellow PS shows turbidity reductions higher  than  98%,  specific  efficiencies  higher  than  99%  and  polymer recovery higher than 90% after 30 min (Table S9). For black PS, 99.8% turbidity reduction is obtained in limonene with 120 min centrifugation time, with a specific efficiency of 99.8% and 97% polystyrene recovery. The  detailed  mass  balance  results  are  presented  in  Table  S9  of  the Supporting Information.

3.3.3. Scale-up considerations

The scale-up consideration was only performed for centrifugation as the  lab-scale  dead-end  filtration  did  not  show  promising  results  and furthermore, the filtration results are given as flux in L ⋅ m 2 ⋅ h 1 , which means that the scaling up can be performed by multiplying the obtained flux with the total filter area of the industrial filter. For the scale-up considerations of the centrifuge, the Sigma theory was used, which de scribes  the  solids  separation  ability  of  a  particular  continuous-flow centrifuge and is given by the ratio of the volumetric flow rate, Q , and the equivalent separation area, Σ [58]. Σ is  considered as a physical characteristic of the centrifuge and is independent of the properties of the fluid-particle system [58 -60]. The Σ value can be calculated for each type of centrifuge and the relation of Q1/ Σ 1 = Q2/ Σ 2 can be used to scale up from a laboratory test to industrial scale, provided the centrifuges have the same geometry, otherwise an efficiency factor has to be applied [31].

In this work, the application of this direct relation to the laboratory centrifuge is not straightforward, since the laboratory centrifuge is a batch and not continuous centrifuge. For this reason, a simplified scale up consideration is made in this work using equation (13), which relates the  total  volumetric  flow  rate, Q ,  with  the  terminal  velocity  under gravity and the Σ of the centrifuge [59,61].

3.4. Case-study: Removal of colorants from waste PS

3.4.1. Filtration

Filtrations of packaging waste PS were performed in the two solvents using different membranes: 0.1, 0.45 and 1 μ m, with constant stirring (500 rpm). Based on the results of the HIPS filtrations, the filtration tests of waste PS were performed at 20 bar since it has led to the highest flux (Fig. 6) and above this pressure the fluxes were constant for HIPS. So lutions of 5 wt% polymer were prepared. Similar as pure HIPS filtra tions, filtrations with the 1 μ m membrane led to higher fluxes (Fig. 13a), however the turbidity reduction was very low ( < 45%). Very low fluxes were obtained with the 0.1 and 0.45 μ m membrane, compared to the 1 μ m (Fig.13a). This result can be explained by the presence of the PB-PS particles in the waste PS sample, as the flux over time follows a similar behavior as the HIPS samples (Fig. 8). For this reason, the filtrations were also stopped once 10 mL of permeate was collected, which corre sponded  to  a  filtration  duration  time  of  approximately  1-hour.  The polymer mass concentration in the permeate with the 0.1 and 0.45 μ m obtained was lower than 2 wt% (Fig. 13b), whilst the expected free PS concentration  should  be  higher  than  4  wt%,  which  is  the  expected concentration of free PS in HIPS solution. High turbidity reductions were obtained with 0.1 and 0.45 μ m, however the permeates still contained some additives, including dyes or organic pigments that have a certain solubility in the applied organic solvents [20,28,64].
3.4.2. Centrifugation

Centrifugation times of 30 min, 60 min and 120 min were applied on waste PS dissolved in limonene and xylene. The centrifugations were performed at 20 °C with a G-force of 14,052 (see Section 2.5). After 30 min, the turbidity reduction is already higher than 99 % in both solvents for supernatant I (Fig. 14). The polymer concentration in supernatant I remains constant with time, being 4.1 ± 0.08 wt% for xylene and 4.2 ± 0.08 wt% for limonene. This is a decrease of 0.8 wt% compared to the feed polymer concentration, which is coherent with the results observed for the centrifugation of HIPS (Section 3.3.1.). However, even though the  turbidity  reduction  for  waste  PS  (supernatant  I)  reached  values higher  than  99%,  the  supernatant  still  had  a  bluish  color  (Fig.  15), similar as observed for the permeates in filtration. The UV -Vis spectrum shows an absorbance peak at 300 nm and a doublet of peaks in the visible  region  from  600  to  700  nm  for  both  limonene  and  xylene (Fig.  S32-S33,  Supporting  Information),  which  is  typical  for  Cuphthalocyanine  [65].  Cu-phthalocyanine  is  a  blue  organic  pigment (Pigment  Blue  15:1)  typically  used  in  plastic  packaging  which  has partial solubility in organic solvents [66,67]. Thus, further downstream processes are required for complete removal of organic additives/im purities that would go through these solid -liquid processes. Nonethe less, this first step to separate undissolved matter is a big advantage to avoid  clogging  further  on;  for  example  in  adsorption  beds  or  whilst performing nanofiltration.

3.4.3. Two-step separation

A centrifugation followed by filtration of the supernatant (two-step separation) was also performed on the waste sample. In Figure 15 a schematic of the three scenarios (one-step filtration, one-step centrifu gation and two-step separation) is summarized. Scenario 3.4.1. (onestep separation) is only filtration of the waste sample (5 wt%) dissolved in limonene at 20 bar with the 0.1 μ m membrane, which results were already presented in Figure 13a. Scenario 3.4.2. is only centrifugation (120 min) of the waste sample (5 wt%) dissolved in limonene, which results were presented in Figure 14. Scenario 3.4.3. (two-step separa tion) is centrifugation of the waste sample (5 wt%) in limonene at 120 min followed by filtration of the supernatant (mixture of both super natants of region I and II) at 1.5 bar with the 0.1 μ m membrane.

The filtration curves of Scenario 3.4.1. and 3.4.3. are depicted and compared in Figure 15. The results show that with one-step separation the flux curve is constant over time and very low compared to a two-step separation.  After  centrifugation  most  of  the  particles  present  in  the waste are sedimented ( cpolymer , supernatant = 4.2 wt%) and the filtration of the supernatant at 1.5 bar shows a decrease of flux with time, indicating that fouling occurs, possibly originating from some still present inor ganic  additives  in  the  supernatant.  In  fact,  the  turbidity  further  de creases from 11 to 3 NTU, indicating that some particles were retained on the membrane [57]. Thus, a combined initial centrifugation followed by filtration might be a sequence to consider when developing process schemes for dissolution recycling of PS waste. Adsorption could also be an alternative process to perform after centrifugation for the removal of organic substances such as pigments.

4. Conclusions

In this work, the potential of filtration and centrifugation as cleaning techniques for undissolved particles, such as PB-PS particles and pig ments,  in  the  dissolution-based  recycling  of  polystyrene-based  waste was studied. The results indicated that 1 μ m membranes do not retain the PB-PS particles completely and the filtration with 0.1 and 0.45 μ m led to very low fluxes compared to the 1 μ m. The application of filtration models  revealed  that  a  combination  of  cake  filtration  and  standard blocking occurs for the PB-PS particles, with cake build up being the main contributor to the overall flow resistance. These results indicate that a combination of membranes would not succeed for the separation of the rubber particles. The filtration of TiO2 and Cr/Sb/Ti oxide results in higher fluxes when compared to carbon black. The application of the filtration  model  indicated  complete  blockage  for  TiO2  and  Cr/Sb/Ti oxide as the underlying fouling mechanism, whilst for carbon black a combination of complete blocking and cake build-up occurs, with the cake build-up being the main contributor to the overall flow resistance.

In a second part, the centrifugation of both HIPS and pigments was studied.  High turbidity reductions (100%) are obtained after 30 min centrifugation time (in a lab centrifuge) for both HIPS in limonene and the free polystyrene recovery was in all cases higher than 80% reaching up to 86%. The centrifugation of pigments resulted that TiO2 and Cr/Sb/ Ti oxide were 100% removed after 30 min in limonene and for carbon black higher centrifugation times are required for completely removal. A simplified scale up consideration was performed based on the Sigma theory and the results suggested that an industrialized centrifuge (for example a tubular bowl centrifuge with an inside diameter of 0.1 m and max g-force of 13 200) is promising to separate the studied pigments (TiO2 and Cr/Sb/Ti oxide) and the PB-PS particles of both HIPS samples. Carbon  black  is  a  more  complicated  pigment  to  remove  by  both centrifugation and filtration.

Finally, for a real waste sample consisting of PS rigid packaging, a two-step separation processes resulted in approximately 100 % turbidity reduction, showing a high potential to remove the PB-PS particles and a large amount of insoluble pigments.

1. Introduction

The acceleration of the replacement of electronic products results in the generation of large amounts of electronic waste (e-waste) (Ma et al., 2016).  Actually,  e-waste  is  one  of  the  fastest-growing  waste  streams globally, increasing at a rate of 3 % -5 % annually (Shittu et al., 2021). It is projected that by 2030, the amount of e-waste will rise to 82 million tons with 27.4 % of plastics (The United Nations Institute for Training and Research, 2024).

Historically, precious metals were at the heart of e-waste disposal; recycling of plastic components has not been a priority enough (Huang et al., 2009; Li and Xu, 2010; Ma et al., 2012). For example, the e-waste plastics  were  largely  disposed  of  through  incineration  or  landfilling, rather than being effectively recycled (Wu et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2020; Zhou  and  Xu,  2012).  E-waste  contains  over  15  types  of  polymers, including  acrylonitrile  butadiene  styrene  (ABS),  polypropylene  (PP), high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), polystyrene (PS), polycarbonate (PC), polyethylene (PE), polyurethane (PU), polyamide (PA), polyphenylene

A B S T R A C T

The acceleration of the replacement of electronic products results in large amounts of electronic waste (e-waste). This stream of waste has become one of the most pressing global issues. Traditional methods such as landfilling and incineration are insufficient for addressing the challenges of mixed plastics in e-waste. While solvent-based recycling has emerged as a promising solution for high-purity separation and additive removal, previous studies often employed toxic solvents and lacked comprehensive techno-economic analysis. To address these research gaps, this study developed a novel DCM/EtOH-based method for separating and recycling PC/ABS mixtures from real-world e-waste streams. The process achieved 88 % PC recovery (purity range: 80 -89 %) and 104 % ABS recovery (purity range: 89 -92 %) via fractional dissolution, while successfully removing organic phosphorus flame retardants. Economic analysis revealed that recycling one ton of e-waste plastics using this method gen erates 766 USD net profit. This is attributed to 91 % energy savings and 10.2 tons of CO2  emissions reduction. Additionally, under the conditions of the Chinese labor market, this process can create 270,000 job opportunities by recycling 12 million tons of domestically generated e-waste annually. These findings demonstrate the tech nical feasibility and economic competitiveness of the proposed method, offering a sustainable solution for ewaste plastic management. Future research should focus on solvent recovery optimization and large-scale pilot validation.

There are several ways to handle plastic waste, including mechanical recycling, incineration, landfill, and chemical recycling. Among them, landfill and incineration will create secondary pollution, and incinera tion will also bury the potential value of resources, while mechanical recycling  and  chemical  recycling  are  the  real  recovery  (Zhao  et  al., 2022). However, for with mechanical recycling, the mechanical prop erties of recycled plastics typically degrade (Zhao et al., 2022), so it is difficult  to  reapply  the  products  to  the  same  application  scenarios, resulting in the continuous decline of product quality and value. Addi tionally,  mechanical  recycling  faces  challenges  in  separating  mixed plastics and removing various additives (Evangelopoulos et al., 2019; Hopewell  et  al.,  2009).  In  the  long  run,  chemical  recycling  is  more conducive to the sustainable use of resources and plays a crucial role in the transition to a circular economy (Asgher et al., 2020; Tiwari et al., 2023).  But  it  often  needs  to  overcome  technical  difficulties,  and  the

recycling process requires more stringent conditions such as high tem peratures.  Comparatively  speaking,  the  solvent  recovery  method  can achieve  high-purity  and  high-quality  recovery  from  plastic-to-plastic under relatively simple operation steps and milder recovery conditions (Ibrahim et al., 2023).

Generally, the dissolution-precipitation method is suitable for a wide range of polymers and allows for the selective separation of different polymers while maintaining their structural integrity, which is crucial for high-quality recycling (Ügdüler et al., 2020; Weeden et al., 2015). Because  of  this,  solvent-based  plastic  recovery  method  (SRPM)  has attracted the attention of scholars. For example, the solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation method uses a mixture of toluene/acetone and dimethyl sulfoxide/water to achieve separation and recovery of PE, ethylene  vinyl  alcohol  (EVOH),  polyethylene  terephthalate  (PET) multilayer  film  polymers  (Walker  et  al.,  2020).  Acetone/dichloro methane solvent combination can continuously separate and extract PC from e-waste at room temperature (Weeden et al., 2015). N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP)/water solvent combination achieves partial removal of phosphorus based flame retardants while separating and extracting PC  from  e-waste  (Yu  et  al.,  2023).  Apparently,  SRPM  enable  a original-grade  plastic  recycling.  Furthermore,  in  terms  of  reducing greenhouse gas emissions, SRPM results in carbon emissions that are two times lower than those from pyrolysis and three times lower than those from incineration. This makes SRPM not only a more sustainable option but also a promising solution for improving the environmental impact of plastic recycling (Vollmer et al., 2020).

However, several challenges remain in SRPM, including the selection of  solvent  combinations, optimization of SRPM conditions and costs, simultaneous recycling of multiple plastics, and management of solvent usage  ratios.  Based  on  a  new  idea  of  solvent  recovery  (one  solvent combination separates two plastics successively), an SRPM for PC/ABS mixed plastics is established, which can reduce the use of organic sol vents as much as possible and ensure the quality of plastic recovery. At the same time, through the preliminary cost-benefit estimation, the huge market potential and broad application prospects (economic benefits, employment  opportunities,  energy  conservation  and  emission  reduc tion,  resource  conservation,  waste  recycling)  of  the  solvent  recovery method in  the  field  of  plastic  recycling  are  verified,  which  provides certain quantitative reference and experimental support for the subse quent research in the field of solvent recovery.

2. Material and methods

2.1. Materials

Dichloromethane (DCM) and 95 % ethanol solution (EtOH) were purchased from Xilong Technology Co., Ltd. (China), both are analytical grade reagents. The standard of polycarbonate (PC) and acrylonitrilebutadiene-styrene copolymer (ABS) were purchased from Chi Mei In dustries  in  Taiwan,  China.  Triphenyl  phosphate  was  purchased  from Shanghai Honghu Technology Co., Ltd. (China). The actual sample was a computer plastic casing contains of PC (65 %), ABS (8.5 %), talc (15 %), phenyl phosphate (11.4 %), and pigment (0.1 %) in weight. The specific type of phenyl phosphate ester present in the actual sample is unknown, it  is  therefore  triphenyl  phosphate  (TPP),  a  commonly  used  organic phosphorus flame retardant (OPFR) in electronic products, was selected as the surrogate of the exact phenyl phosphate ester.

2.2. Solvents selection

Hansen solubility parameter theory (HSP) can be used to select po tential solvents for various polymers. By calculating the relative energy difference (RED), which is the ratio of the distance between the solvent and solute  in  three-dimensional  space  Ra  to  the  radius  of  the  solute solubility sphere R0, it can be preliminarily selected whether the solvent is  a  good  solvent for the solute. RED < 1,  good solvent; RED > 1,  antisolvent;  RED ≈ 1,  boundary  condition.  The  Ra  can  be  calculated  with formula (1).

( Ra ) 2 = 4 ( δ D1 δ D2 ) 2 +( δ P1 δ P2 ) 2 +( δ H1 δ H2 ) 2 (1)

The HSP value includes three types of interactions, dispersion force ( δ D), polarity force ( δ P) and bonding force ( δ H). Where subscript 1 and 2 represent solvent and solute.

In addition, the HSP value of the mixed solution is linearly related to the volume ratio of each liquid component. For example, the δ D value of a mixture can be calculated according to formula (2):

δ Dm = δ D 1 × V 1 + δ D 2 × V 2 (2)

where subscript 1 and 2 represent different solvents, and V represents their volume proportions. The calculation procedures for δ P and δ H is the same as that for δ D.

In the process of solvent selection, we comprehensively considered the factors such as solubility, cost, toxicity and recovery conditions of the solvent, and tried to improve the environmental friendliness of the recovery process as much as possible on the premise of ensuring the effect of dissolution and recovery.

In  this  study,  in  order  to  reduce  the  use  of  organic  solvents,  we decided to use a solvent combination to separate two kinds of plastics successively, which puts forward new requirements for the choice of solvents and anti-solvents, that is, solvents need to be able to dissolve PC and ABS at the same time, and anti-solvents need to be able to precip itate  PC and ABS successively with increasing volume in the system, while taking into account the chemical characteristics of green and low toxicity. Solvent screening results for ABS and PC are shown in Table 1 and Fig. 1. PC and ABS solubility parameters were respectively obtained from  Hansen  (2007) and  Lu  and  Chen  (2023).  RED  calculations  are provided in Table 1. Finally, DCM was selected as the optimal solvent based on toxicity, cost, dissolution efficiency, and recovery conditions.

The same mass plastic samples were placed into various solvents of the same volume to observe the dissolution behavior. The results indi cated  that  DCM  exhibited  better  solubility  for  both  PC  and  ABS. Therefore,  DCM  was  chosen  as  the  solvent  for  further  experiments. Specifically, 1 g PC could completely dissolve in 10 mL DCM; this figure for ABS is 15 mL. To ensure simultaneous dissolution of PC and ABS, 15 mL of DCM was finally selected. Due to the good solubility of DCM in both PC and ABS, the selected anti-solvent must be able to gradually precipitate PC and ABS separately from the mixture of itself and DCM with its volume increasing. After the particles were fully dissolved under stirring, the solution was transferred to a centrifuge  tube  and  added  different  volumes  of  EtOH  while  stirring. Record the volume changes of added EtOH, let the solution stand for 30 min,  then  centrifuged  the  solid  and  solution.  Weigh  the  mass  of  the precipitated solid after the residual solution was completely removed. The same procedure was used to obtain the separation point of 0.10 g ABS.

Using the separation points obtained above, dissolution and sepa ration experiments were conducted on the mimicked e-waste plastics. Place 1 g mimicked sample in a 50 mL conical flask and add 15 mL DCM. After all solids were dissolved, transfer the solution to a centrifuge tube and add 12 mL EtOH under stirring conditions. Let the solution stand for 30  min  and  centrifuge  to  separate  the  solid  (PC)  and  solution.  The separated solution was further mixed with about another 7 mL EtOH under stirring. After standing for another 30 min, the solid (ABS) and solution  were  separated  by  centrifugation.  After  the  solution  was completely removed, add another 10 mL EtOH and shake the container to extract organic phosphorus components (TPP). Using the same pro cedures for effectively separating and recovering PC and ABS from the mimicked sample, the separation and recovery of the computer plastic casing were conducted to further verify the method.

The  resolution  of  each  sample  is  4  cm 1 ,  and  the wavenumber range is 4000-650 cm 1 . 3. Results and discussion

3.1. Separation point

Overall, precipitation increased with the addition of EtOH (Fig. 2). At the initial stage, the solution changed from transparent to turbid; no significant  precipitation  occurred.  Once  a  critical  EtOH  volume  was reached, adding small amounts of EtOH caused a rapid increase in the precipitation, reaching approximately 90 %. At last, the precipitation amount tended to stabilize with the addition of EtOH.

For PC solution (Fig. 2a), when 5 mL EtOH was added, the solution remained transparent. However, when 6 mL EtOH was added, the so lution shifted from transparent to turbid. After another 6 mL added and the solution was left to stand for 30 min, stratification occurred. The upper layer was a milky white solution, while the lower layer remained transparent. When the amount of EtOH added reached 10 mL, the pre cipitation rate increased to 91 %; this figure for 24 mL EtOH was ~95 %. Between 10 mL and 24 mL, the precipitation rate showed sustained stability with slight growth.

For ABS (Fig. 2b), when 12 mL EtOH was added, no precipitation was observed. However, when 13 mL of EtOH was added, a large number of suspended  fine  particles  appeared  in  the  solution  after  settling.  The precipitation rate reached 87 % at 19 mL and ~90 % at 24 mL. There fore, the separation point for PC should be DCM: EtOH = 15 mL: 12 mL; the separation point for ABS should be DCM: EtOH = 15 mL: 19 mL.

3.2. Simulation experiment

Four types of solids were obtained from the simulation experiment with the mimicked sample. Specifically, PC and ABS were respectively obtained from the first and second centrifugation solid; residues of PC and ABS remained on the inner wall of the container after evaporation of the solvent; TPP solid was obtained after evaporating EtOH extract from residues inside the containers. The average recovery rates were 96 % (PC), 82 % (ABS), and 71 % (TPP), respectively. Infrared spectroscopy analysis revealed that the recovered PC sample exhibited a similarity of 98 % (Fig. 3a) compared to the standard spectrum; the similarity for the recovered  ABS  and  TPP  were  77  %  (Figs.  3b)  and  96  %  (Fig.  3c), respectively.

Additionally,  the  infrared  spectrum  of  the  recovered  ABS  sample displayed a characteristic ester group peak at 1763 cm 1 ,  along with three consecutive C-O bond characteristic peaks at 1229 cm 1 ,  1191 cm 1 , and 1161 cm 1 (Fig. 3b). No characteristic peak appeared in the standard  spectrum.  These  features  suggest  the  presence  of  a  small

For the actual e-waste samples, the average recovery rates of PC and ABS were 88 % and 103 %. The spectra are presented in Fig. 4. 3.4. Comparison with other SRPMs

Table 3 summarizes the existing SRPMs. Current SRPMs have pre dominantly focused on continuous extraction using multi-solvent com binations  (Walker  et  al.,  2020;  Weeden  et  al.,  2015;  Achilias  et  al.,

2009a). These approaches exhibit high solubility selectivity and produce high-purity,  high-quality  recovered  plastics.  However,  they  typically demand the use of multiple organic solvents. Notably, the use of organic solvents remains unavoidable in SRPMs for achieving optimal dissolu tion efficiency. Consequently, the development of green, efficient sol vent alternatives has increasingly emerged as a research priority.

Some studies have explored using NMP as a substitute for DCM to recover PC from e-waste (Chandrasekaran et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2023). However,  while  NMP  mitigates  toxicity  risks,  its  high  boiling  point (204 °C) drives up recovery costs and carbon emissions. Further, NMP costs 2 -3 times that of DCM. Meanwhile, the use of anti-solvents re quires  careful  evaluation  of  their  potential  toxicity  and  impacts  on materials  throughout  the  recycling  process  (Chandrasekaran  et  al., 2018; Yu et al., 2023).

Unlike existing methods, the approach developed in this study ach ieves sequential precipitation of PC and ABS using a single solvent sys tem (DCM/EtOH). Its key characteristics include.

3.5. Recovery cost estimation

To assess the method ' s feasibility and economic viability for largescale  production,  a  preliminary  cost-benefit  analysis  was  conducted. For this analysis, we assumed waste plastics from e-waste metal recy cling could directly enter the solvent-based recycling process enabling cost reduction. Additional estimation assumptions include: Waste plas tics have the same chemical composition as the PC/ABS mixtures tested in simulation experiments; The production line has a daily throughput of 1 ton of e-waste (Table 2); The solvent recovery system has 99 % recy cling efficiency (1 % loss rate; Table 2); Capital equipment is linearly depreciated over a 10-year lifespan (10 % annual rate; Table 2).

Initial investment included equipment cost and initial solvent cost. The e-waste plastics processing include grinding, dissolution with stir ring, solid-liquid separation, rotary evaporation, and drying. To imple ment  these  processes  in  actual  production,  the  required  equipment includes  grinders,  dissolution  mixers,  evaporators,  condensers,  and dryers. Based on the assumed daily processing capacity of one ton of ewaste  plastic,  the  specifications  for  the  required  equipment  were calculated. Specifically, a search was conducted on international plat forms  to  gather  data  for  15  sets  of  relevant  information  across  four different types of equipment. These data includes key elements such as equipment price and power, which serve as the foundation for subse quent cost estimation. Distribution fitting was performed on 60 sets of collected market price data for equipment was performed. On this basis, the total cost of the five types of equipment was estimated with Monte Carlo simulation. The simulation yielded a median equipment cost of ~28,430  USD,  the  5th  percentile  is  ~23,110  USD,  and  the  95th percentile is ~36,000 USD (Table 2 and Fig. 6a).

According to calculations, processing one ton of e-waste plastic re quires ~17 tons DCM and ~13 tons EtOH as initial solvents. For per ton of e-waste plastic recovered, ~0.17 tons DCM and ~0.13 tons EtOH (1 %) need to be supplemented (Table 2). The solvent cost can be estimated by fitting the price data of DCM and EtOH collected from January to August 2024 on Chemical Book. Using these fitted price distributions, both the initial solvent cost and the supplementary loss cost per ton of ewaste plastic were estimated via Monte Carlo simulation. The median initial solvent cost is ~17,270 USD, the 5th percentile is ~15,890 USD, and the 95th percentile is ~18,760 USD (Table 2 and Fig. 6b). To ensure the normal operation, the lost solvent must be replenished, i.  e. ,  the supplementary loss cost. The median daily supplementary loss cost is ~173 USD (Table 2).

Operating cost included energy cost and solvent recovery cost. The primary energy cost in the solvent-based method for recycling e-waste plastics  arises  from  the  power  consumption.  Based  on  the  operating steps,  the  energy  cost  was  divided  into  two  parts.  The  energy  con sumption for the crushing, grinding, dissolution, and drying steps was determined with the power consumption formula (3):

Fig. 6. Cost-benefit analysis (cost, economicsbenifits, emissions reduction, and job opportunities) of solvent-based plastic recovery method recovers PC/ABS from e-waste via Monte Carlo simulation.

E = ∑ n i = 1 Pi × t i (3)

where  Pi represents  the  power  of  the  device,  while t represents  the working time. The operating times of the crusher, grinder, dissolution mixer, and drying mixer are 4 h, 4 h, and 24 h, respectively. Power parameters of the collected dataset were calculated through Monte Carlo simulation  to  determine  the  required  energy  consumption  of  the equipment.

The solvent recovery system operates based on distillation principles. Assuming 100 % conversion of electrical energy to thermal energy, the energy consumed during condensation processes is theoretically equiv alent to the latent heat of vaporization required for solvent evaporation. This energy exchange is calculated using the latent heat formula (4):

Q = cm Δ T (4)

Where Q is the energy required to vaporize the solvent, c is the specific heat capacity of the solvent, m is the mass of the solvent, and Δ T is the temperature difference between room temperature and boiling temperature.

Based on the national average industrial electricity price of 0.0089 USD/kWh in China in 2021 (State Grid Corporation of China, 2021), the estimated  energy  cost  required  to  process  one  ton  e-waste  plastic  is

~160  USD/ton,  the  5th  percentile  is  ~150  USD/ton,  and  the  95th percentile is ~171 USD/ton (Table 2 and Fig. 6c).

Additionally, assuming an annual maintenance cost of ~3500 USD, with a fixed asset depreciation rate of 10 %, in summary, the results show that the cost of solvent-based recycling of electronic waste plastic is ~355 USD/ton, the 5th percentile is ~340 USD/ton, and the 95th percentile  is  ~372  USD/ton (under a 10-year cycle and a daily pro cessing capacity of 1 ton) (Table 2 and Fig. 6d).

3.6. Benefit of e-waste plastics recovery

To evaluate the economic benefits of s olvent-based processes for ewaste plastics, a statistical analysis was conducted based on the prices of virgin  PC  and  ABS  from  professional  plastic  trading  platforms.  The economic benefits of the solvent recovery process are determined using formula (5):

P =( X 1 × A 1 + X 2 × A 2 ) ( E 1 + E 2 + M ) (5)

Where P represents profit, X1 and X2 represent the recycling volume of PC and ABS, A1 and A2 represent the average price of the two plastics, E1 represents  solvent  cost,  E2  represents  energy  cost,  and  M  represents equipment maintenance cost. The calculation results show that recy cling one ton of e-waste plastic generates a profit ~766 USD/ton, the 5th percentile is ~627 USD/ton, and the 95th percentile is ~971 USD/ton (Table 2 and Fig. 6e), the net profit margin is 68.4 % when taking the median.

Based on our calculations, the energy intensity of the solvent-based recycling method is 9 % of the energy required for producing equiva lent quantities of fossil-fuel derived PC (113 MJ kg 1 ) and ABS (95 MJ kg 1 ) (Vink et al., 2010). This represents a 91 % (Table 2) reduction compared to conventional petroleum-based production.

Significant carbon reduction is also achieved through this recycling methodology.  The  carbon  emission  reduction  is  calculated  using  the following formula (6):

EC = P × EFn (6)

Where EC represents the reduced carbon dioxide emissions, P represents energy savings, and EFn is the national average CO2 emission factor for electricity. According to the 2021 EFn (0.5366 kg CO2/kWh) (Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People ' s Republic of China, 2024), the solvent based recycling method reduces ~10.2 tons CO2 emissions, the 5th percentile is ~10.11 t, and the 95th percentile is ~10.24 t (Table 2 and Fig. 6g) by recycling one ton waste plastic compared to the original production.

With the increasingly severe global climate problems, peak carbon dioxide emissions and carbon neutrality have become the core goals of the  future  development  of  more  and  more  countries.  The  European Union has made it clear in legal form through the European Climate Law: by 2030, the net greenhouse gas emissions need to be reduced by at least 55 % compared with 1990; by 2050, achieve climate neutrality at the economic and social levels, and achieve negative emissions after 2050. The Chinese government has defined the carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals in relevant documents: strive to achieve carbon peaking by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060. The results show that the sol vent recovery method has significant potential in the field of carbon emission reduction, and this technical path will provide strong support for  countries  to  promote  green  transformation  and  achieve  carbon emission reduction targets as scheduled.

E-waste recycling can create significant job opportunities. A 2021 study found that metal recycling alone generates 2.03 million annual job opportunities in China (Yang et al., 2021). Plastic recycling, as a critical supplement to metal recovery, enhances employment potential through additional processing steps. Based on China ' s 2023 per capita wage of 9558 USD/year (National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2024), recycling 12 million tons of domestically generated e-waste (containing 27.4 %

plastic) could create ~270,000 new jobs, the 5th percentile is ~222, 650, and the 95th percentile is ~340,270 (Table 2 and Fig. 6h).

The results show that the solvent recovery method has great market potential (economic profits and employment opportunities) and broad development  prospects.  Compared  with  petroleum-based  plastic  pro duction,  it  requires  less  energy  and  emits  less  CO2,  supporting  the development of a green economy and resource-recycling society.

The cost-benefit analysis  is  based  on  preliminary  laboratory-scale accounting.  Intended  to  provide  a  simple  quantitative  reference  for the method ' s practical application, the analysis itself carries some un certainty. Apparently, such calculations cannot fully capture the com plexities  of  real-world  industrial  production.  In  practical  industrial settings,  socioeconomic factors are far more complex than in experi mental simulations. Dynamic market shifts, raw material price fluctua tions, equipment depreciation, environmental protection requirements, and policies and regulations may all affect cost structures and economic benefits.  Thus,  the  method ' s  feasibility  in  actual  production  requires accounting for multiple factors: market supply and demand, regional resource allocation, economies of scale, the external environment, and government policies.

4. Conclusion

This study presents a solvent-based recycling system for the separa tion and high-purity recovery of PC/ABS from e-waste streams; at the same time, it removes organic phosphorus flame retardants via selective dissolution.  Under  current  market  and  technological  constraints,  the method achieves 88 % PC recovery efficiency and 104 % for ABS, cuts energy consumption by 91 % and CO2 emissions by 10.2 tons compared with  virgin  plastic  production,  and  demonstrates  economic  viability with a 68.4 % net profit margin. These findings fully demonstrate the method ' s broad potential in waste plastic recycling. Overall, compared with  petroleum-based  plastic  production,  the  solvent-based  recycling technology for e-waste plastics proposed in this paper has obvious ad vantages. It produces high-purity products, saves energy, reduces carbon emissions, brings good economic benefits, and can create more job op portunities.  Especially,  the  method  uses  as  few  types  of  low-toxicity solvents  as  possible.  This  reduces  potential  environmental  harm  and ecological risks, making it environmentally friendly. As noted earlier, solvent recovery technology is still in development, with many chal lenges remaining to achieve true scaling and industrialization. Never theless,  given  the  strong  performance  and  potential  outlined  in  this study,  the  solvent  recovery  method  is  poised  to  become  a  critical pathway for advancing the sustainable utilization and development of global plastic resources.

APPLIED SCIENCES AND ENGINEERING

Pigment removal from reverse- printed laminated flexible films by solvent- targeted recovery and precipitation

Tianwei Yan 1 , Charles Granger 1 , Kevin L. Sánchez- Rivera 1 , Panzheng Zhou 1 , Steven Grey 2 , Kevin Nelson 2 , Fei Long 3 , Ezra Bar- Ziv 3 , Reid C. Van Lehn 1,4 , Styliani Avraamidou 1 , George W. Huber 1 *

The solvent- targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process separates and recovers the constituent resins in multilayer  plastic  packaging  films  by  selective  polymer  dissolution.  In  this  work,  the  cause  of  coloring  in  the STRAP- recycled polyethylene (PE) resins from postindustrial printed films was identified as decomposed diarylide pigments. Two different approaches are needed to completely remove the dissolved colorants during the STRAP process including (i) adding an activated carbon (AC) adsorbent to the solvent after polymer dissolution and (ii) proper mechanical filtration of the polymer- solvent cake to remove as much solvent from the cake as possible. Colorless recycled PE can be produced by a combination of the proposed approaches (choosing the proper solvent, adding an AC adsorbent, and doing proper mechanical filtration) with minimal accumulation of colorants in the recycled STRAP solvents. This study demonstrated that high- quality STRAP low- density PE can be obtained from printed plastic films, enhancing the potential circularity of these packaging materials.

INTRODUCTION

Over the last ~ 70 years, plastic materials have become indispensable to modern society beginning with their large- scale production after World  War  II  ( 1 ).  Their  durability,  low  cost,  and  versatility  have driven an exponential growth of plastics production ( 1 -3 ). However, this growth has led to end- of- life issues, such as waste accumulation and environmental plastics contamination.

Flexible plastic packaging is particularly challenging to recycle as it  typically  includes  several  layers  of  distinct  polymers  for  their moisture and oxygen barrier properties, sealability, and mechanical strength ( 4 , 5 ). Tie layers, adhesives, additives, and inks add further complexity  to  the  composition,  resulting  in  incompatibility  with traditional recycling technologies ( 5 ). Ineffective separation and purification of different polymers result in downgraded recyclates with deteriorated properties.

Virgin plastics are usually colorless plastic materials while inks are  typically  added  to  most  plastics  to  improve  the  aesthetic  demands for products ( 6 ). After mechanical recycling, colorants often cause recycled plastics to appear gray or black ( 7 ), making them distinguishable from colorless virgin plastics. A recent report evaluated mechanically  recycled  low- density  polyethylene  (LDPE)  printed flexible  packaging with pigments and ink binders ( 8 ).  The  results indicated that the presence of ink introduced yellowish or brownish tones to the recycled films as well as reduced transparency and pigment aggregates, e.g., 'black specks. '

Color  removal  from  recycled  polymers  is  difficult  because  the high color strength of colorant species and high color sensitivity of human eyes lead to recognizable color in the recycled plastic materials even with minimal retention of colorants. The retained colors can adversely affect customer perception of the recycled plastic products ( 9 ). For example, yellow color is commonly associated with age and degradation ( 10 -12 ). The adverse impact of colors in recycled resins is reflected in the price difference between colored and colorless postconsumer plastics ( 8 , 13 -17 ). Taking high- density polyethylene (HDPE) as an example, the price of mixed color HDPE bales is one- half  to  one- third  of  colorless  baled  HDPE  ( 8 , 13 -17 ).  Therefore, effective removal of colors from recycled polymers is critical for improving the product value of recyclates.

Understanding colorants  is  crucial  for  effective  color  removal. Colorants are diverse in chemical compositions and physical properties and are classified as pigments or dyes. Pigments are designed to reside in discrete particles while dyes are designed to be soluble in solvents ( 18 ). For plastic packaging printing, organic pigmentbased inks are most common because dyes tend to bleed and leach with incompatible plastics ( 6 ). Pigments require binders and additives in the inks to disperse properly on printed areas. A myriad of chemical compositions and structural variants bring distinct physical and chemical properties. Making it challenging to remove all pigments with one single method. Common colorants and their chemical families are listed in table S1.

The  undesired  color  and  poor  appearance  of  recycled  plastics have troubled plastic recyclers since the 1980s ( 19 -23 ).  Deinking pretreatments have been developed to remove inks from a plastic's surface ( 24 ). However, when ink is printed on an inner layer of flexible packaging (i.e., reverse- printed laminated films), the effectiveness  and  rate  of  deinking  are  compromised  ( 25 ).  Consequently, recycling technologies are emerging to create higher- quality recycled  plastics.  Dissolution- based  recycling  has  gained  interest  as  a complementary  method  to  traditional  mechanical  recycling.  This approach can extract valuable polymer components from multilayer films and remove additives and impurities with distinct solubilities (e.g., pigments) ( 24 , 26 , 27 ).

Solvent- targeted  recovery  and  precipitation  (STRAP)  is  a dissolution- based process that recycles multilayer films by using a

series of solvents to selectively recover the constituent resins of the material guided by thermodynamic calculations of polymer solubility ( 5 , 25 , 28 -30 ). The STRAP process has been successful in recovering polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from multilayer films with high purity, efficiency, and reduced color ( 25 , 28 ). The STRAP process units (Fig. 1) include the following:

Dissolution: shredded plastics are mixed with a hot solvent to dissolve the targeted layer.

Hot filtration: hot dissolved plastics are separated from solid residue.

Precipitation: the polymer solution is cooled to precipitate the plastic (antisolvents are not used in STRAP to minimize costs and environmental impact) ( 31 ).

Mechanical separation: solvent is mechanically separated from precipitated polymer.

Drying: solvent retained in the polymer is evaporated.

Extrusion: the polymer is extruded and pelletized.

Solvent recovery: as much solvent as possible is recovered to be recycled.

Solvent cleaning: solvent is purified, ideally with adsorbents, to avoid contaminant buildup.

Colorants  that  pass  through  the  hot  filtration  step  could  be trapped in the purified polymer during the precipitation step. Colorants in general have a low volatility and cannot be removed during the drying step shown in Fig. 1; thus, any soluble colorants would likely deposit onto the recovered polymer.

In two previous cases, STRAP removed white, yellow, and black colorants from PET and blue colorants from PP via selective dissolution of the inks ( 25 , 28 ). In these instances, colorants were removed  from  the  color- rich  final  products  in  a  secondary  wash step. This extra wash step adds additional cost, emissions, and energy consumption ( 17 ).  Therefore,  we  aim to optimize the color removal approach.

We also previously attempted to isolate colorless postindustrial waste (PIW 1) PE from a multilayer reverse- printed laminated polyester film using a single solvent STRAP system ( 25 ). The resulting PE was then manufactured into a cast film and characterized ( 32 ). Although we removed a large fraction of the colorants (Fig. 2A), the film still had a light but noticeable yellow color (Fig. 2B) ( 25 , 32 ). Ideally, colorless recycled plastic should be produced using a single solvent to maximize financial and environmental benefits, given the high impact of organic solvents ( 17 , 25 , 32 ).

Other dissolution- based methods have observed similar issues. For example, Creasolv's Indonesia plant produces yellow- green recycled PE (rPE) from waste sachets ( 19 , 33 ), likely caused by remaining mixed pigments and other impurities. The yellowing of plastics, however, is common and not limited to dissolution- based recycling. Causes of yellowing can include oxidation of phenolic antioxidant ( 34 ), polymer degradation ( 35 -37 ), pigment retention ( 25 , 28 ), catalyst  choice  ( 38 ),  and  formation of chiral supramolecular structure via irradiation ( 12 ). Degradation of the bulk polymer, adhesives, or ink binders in printed films may produce yellow colorants in recycled plastic ( 1 , 12 , 34 , 36 , 37 ).

In this work, we aim to identify the composition of remaining colorants and demonstrate a method for the nearly complete removal of color from reverse- printed laminated multilayer flexible films made of PE, EVOH, and PET, with polyurethane (PU) inks. The challenge is to identify the color source in the recovered resins and understand colorant solubility and accumulation during the STRAP process. We then show how the processing of the  reverse- printed  laminated  film  can  produce  colorless  polymer resins.

RESULTS

Color source in rPE from STRAP

To determine the exact cause of rPE coloring after the STRAP process, we first conducted experiments with various ink- free films to confirm  that  other  components  do  not  cause  yellowing  during STRAP ( 5 ). Therefore, the possible coloring components in reverse- printed laminated films are PU adhesives and inks. PU adhesives are used to bind together different layers in a multilayer film. Inks consist of solvents, colorants, and additives for printing, durability, and other aesthetic needs ( 8 , 39 ). Pigment- based inks also require the presence of binders to properly disperse pigments on the printed area. PU and nitrocellulose (NC) are the most common ink binders in multilayer films ( 8 ).  Any of these components can potentially cause discoloration when recycled ( 8 , 12 , 35 , 36 ).

A multilayer plastic waste is fed into the process (stream 1) and a single purified polymer is recovered (stream 11) with nearly all color removed. Fig. 2. Recovered PE from a reverse- printed laminated multilayer film via STRAP. ( A ) The coloring issue was mitigated after solvent optimization ( 25 ). ( B ) The cast film made from STRAP resins was still noticeably yellow ( 32 ).

STRAP was applied to eight samples consisting of virgin LDPE plus various combinations of PU adhesive, PU ink, and/or NC ink extenders (ink binders, solvents, and additives, i.e., inks without pigments) to identify any possible degradation reactions that might cause yellowing during the STRAP process in the absence of pigments (Fig. 3). 'Before STRAP' samples were hot pressed (method 1) at 190°C, while ' After STRAP' samples were dissolved in dodecane at 95°C, filtered with a 600- μ m filter, precipitated at 25°C, dried  under  vacuum  at  110°C,  and  hot  pressed  (method  1)  at 190°C. Compressed films of the samples before and after STRAP are shown in Fig. 3.

Sample 1 showed no yellowing before or after STRAP, indicating that degradation of the bulk polymer or any additives in the virgin resin is not the cause of yellowing. Slight yellowing was observed before STRAP for samples 2, 3, and 6, which is hard to see in Fig. 3. Samples 4, 5, 7, and 8 all show heavy yellowing before STRAP , indicating that NC ink causes this color change during the film hot compression. The PU adhesive and PU inks can also degrade but only form a slightly yellow color. Samples 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8 after STRAP showed no notable yellowing, while samples 4 and 5 after STRAP showed yellowing as in the pre- STRAP samples yet to a lesser degree. These results demonstrate that STRAP effectively reduced the yellow color of all samples caused by insoluble PU and NC. The reason for samples 4 and 5 yellowing is that some of the small NC particles passed through the relatively coarse filter in this experiment. The difference between samples 4 and 5 and samples 7 and 8 is that samples 4 and 5 did not contain the PU adhesive. The PU adhesive thus binds to insoluble agglomerates and other insoluble components  to  help  filter  off  NC  from  the  dissolved  polymer  (Fig.  3B). More importantly, the hue and heterogeneous dispersion caused by insoluble NC and PU do not match with the uniform green- yellow  hue  in  our  STRAP- recovered  PE  from  printed  films  (Fig.

2B). Therefore, it can be reasonably assumed that none of the components  in  this  experiment  are  the  main  source  of  yellowing  in STRAP- recovered PE. This leads to the hypothesis that PE yellowing is likely caused by pigments in inks.

Pigment selection and solubility measurements

An extended conclusion from the above STRAP experiments with adhesives and binders is that insoluble pigment particles can adhere to the ink binders and be removed more easily via filtration. Inorganic pigments exhibit extremely low solubility in STRAP organic solvents and may be targeted via filtration. Organic pigments are often partially soluble in STRAP solvents, making the color removal process more challenging. The following work focuses on methods to reduce the color caused by organic pigments in dissolution- based recycling.

Organic pigments are frequently used in plastic packaging due to their higher color strength, brighter hues, and higher transparency, which can reduce costs compared to inorganic pigments ( 6 ).  Y et, these  pigments  have  lower  solvent  resistance  against  organic  solvents than inorganic pigments. The industry continuously seeks pigments  to  achieve  specific  hues  with  single  components  and  high color fidelity ( 40 ). A large array of chemical structures is available in synthetic pigments, and it is impractical to explore every variant's property. In addition, ink manufacturers often keep their formulations  confidential.  Despite  the  vast  number  of  individual  organic pigments,  common  categories  of  organic  pigments  by  chromophores  include  azo,  phthalocyanine,  quinacridone,  and  isoindolinone as shown in Fig. 4A ( 6 , 18 , 41 , 42 ). Azo pigments are broadly used in red, orange, yellow, and violet colors, and phthalocyanines are prevailing as blue and green pigments ( 43 ). Quinacridones and isoindolinones  are  more  commonly  applied  in  high- performance scenarios  ( 6 ).  Within  each  of  these  categories,  the  variants  share similar structures leading to similar solubilities and, thus, are representative of properties of organic pigments in printing. Among the tested  pigments,  Yellow  12,  Blue  15,  and  Red  57:1  are  commonly used  in  the  four- color  (CMYK,  i.e.,  cyan,  magenta,  yellow,  and black) printing process ( 8 ).

Typically, during STRAP of the printed multilayer film samples, a yellow- green PE solution is collected after hot filtration. After precipitation and mechanical filtration, solvent and polymer are separated, although both still have an undesired color. Toluene produces more intensely colored PE while alkanes give a reduced yet recognizable yellowness (Fig. 2A) ( 25 ).  As we will show here, the colorants that contaminate recovered PE are soluble but require heating and have higher solubility in aromatics than aliphatic solvents. Determining the exact source of this coloring is critical for understanding and resolving this issue in the STRAP process.

In Fig. 4, we categorized the tested pigments in groups by their dissolution behavior in dodecane (method 2). A large fraction of organic pigments (Red 57:1, Blue 15:4, Green 7, Yellow 110, and Violet  19)  showed  no  visually  notable  solubility  at  both  20°  and 120°C (Fig. 4B). The low solubility is caused by their stronger intermolecular interaction from large π - conjugated molecular structures, hydrogen bonding (Violet 19) ( 44 ), and/or ionic form (Red 57:1). As a result, no obvious contribution to PE yellowing is anticipated from this group of pigments. In the second group, Yellow 1 and Orange 5 are soluble at 20°C in both toluene and dodecanes (Fig. 4C), due to their low polarity and low molecular weight ( 42 ). Extracting the printed film samples with dodecanes under the same conditions resulted in no recognizable colorant dissolution as the solubility test, which indicates that our printed film samples do not contain these room temperature soluble monoazo pigments. This result agrees with the fact that monoazo pigments are incompatible with polyolefins due to bleeding and leaching issues ( 6 ). Dioxazine pigment (Violet 23) displayed conditional solubility (Fig. 4D), as it slightly dissolved in dodecanes at 120°C with a light color, while fully precipitated and removed upon cooling to 20°C and filtration. This  matched  the  observations  from  STRAP  experiments  about solubility dependence on temperature. However, the dissolved color is relatively weak, and the blue- shade violet is the complementary color of yellow- green in the STRAP- recovered PE ( 45 ). Violet 23 is also not the main cause of PE coloring. Even if Violet 23 is present in the printed film and partially dissolves during STRAP , its color in the recovered PE will be masked by the dominating yellow- green colorant.

The dissolution behavior of diarylide orange and yellow pigments (Orange 13 and Yellow 12) is different from the other three groups. These two pigments showed no visually recognizable dissolution at 20°C, yet the dodecanes turned yellow- green after heating with the pigments at 120°C as shown in Fig. 4E. The difference between diarylide and dioxazine pigments is that Violet 23 remained insoluble in dodecanes upon cooling to 20°C, while the yellow color in hot solution of Orange 13 and Yellow 12 stayed at 20°C. This distinct solubility indicated that the dissolved coloring species have different chemical structures from the initial pigments. Literature suggests that diarylide yellow and orange pigments have lower thermal stability and decompose into monoazo species at high temperatures (above 200°C) as shown in Fig. 4F ( 46 ). These monoazo species have a higher solubility in organic solvents than the pristine diarylide species due to the reduced molecule sizes. A recent study on plastic recycling with inks confirmed through thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) that the decomposition of diarylide yellow occurs above 100°C ( 8 ), indicating the likelihood of forming these more soluble colorants under the STRAP conditions ( 46 ).

Ultraviolet- visible spectroscopy (UV- Vis) of the heated Y ellow 12 solution in dodecane detected absorption peak shifting compared to the Yellow 12 solution prepared at 20°C (Fig. 5A), validating the molecular structural change of diarylide pigments upon heating. The maximum absorbance of heated (decomposed) Yellow 12 matched with the STRAP- recovered dodecanes used on the printed multilayer  film  (Fig.  5A),  further  supporting  the  hypothesis  that  diarylide derivatives contribute to PE yellowing.

Temperature plays an important role in colorant transformation. Raising the dissolution temperature from 20° to 100°, 120°, and 140°C increased the absorption peak at 420 nm with temperature and time as shown in Fig. 5A. The ratio of this peak over the other peak at 370 nm decreased with rising temperature. At 160°C, absorption increased drastically with a hypsochromic shift (Fig. 5A), suggesting accelerated formation and further structural evolution of soluble colorants. This change at 160°C aligns with reported TGA profiles of diarylide pigment, in which its first decomposition peak is at 162°C ( 8 ). After removing undissolved pigments, heating the yellow dodecane solution at 160°C still resulted in a noticeable increase in absorbance with a hypsochromic shift, demonstrating that dissolved color species also undergo changes at high temperatures (Fig. 5A, black arrow).
