4.4. Model Fitting

For both the model based on chain disentanglement and the first-order model, the parameters, resulting from the regression of the model on the experimental data, are provided in Table 3 . Additionally, the TIC, MRE, and 95% CI values are presented as well. The first observation is that, considering their TIC < 0.3, both models for all tested solvents are valid descriptions for the dissolution profile. [73] However, when looking at the MRE, it can be said that the first-order diffusion model is more accurate in describing the dissolution profiles of MEK

and 2-MeTHF. The confidence intervals of the model parameters underpin this observation, as the percentage error is smaller for these solvents. In contrast, by following the trends of the MRE and the 95% CI, the chain disentanglement model appears to be more accurate with regard to the NMP dissolution profile. Finally, for cyclohexanone, it can be said that there is no discernible difference in the accuracy of both models, with MREs of 9.7% for the chain disentanglement model and 8.9% for the first-order diffusion model.

Additionally, the value of the activation energy in the chain disentanglement model shows that the effect of a change in the dissolution temperature on the dissolution rate is the highest for cyclohexanone, followed by NMP, then 2-MeTHF, and finally MEK. The first-order diffusion model also predicts that the cyclohexanone dissolution rate is more sensitive to temperature changes than NMP, MEK, and 2-MeTHF. In this model approach, MEK and 2-MeTHF appear to be equally sensitive. This can be confirmed when looking at the data in Figure 7 , where for cyclohexanone, e.g., the particle size independent chain disentanglement rate and diffusion coefficient increase by 376% at 60 °C relative to the 30 °C baseline experiment. text: In the following section, the resulting dissolution profiles of the different models will only be presented for NMP and 2-MeTHF. The profiles of MEK and cyclohexanone can be found in section 5 of the Supporting Information. Comparing both models for NMP with the experimental data, as shown in Figure 8 , leads to the conclusion that the chain disentanglement model is generally a better representation for this solvent. This is also confirmed when looking at the TIC and MRE of the chain disentanglement model, which are 0.024 and 5.5% respectively, compared to the first-order model, where the TIC is 0.040 and the MRE is 7.6%. Additionally, Figure 8 reveals that the first-order model mostly overestimates the dissolution time for 2190 and 2990 μ m particles, while underestimating for the smaller 1090 μ m particle sizes. The reason for this could be found by comparing the particle size dependency of both models, where the first-order diffusion model only accounts for the initial particle size, r0, while the chain disentanglement model accounts for the change in the particle size over time.

When looking at 2-MeTHF ( Figure 9 ), having a TIC of 0.024 and MRE of 6.9%, the first-order model provides a better fit for all performed experiments, independent of temperature or particle size, compared to the chain disentanglement model with a TIC of 0.037 and MRE of 9.3%. For 2-MeTHF and MEK, the chain disentanglement model generally underestimates the dissolution time in all cases. A possible explanation for the better fit of the first-order model could be that these two solvents have a lower affinity for the polymer, therefore taking longer for the polymer to dissolve than predicted, as well as not dissolving the polymer completely in some cases. This is also one of the downsides of both models, as they cannot predict the equilibrium end-concentration of the dissolution experiments ( ω 2, eq ) when there is a solubility limit. Therefore, this concentration has to be determined experimentally.

Finally, a spider diagram is provided in Figure 10 , where the MRE of both models is plotted, individually for every experiment. This also confirms the previous statements, where it is clear that the first-order kinetics provides an all-round better description of the dissolution profiles for MEK and 2-MeTHF, while it does not for NMP. This leads to the conclusion that the chain disentanglement model, within this experimental design, seems to be more suitable for the description of good to very good PVC solvents like NMP and cyclohexanone. The chain disentanglement model for NMP is considerably better at describing the dissolution profile at temperatures around or below the glass transition temperature of the polymer sample. This difference was less pronounced at higher temperatures. It would be interesting to see if the conclusions of this research hold true when moving toward even higher dissolution temperatures (e.g., 100 -150 °C) as well as larger particle sizes, e.g., 10 -50 mm.

The inclusion of reactor and process parameters such as stirring speed could also prove useful in further developing an industrially relevant model.

5. Conclusion

A full factorial experimental design was conducted on a plasticized PVC sample, containing DINCH, with a varying average particle size (1090, 2190, and 2990 μ m) and temperature (30, 45, and 60 °C). In every experiment, 10 wt% solutions of the sample in one of the following four solvents were prepared: NMP, cyclohexanone, MEK, and 2-MeTHF. Using a combination of GC/MS to measure the plasticizer in solution and Py-GC/MS to measure the amount of PVC in solution, it was found that overall, both the plasticizer and the polymer dissolved at the same rate. These findings were backed up by analyzing a different P -PVC sample where the plasticizer was DEHP. This could indicate that the overall dissolution behavior of P -PVC is governed by the disentanglement of the PVC matrix. Concerning the kinetic dissolution experiments, it was found that in general, the order from fastest to slowest solvents for PVC dissolution was NMP, cyclohexanone, MEK, and 2-MeTHF. It was also noticed that both MEK and 2-MeTHF could not completely dissolve the sample at temperatures around or below the glass transition temperature of the P -PVC sample. Furthermore, as expected, reducing the particle size of the sample as well as increasing the temperature, positively affected the dissolution speed regardless of the solvent used. It was found that the dissolution times for the prepared 10 wt% P -PVC solutions were at most around 120 min. This was the case for both 2-MeTHF and MEK at 30 °C and with 2990 μ m particles. In contrast, the fastest dissolution time was 5 min in NMP at 60 °C and with 1090 μ m particles.

Next, two models are proposed to describe the dissolution profile: a chain disentanglement-based model and a first-order diffusion model. It can be concluded that both models are capable of describing the dissolution profile of a real P -PVC sample, with an MRE of 12.1% or less. It appears that the chain disentanglement model is generally more accurate in describing the dissolution profile of good solvents, like NMP, whilst the firstorder model excels at describing the dissolution profile of slower solvents like MEK and 2-MeTHF. It would be interesting to expand the dissolution experiments to more solvents, higher temperatures, and a wider range in particle sizes, in order to further calibrate both models. Further efforts should also be made in developing a theoretically based formula for the disentanglement rate with respect to macroscopic parameters. This includes material properties (such as molecular weight, detailed particle geometry, solubility parameters, etc.) as well as reactor and process parameters (such as stirring speed, reactor geometry, etc.). In essence, a more advanced understanding of the specific process of chain disentanglement in a practical context. Finally, the simplicity of both models could allow for easy integration into process simulation software, such as Aspen Plus, for example, to perform energy optimization studies. Additionally, understanding the dissolution behavior of polymer waste can aid the industry toward an increase in the dissolution rate, which could, for example, allow for the use of smaller reactors. These vital improvements can pave the way for a viable dissolution-based PVC recycling process in the future.

Solvent-based recycling approaches are receiving industrial and academic interest for their ability to produce high-quality plastic resins from a variety of plastic waste sources without breaking the polymer chains. Here we highlight the development of solvent-based technologies, focusing on the underlying principles, techno-economic and life-cycle analyses, and commercialization. The basic steps in solvent-based recycling include plastic size reduction, plastic dissolution, filtration or centrifugation, and optional additional cleaning steps such as adsorption, precipitation and solvent removal. Impurities that build up in the solvent must also be removed. The goal of solvent-based technologies is to produce a high-quality resin without plastic contaminants or other added substances. Disadvantages of these solvent-based technologies are their physicochemical complexity and the difficulty in scaling up to achieve continuous operations with high polymer and solvent yields and throughputs. Chemical engineering is thus critical in bringing solvent-based recycling technologies to market.

Global annual plastic production reached 413.8 million metric tons in 2023, while the recycling rate was only 9.6% (ref. 1). Globally, most plastic waste is either landfilled or disposed of in open pit dumps. It is estimated that 2-5% of all plastic produced ends up in the ocean 2 . Mechanical recycling is the main current approach to recycle plastics 3 . In mechanical recycling, plastics undergo sorting, separation, grinding, cleaning by (friction) washing, sink-float separation (to separate heavier polymers such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from polyolefins), drying and then re-extrusion. Although some color sorting is possible before mechanical recycling, the recycling process does not remove colors or other common additives, nor is it capable of eliminating many other impurities such as adhesives. Beyond mechanical recycling, several chemical recycling technologies, such as plastic pyrolysis and polyester methanolysis 4,5 , are being developed and commercialized. These technologies are typically integrated with existing petrochemical infrastructure, such as steam-cracking or PET polymerization 6 . Researchers have discussed various plastic waste recycling technologies and their implications. For instance, Tiwari et al. provided a comprehensive analysis of mechanical and chemical recycling methods of plastic waste, highlighting the challenges in plastic sorting and segregation 7 ; Zhang et al. covered the technological mechanisms and development status of mechanical and chemical recycling technologies 8 ; additionally, Li et al. provided a comprehensive review of plastic recycling, detailing the chemistry, engineering and technological aspects of various plastic recycling methods 9 .

Flexible packaging plastic is a complicated waste stream to recycle because moisture, dirt, other polymer layers, adhesives and inks build up during the mechanical recycling process 10,11 . For example, multilayer flexible packaging is composed of multiple polymer and adhesive layers, each with varying chemical compositions and properties. These complex combinations can make it challenging to recycle films and to produce high-quality products via mechanical or chemical recycling methods 12 . Solvent-based recycling, also called dissolution-based recycling, is a promising solution that separates individual polymers from multipolymer streams and simultaneously allows deep cleaning of the dissolved polymers. In addition to films, this approach is well suited to other combinations of materials such as mixed plastic bales 13 , electronic 14,15 and automotive waste 16 , and multicomponent flooring 17 . Dissolution-based recycling can also be applied to monomaterial waste streams to perform deeper removal of impurities, while keeping the polymer chains intact.

Dissolution-based plastic recycling has several advantages compared with mechanical recycling. The process produces a high-quality virgin-like resin where impurities, other polymers and other unintentionally added substances (such as color bodies, often referred to as 'non-intentionally added substances') can be removed. Although dissolution-based recycling is often still classified under 'mechanical' recycling because it does not break the polymer chains, traditional mechanical recycling cannot achieve the same level of impurity removal. Therefore, dissolution-based recycling is categorized as 'physical' recycling 18 . This approach recovers high-quality polymers, leaving polymer chains intact. However, dissolution-based technologies also have several challenges that must be overcome for them to be implemented commercially.

In this Review, we discuss current academic research, industrial processes and future research needs of dissolution-based recycling technologies. We first review the basic underlying principles and commercial activities of dissolution-based technologies. We then discuss thermodynamic principles, experimental laboratory studies, and techno-economic analysis (TEA) and life-cycle assessment (LCA) studies. We close with key recommendations for future research.

Process and unit operations overview

Figure 1 shows simplified block flow diagrams of current commercial dissolution-based plastic recycling plants. There are variations in the technology, but in general dissolution-based recycling of waste polymers involves several fundamental steps: (1) preprocessing (such as shredding/downsizing, densification, metal removal, washing and drying), (2) dissolution of targeted polymer, (3) separation of the dissolved polymer from the remaining non-dissolved material, (4) precipitation of the dissolved polymer, (5) separation of the precipitated polymer from the solvent, (6) drying and solvent purification from the nondissolved polymer and precipitated polymer and (7) resin production. This section discusses each step of the process, highlighting some of the key technical considerations, state-of-the-art approaches and remaining challenges. More details of the processes are covered in the following sections.

Feedstocks and preprocessing

Dissolution-based recycling methods have been reported in the literature for a wide range of feedstocks. Table 1 references recent literature reflecting some of the most widely recognized work on this topic with feedstocks including electronic waste, plastic packaging, foams, plastic bottles, automotive materials and others. Additionally, solvents have been used for the removal of colorants, adhesives, plastic additives and odor 21-25 . While the technology needs time to mature and expand, dissolution-based recycling will likely fill a role in processing complex but low-variability waste streams, such as many of those listed in Table 1, that allow simplification of the preprocessing steps.

Preprocessing of plastic waste involves the following steps: (1) collection and transportation, (2) sorting and separation, (3) size reduction (typically to less than 2 mm) 26 , (4) cleaning, (5) drying and (6) additional processing (such as decontamination, densification, microperforation and thermal conditioning). Quality control is critical to ensure that the undesired components are removed. The collection and sorting of the waste feedstock is one of the most challenging steps in this process. It plays a pivotal role in the whole recycling process to determine the solvent type and operating conditions. Most material recovery facilities use a series of sorting processes including optical methods such as near-infrared spectroscopy, which typically have accuracies of above 90% at object level (an object can consist of different polymers) 27 . Dissolution-based recycling plants can process sorted bales, and even shredded and washed waste, or undertake some of these steps in house 9 .

Dissolution

The shredded plastics are mixed with a potentially heated solvent in a dissolution vessel. Solvent choice and temperature depend on the target polymer. Ideally, only the targeted polymer is dissolved, without dissolving other polymers and small additives including pigments, which facilitates their separation. The viscosity of the solution, an important parameter for the whole process, can be influenced by concentration, temperature, pressure and polymer-solvent interactions 28 . Generally, for dissolution-based plastic recycling, the recommended polymer concentration is 5-20 wt% (ref. 28). A concentration above 10 wt% often results in a very viscous solution, depending on the polymer type, molecular weight and operating conditions. For example, at 155 °C and 20 MPa, the viscosity of the PE solution (1 wt%, weightaveraged molecular mass of 2,150 g mol -1 ) is approximately 0.125 mPa s, and it increases to 0.15 mPa s when the pressure is raised to 40 MPa (ref. 28); for the combination of PS/ o -xylene at room temperature (RT), the entanglement concentration is 13.9 wt%, and the viscosity is noticeably increased at this concentration, reaching ~0.9 Pa s (ref. 29). High viscosity of the polymer solution often leads to difficulties in material flow, separation and post-process cleaning. Polymer solutions are typically categorized as either Newtonian or non-Newtonian fluids on the basis of how the fluid viscosity changes upon the application of shear stress. Researchers have proposed the Carreau and Yasuda-Armstrong-Cohen model to describe both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids 28 . These model parameters require modification for each polymer-solvent combination, as the complexity of the polymer solution viscosity requires further study 28 .

Separation of dissolved polymer from undissolved material

The undissolved material needs to be separated from the viscous polymer solution. Equipment such as centrifuges, strainers, centrifugal sifters and candle filters can be used for this step. For example, centrifugal filters with a rotary knife/brush with fixed screens can be used in this step. In such equipment, material is fed into the chamber, where the rotating knife/brush pushes the material against the screen. Solvent and finer particles pass through the screen to the next step, while larger undissolved particles are pushed out 30 . As an alternative to centrifugation, filtration is often applied to remove undissolved particles. Filter media must be carefully selected to avoid clogging, often consisting of multiple steps aimed at removing increasingly smaller particles. A common filtration method is candle filters, which use cartridges to filter fluid and trap impurities and particles. These candle filters can often remove smaller-sized impurities (down to a nominal size of 0.5 μm) from the fluid 31 .

Post-cleaning dissolved substances

Additional cleaning steps may be necessary to remove contaminants that are not removed by filtration. Such contaminants often include dissolved dyes, organic and inorganic pigments, residue pigments and other undissolved particles that have passed through the previous filter size. Currently, adsorption is the predominant method to achieve this step. For example, Procter and Gamble has reported using adsorbents selected from metal oxides, covalent organic frameworks, metal-organic frameworks and zeolitic imidazolate frameworks to remove contaminants from the polymer solution 32 . Other adsorbents that can be used include activated carbon, Fuller's earth and/ or quartz sand to remove the colorants and other dissolved additives from the polymer solution 33 . Another approach for post-cleaning is ion exchange; however, it is not yet widely adopted, with rather limited information available 34 .

Precipitation of dissolved polymer and solvent separation

The cleaned polymer is then precipitated from the solution by one of three different approaches: (1) adding antisolvent, (2) changing the temperature or pressure of the solvent or (3) evaporation of the solvent. The selection of the appropriate method in this step depends on the types of polymer and solvent used in the process. If possible, antisolvents should be avoided because they introduce the need for costly separation steps, such as distillation, to separate solvent from antisolvent. The second method is useful if the polymer-solvent interaction is highly dependent on temperature or pressure, and the third option is often preferred when the solvent has a low boiling point. More information on the methods used for various polymer-solvent systems is included in Tables 1 and 2. During this stage, a notable challenge is the gelation of polymers (a process where the precipitated polymer and solvent form a single gel-like phase instead of distinct liquid and solid phases) during precipitation, which leads to complications in subsequent separation of precipitates from the solvent 35 . After precipitation, the precipitated polymer will be separated from the solvent. Researchers have used methods such as decantation 32 and filtration to remove the solvent 36 . Even in complex mixed plastic wastes that contain ten different plastics, laboratory-scale experiments recovered 89 wt% or higher for each polymer 37 .

Solvent recovery and purification

After the separation steps, the undissolved material and precipitated polymer contain certain amounts of solvent. These remaining solvents must be recovered for safety, environmental and economic reasons. Solvents are removed from the solid materials by further drying, often with a vacuum followed by condensing the vapors; however, quantitative studies on this aspect are still lacking. In addition, impurities in the solvent after dissolution can include organic or very fine inorganic color bodies, phthalates, rubbers/gels and smaller fragments of the plastics. Low levels of impurities (less than 0.5 wt%) can be removed by adsorption 32 . The solvent often needs to be purified before reuse to remove the impurities or any antisolvent used in the process. In this case, a distillation step is required to separate the solvent from the antisolvent. In the case of precipitation without antisolvent, the solvent might be recovered by a simpler evaporation step. Although solvent purification technologies have undergone extensive studies, integration of these methodologies into recycling processes presents challenges due to the diverse spectrum of contaminants produced during the process.

Final resin properties

The final purified and extruded resins need to be qualified in the downstream application to make sure the products meet consumer needs. The quality (for example, purity and resulting mechanical and thermal properties) of the recovered resin can be assessed across various categories such as Fourier transform infrared spectra, melt flow index, crystallinity and thermomechanical properties (for example, tensile strength and thermal stability). Studies have shown that the crystallinity 38 and mechanical properties 39 of solvent-extracted polymers are affected by the process. Limited studies on the purity of solventrecovered polymers have been carried out. Recently, Deng et al. used dimethyl isosorbide to extract PET from a PET-PS-PVC-PE-PLA blend. No characteristic peaks associated with additives were observed in the 1 H NMR spectra of the recovered PET, showing the high purity of the recovered polymer 40 . Property changes of the recovered polymers can be attributed to the minor degradation of the polymer chains during the dissolution/precipitation stage, the presence of mixtures of polymer architectures in the input material 41 or the removal/degradation of some additives during the process 42 . Thermodynamics of polymer solubility

Understanding solvent-polymer thermodynamic properties allows for the selection of a suitable solvent and operation conditions for dissolution and precipitation. While some solvents and antisolvents have been identified and tabulated for common polymers 9 , identifying solvents that enable the selective dissolution of a single polymer component from a multicomponent mixture of plastic waste remains a challenge. Figure 2 summarizes four broad categories of theories and computational models that can efficiently guide solvent selection by predicting polymer solubility.

BOX 1

Fundamentals of polymer dissolution

Classical solution theories for polymers focus on the thermodynamics of polymer-solvent mixing, which is governed by the Gibbs free energy of mixing Δ G mix = Δ H mix -T Δ S mix . A polymer and a solvent will mix if Δ G mix < 0. Flory-Huggins theory 47 is the most prominent solution theory and uses a mean-field lattice model to derive equation (1):

∆ G mix = RT [ n 1 ln Φ 1 + n 2 ln Φ 2 + n 1 Φ 2 χ 12 ] (1)

In equation (1), R is the ideal gas constant, T is the temperature, component 1 is the solvent, component 2 is the polymer, ni is the number of moles of component i and ϕ i is the volume fraction of component i . The first two terms account for the combinatorial entropy contribution to Δ S mix , while the third term uses the parameter χ 12 to account for polymer-solvent interactions that contribute to Δ H mix . Solubility parameters are another powerful tool to predict polymer dissolution. Most solubility parameter systems adopt the 'like dissolves like' concept and postulate that materials with similar parameter values will be miscible 56 . Notable examples include the Hildebrand parameter and HSPs 60 . The Hildebrand solubility parameter is derived from a material's cohesive energy density and has reasonable predictive accuracy for non-polar systems, but is limited when there are strong polar or specific interactions such as hydrogen bonds. HSPs extend this concept to three parameters that assess the chemical similarity between a polymer and a solvent on the basis of dispersion ( δ D ), polar ( δ P ) and hydrogen-bonding ( δ H ) interactions. Polymer-solvent interactions are quantified by their virtual distance R a as shown in equation (2).

R 2 a = 4 ( δ solvent D -δ polymer D ) 2 +( δ solvent P -δ polymer P ) 2 +( δ solvent H -δ polymer H ) 2 . ŷ2Ÿ

Each polymer has an interaction radius R 0 ; solvents with R a < R 0 are predicted to dissolve the polymer.

Polymer solution theories and solubility parameters have laid the foundation for polymer dissolution behaviors and solubility predictions (Box 1). Phase diagrams based on Flory-Huggins theory have provided physical insight into the key contributions to the free energy associated with polymer-solvent mixing, Δ G mix , at different temperatures and compositions. However, Flory-Huggins theory is a highly simplified physical model and cannot capture all features of a polymer solution, such as the volume change of mixing, the energetically favorable arrangements of molecule segments, or the composition dependence of the interaction parameter 43 . Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) are more frequently used to guide solvent selection. HSPs have been tabulated for a wide range of polymers and solvents and are a benchmark method for screening solvents to dissolve polymers 44 . While parameter systems such as HSPs have many successful applications, they only qualitatively predict whether a polymer should dissolve in a target solvent, and generally are less accurate at temperatures other than RT.

Recent studies have applied modern molecular models and computational methods to evaluate polymer solubility in various solvent systems. For example, Zhou et al. 45 developed a computational approach to predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities using molecular-scale models. This approach employs molecular dynamics simulations, conformational sampling techniques and the conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) 46 . COSMO-RS is a statistical thermodynamics model that can perform solid-liquid and liquid-liquid equilibrium calculations to calculate polymer solubilities. This approach can rapidly predict quantitative polymer solubilities at different temperatures and in both single- and multicomponent solvent systems. Results using this approach have been tabulated as part of a computational polymer solubility database that includes over 10 polymers and 1,000 solvents at multiple temperatures. The database has paved the way to new studies that integrate solvent screening, TEA, LCA and process optimization 35,43,47 and has successfully been used to guide the design of multistep processes for polymer dissolution and separation in complex mixtures 37 . Following a similar approach to identify new green solvents, Soyemi and Szilvási 48 established a solvent library that contains over 9,000 glycerol derivatives and predicted their physicochemical properties using quantum chemical methods, COSMO-RS and machine learning models. The predicted properties included densities, dipole moments, water solubilities, octanol-water partition coefficients, melting points and HSP values. Potential solvent candidates and dissolution strategies for six common polymers were identified on the basis of the predicted data.

Most recently, machine learning methods have been developed to predict properties relevant to polymer dissolution. Chandrasekaran et al. 49 introduced a solvent/antisolvent classification model using a deep neural network, which Aoki et al. 50 extended to predict temperature-dependent Flory-Huggins interaction parameters. Ethier et al. 51 combined Flory-Huggins theory with neural networks to improve model interpretability and accuracy. Sanchez-Lengeling et al. 52 introduced the Gaussian process HSP, a Bayesian method for HSP determination. Kurotani et al. 53 used an in-phase deep neural network to predict solubility parameters. Kern et al. 54 proposed fingerprints of polymers and solvents for room-temperature solubility prediction. These studies largely focus on qualitatively classifying solvents and antisolvents for target polymers or predicting solubility parameters, but a research gap remains in developing machine learning models to quantitatively predict polymer solubilities. Training these models also requires large-scale and high-quality data on polymer solubility, requiring the development of standardized, high-throughput experimental solubility measurement approaches 55 .

This previous discussion has largely focused on polymer solubility at ambient pressure. Another important factor that influences both the enthalpy of mixing (Δ H mix ) and the entropy of mixing (Δ S mix ) is solvent density 56,57 . In a homogeneous solution, the contribution of pairwise interactions to Δ H mix is roughly proportional to the density, which approximately determines the number of interactions per volume. Increasing solvent density for a system with favorable polymer-solvent interactions can thus increase polymer solubility 57 . However, if there are large differences in the densities of the solvent and polymer, the corresponding change in volume upon mixing also contributes to Δ S mix (ref. 56). Unlike the combinatorial entropy, which always promotes mixing, the non-combinatorial contribution to Δ S mix due to this density difference disfavors mixing by reducing the entropy of the lower-density (typically solvent) component. This behavior leads to phase separation at temperatures above the lower critical solution temperature 56 ; at high temperatures, the solvent density decreases to a much greater degree than the polymer density and the non-combinatorial entropy is highly unfavorable. The impact of solvent density on polymer solubility has motivated interest in supercritical fluids as solvents for polymer dissolution 58 . Unlike typical solvents, which are nearly incompressible, the density of a supercritical fluid can be varied from gas-like to liquid-like by manipulating the pressure. Increasing the pressure of a supercritical fluid such that its density approaches that of a target polymer will drive dissolution by reducing the unfavorable non-combinatorial entropy 57 . Pressure variations can also lead to differences in solubility for polymers with similar chemical properties but distinct densities (for example, low-density PE (LDPE) versus high-density PE (HDPE)) 59 . The addition of pressure as a 'knob' to tune the properties of supercritical fluids has motivated the use of solvents with low critical temperatures and pressures, such as carbon dioxide, ethylene propane and butane, to dissolve and purify polymers; one such example is the PureCycle process (discussed below).

Together, the exciting developments in physics-based and datadriven predictions of polymer solubility support the ability of modern computational methods to screen large sets of solvents, including new solvents for which experimental data may not be available. Ongoing challenges include treating variations in polymer solubility associated with molecular weight, crystallinity 60 and the presence of small-molecule components, such as common additives, pigments or contaminants in plastic waste 61 . Predictive methods for solubility are also less established for supercritical fluids than for typical solvents. Current methods rely on equation-of-state models, such as the perturbed chain-statistical associating fluid theory equation of state 62 , and some recent methods have developed machine learning methods or extended COSMO-RS models appropriate for predicting solubility in supercritical carbon dioxide 63 , but more generalizable methods are needed. Other challenges include predicting solution properties other than solubility, such as viscosity, that will influence the design of solvent-mediated recycling methods 28 . For example, thermodynamic models to understand solubility are also useful for understanding the thermodynamics of precipitation as a method to recover dissolved polymer resins from solution. However, polymer crystallization during precipitation depends upon the thermodynamics of nucleation, which remains challenging to predict 64 . The kinetics of polymer crystallization during precipitation can likewise greatly affect the properties of the recycled materials. For example, crystallization temperature, cooling rate and the application of high shear strain are typical factors to control the crystal structure and morphology of polymers 64 . Therefore, while polymer solubility is a critical factor in solvent selection, both thermodynamic and kinetic factors need to be considered in process design. Because the thermodynamic properties of solvents, polymers and impurities strongly influence the operating conditions of the recycling process and its overall economic and environmental performance, another important challenge is the co-design of solvents and of the recycling process (particularly when diverse polymers and impurities are present in the input waste feedstock) 65 .

Commercial activities in dissolution-based recycling

Summary of current dissolution-based plastic recycling plants Table 2 summarizes several pilot- and industrial-scale dissolutionbased recycling technologies that have been reported, including their nameplate capacities, locations, required feedstocks, products and the solvents and dissolution conditions. The current operational status of each of these facilities is not clear.

CreaSolv

CreaSolv is a plastic recycling process developed by the Fraunhofer Institute for Process Engineering and Packaging IVV 66,67 . According to their official website, the process involves solvent selection, targeted polymer dissolution, removal of contaminants from the solution, precipitation of the polymer, drying and final product processing 68 . The process flow diagram is summarized in Fig. 1a. CreaSolv did not disclose the specific types of solvent they use for their process, apart from defining HSP domains in their patent series 69 . As shown in Table 1, CreaSolv has three small industrial facilities or pilot plants that produce (1) PE from sachets, (2) PS from foam waste and (3) PVC from floor covering.

APK Newcycling

APK Newcycling operates an 8,000-ton-per-year plant in Merseburg, Germany, that has been in operation since June 2018 70 . Their process extracts PE and PAs from post-industrial multilayer plastic wastes. According to one of the patents published in 2022, the process involves the shredding and categorization of feedstock, washing and separation through density differences, dissolution of targeted polymer, solid and liquid separation using a centrifuge, cross-flow filtration with a membrane for purification, flash evaporation and devolatilization for polymer extraction, and extrusion to produce final product (see Fig. 1b) 71 . The company has partnered with Coperion to incorporate ZSK twin-screw extruder technology into its process, ensuring efficient polymer devolatilization and extrusion 72 .

Polystyvert

Polystyvert has demonstrated a 600-ton-per-year plant since August 2018 in Montreal, Canada, focusing on the recovery of PS 73 . According to a patent published in 2023, the process uses PS waste, such as foam packaging, as feedstock 74 .The material is dissolved in p -cymene, followed by filtration and precipitation using a non-polar antisolvent such as heptane or hexane. The precipitated PS undergoes several washing and separation steps to remove impurities, after which it is dried and extruded. The process flow diagram can be found in Fig. 1c. One of the key innovations lies in its solubilization stage, where the solvent is also able to dissolve various non-polar additives such as hexabromocyclododecane and silicone oils. The dissolution equipment utilizes a metallic grid to help push the expanded PS into the solvent, which further reduces the dissolution time 75 . To advance the commercial scale-up of this technology, Polystyvert partnered with INEOS Styrolution in 2021 74 .

PureCycle

PureCycle Technologies is commercializing a proprietary process developed by Procter and Gamble that uses supercritical butane to recycle PP plastic waste into high-quality resin. The company worked with KraussMaffei, a company that specializes in degassing extruders, to upscale its process 76 . A simplified process flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1d ref. 32. The process begins with preprocessing feedstock. According to a report published by Leidos, the preprocessing for high-purity PP wastes involves feedstock de-baling, shredding, metal removal, granulating and agglomeration 77 . After preprocessing, the feedstock is fed into an extruder to melt the material and remove solid impurities. The melted PP is then fed into a light extraction column, to extract and remove light, soluble impurities. The solvent is then directed to a flash tank for separation. The remaining PP-solvent mixture enters a mixing column to fully dissolve the PP. Subsequently, the mixture moves into a settler, and the heavy phase is conveyed out of the settler for scrap storage. Additionally, the PP-solvent mixture from the settler passes through candle filters to remove insoluble solid impurities, after which adsorption columns are utilized to remove remaining impurities. The PP solution is then reheated to further remove the solvent. The PP undergoes further pelletization for storage or reprocessing as needed.

STRAP

STRAP is building a 200-ton-per-year pilot system, which can process mixed plastic wastes including multilayer plastic to extract highquality resin, in the United States 30 . Figure 1e shows the simplified process flow diagram of STRAP. After the feedstock is preprocessed, it is selectively dissolved and undergoes hot filtration. The undissolved material is discharged and dried to recover solvent, while the solution undergoes hot adsorption to remove small-sized impurities. The solution is then cooled to allow precipitation, after which the precipitated polymer is separated and dried for resin production and the solvent is purified to be reused in the process. Impact of dissolution-based recycling on quality of recycling

Dissolution-based recycling processes have the potential to provide economic and environmental benefits by reducing resource consumption and improving the quality of recycling. Therefore, next to technical quality of the outputs, TEA and LCA studies play a vital role in assessing and guiding the design of these technologies.

Technical quality of recycled materials

In several studies, solvent treatment did not significantly affect the mechanical, rheological or thermal properties of the final polymer 78,79 . However, in some cases, slight differences in the molecular weight, thermal properties and melt processability of the recovered polymer were observed due to possible degradation or cross-contamination with other components present in the system 80,81 . Another factor that can influence the polymer properties after recycling is solvent retention, which can change the melt behavior of the polymer by reducing its viscosity and which can affect the final use (for example, in food-grade applications) 81 . Additionally, differences in the process design, such as using different dissolution solvents and processing temperatures, can influence the polymer properties 25 . Property comparisons are important to understand whether dissolution-based antisolvent, cooling or other. A positive percentage represents an increase in GHG emissions while a negative percentage represents a decrease in GHG emissions. All referenced values can also be found in Table 3.

recycling processes can produce high-quality polymers, and additional attributes to characterize include tensile strength, flexural strength, impact strength, membrane performance and polymer solution characterization (density, refractive index, viscosity) 25 . The materials recovered via dissolution-based processes can have potential applications in packaging films, membranes, glues, paint additives, natural/fiber composites and textiles, depending on the recovered material and its properties. Therefore, dissolution-based processes can help produce high-quality products from diverse feedstocks that are hard to recycle (Table 2) and be used as a separation technology for multicomponent complex waste. Some limitations include separating mixtures with specific polymers that are challenging to dissolve (for example, PET and nylons). Previous approaches have overcome this issue by leaving the challenging component (for example, PET) at the end of the separation sequence and recovering it as a residual solid without being dissolved 25 . Two other challenges are the separation of different grades of the same polymer and the removal of impurities such as dyes, which impact the color and final use of the recycled materials. Often, in the case of these more challenging separations, costly process steps such as elevated temperatures, pressures or added separation steps are required to achieve high-quality resins 13,82-85 . More research is needed to outline the tradeoffs between product quality and process costs. Demonstrating the food safety of polymers recovered from dissolution recycling also needs further research. Nevertheless, at least on a theoretical basis, dissolution-based recycling has the potential to overcome these challenges and produce virgin-like resins.

Economic analysis

Academic and industry reports have shown that the economic feasibility of dissolution-based processes depends strongly on the precipitation method, feedstock type, recovered polymers, economies of scale (plant capacity) and solvents (type and recycling rate) 13,82,84,85 . Table 3 summarizes key variables for different processes in various stages of development. The processes were differentiated by name and precipitation method including antisolvent (A), cooling (C) or other (O), which comprise a combination of methods. These data are primarily based on laboratory studies, rather than on commercial data, which are difficult to obtain. While estimates of economic and environmental impacts from laboratory data can have limited accuracy, comparing different processes and studies helps identify the main impact drivers and general trends.

Table 3 presents the capital costs for different processes at different plant capacities. These costs are heavily dependent on the required type of equipment. A trend of similar costs in processes with equal capacities and assumptions can be seen (for example, antisolvent-PET and cooling-PET) 86 . However, the technology that uses antisolvent as a precipitation technique results in higher capital costs. The same trend can be observed comparing STRAP-A, which uses antisolvent, and STRAP-B, which uses cooling 87 . These studies have reported that the need for distillation steps to separate the solvent/antisolvent mixture and the required process utilities lead to higher capital and operating costs. In addition, it has been reported that the solvent/polymer ratio and non-feedstock inputs (mainly solvent) are large contributors to process economics 87 . Therefore, high polymer concentrations with high solvent recycling rates are typically necessary to achieve profitability.

Feedstock type and composition are also key economic drivers; some processes may have to purchase feedstock with prices depending on the quality and availability, while others may receive a tipping fee for accepting waste 86 . To date, there is no clear trend between feedstock quality and cost. Some companies, such as PureCycle, have invested in sorting technologies to source ideal feedstocks, but this does not mean that high-quality low-cost feedstocks such as post-industrial waste are not available 88 .

Feedstock composition plays a key role because prices of recovered materials can vary (for instance, HDPE may sell for US$1 kg -1 and EVOH may sell for US$8 kg -1 ) 89,90 . These differences can drive process profitability and design (number of solvent washes to recover all polymers or only the most valuable components). It is also important to highlight that certain polymers require higher energy inputs to dissolve (due to unfavorable thermodynamics), and contaminated feedstocks may need prewashing and other purification steps 91 . Solvent choice impacts energy requirements for solvent removal and affects product use (for example, only some solvents may be suitable for food contact applications).

Many studies report that dissolution-based recycling can produce high-quality recycled resins at prices competitive with those of virgin polymers (using the minimum selling price (MSP) as a metric) 86,87,91 . The recovered resins are typically cleaner than mechanically recycled resins and more valuable than the oils or monomers produced by chemical recycling, offering a competitive advantage over other recycling methods 84 . This suggests that dissolution-based recycling can be profitable despite initial capital expenditures, if there is sufficient volume to achieve favorable economies of scale. The larger commercial processes aim to recycle at 20,000-50,000 metric tons per year 70,77 ; this is the current best indicator for necessary scale, but operational data sre lacking. It is important to note the significant uncertainty in current academic and industrial preliminary estimations, which require more detailed studies in pilot systems.

Feedstock selection can have a large impact on capital costs for dissolution recycling plants and should be carefully considered during the commercialization of this new technology. Cleaner feedstocks such as post-industrial multilayer waste require fewer preprocessing and contaminant removal steps, which can considerably lower capital expenses. Similarly, colorless plastic waste may require fewer treatment steps and save costs. If available, plastic waste containing only two polymers presents an opportunity for plants to recover two products with a single solvent, improving the plant's economic efficiency. If possible, early commercial solvent-based recycling plants should focus on 'ideal' feedstocks first, moving to more complicated waste streams as the technology is better tested and understood.

Environmental impact analysis

The environmental impacts of dissolution-based processes have been quantified by various LCA methodologies. Most studies only report the climate change impact or equivalent greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of the process 82,92 . However, other environmental metrics, such as resource use, water use, land use, toxicity, material circularity and others, can also be relevant, as the single metric of climate change is likely insufficient in determining all environmental impacts of a process 9 . For instance, modern engineered landfills are the most used plastic waste management process, and generate minimal GHG emissions, although their environmental impacts related to soil and groundwater pollution are substantial 9 . Additionally, current LCA approaches have not standardized the selection of system boundaries 93 . This lack of consistency hinders the comparison between approaches and can result in inconsistent or misleading conclusions 94 .

Table 3 provides a summary of the climate change impact and key drivers reported by different references. Most studies use a cradle-togate approach, and depending on the type of waste (post-industrial or post-consumer) some approaches include pretreatment 9,86 . A common environmental impact driver in the processes that use antisolvent is steam, which is required to separate the solvent-antisolvent mixture via distillation. The climate change impacts reported with the virgin production alternative are compared in Fig. 3. It is important to note that these studies may use different assumptions, and reported values may become outdated with updates to technology or LCA methodology. It can be found that, in general, the processes with a higher environmental impact than the virgin alternative use antisolvent as a precipitation method. The specific increase in GHG emissions appears in Fig. 3 as a positive percentage highlighted in red. This impact is a direct result of the energy required to separate the solvent and antisolvent and to recycle them. On the other hand, the processes that use cooling or other methods have a lower climate change impact than virgin polymer production because of lower energy requirements. These methods also include solvent recovery and recycling, but the energy demand is lower because there are no solvent mixtures (see the above discussion for more details on solvent recovery). These results again highlight the need to identify solvents that lead to favorable process designs and operating conditions. The lowest emissions were reported by the company Polystyvert, followed by Solvent-based PLA and STRAP-PP I. Some important characteristics of the Polystyvert-commercial process are the use of low operating temperatures, an essential oil as solvent and the removal of the flame retardant hexabromocyclododecane 95 . However, there are no publications available that outline their LCA assumptions and methodology. The other processes with low reported impacts recover only one component and do not use antisolvents for the precipitation. Previous studies reported the solid/liquid ratio and process energy consumption as the main contributors to GHG impacts and identified that high solvent recycling rates are essential to reduce emissions 9 . Furthermore, the environmental benefits of the different dissolutionbased processes are a function of the material that is treated and the number of recovered polymers 42,48 . All commercial processes report a reduction in climate change impact and use multicomponent waste as feedstock 67,77 .

As shown in Fig. 3, reported dissolution processes without antisolvents have a GHG impact of approximately 1-2 kg CO 2 -equivalent per kg plastic produced, roughly 50% lower than virgin resin production. This is also lower than typical reported emissions for other advanced recycling methods such as glycolysis or pyrolysis 96-98 . In general, other impact categories such as energy consumption follow a similar trend 82,84 . However, comparison across analysis methods is challenging, as factors such as energy mix and waste credits can have a major impact, further highlighting the need for consistent LCA approaches.

Almost all chemical processes have economic and environmental trade-offs; however, the evaluated dissolution-based recycling processes agree on common drivers for cost and GHG emissions. For instance, the need for high solvent recycling rates and cooling as a precipitation method has been consistently shown to lead to economic and environmental benefits (mainly focusing on GHG emissions). Of course, solvent consumption is also related to the polymer concentration used in the system. While reducing solvent use lowers environmental impact, it also increases solution viscosity, and maintaining a viable working viscosity takes precedence over minimizing solvent consumption. There is still significant uncertainty in current TEA and LCA approaches; therefore, these conclusions may change as dissolution-based technologies evolve and other environmental metrics are evaluated.

Challenges for commercialization

It is unknown if commercial dissolution-based technologies are operating at full capacity. Several of the facilities have been reported to have operational challenges, which are to be expected for pioneer process plants. For instance, a PVC recycling plant in Europe that was designed to recycle 10,000 ton yr -1 of PVC ceased to operate in 2018 68 . Publicly available information indicated that this closure was partly due to the new legislation that identified the phthalates used in their process being hazardous 99 . Another 49,000-ton-per-year plant built in North America is currently operating at lower than its design capacity 100 . It is thus clear that dissolution-based recycling still has several challenges, often related to chemical engineering. First, a solvent must be chosen that only dissolves the targeted polymer and only minimally dissolves any of the other polymers, the pigments or any additives. The undissolved solids are then removed by filtration or centrifugation from a viscous polymer solution without clogging. Depending on the polymer, the dissolution temperature can also be relatively high (for example, >130 °C for polymers such as PP and PET) 45,101 , which means that the processes, equipment, tubing and so on need to withstand high-temperature solvent environments, while every cold spot can induce polymer precipitation and clogging. After the solid-liquid separation, the dissolved impurities should be removed, for example by an adsorption bed. However, adsorption from mostly apolar solvents of additives is not well studied 61 , compared with, for example, adsorption in wastewater treatment, in which the process starts from a polar matrix (water). Afterwards, the polymer must be precipitated from the solution, which could cause gel formation if not well operated 35 . Avoiding gel formation and forming good polymer precipitates is a challenge in dissolution-based recycling. Limiting solvent entrapped in the precipitates reduces the need to remove high amounts of solvent from the resulting gel. The polymer has to be dried to the appropriate level (typically in the ppm range). Dissolution-based recycling thus requires a completely different plant design compared with traditional mechanical recycling plants, as dissolution plants could deal with volatile/ flammable solvents 102 . Therefore, correct safety/hazard engineering controls need to be built into any system. Further details regarding the chemical engineering challenges associated with the commercialization of dissolution-based plastic recycling are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Key recommendations for the future

Dissolution-based plastic recycling technologies have shown considerable potential in producing high-quality resins from diverse plastic waste streams. The thermodynamics of pure polymer-solvent interactions are well documented, and TEA and LCA data indicate that these methods are potentially cost-effective and environmentally sustainable, with several companies now developing industrial plants.

However, several challenges must be addressed to advance this technology. (1) Preprocessing and sorting: enhanced techniques for sorting plastic waste are crucial to optimize the recycling process. (2) Additives in plastics: research is needed to better understand what happens to additives during dissolution and how to remove additives if desired. (3) Polymer solution properties: improved predictions and management of polymer solution properties, such as viscosity, are essential for optimizing the dissolution and precipitation stage of the process. (4) Solvent reuse and impurity accumulation: investigating the impact of impurity build-up in reused solvents and develop methods to mitigate their effects is vital. (5) Recovered-resin properties: further study is required to understand and enhance the properties of recovered resins for various applications.

Some of the above challenges can be addressed in part by policy. For example, improved sorting practices can be required, or dangerous additives can be outlawed. However, many of the challenges related to dissolution recycling are chemical engineering challenges. By addressing these challenges through targeted research and development, dissolution-based plastic recycling technologies can be optimized and integrated into the broader plastic recycling landscape, providing a sustainable solution for managing plastic waste, and making them a key solution for sustainable plastic waste management.

Deinking of Water-Based Ink Printing from Plastic Film Using Nonionic Surfactants

Hatice Gecol a, *, John F. Scamehorn b , Sherril D. Christian b , Brian P . Grady b , c

and Fred E. Riddell

a Chemical Engineering, University of Nevada-Reno, Reno, Nevada 89557, b Institute for Applied Surfactant Research, University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma 73019, and c Kimberly-Clark Corporation, Neenah, Wisconsin 54956

ABSTRACT: When plastic film packaging is processed for reuse, residual ink colors the polymer and makes the polymer less stiff, weaker, and denser than the original material. These problems can be avoided if the printing is removed from the plastic film surface. In this study, a commercial polyethylene film with water-based ink printing was deinked (the ink was removed) using nonionic surfactants under a variety of conditions, and the effect of some parameters related to the deinking process were quantified and optimized. Nonylphenol polyethoxylate,  ethoxylated  alcohol  at  a  pH  of  10,  and ethoxylated amine at either acidic, neutral, or basic pH level were identified to be effective at deinking. The hydrophiliclipophilic balance (HLB) value and the cloud point are useful parameters for characterizing the effectiveness of nonionic surfactants. For optimal deinking, the HLB of the nonionic surfactants should be as small as possible or the cloud point as low as possible without the deinking temperature substantially  exceeding  the  cloud  point.  Information  related  to scaleup of the process was also developed. Soaking plastic film in surfactant solution prior to mechanical agitation significantly decreased the needed agitation time to achieve a given level of deinking. Deinking decreases as the plastic/solution ratio  (consistency)  increases,  and  cutting  plastic  film  into smaller pieces improves the deinking at moderate consistency. Increasing agitation speed also enhances the deinking. Experiments performed with pilot-sized paper deinking apparatuses demonstrated that deinking of plastic film using surfactants is technically feasible.

Replacement of plastic in packaging by other materials such as paper, foil, and glass has been considered as an alternative to reduce plastic waste, but this would result in a 400% increase in the weight of waste, a 200% increase in energy consumption in making the alternatives, and a 210% increase in cost (2). Plastic packaging improves product security  and  reduces  spoilage  and  contamination  of  food products. The market demand for plastic film packaging in the United States is projected to grow at an annual rate of 3.1%, which will also increase the amount of plastic film requiring disposal or recycle (5). Limitations in the technology of sorting, cleaning, and reformulating the recyclate limit the plastic recycling rate. Since the source is better defined, in-plant plastic recycling is more successful than recycle of post-consumer plastic. However, if the plastic film is printed, re-extrusion of this plastic results in a product that can only be used to make low-value colored products such as trash cans, pipes, and signposts. Repelletized colored resins can crack owing to gases associated with ink decomposition (3,6,7). Effective film deinking technology could permit reuse of the polymer to produce clear films. Possible alternatives for plastic film deinking include using either organic solvents or surfactants. However, surfactants have an advantage over organic solvents since the former are more environmentally compatible (6).

Polymers used for films include low-density polyethylene (LDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polyethylene terephthalate, ethylene vinyl acetate, polyvinyl chloride, and polypropylene. The highest-volume resin used is LDPE because of its toughness, sealability, inertness, and action as a moisture barrier. LDPE has greater clarity and flexibility than HDPE, making it particularly valuable for clear films. Most plastic packaging is made of either LDPE, HDPE, or a mixture of LDPE and HDPE (8-10).

The plastic film surface is almost always treated with one of several alternative surface treatment processes before printing to increase the surface energy of the plastic surface and enhance ink wettability. These surface treatments include flame treatment, corona discharge, plasma treatment, and ultraviolet treatment. Treatment with corona discharge is  common  and  involves  application  of  high  voltage (~10,000 V) to an electrode that is positioned a short distance from the plastic film. The air between the electrode and the plastic is ionized, and this corona of ionized air oxidizes the surface (11). Water-based or oil-based (solventbased) ink is used for printing the plastic film surface with flexographic or gravure printing processes. Water-based inks occupy a large and increasing fraction of plastic film inks since environmental regulations are restricting the percentage of volatile organic compounds from printing press emissions and the use of water-based inks can reduce capital costs (12-15).

In this paper, the use of nonionic surfactants of varying structure for plastic film deinking is investigated. Nonionic surfactants are often less expensive and more biodegradable than cationic and amphoteric surfactants. The effects of important parameters are quantified by simple soak and shake experiments. Then two larger-scale apparatuses (a pulper and a flotation cell) are used to simulate pilot-scale deinking.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES

Our  previous  studies  indicated  that  water-based  ink printing could be partially removed from plastic film surfaces with water at pH of 11 or 12 under mechanical action, presumably because the ink binder (acidic acrylate) has a higher  solubility  at  high  pH  (6).  Aqueous  solutions  of cationic, amphoteric, or nonionic surfactant were identified to be effective deinking agents at pH levels less than 11. Cationic surfactant (i.e., hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide and hexadecyl pyridinium chloride) is as effective at deinking, showing high efficiency at surfactant concentrations both above and below the critical micelle concentration (CMC) over a pH range of 5 to 12. Amphoteric surfactant (i.e., dimethyl dodecylamine oxide) was found to be effective above the CMC over a wide pH range. Nonionic Materials. Nonylphenol polyethoxylate (NPEO 10 , trade name Igepal CO-660) was obtained from Rhodia (Cranbury, NJ). Ethoxylated alcohols (AEO X , trade name Witconol SN-50, SN-70, SN-90, SN-120, 610-30, and TD-100) and ethoxylated amines, which are primary tallow amines (AMEO X+Y , trade name Varonic T-202, T-205, T-210, and T-215), were from the Witco Corporation (Greenwich, CT). Some characteristics of these surfactants are given in Table 1. All surfactants were used as received. The water was double deionized.

The plastic film was composed of 70% LDPE and 30% HDPE. It was reversibly printed with a pattern composed of multicolor water-based ink (black, white, purple, pink, and orange) by flexographic printing after surface treatment with corona discharge. The printed pattern was then coated with white ink to give an opaque appearance and to protect the ink layers (6). This film was commercial plastic packaging supplied by the Kimberly-Clark Corporation (Neenah, WI). The clear and the printed parts of the plastic film were segregated for this study, and the clear parts of plastic film were used as a standard for the comparison with deinked plastic film strips.

Methods. All glassware was cleaned with a regular lab detergent  and  then  acid-washed  with  Nochromix ® solution (Godax Laboratories Inc., Takoma Park, MD) for at least an hour. Surfactant solutions were always prepared fresh with double-deionized water for each experiment, and the pH level of the aqueous surfactant solution was adjusted immediately with sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid before the deinking experiment was conducted. A representative sample printed with multicolors of water-based ink (white, black, orange, purple, and pink) was cut from the printed area of the plastic packaging to the size of 1 × 1 in. unless otherwise specified and soaked in the surfactant solutions. The effect of process parameters was studied in experiments performed with 20 mL of surfactant solutions including 20 irregularly shaped porcelain beads in 30-mL glass vials. The glass vials were placed in a water bath at a monitored temperature when the effect of soaking prior to agitation was studied. These samples were agitated for varied time periods with a portable  reciprocating  action  shaker  (Model  R-2;  New Brunswick Scientific, Edison, NJ) at the speed of 350 strokes per minute with a 1-in. stroke length. After agitation, plastic film strips were taken out of the washing bath, rinsed with deionized water, and air dried. A shaker was placed in an incubator (Fisher Scientific) when temperatures other than room temperature were used. In addition, several experiments to demonstrate scaleup were performed with 2 L of surfactant solutions by using either a Denver Laboratory Model D-12 Flotation Machine with the attrition scrubber kit (Denver Equipment Company, Denver, NC) or a TMI D-111 disintegrator (Testing Machines Inc., Islandia, NY). The Denver flotation cell (Fig. 1) is commonly used for pilot-scale paper deinking studies to separate ink from paper fibers after pulping. In these flotation deinking experiments, ink particles attach to air bubbles and are collected as froth from the top of the solution. For this work, the Denver flotation cell was converted to a scrubber by removing the air valve and replacing the impeller with a one-piece double-attrition propeller. The agitation speed of this machine can be adjusted between 500 and 3500 rpm. The TMI disintegrator (Fig. 2) is a pulper used for pilot-scale paper deinking to disintegrate waste paper. Besides agitation, the TMI disintegrator (Fig. 2) provides a beating effect due to the attached spiral fins on the internal part of the pulping tank. The agitation speed of the disintegrator is limited to 3000 rpm. After deinking experiments  with  these  machines,  the  washing  bath  was drained, and deinked plastic film strips were rinsed several times with water and dried in a vacuum oven overnight.

Each deinked plastic film sample was first visually evaluated and then analyzed using a HunterLab UltraScan™ Spectrocolorimeter system (Hunter Associates Laboratory, Inc., Reston, VA) in regular transmission mode. The HunterLab UltraScan Spectrocolorimeter system consists of an UltraScan optical sensor (SN-7834) with a sensor interface unit and an IBM computer including data evaluation software. In the regular transmittance mode, the intensity of the light passing directly through the plastic film is measured as a function of wavelength. The total color difference (DE*) between the standard (clear plastic film) and the deinked sample was determined at the chosen standard illuminant (D65, representing daylight with a correlated color temperature of 6500 K) and observer (10° standard observer). An average value from six measurements for each sample is reported. The lower the value of DE*, the better the deinking. More details about this procedure are given in Reference 6.

FIG. 1. Denver flotation cell (Denver Equipment Co., Denver, NC).

Clear plastic film, printed plastic film, and deinked plastic film were separately extruded either as pellets or as a film with a KL-100 Killion Extruder at 232°C. Processing temperatures of 160-240°C for LDPE and 200-280°C for HDPE are recommended (9). Cross-sectional areas of the re-extruded pellets were analyzed with a transmittance electron microscope (TEM; JEOL 2000 FX, Peabody, MA) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer attached to the TEM. Samples for  the  TEM  were  prepared  with  600  Ultramicrotomy attached with FS-100 Cryosectioning (Microstar Technologies, Huntsville, TX) at -120°C and picked up with 200mesh nickel or copper folding grids.

FIG. 2. TMI disintegrator (Testing Machines Inc., Islandia, NY).

For stress-strain property measurements, re-extruded film strips were first pressed with a Carver M Press (Carver Inc., Wabash, IN) including a Carver 2101 heating plate at approximately 150°C in order to achieve uniform thickness and then cut with an ASTM standard D-1708 die (16). The samples were stretched with an Instron TT-C-L tensile tester (Instron Co., Canton, MA), which had a computerized data acquisition system, at a rate of 0.51 cm/min at room temperature. Measurements were repeated three times for reextruded clear, printed, or deinked film. The differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) data for pellets produced from clear,  printed,  and  deinked  plastic  films  were  obtained using  a  liquid  nitrogen-cooled  Mettler-Toledo  DSC820 (Columbus, OH). Samples were placed in 40-µL aluminum pans. Thermograms were recorded from 20 to -150°C and from -150 C to 150°C at a heating rate of -10 and 5°C/min, respectively. From the DSC curve, the melting temperature (T m ) and the heat of fusion, which is the melting peak area, were obtained. The crystallinity of the polymer was calculated by dividing the measured heat of fusion by the heat of fusion of 100% crystalline polyethylene (290 J/g). Polymer produced from the printed part of the plastic film had 8.6 wt% ink; therefore, the crystallinity of this sample was corrected by dividing the calculated crystallinity by the mass fraction of polymer (0.914).

The  densities  of  the  re-extruded  plastic  films  were measured  according  to  ASTM  standard  D-1505  (17)  by use of the DC-4 Techne Density Gradient apparatus (Techne Incorporated, Princeton, NJ). This test method was based on observing the level of plastic pellets in a density gradient liquid column and then comparing it with standard glass floats of known density. An isopropanol/water (50:50 vol%) mixture was used as the liquid in the density gradient column.

The procedure of ISO 1065, method A-Determination of the cloud point in aqueous solution (18), was followed for the measurement of the cloud points of AMEO 2 , AMEO 5 , AMEO 10 , and AMEO 15 . This method does not monitor the effect of pH on the cloud point. For this study, the pH level of the surfactant solution was adjusted between 4 and 11 using sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid. A surfactant solution (15 mL of 1 wt%) in a test tube was placed in a water bath filled with ethylene glycol. The temperature was increased to 100°C and then decreased until the cloudy appearance of the solution disappeared. This temperature was recorded as the cloud point of the surfactant.

To determine whether AMEO 5 protonates, titration (60 mL of 5 mM, prepared based on the maximum value of its molecular weight) was performed with 0.25 N Fisher-brand sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid. Eppendorf micropipettes, 100 and 1000 µL, were used to add a defined amount of acid or base into the surfactant solution, and the pH of the solution was monitored with an Accumet model 50 pH meter (Fisher Scientific, Fair Lawn, NJ). Surfactant solution was first titrated with hydrochloric acid to pH 2 or with sodium hydroxide to pH 12. The solution titrated to pH 12 was back-titrated with hydrochloric acid to pH 2. A similar titration was also performed using water for comparison of titration curves.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Quantification of deinking process parameters. Deinking involves the removal of, first, white ink coating and then colored ink layers from plastic film. Surfactants NPEO 10 , AEO X , and AMEO X+Y (some characteristics of these are given in Table 1) were chosen as model nonionic surfactants for this study. The solution of NPEO 10 was identified to be effective at deinking above the CMC at room temperature and pH 10 after 4 h of agitation (6). There is substantial controversy over the toxicity and environmental impact of the NPEO X class of nonionic surfactants (19-22).

FIG. 3. The total color difference (DE*) between the deinked plastic film using either NPEO 10 , AEO 5 , or AMEO 5 and clear plastic film as a function of  pH. NPEO, nonylphenol polyethoxylate; AEO, ethoxylated alcohol; AMEO, ethoxylated amine.

Ethoxylated alcohols are nonionic surfactants that are extensively used in the paper-deinking processes (23). They are relatively inexpensive and exhibit excellent wetting and detergency properties, especially for oily soil removal (24). An ethoxylated alcohol, AEO 5 (whose properties are shown in Table 1), was tested in deinking of plastic packaging at a concentration of 25 mM, at room temperature, at pH from 3 to 12. The resulting DE* values are presented in Figure 3, and a decrease in DE* values indicates a decrease in printed ink residue on plastic film, i.e., an increase in the amount of deinking. As seen in Figure 3, the deinking level achieved with AEO 5 is comparable to that achieved with NPEO 10 . No deinking was achieved with AEO 5 at acidic and neutral pH levels, but the deinking process started at basic pH level and increased with increasing pH. Therefore, ethoxylated alcohols can be effective deinking agents at a process pH of 10 or greater.

FIG. 4. Titration of AMEO 5 . For abbreviation see Figure 3.

FIG. 5. DE* between the deinked plastic film using 25 mM NPEO 10 [room temperature (room T) and pH = 10] and clear plastic film as a function of agitation time. For abbreviations see Figure 3.

Ethoxylated amines are classified as nonionic surfactants, but they behave as cationic surfactants in acid solution and at low ethylene oxide levels owing to the presence of a nitrogen atom (24,25). For example, the titration of AMEO 5 with hydrochloric acid, shown in Figure 4, demonstrates  that  AMEO 5 protonates under acidic conditions. Ethoxylated amines exhibit good emulsification and wetting properties at both acidic and alkaline pH levels, and are used as dye leveling agents in the textile industry and as dispersing agents for pigments in oil-based paints (23,24). The AMEO 5 (properties shown in Table 1) was tested for the deinking of plastic film. Experiments were performed with 5 mM AMEO 5 at room temperature by varying the pH levels from 3 to 12. Unlike NPEO 10 and AEO 5 , AMEO 5 (Fig. 3) accomplishes deinking at acidic, neutral, and basic pH levels, and residual ink on plastic film decreases with an increase in acidity or alkalinity. This result is comparable to that obtained  with  cationic  surfactant  (6).  Hence,  ethoxylated amines also can be used effectively for deinking of plastic film over a wide pH range.

The effect of agitation period on deinking was investigated with or without soaking the plastic strips in surfactant solution prior to agitation. Experiments were performed with 25 mM NPEO 10 at room temperature at a pH of 10. Agitation time was varied from 0 to 240 min. The resulting DE* values are presented in Figure 5. The residual ink on film decreases as the agitation time increases from 0 to 180 min and stabilizes at 180 min when the plastic film strips are agitated without soaking them in the surfactant solution prior to the agitation step. However, pre-soaking the plastic film in a surfactant solution for 24 h significantly decreases the residual ink on film for a given agitation time, but the value at which the DE* stabilizes at long times is identical in the two cases.

FIG. 6. DE* between the deinked plastic film using 25 mM NPEO 10 (pH = 10) and clear plastic film as a function of agitation time at varied temperatures (plastic film was not soaked in surfactant solution prior to agitation). For abbreviations see Figures 3 and 5.

The effect of temperature on the deinking process was also investigated with NPEO 10 and the resulting DE* values are presented in Figures 6 (samples were agitated without pre-soaking) and 7 (plastic film was pre-soaked in surfactant solution for 24 h). Experiments were conducted with 25 mM NPEO 10 at a pH of 10. As seen in Figure 6, the residual ink on film decreases as the temperature is increased from room temperature (~25°C) to 60°C, but less ink is removed when the temperature is increased to 75°C. Nonionic surfactants become turbid when they are heated to the cloud point, a temperature at which the solution separates into two phases, the micelle-rich phase and the micelle-poor phase (26). As seen in Table 1, NPEO 10 has a cloud point of 60-65°C (27). If it were not for a phenomenon such as a phase  change,  deinking  would  be  expected  to  improve monotonically with increasing temperature. The increase in DE* after the minima as a function of temperature shown in Figure 7 seems likely to be related to the cloud point being exceeded. In laundering, optimal removal of nonpolar oil phases from fabrics occurs if the washing bath temperature is 15-25°C above the surfactant cloud point. However, the optimal removal of polar oil phases or blends of nonpolar and polar oil phases from fabric occurs at wash temperatures 0-30°C below the surfactant cloud point (28). Ink appeared to behave like polar oil in the paper deinking process (28,29). Although the optimal deinking temperature was not determined with accuracy, an optimal temperature in the vicinity of the cloud point is consistent with these guidelines for fabric detergency behavior.

The HLB value is used to characterize surfactants and is calculated from the structure of the molecule or obtained from experimental emulsification data (30,31). The higher the HLB value, the more water-soluble it tends to be and the higher the cloud point tends to be.

The  effect  of  the  HLB  of  ethoxylated  alcohols  and ethoxylated amines on deinking at room temperature was studied here. The HLB of the ethoxylated alcohols was varied by changing either the number of ethylene oxide (EO)
