The HLB of the ethoxylated amines was varied by changing only the number of EO groups from 2 to 15. Increasing the number of EO groups increases the HLB number, so the surfactant becomes more water soluble (Table 1). Adding EO groups to the surfactant also elevates the cloud point of the surfactant. On the other hand, increasing the carbon chain number decreases the HLB number and cloud point of the surfactants (Table 1).

Plastic packaging strips were soaked for 24 h in 20 mL of 25 mM AEO 3 , AEO 5 , AEO 7 , AEO 10 , A 6 EO 3 , A 13 EO 10 , and NPEO 10 (each solution had only one plastic strip of 1 × 1 in. dimensions) at pH 10, then 20 porcelain abrasives were added to the solutions and agitated for 15 min. As one can see in Figure 8, decreasing the EO number increased the deinking capacity of the surfactant except for AEO 3 . The solution of AEO 3 was the only one in which a milky phase appeared, indicating that the surfactant cloud point is below room temperature. Extrapolation of the cloud point data (Witco Detailed Product Report, 1 wt%, pH = 6.5-7) in Table 1 results in an estimated cloud point of AEO 3 of 15°C. The higher level of deinking was achieved with AEO 5 (Fig. 8), which  is  consistent  with  an  optimal  temperature  being around the cloud point. As seen in Figure 9, increasing the carbon chain length also increased the deinking capacity of the surfactant.

The HLB of the ethoxylated amines was varied by changing the EO number. The ethoxylated amines studied here were reported to have no cloud points between 0 and 100°C (32). However, the cloud point for AMEO 5 was determined as 40.5°C at pH 8, 28°C at pH 9, 26.5°C at pH 10, and 25.5°C at pH 11. The cloud point for AMEO 10 at pH 10 and 11 was 98°C. At temperatures between 1 and 100°C, AMEO 2 was cloudy at pH 5 to 11. However, AMEO 2 at pH 4, AMEO 10 at pH 4 to 9, and AMEO 15 at all pH levels formed clear solutions. Deinking experiments were performed at room temperature and at pH values of 5 and 10 by first soaking plastic packaging samples in 5 mM surfactant solutions for 24 h and then by shaking the samples for 15 min. The resulting DE* values are presented in Figure 10. As one can see in Figure 10, the deinking capacity of the surfactant increases with decreasing EO number (similar to Fig. 8) except for AMEO 2 . Better deinking was achieved with AMEO 5 at the highest pH studied.

Since AMEO 5 is effective at deinking of water-based ink at acidic, neutral, or alkaline pH levels (see Fig. 3), the effect of agitation period at deinking with or without soaking the plastic strips in surfactant solution was investigated. Experiments were performed with a surfactant concentration of 5 mM

AMEO 5 at room temperature at pH of 5, 7, and 10. Agitation time was varied from 0 to 240 min. As seen in Figure 11, the residual ink on film decreased (deinking level increased) as agitation time increased from 0 to 60 min and stabilized at 60 min. AMEO 5 deinks more effectively if the surfactant solution is acidic (pH 5) or basic (pH 10) than if it is neutral.

The effect of soaking on deinking prior to mechanical agitation was also investigated with 5 mM AMEO 5 at pH 10. Soaking plastic samples in surfactant solution (Fig. 12) increased the deinking level and decreased the needed agitation time for the optimal level of deinking. As seen in Figure 12, increasing the soaking period from 30 min to 1 h decreased greatly the residual ink on film (increased the deinking level); however, further increase of the soaking period from 1 h to 24 h did not cause any significant change on the deinking level. On the basis of the information in Figures 5 and 12, long soaks (>1 h) prior to agitation do not benefit deinking substantially, especially with extended agitation times.

The effect of plastic film consistency (plastic/solution ratio) on deinking was studied by varying it from 0.1 to 5% using 20 mL of 5 mM AMEO 5 at pH 10. Plastic film strips were soaked in the surfactant solution for 1 h prior to an agitation period of 20 min. As seen in Figure 13, an increase in  consistency  increased  the  residual  ink  on  film.  The amount of residual ink on film was also varied from one plastic strip to another in the same batch when the consistency was 1, 2.5, or 5%. However, the size of the plastic film strips affected the level of deinking. Three experiments were performed with 2.5% consistency. Plastic film for each experiment was cut to 1 × 1, 1 × 0.5, or 1 × 0.25 in. As seen in Figure 14, a decrease in the width of the plastic film strip from 1 to 0.5 in. decreased the residual ink on film and increased the uniformity of the deinking among different samples. However, a decrease in width from 0.5 to 0.25 in. did not significantly change the deinking level. Error bars in Figures 13 and 14 represent the 90% confidence interval (for each batch, the DE* values of all the deinked plastic film strips were determined. The mean and lower/upper limits of the error bar for the DE* values were calculated with the method stated in Ref. 33). The size of plastic film strips in the deinking process may be important in the recovery of plastic film pieces after the deinking operation.

Visual evaluation of the deinked plastic film samples indicated that black ink is more difficult to remove than other colors studied here.

Scaleup of deinking. Deinking experiments were scaled up from 20 mL to 2 L by using either a Denver flotation cell or a TMI disintegrator. The surfactant concentration was kept at 5 mM and the process pH was 10 with surfactants AEO 5 and AMEO 5 . The printed part of the plastic film at 1% consistency (20 g plastic film in 2000 mL solution) was first cut to the size of 1 × 1 in., soaked in the surfactant solution for 1 h, and then agitated in the Denver flotation cell or the TMI disintegrator for 20 min. The agitation speed of the Denver flotation cell was varied from 1000 to 3000 rpm. The experiment with AEO 5 was performed at only 1000 rpm with the Denver flotation cell because AEO 5 created a large amount of foam during agitation. After deinking, the plastic film pieces were collected, rinsed with water, and dried in a vacuum oven overnight. From each batch, 30 plastic film pieces (around 3 wt% of the total plastic film) were arbitrarily picked and analyzed with the HunterLab UltraScan Spectrocolorimeter. Figure 15 shows the average DE* between clear plastic film and deinked plastic film (with a 90% confidence interval) as a function of agitation speed. Increasing the agitation speed from 1000 to 3000 rpm with the Denver flotation cell decreased the relative residual ink amount on film when AMEO 5 was used as a surfactant. The Denver flotation cell and the TMI disintegrator at 3000 rpm resulted in almost the same level of deinking, but, owing to the beating effect, using the TMI disintegrator provided a more uniform deinking among plastic  film  pieces  than using the Denver flotation cell. The plastic film deinks better with AEO 5 than with AMEO 5 at 1000 rpm when the Denver  flotation  cell  is  used  (Fig.  15).  However,  foam  that formed with the use of AEO 5 created several problems during the agitation and rinsing stages. Addition of defoamer to the AEO 5 solution might eliminate these problems. Furthermore, experimental observation indicated that AMEO 5 acted as a flocculant since the majority of the particles from the washing bath settled down. The agitation speed affected the settling period of the ink particles. For the washing bath that was collected from the plastic film deinked at 3000 rpm, complete ink particle settling took 24 h. However, settling took 3 and 7 d for washing baths collected from the plastic film deinked at 2000 and 1000 rpm, respectively. On the other hand, AEO 5 acted as a dispersant because the majority of the ink particles stayed suspended in the washing bath after the deinking.

FIG. 15. DE* between clear plastic and water-based ink printed plastic film treated with 5 mM AMEO 5 and AEO 5 and at pH 10 at large scale (2 L) as a function of agitation speed. Error bars represent the 90% confidence interval. For abbreviations see Figure 3.

Hence, these experiments, performed with either a Denver flotation cell or a TMI disintegrator, show that deinking of plastic film using these surfactants is technically feasible.

Physical properties of re-extruded plastic films. Ink aggregates in the plastic structure are expected to reduce the strength of the plastic. Particle agglomeration is a weak point in the material and causes the material to break easily  when  stress  is  applied  to  it  (34).  Therefore,  the stress-strain properties of re-extruded samples from clear, printed,  and  deinked  plastics  were  determined.  Stressinduced crystallinity was observed during stretching of all samples. Measurements were repeated three times for each sample, and the stress-strain properties with a 90% confidence interval are presented in Table 2. Ink makes the plastic less stiff (modulus is decreased) and weaker (ultimate strength and elongation at break are decreased). Therefore, plastic heavily contaminated with printing is not a suitable raw material for clear plastic film production due to poorer physical properties and color from residual ink. However, deinking printed plastic film with either AMEO 5 or AEO 5 changes the color; reduces the density; and raises the modulus, the ultimate strength, and the elongation at break to a level basically equivalent to that of clear plastic film (Table 2). On the other hand, ink in repelletized polymer or the treatment with surfactants does not change the fractional crystallinity or melting temperature of the polymer (see Table 2).

Critical Assessment of the Hildebrand and Hansen Solubility Parameters for Polymers

Shruti Venkatram, Chiho Kim, Anand Chandrasekaran, and Rampi Ramprasad *

School of Materials Science and Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, 771 Ferst Drive NW, Atlanta, Georgia 30332, United States

*

Supporting Information

ABSTRACT: Solubility parameter models are widely used to select suitable solvents/nonsolvents for polymers in a variety of processing and engineering applications. In this study, we focus on two well-established models, namely, the Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameter models. Both models are built on the basis of the notion of ' like dissolves like ' and identify a liquid as a good solvent for a polymer if the solubility parameters of the liquid and the polymer are close to each other. Here we make a critical and quantitative assessment of the accuracy/utility of these two models by comparing their predictions against actual experimental data. Using a data set of 75 polymers, we fi nd that the Hildebrand model displays a predictive accuracy of 60% for solvents and

76% for nonsolvents. The Hansen model leads to a similar performance; on the basis of a data set of 25 polymers for which Hansen parameters are available, we fi nd that it has an accuracy of 67% for solvents and 76% for nonsolvents. The availability of the Hildebrand parameters for a large polymer data set makes it a widely applicable capability, as the Hildebrand parameter for a new polymer may be determined using this data set and machine learning methods as we have done before; the predicted Hildebrand parameter for a new polymer may then be used to determine suitable solvents and nonsolvents. Such predictions are di ffi cult to make with the Hansen model, as the data set of Hansen parameters for polymers is rather small. Nevertheless, the Hildebrand approach must be used with caution. Our analysis shows that while the Hildebrand model has a predictive accuracy of 70 -75% for nonpolar polymers, it performs rather poorly for polar polymers (with an accuracy of 57%). Going forward, determination of solvents and nonsolvents for polymers may bene fi t by developing classi fi cation models built directly on the basis of available experimental data sets rather than utilizing the solubility parameter approach, which is limited in versatility and accuracy.

■ INTRODUCTION

Solvent selection is critical to applications involving polymers. 1 For instance, polymer recycling requires designer solvents that degrade polymers in a controlled manner with environmentally compatible byproducts. Drug delivery systems require chemically permeable polymers to e ff ectively operate in biological environments. Solvent selection is critical to avoid phase segregation during polymer synthesis and to develop stable formulations that meet environmental, safety, and quality standards. 1 -3

The need to identify suitable (non)solvents for polymers has led to the development of quantitative models of polymer -solvent compatibility governed by the notion of ' like dissolves like ' . 4,5 In essence, a solvent with a cohesive energy density similar to that of a polymer is expected to be a good solvent for the polymer. The cohesive energy density of a condensed substance is a measure of the intramolecular bond strength and is de fi ned as the energy necessary to isolate a unit volume of the molecules making up the substance from each other.

Two widely used measures of solvent -polymer compatibility are the Hildebrand 1,5 -7 and Hansen 4 -7 solubility parameters. The Hildebrand model utilizes a single parameter, δ , de fi ned as the square root of the cohesive energy density, to determine whether a substance is a good solvent or nonsolvent for a polymer. Solvents with δ values di ff erent from that of a polymer by more than 2 MPa 1/2 are deemed nonsolvents, and those within ± 2 MPa 1/2 of the polymer δ value are considered good solvents; the factor 2 MPa 1/2 was determined on the basis of empirical considerations. Figure 1a pictorially depicts the Hildebrand solubility criterion.

The Hansen model utilizes three parameters, δ D, δ P , and δ H, to quantify solvent -polymer compatibility. These three parameters represent the dispersion, polar, and hydrogenbonding components, respectively, of the Hildebrand parameter δ , such that, δ 2 = δ D 2 + δ P 2 + δ H 2 . Those solvents within a sphere of radius R = 8 MPa 1/2 centered at a point corresponding to a polymer are deemed to be good solvents for that polymer, and those solvents falling outside the sphere are considered nonsolvents. Again, the factor 8 MPa 1/2 was determined on the basis of empirical considerations. Figure 1b pictorially depicts the Hansen solubility criterion.

In this study, we critically assess the performance of both the Hildebrand and Hansen models by directly comparing their predictions against actual experimental data (collected from the Polymer Handbook ) on solvents and nonsolvents for a benchmark set of polymers. The model predictions were based on the criteria described above and portrayed in Figure 1. A challenge we had to overcome in this study is that the Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameters are available for only limited numbers of polymers (although the solubility parameters are available for numerous solvents). For those polymers for which experimental data on solvents and nonsolvents were available but the Hildebrand parameter was not available, a previously developed machine learning (ML) model 8 was used fi rst to predict the Hildebrand parameter, followed by application of the criterion discussed above to predict solvents and nonsolvents. The Hansen model values were available for only 25 polymers  too few to train a ML model. Thus, Hansen model assessments were performed only for these 25 polymers.

Overall, we conclude that both the Hildebrand and Hansen parameters provide limited accuracy. For a data set of 75 polymers, we fi nd that the Hildebrand model predicts solvents with an accuracy of 60% and nonsolvents with an accuracy of 76%. The Hansen model is similarly evaluated using a data set of 25 polymers for which the Hansen values are available. We fi nd that its predictive capability is similar to that of the Hildebrand model, with a predictive accuracy of 67% for solvents and 76% for nonsolvents. The quantity and diversity of polymers for which the Hildebrand parameters are available (and the Hansen parameters are not) makes it a suitable candidate to predict solvents and nonsolvents for polymers. For new polymers, this data set and ML methods can be used to predict the Hildebrand parameter. However, the performance of the Hildebrand parameter is not uniform across the chemical space of polymers. From this study, we fi nd that the Hildebrand model ' s predictive capability is better for nonpolar polymers (with an accuracy of 70 -75%) than for polar polymers (with an accuracy of 57%). To overcome these limitations, the next steps for more accurate solvent predictions for polymers could be to use the experimental data sets as is with classi fi cation models rather than go through the intermediate route with solubility parameters. This approach may lead to a higher success in capturing complex relationships between polymers and solvents.

Therefore, to apply solubility models, generic compounds (e.g., alcohols) found in data sources were replaced by speci fi c common organic solvents (e.g., methanol, ethanol, etc.) to allow for the application of solubility models. To assess the solvent prediction capability of the Hildebrand model, a benchmark polymer data set (shown in Table 2) containing 75 polymers classi fi ed into four categories, viz., 12 amorphous nonpolar polymers, 17 amorphous polar polymers, 21 semicrystalline nonpolar polymers, and 25 semicrystalline polar polymers was used. Since the Hildebrand solubility parameters were not available for all of the polymers (although the solubility parameters are available for most solvents), the Hildebrand values for the polymers in the data set were predicted using a previously developed Gaussian process regression (GPR) ML model. 8

To train the machine learning model, 113 polymers were used, and all of them are plotted in Figure 2. The model performance was assessed using a learning curve in the work by Kim et al. 8 However, the fi nal model used for the prediction of the solubility parameter uses all 113 data points to ensure maximum diversity, and therefore, there is no validation set. The root-mean-square error for the model prediction is 0.49 MPa 1/2 , and the model performance plot is shown in Figure 2. Each polymer in this data set has corresponding experimentally determined solvents and nonsolvents that are documented in the Polymer Handbook by Brandup et al. 9,12 -40

Figure 2. Performance of the Hildebrand solubility machine learning model developed using Gaussian process regression (GPR) for the prediction of unknown polymer Hildebrand solubility values.

The evaluation of the solvent prediction capabilities of the Hansen model was conducted using 25 polar and nonpolar polymers (shown in Table 3). The size of the polymer data set was constrained by the scarcity of data for the Hansen parameter. The Hansen parameters for polymers were collected from the o ffi cial Hansen parameter website. 41,42 For comparison, the data set was also assessed using the Hildebrand model, where the parameter values were obtained using the ML model described above. Each polymer in this data set has corresponding experimentally determined solvents and nonsolvents that are documented in the Polymer Handbook by Brandup et al. 9 The Hildebrand and Hansen parameter values for all of the solvents and nonsolvents were obtained from the literature. 9,42

Assessment Procedure. To assess the Hildebrand model, the benchmark polymer data set and its associated experimental solvents and nonsolvents (as described above) were evaluated using the miscibility criterion depicted in Figure 1a. Similar Hildebrand parameters indicate miscibility, i.e., the di ff erence between the Hildebrand parameters of a miscible solvent -polymer pair should not exceed ± 2 MPa 1/2 . For nonsolvent -polymer pairs, the di ff erence between the Hildebrand parameters must be greater than ± 2 MPa 1/2 . The (non)solvent prediction accuracy was calculated using this miscibility criterion for each (non)solvent -polymer pair. 6,7

Likewise, the Hansen model was evaluated using the aforementioned data set and its associated solvents and nonsolvents. The miscibility criteria depicted in Figure 1(b) is used to assess the model where miscible polymer -solvent pairs are within ± 8 MPa 1/2 and polymer-nonsolvents are greater than ± 8 MPa 1/2 . Each (non)solvent -polymer pair was evaluated using this criterion. 4,41 -43

For every polymer in the Hildebrand and Hansen data sets, the (non)solvent prediction accuracy was calculated as the percentage of (non)solvents correctly predicted by the solubility models. Then, to estimate the performance of these models across the polymer space, the population statistics for each data set was determined using a wellestablished statistical resampling method called bootstrapping. The bootstrap method is a statistical technique for estimating the mean and standard deviation of a population by averaging

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Assessment of the Hildebrand Solubility Parameter Across Di ff erent Polymer Classes. The performance of the Hildebrand parameter for solvents and nonsolvents for the four distinct classes of polymers is shown in Figure 3. The

Figure 3. Performance of the Hildebrand parameter for 75 polymers across polymer classes for solvents and nonsolvents.

Hildebrand parameter was originally developed for amorphous nonpolar polymers, and its prediction capability is known to falter for semicrystalline and polar polymers. 7 Here we evaluated its prediction capabilities quantitatively across four di ff erent polymer classes: amorphous polar, amorphous nonpolar, semicrystalline polar, and semicrystalline nonpolar. The Hildebrand approach predicts solvents for nonpolar polymers more accurately than for polar polymers. The solvent predictions for amorphous nonpolar and semicrystalline nonpolar polymers reach accuracies of 77% and 72%, respectively. However, the performance deteriorates for polar polymers: 59% for amorphous polar polymers and 57% for semicrystalline polar polymers. At greater than 78%, the parameter performance is uniformly satisfactory for nonsolvent prediction for all polymer classes.

The performance trend of the parameters for solvents can be explained by the nature of the interactions captured by the Hildebrand parameter and the interactions at play for various classes of polymers. The Hildebrand parameter essentially captures the total cohesive interactions, which include the dispersion forces, dipole -dipole interactions, and hydrogenbonding interactions for a molecule. For nonpolar polymers, which do not have noteworthy polar or hydrogen-bonding contributions, the total cohesive energy su ffi ces as the primary criterion for solubility. For polar polymers, speci fi c interactions like hydrogen bonding play a crucial role that the Hildebrand parameter, as a single parameter, is unable to explicitly capture. For instance, polycarbonate (PC) and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) are well-known polar amorphous polymers. Acetone is a solvent for PMMA but is a nonsolvent for PC, and yet the three systems have similar Hildebrand parameters. Acetone is a polar aprotic solvent and therefore does not have hydrogen atoms that can form hydrogen bonds during solvation. Therefore, the PMMA -acetone solubility can be explained by a polymer-speci fi c polar or hydrogen-bonding interaction that is absent in the PC -acetone interaction, which the single-parameter Hildebrand model is incapable of predicting. 1,7,44 Additionally, the solvent and nonsolvent temperatures also play an important role in solubility by altering the free energy of mixing, which the parameter does not consider. For nonsolvents, the Hildebrand parameter has a reasonable level of accuracy since the criterion is based on exclusion.

Despite its disadvantages, the Hildebrand parameter can be used to predict solvents for nonpolar polymers with reasonable accuracy and to predict nonsolvents for all classes of polymers. Additionally, the Hildebrand parameter has an expansive data set for polymers, and we have utilized this to train an ML model that predicts the parameter values for a new polymer or polymers absent from the data set. This development has led to a user-friendly ML-based screening tool to predict solvents and nonsolvents for a queried polymer using the Hildebrand parameter. This tool is implemented at www.polymergenome. org.

Assessment of the Hansen Solubility Parameter and Its Comparison to the Hildebrand Parameter. The performance of the Hansen and Hildebrand solubility parameters for 25 polymers and their associated solvents and nonsolvents is shown in Figure 4. As expected, we fi nd that the average solvent prediction accuracy of the Hansen model (69%) is higher than that of the Hildebrand model (60%). The nonsolvent accuracies of the two methods are equal (76%).

The Hansen parameter was developed to overcome a major inadequacy of the Hildebrand parameter by the inclusion of

Figure 4. Performance of the Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameters for 25 polymers for solvents and nonsolvents.

the polar and hydrogen-bonding contributions. 42 However, the di ff erence between the accuracies of the parameters for polymer systems, especially polar polymers, is not striking. We fi nd that the Hildebrand parameter is equivalent to or outperforms the Hansen parameter in solvent predictions for 12 polar polymers, which constitute 48% of the Hansen data set. The reasonable nonsolvent accuracy implies that the parameters can be used interchangeably for this purpose.

The Hansen parameter ' s lack of signi fi cant improvement can be attributed to two reasons. First, the parameter is heavily biased toward its dispersion component, which captures the nonpolar interactions of a molecule. The dispersion component has a multiplier of 2 attached to it, which diminishes the contributions of the polar and hydrogenbonding parameters. Second, polymer solubility is a complex process involving swelling, di ff usion, and solvation processes that are often dependent on the polymer structure and other physical attributes like the solvation temperature and solvent concentration. 1 These parameters are not represented in the Hansen model or the Hildebrand model, and their inclusion could be used to develop a better solubility model.

■ OUTLOOK

The heuristic nature of the Hildebrand and Hansen models renders them easy to use but results in signi fi cant drawbacks and limitations. Polymer solubility is an inherently complex process and depends on a multitude of chemical, morphological, thermodynamic, and kinetic factors. Quantifying such a phenomenon using a limited number of manually fi tted parameters is an exceptionally challenging endeavor. 45 For instance, both the Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameters are completely unable to capture the speci fi c nature of the interaction of water with polymers. 1,41 Another major drawback is the limited availability of the model parameter values for polymers, especially for the Hansen model. 4 Indeed, in some cases con fl icting values of the Hansen parameter have been reported for the same polymer. 46 Moreover, for a newly designed polymer, it is di ffi cult to obtain a measurement of the Hildebrand parameter or an estimate of the Hansen solubility parameter. Other solubility models, like the χ parameter, have speci fi c values/parameters for polymer -solvent pairs at given temperatures and concentrations, making it di ffi cult to generalize to unexplored chemical space. 47

To overcome these drawbacks, the solvent/nonsolvent data could be directly used to train an ML classi fi er and therefore bypass the requirement of obtaining intermediary solubility parameters. Such an approach is likely to possess signi fi cant advantages over the Hildebrand and Hansen criteria because of its ability to learn from a larger chemical space without the requirement of generating empirically derived parameters. Modern ML algorithms like deep neural networks could capture the highly nonlinear multivariate mapping between the characteristics of a polymer and its solubility in a given solvent.

■ CONCLUSIONS

This study critically examines and establishes a predictive baseline for two well-established solubility models (based on the Hansen and Hildebrand solubility parameters) that are widely utilized to characterize polymer solubility in solvents. This comparative study could be used to make informed decisions when utilizing the models for solvent predictions and could also be used as a baseline for new polymer solubility models. Key fi ndings from this study are summarized below:

We fi nd that the Hildebrand model has a better solvent prediction accuracy for nonpolar polymers than for polar polymers. The nonsolvent prediction accuracy is uniformly high for all polymer classes. The higher solvent prediction accuracy for nonpolar polymers can be attributed to the accurate representation of van der Waals forces by the Hildebrand parameter. The lower solvent prediction accuracy for polar polymers occurs because polar and hydrogen-bonding contributions are lacking in the single-parameter Hildebrand model.

We fi nd that the Hildebrand and Hansen models have similar prediction accuracies for solvents and nonsolvents for polymers. Considering that the Hansen model was developed as an improvement of the Hildebrand model, the insigni fi cant di ff erence in the two models ' performance can be attributed to the scarcity of available data for the Hansen model and the complexity of polymer solubility, as neither model captures factors like temperature, concentration, or polymer molecular weight.

Traditional solubility parameters provide a simple and powerful gateway to understand polymer solubility by utilizing parameters that attempt to capture forces pertinent to solvation. This is particularly true of the Hildebrand approach, which may be widely used for a large portion of the polymer chemical space (e.g., using ML methods, as has been done at https://www.polymergenome.org). However, the limited number of parameters such models contain are insu ffi cient to capture the full complexity of polymer -solvent interactions. In the future, we aim to bypass the use of traditional solubilityparameter-based models and utilize experimental data as is with numerous potentially relevant features and ML algorithms to determine a unique structure -property mapping of solvent and polymer structures to their miscibility.

ABSTRACT: Surfactant-mediated binder removal is critical for deinking pretreatment in plastics recycling, yet the molecular mechanisms governing surfactant performance remain poorly understood. We used all-atom (AA) and coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations alongside alkaline surfactant washing experiments to investigate interactions between a series of surfactants and a polyether urethane (PEU) binder in solution and on a polyethylene (PE) surface. Experiments reveal a range of de-inking e ffi ciencies, ranging from < 25 to > 95% depending upon surfactant headgroup charge and tail length. AA simulations reveal that charged surfactants reach stable levels of surfactant coverage, while nonionic surfactants aggregate on the binder. CG umbrella sampling calculations quantify the thermodynamics of binder desorp- Supporting Information

tion in water. In ∼ 0.25 M surfactant solutions, up to a 52% reduction in the free energy barrier is computed, with trends in good agreement ( R 2 = 0.92, Pearson ' s r = -0.96, Spearman ' s ρ = -0.83) with experimental de-inking e ffi ciencies. We fi nd that charged surfactants are more e ff ective than nonionic surfactants for de-inking and propose three regimes of surfactant de-inking processes: good de-inking occurs in surfactants that promote PEU desorption with a low radius of gyration ( R g ); moderate de-inking occurs when surfactants stabilize PEU but increase R g ; poor de-inking occurs in surfactants that aggregate on the binder and promote extensive anchoring to the surface. Overall, these molecular-level insights have the potential to guide the design of surfactant formulations for plastics recycling applications.

KEYWORDS: plastic recycling, ink removal, molecular dynamics simulations, polyurethane, surfactant, umbrella sampling

■ INTRODUCTION

Global plastic production is expected to rise to 884 million tons by 2050, yet less than 10% of plastics are currently recycled, and many recycled materials have reduced value due to altered physical properties. 1 -3 Mechanical recycling, a process in which plastics are rinsed and re-molded via extrusion, is the most prevalent approach for recycling plastics. 4 A major challenge for mechanical recycling is that it cannot remove embedded or strongly adsorbed contaminants. For example, roughly 70% of plastic fi lm waste is printed with inks, which need to be removed to reintegrate printed plastics into manufacturing streams. 5,6 Incomplete removal of printed inks from plastic substrates can alter the color and transparency of the recycled plastics, create defects that impact the mechanical properties of the recycled fi lms, and introduce odorous or migratable degraded ink species. 7,8

Inks consist of a solvent, binding resins (i.e., binders), organic or inorganic pigments, and additives such as wax, plasticizers, surfactants, and antioxidants that are essential for the manufacturing or end use of the material. 9 -11 Inks are typically printed on plastics by fl exographic or gravure processes, often immediately after surface treatment by corona discharge or fl ame treatment, which increases the surface energy of plastics and promotes ink adhesion. 9,10,12 Adhesion is mediated by the binder. Common binders include cellulose-based polymers, polyurethanes, and acrylates because these materials have strong adhesion to the functionalized surface, high pigment dispersibility, fast solvent release upon heating, and impart good gloss, toughness, and fl exibility to the product. 9,10 However, the strong adhesion promoted by the binder then inhibits ink removal during recycling, motivating the development of tar-

Some technologies have emerged for recycling printed postindustrial plastic waste. One approach involves fi ltration, homogenization, and degassing of the hot melt during extrusion. 13,14 This process has been patented by EREMA and is e ff ective for low ink loads, but the products of this process are generally still downcycled into lower grade products. 13 Other approaches rely on exposing the plastics to organic solvents in which the inks are soluble; however, this is mainly oriented towards multilayer fi lms and is less desirable due to the cost and potential residues of organic solvents. 15,16 These considerations have motivated the development and implementation of de-inking processes for highly printed single-layer fi lms and rigid plastic materials (i.e., rigids) that rely on washing the ground plastics in a caustic aqueous solution with surfactants before drying, pelletizing, and extruding them into clear fi lms.

Scamehorn et al. explored the e ffi ciency of surfactants for de-inking in a series of papers. 6,17 -21 This work found that surfactant type (cationic, anionic, amphoteric, or nonionic) and concentration, ink type (solvent or water-based), solution pH, experiment duration, and mechanical agitation all impacted de-inking of plastic fi lms and rigids. Surfactant-mediated deinking was demonstrated at the semi-industrial scale in the Cadel Deinking plant (now KEYCYCLE, an EREMA group subsidiary) using 0.1 -5% by weight cetrimonium bromide (CTAB), dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide (DTAB), or dodecyl sulfate (SDS) surfactant solutions between pH 11 and 13. 22 Another patented process from Duchenaud Uni fl exo used nonionic surfactants, including alkoxylated alcohols (AEOs) or alkyl polyglycosides (APGs), along with an organic solvent and an alkaline aqueous solution to achieve high deinking e ffi ciency. 22 The Italian companies Sorema and Gamma Meccanica use a similar approach with the former commercializing a batch de-inking line and the latter o ff ering ECO CLEAN with detergent formulations for fl exible printed fi lms. 22,23 Recently, surfactant-based de-inking mechanisms have been tested in advanced plastics recycling technologies. Ügdüler et al. reported that the addition of cationic surfactants improved the removal of cellulosic and acrylic inks, 24 although Sánchez-Rivera et al. found that surfactant-based de-inking was less e ff ective for color removal with multi-layered reverseprinted plastic fi lms. 25 In a related application, aqueous surfactant solutions with small amounts of a good solvent for the ink have been used for the removal of hydrophobic polymer coatings from artistic surfaces. 26,27 While there is signi fi cant interest in surfactant-based de-inking, the mechanism of the process remain poorly understood, limiting the ability to rationally optimize surfactant formulations and other process parameters.

De-inking above the surfactant critical micelle concentration (CMC) is hypothesized to proceed by a process similar to textile laundering that consists of three steps: surface wetting, solubilization, and ink detachment and dispersion. 6 Good wetting of the plastic surface through the formation of a surfactant monolayer is expected, which reduces the ink-water and plastic-water surface tensions. 19 Next, hydrophobic segments of the binder are solubilized into surfactant micelles while larger binder fragments are stabilized by surfactant adsorption onto their surfaces, as has been discussed for cross-linked binders. 6 Additional stabilization may arise through electrostatic interactions for charged binders or ion-dipole interactions for binders with π -electron rich aromatic rings. 6 Once detached, inksurfactant complexes are dispersed and prevented from readsorbing to the surface by electrostatic repulsion with the surfactant-wetted surface. 6 As in typical laundering, surfactants that e ffi ciently solubilize hydrophobic compounds and stabilize detached particles are preferred. For example, previous work reported complete de-inking using CTAB at a concentration 4 × the CMC, tetradecyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB) at 8 × the CMC, and DTAB at 24 × the CMC for a solvent-based epoxy ink screen-printed on high-density polyethylene. 19 Cationic surfactants are generally preferred for deinking because binders like nitrocellulose and acrylates become negatively charged through alkaline hydrolysis, leading to strong electrostatic interactions. 6,28 However, anionic, amphoteric, and nonionic surfactants have also been tested with varying results under di ff erent conditions. 6,20,21 Despite continued interest in surfactant-based de-inking, it is not clear how molecular-scale surfactant organization impacts the underlying interfacial phenomena of surface wetting and binder solubilization and detachment. This knowledge gap, along with continued uncertainty regarding molecular mechanisms of de-inking, motivates mechanistic investigation of surfactant-mediated de-inking through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which have provided useful insights for a range of related phenomena. 29 -34

In this work, we used all atom (AA) and coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations alongside alkaline surfactant washing experiments to investigate the interactions between CTAB, TTAB, DTAB, STS, SDS, DOSS, DDAO and AEO5 surfactants and a high molecular weight polyether urethane (PEU) binder in solution and on a polyethylene (PE) surface. To model appropriately large system sizes while retaining molecular-scale chemical details, we develop a CG PEU model and show through desorption free energy calculations that charged surfactants favor de-inking while neutral surfactants only slightly promote de-inking relative to water. Experimental alkaline surfactant washing trials show the same rank-ordering of surfactant de-inking e ffi ciency, providing experimental support to corroborate that simulated desorption free energies for the simpli fi ed simulation systems can predict de-inking. Based on these fi ndings, we propose three regimes of de-inking (good, moderate, and poor) which are related to the packing e ffi ciency of surfactants around the binder as is demonstrated by the coverage levels and morphology of the binder in di ff erent surfactants throughout the desorption process. Together, these results provide quantitative insights into the thermodynamics of surfactant-mediated de-inking and elucidate di ff erent aspects of the mechanism of this process.

■ METHODS

Materials Studied

PEU was selected as a representative binder due to its widespread use in solvent-based ink formulations. 11,35 PEU binders exhibit weightaverage molecular weights from 10,000 to 250,000 g/mol, with polyether polyol segments typically 400 -600 g/mol (but ranging from 50 to 3000 g/mol). 11 Experimental alkaline surfactant (2 wt %) wash trials used a 1 g (2 × 2 cm) printed LDPE surface which underwent surface corona treatment prior to printing to improve ink adhesion. The printed surface had a typical molecular weight PEU binder and PB15:4 was used as pigment.

To ensure computational feasibility while remaining within experimental ranges, we modeled an AA PEU chain (13,201 g/mol; 32 repeat units) with a 160 g/mol polyol segment (Figure 1). A higher molecular weight PEU chain (30,173 g/mol; 35 repeat units) incorporating a 593 g/mol polyol segment was also studied (SI Figure S1). The CG PEU model comprised a 24,282 g/mol chain with 44 repeat units (540 g/mol), each of which contained a single 162 g/mol polyol segment, and terminal groups of 90 and 432 g/mol. Curing agents that promote crosslinking and improve adhesion of the ink to the substrate and the physical properties of the product are common, but we do not consider crosslinked binders in this work. 11 Similarly, other ink components, such as pigments, were omitted from the simulations to focus on the role of surfactant-binder interactions that could generalize beyond any single speci fi c ink formulation. We selected PE as a substrate for desorption free energy calculations of the PEU binder because it is the most commonly used polymer in packaging and several studies have investigated the de-inking of fl exible LDPE fi lms and HDPE rigids. 4,6,18,19 The CG PE model consisted of 85 chains, each comprising 200 CG beads (14,400 g/mol chains) which is a rather low approximation of commercial PE molecular-weight distributions but is suitable for this interface-focused study. 36

Surfactants were selected based on a wide range of de-inking studies 6,17 -21 and were all modeled at concentrations above their CMC to re fl ect our experimental conditions (Figure 1; see fi gure for surfactant names and acronyms). Quaternary ammonium surfactants are widely used in detergent formulations and have demonstrated good de-inking, so we selected surfactants with variations in alkyl tail length. Similarly, we selected anionic surfactants with varying tail length (STS and SDS) and morphology (DOSS) that have been tested in de-inking experiments. Amphoteric (DDAO) and non-ionic surfactants (AEO, AMEOs, etc.) have been tested in de-inking experiments as well so we selected a representative non-ionic AEO 5 surfactant for comparison to the charged surfactants.

Alkaline Surfactant Washing

1 g (cut into 2 × 2 cm pieces) plastic samples were placed in 50 mL of a 2% aqueous NaOH solution with surfactant concentrations at 10 × the CMC, as has been done in previous studies. 6 The printed plastics were placed in a pre-heated 80 °C solution for 30 min at 300 rpm (Figure 2a). The samples were then recovered, fi ltered, and dried in a vacuum oven overnight at 60 °C prior to scanning.

Figure 2. Overview of experimental methods and MD simulation systems. (A) Schematic of experimental work fl ow: printed plastics were placed in an 80 °C solution for 30 min at 300 rpm. The samples were then recovered, fi ltered, and dried in a vacuum oven overnight at 60 °C. (B) Representative simulation snapshot from the initial con fi guration of an AA simulation of the PEU 32mer (orange) in a solution with 120 CTAB surfactants (headgroup in cyan, tail group in purple). Water molecules and counterions are included in the simulations but not shown in the snapshot. (C) CG system with a PE thin fi lm, surfacebound PEU, and a surfactant. The color scheme follows the same scheme as (A) with the PE fi lm shown in brown. (D) CG mapping approach for PEU and CTAB. Groups of atoms are colored by corresponding CG bead type, with bead names following MARTINI 3 conventions. A similar mapping approach was followed for other surfactants as described in the Supporting Information.

Residual Color Pixel Analysis

Plastic samples before and after surfactant treatment were scanned using a Canon LiTE 400 scanner at 600 dpi resolution. The resulting images were analyzed using ImageJ software to quantify ink removal. A threshold value was applied to each scanned image to identify and count the remaining ink pixels after treatment. De-inking e ffi ciency was calculated by comparing the pixel count of treated samples to the initial untreated sample, allowing for quantitative assessment of ink removal performance across di ff erent surfactant formulations.

All-Atom Molecular Dynamics Simulation Parameters

For AA MD simulations, all system components were parameterized using the Generalized Amber Force Field (GAFF). 37 GAFF has been widely validated for reproducing experimental surfactant interfacial properties, including interfacial and surface tensions of ionic and nonionic surfactants, surface excess concentration at the CMC, and selfassembled morphologies with reasonable accuracy. 38 -41 Water was modeled using the TIP3P force fi eld. MD simulations were performed using a leapfrog integrator with a 2 fs timestep using Gromacs

2021.5. 42 Verlet lists were generated using a 1.2 nm neighbor list cuto ff . Van der Waals interactions were modeled with a Lennard-Jones potential that was smoothly shifted to zero between 1.0 and 1.2 nm. Electrostatic interactions were calculated using the smooth Particle Mesh Ewald method with a short-range cuto ff of 1.2 nm, grid spacing of 0.14 nm, and 4th order interpolation. All bonds with hydrogen atoms were constrained using the LINCS algorithm. Temperature coupling was controlled with the velocity-rescale thermostat at 300 K with a relaxation time of 1 ps. The Parrinello-Rahman barostat was used with a 5 ps time constant and an isothermal compressibility of 4.5 × 10 -5 bar -1 . Initial velocities were generated from a MaxwellBoltzmann distribution at 300 K.

To investigate the solubilization of PEU oligomers by surfactants, 6 each system was initialized within a cubic box containing a single polymer with an 11.79 nm distance between the polymer and box edge (Figure 2b). The box was solvated with 48,120 water molecules, 120 surfactant molecules, and 120 neutralizing sodium or chloride counterions as needed. Note that chloride counterions were used instead of bromide for cationic surfactants due to their more common usage in MD force fi elds. This choice was further justi fi ed by preliminary experiments which showed that CTAB and cetrimonium chloride yielded similar de-inking e ffi ciencies (data not shown). The system underwent steepest descent energy minimization and was equilibrated for 3 ns in an NPT simulation at 300 K and 1 bar. A 200 ns NVT production simulation was then performed for each system at the same temperature using the same thermostat. The solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) was computed as:

SASA i = 4 π r i + r probe �  2 N ∑ N j = 1 σ ij (1)

where r i is the van der Waals radius of atom i , r probe is the probe radius (0.1914 nm), N is the number of test points distributed on the expanded sphere ( r i + r probe ), and σ ij equals 1 if test point j on atom i does not lie within the expanded sphere of any neighboring atom, and 0 otherwise (illustrated in SI Figure S2a). The total SASA of the molecule is then:

SASA = ∑ N atoms i = 1 SASA i (2)

and is implemented in GROMACS using the double cubic lattice method (DCLM) to de fi ne test points per atom. The probe radius was set to 0.1914 nm to ensure consistency between AA and CG SASA calculations. 43,44

Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics Simulation Parameters

For CG MD simulations, all system components were parameterized using the MARTINI 3 force fi eld. 44 MARTINI employs a parameterization strategy in which nonbonded interactions are calibrated against experimental partitioning free energies while bonded interactions are derived from reference AA simulations. 44 As such, CG models parameterized against AA (GAFF) reference data are expected to inherit the reasonable experimental agreement demonstrated by the underlying AA force fi eld. 44 For surfactants, bead types were chosen based on literature precedents for CTAB, TTAB, DTAB, 45 and AEO5 46 (Figure 2d). Polymer bead types were based on mapping schemes previously described for other systems using the MARTINI 3 forcefi eld. 44,47,48 The bead types of polar functional groups were iteratively updated until the computed SASA and radius of gyration (R g ), de fi ned as the mass-weighted root-mean-square distance of all atoms from the center of mass of the molecule (illustrated in SI Figure S2b), 49 for the CG system in representative ' good ' and ' poor ' solvents showed good agreement with an AA system of the same size. For example, increasing the attractiveness of the carbamate functional group in the urethane bond (P3 to P6) and increasing the repulsiveness of the ether bond in the soft segment of PEU (SN3 to SN1) resulted in good agreement between AA and CG models for PEU in water (discussed in more detail in the Results). Bonded interactions for the CG models were initialized by de fi ning bonds and angles with generic force constants. These parameters were then iteratively updated for both surfactants and a PEU trimer using Swarm-CG, which employs a particle swarm optimization algorithm to minimize the di ff erence between CG and mapped AA bond/angle distributions (SI Figures S3 -10). 50

The trimer parameters served as inputs for a custom polyply fi le, which builds the polymer chain by repeating the central repeat unit of the trimer while preserving the terminal units to capture endgroup e ff ects. We constructed a 24,282 g/mol CG PEU binder topology, though this approach is generalizable to PEU chains of arbitrary lengths. The fully extended contour length ( L c ≈ 118 nm) was estimated by summing the equilibrium bond lengths along the shortest backbone path through the CG topology, providing a reference scale for interpreting desorption distances. This molecular weight was chosen to balance approximating physical binder molecular weights (10,000 + g/mol) with practical simulation system size constraints.

The thin fi lm system was constructed by generating a PE layer with 85 chains, each containing 200 CG beads (representing 400 ethylene repeat units) yielding a 1.1 g/cm 3 slab spanning 6 nm in the z direction and 17 nm in the x and y directions using polyply (Figure 2c). 51 A 13,583 nm 3 water box (100,000 CG water molecules) with dimensions of 17 × 17 × 47 nm 3 was added at the edge of the PE fi lm to ensure adequate room for desorption of PEU. The system underwent steepest descent energy minimization and was equilibrated for 5 ns in the NPT ensemble using a semi-isotropic barostat. The binder was then added in solution (replacing solvent molecules) and the system was equilibrated in the NVT ensemble for 3 ns. To generate a PE-adsorbed initial con fi guration, the binder was pulled toward the PE surface in the z -direction over 2 ns using a moving harmonic restraint with a force constant of 1000 kJ/mol · nm 2 and a pull rate of 0.008 nm/ps. This pulling step was used solely for system preparation; the pulling restraint was then removed, and the adsorbed system was equilibrated for 1.2 μ s in the NVT ensemble, allowing for complete spreading of PEU on the PE surface as veri fi ed by convergence of the PEU R g and end-toend distance (SI Figure S11). Restraints were added to PE in the presence of PEU and in subsequent simulations to avoid intercalation of the PEU into PE or distortion of the thin fi lm structure. Surfactants were then added to the system using random coordinates between 8 and 40 nm in the z direction and spanning the xy plane to ensure no initial contact between the surfactants and PE surface. All surfactant systems were simulated at a concentration of 0.25 M except AEO 5 , which was simulated at ∼ 0.18 M due to instability during NPT equilibration at higher concentrations arising from its lower aqueous solubility. Additionally, DDAO systems were simulated at 315 K (42 °C) rather than 300 K (27 °C) to suppress an arti fi cial water freezing artifact associated with the MARTINI 3 force fi eld in systems containing solid surfaces and charged species, as discussed further in the Results. Although our de-inking experiments are performed at ∼ 80 °C, our primary simulations were carried out at 27 °C (300 K). This is done to establish our methodology under conditions where MARTINI 3 is best benchmarked, as the force fi eld is parameterized against experimental partitioning free energies at 298 K and may exhibit temperature transferability limitations away from this reference. 52 -54 Additional simulations performed at 0.15 M and at 27/80 °C verify that trends in desorption free energies are robust to concentration and temperature; these are discussed in the Results and Supporting Information. Simulations performed at 0.25 M and 27 °C with additional 0.25 M NaCl further verify robustness to salinity and approximate the ionic strength of the experimental 2 wt % NaOH de-inking solution. Di ff erent random coordinates were used for each independent simulation replica. Each system then underwent energy minimization, 5 ns of semi-isotropic NPT equilibration, and 3 ns of NVT equilibration.

All CG MD simulations were performed using a leapfrog integrator with a 20 fs timestep using Gromacs 2021.5. 42 Verlet lists were generated using a 1.1 nm neighbor list cuto ff . Van der Waals interactions were modeled with a shifted Lennard-Jones potential. Electrostatic interactions were calculated using the reaction- fi eld method with a cuto ff of 1.1 nm and a dielectric constant of 15. Temperature coupling was controlled with the velocity-rescale thermostat at 300 K with a relaxation time of 1 ps. The Berendsen barostat was used with a 4 ps time constant and an isothermal compressibility of 3 × 10 -4 bar -1 . Position restraints were applied to PE atoms with a force constant of 400 kJ/mol · nm 2 . Initial velocities were generated from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 300 K.

Umbrella Sampling Simulations

CG umbrella sampling (US) simulations were performed to compute the free energy for desorbing the PEU binder from PE. Dz was de fi ned as the collective variable for US and quanti fi es the distance, projected onto the z -axis, between the center of mass of PEU and the center of mass of PE. Dz is reported in units of nm and was calculated in GROMACS. The ratio Dz / L c serves as a measure of chain anchoring to the surface: small Dz / L c indicates more favorable detachment of adsorbed segments, while large Dz / L c re fl ects persistent polymersurface contacts (trains) that must be sequentially peeled before full desorption. 33,55 All US simulations used an umbrella potential between the reference groups with a force constant of 1000 kJ/mol · nm 2 . US was performed using independent simulation windows restrained to values of Dz from 3.0 to 18.0 nm (or until desorption) in 0.25 nm increments. US windows were simulated sequentially in increasing increments of Dz , with the fi nal con fi guration of each window used as the initial con fi guration for the next window corresponding to an increased value Dz . This approach ensured that surfactants remained in contact with PEU throughout all windows during the desorption process. All windows starting at 3.25 nm were simulated for 50 ns, except for a 2 μ s equilibration that was performed for Dz = 4.75 nm. This distance corresponds to the transition of PEU from a spread to droplet con fi guration on the PE surface, at which surfactants were found to aggregate on the protruded PEU polymer (SI Figure S11). Additional equilibration for this window maximized PEU-surfactant interactions during desorption and led to lower free energy and more consistent replicate results. Potentials of mean force (PMFs) were calculated using the Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM). 56 Convergence was assessed by varying beginning cuto ff times as well as varying the segments of beginning and end times (SI Figures S12 and S13). To analyze the US trajectories, the SASA and R g for the complete trajectories were calculated.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Experimental De-Inking Reveals Distinct Performance Di ff erences

To establish a baseline understanding of surfactant performance in polymer de-inking, we fi rst conducted experimental de-inking trials on materials that our computational models were designed to represent. We selected eight surfactants spanning cationic, anionic, zwitterionic, and nonionic surfactants with CMCs ranging from 0.76 to 16 mM (Figure 1). These choices were intended to probe how surfactant headgroup chemistry, chain length, and self-assembly behavior in fl uence de-inking e ffi ciency.

Figure 3 summarizes measured de-inking e ffi ciencies. CTAB demonstrated the best de-inking e ffi ciency with 95.4% ( ± 2%) color removal compared to all other surfactants. The shorterchain quaternary ammonium surfactants DTAB (88.9% ± 3%) and TTAB (89.4% ± 4%), along with the anionic STS (87.9% ± 5%), exhibited comparable de-inking e ffi ciencies, forming a second group of comparable performance. SDS (72.1% ± 13%) and DDAO (71.3% ± 18%) showed moderate de-inking capability but with notably higher variability between replicates. The nonionic surfactant AEO5 (23.8% ± 15%) and the branched surfactant DOSS (7.2% ± 8%) were the poorest performers, achieving minimal ink removal from the plastic substrates. These results indicate that there is no simple relationship between de-inking and surfactant properties like the CMC, headgroup charge, or tail group length, motivating computational analysis to investigate the origin of the observed de-inking trends.

Figure 3. Experimental de-inking e ffi ciency of various surfactants after alkaline washing. Ink removal percentages show that CTAB achieves the best performance ( > 95%) while DTAB, TTAB, and STS achieve good performance ( ∼ 89% removal), SDS and DDAO demonstrate moderate performance ( ∼ 72%), and DOSS and AEO 5 exhibit poor de-inking performance ( < 25%). Error bars represent standard deviation across experimental replicates. Representative photographs of washed plastic fi lm samples (bottom) illustrate the contrast between high ink removal (left) and low ink removal (right) conditions.

Surfactant Charge Leads to Di ff erences in Solution-State Binder Coverage

Our experimental results suggest that increasing the alkyl tail length of ionic surfactants improves de-inking while introducing branched or zwitterionic/nonionic surfactants inhibits deinking. As a fi rst step toward understanding the molecularscale interactions governing these trends, we performed unbiased, all-atom MD simulations to quantify surfactant interactions with the PEU binder in aqueous solution. Based on previous reports that surfactants with longer tails favor deinking due to increased adsorption of the tail to hydrophobic parts of the binder, 17 we hypothesized that the bestperforming surfactants from our experiments would have the greatest binder coverage in our simulations.

We fi rst simulated the PEU binder in water in the absence of any surfactant, which led to the collapse of the polymer into a single, nearly spherical globule whose SASA is shown in Figure 4. This conformation is consistent with the behavior of polymers in poor solvents and the hydrophobic nature of the binder. Coverage of the binder surface by surfactants would thus be expected to decrease the SASA, thereby increasing binder stability in solution which could correlate with improved de-inking. We observe surfactant coverage of the binder that is generally consistent with experimental de-inking trends, with longer alkyl tail lengths producing greater coverage based on analysis of the SASA (Figure 4). Among the cationic surfactants, CTAB exhibited the greatest coverage (lowest SASA), followed by TTAB and then DTAB as the tail length decreased. A similar trend was observed for the anionic surfactants, with STS exhibiting greater coverage than SDS. However, DOSS exhibited very high coverage with a SASA near zero despite its poor deinking e ffi ciency (Figure 3), indicating that binder coverage alone does not fully explain the de-inking trends. Unlike most charged surfactants, the zwitterionic and uncharged surfactants DDAO and AEO5 tended to form a single aggregate with the binder, leading to low SASA and few surfactants remaining in solution. These simulations were also repeated with a 30,173 g/mol PEU binder with a larger polyol unit, which yielded consistent surfactant coverage trends, with the exception that DTAB exhibited the greatest coverage among the cationic surfactants (SI Figure S1). These results motivated further investigation of the de-inking ability of di ff erent surfactants as binder coverage alone does not align with the de-inking results in Figure 3 or prior experimental reports of the best surfactants for de-inking. 6,17 -21

Figure 4. Equilibrium coverage of PEU 32mer by various charged and neutral surfactants from all-atom simulations. The SASA of PEU in water (HOH) and various surfactant solutions, time-averaged over the fi nal 50 ns of each 200 ns run, is shown at top. Error bars indicate the standard deviation over time. Simulation snapshots show the equilibrium structures of the PEU 32mer in TTAB, (a representative charged surfactant) and DDAO (a representative neutral surfactant).

Semi-Automated Coarse Graining Procedure Yields Accurate Models

Because surfactant coverage of PEU in solution was insu ffi cient to explain trends in de-inking e ffi ciency, we next sought to model a more complete process of surfactant-mediated desorption of PEU from a PE thin fi lm. Such simulations are too computationally expensive to perform at AA resolution, motivating the development of a CG simulation representation of the PEU and surfactant systems. As detailed in the Methods, we parameterized PEU and the surfactants using the MARTINI 3 CG force fi eld, 44 with CG bead types (which de fi ne nonbonded interactions) summarized in Figure 2. PEU bonded parameters were obtained based on a CG PEU trimer input to polyply and these generally agreed well with the AA bonded parameters (SI Figure S3).

Accurate parameterization of the solution properties of the CG PEU model was con fi rmed by comparing the structural properties of PEU (13,200 g/mol, 32 repeat units) in water (a ' poor ' solvent) and dimethylacetamide (DMAc; a ' good ' solvent) using both AA and CG simulations (Figure 5a). Good agreement was obtained in water with SASA and R g values of 56.3 nm 2 and 1.3 nm for the AA model and 49.3 nm 2 and 1.2 nm for the CG model (Figure 5b). In DMAc, higher SASA and R g values of 165.3 nm 2 and 2.8 nm were obtained for the AA model compared to 92.5 nm 2 and 1.9 nm for the CG model. Since we are primarily concerned with the solution behavior of PEU in water, and the CG model does correctly predict larger SASA and R g values in DMAc compared to water, the larger deviation between AA and CG structural parameters in DMAc was considered acceptable. Close agreement between the AA and CG SASA values for a single surfactant in water with one counterion were also obtained for all surfactants (Figure 5C) after adopting literature mapping schemes and parametrizing bonded parameters using SwarmCG (SI Figures S4 -S10). 50 We further computed the water contact angle on the CG PE surface using a sessile drop method, as detailed in the Supporting Information (SI Figure S14). The water contact angle was computed to be 100.2 ° , which agrees well with experimental values of 96 -103 ° for virgin LDPE. 12,57 Overall, these comparisons indicate that the MARTINI 3 CG parameters can reliably reproduce AA or experimental values for the custom components of our system.

Figure 5. CG model validation against AA models for PEU 32mer and surfactants. (A) Simulation snapshots of AA and CG PEU in water (a ' poor ' solvent) and DMAc (a ' good ' solvent). (B) Mean SASA and R g values of AA and CG PEU in water and DMAc. Error bars represent the SASA and R g standard deviation for a single 100 ns simulation. (C) Mean SASA for AA and CG surfactants in water.

CG Models Predict Surfactant-Mediated Decrease in Binder Desorption Free Energy

Using the CG PEU and surfactant models, we next investigated the hypothesis that surfactants decrease the free energy required to desorb the PEU binder from PE. Surfactant-mediated decreases in the desorption free energy relative to desorption in water are expected to correlate with experimental de-inking, and calculation of the free energy of desorption is expected to permit quantitative comparisons between di ff erent surfactants. We fi rst con fi rmed that PEU was equilibrated on the PE surface by observing convergence of the R g and end-to-end distance (SI Figure S11). During equilibration, some surfactants (independent of type) adsorbed to the PE surface along with the PEU, while some surfactants remained in solution and formed micelles because all systems were simulated at surfactant concentrations signi fi cantly in excess of the CMC. Prior to PEU desorption, we observed the formation of a monolayer of approximately 200 surfactants on the PE surface, corresponding to an area per molecule of 1.45 nm 2 ( ∼ 1 surfactant per 40 CH 2 groups) and a net surface charge density of roughly

+ 3.0 q/nm 2 for cationic surfactants and -3.0 q/nm 2 for anionic surfactants (SI Figure S15). The calculated area per molecule agrees well with experimentally reported CTAB minimum areas per molecule of 1.18 -1.60 nm 2 at the hydrophobic air-water interface. 58 The fi nal system con fi guration prior to US thus consisted of a PE surface to which the PEU was adsorbed, with excess PE area covered by a surfactant monolayer and surrounded by a solution of surfactant micelles.

To model PEU desorption, US was performed using a sequential approach as described in the Methods. Potentials of mean force (PMFs) associated with desorption in pure water (HOH) or in a 0.15 M CTAB solution at 27 °C are compared in Figure 6A; results at 0.25 M are presented below. Although our de-inking experiments are performed at 80 °C to accelerate de-inking kinetics, 24 our primary simulations were performed at 27 °C, where the MARTINI 3 force fi eld is most reliable. 52 -54 Since both experiments and simulations are performed well above the CMC of each surfactant, this temperature di ff erence is not expected to alter the underlying driving forces captured by our PMFs. Additional simulations at 80 °C were also performed to con fi rm the robustness of this approach, as discussed below. Similarly, experiments were performed in 2% NaOH but all simulations were performed without added electrolyte because the MARTINI 3 force fi eld models a weakly screened environment by setting a system-wide dielectric constant of 15 and using a short-range electrostatic potential. Prior experimental studies of the e ff ect of salinity on de-inking using charged surfactants suggest that salt contributes to de-inking predominantly through reducing the surfactant CMC, 18 but as all simulations are performed at concentrations substantially higher than the CMC added salt is not expected to in fl uence the simulation results, as con fi rmed by additional simulations described below.

Figure 6. Analysis of umbrella sampling (US) simulations of PEU desorption from a PE thin fi lm in water and in the presence of 0.15 M CTAB at 27 °C. Data for two independent simulation replicates (labeled as REP1 and REP2) are shown separately to demonstrate simulation reproducibility. (A) PMF of PEU desorption in water (HOH) and in CTAB solution (top), and simulation snapshots of the three-step desorption mechanism (bottom): I, PEU transitions from a spread to a globular conformation, enabling surfactant interaction; II, surfactant stabilization of the highR g PEU desorption intermediate; III, detachment of the PEU anchor, which occurs at a variable pulling distance across replicates. (B) PEU SASA as a function of distance from the PE surface (top), with high SASA suggesting less stabilization of PEU during desorption, and PEU R g as a function of pulling distance (bottom), with high R g indicating energetically unfavorable conformations during desorption.

Two PMFs are computed for both systems, initiated from independent initial con fi gurations, to quantify uncertainty. Both sets of PMFs show well-de fi ned global minima for Dz = 3.5 nm, indicating a thermodynamic preference for the PEU to adsorb to the PE surface as expected. The PMF then increases with D z until plateauing for large values of Dz , corresponding to the PEU fully desorbing into the surrounding solution. Since the PMF can be interpreted as the variation in the free energy as a function of Dz , we thus associate the di ff erence in the PMF between its global minimum value (arbitrarily set to a value of zero) and its plateau value as the magnitude of the desorption free energy. Smaller values of the desorption free energy indicate that desorption can more readily occur, which we would associate with increased de-inking in experiments. Figure 6A shows that, as expected, the two PMFs for desorption in CTAB correspond to substantially lower desorption free energies (330 and 510 kJ/mol) than the two PMFs for desorption in pure water (830 and 890 kJ/mol), representing a reduction of up to 500 kJ/mol (discussed further below). These data indicate that surfactant molecules can reduce free energy barriers for desorption, in agreement with our core hypothesis that desorption thermodynamics in fl uences de-inking e ffi cacy.
Surfactants A ff ect PEU Structure During Desorption

Figure 6A shows simulation snapshots that illustrate key structural changes in the PEU binder during desorption. These metrics, namely SASA and R g , are further quanti fi ed in Figure 6B. We additionally computed the relative shape anisotropy κ 2 , a dimensionless descriptor derived from the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor that is bounded between 0 (for a spherical mass distribution) and 1 (for a fully linear, extended mass distribution), to distinguish isotropic from anisotropic changes in chain conformation during desorption (SI Figure S16). 59,60 PEU fi rst adopts a con fi guration that can favorably interact with the surfactant micelles present in solution. The structural change in PEU during this onset of desorption is marked by a decrease in R g at Dz = 4.75 nm. The PEU SASA decreases substantially at this value of Dz for the CTAB solution, signifying interactions between the PEU and surfactants in solution (Figure 6B). As Dz increases, simulation snapshots and R g values for desorption in pure water show that PEU detaches gradually rather than all at once, elongating away from the surface and increasing both R g and SASA. This elongation is accompanied by a sharp rise in κ 2 toward 1, con fi rming that the increases in R g during desorption are anisotropic and prolate in character, with the chain adopting a rod-like conformation while remaining in contact with the surface. We refer to this elongation process in which some segments remain adsorbed prior to complete desorption as ' anchoring ' . In the presence of CTAB, surfactants remain in contact with the binder to stabilize it during the desorption process, leading to lower SASA and R g values and a suppressed peak κ 2 relative to the water-only control. For the plateau region of Dz , the PEU is completely desorbed from the surface and collapses into a globule in pure water, leading to decreased SASA and R g values. In CTAB, the same globular conformation is observed based on the R g values, yet the SASA remains low due to coverage by the surfactant. These structural changes accompany the gradual rise in the PMF between the global minimum and the plateau and re fl ect the sequential detachment of adsorbed polymer segments from the PE surface. This is consistent with previously reported two-phase polymer desorption regimes in which adsorbed and desorbed states coexist at intermediate Dz . 55 Thus, the distance at which the polymer desorbs re fl ects the extent of chain anchoring, with surfactants that reduce anchoring generally yielding lower desorption free energies. SI Figure S16 further supports this behavior by showing relative di ff erences in peak κ 2 across surfactants, which separate the chains into distinct mild- and strong-anchoring groups.

Based on our analysis, we delineate three mechanistic steps in the surfactant-mediated desorption process, each associated with characteristic D z values during US and illustrated by representative simulation snapshots in Figure 6A. (I) Dissociation : the binder is dislodged from its equilibrium spread con fi guration on the PE surface, reaching an R g minimum at Dz = 4.5 nm that is characterized by a droplet-like con fi guration that facilitates interactions with surfactants. (II) Stabilization : Surfactant micelles subsequently stabilize the partially detached binder to maintain its low R g and SASA values. Di ff erences in the PMF slopes emerge between Dz = 4.5 nm (e.g., water vs CTAB) and arise through 7.5 nm (e.g., fi rst and second water replicates). (III) Desorption : the binder is completely removed from the PE surface, which occurs for values of Dz as small as 8.5 nm ( ∼ 7% of the fully extended contour length, L c ≈ 118 nm) in the presence of CTAB or as large as 20 nm ( ∼ 17% of L c ) in the presence of neutral surfactants (see below). Comparing the PMFs indicates that larger desorption free energies are correlated with higher SASA and R g values. High SASA values indicate less surfactant coverage of the binder during desorption and high R g values indicate stronger binder anchoring to the PE surface, which leads to the binder adopting unfavorable extended conformations as it continues to be pulled.
Desorption Free Energies Relate to De-Inking E ffi ciencies across Surfactants

To further quantify the reduction of the free energy barrier for binder desorption and investigate di ff erences owing to surfactant morphology, we performed umbrella sampling simulations for the additional surfactants listed in Figure 1. In pure water at 27 °C, the mean free energy of PEU desorption for two replicates is 895 kJ/mol (Figure 6b) or 7.73 kT/nm 2 (SI Figure S17). This is a substantial energy barrier that is addressed in industrial de-inking processes by employing a combination of elevated temperatures, mechanical agitation, extended residence times ( ∼ 0.5 -1 h), and controlled addition of feedstock and surfactants. 61 Due to the long timescales associated with desorption in our umbrella sampling approach, our simulations were performed at high concentrations ( ∼ 0.15 and 0.25 M) compared to prior de-inking experiments ( ∼ 0.05 M or 0.1 -5% by weight) 61 as this increases the likelihood of surfactant interactions with the binder during the simulations. Figure 7a compares corresponding desorption PMFs. In ∼ 0.25 M surfactant solutions at 27 °C, the CTAB system had the lowest desorption free energy of 430 kJ/mol or 3.7 kT/ nm 2 , which is a ∼ 52% reduction in the energy barrier for desorption relative to water. The TTAB (550 kJ/mol), DTAB (570 kJ/mol), STS (510 kJ/mol) and SDS (590 kJ/mol) systems all had similar desorption free energies between 500 and 600 kJ/mol (4.4 -5.1 kT/nm 2 ). The DDAO system was simulated at a slightly elevated temperature of 42 °C due to freezing of the system at room temperature after 1 -2 μ s of total simulation time (an issue which has been reported in MARTINI 3), 54

The AEO5 system was tested at ∼ 0.18 M due to its lower aqueous solubility (see Methods) and exhibited a high desorption free energy (840 kJ/mol; 7.24 kT/nm 2 ) that was only slightly better than water. Overall, our simulation results for the di ff erent surfactants tested agree well with our experimental results. Across the six surfactants that share a common surfactant-mediated desorption mechanism (CTAB, TTAB, DTAB, STS, SDS, AEO 5 ), a strong negative correlation ( R 2 = 0.92, Pearson r = -0.96) was observed between the simulated PEU desorption free energy and experimental ink removal e ffi ciency (Figure 8), confi rming that surfactants which lower the free energy of binder desorption yield better de-inking performance. CTAB was the best-performing surfactant with the highest experimental deinking e ffi ciency and the greatest reduction in the desorption free energy barrier relative to water. TTAB, DTAB, and STS were all e ff ective but distinctly worse than CTAB and had comparable deinking e ffi ciencies in our experiments and similar desorption free energies in simulations. In experiments, SDS had lower de-inking e ffi ciency than other linear ionic surfactants, consistent with our simulations where SDS exhibited the highest desorption free energy among that class of surfactants. Furthermore, AEO5 had the worst de-inking e ffi ciency in our experiments and the largest desorption free energy in simulations among the six linear surfactants. DOSS was excluded from the linear correlation in Figure 8 due to high standard error between simulation replicates arising from vesicle and bilayer formation (SI Figure S18), and DDAO was excluded because it desorbs through a distinct wetting-based mechanism rather than the surfactant-mediated pathway shared by the other linear surfactants (SI Figure S19; discussed in more detail below). Corresponding analysis of all eight surfactants is provided in SI Figure S20, where a logistic regression model ( R 2 = 0.80) captures the rank ordering across all eight surfactants, including DOSS and DDAO, indicating that the desorption free energy reasonably classi fi es good vs. poor de-inking performance across all surfactants. The numerical values of the desorption free energies from our simulations also align with literature results on laundering processes, where arachidic acid removal from PE in SDS showed a 54% free energy reduction relative to water (15.7 -7.2 kT/nm 2 ), supporting the magnitude of surfactant-mediated reductions in the desorption barrier that we observe. 62 DDAO is the only surfactant with a notable discrepancy between experimental de-inking and simulated desorption, with an average desorption free energy comparable to that of CTAB, the best-performing surfactant, yet experimental de-inking e ffi ciencies that were more similar to SDS as a moderately e ff ective surfactant. As discussed in more detail below, we attribute this result to a unique desorption mechanism that leads to high variability in simulations and experiments.
