Binder Coverage and Morphology Dictates Desorption E ffi ciency

Motivated by the encouraging alignment between simulated desorption free energies and experimental de-inking e ffi ciencies, we next investigated desorption mechanisms and how they relate to surfactant interactions. In the simulations, the best surfactants for de-inking promote low binder SASA values (high surfactant coverage of the binder) and low R g values (more favorable binder conformations) (Figure 7b). Di ff erences in the distance the binder is pulled from the surface before desorption were also observed, with smaller D z values indicating favorable de-inking and larger Dz values indicating unfavorable anchoring of the binder on the surface. For example, in CTAB, binder desorption occurs at Dz = 8.5 nm ( ∼ 7% of the fully extended contour length, L c ≈ 118 nm), whereas in water desorption occurs at Dz = 12.25 nm ( ∼ 10% of L c ). In STS ( Dz = 8.25 nm, ∼ 7% of L c ), SDS ( Dz = 18.25 nm, ∼ 15% of L c ), TTAB ( Dz = 12.75 nm, ∼ 11% of L c ), DTAB ( Dz = 9.0 nm, ∼ 8% of L c), DDAO ( Dz = 7.5 nm, ∼ 6% of L c ), and AEO5 ( Dz = 22.75 nm, ∼ 18% of L c ) the binder desorbs at di ff erent distances of Dz and we fi nd that anchoring corresponds to higher desorption free energies. Based on these results, we propose three regimes of good, moderate, and poor de-inking, which are impacted by the charge and hydrophobicity of the surfactants (Figure 7c). Good de-inking is characterized by desorption free energies less than roughly 4 kT/nm 2 and is primarily observed in systems like CTAB where the binder maintains low SASA and R g values throughout the entire desorption trajectory. Moderate de-inking occurs between 4 and 5 kT/nm 2 such as in DTAB, TTAB, STS and SDS. These systems display low SASA but high R g values during desorption due to good surfactant coverage of the binder but ine ff ective solubilization, and thus some anchoring, in the smaller hydrophobic cores of their micelles. Poor de-inking occurs above 5 kT/nm 2 such as in pure water, DOSS, and AEO5. Speci fi cally, nonionic AEO5 surfactants aggregated on the binder leading to unfavorable and extensive anchoring of the binder. As we further verify below with a custom nonionic surfactant, this highlights the importance of charge in the surfactant-mediated desorption process. Branched DOSS surfactants assembled into bilayers and vesicles in solution instead of micelles (SI Figure S18) and thus do a worse job of stabilizing the binder near the PE surface, which we also verify below with custom vesicle-forming cationic surfactants.

DDAO is the only system that appears to proceed by a distinct de-inking mechanism in which wetting of the PE promotes desorption rather than stabilization of the binder by micelles. Due to the zwitterionic nature of DDAO and its neutral CG headgroup, all DDAO surfactants in the system coat the PE surface. This leads to a substantial reduction in the desorption free energy that is comparable to the reduction associated with charged surfactants. We also observe large disc-like micelles (i.e., bicelles) 63,64 after 1 -2 μ s of simulation time in our DDAO system. At lower temperatures, bicelle formation results in arti fi cial ordering and nucleation of water, a known artifact in MARTINI 3. 54 This freezing artifact can occur at room temperature, particularly in the presence of nucleation sites such as solid surfaces and in highly charged systems. 65 At 42 °C, this artifact is largely suppressed, occurring in only one out of four replicates; however, bicelle formation itself still occurs and, as shown in SI Figure S19, the bicelles tend to adsorb onto the PE surface rather than interacting with the PEU binder from solution. This is consistent with a wettingdominated de-inking pathway rather than micellar solubilization. 66 Taken together, the high variability for DDAO in our experimental results (Figure 3) may be explained by favorable wetting phenomena on the one hand, and the formation of bicelle structures on the other. Future work is needed to confi rm this behavior of zwitterionic surfactants.

To assess the robustness of our simulation fi ndings, we repeated desorption simulations at a lower surfactant concentration ( ∼ 0.15 M and 27 °C; SI Figure S21), at an elevated temperature ( ∼ 0.15 M and 80 °C; SI Figure S22), and with additional NaCl for CTAB, SDS, and AEO 5 ( ∼ 0.25 M surfactant and salt at 27 °C; SI Figure S23). Although individual desorption free energies varied across all conditions, we consistently found that surfactants promoting a low SASA and R g have the lowest desorption free energies, with CTAB the clearest example. For the salinity comparison, trends in PMFs and structural observables were preserved between simulations with and without added salt for CTAB, SDS, and AEO 5 . The exception remains DDAO, which at 80 °C desorbs via the wetting mechanism discussed above. This con fi rms the main mechanistic fi ndings from our desorption simulations: the lowest desorption free energies are achieved when the binder undergoes minimal conformational changes (maintains a low R g ) due to good coverage and solubilization (low SASA) by charged surfactant micelles.

Tail Length Modulates Surfactant Packing in the De-Inking Process

To test the impact of surfactant tail length and further clarify differences between DTAB (12 carbon), TTAB (14 carbon), and CTAB (16 carbon) de-inking e ffi ciency, CG models of quaternary ammonium surfactants with 4, 8, 20, and 24 carbon tails were constructed (Figure 9a). Mapping involved incrementally adding C1 (4 carbon) bead units to the headgroup and SwarmCG was used to obtain accurate bond and angle parameters. US was then performed at ∼ 0.25 M and 27 °C. Additionally, to verify the importance of charge, US was performed for a neutral system in which the charge was arti fi cially set to zero for the STS headgroup (and no counterions were added).

The 4-carbon surfactant formed molecular clusters instead of micelles and was only slightly better than water with a desorption PMF of 800 kJ/mol (desorption Dz = 20 nm, ∼ 17% of L c ; Figure 9b). This demonstrates that introducing charge alone is not su ffi cient for good or moderate de-inking and stabilizing interactions with surfactant micelles are necessary. In the neutral STS system, we found that the desorption PMF increased from 500 to 700 kJ/mol at 0.25 M mol ( Dz = 13 nm, ∼ 11% of L c ). We observed behavior consistent with the AEO 5 simulations in which the neutral STS aggregated on the binder causing anchoring and high R g conformations before desorption (Figure 9c). This aggregation behavior suggests that charged headgroups mediate the assembly of micelles around the binder oligomer during desorption, consistent with the solubilization mechanism discussed above for smaller binder segments. 6 The increase in desorption PMF upon removing headgroup charge also suggests that electrostatic repulsion between the charged surfactants assembled around the PEU and the charged surfactants on the surface helps promote desorption. Across the remaining tail lengths, the 8-carbon ' BTAB ' variant had a desorption free energy of 400 kJ/mol ( Dz = 7.75 nm, ∼ 7% of L c ), while the 20-carbon ' ETAB ' system (600 kJ/mol; Dz = 12.5 nm, ∼ 11% of L c ) and 24-carbon ' FTAB ' system (500 kJ/mol; Dz = 11.5 nm, ∼ 10% of L c ) demonstrated desorption behavior most like DOSS, which also formed vesicle-like structures. In these systems, de-inking is contingent on the binder interacting with a single vesicle in solution whereas in the systems with linear ionic surfactants, the presence of multiple micelles in solution increased the likelihood of the binder being stabilized during desorption. Together, these results demonstrate that optimal de-inking performance is based on balancing tail length and charge to promote the formation of multiple stable micelles that can stabilize the desorbing binder.
Residual Surfactant Molecules Remain on PE after De-Inking

Simulations also reveal that surfactants remain adsorbed onto the PE surface after binder desorption (visible in the snapshots in Figures 6A and 7C). SI Figure S24 details that concentrations ranging from 0.4% (DOSS) up to 10.5% (CTAB) of the total amount of surfactant added adsorbs to the bare PE surface (the opposite surface from which PEU desorbed). This adsorption was also con fi rmed experimentally, by performing pyroGC-MS experiments (SI Tables S2 and S3) on the washed plastic fi lms (tap water + 2 wt %. caustic soda + 10x CMC surfactant) after drying them at 60 °C. Experimentally, the total remaining surfactant concentrations range from 0.3 g surfactant/kg plastic (DOSS) to 12 g surfactant/kg plastic (DTAB) (SI Table S4), which corresponds to 0.05 -1.15% of the total amount of surfactant added. Simulations predict higher absolute values ranging from 3.7 g/kg (DOSS) to 66 g/kg (CTAB), corresponding to 0.4 -10.5% of total surfactant added. This di ff erence is expected, as simulations capture total surfactant adsorption onto the PE surface, whereas experimental values re fl ect residual surfactant remaining after a post-washing step. To compare relative trends, each dataset was internally normalized to its respective maximum value (SI Figure S24). Across both datasets, DOSS exhibits the lowest relative surface loading (6% simulated, 2% experimental) and the anionic surfactant trend (STS > SDS) is consistent, for STS (53% sim., 14% exp.) and SDS (44% sim., 8% exp.). However, the cationic surfactant series exhibits an inverse trend with DTAB (100%) having the most residual surfactant after washing in experiments, followed by TTAB (58%) and CTAB (4%). In simulations, surfactant adsorption increases with tail length (CTAB 100%, TTAB 97%, DTAB 82%). This suggests that longerchain cationic surfactants adsorb more strongly during deinking but are more readily removed during washing, whereas shorter-chain DTAB may form more wash-resistant interactions with the PE surface. These results con fi rm that surfactants which are often applied in water-based mechanical recycling have the tendency to stay adsorbed on the plastics in rather high amounts. This highlights the need for post-washing or assessment of the behavior of these surfactants during extrusion, as remaining surfactants might a ff ect human health when such recyclates would be used in high-value applications. 8

■ CONCLUSIONS

Printed plastics hinder widespread mechanical recycling because remaining inks degrade the mechanical strength and optical clarity of recycled fi lms. 6,7 A promising solution is alkaline washing with surfactants prior to extrusion to minimize residual ink in the recyclate. 6,7,17 -21 However, the molecular mechanisms of surfactant-based de-inking remain poorly understood, limiting the rational optimization of surfactant formulations and process conditions for industrial applications. In this work, alkaline surfactant de-inking experiments revealed that CTAB achieves the best de-inking performance ( > 95%) while DTAB, TTAB, and STS achieve good performance ( ∼ 89% removal), SDS and DDAO demonstrate moderate performance ( ∼ 72%), and DOSS and AEO 5 exhibit poor de-inking performance ( < 25%). To investigate these results on the molecular scale, AA MD simulations of surfactant coverage of binders in solution were performed and it was found that charged surfactants reach equilibrium levels of surfactant coverage, while nonionic surfactants aggregate on the binder. However, these results did not distinguish between the performance of cationic surfactants, so we developed a CG model with custom PEU parameters to quantify binder desorption free energy in the presence of di ff erent surfactants. charged surfactants stabilize the binder and reduce the energy barrier for desorption by up to 52% while neutral surfactants aggregate on the binder, causing anchoring of the binder on the surface and performance that is only slightly better than water. The exceptions are DOSS, which forms vesicles and bilayers rather than micelles, leading to high variability across simulation replicates and ine ff ective binder solubilization, and DDAO, where surfactant molecules adsorb to the PE surface and promote binder desorption by a distinct wetting mechanism rather than the surfactant-mediated pathway observed for the other surfactants.

Based on these results, we propose three regimes of good, moderate, and poor de-inking, which are impacted by the charge and hydrophobicity of the surfactants. Good de-inking is observed in systems like CTAB where the binder maintains low SASA and R g values throughout the entire desorption trajectory. Moderate de-inking occurs in DTAB, TTAB, STS and SDS, which display low SASA but high R g (i.e., anchoring) values due to good surfactant coverage of the binder but ine ff ective solubilization in their smaller micelle cores. Poor de-inking occurs in pure water, nonionic surfactants, and surfactants that form non-micellar self-assembled structures. In Figure 10, we depict good de-inking where surfactant micelles promote desorption by better solubilizing the binder. We distinguish this from poor de-inking which is characterized by surfactant aggregation on the binder and extensive anchoring to the substrate. Overall, our simulations reveal the importance of charge and hydrophobicity in promoting binder desorption with good coverage (low SASA) and minimal conformational changes (low Rg ), and provide insights into the role of PEU structure and morphology during de-inking processes.

These results relate surfactant structure to de-inking performance, which can guide surfactant selection and the design of e ff ective formulations in plastics recycling pretreatment wash steps. For example, we can explore how selecting surfactants from curated databases based on properties like charge, adsorption e ffi ciency, and maximum surface excess concentration impacts de-inking e ffi ciency. 67 To enable screening a wider range of components, we can de fi ne collective variables, lowdimensional projections that adequately capture the thermodynamics of our system, to explicitly bias surfactant solubilization of the binder along with binder conformational changes during surfactant-mediated desorption. 68 Once these methods are established, our systems are well-suited for studying de-inking of a wide range of more complete ink formulations (i.e., binders complexed with organic pigments) to better understand how pigments interact with surfactant micelles to minimize pigment staining of the recyclate. 22 Furthermore, we seek to explore the desorption e ffi ciency of other common binders like nitrocellulose, cellulose acetate propionate (CAP), polyvinyl butyral (PVB), and acrylates, which possess a net negative charge due to alkaline hydrolysis. 6,28 We can further extend these approaches to understand de-inking mediated by organic solvents beyond water during plastics recycling processes. 15,16,25,69,70 Finally, we aim to investigate the impact of PE corona treatment, which is common immediately before printing to increase the surface energy and adhesion of ink formulations, on binder desorption free energies from a functionalized surface in water and in the presence of surfactants. 12 These e ff orts will help us to develop increasingly realistic and experimentally validated simulations that capture the complexities of industrial recycling conditions and enable predictive formulation design.

Removal of solvent-based ink from printed surface of high-density polyethylene bottles by alkyltrimethylammonium bromides: Effects of pH, temperature, and salinity

Arubol Chotipong a , John F. Scamehorn b , Thirasak Rirksomboon a , Sumaeth Chavadej a , Pitt Supaphol a , ∗

a

The Petroleum and Petrochemical College, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok 10330, Thailand b Institute for Applied Surfactant Research, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73019, USA

Received 15 January 2006; received in revised form 15 October 2006; accepted 23 October 2006 Available online 26 October 2006

Abstract

TheeffectsofpH,temperature,andsalinityontheremovalofsolvent-basedinkfromhigh-densitypolyethylene(HDPE)surfaceswereinvestigated using three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively). Ink removal increases with increasing concentration, increasing pH, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. The zeta potential of ink becomes more positively charged with increasing pH as well as concentration and alkyl chain length of CnTAB, indicating that adsorption of CnTAB on ink pigment occurred more readily with an increase in any of those parameters. The solubilization of epoxy ink binder was found to increase with increasing surfactant concentration, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. Adsorption of cationic surfactant onto the ink pigment particles and solubilization of ink binder molecules into surfactant micelles are important mechanisms causing ink removal from the plastic surface. © 2006 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Deinking; Alkyltrimethylammonium bromide; High-density polyethylene; Zeta potential; Solubilization

1. Introduction

Steady growth of demand in plastics leads to increasing demand for natural gas and petroleum as the raw materials for plastic production. An increase in the utilization of plastics translates into a steady growth of plastic wastes as a consequence. A means for dealing with such a problem is through recycling, but it has been reported that recycled plastics often bear poor physical and mechanical properties in comparison with those of virgin polymers [1,2]. For printed plastics, the presence of residual inks can be a primary cause of the deterioration of polymer properties. Previous work, for example, reported the deterioration effect of residual ink on physical properties of re-extruded polyethylene [3]. Therefore, removal of ink from the plastic surface prior to recycling is a prerequisite. Generally, ink can be removed by either physical [4] or chemical [3,5-7] means.

Chemically, ink can be removed by organic solvents, but, due to their toxicity, alternative deinking media are desirable. Due to their biodegradability, non-toxicity, and non-volatility, aqueous solutions of surfactants are considered good alternatives for such a task.

Previous studies on surfactant-based deinking process have been carried out on surfaces of either plastic films [3,5,7] or rigid plastics [6] in order to remove either water-based [3,5] or solvent-based [6,7] ink using an anionic surfactant [3], nonionic surfactants [3,5,7], an amphoteric surfactant [3,7], or cationic surfactants [3,6,7]. For either water- or solvent-based ink, cationic surfactants were the most effective in ink removal at concentrations well above their critical micelle concentration (CMC) and at high pH levels (generally greater than or equal to 11) [3,6,7]. Furthermore, increased temperature during deinking, increased pre-soaking time in the surfactant solutions prior to mechanical agitation, and increased shaking time helped increase deinking efficiency [5-7]. The cationic surfactants which have been previously investigated were hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB;

C16H33 + N(CH3)3Br -) [3,6,7] and hexadecylpyridinium chloride (CPC; C16H33 + N(C5H5)Cl -) [3], but CPC was found to degrade at high pH levels.

In the first paper of this series [8], we reported the use of three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively) to remove blue solvent-based ink from a printed surface of high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottles. All studies were carried out at a fixed temperature and pH of 30 °C and 12, respectively. Both the increase in the alkyl chain length and the surfactant concentration increased the deinking efficiency. Complete deinking was achieved at concentrations of about3,8,and24timesoftheCMCofCTAB,TTAB,andDTAB, respectively. For CTAB, ink removal began at a concentration close to its CMC and increased significantly at concentrations greater than its CMC, while, for TTAB and DTAB, significant deinking was only observed at concentrations much greater than their CMCs. Both the wettability of the surfactant on the ink surface and the solubilization of ink binder in the surfactant micelles increased with an increase in both the alkyl chain length and the surfactant concentration. Finally, we proposed a mechanism for the removal of a solvent-based ink from the HDPE surfaces as consisting of four main steps: (1) surfactant adsorption on both printed and unprinted HDPE surfaces; (2) solubilization of ink binder in micelles; (3) detachment of ink pigment from HDPE surfaces; (4) stabilization and dispersion of the detached ink particles.

In the present contribution, the effect of pH, temperature and addition of a simple salt, sodium chloride, on deinking for this same system using DTAB, TTAB and CTAB was studied. The effect of their concentration on zeta potential of ink particles and solubilization of ink binder pigment particles was investigated under different deinking conditions (i.e., pH 11-12; temperature = 30, 35, 40, and 45 °C; and addition of 0.1 M sodium chloride salt (NaCl)) from that performed in our previous work [8] (i.e., pH 12 and temperature = 30 °C).

2. Experimental details

2.1. Materials

High-density polyethylene (HDPE) sheet samples were obtained from commercial drinking water blow-molded bottles produced by SVB Drinking Water Company (Thailand). Printing of these bottles was done at CK-Plastic Company (Thailand). Prior to printing, the HDPE bottles were flame-treated. A blue solvent-based ink formulation (UPE-B4009/2) from Uni Ink Company (Thailand) was screen-printed on the treated HDPE surfaces. The printed parts of the bottles were then cut into 8 mm × 40 mm sheets.

N -dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide (DTAB) (99% purity; powder) and n -tetradecyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB) (98% purity; powder) were purchased from Aldrich (USA), while n -hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) (98% purity; powder) was purchased from Fluka (Switzerland). Sodium chloride (NaCl) was purchased from Aldrich (USA). Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) (98% purity), purchased from EKA Noble (Sweden), and hydrochloric acid (HCl) (AR grade), purchased from BHD (Germany), were used for pH adjustment. All of these chemicals were used as-received.

Ink powder was prepared by mixing the as-received ink with an appropriate solvent and the mixture was evenly pasted onto a 15 in. × 10 in. glass plate. The layer of ink was made as thin as possible to hasten the drying. The painted glass was later dried in an oven at 60 °Cover night, after which time the ink was scraped off from the glass surface, ground in a mortar, and finally sieved into powder of about 100 mesh or less (i.e., <150 𝛍 m). The asprepared ink powder was kept in a desiccator prior to further use. The chemical composition of the ink powder was investigated by a Fourier-transformed infrared spectrometer (FT-IR; Bruker Vector 3.0), operating at a resolution of 4 cm -1 and a frequency range of 4000-400 cm -1 .

2.2. Zeta potential measurement

Averysmallamountoftheas-preparedinkpowderwasadded into a CnTAB solution. The pH level of the mixture was adjusted to either 11 or 12 and the mixture was stirred for 24 h. The temperature of the mixture was equilibrated at 30 ± 1 °C. The as-prepared mixture was then transferred to an electrophoretic cell of a zeta meter (Zeta Meter, 3+), equipped with a microscope module. After applying a suitable voltage according to the solution conductivity, the time for any visible ink particle to move for a certain distance was measured. For a given data set, at least 20 ink particles were monitored, from which the average time was calculated. The average time was then used to calculate the average zeta potential value for that particular data set.

2.3. Deinking experiments

Toinvestigate the effects of alkyl chain length, surfactant concentration, pH, temperature, and salinity on deinking efficiency, DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB solutions were prepared at different concentrations, pH levels (i.e., between 11 and 12), temperatures (i.e., between 30 and 45 °C), and salinity (i.e., with or without 0.1 M NaCl). The as-prepared printed HDPE specimens were first pre-soaked (without shaking) in a 15 mL surfactant solution for 2 h and further soaked while being shaken at 200 cycles/min for another 2 h in a shaking water bath. Then, the specimens were washed with deionized water and later dried in open air at room temperature overnight. The amount of ink on the plastic before and after deinking was measured using the optical scanning method [6]. In this method, each plastic specimen was carefully positioned on and scanned by a HP ScanJet 4C optical scanner using the factory settings. The scanned files were analyzed by a copy of Adobe Photoshop 5.5 by counting the number of pixels (proportional to the amount of ink present) on the plastic surface. The amount of ink removed (%) was then calculated based on the following relationship [6]:

ink removed (%) = [ pixelsbefore deinking -pixelsafter deinking pixelsbefore deinking ]

2.4. Critical micelle concentration measurement

At 30 ± 1 °C, the critical micelle concentration (CMC) of pure DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB solutions was determined based onconductivity, using a conductivity meter (Orion, 125). Surface tension values, used to determine the CMC of the CnTAB solutions in the presence of 0.1 M NaCl, were measured by a drop shape analyzer (KR ¨ USS, DSA10-Mk2). The temperature was maintained at 30 ± 1 °C. For both surface tension and conductivity, the CMC is the surfactant concentration at which there is an abrupt change in the slope of the property values as a function of the surfactant concentration.

2.5. Solubilization measurement

Theconcentration of solubilized ink in CnTAB solutions with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl was indicated by first mixing 10 mg of the as-prepared ink powder in a 15 mL CnTAB solution at pH 12 in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask. The flask was then placed in a shaking water bath with the temperature of the water being varied between 30 and 45 °C and the shaking frequency of the sample stage being set at 200 cycles/min for 4 h. The solution was later filtered to remove undissolved ink particles using filter paper (Whatman no. 7402-001; average pore size = 0.2 𝛍 m). The UV absorbance of the filtrate was measured by a UV-visible spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, UV-2550) at a wavelength of 273.8 nm. The absorbance for accurate measurement is in the range of 0.1-0.8. If the sample solution showed an absorbance greater than this range, it was further diluted. The absorbance versus the concentration of CnTAB solutions is a qualitative measure for ink binder solubilization in the CnTAB solutions as increased absorbance corresponds to increased solubility of the binder in the surfactant solutions due to increased solubilization in micelles.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Zeta potential of ink

The effects of initial concentration and pH on zeta potential of ink in CnTAB solutions are shown in Fig. 1. For a given type of CnTAB solution, the zeta potential of ink pigment particle at pH 12 is consistently greater than that at pH 11 over the entire concentration range investigated. For a given pH, an increase in the initial concentration of the CnTAB solutions increases the zeta potential of ink pigment particles due mainly to the adsorption of the positively charged head groups of the CnTAB monomers onto the initially negatively charged ink pigment surfaces. This was possible because the point of zero charge (PZC) of the ink particles in water was observed at a pH of about 3.3 [8], which means that the ink particles exhibit a positive charge at pH < 3.3, while they are negatively charged when pH > 3.3. The particles became more negatively charged with increasing pH. As a result, the absorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink particles could occur much better at pH 12 than at pH 11, causing the particles to become more positively charged at pH 12. This 'charge reversal' effect is commonly observed when ionic surfactants adsorb onto oppositely charged solid surfaces. In the presence of cationic surfactants, the zeta potential reaches a plateau at approximately the CMC because surfactant adsorption onto solids levels off above the CMC due to the surfactant monomer concentration (and therefore thermodynamic activity) becoming constant when micelles form at or above the CMC.

Fig. 1. Zeta potential of ink in (a) CTAB, (b) TTAB, and (c) DTAB solutions as a function of concentration (in a linear scale) at pH levels of 11 and 12.

Fig. 2 shows the effects of alkyl chain length and pH on the zeta potential of ink pigment particles in CnTAB solutions. For a given initial concentration and pH of CnTAB solutions, the zeta potential of pigment increased with increasing alkyl chain length both below and above the CMC. The longer the alkyl chain length, the stronger the van der Waal interaction of the tail groups with the pigment surface [8], which, in turn, helps render more CnTAB monomers to adsorb onto the particles.

Fig. 3 shows the FT-IR spectrum of the solvent-based ink used in this study. A typical composition of screen-printing ink for HDPE bottles usually comprises 5% organic pigment, 11% titanium dioxide pigment, 82% epoxy resin, and 2% napthenate catalyst [9]. Since the majority of the ink formulation contains epoxy resin as the binder, it is expected that chemical fingerprints obtained in the FT-IR spectrum should belong to those of the epoxy resin. Normally, the epoxide group exhibits a weak C-H stretching peak around 3050-2990 cm -1 , while aromatic rings show absorption peaks over the wave number range of about 870-670 cm -1 [10]. According to Fig. 3, the absorption peak at about 3026 cm -1 and the absorption peaks at about 870-670 cm -1 were evident. Under the strongly basic condition of the deinking process, the cationic head groups of the CnTAB monomers can associate with the negative moieties of the epoxy molecules (due to the opening of the epoxide rings) via electrostatic interactions, thus enhancing the adsorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink surfaces [8], although the epoxy molecules are simultaneously being solubilized into micelles as will later be discussed, making the deinking process quite complex.

Fig. 2. Zeta potential of ink in CnTAB solutions as a function of concentration (in a semi-logarithmic scale) at pH levels of (a) 11 and (b) 12. Dashed lines refer to CMC values.

Fig. 3. FT-IR spectrum of ink powder.

Fig. 4. CMC of CnTAB solutions as a function of temperature.

The adsorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink pigment surfaces is driven by both electrostatic and van der Waal forces. Since the possibility for the formation of negatively-charged moieties of the epoxy binder and on the pigment (e.g., TiO2) surfaces themselves is greater at a higher pH, increasing the pH value also renders greater adsorption of CnTAB monomers onto the ink pigment surfaces. On the other hand, pH does not affect the van der Waal interactions between the tail groups of the adsorbed CnTABmonomersandthehydrophobicpartofthepigment surfaces greatly. In addition, the van der Waal interactions should increase with the length of the hydrophobic part of the CnTAB molecules. We cannot, however, differentiate between the adsorption of CTAB onto the pigment particles themselves or onto epoxy molecules attached to the pigment surface.

3.2. Critical micelle concentration

3.2.1. Effect of temperature

Plots of the CMC values of CnTAB solutions over a temperature range of 25-50 °C are illustrated in Fig. 4. The CMC of these CnTAB solutions increased very slightly with increasing temperature. Specifically, the CMC values increased from about 0.93 mM at 25 °C to about 1.28 mM at 50 °C for CTAB, from about 3.67 mM at 25 °C to about 4.06 mM at 50 °C for TTAB, and from about 16.1 mM at 25 °Cto about 17.8 mM at 50 °Cfor DTAB. This mild effect of temperature on CMC of ionic surfactants is commonly observed [11] and necessary to know in this work to interpret the temperature dependence of deinking.

3.2.2. Effect of salinity

TheCMCsofCnTABwithandwithout0.1MNaClareshown in Table 1. There is good agreement between the two methods of measurement except in one case where we will use the conductivity values in the absence of added NaCl since the change in the slope of the curve used to obtain the CMC is sharper in that case. The CMCs of CnTAB without NaCl addition were 0.96, 3.75 and 16.29 mM, for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively, whereas, in CnTAB solutions with 0.1 M NaCl, the CMCs were reduced to 0.04, 0.74 and 12.77 mM for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively. The reduction in the CMC with increasing alkyl chain length and the added electrolyte is well known for a cationic surfactant and the values shown here are quite in line with a similar system [11].

3.3. Solubilization

3.3.1. Effect of temperature

The effects of temperature and concentration on solubilization of epoxy binder from the ink in CnTAB solutions are shown in Fig. 5. The concentrations of the CTAB and TTAB solutions for solubilization studies were in the same ranges as those in the deinking experiments; i.e., 0.96-4.8 mM and 15.0-30.0 mM, respectively. For DTAB solutions however, the concentration range for the solubilization studies was very low (i.e., about 24.4-57.0 mM or about 1.5-3.5 × CMC) as compared to about 293-382 mM or about 18.0-23.5 × CMC used in the deinking experiments because high concentration of surfactant can solubilize essentially all epoxy molecules, so there is no effect of surfactant concentration at high concentrations.

text: In our previous work [8], solubilization studies were carried out at pH 12 and 30 °C. We found that the solubilization of ink binder in CnTAB micelles increased with an increase in both the alkyl chain length and the concentration of CnTAB. In this work, the temperature was varied between 30 and 45 °C. Apparently, for any given CnTAB concentration, the solubilization of ink binder within the micelles decreases with increasing temperature. Interestingly, the effect of temperature on the decrease in the solubilization of ink binder in CTAB micelles was more pronouncedathigher concentrations. The results could be explained based on the effect of temperature on the CMC values and the aggregation numbers of CnTAB. As mentioned earlier, a slight increase in the CMC values with increasing temperature is evident (see Fig. 5) and this leads to a smaller fraction of surfactant being in micelle form, however, this factor will have a small effect on solubilization capacity at the surfactant concentrations used here. An increase in the temperature causes the aggregation number to decrease [12,13]. The decreased aggregation number translates into less micellar volume that can accommodate solubilized ink binder [14].

Among the three surfactants investigated, the effect of temperature on solubilization of ink binder in TTAB solutions is more pronounced than for DTAB or CTAB. It is possible that the effect of the particular alkyl chain length of TTAB monomers affects the size of micelles more than CTAB and DTAB. It was reported that the size of TTAB micelles decreases with increasing temperature [13]. Specifically, the aggregation number of TTAB micelles decreases from about 157 at 5 °C to about 72 at 81 °C[14],whiletheCMCincreasesfromabout3.7 mMat20 °C to about 7.1 mM at 80 °C[15]. The decrease in the size of TTAB micelles with increasing temperature is relatively more important than those of CTAB and DTAB, as evidenced by greater temperature dependence of solubilization in TTAB.

3.3.2. Effect of salinity

The effect of NaCl addition on the solubilization of ink in CnTAB solutions is illustrated in Fig. 6. The experiments were carried out at pH 12 and 30 °C. For all surfactants, the addition of NaCl significantly improved the solubilization of ink binder. The difference in the solubilization of ink binder in CnTAB in comparison with that with NaCl salt addition was found to be more pronounced at higher CnTAB concentrations, except for DTAB. The addition of NaCl contributes two main effects regarding to the solubilization capacity of ink binder. First, it lowers the CMC, which results in the improvement in the solubilization capacity of ink binder at low surfactant concentrations. Second, the aggregation number is increased when NaCl is added.

Fig. 6. Solubilization capacity of ink components in (a) CTAB, (b) TTAB, and (c) DTAB solutions with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl at pH 12 and 30 °C as a function of concentration.

3.4. Deinking

3.4.1. Effect of pH

Fig. 7 shows the ink removal as a function of pH for different values of normalized CnTAB concentration (i.e., CnTAB concentration divided by corresponding CMC value). These measurements were carried out at a fixed temperature of 30 °C. Evidently, deinking is not possible in surfactant-free basic solutions. For a given type and concentration of CnTAB solutions, the amountofinkremovalincreasedmonotonicallywithincreasing pH of the solutions. For any given CnTAB concentration, the lowest pH value at which deinking began is about <11.0, <11.5, and 11.5 for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively. Significant deinking (i.e., at least 40% of ink removal) was observed at about 2 × CMC and pH of about 11.5 for CTAB, 6 × CMC and pH of about 11.8 for TTAB, and 16.5 × CMC and pH of about 11.7 for DTAB, respectively. Evidently, for a given pH, the amount of ink removal increased monotonically with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB. Fig. 7 also shows that complete deinking was observed at concentrations of about 4, 8, and 24 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively [8]. Clearly, the effect of pH on deinking is less pronounced with CnTAB having a longer alkyl chain length. As previously mentioned, longer alkyl chain length helps promote the adsorption of CnTAB monomers onto the ink pigment surfaces (as evidenced from the observed increase in the zeta potential of ink particles with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB; see Fig. 2) and adsorption of surfactant on both printed and unprinted HDPE surfaces is the first step in the deinking process of solvent-based ink from HDPE surfaces [8].

Fig. 7. Percentage of ink removal from printed HDPE surfaces in (a) CTAB, (b) TTAB, and (c) DTAB solutions at various normalized concentrations at 30 °C as a function of pH.

3.4.2. Effect of temperature

Fig. 8 shows the ink removal as a function of temperature for different values of normalized CnTAB concentration. These measurements were carried at a fixed pH of 12. Deinking is not significant in surfactant-free basic solutions at any temperature. The amount of ink removal decreases monotonically with increasing temperature for all surfactants and concentrations. ForCTAB,significantdeinking(i.e., at least 40% of ink removal) was observed at concentrations greater than about 1 × CMC when the temperature is 30 °C. At 35 °C, significant deinking is only observed at 5 × CMC. For TTAB, significant deinking is only observed at 30 °C, provided that the concentrations are greater than about 5 × CMC. For DTAB, at 30 °C, significant deinking is observed at all concentration ranges investigated. However, at 35 °C, significant deinking is only observed at a concentration of 22 × CMC or greater.

Fig. 8. Percentage of ink removal from printed HDPE surfaces in (a) CTAB, (b) TTAB, and (c) DTAB solutions at various normalized concentrations at pH 12 as a function of temperature.

The observed decrease in the deinking performance with increasing temperature is in accord with the observed decrease in the solubilization capacity of ink in CnTAB solutions with increasing temperature for all surfactants and concentrations.

Fig. 9. Percentage of ink removal from printed HDPE surfaces in CTAB solution with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl at pH 12 and 30 °C as a function of concentration: (a) on a normal scale and (b) on a normalized scale (i.e., concentration/CMC).

According to the four-step mechanism for the removal of solvent-based ink from the HDPE surfaces proposed in our previous work [8], solubilization of the ink binder in CnTAB micelles was postulated to be the most important step for deinking, a hypothesis which is supported by this subsequent work.

3.4.3. Effect of salinity

Figs. 9-11 show the removal of ink from HDPE surfaces in CTAB,TTAB,andDTABsolutions as function of concentration and normalized concentration with or without the addition of 0.1 M NaCl. These experiments were carried out at a fixed pH of 12 and a fixed temperature of 30 °C. Without the presence of the salt, complete deinking of printed HDPE surfaces was observed at about 2.9, 30, and 380 mM for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB, respectively. With the salt added, it was observed at about 1.5, 8.2, and 305 mM, respectively. The result indicated again that deinking efficiency increased with increasing alkyl chain length and salinity. Marked improvement in the deinking efficiency was obtained in the TTAB solutions when the salt was added into the solutions, while, in the cases of CTAB and DTAB, only marginal improvement was observed.

The significant improvement in the deinking performance of TTAB with salt addition over those of CTAB and DTAB can be explained based on the results from the solubilization studies (see Fig. 6), where the presence of NaCl increased the solubilization capacity of ink binder in the TTAB solutions in a much greater extent than it did with the CTAB and DTAB counterparts. For examples, at the concentration where CTAB solutions with added salt showed complete deinking (i.e., 1.5 mM), the solubilization capacity for that particular concentration was not very different from that when no salt was present (see Fig. 6a). On the other hand, for TTAB, at the concentration where complete deinking was observed in the presence of salt (i.e., 8.2 mM), the solubilization capacity for that particular concentration was far greater than that when no salt was added (see Fig. 6b). Based on these observations, the observed significant improvement in the deinking efficiency of TTAB solutions in comparison with the other two surfactants is reasonable.

Fig. 10. Percentage of ink removal from printed HDPE surfaces in TTAB solution with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl at pH 12 and 30 °Cas a function of concentration: (a) on a normal scale and (b) on a normalized scale (i.e., concentration/CMC).

Fig. 11. Percentage of ink removal from printed HDPE surfaces in DTAB solution with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl at pH 12 and 30 °Cas a function of concentration: (a) on a normal scale and (b) on a normalized scale (i.e., concentration/CMC).

If we are to consider the deinking performance as a function of normalized concentration with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl, it is obvious that, without the presence of salt, complete deinking was observed at a concentration equivalent to about 3, 8, and 23.5 × CMCfor CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB, respectively. On the other hand, with the presence of salt, complete deinking was observed at about 40, 11, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively. Apparently, with or without the presence of salt, complete deinking was only observed at concentrations greater than the CMC for all surfactant solutions studied.

4. Conclusions

The present contribution investigates the effects of pH, temperature, and salinity on the removal of solvent-based ink from high-density polyethylene (HDPE) surfaces based on the use of three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively). The critical micelle concentration (CMC) values of these surfactant solutions was found to increase very slightly with increasing temperature and decreased significantly with the addition of 0.1 M NaCl. Ink removal was found to increase with increasing concentration, increasing pH, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. The zeta potential of ink became more positively charged with increasing pH as well as concentration and alkyl chain length of CnTAB, suggesting that the adsorption of CnTAB molecules on ink pigment occurred more readily with an increase in any of those parameters. The solubilization of epoxy ink binder was found to increase with increasing surfactant concentration, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. Without the NaCl salt addition, complete deinking was observed at a concentration equivalent to about 3, 8, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB, respectively, while, with the salt addition, it was observed at about 40, 11, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively.

Computational methods in solution-based plastics purification

Ali Altamimi 1 and Reid C Van Lehn 1,2

Plastic waste can be recycled into resins with near-virgin properties by solution-based purification processes that selectively dissolve polymers, remove contaminants, or detach printing residues. In this review, we examine computational methods for predicting the behavior governing solution-based plastic purification, motivated by the vast polymer-solvent-contaminant compositional space. We discuss thermodynamic and machine learning methods for predicting polymer-solvent and polymer-contaminant interaction and review physics-based molecular dynamics simulations that resolve molecular-scale phenomena within polymer matrices inaccessible to screening methods. We highlight how these methods have informed experimental design for dissolution-based recycling and solvent-based contaminant removal. Finally, we discuss the prospective role of agentic AI in integrating these computational tools with real-time sorting data to adapt purification conditions to the compositional variability of real post-consumer feedstocks. This review charts a path toward computationally guided solutionbased purification workflows that can respond to the complexity

inherent in plastic waste streams.

Introduction

Recycling post-consumer plastic waste to produce polymer  resins  with  properties  comparable  to  virgin materials remains a challenge that is essential to achieving circularity in the plastics industry [1-4]. The underlying difficulty stems  from  the complexity  of plastic waste streams, which include numerous polymers and  difficult-to-remove  components  introduced  during manufacturing  and  end  use.  For  example,  multilayer films  present a  compatibility  issue upon  remelting that degrades the mechanical properties of recyclates, while printing  residues,  which  contain  polymer  binders  and pigments, compromise both the mechanical and optical properties  of  the  final  recyclate  [2,5].  Plastic  waste  can also  contain  intentionally  and  non-intentionally  added substances (which we refer to as contaminants) that are persistent, bioaccumulative, or toxic, restricting the use of  contaminated recyclates in applications such as food packaging [6,7].

Addressing these limitations has motivated the develop ment of solution-based purification approaches, in which plastic  waste  is  contacted  with  a  liquid  medium  to  se lectively remove or recover target components (Figure 1) [4,5,8-10]. Solvent-based washing, exemplified by Norec ® ,  can  remove  inks  and  leach  non-volatile  con taminants from a swollen polymer matrix [8,9]. Aqueous surfactant  washing,  employed  by  companies  like  Cadel Deinking (now KEYCYCLE) and Sorema, targets printing  residue  removal  [8-10].  Dissolution-based  re cycling recovers purified polymer resins without chemical degradation and can separate the individual polymers in multilayer  films,  as  demonstrated  by  processes  such  as CreaSolv ® ,  Newcycling ® ,  PureCycle ® ,  and  Solvent-Tar geted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP™) [4,11]. The feasibility,  selectivity,  and  scalability  of  these  processes are  governed  by  molecular-scale  interactions  between plastics, contaminants, and the liquid medium [4]. Iden tifying  optimal  process  conditions,  however,  is  challen ging due to the vast polymer-solvent-contaminant compositional  space,  the  inherent  complexity  of  poly meric  materials,  and  the  variability  of  real  feedstocks, motivating the development of computational methods to navigate this design space.

In this review, we examine computational approaches for understanding  and  predicting  the  thermodynamic  be havior  that  governs  solution-based  plastic  purification. We begin with thermodynamic methods for predicting polymer-solvent-contaminant interactions, including machine learning  (ML)  approaches  for  accelerating  so lubility  predictions  and  property  screening  across  large chemical spaces. Computational methods for predicting polymer dissolution

A  first  challenge  in  a  solution-based  plastic  purification process is solvent selection, which requires the prediction of polymer-solvent interactions. Polymers present unique thermodynamic complexities arising from their high mo lecular  weights,  polydispersity,  chain  connectivity,  and conformational flexibility, which complicate the definition of representative molecular structures for thermodynamic calculations [12,13]. For semicrystalline polymers, an ad ditional solid-state reference contribution to the dissolu tion free energy, requiring knowledge of melting temperature and enthalpy of fusion,  must  be  accounted for, which can vary depending on resin type [14].

Semi-empirical  approaches,  including  Hildebrand  and Hansen  solubility  parameter  models  and  Flory-Huggins theory, have traditionally been used to quantify polymersolvent  compatibility  using  a  small  set  of  descriptors [15-18]. While simple and widely used, with parameters available in established databases, these methods achieve only moderate predictive accuracy; for example, a recent study  found  that  Hansen  solubility  parameters  correctly identify good and nonsolvents in 67% and 76% of cases, respectively [18]. Equation of state (EOS) models, parti cularly perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT),  offer  improved  treatment  of  temperatureand pressure-dependent polymer-solvent thermo dynamics,  but  require  experimentally  fitted  parameters that  must  be  refit  for  novel  systems  or  chemically  com plex mixtures [19]. COSMO-RS (Conductor-like Screening  Model  for  Real  Solvents)  addresses  this  lim itation by leveraging quantum-chemically derived charge densities  to  calculate  activity  coefficients,  from  which solubility,  miscibility,  and  partition  coefficients  can  be obtained [20]. Recent approaches have used COSMO-RS to  predict  the  solubilities  of  polymers,  biopolymers,  and biomass  materials  [21,22].  For  example,  Zhou  et  al.  de veloped a temperature-dependent solubility database by combining  conformational  sampling  based  on  all-atom (AA)  MD  simulations  with  COSMO-RS  calculations using  experimental  thermal  data  to  approximate  the  fu sion free energy of the polymer resin [11,14,23]. COSMORS polymer predictions were found to accurately predict activity  coefficients  across  a  range  of  molecular  weights, provided that MD-sourced conformers having undergone DFT  optimization  with  a  small  basis  set  are  used  to generate  realistic σ -profiles  that  accurately  capture  the residual  chemical  potential  and  that  the  combinatorial contribution,  a  separate  additive  term  derived  from  mo lecular volume, is included [12].

ML models offer the ability to screen polymer-solvent interactions across large chemical spaces at low compu tational cost once trained on sufficient data. ML efforts have been reviewed [17] and span a range of prediction targets from Hildebrand solubility parameters [18,24,25] to  binary  good  solvent/non-solvent  classification  using deep  learning  [26,27] and  large  language  models  [28]. While  these  approaches  are  useful  for  many  screening applications,  they  may  not  be  suitable  for  applications requiring  more  detailed  thermodynamic  information, such  as  temperature-dependent  solubility.  Other  pre dictions  have  pushed  toward  more  experimentally  re levant outputs like cloud-point temperatures [13], weight-based  infinite  dilution  activity  coefficients  [29], and PC-SAFT EOS parameters that enable full polymer-solvent  phase  equilibria  calculations  [19].  Ad ditionally,  efforts  have  standardized  polymer  solubility experiments  and  tested  multiple  concentrations  to  en able classification of soluble, insoluble, and partially so luble polymer-solvent combinations [30].

Recently,  these  computational  methods  have  been  ap plied to choose solvents for dissolution-based plastics re cycling. Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) have guided  solvent  selection  for  polyethylene  (PE),  poly propylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene  (ABS),  polyethylene  terephthalate  (PET),  poly vinyl  chloride  (PVC),  and  ethylene-vinyl  acetate  (EVA) solvent-based  recycling  processes  [31-33].  For  example, in single-polymer dissolution-precipitation recycling, HSPs were used to identify an acetone-water system for ABS recovery  from  toy  waste  and  biobased  solvents  for rigid  PVC  recycling  [32,33].  Similarly,  COSMO-RS  has been applied to screen candidate solvents for dissolutionbased recycling of PET, PS, PVC, ABS, and high density polyethylene (HDPE), including virtual screening of over 9000  ionic  liquids  for  PET  dissolution,  identification  of selective  solvents  for  PVC  removal  from  mixed  waste streams, and optimization of dissolution-precipitation processes for PS and ABS recovery from e-waste [34-36]. This  approach  has  been  applied  extensively  for  the STRAP  process,  where  COSMO-RS  enabled  selective sequential dissolution of  PE, ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH),  and  PET  from  one  another  in  commercial multilayer  films  with  near-complete  material  recovery [11].  An  expanded polymer solubility database was sub sequently applied to printed films containing poly urethane inks, biopharmaceutical bags,  postconsumer shrink-wrap, and post-industrial mixed plastic waste containing up to ten polymers [14,23,37-39].

Several  critical  gaps  remain  to  broaden  the  utility  of computational  methods  for  solvent  selection.  From  a thermodynamic perspective, many current models treat the effect of molecular weight on polymer-solvent thermodynamics  using  simplified  or  monodisperse  re presentations,  limiting  their  accuracy  for  polydisperse industrial  polymers  whose  molecular  weight  distribu tions  can  span  orders  of  magnitude  [12,13].  Extending these  models  to  solvent  mixtures,  where  phenomena such as preferential solvation and cosolvency effects in troduce  complexity,  and  to  polymer  mixtures,  where dissolved  polymers  alter  solvent  quality,  could  also  in crease  opportunities  to  tune  selectivity,  reduce  cost,  or enable  greener  solvent  systems  [40-42].  Beyond  ther modynamics, computational studies should continue to address kinetic factors, such as dissolution rates and so lution viscosity, as well as precipitation phenomena like crystallization and physical gel formation [31,40,43-45]. Addressing these challenges will require closer integration  of  molecular  and  process  models,  ML  ap proaches that leverage computational descriptors to generalize  beyond  limited  experimental  datasets,  and systematic experimental data collection performed with predictive modeling in mind.
Computational methods for predicting contaminant removal thermodynamics

Whereas dissolution-based processes remove a con taminant  polymer  by  selectively  dissolving  it  from  the target resin, purification also requires removing nonpolymer  contaminants  such  as  additives,  plasticizers,  and printing  residues.  Similar  computational  methods  have been applied to guide solvent-based washing processes for contaminant removal, in which the solvent swells but does not  dissolve  the  polymer,  allowing  contaminants  to  leach into the solvent phase [8,36,46]. This process is governed by  solubility  and  diffusivity:  the  partitioning  of  the  con taminant  into  the  solvent  should  be  thermodynamically favorable,  and  the  migration  of  the  contaminant  through the swollen polymer matrix must proceed at a practical rate [36,46].  HSPs  have  been  applied  to  guide  solvent  selec tion, with the Relative Energy Difference (RED), defined as the Hansen distance (Ra) normalized by the interaction radius R0 (RED=Ra/R0), used to predict partitioning; sol vents  whose  parameters  fall  close  to  those  of  the  target contaminant  are  expected  to  yield  higher  extraction  effi ciency,  while  the  solvent's  RED  with  respect  to  the polymer  is  kept  above  1  so  that  it  does  not  dissolve [35,36,46].  A  combined  computational  approach  was  de veloped  for  the  removal  of  brominated  flame  retardants (BFRs)  from  ABS  plastic,  which  used  HSPs  to  identify candidate solvents that dissolve the BFR while leaving the polymer intact [36].  Similarly,  Zhou  et  al.  extended  their COSMO-RS-based  screening  framework  to  predict  con taminant  partition  coefficients  (LogP)  between  a  solvent phase and a polymer phase, enabling solvent selection for both  contaminant  leaching  and  contaminant  removal  in tegrated into the STRAP process [46].

These  limited  studies  highlight  potential  opportunities for  computational  methods  to  predict  contaminant  re moval,  but  several  challenges  point  to  important  oppor tunities  for  future  work.  First,  the  chemical  space  of potential  contaminants  is  vast;  the  PlastChem  database catalogs over 16 000 chemicals associated with plastics, of which over 4000 are hazardous, highlighting the need to combine  thermodynamic  methods  with  ML  approaches capable of rapidly screening conditions that better control the removal of families of contaminants [6]. Second, while these  methods  focus  on  the  thermodynamics  of  con taminant removal, contaminant removal is also governed by kinetic factors such as diffusion through polymer ma trices  [47,48].  Empirical  diffusivity  models  have  been used to estimate migration of contaminants in food con tact applications, demonstrating that diffusion coefficients decrease  with  increasing  migrant  molecular  weight,  in crease  exponentially  with  temperature,  and  depend  on polymer  chain  flexibility  [8,49].  However,  studies  ap plying these techniques to plastic contaminants are lim ited.  Third,  larger  contaminants  such  as  TiO2 pigment particles  are  not  well  described  by  thermodynamic  fra meworks  that  do  not  account  for  colloidal  interactions [32,50]. Fourth, these methods do not capture interfacial phenomena,  such  as  the  detachment  of  contaminants from polymer surfaces, which are central to processes like ink  removal  and  delamination  [10].  These  limitations motivate  the  use  of  particle-based  simulation  methods, which can provide mechanistic insight into contaminant removal  while  also  informing  process  optimization  stra tegies, such as surfactant selection for aqueous de-inking.
Molecular methods for mechanistic insights

Physics-based  MD  simulations  complement  thermo dynamic and ML-based approaches by directly resolving the molecular-scale structural and dynamic phenomena governing  processes  such  as  solvent  penetration,  con taminant  diffusion,  and  other  interfacial  interactions [51,52].  In  AA  MD  simulations,  every  atom  is  re presented explicitly with its own interaction parameters defined by a force field [53], which makes certain solu tion-based  recycling  phenomena  computationally  in feasible to model. For example, it has been established that molecular simulations are limited in their ability to capture dissolution kinetics due to the length and time scales  of  atomistic  models;  the  physics  of  polymer  dis solution has been reviewed in detail elsewhere [51,54]. AA MD simulations have been applied to more tractable phenomena in solution-based plastics purification, such as the penetration of polymers by solvents, a process that precedes  polymer  dissolution  [55].  Studies  have  also used  molecular  simulations  to  predict  the  leaching  of additives  and  plasticizers  from  polymers  [56].  While contaminant removal is dictated by solvent penetration and  additive  leaching,  MD  has  seen  limited  use  in guiding  solvent  selection  for  this  application;  recent work  has  compared  candidate  solvents  for  separating additives  from  PVC  [57],  but  capturing  these  relation ships  across  the  broad  range  of  relevant  polymers  and contaminants continues to present modeling challenges.

Coarse-grained  (CG)  MD  simulations  group  atoms  into effective  'beads'  to  access  longer  timescales  and  larger length scales while retaining a semi-quantitative level of accuracy. For example, the MARTINI CG model maps groups  of ∼ 4  heavy  atoms  onto  beads  and  has  enabled systematic  CG  modeling  of  a  broad  range  of  polymer systems  [58].  CG  simulations  have  been  valuable  for studying  slow  transport  and  interfacial  phenomena,  in cluding  plasticizer  migration  in  PVC  [59],  solvent  diffu sion  in  PS  dissolution  [52],  solvent  swelling  of  polymer brushes  [60],  and  solvent  evaporation  from  polymercontaining  systems  [61],  where  the  extended  timescales accessible at the CG level are essential to capturing the underlying  physics.  The  behavior  of  contaminants  as medium-sized molecules embedded in polymer matrices has  also  been  investigated  [62,63],  including  leaching dynamics  that  are  relevant  to  contaminant  removal  in recycling  contexts  [64].  Beyond  transport  phenomena, CG simulations  have  been  coupled  with  the  PC-SAFT EOS to better describe complex phase behavior [65], and have  been  used  to  characterize  polymer-solvent  inter facial  structure  [66].  CG  approaches  have  recently  been extended  to  surfactant-mediated  de-inking,  a  pretreat ment  process  in  which  ground  plastics  are  washed  in surfactant solutions to remove printing inks from singlelayer  films  and  rigid  materials  [10].  Altamimi  et  al.  le veraged  CG  MD  simulations  to  quantify  binder  deso rption free energies in the presence  of a range of surfactants,  demonstrating  that  charged  surfactants  re duce the energy barrier for binder desorption to achieve increased  experimental  de-inking  efficiency  [67].  These results  provide  molecular-level  guidance  for  surfactant selection and motivate future studies to consider pigment dispersibility  in  surfactant  micelles,  corona  treatment  of polymer surfaces, and a broader range of binder types.

Together, these studies provide a foundation for modeling dissolution-precipitation  behavior  and  the  interfacial  phe nomena  that  govern  solvent-based  purification  processes. Looking ahead, performing AA or CG MD simulations at higher throughput could enable predictions of contaminant removal  or  de-inking  efficiency  to  optimize  formulations for  solvent  washing,  and  could  potentially  be  combined with  ML  methods  to  explore  associated  design  spaces using  physics-based  descriptors.  To  date,  however,  MD studies  of  solvent-based  purification  have  focused  largely on  conventional  organic  solvents.  Ionic  liquids  and  deep eutectic  solvents  remain  comparatively  underexplored  in this context, even though explicit simulations have begun

Integration of computational predictions in plastics purification

In the preceding sections, we highlighted computational methods  that  can  screen  large  libraries  of  polymers, solvents, and contaminants and demonstrated their use in informing process design. A potential opportunity for future development is the integration of these methods with  AI  to  process  real-world  feedstocks.  Agentic  AI systems, in which autonomous AI agents plan and exe cute multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention, are  well-suited  for  these  challenges  [71,72].  Such  sys tems can orchestrate the computational tools discussed in  this  review  alongside  real-time  sensor  data  and  ex ternal regulatory information, enabling process re commendations that adapt to variable feedstock compositions and evolving contaminant regulations. To illustrate  this  vision,  we  consider how agentic AI could be  integrated  across  the  plastics  recycling  process,  in cluding sorting at advanced materials recycling facilities (MRFs), pretreatment, and reprocessing (Figure 2).

MRFs separate commingled recyclables and sort plastics into commodity bales [73]. Advances in near-IR imaging, AI-assisted  robotic  sorting,  and  complementary  spectro scopic  methods  now  enable  near-real-time  identification of polymer type and, increasingly, chemical contaminants in waste streams [74-76]. These techniques are well es tablished  for  single-layer  plastics,  while  identification  of multilayer  materials  is  more  challenging  and  remains  an area of active development [77]. Coupling these detection capabilities  with  the  thermodynamic  and  ML  tools  dis cussed above could help assess whether a contaminated feedstock  requires  additional  purification,  thereby  in tegrating upstream contaminant identification with downstream process selection. For example, detection of regulated  contaminants  could  flag  a  feedstock  for  a  tar geted solvent-based leaching step, heavily printed plastics could  be  routed  to  aqueous  washing,  while  relatively clean  feedstocks  proceed  with  venting-only  mechanical recycling.  Complementary  modeling  of  chemical  migra tion through food contact materials could further inform pretreatment  by  predicting  migration  rates  through  dif ferent  polymers  [78].  More  broadly,  the  rich  material characterization data generated by these sensing systems creates  an  opportunity  for  agentic  frameworks that  relay feedstock  information  downstream  and  adaptively  re commend process adjustments to recycling and purifica tion conditions in response to material variability.

Downstream of  automated  sorting  and  contaminant  iden tification,  adaptive  process  control  could  guide  decisionmaking  across  recycling  approaches,  though  its  feasibility varies substantially with process complexity. This has been pursued  in  mechanical  recycling  through  real-time  spec troscopic  analysis  and  in-line  melt  rheometry  to  adjust processing parameters in response to feedstock varia bility  [79,80];  however,  such  control  is  constrained  to  a narrow  range  of  process  parameters.  In  dissolution-based recycling, adaptive approaches are a more challenging pro spect due to cost and safety constraints, but agentic process design with human oversight could align solvent selection, temperature,  and  processing  time  with  incoming  polymer composition and contamination state. For contaminant re moval, thermodynamic frameworks could be integrated into agentic  workflows  that  autonomously  screen  new  con taminant  chemistries  and  recommend  process  conditions for adaptive, feedstock-aware purification.

To  our  knowledge,  no  integrated  agentic  system  cur rently  exists  that  connects  upstream  feedstock  char acterization with downstream process optimization across any plastics recycling pathway. However, the de ployment  of  AI  agents  in  chemical  engineering  is  ac celerating, with companies beginning to integrate agentic  AI  platforms  into  plant  operations,  and  ex tending these approaches to recycling facilities re presents a promising future direction [71].

Conclusion

Solution-based  plastics  purification  encompasses  a  broad and interconnected set of challenges, ranging from selec tive  dissolution  for  separating  polymers  in  multilayer  and mixed-plastic  waste,  to  solvent-  and  aqueous-based  con taminant  removal,  that  benefit  from  a  combination  of computational approaches to accurately guide process de sign.  Thermodynamic  approaches  such  as  COSMO-RS provide  accurate  predictions  of  polymer-contaminant-sol vent  interactions,  molecular  simulations  reveal  the  me chanistic detail of interfacial and transport phenomena that screening-level  methods  cannot  access,  and  ML  models offer  the  throughput  needed  to  navigate  vast  chemical spaces when adequate training data is available. Refining these methods, however, requires broader standardization of  condition-resolved  experimental  datasets,  molecularweight-dependent  solubility  predictions  for  polydisperse industrial  polymers,  more  broadly  applicable  contaminant leaching models for swollen polymer matrices, and higherthroughput,  physically  realistic  simulation  frameworks  to guide the rational design of surfactant formulations. Looking  forward,  integrating  upstream  sensing,  thermo dynamic  screening,  and  agentic  AI  frameworks  into  uni fied, feedstock-adaptive workflows, with appropriate human oversight,  offers  a  promising  path  toward  compu tational  guidance  that  can  better  accommodate  the  varia bility inherent in real post-consumer plastic waste streams.

Screening the Impact of Surfactants and Reaction Conditions on the De-Inkability of Different Printing Ink Systems for Plastic Packaging

Jinyang Guo 1, *, Cong Luo 1 , Christian Wittkowski 2 , Ingo Fehr 2 , Zhikai Chong 1 , Magdalena Kitzberger 1 , Ayah Alassali 1 , Xuezhi Zhao 3 , Ralf Leineweber 2 , Yujun Feng 3 and Kerstin Kuchta 1, *

2 Siegwerk Druckfarben AG_Co.KGaA, Alfred-Keller-Str. 55, 53721 Siegburg, Germany

3 Polymer Research Institute, State Key Laboratory of Polymer Materials Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu 610065, China

Correspondence: jy.guo@tuhh.de (J.G.); kuchta@tuhh.de (K.K.); Tel.: +49-40-428783108 (J.G.); +49-40-428783054 (K.K.)

Abstract: One of the major applications (40% in Europe) of plastic is packaging, which is often printed to display required information and to deliver an attractive aesthetic for marketing purposes. However, printing ink can cause contamination in the mechanical recycling process. To mitigate this issue, the use of surfactants in an alkaline washing process, known as de-inking, has been employed to remove printing ink and improve the quality of recyclates. Despite the existence of this technology, there are currently no data linking the de-inking efficiency with typical printing ink compositions. Additionally, it is necessary to investigate the de-inking process under the process parameters of existing recycling plants, including temperature, NaOH concentration, and retention time. This study aims to evaluate the performance of commonly used printing inks with different compositions under various washing scenarios for plastic recycling in conjunction with different de-inking detergents containing surfactants or mixtures of surfactants. The results indicate that the pigments applied to the ink have no significant effect on the de-inking process, except for carbon black (PBk 7). Nitrocellulose (NC) binder systems exhibit high de-inkability (over 95%) under the condition of 55 °C and 1 wt.% NaOH. However, crosslinked binder systems can impede the de-inking effect, whether used as a binder system or as an overprint varnish (OPV). The de-inking process requires heating to 55 °C with 1 wt.% NaOH to achieve a substantial effect. Based on the findings in this work, breaking the Van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, and covalent bonds between the printing ink and plastic film is an essential step to achieve the de-inking effect. Further research is needed to understand the interaction between surfactants and printing inks, enabling the development of de-inkable printing inks and high-performance surfactants that allow for de-inking with less energy consumption. The surfactant and NaOH have a synergistic effect in cleaning the printing ink. NaOH provides a negative surface charge for the adsorption of the cationic head of the surfactant and can hydrolyze the covalent bonds at higher concentrations (>2 wt.%).

1. Introduction

According to recent statistics, the global consumption of plastic exceeded 400 Mio. Mg in 2019, while nearly the same amount was generated as plastic waste [1]. In Europe, the annual plastic consumption was reported to be 50 Mio. Mg in 2020, with 40% being used for packaging applications [2]. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) accounted for 8.8 Mio. Mg/a and most of it was used in the form of a flexible film [3]. Other polymers (e.g., high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polypropylene (PP)) can also be converted into flexible packaging such as pouches, bags, sleeves, and labels [2,4,5].
