Methods

Rationale and conceptual considerations

We built a comprehensive and globally applicable inventory of all known plastics chemicals and developed an innovative framework combining hazard and grouping components with the aim to facilitate a transition towards safer plastics. We define plastic chemicals as all chemicals that can be present in plastic materials and products, including the polymer backbone, intentionally added substances (that is, starting substances, processing aids and additives) and NIASs (for example, impurities, unreacted intermediates, reaction by-products and degradation products). The fact that some plastic chemicals may have additional uses in non-plastic applications has no bearing on their inclusion. Contaminants sorbing to plastics during use or end-of-life are not considered plastic chemicals. See complete definitions in Supplementary Text 1.

To identify chemicals of concern in plastics, we developed and applied a hazard-based approach. In brief, we classified a plastic chemical as of concern on the basis of the criteria of persistence, bioaccumulation, mobility and toxicity. The rationale for taking this approach is threefold. First, we argue that plastics should not contain hazardous chemicals, to protect human health and the environment. Although this approach might be considered conservative, it enables scientists and businesses to improve the safety of plastics and proactively prevent potential harm in a timely and efficient manner. Second, we posit that exposure to most plastic chemicals is probable given that most are not covalently bound to the polymer. This is backed by empirical evidence showing that 83% of the 1,788 chemicals tested for release from plastic food contact materials indeed migrate into foodstuff 17,25 . Third, we reason that an alternative risk-based approach is neither efficient nor effective-and often infeasible-to identify chemicals of concern owing to numerous practical challenges, blind spots and high implementation costs that would unduly delay a transition to safer plastics.

Apart from the identification of chemicals of concern, we collected additional evidence on the use, presence and release of plastic chemicals. We use this information to link chemicals to specific polymer types, shed light on which compounds are intentionally added to plastics (commercial use) and infer their exposure potential. Although the last of these is only qualitative, it suggests that human and environmental exposures to these chemicals are probable, given that scientific studies demonstrate their migration or volatilization into foodstuff or environmental media.

We grouped plastic chemicals on the basis of their structure to efficiently address chemicals of concern as well as regrettable 'drop-in' substitutions (that is, replacing a chemical of concern with a structurally very similar compound). We assumed a chemical without hazard data is 'guilty by association' if it is part of a group that consists of many known chemicals of concern. This is supported by ample evidence available for certain groups, such as bisphenols 50 , as well as the fact that the structure of a chemical determines its hazards. In combination with the hazard-based approach, such chemical grouping offers a robust framework to improve the chemical safety of plastics in a timely and efficient manner.

Building the PlastChem inventory

We built the PlastChem inventory by: compiling and harmonizing information from seven prior databases; retrieving additional and updated information on hazard classifications and regulatory status from 15 authoritative sources (latest update August 2023) to identify chemicals of concern; integrating data on the use, detection and release of chemicals in and from plastics; and grouping the chemicals on the basis of their structure (Extended Data Fig. 1). All data engineering work was performed using R (R Consortium, 2023) and Microsoft Excel (see Data and Code availability).

Core of the PlastChem inventory

We compiled and harmonized information from prior databases that had identified chemicals in plastics, relying on six peer-reviewed and one regulatory source. As a first step, we retrieved lists of plastic chemicals from seven sources, including: the dataset of ref. 27; the database of Chemicals associated with Plastic Packaging (CPPdb, version 1) 28 ; the European Union (EU) list of Authorized Substances Annex I, Plastic Food Regulation 10/2011/EU (PFCRdb) 31 ; the Food Contact Chemicals database (FCCdb, version 5) 29 ; the PlasticMAP dataset 26 ; the dataset on Migrating and Extractable Food Contact Chemicals (FCCmigex, version February 2023) 17 ; and the LitChemPlast dataset (version June 2023) 25 . Given the scale of the results, we deemed verifying the original sources not feasible and accepted the entries in the seven databases as plastic chemicals.

To identify chemical structures, compile data from various sources and assemble the inventory, we used CAS RNs or chemical names (when CAS RNs were invalid or unavailable) with the automatic Application Programming Interface services of PubChem. The information retrieved included the PubChem Compound Identification (CID), molecular formula, molecular weight, canonical SMILES, isomeric SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, IUPAC name, predicted octanol/water partition coefficient (XLogP), exact mass, monoisotopic mass, topological polar surface area, complexity and charge. CAS RNs were validated according to CAS guidelines 51 . Further details are available in Supplementary Text 2.

Despite thorough quality assurance and control, some uncertainties may remain in the inventory (Supplementary Text 2). For example, 400 duplicates were identified, originating from the use of multiple names for the same chemical or from non-unique CAS RNs that correspond to multiple substances. These duplicates are shown in an additional file in the inventory. Of these, 188 chemicals were manually selected by expert judgement for inclusion in the main inventory, as they were deemed the most likely matches for the corresponding CAS RNs. Although we validated and curated the CAS RNs to reduce duplication, additional duplicates may still exist.

Information on functions and regulation

Additional information on the known functions of plastic chemicals and their regulatory status is also included in the PlastChem inventory. Briefly, the functions were gathered from ref. 27, CPPdb 28 and PlasticMAP 26 , aligned to a common terminology and assigned larger functional classes (starting substances, additives, processing aids and NIASs). See further details in Supplementary Text 3.

To integrate regulatory information, we compiled information from the Basel, Stockholm and Minamata Conventions, along with the Montreal Protocol, to identify the chemicals globally regulated under Multilateral Environmental Agreements at present. In addition, we also included regional and national lists of chemicals that were easily accessible, including chemicals regulated in the EU, Japan, the Republic of Korea and the USA, along with those substances regulated under the Rotterdam Convention. See further details in Supplementary Text 6.

Identification of chemicals of concern

Hazard information was collected from 15 regulatory sources, some of which aligned with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling (Supplementary Table 4). This information is consistent with the principles outlined in the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability 52 and the updated Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures regulation 36 . We did not include hazard information from the scientific literature because relevant studies are either already synthesized in the regulatory sources or would require individual quality assessment, data extraction and analysis. Accordingly, we consider the regulatory sources used as authoritative.

We applied a stepwise process to harmonize the compiled hazard information and translate it into a single hazard score per chemical. First, chemicals with hazard data for a specific trait (for example, carcinogenicity) were assigned a score ranging from 0 to 2, with 0 indicating non-hazardous, 0.5 indicating less hazardous, 1 indicating hazardous, and 2 indicating very hazardous (Supplementary Table 5). Chemicals with hazard evaluations under development, postponed or pending received a score of 0.25 to reflect that these are undergoing assessment but have not been classified yet. A blank indicates that no information is available. In cases of multiple classifications per source, we used the highest scores for each trait, with regulatory information taking precedence over industry data. As a second step, we aggregated the individual scores per trait into a single score for each hazard criterion (P, B, M and T) using the highest score whenever multiple traits within a criterion had information, retaining the 0-2 scoring system as described above. Finally, the maximum score across the P, B, M and T criteria resulted in a unique hazard score for each chemical that we used to identify chemicals of concern when the score was ≥1, indicating that a chemical of concern fulfils at least one hazard criterion. Additionally, we calculated the sum of hazard scores across the P, B, M and T criteria, ranging from 0 to 8, and provide an evidence score reflecting the number of sources that classify a chemical as hazardous for the same criterion, ranging from 0 to 31. Further details are available in Supplementary Text 4.

Use, presence and release information

We compiled and harmonized data on the use, presence and release of chemicals in plastic polymers from FCCmigex 17 , PlasticMAP 26 and LitChemPlast 25 . Presence data were derived from studies performing extraction experiments (for example, with solvents); release data came from studies performing migration experiments (for example, with food simulants). Chemicals with release data were assigned a score of 2, and those with only presence data received a score of 1. Data on the commercial use of plastic chemicals were sourced from PlasticMAP and given lower priority (score of 0.5 if no presence or release data are available). Chemicals with inconclusive information were scored 0.25, and substances that were analysed but not detected in experimental studies were scored 0. Finally, chemicals without data received a blank. See Supplementary Text 5 for further details.

Grouping and groups of concern

Plastic chemicals were grouped on the basis of their structures following two approaches (details in Supplementary Text 7). In brief, the first approach consisted of searching a predefined set of keys in the chemical names to identify inorganic compounds, organometallics and metalorganics, UVCBs, polymers and mixtures. This was followed by searching the name and chemical symbol of respective elements in the chemical names and SMILES to identify organohalogens, organophosphates, organosilicons and various chemicals containing certain metal(loid) elements. The second approach consisted of matching chemicals in the PlastChem inventory with existing lists of chemical groups (list in Supplementary Text 7). In addition, we applied expert judgement to identify PFASs from all organofluorine chemicals, as well as those PFASs and chlorinated paraffins regulated under the Stockholm Convention.

Groups of plastic chemicals were prioritized on the basis of the number of chemicals of concern they contain. As some groups of chemicals lack hazard data, our prioritization considers only groups with sufficient information. Starting with more than 100 initial groups, we isolated relevant groups by excluding groups that were too large and unspecific (for example, mixtures), groups that are regulated internationally, and groups with too few members. The final selection of prioritized groups was ranked on the basis of the proportion of known chemicals of concern they contain. This follows the rationale that groups consisting of many hazardous chemicals have more evidence for being concerning. Priority was assigned to groups for which ≥40% of the members are chemicals of concern or if additional scientific considerations pointed towards group-specific hazards (details in Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Table 9).

During the grouping, we also identified some technical challenges. Notably, no single automated tool is available to consistently group large numbers of chemicals. Instead, a combination of various techniques is required. For example, we used an algorithm 53 to identify homologue series containing repeating units of -CH 2 -, -CF 2 -, -CF 2 O- or -CF 2 CF2O-, covering more than 2,000 substances. Additionally, it is possible to identify UVCBs, polymers and other mixtures using predefined keyword searches 47 . However, in both cases, the subsequent assignment into more specific groups (for example, PFASs) requires manual inspection and expert judgement. This is due to a lack of machine-processable structural identifiers for these substances. Therefore, the manual curation of grouping and certain entries may have introduced some inconsistencies in our inventory. More work is needed to improve the availability of unique structural identifiers for chemicals on the global market, and to develop cheminformatics tools for grouping.

Keywords: Plastics recycling PVC Biobased solvents Physical recycling Solvent and non-solvent selection Hansen Solubility Parameters

1. Introduction

The global production of plastics has increased tremendously in the last decades  resulting  in a  concurrent  increase  in  plastic  waste (European  Parliament,  2021;  PlasticsEurope,  2024).  From  the  413.8 million  tons  (Mt)  produced  in  2023,  only  8.9  %  and  0.5  %  can  be attributed  to  post-consumer  recycled  and  bio-based  plastics,  respec tively (PlasticsEurope, 2024). Hence, more than 90 % of the produced plastics are still made from virgin and fossil-based polymers, stressing the need of a proper end-of-life waste management. In Europe, only 32 % of plastic waste is recycled, whereby the remaining is either incin erated (43 %) or landfilled (25 %), causing harm to the environment (European Parliament, 2021). Consequently, there is increasing regu latory pressure on recycling targets and recyclability. Several initiatives have been launched to tackle plastic pollution and accelerate the tran sition to a circular and resource-efficient plastics economy. The Euro pean Plastics Strategy, part of the EU ' s Circular Economy Action plan, seeks to revolutionize the way plastic products are designed, produced, used and recycled within the EU (European Commission, 2018). A B S T R A C T

For  the  first  time,  rigid  polyvinyl  chloride  (PVC)  waste  has  been  successfully  recycled  using  a  dissolutionprecipitation  approach  with  biobased  solvents.  Hansen  Solubility  Parameter,  HSP,  predictions  guided  the  sys tematic selection of solvents, while a modified HSP approach was developed to estimate the required non-solvent amounts for efficient polymer precipitation. Among the tested biobased solvents cyrene, γ -valerolactone (GVL) and 2-methyltetrahydrofuran demonstrated excellent dissolution performance, with water, methanol or isopropanol serving as effective non-solvents. The GVL-water system was the most efficient, requiring less than 10% non-solvent to achieve nearly complete separation and recovery of both the polymer and inorganic fraction without inducing polymer degradation. This optimized system was applied to a commercial PVC formulation for window frames, an end-of-life  PVC  window frame and a rigid PVC tube, achieving over 95% polymer recovery. Additionally, the process  successfully  removed  more  than  99%  of  inorganic  fillers,  enabling  the  selective  purification  and  covalorization of CaCO3  or the valuable TiO2.

instance, Vinylplus has set a goal to incorporate 1 Mt of recycled PVC waste  in  new  products  by  2030  (Vinylplus,  2020).  To  achieve  these recyclability commitments, new efficient plastic recycling methods and measures to stimulate the market for recycled plastic are key.

With a consumption volume of more than 50 Mt worldwide, PVC is one  of  the  most  extensively  utilized  plastics  in  the  world  (Statista, 2023a). Its widespread application in e.g. construction, electronic and healthcare applications, can be attributed to its good physical, chemical and weathering properties  combined with low cost  and various  pro cessing possibilities (Titow, 1990). Even if the mechanical recycling of PVC is well established (Plinke, 2000; Schyns and Shaver, 2021), only 24.3  %  of  all  PVC  waste  generated  in  2023  in  Europe  was  recycled (VinylPlus, 2024). PVC recycling remains highly challenging due to the versatility of the waste streams and the presence of multiple and varying amounts of additives (e.g. plasticizers, heat stabilizers, pigments) (AitTouchente  et  al.,  2024;  Ragaert  et  al.,  2017;  Ügduler  et  al.,  2020). Moreover, partial degradation of the PVC during reprocessing can in fluence the applicability and economic value of the recyclate (Hoff and Jacobsson, 1981; Lase et al., 2022).

To address these limitations, chemical recycling has gained signifi cant popularity in recent years (Klotz et al., 2024). In this process the polymer  is  converted  at  higher  temperatures  into  lower  molecular weight substances that can be reused as building blocks for the pro duction of chemicals, polymers or fuels (Parida et al., 2024). Various chemical recycling technologies for PVC and its derivatives have been extensively reviewed by Lu et al. (Lu et al., 2023). However, the high chlorine content of PVC, which constitutes at least 57 wt% of its mass, presents significant challenges, as it can lead to the formation of highly corrosive hydrogen  chloride  and  chlorinated  organic  compounds (Rahimi and García, 2017). In this sense, the dissolution-precipitation process, or physical recycling, is a promising alternative in which plas tic waste is dissolved in a selective solvent and subsequently precipitated using a low-solvating non-solvent (Li et al., 2022; Ügduler et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2018a). This methodology is an interesting intermediate solution for PVC as it operates at mild conditions, limiting dechlorina tion and allowing to recover intact polymer (Sherwood, 2020; Ügduler et al., 2020). It has also successfully been applied in the past to recycle soft  PVC  at  pilot  scale,  i.e.,  in  the  VinyLoop ® plant  in  Ferrara-Italy (Vandenhende,  2001;  VinylPlus,  2017).  Nevertheless,  this  plant  was closed due to changing sustainability regulations that hampered eco nomic viability, stressing the need of continued innovations to maximize sustainability and economic feasibility.

Currently, the physical recycling process still relies heavily on con ventional  organic  solvents  (Zhao  et  al.,  2018b).  For  PVC  it  concerns solvents such as dichloromethane, tetrahydrofuran (THF), toluene and xylene, which are hazardous for the environment, limiting their appli cation at industrial level. (Achilias et al., 2009; Kampouris et al., 1986; Sánchez-Rivera  et  al.,  2025;  Sperber  and  Rosen,  1976)  Also,  the VinyLoop ® process used a solvent mixture based on methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) with a low life cycle score (Vandenhende, 2001). To increase the overall sustainability of the process, it remains thus key to identify new powerful  green  solvent  systems.  Especially  solvents  that  can  be  pro duced from renewable sources, i.e., biobased solvents, are of particular interest. Very recently, solvents such as d -limonene, α -pinene and GVL were successfully applied for the dissolution-based recycling of poly styrene (Kazuyuki, 2015; Kol et al., 2023; Mangalara and Varughese, 2016),  high-density  polyethylene  (Aparício  et  al.,  2024)  and  poly ethylene  terephthalate  (Chen  et  al.,  2021).  Yet,  to  date,  no  suitable biobased solvents have been identified for the physical recycling of PVC.

Aside from being green, also the solvent ' s functional efficiency is of utmost importance. Especially in the case of the non-solvent, a high excess is applied to precipitate the polymer, which is undesirable from a sustainability perspective given the high energy demand associated with its  recovery  (Zhao  et  al.,  2018b).  The  Hansen  Solubility  Parameters (HSP) have demonstrated their utility as a guiding tool for solvents, but have been seldomly applied for the selection of non-solvents. In these studies, the non-solvents are chosen based on only their HSP neglecting the  influence  of  the  initial  solvent  on  the  precipitation  at  low  nonsolvent  excess  (Gorre  and  Tumolva,  2020;  Hansen,  2012;  Lu  and Chen, 2023; Venkatram et al., 2019). To overcome this limitation, very recently, an adapted approach has been proposed using the HSP of the solvent:non-solvent  mixture  instead.  This  approach  was  successfully applied to recycle acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, but its validation on other polymeric systems is still missing (Lu and Chen, 2023).

Beyond optimizing solvent use, the overall sustainability and eco nomic feasibility of recycling can be further improved by maximizing material utilization, such as through the co-valorization of additives. Rigid PVC contains significant amounts of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and titanium dioxide (TiO2) to improve rigidity, thermal stability or as a pigment.  Given  its  market  price  of  approximately  3 € /kg  (Statista, 2023b), especially the co-valorization of TiO2 can allow to improve the economic feasibility of the recycling process. Although TiO2  recovery from paint and wastewater has been previously achieved through py rolysis or filtration, to our knowledge, the simultaneous purification of both  the  polymer  and  valuable  inorganic  fillers  via  dissolutionprecipitation  has  not  been  reported  yet  (Karlsson  et  al.,  2015;  Ravi and Kumar Golder, 2024). Recently Kol et al. reported complete sepa ration  of  pigments  from  polystyrene  waste.  However,  the  resulting inorganic fraction was not subjected to further purification (Kol et al., 2023).

The objectives of this research are: [i] to introduce a novel approach to the physical recycling of rigid PVC using bio-based solvents; [ii] to enable the co-valorization of CaCO3 and TiO2; and [iii] to demonstrate the effectiveness of Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP) as a practical tool  for  selecting  suitable  bio-based  solvents  and  non-solvents.  The recycling process was first optimized with virgin PVC, and the estab lished  conditions  were  successfully  extended  to  commercial  formula tions  and end-of-life rigid PVC materials. Furthermore, the inorganic fraction  was  selectively  purified  to  recover  TiO2  or  CaCO3,  and  the recycled  PVC  was  characterized  to  evaluate  its  purity  and  structural integrity. This work highlights a sustainable, dual-recovery strategy that enhances  both  material  circularity  and  resource  efficiency  in  PVC recycling.

2. Experimental

2.1. Materials

Virgin PVC powder without additives was received from Centexbel, commercial PVC flakes designed for window profiles and a shredded end-of-life  mixture  were  obtained  from  a  window  producer,  and  a commercially produced rigid PVC tube was sourced from a construction site.  The PVC tube was cryogenically ground using a Pulvurisette 14 equipped with a 1 mm sieve before use. The remaining materials were used as received.

Commercially available biobased solvents cyrene, diethyl carbonate, GVL,  p-cymene,  d-limonene  and  2-methyl  tetrahydrofuran  (m-THF) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Ethyl acetate (EtOAc), cyclohexa none, anisole, MEK, THF, acetone, cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME), methanol (MeOH), ethanol (EtOH), isopropanol (IPA) and hexane were purchased from VWR Chemicals. All solvents were used as received.

2.2. Methods

2.2.1. Instrumental characterization

PVC Molecular weight was determined by SEC, using a Waters sys tem with an HR5E column connected to an RI and UV detector. The instrument was calibrated with polystyrene internal standards (1920 -1500000 g ⋅ mol 1 ) and eluted with THF. Ash content analysis was performed in triplicate for each sample in a Thermo Fisher Scientific Thermolyne muffle furnace. Approximately 100 mg of the dried material was added into a pre-weighed aluminum cup. The samples were placed in the muffle furnace and following heating profile was used: heating to 250 °C at 5 °C/min, isothermal for 5 min, heating until 550 °C at 5 °C/ min, isothermal for 4 h, cooling to 105 °C. Afterwards the sample was cooled to room temperature and weighed to determine the ash content. Determination of the CaCO3, TiO2 and Zn content was done by ICP-AES using a Thermo Fisher Scientific iCAP Pro XP system. 50 mg of polymer was weighed in a Teflon recipient of 18 mL. 1.5 mL nitric acid Pico-Pure Plus and 1.5 mL hydrofluoric acid were added to the sample. The sample was digested in an Anton Paar Multiwave 7000 microwave digestor, by heating it at 250 °C for 3 h. After cooling down to room temperature, the sample was transferred to a test tube and neutralized with 16 mL of a 4 % boric acid solution. The sample was diluted to a total of 50 mL using ultrapure water and measured. Elemental quantities of calcium (Ca), titanium (Ti), and zinc (Zn) measured by ICP-AES were converted into the amounts of their respective target compounds, such as CaCO3 TiO2 using the stochiometric information. The limit of quantification (LOQ) was 10 mg/kg for Ca and Zn and 5 mg/kg for Ti, and a limit of detection (LOD) being half of LOQ.

Quantification of the residual solvent in the recovered polymer was A. Aerts et al.

done by quantitative GC-FID using a Thermofisher Scientific trace 1600/ 1610 GC system equipped with a DB-5MS column (60 m x 0,25 mm ID x 0.25 µ m),  and  using  helium  as  a  mobile  phase.  A  known  amount  of polymer was dissolved in THF and 1 µ L of solution was injected at a temperature of 300 °C. The temperature of the column was kept first for 2 min at 45 °C, then increased to 265 °C at 15 °C/min and kept constant for a total run time of 30 min. Calibration of the instrument was per formed using seven standard solutions of m-THF, cyrene and GVL with a concentration ranging from 10 to 5000 µ g/g in THF. For each solvent a calibration curve was generated with an R 2 of 0.99. The relative stan dard deviation of the measurements was 0.61 %, 0.48 % and 0.61 % for m-THF, cyrene and GVL respectively. Additionally, two separate quality control solutions were analyzed to ensure accuracy. The LOD and LOQ were 10 mg/kg and 25 mg/kg, respectively.

Tensile tests of the PVC dog bones (see 2.2.7) were conducted on an Instron  6800  single  column  tensile  tester  using  pneumatic  clamps equipped with a 1kN load cell. Two to four replicates were measured for each sample. The tensile tests were performed at ambient temperature with a cross head speed of 5 mm ⋅ min 1 and hence a strain rate of 3 ⋅ 10 -3 s 1 .

2.2.2. Experimental solvent selection

Experimental solubilization tests of pure PVC were performed using a set of selected solvents that were selected based on the HSP parameters (see supplementary information). A known weight of PVC powder was combined with the selected solvents (in total 2 g of mixture) in 4 mL glass vials at polymer concentrations between 5 wt% and 25 wt%. The sealed vials were placed in a Thermal Shake Lite shaker at 40 °C and 1200 rpm for 30 min. Samples were visually inspected, and when the PVC was not completely dissolved the temperature was increased by 5 °C  for  another  30  min.  This  process  was  repeated  until  complete dissolution was observed or the maximum temperature of 100 °C was reached. Temperatures exceeding the boiling point of the solvents were not considered.

2.2.3. Experimental non-solvent selection

For the selected biobased solvents, i.e., cyrene, GVL and m-THF, the PVC precipitation was investigated for non-solvent concentrations be tween 2 wt% to 60 wt% in the mixture. The non-solvent was added slowly while stirring the mixture at 60 °C. The precipitated phase was separated by decantation, washed with an extra amount of non-solvent and dried in a vacuum oven at 85 °C for at least 12 h. Precipitate yields were calculated considering the initial mass of PVC used in the disso lution  step  and  the  recovered  polymer  mass  after  precipitation  and drying. These were corrected for the residual solvent in the polymer using Equation (1):

Ya = Y * ( 100 S ) 100 (1)

With Ya (%) the actual yield, Y (%) the yield after precipitation and S (%) the percentage of solvent measured by GC-FID.

2.2.4. Dissolution-precipitation of commercial PVC and end-of-life materials

10 g of polymer was stirred in 100 mL of GVL at 70 °C overnight. When dissolved, the samples were centrifugated at 40 °C and 11,000 RCF, and separated in an insoluble and supernatant fraction. The su pernatant was heated to 60 °C and stirred for 30 min. 26 mL of water was added to precipitate the polymer and left stirring for 30 min, after which the supernatant was decanted. The recovered polymer was first washed with water, cold pressed to remove the excess solvent, and then dried overnight in a vacuum oven at 70 °C. Lastly, the polymer was cryo genically ground for further drying using supercritical CO2 extraction

The insolubles obtained from the via centrifugation, were washed with GVL and centrifuged again at 40 °C and 11,000 RCF. The washed insolubles were dried in the vacuum oven overnight at 70 °C and used for isolation of the CaCO3 and TiO2.

2.2.5. Drying the recovered PVC via supercritical CO2  extraction

Supercritical CO2 extraction was used to completely dry the recycled PVC before compounding. This was performed using a laboratory scale JASCO SFE system from JASCO Isogen Life Science using a flow-through extraction cell (Elst et al., 2018). The cell was filled with 4 to 4.5 g of dried and ground PVC sandwiched between two layers of glass wool. The extraction was performed during 3 h using pure CO2, a flow rate of 1 mL ⋅ min 1 , temperature of 50 °C and pressure of 35 Mpa. Afterwards, the polymer was collected and analyzed for solvent content. The system was rinsed using IPA.

2.2.6. Compounding PVC into dog bone tensile bars

Minicompounding to tensile dog bones was done using a Thermo Fisher ™ HAAKE ™ miniCTW equipped with a Force Feeder system to guarantee  continuous  flow  of  the  material  and  an  air-cooled  screw feeder to avoid clogging of the system. The MiniCTW is combined with the MiniJet injection moulder to shape the dog bones. PVC dog bones were  compounded  using  the  co-rotating  configuration  with  direct extrusion at 190 °C with a screw speed of 80 rpm. The PVC was directly extruded to the MiniJet cylinder heated to 200 °C and to be injected into an ISO 5A mold at 95 °C. The injection was performed with a pressure of 950 bars within 10 s and a post pressure of 10 s at 700 bars was applied.

2.2.7. Isolation of CaCO3  and TiO2  from the insoluble fraction

The inorganic fractions were purified using a thermal treatment to remove  the  remaining  organic  residues  followed  by  a  double  acid treatment to recover TiO2. The thermal treatment was performed using the previously described ashing conditions (see 2.2.1). The residues with high TiO2 content were suspended 1 M HCl solution (1 g in 10 mL) and stirred  at  room  temperature  for  3  h.  The  resulting  suspension  was centrifuged at 4500 RCF for 45 min to separate TiO2 from the dissolved CaCl2. The TiO2  was washed with deionized water and centrifuged an additional three times. The purified TiO2  was then dried in a vacuum oven at 105 °C overnight. Those steps were repeated with 30 mL HCl solution. ICP-AES was employed to assess the final purity. In the case of the PVC tube, the TiO2 content was very low, and instead the recovery of CaCO3 was targeted by applying solely the thermal treatment.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Theoretical selection using HSP

3.1.1. Solvents

Recent studies have explored the use of biobased solvents for the physical recycling of various plastics. Various terpenes and terpenoids were evaluated for their ability to recycle polystyrene based plastics whereby d -limonene was proven to be successful for both expanded and high impact polystyrene (Kazuyuki, 2015; Kol et al., 2023; Mangalara and Varughese, 2016). Similarly, d-Limonene was investigated for the recycling of high-density polyethylene achieving approximately 78 % polymer and 57 % solvent recovery. For this material, however, the highest recovery was obtained with α -pinene also allowing to keep the structural integrity of the recycled polymer intact (Aparício et al., 2024). Another biobased solvent, GVL, was applied successfully for the physical recycling of polyethylene terephthalate (Chen et al., 2021). However, to the  best  of  our  knowledge,  no  suitable  biobased  solvents  have  been identified for PVC yet. In this study, the theoretical solvent selection for the dissolution of PVC was performed using HSP. HSPiP software was used for the solvent selection (see supporting information), with the following parameters for PVC: δ d = 18.8, δ p = 9.2 and δ h = 6.3. Fig. 1 shows the HSP sphere for PVC with R0 equal to 8.0. A list of conventional organic solvents and commercially available biobased solvents such as cyrene, diethyl carbonate, GVL, p-cymene, methyl oleate, d-limonene, 1butanol, m-THF, EtOAc and EtOH were included in the study and their A. Solvents inside the solubility sphere of PVC show RED < 1 (Equation S2, see supplementary information),  represented  in  blue  (1 -14)  and  thus  were  classified  as good solvents. Solvents outside the solubility sphere of PVC, represented in orange (15 -26), were considered as poor solvents. In this regard, cyclohexanone and cyrene are considered among the best, and water and methanol (MeOH) among the worst investigated solvents. The most promising biobased solvents from the studied group, i.e.,  cyrene,  GVL  and  m-THF,  were  selected  for  further  experimental work. Solvents were ranked in order of compatibility with PVC based on their HSP ( δ d, δ p, δ h), distance to PVC (Ra, Equation S1, see supple mentary information), boiling point (BP), melting point (MP), molecular weight (MW) and GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) solvent sustainability classi fication as presented in Table S1 (see supplementary information). Ac cording to the GSK solvent sustainability guide the priority categories considered  in  this  classification  are  VOC  emissions,  health  hazard, flammability and explosion potential and reactivity and stability. All three of the selected biobased solvents received good to excellent ratings in these categories with cyrene and GVL even achieving a green rating for VOC emissions, flammability and explosion potential and reactivity and stability (Alder et al., 2016).

3.1.2. Non-solvents

The theoretical selection of non-solvents for the precipitation of PVC was  also  performed  using  the  HSP.  In  the  previously  reported  ap proaches, the prime criteria for selection non-solvents is that their RED as compared to the polymer is larger than one (Venkatram et al., 2019). While this approach is effective at the typical large non-solvent excess, it faces  limitations  when  lower  non-solvent  dosages  are  targeted  to enhance the sustainability. Under these conditions, the initial solubili zation  solvent  remains  at  relatively  high  concentrations,  which  can interfere  with  precipitation  performance.  Therefore,  in  this  study,  a novel approach was applied based on the HSP of the solvent:non-solvent mixture to assess the non-solvent behavior. A good solvent:non-solvent pair was defined as the combination of a good solvent with a non-solvent that allows to increase the RED of the mixture above one over a small concentration span. Water, MeOH, EtOH, IPA, hexane, toluene, EtOAc and acetone were evaluated as potential non-solvent candidates in the presence  of  the  selected  biobased  solvents  cyrene,  GVL  and  m-THF. Hexane  was  not  evaluated  in  the  system  with  GVL  because  of  its immiscibility.

In  Fig.  2,  the  HSP  distance  (Ra)  between  the  solvent:non-solvent mixtures and PVC at different solvent:non-solvent ratios is illustrated. In this way, the best non-solvent candidates and their required amounts for PVC precipitation were identified. According to the R a  values be tween solvent:non-solvent mixtures and PVC, water could be considered to be the best non-solvent to precipitate PVC in combination with cyrene and GVL as solvent. In both cases, a water concentration of maximum 20 wt% (ratio 80:20, solvent:non-solvent) was theoretically sufficient for the precipitation of PVC, which is significantly better compared to the typical 300 % of non-solvent used for polymer precipitations (Achilias et  al.,  2009).  A  sharp  increase  of  the R a  values  was  observed  with increasing  water  content,  which  can  be  explained  by  the  elevated hydrogen bond and polarity parameters of water as compared to PVC and  the  selected  biobased  solvents.  Unfortunately,  the  miscibility  of water and m-THF is limited and hence water could not be considered as a good non-solvent for the precipitation of PVC from a solution in mTHF.

Next to water, MeOH showed good non-solvent capabilities at ratios higher  than  50:50  (solvent:MeOH) in  all  three  investigated  biobased solvents.  The  non-solvents  MeOH  and  hexane  exhibited  the  most promising results when using m-THF as a solvent. Nevertheless, since hexane is linked to serious environmental and health problems, and it is classified as red according to the GSK solvent sustainability guide, (Alder et al., 2016) MeOH is preferred over hexane. When comparing MeOH and EtOH as non-solvents, the increase of the alkyl chain length, led to a decreased hydrogen bond and polarity parameters of the non-solvent, hence it showed an increased similarity to the PVC parameters, which resulted in reduced non-solvent capabilities for the precipitation of the polymer. Therefore, IPA showed less potential for the precipitation of PVC compared to MeOH and EtOH in the case of the three evaluated biobased solvent systems. As expected, EtOAc and acetone, located in side the solubility sphere of PVC, showed unfavorable results as non -solvent  for  PVC  precipitation,  even  at  the  highest  evaluated  nonsolvent concentration of 75 wt% (1:3 solvent:non-solvent), because of the similarity of their HSP to the selected biobased solvents and PVC. This  indicates  that  these solvent mixtures could be better solvents for PVC dissolution compared to their individual counterparts, being an interesting case for a follow-up study.

3.2. Experimental selection of the solvents and non-solvents

3.2.1. Solvents

Solvents  inside  and  outside  of  the  solubility  sphere  of  PVC  were experimentally tested to evaluate the accuracy of the HSP predictions for this system. A temperature interval of 40 -100 °C was selected for the dissolution experiments unless the boiling point of the solvent was lower than the desired temperature. Pressurized conditions were avoided and hence, the temperature was kept below the boiling point. Dissolution experiments started at 40 °C for  30  min  in  a  thermal  shaker,  and  if visually incomplete dissolution of PVC was reached, the temperature was increased 5 °C for 30 extra minutes. This process was repeated until PVC was visually completely dissolved. The effect of polymer concen tration  (5 -25  wt%)  on  the  dissolution  was  investigated  for  selected solvents  and  the  results  are  represented  in  Fig.  3.  The  individual experimental data are shown in Table S2 (see supplementary informa tion),  where  the  solvents  were  ranked  in  descending  order  for  HSP predicted affinity to PVC. The results demonstrate that solvents with theoretically high PVC-dissolving capabilities, including cyclohexanone, cyrene, GVL, anisole, THF, MEK, and m-THF, successfully dissolved the polymer at concentrations ranging from 5 wt% to 15 wt%. Among these, THF  and  cyclohexanone  were  specifically  observed  in  literature  to effectively separate PVC from PET (Grause et al., 2017). In the case of cyclohexanone and GVL, complete dissolution of PVC was reached at even higher polymer concentrations up to 20 and 25 wt%. A general trend was observed, where an increased PVC concentration led to more viscous solutions and higher dissolution temperatures. Solvents such as acetone,  CPME,  and  EtOAc,  were  unable  to  dissolve  PVC  under  the investigated conditions, despite being within the HSP solubility sphere of PVC. Although these solvents are poor at dissolving the polymer, they can  still  induce  PVC  swelling,  enabling  the  extraction  of  additives (Kumar  et  al.,  2020).  Additionally,  as  predicted  using  HSP,  solvents located  outside  the  PVC  solubility  sphere,  such  as  d-limonene,  pcymene, and diethyl carbonate, were unable to completely dissolve PVC at any of the investigated conditions.

Based on these findings, cyrene, GVL, and m-THF emerged as the most promising biobased solvents for PVC dissolution and were subse quently selected for further experimental investigation. Although HSP does  not  provide  direct  quantitative  predictions  of  solubility,  it  has proven to be a valuable and practical tool for identifying solvents with high potential for dissolving PVC.

3.2.2. Non-solvents

Experimental dissolution and precipitation experiments were carried out with pure (virgin) PVC (V-PVC) using the selected biobased solvents: cyrene,  GVL  and  m-THF.  The  more  efficient  non-solvent  candidates would be the ones that could lead to the maximum precipitation yield of PVC while using the lowest amount of non-solvent. An initial screening of  non-solvents,  from  the  most  suitable  candidates  according  to  the theoretical prediction such as water and methanol and the less preferred solvents such as EtOAc and hexane, was performed. The results were summarized in Table S3 (see supplementary information). PVC precip itate yields were affected by three key factors: the choice of solvent, the non-solvent, and the non-solvent concentration. Initial screening of the A. Aerts et al.

selected non-solvents revealed that water was the most effective nonsolvent for PVC precipitation when cyrene and GVL were used as sol vents, aligning with the HSP predictions represented in Fig. 2. Experi mentally, MeOH also demonstrated strong non-solvent capabilities in combination with cyrene and GVL, though MeOH consistently exhibited lower efficiency compared to water, as higher volumes of MeOH were required to achieve comparable precipitation yields. With alcohols of increasing chain length, non-solvent efficiency decreased, necessitating larger  volumes  to  attain  complete  PVC  precipitation.  These  experi mental  trends  are  consistent  with  HSP  predictions  for  the  mixtures. Furthermore, PVC precipitation in the presence of m-THF was less effi cient  compared  to  when  cyrene  or  GVL  were  used  as  solvents,  also consistent with the predictions made using HSP. However, the experi mental screening revealed that IPA unexpectedly performed as a more effective non-solvent than ethanol, which can be attributed to its bulkier molecular structure, leading to a reduced affinity for PVC. As predicted, EtOAc is an inefficient non-solvent since it was impossible to precipitate the polymer at any of the investigated concentrations in the three bio based  solvents.  While  HSP  generally  provides  reliable  predictions  of solvent and non-solvent behavior, there are instances where it exhibits some inaccuracies. HSP does not account for factors such as solvent geometry, temperature, or polymer concentrations, but these parame ters significantly affect the experimental solubility of polymers. More over,  Venkatram  and  coworkers  observed  that  HSP  tends  to  exhibit slightly  greater  inaccuracies  when  predicting  the  solubility  of  polar polymers such as PVC compared to apolar polymers (Venkatram et al.,

2019).

The initial solvent screening resulted in the best non-solvents for the precipitation of PVC being water and MeOH for the systems with cyrene and GVL as solvents and being MeOH and IPA in combination with mTHF.

Those selected cases were further investigated to identify the optimal conditions for the precipitation of  PVC and the results are shown in Fig. 4 (see also supplementary information Table S4 and Fig. S1). This figure presents the yield of recovered PVC (Equation (1) as a function of non-solvent concentration for the systems with cyrene, GVL and m-THF as well as the SEC chromatograms of the polymer clearly proving that there  is  no  PVC  degradation  after  the  purification  via  dissolutionprecipitation (Fig. 4d). The utilization of water as non-solvent in com bination with cyrene or GVL as solvent led to maximal PVC recovery using less than 10 % (9:1 solvent:non-solvent) of water. When using MeOH  as  non-solvent,  the  maximum  yield  of  PVC  precipitate  was reached at MeOH concentrations of at least 25 wt% (3:1 solvent:nonsolvent) and 30 wt% (7:3 solvent:non-solvent) for systems with cyrene and GVL, respectively. As observed during the screenings, the precipi tation of PVC from m-THF was less effective, resulting in maximal re covery using at least 50 wt% MeOH and IPA (1:1 solvent:non-solvent). However, this is still lower than the traditionally applied 1:3 ratio of solvent:non-solvent  for  the  precipitation  of  polymers  (Achilias  et  al., 2009; Chen et al., 2021; Kampouris et al., 1986). In summary, in this study it was demonstrated that under the investigated conditions, rela tively low amounts of non-solvent < 12 % (22:3 solvent:non-solvent) are A. Aerts et al.

The theoretical HSP non-solvent predictions were in general in-line with the experimental data, and hence, they could be applied for fast selection of non-solvents and providing a first idea on required quantities of nonsolvent for the precipitation of PVC in a particular system.

3.2.3. End-of-life materials

The most promising combinations, being GVL or cyrene and water as the solvent:non-solvent combination was applied to commercial PVC and end-of-life materials. Three materials were selected for the recycling of the  PVC  using  the  optimal  solubilization-precipitation  procedure:  a commercial PVC formulation to produce window frames as a reference, a PVC window frame and an end-of-life rigid PVC tube (Fig. 5a-c). Those materials were analyzed for inorganic content and ICP-AES was used to identify  elements  and  quantify  various  inorganic  additives,  including TiO2, CaCO3 (Fig. 5d and e). An inorganic content of 13.2 %, 9.8 % and 9.1 % was obtained for the commercial PVC, the window frame and the tube, respectively. The ICP-AES results (Fig. 5e) clearly showed that sig nificant amounts of Ti and Ca were detected, originating primarily from the TiO2 and CaCO3 that are present in the material. This is in in-line with expectations since those additives are mainly added as a pigment or to tune  the  material ' s  properties  and  increase  strength  and  durability. Additionally, small amounts of Zn ( < 0.2 %) were observed, likely linked to  Ca/Zn-stearates  that  are  commonly  added  as  a  stabilizer.  The  Ca amount that can originate from this stabilizer was estimated to be at most 0.5 %, which is negligible as compared to the total Ca amount, supporting the hypothesis that the Ca originates primarily from the CaCO3.

The  PVC  materials  were  solubilized  in  selected  solvents  for  their purification.  However,  cyrene  resulted  in  an  inseparable  gel  of  in solubles and  the polymer  (see supplementary  information);  and

4. Conclusions

This  study  demonstrates  that  while  HSP  do  not  provide  direct quantitative predictions of solubility, it serves as a powerful and prac tical tool for selecting solvents to efficiently dissolve PVC and optimize solvent:non-solvent  combinations  for  selective  polymer  precipitation. Using HSP predictions combined with experimental verification, GVL and  water  was  identified  as  the  optimal  solvent  system  for  the dissolution-precipitation purification of rigid PVC and CaCO3 and TiO2. We achieved a recovery of over 95 % of the material with a minimal nonsolvent  addition  of  less  than  10  %,  while  preserving  the  structural integrity of the polymer. Furthermore, the developed method proved to be highly effective across three distinct types of PVC, including end-oflife materials such as a PVC window frame and a tube, achieving over 99 % removal of inorganic fillers. The purified PVC exhibited properties comparable to virgin PVC, with only minor deviations, demonstrating the  potential  for  high-quality  material  recovery.  Additionally,  we established a viable route for the selective recovery of inorganic com ponents: CaCO3 was successfully extracted from PVC tubes via thermal treatment, while TiO2 was efficiently recovered through a combination of  thermal  treatment  and  acidified  water  washing.  These  findings highlight  the  potential  of  solvent-based  recycling  as  a  scalable  and sustainable approach for rigid PVC recovery, contributing to improved material  circularity  and  resource  efficiency.  However,  although  real end-of-life materials were used in this study, implementing this tech nology for mixed waste streams requires further investigation into the effects of various materials and additives. Additionally, since the purity of end-of-life materials depends on the efficiency of pre-sorting tech nologies, their role in ensuring process effectiveness across diverse and complex waste compositions must be carefully considered.

Use of cationic surfactant to remove solvent-based ink from rigid high density polyethylene surfaces

Duangkamol Songsiri a , Swe Swe Min a , John F. Scamehorn b, *, Somchai Osuwan a , John W. Ellis a

a Petroleum and Petrochemical College , Chulalongkorn Uni p54 ersity , Bangkok 10330, Thailand b Department of Chemical Engineering , Institute for Applied Surfactant Research , The Uni p54 ersity of Oklahoma , Norman , OK 730019, USA

Received 30 April 2001; accepted 24 December 2001

Abstract

Increasing space limitations for disposal of solid waste and shortages of raw materials for plastic have increased the need for recycling. However, printed plastic surfaces cannot be effectively recycled unless the inks are removed. The use of surfactants for deinking rather than organic solvents or chlorine bleaches is environmentally attractive. In this study, the effect of cationic surfactant concentration, pH, process temperature, pre-soaking time, shaking time and abrasion were investigated for blue solvent-based ink on rigid high density polyethylene surfaces. The cationic surfactant ( n -hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide) was effective only at concentrations above the critical micelle concentration (CMC) and at high pH levels (11.75 and above). Both below and above the CMC, ink removal was promoted by increasing temperature, pre-soaking time and shaking time. The presence of an abrasive also helped to detach the loosened ink from the plastic surface. Solubilization appears to be an important mechanism aiding deinking. © 2002 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords : Surfactant; Deinking; Plastic container; Recycling; Solvent-based ink

1. Introduction

The use of rigid plastic packaging (e.g. milk bottles) has rapidly increased for many applications because of its light weight, strength, durability, moldability, colorability and relatively

low energy requirement in converting resin to manufactured products. In the future, increasing scarcity of raw materials for virgin plastic will make recycling more attractive. Moreover, most of the used plastics go to landfills, thereby increasing solid waste disposal problems. Plastic waste generation increases annually, but only a small proportion of this waste is recycled, forcing both governments and industries to seriously consider plastic recycling.

At present, polymers produced from recycling are not as valuable as virgin polymers because the residual ink colors and changes the physical properties of the polymer [1]. These problems can be avoided if ink is removed from the plastic surface before recycling. Possible alternatives for plastic deinking include using either organic solvents or surfactants; however, the use of surfactants has an important advantage in being environmentally friendly.

The use of surfactants to remove ink (deink) from a polymer surface is an example of a surfactant-based separation process [2,3]. Deinking is fundamentally a laundering process. The adhesion of ink to plastic packaging materials and soil to clothing is due to van der Waals, electrostatic and chemical bonding, among other forces. Similar to laundering, deinking is a two step process: (i) detachment of soil (ink) from the substrate (plastic surface); and (ii) dispersion of soil in a washing bath by mechanical action [4,5]. The effect of surface tension, surfactant adsorption, wetting, dispersion and solubilization are all important in the deinking process. It is well known that single component liquids wet substrates that have higher critical surface tension values than the liquid surface tension [6-8]. During printing, the lower surface tension of the ink causes it to wet the polymer surface and adhere to the surface better [9]. The removal of ink from polymer surfaces with the use of aqueous solutions of surfactant is aided by adsorption of surfactants onto the polymer and ink surfaces, thereby decreasing the interfacial tension values of both polymer-water and inkwater. If the reduction of interfacial tension is so strong that the sum of the interfacial tensions of polymer-water and ink-water is equal to or less than the ink-polymer interfacial tension, it is thermodynamically favorable for the ink to detach from the polymer surface [5,10]. Rubbing of the polymer surface against another solid (e.g. other polymer or abrasive) and shearing forces from agitation help remove loosened ink and keep the detached ink dispersed [1,4,10-13]. Solubilization [14] of molecularly dispersed dyes or binder molecules into micelles can also contribute to deinking. In previous studies of deinking of polyethylene film, solvent-based inks were found to be much more difficult to remove than water-based inks [1,11]. Studies of the effect of surfactant type on deinking of rigid polyethylene surfaces [12] and polyethylene film [1] have shown that cationic surfactants are more effective than anionic and nonionic surfactants and have equal or greater effectiveness as amphoteric surfactants. In this research, the effect of processing parameters on the effectiveness of deinking focused on the removal of screen-type solvent-based blue ink printed on flame-treated high density polyethylene (HDPE) blow molded bottles using a cationic surfactant.

2. Experimental

2.1. Materials

Plastic containers used for this research were all composed of HDPE and printed with blue color solvent-based ink by the screen printing process. Prior to printing, the containers were flame-treated in order for the ink to adhere well to the surface. All the containers were treated and printed by SVB Drinking Water Co., Thailand. Plastic samples ( p58 8 × 40 mm) containing blue-colored printed ink were cut from the printed area of the plastic bottles. Small irregular shapes of ceramic pieces were used as the abrasive material in order to facilitate the detachment of loosened ink from the rigid plastic surfaces. The abrasive was composed of refractory insulators (used for electrical wire) of tubular shape p58 5 mm diameter and 5 mm in length. The hole in the center was p58 3 mm in diameter. Ceramic beads [1] or zirconium silicate grinding beads [13] have been used as abrasives

in other studies.

The cationic surfactant, n -hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide or cetyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB), having 98% purity in powder form, was supplied by Fluka Co., Switzerland. It was used as received without further purification. Sodium hydroxide with 98% purity, which was used for pH adjustment, was supplied by EKA Nobel Co., Sweden.

2.2. Analysis before deinking process

The amount of ink present on each sample before deinking was determined by using an optical scanning method. For optical scanning, each plastic sample was carefully positioned on the scanner and scanned at optimum conditions (standardized) using a HP scanJet 4c scanner. In order to prevent the reflection from the white surface of the scanner cover, a black poster board was placed behind the sample during scanning. After scanning, an image file was imported into an Adobe PhotoShop program to quantify the amount of ink (pixels) present on the plastic surface.

2.3. Deinking

Each CTAB solution was prepared with distilled water at room temperature and stirred with a magnetic stirrer to produce a homogeneous solution. The surfactant solution was warmed up slightly to 40 °C to speed up dissolution (since dissolution is slow in water at room temperature). The pH level of the surfactant solution was then adjusted by adding a sodium hydroxide solution from a burette. All pH measurements were carried out using a Benchtop pH / ISE meter Model 920A with Triode pH electrode Model 9157BN. After analyzing the samples (before deinking) by the optical scanning method, each sample was placed in a 15-ml surfactant solution in a conical flask. The samples were then allowed to soak for either 2 h in the presence of 25 irregular-shaped ceramic pieces (abrasive material) or for various times in the absence of ceramic pieces. All samples were allowed to soak by standing the flasks in a temperature controlled water bath. After soaking, the flasks were shaken in the temperature controlled shaking water bath (GFL model 1086) at 200 oscillations per minute. After shaking, the samples were removed from the flasks, washed several times with distilled water and air-dried. Each experiment was repeated at least twice.

2.4. Analysis after deinking process

The extent of deinking of the samples were first evaluated visually. The deinked plastic samples were rescanned on the HP ScanJet scanner using the identical procedure and conditions as used for the original samples. The amount of ink removed (%) was determined using the following relationship:

Ink removed (%)

= [(pixels before deinking -pixels after deinking ) / pixels before deinking ] × 100.

3.1.1. Effect of CTAB concentration and abrasi p54 e

As shown in Figs. 1 and 2, in the absence of ceramic pieces, there is no significant ink removal from the plastic surfaces below the CMC, while there is substantial removal when abrasives are present, except when no surfactant is present and very little removal occurs. There is a CTAB concentration range in which deinking increases rapidly to 100%; in the absence of abrasives, this concentration range is p58 150% higher than in the presence of abrasives. For example, 50% deinking occurs at 1.0 mM CTAB with abrasives and at 2.5 mM CTAB without abrasives. In either case, complete (100%) deinking occurs at a CTAB concentration of 5 mM. So, abrasives speed up deinking, but are not necessary for complete deinking. The separation of abrasives from recovered plastic and from ink might make abrasives undesirable. If abrasives are discarded with detached ink, this results in an increase in the mass of solid waste requiring disposal.

3.1.3. Effect of shaking time

text: Figs. 5 and 6 show that shaking time can have a substantial effect on ink removal. Comparing Figs. 4 and 6, there is sometimes an inhibition period of time for both pre-soaking and shaking, during which little deinking occurs, followed by a narrow period of time (we will call this the detachment period) during which ink removal increases rapidly to near completeness. From a design viewpoint, it is important to choose residence times for pre-soaking and shaking which are at the end of the detachment periods for each. Longer pre-soaking times permit shorter shaking times and longer shaking times permit shorter pre-soaking times, so there is an economic optimization required to determine design conditions. For example, p92 90% ink removal can be attained at a CTAB concentration at the CMC with 5 h pre-soaking and a standard 2 h shaking time, while with 2 h pre-soaking, 4 h shaking time is needed to yield p92 90% deinking. Since pre-soaking tanks generally require much less capital expense than agitated process units, pre-soaking can improve process economics.

3.1.5. Effect of temperature

text:
Higher temperatures can substantially increase deinking efficiency, as shown in Figs. 9 and 10. At 45 °C, p92 90% ink removal was observed even at a CTAB concentration of only 25% of the CMC. Higher temperatures can increase energy costs and require robustness of process equipment materials (particularly at the high pH levels anticipated). Note that the CMC referred to here is that at 25 °C. Since the CMC is only mildly dependent on temperature for ionic surfactants [15], temperature corrections were not made. So, for example, when the CTAB concentration is referred to as at the CMC, this is not entirely accurate at 45 °C. In terms of the fairly large concentration increments used here, this is not a significant consideration.

Qualitative observations give some insight into the mechanisms of deinking. When significant deinking occurred, the wash solution was always blue in color. The greater the degree of deinking, the bluer the color. At 30 °C, particles were observed in solution and the remaining ink on the polymer surface was hard. At 45 °C, the particles in the solution were observed to be larger than at 30 °C. At 45 °C, the residual ink on the polymer was soft and sticky.

3.2.

Mechanisms of deinking

One problem with understanding physical mechanisms of ink removal is the ill-defined nature of the inks and binder due to their complexity and due to the proprietary nature of their formulation. However, the results here can give some insight.

The surfactant can aid detachment by mechanisms such as adsorption on ink and plastic surfaces, decreasing ink / water and plastic / water interfacial tensions, making detachment more thermodynamically favorable. This is a common mechanism aiding detergency of both particulate and oily soils [5,16]. Surfactant can sometimes 'liquefy' soil, an ill-defined term implying that the soil can either flow and be removed by the roll-back mechanism [4,5,10,16] or can be shaken up into little pieces as surfactant diffuses or penetrates into the soil and loosens it up. The surfactant can also improve wetting, aiding a water layer to form between ink and polymer surface. The wetting enhancement is due to surfactant adsorption on ink and plastic-trapped air is displaced. The surfactant can aid in antiredeposition (preventing the ink from readsorbing) by dispersing solid ink particles by adsorbing in the ink surface, emulsifying liquid ink droplets and solubilizing ink molecules in micelles [1,5,11,14,17].

The surface area of the polymer and ink are low enough that the final concentration of surfactant in solution is probably not significantly lower than the initial concentration. Above the CMC, the primary function of incremental surfactant is to solubilize ink molecules within micelles. A secondary advantage could be the micelles disassociating to provide surfactant monomer, speeding up rate-driven processes. However, over the time periods covered here (hours), this is generally not a significant factor, so solubilization can be deduced as an important mechanism of ink uptake by the solution. This implies that a significant amount of ink is molecularly dispersed in order to be solubilized, instead of being present as particles or droplets. Another possibility is that the micelles are solubilizing the ink binder.

Both pre-soaking and shaking time are important. It is possible that either the rate of surfactant adsorption or rate of penetration or liquefaction can be the rate-determining step here. The beneficial effect of abrasives at short times imply that it is the rate of detachment of ink after surfactant adsorption has occurred which may be limiting, also consistent with no significant deinking with abrasive, but no surfactant. Solubilization is a very fast process [18] and is probably not rate-determining.

Detergency is generally more effective at high pH, as more negative charges are imposed on the contaminant and on the substrate, making them more repulsive from each other [5,8,10]. This would make ink detachment and antiredeposition easier in this case. The ink particles can be attached to the surface by binders. Attenuated total reflection (ATR) FTIR [12] indicated that the ink binder contained ester groups for this system. The intense C = O stretching bond of saturated aliphatic ester groups is in the frequency range of 1750-1735 cm -1 [19] in agreement with the spectrum observed for this ink. Sodium hydroxide, which was used for pH adjustment, is hypothesized to break up the ink binder by hydrolyzing the ester groups, especially at pH 12 [11,12]. A study of selective froth flotation to separate two polymers from each other has shown that the polymer surface hydrophobicity can be dependent on pH [20]. This wettability dependence on pH may be a factor here and will be a focus of future work.

The improvement in deinking with increasing temperature is probably due to rate effects, since surfactant adsorption decreases with increasing temperature [21] and solubilization is only mildly temperature dependent [22].

4. Conclusions

Increasing pH, temperature, pre-soaking time, shaking time, surfactant concentration and adding abrasives improve deinking. Complete deinking is attainable under reasonable process conditions and this work shows some variable effects useful in process optimization.

ABSTRACT

Polyolefins are widely employed as external skins for flexible packaging, yet their nonpolar, hydrophobic surfaces present challenges for high- resolution, wear- resistant printing. Converters have traditionally relied on surface treatments, such as corona treatment, to increase surface free energy (SFE) and promote compatibility with solvent- based inks. While water- based inks offer sustainability advantages and reduced volatile organic compound exposure over solvent- based inks, their adhesion to polymer substrates is inconsistent and generally not robust. Industry guidelines suggest SFE differentials between ink and substrate are the only factor influencing adhesion; however, this factor may not completely describe the ink- substrate interactions. The adhesion performance of water- based inks was evaluated on polyethylene, ethylene acrylic acid copolymer, ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer, and polyamide. Polymer films were examined pre-  and post- corona treatment to assess changes in surface energy, chemistry, and topography on ink printability and durability. To achieve acceptable print durability, these polymers all required corona treatment, leading to chemical and morphological modifications to the film surface. Results demonstrated that surface chemistry and topography are stronger indicators of water- based ink adhesion than SFE alone. These findings establish a framework for optimizing the durability of water- based inks on polyolefins and related substrates through targeted surface treatment strategies.

1   |   Introduction

The surface printing of flexible polymer packaging is crucial for  aesthetic  and  informational  reasons.  Enhancing  a  product's attractiveness and functionality to consumers is a significant factor in the supply chain processes involved in finished goods  production.  Flexible  packaging  articles  are  typically produced with polyolefins (e.g., polyethylene) as external skin layers  due  to  their  abuse  resistance,  durability,  flexibility, and  corrosion  resistance  properties,  in  addition  to  low  cost and ease of processing. However, due to polyolefins' chemical structure  and  their  resulting  low  surface  free  energy  (SFE), these polymers cannot form strong bonds with ink, overprint varnish, or lacquer coatings [1]. To overcome adhesion issues common with  low  SFE  materials,  packaging  producers  (referred to in the industry as converters) apply a combination of  surface  treatment  and  organic  solvent- based  ink  systems to enable surface printing of these materials. With the global movement towards more sustainable solutions, traditional organic  solvent- based  ink  systems  have  been  criticized  due  to

the environmental impacts of the raw materials of the inks [2]. Additionally, there are health concerns for industry workers over prolonged exposure to these inks associated with inhalation and contact with volatile organic compounds present in organic solvents [3]. Water- based ink systems are considered more environmentally friendly, eliminate workers' exposure to organic solvents, and can produce higher- definition imaging  than  solvent- based  inks  [4].  Digital  printing,  also  called inkjet printing, which uses water- based ink systems, has been touted  as  the  future  of  printing  technology  for  packaging graphics [5, 6]. This research examines how polymer selection and corona surface treatment impact the printability of water- based ink systems.

Interactions  between  inks  and  substrates  are  critical  during printing. The adhesion of the ink to the outer layer of the packaging film is hypothesized to be determined by the interactions between polar and nonpolar (dispersive) components of the inks and the polymer films. The greater the similarity between the polar and dispersive components of inks and substrates, the better the wetting and adhesion on the surface of the printing substrate. Increasing the surface density of polar functional groups and the resulting increase in SFE can overcome poor wetting and adhesion on polymer surfaces. A guideline commonly used in  industry  is  that  the  SFE  of  the  printing  substrate  typically needs to be 15-20 dynes/cm higher than the ink's surface tension to achieve proper adhesive bonding. To the authors' knowledge, no comprehensive study has critically assessed the overarching applicability  and  limitations  of  this  industrial  guideline.  This study evaluates this widely used industry guideline on surface energy differences, specifically studying SFE and other physical and chemical factors that may contribute to ink adhesion and durability.

There  are  several  methods  that  converters  can  use  to  modify polymer  film  surfaces  prior  to  printing,  promoting  ink  adhesion,  including  corona  treatment,  flame  treatment,  plasma treatment, and chemical treatment [7, 8]. Generally, these surface  treatments  are  designed  to  increase  the  SFE  of  the  film by ~15-20 dynes/cm compared to the neat film by introducing reactive  groups  that  bond  with  the  ink  on  the  surface  [9-13]. A  typical  water- based  ink  has  a  surface  tension  in  the  range of  25-30 dynes/cm. Using the industry guideline that the substrate surface tension should be 15-20 dynes/cm higher than the ink, the target surface energy of the print substrate should be 40-50 dynes/cm to achieve acceptable adhesion [3].

Methods such as corona treatment are widely used in industry to promote surface oxidation that can increase the adhesion between solvent- based  inks  and  polyolefin  surfaces  [9].  When  a film  is  subjected  to  corona  treatment,  the  treatment  produces polar  and  hydrophilic  functional  groups  on  the  surface,  such as  hydroxyl  ( OH),  carboxyl  (R COOH),  carbonyl  (C O), or  ester  (R CO OR) groups [10,  13].  Introducing  these  polar groups on the film surface increases the SFE and subsequently improves the wettability and adhesion properties between the liquid  ink  and  the  polymer  film  [13].  A  drawback  of  corona treatment is that the treatment effects decrease over time as non- functionalized polymer chains diffuse from the bulk to the surface. As a result, films often need to be retreated if they are not printed immediately [14, 15]. While these surface treatments are commonly used in typical packaging polyolefins, they are not always available (capital expense), may not produce adequate oxidation to increase the surface energy of these films and have the limitation of needing to print very soon after treatment. Another consideration is that different polymers have varied responses to these surface treatments, resulting in variable levels of oxidation and, in some cases, detrimental responses to treatment, such as chain scission [10].

A wide variety of polymers are used in packaging films, each exhibiting  a  range  of  surface  and  bulk  properties.  This  study focuses on a group of polymers extensively utilized in packaging films to explore how their surface characteristics influence printability and print stability. Polyethylene is used as a model nonpolar polymer for comparison with the other selected polymers. The selected polymers in this study that possess inherent latent  functionality  include  ethylene  acrylic  acid  copolymer (EAA),  ethylene  vinyl  alcohol  block  copolymer  (EVOH),  and polyamide (PA) (Figure 1).

Polyethylene  (PE)  is  the  most  commonly  used  polymer  in flexible packaging [9]. PE has the least complex structure in polymers, with only methylene (CH 2 ) repeat units, which are nonpolar and relatively inert. PE and other nonpolar polymer films are difficult to print on due to their nonpolar and hydrophobic  nature,  as  indicated  above.  Without  any  hydrophilic functional groups, PE must be surface- treated to create functional groups that can provide favorable interactions with the inks to improve printing.

EAA copolymers are used in the packaging industry to adhere to polar substrates or act as interlayer adhesion layers between coextruded  multilayer  polymer  films  [16].  Occasionally,  EAA has also been used on external surfaces where increased adhesion is desired for the surface. The carboxylic acid groups from the acrylic acid content [10] in EAA can serve as reactive functional groups and orient to the surface, and this polar surface functionality promotes adhesion with polar inks.

EVOH was selected as one of the polymers due to its surface energy value of 41-45 dynes/cm [17], which is comparable to corona- treated PE. EVOH is a random copolymer of PE and poly  (vinyl  alcohol)  (PVA).  PVA  contains  an  aliphatic  C C backbone and pendant OH groups, and these polar groups render  the  copolymer  hydrophilic  [17].  EVOH  is  commonly used in packaging as a barrier layer to protect the contents due to its performance as a barrier to various gases. The selection of EVOH for this study is based on its hydrophilic nature, desirable SFE values, and functional groups available for interactions with ink.
