PA also has a higher native surface energy that falls in the typical range of 48-51 dynes/cm [18] and has available amide functional  groups  ( CONH 2 ).  Commercial  polyamide  comes  in  a variety of grades based on monomer structure (e.g., PA6, PA66, copolymer PA6/66). PA6/66 is often used in packaging for film strength, barrier properties, and improved processing compared to PA6 and PA66 grades, and can be used throughout multilayer structures, including as an exterior skin layer. Due to its prevalent use in commercial applications, the copolymer PA6/66 is the form of PA selected for this study.

Most of  the  literature  data  targeting  improved  adhesion  between water- based ink and polymer film surfaces has focused on  the  ink  composition  [19,  20].  Limited  research  has  been performed that modifies the polymers and their surface characteristics  while  maintaining  the  constant  ink  composition. Also,  how  the  surface  treatment  alters  the  surface  topography and correspondingly changes the ink adhesion behavior is not well understood. This study aims to provide a new understanding of the critical surface characteristics of polymer films to achieve acceptable ink adhesion and durability in digital print applications.

2   |   Experimental

2.1   |   Materials

2.1.1   |   Film Preparation

The  test  samples  used  in  this  study  are  multilayer  polymer films  produced  on  a  commercial  coextrusion  line  at  Sealed Air Corporation. The bulk layers were produced similarly for all  films  used  in  the  study,  and  only  the  external  skin  layer (5-10 μm layer thickness) was modified. The commercial polymers used for this study include the polyethylene grade linear low- density (LLDPE) octene copolymer PE ExxonMobil Exact 3024,  SK  Primacor  1410  EAA,  BASF  Ultramid  C33  PA6/66 polyamide copolymer, and the Kuraray EVAL E171B, a 44 mol% grade EVOH.

FIGURE  2 |    Illustration  of  multilayer  films  and  exterior  printing surface of interest.

2.1.2 | Printing

The films were printed using a water- based polyurethane ink system  prepared  by  Sealed  Air  Corporation.  The  ink  consists of  the  following  components:  pigment,  polymer,  co- solvent, humectant,  surfactant,  and  water,  with  an  approximate  total solids  content  of  less  than  20 wt%  and  an  initial  surface  tension  of  less  than  ~50  dynes  per  centimeter  upon  application. The printing involves a piezoelectric four- color CMYK process. The  ink  and  the  printing  process  are  described  in  US  Patent Applications US20230118001A1 [21], US 2024/0327662A1 [22], US  2024/0010019A1  [23],  and  US  Patent  US11008478B2  [24]. The films were corona- treated in line with a treatment setting of  1  W/ft 2 (10.76 W/m 2 )  where  applicable.  Films  were  printed on the exterior  layer  only.  All  bulk  layers  remained  the  same throughout the study, and only the surface layer was modified, as illustrated in Figure 2.

2.1.3 | Contact Angle

SFE was evaluated using contact angle measurements collected using a Krüss MSA One- Click SFE surface analyzer. Sessile drop experiments  were  conducted  using  water  (deionized  UHPLC water, Sigma Aldrich, CAS 7732- 18- 5) as the polar probe liquid and diiodomethane (ReagentPlus, 99%, Sigma Aldrich, CAS 75- 11- 6) as the dispersive probe liquid, with a 2 μL drop volume. The Kruss ADVANCE software was used to estimate the contact angle values from the captured images using the Young- Laplace fitting method. The surface free energies for the films were calculated using the OWRK (Owens, Wendt, Rabel, and Kaelble) method [25].

2.1.4 | Ink Adhesion and Durability

Ink durability testing was completed immediately after printing  using  the  ASTM  F2252- 03  tape  adhesion  test  method [26].  A  piece  of  ¾"  3 M  #600  clear  pressure- sensitive  tape was applied across the entire printed surface. The tape was then pulled with a steady, smooth motion at a 45° angle. The tape was then assessed for ink transfer, and a score was assigned based on the amount of ink present on the tape. Rub testing was conducted using a Testing Machines Inc. Digital Ink Rub Tester 10- 20 using ASTM D5264 [27], where samples are  mounted to a sled with the printed side in contact with Kraft paper. The unit then oscillates the sled back and forth for the desired cycle time. For this study, the oscillation cycles were 2 min long, with 100 cycles/min for 200 cycles. The characteristic adhesion and durability tests selected for this study are  based  on  the  commercial  usage  conditions,  specifically printed  ink  resistance  to  scuffing  due  to  repeated  external stressors, such as rubbing contact with other materials during packaging and transport. In this case, the rub testing method provides a representative evaluation of the ink's contact durability in packaging applications.

2.1.5 | Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM)

The  surface  topographies  and  phase  contrast  imaging  of the  film  samples  were  investigated  using  a  Dimension  Icon AFM (Bruker). A silicon NCHV probe with 42 N/m of spring constant  and  320 kHz  of  frequency  was  used  in  all  experiments, and the film sample was mounted on glass slides with double- sided tape. AFM height and phase scans (5 × 5 μm 2  and 50 × 50 μm 2 ) were collected using tapping mode under ambient air conditions.

2.1.6 | Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR)

The samples were characterized using FTIR in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode to examine the functional groups present within the film surface. The equipment was a Nicolet iS20 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, USA) equipped with a SMART iTX ATR accessory (Thermo Scientific, USA) and a diamond crystal. All spectra were analyzed using OMNIC (Thermo Scientific, USA) software. Each sample was run with 32 scans, with a spectral range of 1500-600 cm -1 and a spectral resolution of 0.25 cm -1 .

2.1.7 | X- Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS)

XPS  analysis  was  performed  using  a  Physical  Electronics PHI VersaProbe 5000 station XPS to obtain survey and high- resolution  (HRES)  spectra  of  the  neat  and  corona- treated polymer films. The XPS instrument is equipped with a monochromated  25.0 W  Al  1486.6 eV  source.  To  assess  elemental composition, survey spectra were collected at a pass energy of 117.4 eV and a resolution of ±0.5 eV. For all elements observed in the survey scan, HRES spectra were collected at a pass energy of 23.5 eV and a resolution of ±0.2 eV. All XPS data were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.23PR1.0). Atomic percentages were determined from the survey spectra after processing each elemental region with Shirley backgrounds and applying the Physical Electronics instrument relative sensitivity factors (RSF), which are instrument dependent. All HRES spectra were charge- corrected  by  pinning  the  C1s  aliphatic  (C C/C H) band to  285 eV  and  were  processed  with  Shirley  backgrounds and CasaXPS 's  LA  line  shapes,  which  combine  Gaussian  and Lorentzian peak shape contributions that are typical for polymers [28].

3   |   Results and Discussion

3.1   |   Determining Surface Characteristics Before and After Corona Treatment

3.1.1   |   FTIR

As the printing process depends on the surface characteristics, the film samples were characterized by FTIR and contact angle measurements (and subsequent calculations of SFE) before and after corona treatment. FTIR spectra for all untreated polymer samples  are  shown  in  Figure  3.  For  neat  PE  (control),  peaks at ~2850 and 2920 cm -1 are  attributed to C H stretching, and peaks at 1460 and 720 cm -1 are  associated with C H bending and rocking modes, respectively [29, 30]. For EAA, the peak at ~1700 cm -1  is the identifying peak for this material, which corresponds to the carbonyl stretch of carboxylic acid [29, 30]. For PA, the peaks of interest are 1635 and 1537 cm -1 ,  which correspond to N H bending in amines [28-31]. EVOH is a copolymer of PE and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). A strong peak at 3307 cm -1 indicates OH stretching, which is characteristic of PVA in the EVOH copolymer [30, 31]. Additionally, a peak at 1430 cm -1 is associated with the C H bending mode in PE in the EVOH copolymer [30, 31].

Corona  treatment  directs  a  high- frequency  discharge  at  the polymer surface, leading to surface oxidation and the generation of polar functional groups such as carbonyl groups, among others previously mentioned [10, 13, 32]. These generated polar groups lead to higher surface energy compared to untreated PE and improve the likelihood of adhesion between the liquid and the polymer film. The presence of polar groups such as hydroxyls or carbonyls is desired at the surface and can contribute to increased ink durability performance.

FTIR characterization was conducted after corona treatment for each sample type (Figure 3). Distinct changes in the FTIR spectral peaks due to the corona treatment process were expected. Still, they were not distinctly discernible in this case, as no additional peaks or shifts in peaks were detected (see Figure S1, ESI). The corona treatment settings used in this study were a quick- treat,  or  in- line  corona  treatment  unit  on  the  printing  press. Correspondingly, the specimens were exposed to corona treatment for a short time (< 1 s). Due to the short treatment times, the  corona  treatment  was  expected  to  lead  to  chemical  functionalization over a very thin surface layer. FTIR measurements cannot capture the surface layer exclusively, and the responses from the bulk are dominant in the FTIR spectra obtained here. Instances of marked changes in FTIR spectra are reported in the literature where polymer films were subjected to corona treatment for an extended period of time, with some studies reporting treatment times of seconds-as low as 5 s [33]-and others up to 50 h [34], which are not representative of industrial in- line corona treatment processes (Figure 3). Studies with treatment times similar to this study (~1s) have also been reported in the literature, where treated samples did not display any significant changes in spectral patterns [12].

3.1.3 | XPS

Neat and corona- treated polymer films were analyzed by XPS. Both survey and high- resolution (HRES) spectra were collected to assess the atomic composition and chemical bonding changes in the polymer films due to the corona treatment. Comparison of the HRES spectra for C 1s and O 1s regions, as well as the ratio of O 1s/C 1s atomic percentages, indicates a change in chemical bonding and an increase in oxygen content for the PE, EVOH, and  PA  films,  while  changes  in  the  monolayer  EAA  film  are ambiguous.

As summarized in Table 2, the oxygen content increased after the samples were corona- treated, which was expected. For example,  the  PE  oxygen  content  of  the  PE  sample  after  corona treatment was 18.25%, compared with 1.49% before corona treatment. Also, the carbon content decreased from 98.50% before the corona treatment to 74.47% after the corona treatment. This is expected due to the known functional groups introduced by corona treatment (C O, OH, OOH, and COOH) [10, 13, 32], which explains the increase in the oxygen content as the pre- treatment surface contained only CH 2 functional groups.

The high- resolution  scans  (HRES)  were  also  investigated  and are detailed in Figures S2-S7, and Tables S1-S4 ESI. For PE, the C1s and O 1s HRES spectra indicated an increase in peak intensities for CO (eV) and C O/COOH (eV) functional groups, and a broadening of the overall C1s peak was observed after corona treatment. The EAA sample C1s and O1s HRES spectra for the corona- treated film showed lower contributions of acrylic acid functional  groups.  The  C1s  HRES  peaks  in  the  neat  film  are slightly lower than expected for EAA and PAA- based polymers in the literature. For EVOH, the presence of a carbonyl peak at 288.9 eV in the C1s HRES and a peak at 533 eV in the O1s spectra after corona treatment suggests the formation of carboxylic acid groups. In the PA films, the HRES N1s spectra for the corona- treated  film  show  a  significantly  weaker  polyamide  peak  at

~400 eV compared to the untreated film. An increase in the area percentages for peaks in the ~385.5-386.5 eV region in the C1s HRES spectra associated  with  C O/C OH/O C O  suggests an increase in oxygen species on the corona- treated polyamide surface. The survey scan spectra for the samples are shown in Figure 4, and selected HRES spectra are shown in Figure 5.

3.2   |   Surface Morphological Analysis

AFM was used to examine the changes in surface topography of the film samples before and after corona treatment and how the surface topography relates to the ink adhesion behavior of the polymer films. AFM height and phase images are shown in Figures  6  and  7,  respectively.  Untreated  samples,  specifically PE,  display  fibrous  features,  which  have  also  been  reported previously  in  the  literature  [35-39].  This  has  been  attributed to crystallites present in PE, affected by the orientation of the polymer chains during processing and subsequent quenching. After corona treatment, the PE, EAA, and EVOH films exhibit a  distinct  change  in  surface  topography,  where  the  surface  of the  film  appears  to  have  globule- like  structures,  or  'globular mounds'.  These  were  not  present  before  treatment  but  have been reported in the literature for  polypropylene  after  corona treatment [35-39]. These mounds have been hypothesized to be low molecular weight oxidized material (LMWOM) [35-39] and have also been found to be water- soluble through several characterization  methods.  The  similarities  in  appearance  between the results presented by Strobel et al. [35] for PP and the samples in this study are notable. Given the similarities in structures between the PE and PP, the presence of LMWOM on the surface of  the  samples in this study could be assumed; however, with water- based ink, the treatment effects would be expected to contradict an improvement in ink adhesion.

The corona treatment process used in this  study  is  an  in- line  process  within  the  printing  press,  and the film is treated as it passes through the press, which is the most practical method of treatment for films in preparation for industrial printing. In the case of PA, the film may have needed a longer exposure to corona treatment to have an adequate effect to demonstrate observable changes in film surface morphology and chemistry. This is beyond the scope of the work of this study.

3.3   |   Ink Adhesion and Durability

The films were printed in- line using a digital printing press and evaluated immediately for ink adhesion and durability using the tape- test method and rub evaluation as described in the methods section. An example of the printed image before testing and examples of tape test results are shown in Figure 8.

The  ASTM  tape  standard  test  defines  both  slow  and  fast  tape pulls  to  determine  ink  adhesion  on  a  printed  surface  [26].  The test  method  is  described  in  more  detail  in  the  materials  and methods section. In summary, after an image is printed onto a surface (Figure 8A), a piece of tape is applied to the printed surface smoothly and then pulled off either slowly or quickly according to which test is being conducted. This test method is a measure to assess the strength of adhesion between the ink and the print surface. The amount of ink that is on the tape after it is removed is an indication of the ink's adhesion to the surface. Figure 8B-E are images of the tape after slow and fast tape pulls. If there is a high percentage of ink on the tape and little ink left on the film, as shown on the untreated images in Figure 8 (left side; untreated PE [B] and untreated PA [D]), the ink adhesion is poor. An indication of good ink adhesion would result in little to no ink on the tape after it is pulled off the printed area, as seen in Figure 8C, where the tape test results of treated PE are depicted. Tape test results of treated PA are shown in Figure 8E. After the tapes were pulled, the amount of ink on the tape was evaluated and scored according PE Films Printed image before tape tests to the Durability Rating Scale shown in Table 3. A summary of the results of tape testing and rub evaluations by polymer type and corona treatment level is also available in Table 3.

As shown in Table 3, there were varied results between the polymer films with respect to ink adhesion and durability. If only the  SFE  were  used  as  guidance,  all  corona- treated  film  samples would be expected to outperform untreated PE and EAA. Further,  it  was  anticipated  that  the  higher  native  SFE  of  the PA and EVOH film samples would demonstrate improved performance in untreated film ink adhesion compared to the untreated polyolefin films. However, our results indicate that the corona- treated PE resulted in the best ink adhesion scores, while the corona- treated PA resulted in the poorest post- treatment ink adhesion scores.

The  ink  adhesion  and  durability  testing  results  are  as  anticipated for the treated PE and EAA samples. As a result of corona treatment, both PE and EAA indicated a marked increase in SFE in addition to observed topographical changes through AFM. The adhesion and durability results support the guideline practiced in industry.

However, the adhesion and durability results for the PA and EVOH  samples  are  contradictory  to  the  hypothesis,  where films with surface energies in the range of corona- treated PE would exhibit better ink adhesion and durability even without corona treatment. The PA and EVOH films both demonstrated improved ink adhesion with corona treatment in the tape test, but did not demonstrate durability improvement in rub testing scores, even after corona treatment. The PA samples  were  poorer  in  durability  scores  after  corona  treatment than all other samples. As observed in the contact angle/SFE, AFM, and XPS characterizations, the PA film exhibited minimal changes pre-  and post- corona treatment. The surface topography was relatively unaffected, as observed in the AFM images (Figures 6 and 7). The SFE was minimally affected by corona treatment in the PA films, and while the XPS analysis

A

did indicate a small increase in oxygen content, the increase was not as significant as the better- performing (with respect to  ink  adhesion  and  durability)  PE  and  EAA  films.  EAA showed  a  small  increase  in  oxygen  content  as  analyzed  by XPS (an increase of 2.23% after treatment) but demonstrated a more pronounced increase in SFE as determined by contact angle evaluation. EVOH showed a more pronounced increase in  oxygen  with  XPS  analysis,  with  an  increase  of  15.32%  in oxygen content post- treatment.

The results above suggest that the oxygen content, and more importantly, the reactive groups present on the surface along with surface topography, are more influential for ink adhesion and durability than factors such as high native SFE. While it can be observed that all four polymer types studied were affected by the corona treatment, it can be justifiably concluded that polymer types have varied responses to corona treatments, resulting in varied surface topographies, surface chemistries, and ink adhesion and durability capacity. The types of functional groups, surface density of the functional groups, and reactivity of the functional groups, combined with surface topography, directly influence the level of ink adhesion and durability of the polymer surfaces, signifying that the degree of ink adhesion and durability is more complex than SFE guidelines used in industry. While PE was the most promising substrate for printing in this study, future investigations would be necessary to understand the effects of comonomer content, molecular weight, branching, and other physical attributes of PE grades.

4   |   Conclusions

Industry guidelines for acceptable ink adhesion and durability currently reference SFE differentials as the primary factor in predicting successful printability. Based on this guideline, the SFE of a print substrate should be in the range of 40-50 dynes/ cm to generate successful ink adhesion with a representative water- based ink. The initial hypothesis of this work was that polymer films having native SFE values that are in the same range as those achieved by corona treatment of polyethylene, ca. 41-46 dynes/cm, will have significantly higher ink adhesion and rub- resistance durability compared to a standard polyethylene, with typical SFE values of 28-33 dynes/cm. However, the findings from this study show that polymers with native SFE in the range of 41-46 dynes/cm, due to their chemical composition and surface functional groups, did not demonstrate improved ink adhesion or durability. All polymers tested required corona treatment to demonstrate any notable improvement in ink adhesion and durability. The analysis methods, including ATR- FTIR, contact angle goniometry with resulting SFE calculations, AFM, XPS, and ink adhesion and durability testing, established  baseline  information  for  untreated  samples  and demonstrated surface functionality changes that were expected in  the  corona- treated  samples,  confirming  the  surfaces  were adequately treated and prepared for printing. Combining the results  of  ink  adhesion  and  durability  testing  with  other  analytical  data,  it  was  determined  that  the  influence  of  corona treatment through oxidation, production of surface- active functional groups present at the surface, and topographical modifications  are  more  significant  factors  for  predicting  acceptable ink adhesion and durability than the SFE differences between the ink and the polymer substrates. Polymers with high native SFE values in the range of corona- treated PE (ca. 41-46 dynes/ cm) (i.e., PA, EVOH) did not demonstrate better or improved ink adhesion or durability versus polymers with lower native SFE values (i.e., PE, EAA, ca. 28-33 dynes/cm) either pre-  or post- corona treatment. The observed changes in corona- treated PE and EAA, including oxidation and changes in surface topography, in combination with a higher SFE, led to higher ink adhesion and durability performance in comparison to PA and EVOH. From these  results,  it  can  be  concluded  that  surface chemistry and surface topography combined are more influential factors than SFE alone as a means of achieving improved ink  adhesion  and  durability.  These  observations  and  corresponding  conclusions  provide  updated  guidance  for  flexible packaging converters, as the industry's rule of thumb for using ink and substrate SFE differentials to predict acceptable ink adhesion is not adequate.

1. Introduction

Each year, 21 million tonnes of plastic packaging are produced in the European  Union  (EU)  [1],  of  which  approximately  23  %  consists  of polyethylene  (PE),  a  family  of  polymers  that  includes  low-density polyethylene  (LDPE),  linear  low-density  polyethylene  (LLDPE),  and high-density polyethylene (HDPE) [2]. According to the EU ' s Strategy for Plastic in a Circular Economy, by 2030, all plastic packaging placed on the EU market should be cost-effectively reusable or recyclable [3]. Therefore, the design for recycling of PE-based packaging products has been receiving significant academic and industrial attention [4 -6].

An  important  segment  of  packaging  is  PE  flexible  packaging, commonly referred to as plastic film. These plastic films can be cate gorized into monolayer (one layer of one plastic type), mono-material multilayer (several layers, but only one plastic type), or multi-material multilayer (several layers, several plastic types) [6]. Laminated plastic films, especially mono-material multilayer polyethylene-based (MM-PE) films, have attracted strong interest within the packaging industry over the past decade. Towards closing the material loop, MM-PE films should be recycled in a film-to-film mechanical recycling process, while preserving their desired perfor mance. However, MM-PE laminates typically contain polyurethane (PUR) adhesives between PE film layers, which can affect their recyclability. Herein, three MM-PE films containing different PUR adhesives were studied to assess the effect of the PUR characteristics on the films ' recyclability. The processability of MM-PE laminated films produced via film-blowing extrusion was evaluated, followed by structural, rheological, mechanical, and optical characterization of the recycled films. The composition of the PUR adhesive substantially affects the closed-loop recyclability of the films, and even a small PUR content (2 wt%) can hinder the recycling process. Overall, PUR adhesives reduce the zero-shear viscosity and increase the heterogeneity of the recycled laminates, reducing toughness and increasing haziness. By assessing the morphology and the physicochemical character istics of the PUR adhesives, it is possible to estimate the impact of these materials on the recyclability of MMPE laminates. PURs presenting a higher degree of mixing between hard and soft phases, as indicated by a lower content of hydrogen-bonded groups among hard segments, are preferred for improving the recyclability of MMPE laminates.

Due to the complexity of these multi-material multilayer films, their mechanical recycling is challenging [10].

The environmental performance of mono- and multi-materials plas tic  films  from  the  packaging  industry,  when  assessed  by  life  cycle assessment (LCA), is heavily influenced by their composition [11]. Only the mono-materials packaging systems are currently considered as fully recyclable [11 -13].

In certain applications, including dry food and detergent packaging, mono-material multilayer flexible films can replace the multi-material ones,  which  may  lead  to  improved  recyclability  of  the  films  [6,14]. PE-based mono-material multilayer films (MM-PE) are suitable candi dates for mechanical recycling, as PE is used across all layers [6,12]. Due to the development of these new oriented PE films (MDOPE) with  different  molecular  architectures  and  morphologies,  PEbased layers can offer higher stiffness, puncture resistance, and better optical properties, making them suitable for the replacement of PET in multi material multilayers and developing MM-PE laminates instead [15,16].

Depending on the packaging requirements, multilayer flexible films are  produced  through  co-extrusion  or  lamination  [6].  Since  the  pro duction processes for MDOPE and LDPE layers differ, the MM-PE films are  produced  using  a  lamination  process,  and  PUR  adhesives  are commonly  used  as  a  binder  in  the  final  laminate  structure  of  the multilayer flexible film [17]. PUR is synthesized from the reaction of isocyanates and polyols. Isocyanate ( -NCO) groups undergo addition reactions  with  hydrogen-containing  nucleophiles,  such  as  hydroxyl ( -OH), amino ( -NH2), or carboxyl ( -COOH) groups [18]. PUR adhesives are generally formed from the reaction of an NCO-terminated prepol ymer with a polyester- or polyetherpolyol [19 -23]. Common monomers for polyester synthesis include terephthalic acid (TPA), isophthalic acid (m-phthalic acid), adipic acid, diethylene glycol, neopentyl glycol, and ethylene glycol [24]. Among polyethers, polypropylene glycol (PPG) is one of the most widely used polyols for adhesive formulations [25].

Both aromatic and aliphatic diisocyanates are employed in the PUR adhesive synthesis. Typical aromatic isocyanates include toluene diiso cyanate (TDI) and 4,4 ′ -diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI) [26], while widely used aliphatic options are hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI), isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI), and xylylene diisocyanate (XDI) [27, 28]. The isocyanate index, defined as the molar ratio of NCO to OH groups, is commonly in the range of 1.5 -2 to achieve an optimal balance between reactivity, properties, and processing requirements, and results in a crosslinked PUR adhesive [19,21].

The choice of polyol backbone, the type of the diisocyanate, and the isocyanate  index  represent  the  key  parameters  affecting  the  perfor mance  of  PUR  laminating  adhesives,  including  flexibility,  adhesion strength,  chemical resistance, heat stability,  and retortability  [18,19, 28]. The final structure and morphology of PUR adhesives depend on the chemical structure and molecular weight of the raw materials, the vol ume fraction of the hard and soft segments, and the extent of intra- and inter-molecular interactions in each segment and between hard and soft segments, especially hydrogen bond formation [29 -34]. Additionally, the  content  of  PUR adhesive  used during  film  lamination affects the performance of the adhesive [35,36].

In line with the principles of the circular economy, and to reduce dependence on virgin plastics while minimizing environmental impacts [37,38], the recycled MM-PE ideally will be reused in the same appli cation as the original product, or in applications that demand compa rable  material  properties  [37,39].  Currently,  mechanical  recycling remains  the  dominant  method  for  recycling  of  polyolefins  [40]. Achieving closed-loop film-to-film mechanical recycling of MM-PE re quires that the recycled material be processable through film-blowing, one of the most widely used polymer processing technologies for the production of plastic films [41].

In general, the processability and performance of a final film-blown product are highly dependent on the macromolecular architecture of PE, particularly its molecular weight, molecular weight distribution, and the content and distribution of short-chain branches [42]. However, MM-PE films typically contain PUR adhesives, and due to the presence of polar chemical groups in PUR, such as urethane and ester/ether functional ities, there is an inherent incompatibility of PUR with the non-polar PE matrix during the melt blending stage of mechanical recycling [43,44]. It has been previously found that contaminations will drastically reduce the processing window and the quality of the final film [45]. Conse quently,  it  is  essential  to  investigate  the  influence  of  the  chemical structure of PUR adhesive on the processability and final performance of the  recycled  films  within  the  closed-loop  mechanical  recycling  of MM-PE.

The present study systematically evaluates the recyclability of MM- PE laminated films. Herein, the impact of three different types of PUR adhesives on the processability, mechanical, and optical performance of MM-PE laminates is evaluated in a closed-loop film-to-film mechanical recycling  process.  To  the  best  of  our  knowledge,  no  comprehensive study currently exists for evaluating the recyclability of MM-PE lami nates containing PUR adhesives. This study aims to identify the main effects of PUR adhesives on the film-blowing processability and prop erties of recycled MM-PE films.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Mono-material multilayer polyethylene-based (MM-PE) laminates

Three commercial MM-PE laminates, each one containing a different PUR adhesive (PU1, PU2, and PU3) were evaluated. The composition of the  layers  in  all  the  laminates  was  consistent,  comprising  a  50 μ m MDOPE layer, a 2 g/m 2 PUR adhesive, and a 50 μ m LDPE film as a sealant layer. A film consisting of MDOPE/LDPE without PUR adhesive (PU0) was used as a control.

2.2. Closed-loop mechanical recycling

In this study, closed-loop mechanical film to film recycling refers to the process of converting MMPE laminated films into new films through a shredding, compounding and film-blowing process. At the first step, the laminates were comminuted in a shredder with a 6 mm diameter sieve (Hellweg MDS 340/150). Before the compounding and granulation steps, the shredded flakes were dried for 24 h at 60 °C. The dried flakes were fed into a co-rotating twin screw extruder compounder (KraussMaffei ZE 25R52D) at temperatures ranging from 30 to 230 °C (feeding zone to the die), using both vacuum and atmospheric degassing. The screw rotation speed was maintained at 270 rpm. The resulting pellets were dried again (1 h at 60 °C) before proceeding to the film-blowing step.

The film-blowing process was conducted using a Brabender singlescrew extruder (screw diameter 30 mm; length-to-diameter, L/D = 25) equipped with a melt pressure sensor and a screen changer (100 mesh). The channel depth of the screw in the metering section was 1.66 mm. The film-blowing die had a diameter of 40 mm and a die gap of 1 mm. The barrel temperature was set in the range of 190 -220 °C, and the die head was maintained at 220 °C. Two different screw speeds, 25 and 40 rpm, were set during the production of the film. The cooling fan rate was adjusted for all samples to keep the frost line height (FLH) at 12.5 cm. The blow-up ratio (BUR) and draw-down ratio (DDR) were calculated using Equations (1) and (2), respectively:

BUR = DB DD (1)

BDR = h t × BUR (2)

Where DB is the bubble diameter, DD the die diameter, h the die gap, and t is the film thickness.

The processing for each sample was conducted at two different film thicknesses (25 and 55 μ m), corresponding to two different DDRs. A 25 μ m thickness setup was selected as the critical benchmark for evaluating processability, as thinner films present more challenges in maintaining a stable bubble.

During processing. Afterward, 55 μ m thickness films were produced since thicker films typically present a lower coefficient of variation in the film thickness. These films were then employed for measuring the mechanical and optical properties, as well as for the analysis of the gel particles through optical microscopy. 2.3. Characterization of the PE film layers, PUR, and recycled MM-PE after compounding

Differential  scanning  calorimetry  (DSC),  melt  flow  rate  (MFR), density, and rheological analysis of the laminate layers were performed on  compression-molded  sheets,  which  were  prepared  directly  from discarded shredded films. The compression molding was carried out at 220 °C for 5 min.

2.3.1. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)

Prior to the DSC analysis of PUR adhesives, a reflux technique was employed to dissolve the PE layers of the laminates. For this extraction, approximately 10 g of MM-PE films were placed in a 500 mL roundbottom flask containing 200 mL of p-xylene at 150 °C and kept under reflux for 15 min. After cooling to room-temperature, the sample was filtered to separate the PUR adhesive from the PE solution. The recov ered PUR was further washed with fresh p-xylene to remove residual PE, and subsequently dried under 10 mbar vacuum at 40 °C for 48h. DSC measurements of the extracted PUR adhesives were conducted on a DSC Q2000 (TA Instruments). All DSC measurements were performed under nitrogen atmosphere, using samples of ca. 8 mg. The heating and cooling rates were set to 30 °C/min. The PUR samples were heated from 60 to 120 °C, kept at 120 °C for 3 min, cooled down to 60 °C, and then reheated to 120 °C.

DSC measurements of the lamination PE layers (MDOPE and LDPE) and  the  control  film  (PU0)  were  conducted  on  a  DSC  300  Caliris (Netzsch). All DSC measurements were performed under nitrogen at mosphere, using samples of ca. 8 mg. The heating and cooling rates were set to 10 °C/min. The samples were heated from 0 to 160 °C, following an  isothermal  step  for  10  min,  cooled  to  0 °C,  maintained  at  this temperature for 10 min, and then re-heated to 160 °C. The crystallinity degree ( XC ) was calculated according to Equation (4), where Δ Hm is the measured melt enthalpy, Δ H ∞ m is the theoretical enthalpy of the 100 % crystalline PE (293 J/g) [46].

2.3.2. Melt flow rate (MFR)

The melt flow rate (MFR) of the pure layers (MDOPE and LDPE) was measured in accordance with ISO 1133 -1:2022.  Measurements  were carried out using a melt flow indexer (Tinius Olsen MP1200) at a tem perature of 190 °C under a load of 2.16 kg.

2.3.3. Density

The density of  PE  layers  and  the  control  sample  was  determined using the density method in accordance with ISO 1183 -1:2025 (Method A). MFR strands were first weighed in air using an analytical balance (Mettler Toledo XSE105). Subsequently, the specimens were immersed in ethanol of known density at room temperature, and their apparent weight in the liquid was recorded with a density determination kit.

2.3.4. Attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR)

Infrared spectroscopy analyses were conducted using a PerkinElmer Spotlight 400 FT-IR Spectrometer equipped with a Golden Gate diamond single attenuated total reflectance (ATR) cell. The MDOPE/LDPE films were delaminated and ATR-FTIR measurements were performed on the surface of the PUR layer. The spectra were recorded at a resolution of 2 cm 1 .  Subsequently,  the  spectra  underwent  baseline  correction  and were normalized according to the maximum absorbance observed in the range 1760 - 1700 cm 1 .

2.3.5. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)

A thermogravimetric analyzer (TA Instruments Q500) was used to investigate the mass loss profiles of the compounded samples (7 -8 mg). The samples were analyses in titanium crucibles using three successive dynamic steps: 10 °C/min from 25 to 180 °C; 2 °C/min from 180 to 420 °C; and 10 °C/min from 420 to 550 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere (60 mL/min). The heating rate was set at 2 °C/min in the temperature range of PURs mass loss (180 -420 °C) to increase the resolution of the analysis, accessing the PUR segments degradation steps, given the low concentration of PUR in the films (2 g/m 2 ).

2.3.6. Rheological measurements

For the rheological analysis, the  compounded  samples  were compression-molded into rectangular sheets with thicknesses of (1.0 ± 0.1) mm. Two layers were placed on top of each other to ensure suffi cient material without voids. Any excess material was trimmed prior to measurement.  Zero-shear  viscosity  values  were  calculated  using  the modified rheological model from Carreau (Equation (5)):

η = η 0 [ 1 +( λ ˙ γ ) m ] n 1 m (5)

Where ( η 0 ) represents the zero-shear viscosity, ˙ γ stands for shear rate, and λ , m , and n are the constants of this model [47].

An Anton Paar MCR 702e MultiDrive rheometer with a parallel plate geometry (diameter of D = 25 mm, gap between plates = 1 mm) was employed  for  oscillatory  and  rotational  experiments.  Oscillatory  ex periments were conducted under nitrogen atmosphere over an angular frequency ( ω ) range of 0.126-500 rad/s, at a temperature of 220 °C, with an applied strain of 1 %. The viscosity curves of the samples were ob tained at 220 °C within a shear rate range of 0.001 -10 s 1 under a ni trogen atmosphere.

2.3.7. Mechanical properties

Tensile tests of the recycled films were performed according to the ISO 527 standard, using a Zwick Roell Z020 testing machine equipped with a 100 N static load cell and a video extensometer. Test specimens (ISO 527 type 2) were cut from the films in both machine direction (MD) and transverse direction (TD), using a manual press (Ray-Ran) equipped with a cutting die. During the tensile tests, an initial pre-load of 0.1 N was applied, following a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min up to a strain of 1 % to determine the elastic modulus. Afterward, the test continued at 50 mm/min until the failure occurred. The tear force of the recycled films  was  measured  according  to  the  ISO  6383-1  standard  using  an Instron 5566 tensile test machine at a crosshead speed of 200 mm/min. The impact resistance of the films was measured according to the freefalling  dart  method  (ASTM  D  1709, method  A)  in  an  RDM  FD-1709 falling dart impact tester.

2.3.8. Optical properties

The total light transmission, yellowing index (YI), and haze of the recycled films were measured according to the ASTM E1164 standard, using  a  HunterLab  UltraScan  VIS  spectrophotometer  in  the  trans mittance mode.

2.3.9. Optical microscopy

A polarized optical microscope (Olympus DP27) equipped with a Linkam hot stage device was employed to assess the morphology of the PUR particles dispersed in PE. A temperature of 150 °C was set to melt the PE, facilitating the characterization of the crosslinked PUR particles. PUR particles were evaluated from five pictures of each sample, each representing a 1 cm 2 section of the films. The software Image-J was employed to measure the dimensions of the PUR particles. The reported number of gels corresponds to an equal surface area of 1 cm 2 for all samples.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Characterization of the PE layers and control sample

Fig. 2a shows the viscosity of the laminate layers (MDOPE as the top layer and LDPE as the sealant) as a function of shear rate. MDOPE ex hibits higher viscosity than LDPE at all shear rates, indicating that a higher molecular weight (Mw) grade was used in the production of the MDOPE layer  [48].  Linear  polyethylene  grades  with  higher  Mw  are typically  employed  for  MDOPE  production  to  achieve  films  with enhanced physical performance [49].

The control sample (PU0), which is a blend of 50.3 wt% MDOPE and 49.7  wt%  LDPE,  presents  higher  viscosity  than  MDOPE.  This  higher viscosity can be attributed to crosslinking of PE chains in PU0, resulting from the additional high-temperature processing steps (compounding and film-blowing) occurred during the recycling process [50].

Zero-shear viscosity  values  were  calculated  using  the  modified  rheo logical model from Carreau (Equation (5)) by fitting the curves as shown in Fig. 2a.

The zero-shear viscosities ( η 0) of the MDOPE and LDPE layers, and control sample PU0 were 17823, 3988, and 20872 Pa s, respectively. The MFR values for the samples MDOPE LDPE, and PU0 were 0.52, 1.91, and 0.40 g/10 min, respectively. MFR values are consistent with poly ethylene grades suitable for film production n [49].

The second heating cycle of the DSC thermogram for the laminate layers and PU0 sample is presented in Fig. 2b. Table A.3 in the Sup porting  Information  (SI)  contains  the  melting  points,  enthalpy  of melting,  and  crystallinity  percentages  for  all  layers  and  PU0.  Both MDOPE and LDPE layers display a single melting point, with MDOPE showing a higher melting temperature, indicative of a thicker lamellar structure resulting from its more linear chain configuration [51]. LDPE, with its lower melting temperature, is more appropriate for use as an inner sealant layer [52]. This observation is consistent with the density values, where MDOPE (931 kg/m 3 ) exhibits a higher density than LDPE (921 kg/m 3 ), further confirming its more linear chain structure [51]. The control sample, with a density of 927 kg/m 3 , lies between the two layers.  The  MDOPE  layer  also  exhibits  a  higher  melting  enthalpy, reflecting a higher degree of crystallinity (Table A.3).

In contrast, PU0 exhibits two distinct melting points corresponding to  the  MDOPE  and  LDPE  layers,  suggesting  that  no  substantial  cocrystallization occurs in this blend due to the high degree of branch ing  of  LDPE  [53].  However,  the  melting  point  of  MDOPE  in  PU0  is slightly suppressed due to the presence of LDPE chains which may have either kinetic effect or thermal perturbations, which act as defects and lead to thinner lamellae [53].

Selecting the appropriate grades for MDOPE and LDPE layers can be guided effectively by evaluating the viscosity, density, and MFR values of each layer [54].

3.2. PUR characterization

3.2.1. ATR-FTIR

The FTIR spectra (400 -4000 cm 1 ) of the samples (PU0 -PU3 in Figure A.9) indicates that PU1 is a polyether-based PUR, with a strong band at 1098 cm 1 , referring to the C-O stretching mode vibration in ethers. PU2 and PU3 most likely consist of polyester-based PUs since they do not present absorption peaks associated with ether bands [55]. Fig. 3a presents the ATR-FTIR spectra of the PU0-PU3 sample in the region related to the carbonyl region (1620 -1780 cm 1 ), emphasizing their different compositions and hydrogen-bonding (H-bond) characteristics.

This band shifts to 1680 -1720 cm 1 for H-bonded carbonyl and urethane carbonyl in both soft and hard segments in a disordered phase and ul timately shifts to 1640 -1680 cm 1 for H-bonded carbonyl of urethane groups in an ordered phase of hard segments [33,56 -59]. Additionally, carbonyl bands associated with urea groups forming H-bonds appear in the range of 1620 -1650 cm 1 [33]. Therefore, the carbonyl absorption region was divided into three segments: (i) ordered H-bonded carbonyl groups  (around  1662  cm 1 only  in  case  of  PU3);  (ii)  disordered H-bonded carbonyl groups (around 1706 cm 1 for PU1, 1712 cm 1 for PU2, and 1684 cm 1 for PU3); and (iii) free, non-H-bonded carbonyl groups (1723 -1739 cm 1 )  [33,58]. The FTIR spectra of the carbonyl region were deconvoluted based on these three distinct segments, and the area of each assigned peak was calculated. The deconvolution results for each absorption band are presented in Figure A.10 and Table A.4. Thereafter,  the  hydrogen  bond  index  (HBI)  was  determined  using Equation (6) [29]:

HBI = Sbonded Sbonded Sfree (6)

Where Sbonded represents  the  area  of  the  H-bonded  carbonyl  peak (1660 -1712 cm 1 ),  and Sfree represents the area of the free carbonyl peak (1720 -1740 cm 1 ).  HBI values for all samples are presented in Fig. 3a.

The development of hydrogen bonding networks within the hard segments or between hard and soft segments, and the microphase sep aration between hard and soft phases determine the morphology and properties of PURs [33,60]. Analyzing the FTIR spectra of the samples, it is shown that PU3 exhibits a distinct absorption pattern compared to PU1 and PU2. PU3 shows three strong absorption peaks corresponding to two H-bonded peaks at 1662 and 1684 cm 1 (present in the ordered phase in hard segments and disordered phase within hard-soft segment, respectively)  and  free,  non-H  bonded  urethane  carbonyl  groups.  In contrast, PU1 and PU2 show a single peak in the range of free urethane carbonyl,  while  only  a  shoulder  towards  the  disordered  H-bonded carbonyl groups region between soft and hard segments is observed. The ordered H-bonded carbonyl groups in the hard phase of PU3, as indi cated by the peak 1662 cm 1 , suggest that some of the hard segments are incorporated into the hard phase and developed H-bond with other hard segments [31,61], leading to phase separation between the hard and soft microphases [57]. A small shoulder in the range of 1706 -1712 cm 1 for PU1 and PU2 indicates the presence of weakly H-bonded hard segments [61].  Considering  these  peaks  for  PU1  and  PU2,  it  is  shown  that  a fraction of hard segments is dispersed within the soft segments, resulting in a lower level of phase separation for these samples [57]. The proposed morphology model of PU1 and PU2 is shown in Fig. 4a, and that of PU3 is  depicted  in  4b.  For  simplicity,  the  isocyanate  functionality,  polyol molecular weight, and isocyanate index are assumed to be equal for all three  PURs.  The  HBI  values  indicate  that  PU2  has  a  higher  ratio  of H-bonded urethane carbonyls compared to PU1. However, PU3 presents the lowest ratio of H-bonded urethane carbonyls, while the hard seg ments in PU3 show ordered hydrogen bonds compared to PU1 and PU2, indicating a morphology consisting of packed and phase-separated hard segments  for  PU3,  as  evidenced  by  the  strong  absorption  related  to H-bonded  urethane  carbonyls  at  lower  wavenumbers.  The  type  and symmetry of the isocyanate, the type and molecular weight of the pol yol, and the ratio between these PURs constituents (isocyanate index) are important factors affecting the H-bond network in the final PUR structure. The linear and planar isocyanates enable more H-bonds and higher  ordering  of  the  hard  segments  in  the  hard  domains  [57,61].

3.2.2. DSC

The DSC results obtained during the second heating cycle for the extracted PURs is shown in Fig. 3b. Both the heat flow and the first derivative of heat flow for the PUR samples are shown. PURs presenting high miscibility between the hard and soft segments typically exhibit a single  glass  transition  temperature  ( Tg ),  positioned  between  the Tg values  of  the  hard  and  soft  segments  [67,68].  Among  the  samples studied,  only  PU3  displayed  a  well-defined  glass  transition  at Tg = 9.9 °C, as highlighted by the peak observed in the first derivative of heat flow of this sample. In contrast, PU1 and PU2 exhibited Tg in a broad range of temperature, with estimated average Tg values lower than that of PU3. The broad transition temperatures observed for PU1 and PU2 is attributed to the extensive degree of mixing between the hard and soft segments, being consistent with the FTIR results shown in Fig. 3a [69, 70].

3.2.3. TGA

TGA provides insights regarding PUR composition and microstruc ture, as the thermal degradation of PUR depends on the hard and soft segment types, isocyanate index, and degree of phase separation [30]. Figure A.11 presents the TGA thermograms (mass versus temperature) of PU0-PU3 of samples from 25 to 550 °C, while Fig. 4c depicts the first derivative (DTG) of the mass change as a function of the temperature curves during the initial stage of mass loss (from 190 to 390 °C) for PU0 PU3 samples.

Under a nitrogen atmosphere, PU0 (PE) shows a single step of mass loss  starting  at  350 °C [71], as observed in Fig. 4c. For the samples containing PUR adhesives (PU1-PU3), the mass loss occurs in two or three steps, starting around 200 °C [30]. The thermal degradation of PUR initiates  with  the  breakdown  of  urethane  bonds  from  the  hard segment, and the onset temperature and magnitude of this stage depend on the type of isocyanate and polyol, as well as their ratio. A higher content of the soft segment decreases the rate and intensity of the mass loss observed during this first degradation step [34]. In addition, ure thane groups presenting low amount of hydrogen bonds are less stable and degrade faster [32]. The second and third DTG peaks are related to the decomposition of soft segments which occur at a slower rate than the first step [30]. PU3, presenting a higher content of ordered hard seg ments shows mass loss at higher temperatures [30,72]. PU1 and PU2 show  a  similar  first  DTG  peak,  starting  at  around  195 °C  with  a maximum mass loss rate at 250 °C. However, PU1 shows a higher rate of mass  loss,  indicating  a  possible  higher  content  of  hard  segments. Conversely, PU3 demonstrates a diverse thermal decomposition behavior, starting at a higher temperature compared to PU1 and PU2, and showing the first DTG peak as a shoulder beginning at 210 °C and the second DTG peak with a maximum at around 311 °C. These results suggest that PU3 presents more stable hard domains, such as urethane formed from alkyl-isocyanate and alkyl-polyols instead of aryl-isocyanate  and  aryl-polyol  [32].  Furthermore,  increasing  the crosslinking density or the isocyanate index improves the PURs thermal stability since more energy is required to breakdown the PUR network [30].

The temperatures at which the samples presented 5, 20, and 50 wt% of mass loss during the TGA test (T5, T20, and T50, respectively) were determined and are shown in the inset of Fig. 4c. PU1 starts to degrade earlier in the first step than PU2, for T5, and T20. However, at a higher temperature, the  DTG degradation peak of PU1 happens at a higher temperature than the one for PU2. This behavior is possibly related to the higher content of isocyanates and different types of polyols in the PUR ' s  structures  [34,72].  PU3  presents  a  higher  thermal  stability compared to PU1 and PU2, conceivably due to its ordered hard segment morphology, the content of hydrogen bonds in the hard phase, and a higher crosslinking degree.

3.3. Processability during closed-loop mechanical recycling

During the film-blowing process, numerous bubble instabilities can occur, depending on the polymer molecular structure and processing parameters, such as helical instability, draw resonance, bubble sagging, FLH  instability,  bubble  tearing  and  rupture,  and  width  reduction, limiting  the  production  [42,73,74].  During  the  shredding  and  com pounding steps of MM-PE laminates, no abnormal conditions or differ ences were observed. However, variations in the film-blowing processability  of  the  samples  were  noticed.  Detailed  processability criteria are presented in Fig. 5.

From Fig. 5, it is evident that PU3 imposes a higher load on the extruder drive compared to the other samples. PU1 leads to an extruder load similar to the one of PU0, while PU2 exhibits the minimum extruder load. PU1 and PU3 show similar melt pressures, and higher than PU0. Both extruder load and melt pressure are influenced by the melt vis cosity  and  pressure  of  the  polymer  at  the  extrusion  condition  [75]. Another important parameter for the film production industry is the melt pressure build-up. It is common to incorporate a melt filtration step in the film-blowing line to remove contaminations and gels. However, a faster melt pressure build-up leads to more frequent filter replacements to  prevent damage to the line ' s  head and die. Therefore, lower melt pressure build-up is preferred in the film production industry. Among the samples, PU3 shows the highest melt-pressure build-up, followed by PU1, PU2, and PU0.

During the film-blowing process, maintaining the bubble stability is essential  for  a  stable  process.  In  this  study,  only  bubble  tearing  and width reduction were observed as instabilities, as shown in Fig. 1. From Fig. 5, it is observed that PU3 poses substantially more challenges during the  filmblowing  process,  presenting  39  bubble  tearing  events.  PU2

3.4. Rheological assessment

3.4.1. Linear viscoelastic measurement

The linear viscoelastic properties in terms of storage and loss moduli as a function of angular frequency of PU0-PU3 samples at 220 °C are depicted in Figure A.13. PU3 exhibits storage and loss moduli compa rable to those of PU0. However, PU1 and PU2 show a slight decrease in their storage and loss moduli compared to PU0. Given the similar PE composition across all the samples, this change can be attributed to the structural difference, including types of polyol and isocyanate, hydrogen bond interactions, and isocyanate index among the PUR adhesives and their dispersed particle morphology which is discussed in section 3.6.

The dynamic intersection of storage and loss moduli curves, and the dynamic intersection frequency values of the samples can be seen in Fig. 6a. A higher value of the dynamic intersection or an increase in the crossover  frequency  indicates  a  less  homogenous  system  [76,77].  As such, PU3 shows the lowest degree of homogeneity among the samples, while PU1 demonstrates the highest level of homogeneity among sam ples containing PUR adhesive and its homogeneity level is similar to PU0 (Control sample). PU2 is positioned between PU1 and PU3 based on intersection frequency. The homogeneity of these systems is related to the chemical structure of the PUR adhesives. For instance, polyether polyol-based PUR is expected to have a better affinity with PE. This may result in a more regular morphology for the PUR dispersed phase than polyester polyol-based PUR [78]. From this result it is expected that PU1 presents molecular segments with lower surface energy, thus showing better  affinity  with  PE  chains.  In  contrast,  PU3  contains  more  polar groups, and it is less compatible with the non-polar PE chains. As pre viously described, PU1 is based on a polyether polyol and PU3 is based on a polyester polyol. Also, PU3 showed a higher proportion of hydrogen bonds within the hard phase, which makes PU3 more heterogeneous in the recycled laminate leading to a higher number of instabilities during the film-blowing process. The shift of crossover frequencies to higher values  corroborates  with  the  poor  processability  of  PU3  during  the film-blowing, as it leads to more bubble rupturing [79].

The  cot δ parameter,  derived  from  the  oscillatory rheological analysis, is equal to the ratio of storage-to-loss moduli (in verse of tan δ parameter) and indicates the melt rigidity properties of polymers [81]. The cot δ of the samples at the frequency of 23.5 s 1 were calculated considering the validity of the Cox-Merz rule since the con tent of PUR is low and are shown in Fig. 6a [82]. The value of cot δ of each sample can be found in Figure A.13. A higher value of cot δ is favorable for producing a stable bubble during the film-blowing process [79]. PU0 shows the highest value of cot δ , indicating high melt rigidity and bubble stability. PU1 shows a cot δ value similar to that of PU0, and PU2 and PU3 show lower cot δ values, consistent with the processability results.

3.4.2. Zero-shear viscosity

Viscosity values, particularly at low shear rates, are associated with the molecular characteristics of the polymer chains. The value of vis cosity at the Newtonian plateau, referred to as zero-shear viscosity ( η 0), is indicative of the degree of entanglement, and consequently, the melt strength  of  the  material  [83,84].  Fig.  6b  presents  the  viscosity  of PU0-PU3 samples as a function of the shear rate. From Fig. 6b, one can observe that PU0 and PU1 showed similar viscosity as a function of the shear rate.

In contrast, PU2 and PU3 show lower viscosities across the entire shear  rate  interval,  especially  in  the  Newtonian  plateau,  indicating lower zero-shear viscosities. For a more accurate comparison, the zer oshear  viscosity  values  were  calculated  using  the  modified  Carreau rheological model (Equation (5)) by fitting the curves in Fig. 6b. From this fitting PU1 exhibits a higher value of zero-shear viscosity than PU0. For PU2 and PU3, the zero-shear viscosities drop by 28 % and 13 %, respectively, in comparison to PU0. The zero-shear viscosity value for each sample can be found in the table of Fig. 6b. Higher zeroshear vis cosity indicates higher melt strength and higher stability during filmblowing [85,86]. PU2 and PU3 appear to act as a less viscous compo nent for PE chains, facilitating the macromolecules ' mobility [87,88]. This behavior is similar to the viscosity profile observed in incompatible polymer blends caused by weak interfacial interactions [89]. At high shear rates, the shear-thinning behavior of PE is dominant, and all the samples represent similar viscosity values.

3.5. Mechanical properties

Fig.  7 depicts  the  tensile  modulus,  tensile  strength,  elongation  at break, dart drop resistance, and tear force results for the studied sam ples, both in MD and in TD. To develop new applications for mechani cally recycled plastics in the film industry, high values for dart drop impact  resistance,  elongation  at  break,  tensile  strength,  and  tear strength are preferred. As for tensile modulus, either low or high values may be desirable depending on the specific end-use application.

The average tensile modulus of PU2 in the MD is slightly higher than that of PU0, while it is lower for PU1 and PU3. This may be attributed to the  presence  of  stiffer  PUR  particles  in  PU2,  which  have  a  stronger interface with the PE matrix and act as reinforcing agents within it [90, 91]. In the TD, the tensile modulus follows a similar trend as the MD. However, the absolute TD values are higher, due to the strong orienta tion of PE chains in the MD at high DDR values [92]. At high DDR, the PE melt  undergoes  strong  stretching  in  the  MD  and  is  subsequently quenched immediately after exiting  the  die.  This  rapid  solidification preserves the chain orientation in the MD, while the crystalline lamellae tend  to  stack  preferentially  perpendicular  to  this  direction  [92 -94]. Such a microstructural arrangement reduces stiffness along the MD but enhances  resistance  to  deformation  in  the  TD,  resulting  in  a  higher modulus  in  the  latter  [92 -94].  In  the  TD,  the  films  behave  as  an iso-strain system, where  the crystalline regions, showing  higher modulus  than  the  amorphous  phase,  dominate  the  overall  tensile response [92]. Therefore, the increase in modulus for PU2 is less pro nounced in the TD compared to the MD, as the TD already exhibits a higher initial modulus. In the case of PU3, the decrease in modulus is more significant in the TD than in the MD, likely due to poor stress transfer between the PE and PUR phases [95]. Since the crystalline re gions with higher modulus dominate the tensile behavior in the TD, the material experiences higher stress and its microstructure becomes more sensitive to defects. Finally, PU1 shows a reduction in modulus in the TD similar to that observed in the MD.

For all samples containing PUR adhesive, the tensile strength in both MD and TD shows a slight but statistically significant decrease, associ ated with poor stress transfer between the PE and PUR phases [90]. Only PU2 in the TD shows tensile strength comparable to that of PU0. Overall, considering  tensile  strength  in  both  MD  and  TD,  all  PUR  adhesives behave as incompatible contaminants, with limited stress transfer be tween the PE matrix and PUR domains. This results in films with lower mechanical properties compared to PU0 [90,96].

Regarding the elongation at break, PU1, PU2, and PU0 show similar values in the MD. In the TD, PU2 and PU0 have similar elongation at break values, and PU1 shows a slight reduction in this property. In both MD and TD, PU3 demonstrates a significant reduction in elongation at break (by 55 % and 53 % in MD and TD, respectively). The presence of PU3 particles in the PE matrix decreased the ductility of the PE film by introducing stress concentration points and a weak interface between the components of the blend [90,96,97].

Similar to the tensile test results, the tear force in the TD is higher than in the MD, due to higher chain orientation in the MD [98,99]. PU2 shows a slightly higher tear force compared to PU1 and PU0 in MD. In addition, PU3 recorded the lowest tear force among the samples, 16 % lower than PU0. In the TD, PU2 and PU0 demonstrate similar values of tear force, with PU1 slightly lower than those two samples. Finally, PU3 resulted in a 27 % reduction in the TD tear force compared to PU0, mainly related to the stress concentration caused by the existence of non-compatible PUR particles in the film structure, which promotes the initiation and propagation of cracks [98 -100].

Dart  drop  impact  results  are  substantially  more  sensitive  to  the presence of PUR particles compared to other mechanical properties. The dart drop impact resistance of the samples decreased by 9, 40, and 72 % for PU1, PU2, and PU3 respectively, compared to PU0. The presence of PUR particles resulted in more brittle films with lower deformability, likely due to the stress concentration around the PUR particles and less stress transfer in the PUR/PE interface [96].

3.6. Colorimetric and PUR adhesive particle size

Fig. 8a represents the optical properties of all the samples in terms of total light transmission, YI, haze, and gel size.

All samples exhibited total light transmission values above 89 %, indicating high transparency. However, PU1, PU2, and PU3 showed a statistically significant decrease in light transmission, due to the pres ence of PUR particles. PU1 presented the highest value of light trans mission,  followed  by  PU2,  and  finally  PU3.  Typically,  higher  phase separation between the hard and soft segments of PUR results in lower light transmission, corroborating the results observed for PU3 [101].

Considering the YI, PU1 shows the highest YI value. The yellowing effect is a result of PUR degradation during the thermal process [101, 102]. Isocyanates containing aromatic moieties lead to more yellowing compared to aliphatic ones [103]. The TGA results of PU1, previously discussed (Fig. 4c), indicated that this sample degrades at lower tem peratures and at a faster rate compared to PU2 and PU3 at the extrusion temperature, which leads to the higher YI value.

Irregularities  originating  from  the  polymeric film  production pro cess, rheological properties, and contamination cause the scattering of the light, observed as film haziness [104,105]. 4. Conclusion

In this study, the effect of PUR adhesives on the recyclability of MMPE laminated films was assessed during a closed-loop film-to-film me chanical recycling process. It is shown that the type of PUR adhesive will affect the recyclability of MM-PE films, leading to higher melt pressure build-up and more instabilities during the film-blowing process. Rheo logical investigation of recycled MM-PE laminates containing PUR ad hesives proved to be an effective method to evaluate their processability and large number of instabilities during the film-blowing process.

PURs introduced heterogeneities in the PE matrix, shifting the dy namic intersection of the storage and loss moduli, as well as the fre quency at this intersection, to higher values. Furthermore, the presence of  the  PURs  may  reduce  the  zero-shear  viscosity,  lowering  the  melt strength and causing instabilities, affecting  the  film-blowing  process. PUR adhesives showing higher degree of separation between hard and soft phases with large amount of H-bonding between hard segments, inflict  a  less  stable  film-blowing  process.  PURs  strongly  affect  the A. Ebrahimi et al.

toughness of the PE film by decreasing the dart drop impact resistance and elongation at break. The thermal degradation of PURs caused yel lowing in the recycled films, and larger PUR particles led to a higher haziness.

The recyclability of MM-PE laminated films containing PUR adhe sives can be systematically assessed by investigating the physicochem ical characteristics of the PUR adhesive by FTIR and TGA analysis. The methodology and results of this study can be employed as a framework for  assessing  the  recyclability  of  MM-PE  laminates  containing  PUR adhesives.

This  study  highlights  how  existing  Design  for  Recycling  (DfR) guidelines for PE-based flexibles could be further refined down to the level of the chemistry used in adhesives for MM-PE. Overall, maximizing recycling efficiency requires a holistic approach in which all compo nents, especially those present in minor quantities, such as labels, ad hesives, lacquers, inks, and pigments, are carefully selected and assessed for compatibility with the intended recycling process and each other. Only through such comprehensive material design can true circularity in flexible packaging be achieved.

Green foundation

This work proposes computational methods to identify solvents that can remove hazardous contaminants from plastic waste, thereby facilitating the design of sustainable recycling processes that minimize plastic pollution in the environment.

The computational methods developed in this work quantify contaminant partitioning into di ff erent solvents based on thermodynamically well-defined partition coe ffi cients. The integration of these calculations with previous methods to predict polymer solubility enable contaminant removal from plastic waste, as demonstrated in multiple case studies.

This work could be extended to a broader range of harmful contaminants by integrating the thermodynamic methods with machine learning methods, which could also permit analysis of solvent greenness.

Introduction

Increasing interest in reducing the amount of plastic pollution that ends up in landfills or leaking into the environment has motivated the development of numerous plastics recycling processes, such as mechanical recycling, solvent-based recycling, and chemical recycling ( e.g. , pyrolysis). 1 -4 While substantial e ff ort has been devoted to understanding how these processes can recycle the polymer resins in plastic waste, less is known about the impact of other plastic waste components on recycling processes. 5 Most plastic products are made from base polymer resins mixed with a complex blend of materials collectively known as additives. These additives enhance plastic products by making them safer, more durable, and visually appealing. 6 Additives also reduce production costs and extend the lifespan of plastic materials. 7 There are many di ff erent types of additives, with recent databases including thousands of unique chemical species. 8 -10 For example, plasticizers, such as phthalates and adipates, increase polymer flexibility by reducing intermolecular forces. 11 Stabilizers such as UV absor- Published on 18 May 2026 Licence and permissions

Solvent-mediated contaminant removal from plastic waste using thermodynamic modeling

Panzheng Zhou, † a Ugochukwu M. Ikegwu, † a Elizaveta Radkevich, a Euncheol Ra, a Hadeia Liburd, b George W. Huber, a Victor M. Zavala a and Reid C. Van Lehn * a,c

Plastics recycling is hindered by the compositional complexity of plastic waste, which can include numerous polymer components as well as low concentrations of additives and non-intentionally added substances. These latter small-molecule species, which we collectively refer to as contaminants, can harm human health and will build up in recycled plastic causing environmental and downstream processing challenges if not removed. In this work, we present molecular modeling approaches using the COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) to guide the selection of solvents that are capable of removing targeted contaminants from plastic waste. By considering the thermodynamic partitioning of contaminant species between a solvent phase and polymer phase, we identify guidelines for solvent selection to promote either the low-temperature extraction of contaminants from plastic waste or the removal of contaminants as part of a dissolution-based plastics recycling process. We present four case studies to illustrate the application of the computational approach to the removal of brominated fl ame retardants, phthalates, and selected per fl uoroalkyl substances, and compare to both literature and newly collected experimental data to illustrate model prediction accuracy. The case studies highlight the capability of the modeling approach to help design recycling processes that explicitly account for contaminant removal, thereby increasing product purity during dissolution-based recycling or facilitating chemical recycling of contaminant-free plastics.

bers and antioxidants can prevent degradation caused by heat, light, and oxidation. 12 Flame retardants inhibit combustion by disrupting the burning process. 13 Fillers and reinforcements, such as glass fibers and calcium carbonate, improve mechanical strength and reduce material costs. 14 Colorants, including inorganic pigments ( e.g. , titanium dioxide) and organic dyes, provide coloration and opacity. 15 Antimicrobial agents, such as silver nanoparticles, inhibit microbial growth in medical and food packaging applications. 16 Antistatic agents can minimize electrostatic buildup on plastic surfaces. 17 Other additives include lubricants, nucleating agents, impact modifiers, among others. Additives contribute to the substantial compositional complexity in plastic products. 10

Despite their benefits, some additives raise concerns due to their persistence in the environment and potential health impacts, which have led to regulatory restrictions on their usage. 18 The presence of additives can also pose a challenge for plastics recycling processes due to their potential to be unintentionally present in recycling streams, particularly for post-consumer plastics that are mixed with a wide range of di ff erent plastic products and other types of waste. 19,20 Postconsumer waste plastics can also include non-intentionally added substances (NIAS) that migrate into plastic products from the environment or other waste materials. 21 NIAS also include substances that are present in plastics without intentionally imparting a technical function to the plastic. As such, NIAS include impurities found in starting materials such as monomers, processing aids, colorants and printing inks, cross-linking agents, as well as by-products or intermediates from polymerization reactions. 10 The most common plastics recycling technology, mechanical recycling, does not remove additives or NIAS without specific preprocessing steps, such as washing in surfactant solutions, 22,23 which can lead to these molecules persisting into the final recycled product raising regulatory and health concerns. 24 -27 Similarly, additives or NIAS can impact the e ffi ciency or products of chemical recycling processes. 28 Consequently, we collectively refer to additives and NIAS as ' contaminants ' for the remainder of this work due to their undesirable presence in recycling streams and need for removal.

Because contaminants in plastic waste streams pose a substantial hindrance to plastics recycling due to industrial standards regulating the maximum concentration of these chemicals in pure polymers, processes are required to remove potential contaminants prior to or during plastics recycling. Example processes for contaminant removal include washing in water or surfactant solutions or solvent extraction in organic solvents. 22,23 These processes rely on the selection of solvent or processing conditions to preferentially remove contaminants from the polymer matrix or surface prior to recycling and are often incorporated as pre-processing steps that are applied to waste prior to mechanical or chemical recycling. Alternatively, solvent-based recycling methods that involve the dissolution of polymer resins may also lead to the dissolution of contaminants in the solvent phase, where they can be removed by adsorption. 4,29 For example, Solvent-Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP ™ ) is a solvent-mediated process in which target polymer resins are recovered from multicomponent plastic waste via selective dissolution and precipitation. 30,31 STRAP has been applied to a variety of complex feedstocks 31 -37 and can also lead to the removal of inks which would otherwise be contaminants in the recovered resins. 32,33 There is thus the potential to combine solventmediated contaminant removal steps with polymer recovery steps, thereby intensifying solvent-based plastics recycling processes while improving product quality. Designing any of these solvent-mediated contaminant removal processes is challenging, however, because each category of contaminant encompasses a large family of hundreds of di ff erent chemical compounds and compounds can be present in low concentrations, which can hinder the rational selection of solvent and operating conditions.

To address this problem, in this work we develop computational modeling methods to screen solvents for selectively removing contaminants from plastic waste. Our approach builds upon our prior computational screening methods for polymer solubility to identify solvents capable of extracting classes of di ff erent contaminants without dissolving the target polymer based on thermodynamic calculations. 38 -41 We focus on three categories of contaminants that have recently gained increasing attention due to issues related to toxicity: brominated flame retardants (BFRs), phthalates, and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). We present strategies for contaminant removal from plastic waste by leveraging computational predictions of contaminant partitioning across a broad range of solvents, supported by experimental validation using real-world applications involving these representative contaminants. Comparison to experiments reveals that thermodynamic modeling is suitable for identifying solvents capable of removing target contaminants through leaching or in combination with STRAP, although kinetic e ff ects may also impact the e ffi cacy of these processes. These advances pave the way for the development of sustainable plastics recycling methods like STRAP that can produce high-quality, contaminant-free plastics, thereby diverting plastic materials from landfills for reuse in place of petroleum-derived virgin plastics.

Methods

Summary of computational screening approach

Fig. 1 sketches computational solvent screening methods for two distinct contaminant removal processes that we refer to as (1) leaching and (2) STRAP contaminant removal. Leaching is a commonly employed method for the removal of undesirable chemicals from industrial products. This process involves the immersion of the targeted polymer into a solvent that facilitates the extraction of dissolved contaminants from the solid polymer matrix. 42 Leaching is often utilized in environmental remediation and recycling e ff orts, as it allows for the selective removal of harmful additives that may pose ecological or health risk, ideally without impacting the original target
