material. STRAP contaminant removal refers to the incorporation of contaminant removal steps into a dissolution-based plastic recycling process. In the STRAP process, a target polymer is first dissolved in a selective solvent that does not dissolve other polymer components of the waste. The target polymer is then precipitated by decreasing the temperature or adding a nonsolvent to the solution. Therefore, if properly designed, STRAP can be directly used for contaminant removal by dissolving both a target polymer and contaminants then selectively precipitating the polymer without precipitating the dissolved contaminants. The recycling of pure polymer resins and contaminant removal would be achieved in a STRAP process simultaneously. Fig. 1 illustrates both processes for a single contaminant. Our goal is to develop methods that would permit the simultaneous removal of multiple contaminants using either of the two processes shown in Fig. 1.

We hypothesize that the e ffi ciency of contaminant removal depends on the partitioning behavior of contaminant molecules between a solvent phase and an immiscible polymer phase. Such partitioning behavior can be quantified based on the partition coe ffi cient, log P , which is a thermodynamically well-defined parameter that describes the distribution of a solute between the two immiscible liquid phases. Here, we treat a solid polymer as a liquid phase based on the assumption that contaminants partition into the amorphous region of the polymer matrix with an a ffi nity that can be quantified via log P to guide solvent selection. Based on this assumption, eqn (1) defines the partition coe ffi cient of a single type of contaminant molecule between the two phases, assuming the contaminant is infinitely dilute in each phase.

log P ¼ log c ½  s c ½  p ¼ ð μ p c � μ s c Þ RT ln 10 þ log V p V s   ð 1 Þ

Here, c refers to a specific contaminant, the superscript s indicates the solvent, the superscript p indicates the polymer, [c] s and [c] p refer to the concentration of contaminant c in the solvent and polymer, respectively, μ i j is the infinite-dilution chemical potential of component i in pure liquid phase j , and V j is the molar volume of liquid phase j . A positive partition coe ffi cient (log P > 0) indicates that at equilibrium the contaminant is more likely to partition to the solvent phase, while a negative value (log P < 0) indicates that the contaminant prefers to remain in the polymer matrix. In the context of contaminant removal from plastics, we thus hypothesize that calculating log P can predict the e ffi ciency of contaminant removal to determine the selection of appropriate solvents to remove one or more targeted contaminants from a given polymer. We note that this approach is based on equilibrium thermodynamics, without consideration of kinetic factors that may substantially impact low-temperature leaching. 43 Consequently, log P values determine the maximum theoretical removal capacity to guide solvent selection, whereas practical contaminant removal rates could be governed by mass transfer kinetics that are not considered here.

Thermodynamic property prediction using COSMO-RS

The conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) is used to predict thermodynamic properties that are relevant to contaminant removal, including polymer solubilities, solvent miscibility with contaminants, and contaminant log P values. 44 COSMO-RS is well-suited for this study because it can predict thermodynamic behavior while requiring only input density functional theory calculations (DFT), without requiring new experimental data, which is advantageous for considering the properties of chemically diverse contaminants. Several studies have shown COSMO-RS to predict organic compound solubility and partitioning in liquid phases in strong agreement with experimental measurements, with performance comparable to or more accurate than alternative equation-of-state or continuum-solvation methods. 45 -49 Finally, this approach enables the use of our previous methodology 38,39 to represent the physicochemical properties of polymers using DFT calculations of representative oligomers, as detailed in the SI, to predict contaminant removal.

The COSMO-RS computational property predictions involve several steps. Fig. 2 depicts the methodological workflow adopted to compute the necessary molecular properties of each contaminant, polymer, and solvent employed in this study. First, each selected molecular structure is input to DFT calculations to obtain a screening charge density profile.

Fig. 2 Overview of COSMO-RS calculations. (a) Screening charge densities of three representative species -a polymer (PVC), solvent (THP), and contaminant (Tri-PBDE) -and corresponding σ -pro fi les, which are used for input to all other calculations. (b) Temperature-dependent polymer solubilities shown for low-density polyethylene (LDPE) in three solvents as an example. (c) Liquid -liquid equilibrium calculation to determine contaminant miscibility. The example shows the free energy of mixing for Tri-PBDE in either dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; fully miscible) or water (immiscible).

Examples of the molecular structures are shown in Fig. 2a for an example polymer (PVC), solvent (tetrahydropyran, THP), and contaminant (2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether, Tri-PDBE). This step includes a geometry optimization in implicit water using the conductor-like polarizable continuum model and a single-point calculation in the infinite dielectric constant limit, and is performed with Gaussian 16 at the BVP86/TZVP/ DGA1 level of theory. 50 Examples of the resulting screening charge densities and corresponding σ -profiles for the polymers, solvents, and contaminants from this step are also depicted in Fig. 2a. Screening charge densities for polymers and solvents were obtained from our prior work, 38,39 whereas screening charge densities for contaminants were newly computed using a single energy-minimizing conformer per contaminant molecule. A summary of our previously developed method for obtaining screening charge densities for polymers 38,39 is presented in the ' polymer and solvent modeling ' section of the SI, and a complete list of the 32 solvents considered in this work is included as part of Table S1. Second, COSMO-RS statistical thermodynamics calculations use the screening charge density to calculate the chemical potentials of the compounds. Polymer solubilities, solvent miscibility, and contaminant partition coe ffi cients are then calculated via solid -liquid and liquid -liquid equilibrium calculations. 51,52 In this study, a contaminant is considered miscible in a solvent if the predicted liquid -liquid solubility at a given temperature exceeds 15%. Given that most contaminants exhibited high solubility values (approaching 100%) across multiple solvents, miscibility was treated as a binary property: ' yes ' for solubility values greater than 15% and ' no ' otherwise, with this threshold chosen as a conservative value to account for any potential simulation error. All COSMO-RS calculations were performed using the COSMOtherm19 software with the BP_TZVP_19 parameterization, 53 although the BP_TZVP_FINE_19 parameterization was used when predicting partition coe ffi cients in solvent mixtures for better accuracy. 49 Fig. 2b shows an example of the temperature-dependent solubility curve of polyethylene in three di ff erent solvents obtained from COSMO-RS. Similarly, Fig. 2c shows an example of the free energy of mixing of an example contaminant (tri-PDBE) in two solvents at room temperature to illustrate characteristic curves for a solvent in which the contaminant is fully miscible (DMSO) and immiscible (water). We similarly compute log P values using COSMO-RS, 54,55 although these are not shown in Fig. 2.
Experimental contaminant removal

Experiments were carried out for the phthalate removal case study. Benzyln -butyl phthalate (BBP) was selected for it due to its characteristic peak appearance in gas chromatograms. It appears as one clear peak while some other phthalates have multiple peaks. BBP was physically blended with polyvinyl chloride (PVC, Sigma Aldrich average M w ∼ 80 000 and average M n ∼ 47 000) at a ratio of 1 : 2.5 by mass, respectively, to a total mass of 100 g, then melt-compounded in a twin-screw extruder at 150 °C and a screw speed of 30 rpm under mild conditions to minimize thermal degradation. The produced cylindrical filament was 2 -2.2 mm in diameter which was cut into 4.8 -6 mm long pieces. Three consecutive solvent washes were performed in each solvent at each temperature. Xylenes (Aqua Solutions, Reagent ACS Grade) and dodecane (ThermoFisher Scientific, mixture of isomers) were selected as solvents to assess BBP removal e ff ectiveness at room temperature and at 130 °C. The starting polymer mixture mass was 1.0 g and solvent mass was 75 g. Experiments were conducted in glass pressure tubes to avoid solvent evaporation. The solution and polymer were allowed to stir for 1 hour per wash. After each wash, the polymer was recovered, dried for three hours at 100 °C in a vacuum oven and transferred to the next wash with 75 g of new solvent. For experiments at 130 °C, glass tubes were quenched in ice for 5 minutes prior to solvent recovery. Prior to analysis, all samples were filtered using 0.22 μ mfilters to ensure no PVC was retained in the injected samples. Recovered solvents were analyzed through gas chromatography (Shimadzu GC-2010) with a Phenomenex ZB-5HT Inferno ™ column and N2 as the carrier gas. A calibration curve was used for determining the concentration in samples. The concentrations were converted into mass and compared to phthalate mass in the added polymer mixture to calculate the percent recovery. For experiments at 130 °C, some PVC dissolved (as expected; vide infra ) and precipitated during quenching. The solution was filtered using a 100 -200 μ m wire mesh to separate the solution and the PVC. Precipitated PVC was collected from the mesh while any remaining dissolved PVC and BBP was retained in solution. The collected PVC was then dried and transferred to the next wash.

Results and discussion

Solvent selection criteria for contaminant removal

For a given set of contaminants, we propose di ff erent solvent selection criteria based on the characteristics of the two contaminant removal processes in Fig. 1. These selection criteria depend upon contaminant miscibility, the contaminant partition coe ffi cient, and polymer solubilities in the possible solvents.

The selection criteria for leaching are:

The target contaminants must be miscible in the selected solvent ( i.e. , the solvent can dissolve the contaminants).

Contaminants should have positive partition coe ffi cients (log P > 0); higher values are preferred to limit retention within the polymer.

Ideal solvent candidates will swell but not dissolve the polymer.

These criteria are designed to ensure the preferential retention of the contaminants within the chosen solvent without dissolving the polymer itself. Swelling of the polymer is desired to maximize solvent contact with contaminants within the polymer matrix and to enable e ffi cient mass transport into the solvent phase.

The selection criteria for the STRAP contaminant removal process are:

The solvent can dissolve both the polymer and target contaminants.

The solvent does not dissolve non-target compounds, such as other polymers in the plastic waste.

The polymer can be precipitated from solution either by decreasing the temperature (or by adding an antisolvent).

Contaminants should have positive partition coe ffi cients (log P > 0); higher values are preferred.

The contaminants do not precipitate ( i.e. , they remain miscible in the solvent) under the conditions in (4) that induce polymer precipitation.

These criteria are designed to ensure that target contaminants dissolve along with the target polymer and then preferentially remain in the solvent phase when the polymer precipitates. In this work, we assume that precipitation is induced by a decrease in temperature, as opposed to adding an antisolvent, due to more favorable environmental and economic impacts associated with temperature-dependent precipitation. 56 Following our past work, we set a threshold of 1 wt% as the maximum computationally predicted solubility to achieve precipitation, although in practice lower solubilities are observed experimentally. 31,32,38 -40 Dissolved contaminants removed during this process can be potentially removed from the solvent via additional methods not explicitly discussed here, such as by adsorption. 33

It is computationally expensive to perform property predictions for every exact chemical structure because contaminants in plastic waste (including both BIAS and additives intentionally included in plastic products) are often mixtures of similar chemical compounds. Most of these chemical families include a wide range of di ff erent substances. 10 To conduct feasible property calculations suitable for satisfying the above criteria, we first need to select a set of representative chemicals, then use their molecular structures to perform predictions of interest. In this work, we propose multiple case studies in which we select representative chemical structures for di ff erent classes of contaminants based on common compounds reported in literature. Specifically, given the large number of contaminants classified within each ' priority group of chemicals ' identified by Monclús and co-workers due to their significant risks to human health, safety, and the environment, 10 a representative subset was selected for detailed investigation. This subset comprised of four BFRs, eight phthalates, and twenty-six PFAS. The rationale for selecting these compounds is provided within the corresponding case studies presented in the following sections. Their structures are then input to COSMO-RS to predict miscibility, solubility, and partition coe ffi cients as detailed in the Methods to identify solvents suitable for contaminant removal via leaching or STRAP. Fig. 3 shows the chemical structures of polymers, example common solvents, and example contaminants studied below. The full list and chemical structures of contaminants studied in the work are included in the SI.

Case study 1: BFR leaching from plastic products. As a first case study, we consider solvent selection for the leaching of brominated flame retardants (BFRs) from common polymers including polystyrene (PS), polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). We compare computational predictions to known literature data and identify solvent candidates for BFR removal. BFRs are synthetic chemicals widely used as additives in plastic materials to reduce product flammability. 13,57 Furthermore, BFRs are incorporated as flame-retardant additives into consumer products, particularly electrical and electronic equipment, many of which are predominantly composed of PS. 10 However, they are persistent organic pollutants with bio-accumulative properties. 58 They have been reported at hazardous concentrations in aquatic environments and soils where they can accumulate on PP, PE, and PET microplastics which constitute a significant fraction of microplastics detected in terrestrial and aquatic environment. 59 Exposure to BFRs has been associated with serious health concerns, including cancer, neurobehavioral disorders, and reproductive issues. 57 Common end-of-life plastic management processes, such as mechanical recycling or incineration, are not able to separate BFRs from the target polymer resins, thus posing significant environmental and health risks by releasing hazardous halogenated compounds. 60 Conversely, recent work has indicated the feasibility of solvent-based methods for removing BFRs from waste plastics obtained from electrical and electronic equipment. 61

Fig. 4 shows selected common BFRs and their chemical structures, along with COSMO-RS σ -profiles to illustrate the distinct chemical properties for these molecules. These BFRs were selected due to the availability of literature experimental data reporting the solvent extraction of BFRs from common polymers. 62,63 These literature references provide the opportunity to perform computational screening to select solvents according to the leaching process in Fig. 1, then compare computational predictions to literature results. Hexabromocyclododecane (HBCD), decabromodiphenyl ether (DECA), and 2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether (Tri-PBDE) are designated as ' chemicals of concern ' in the PlastChem database, reflecting their persistence, bioaccumulation potential, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and reproductive toxicity. 10 In addition, polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) form a major class of BFRs and have been detected at extreme concentration levels in waste plastics, particularly ocean plastics. 63 Based on the BFRs and polymers reported in the literature, we thus first performed computational predictions of log P values for BFRs, polymer solubilities, and BFR miscibility to qualitatively compare with experimental observations in the literature.

Fig. 4 Chemical structures of four BFRs modeled and used for qualitative validation of leaching approach. Corresponding COSMO-RS σ -pro fi les for the four BFRs are shown at bottom. The variations in the σ -pro fi les illustrates the chemical diversity within this class of contaminants.

Table 1 presents data on the experimental solvent extraction of the four BFRs introduced in Fig. 4 from di ff erent polymers 62,63 and compared to our computational predictions. HBCD, DECA, and TBBPA-bis-2,3-dibromopropylether (TBBPAdbp) were extracted from PS obtained from discarded television and personal computer housings at 60 °C using di ff erent solvents while tri-PBDE that first adsorbed to PET, PE, PS, and PP polymers from aqueous solution (to represent contaminated environmental plastics) was extracted at room temperature. Experimental procedures used by Singla et al. 63 and Altwaiq et al. 62 for these samples are summarized in the SI. In both experimental studies, the extraction e ffi ciency for each contaminant was calculated as the percentage of the contaminant mass recovered in the organic extract from the plastic relative to the total amount of contaminant introduced onto the plastics. This was quantified using GC/MS or HPLC/UV. Based on our framework for extracting contaminants via leaching, we expect that a target BFR will be extracted if log P > 0 in the selected solvent, the target BFR is miscible in the selected solvent, and the solubility of the polymer in the selected solvent is low, thus fitting the criteria for process 1 in Fig. 1.

text: All experimental results from the extraction of Tri-PBDE using the solvents listed in Table 1 are consistent with our computational predictions. For example, the reported high extraction e ffi ciency of Tri-PBDE with toluene (138.4%) aligns with our predicted values, which indicated favorable miscibility, low polymer solubility (0.8 wt%), and a log P of 1.7. Conversely, the low experimental extraction e ffi ciency observed with methanol (2.1%) agrees with our computational prediction that methanol is a poor solvent for this process, as evidenced by the negative partition coe ffi cient (log P < 0), despite satisfying the other two criteria of BFR miscibility and low polymer solubility. Based on the results summarized in Table 1, extraction e ffi ciencies exceeding 100% are likely attributable to experimental uncertainties in mass balance calculations or may indicate that the extraction solvents coextracted unidentified contaminants or compounds originating from untargeted sources, such as plastic materials used during the experimental procedures. In general, higher log P values correlate with higher extraction e ffi ciencies. Similarly, Table 1 shows high experimental extraction e ffi ciencies for DECA (100%) and TBBPA-dbp (93.8%) that are also in good agreement with our predictions, supported by log P values of 0.6 and 2.3, respectively, along with compliance with low polymer solubility and BFR miscibility requirements at 60 °C. Only the extraction of HBCD from polystyrene using a toluene/

1-propanol mixture deviated from computational expectations; while our predictions suggested preferential extraction at 60 °C, the experimental e ffi ciency was low (7.7%). This discrepancy may arise from kinetic e ff ects since partition coe ffi cients are computed assuming equilibrium, and it is possible that extending the extraction time beyond the 2 hours adopted by Altwaiq et al. could improve the extraction e ffi ciencies as shown for phthalate extraction in Case study 2 (described below). Overall, the data suggest that computational log P predictions correlate well with experimental findings, highlighting the potential of our computational approach to guide solvent selection for BFR removal.

Given the strong agreement between literature data and our computational predictions, we subsequently screened 32 common solvents to identify those capable of simultaneously removing all four selected BFRs from the polymers listed in Table 1 (PS, PET, PE, and PP) at room temperature. The objective was to identify solvents that satisfy the established screening criteria while enabling the removal of all four BFRs rather than optimizing for a single compound. The predicted log P values, BFR -solvent miscibility, and polymer solubilities across di ff erent solvents are summarized in Tables S1 -S4. The results reveal that, even if several solvents have the potential to extract all four BFRs, distinct trade-o ff s are evident. Specifically, solvents demonstrating high e ffi cacy for one BFR often perform sub-optimally for others. Representative examples of these trade-o ff s for BFR removal from polystyrene using five selected solvents are illustrated in Fig. 5. While all five solvents meet the BFR miscibility criteria, variations arise in their ability to satisfy the log P requirements across all BFRs. For instance, N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) exhibit favorable partitioning for HBCD and TBBPA-dbp but are less e ff ective for DECA, as reflected by its low log P value. Conversely, tetrahydropyran (THP) demonstrates favorable partitioning for Tri-PBDE, HBCD, and TBBPA-dbp, but not for DECA, which displays a negative log P value. This example highlights that selecting solvents for BFR removal by maximizing the partitioning of a single compound may not be optimal for removing all possible BFRs. In contrast, even they do not lead to the highest log P values for any individual BFR, benzene and diphenyl ether exhibit consistently favorable partitioning across all four BFRs, suggesting that these solvents are preferred for more broadly removing a wider range of BFRs; selection between these solvents may ultimately depend on economic, availability, environmental, and safety considerations. 40

Fig. 5 Observed trade-o ff s during solvent selection for the removal of all four BFRs from polystyrene. Log P < 0 indicates poor solvents for speci fi c BFR removal (partitioning into the polymer phase) while log P ≥ 0 indicates good solvent for speci fi c BFR removal (partitioning into the solvent phase).

Case study 2: phthalate removal from PVC. The first case study established that computational predictions align qualitatively with experimental literature results for the leaching of BFRs from varied polymers at temperatures close to, or somewhat above, room temperature. In the second case study, we extended the computational screening protocol to identify suitable solvents for removing phthalates from PVC resins. Phthalates are a family of synthetic chemical compounds used in plastics, solvents, and personal care products. In plastic products, phthalates are widely used as plasticizers in the production of flexible and durable plastic materials, particularly PVC. 64,65 Phthalates are often physically integrated into plastics rather than chemically bound, which means they can migrate out of products through wear, heating, or contact with liquids. 66 Short-chain phthalates, such as dimethyl phthalate (DMP), are more volatile and can evaporate into the air, whereas longer-chain phthalates, like di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), tend to leach from plastics into surrounding environments over time. 64,67 Phthalates are also endocrine-disrupting substances associated with numerous adverse health consequences, including elevated risks of cancer, and consequently have been subjected to increased regulation for recycled plastics, motivating their removal. 68,69 Since there are hundreds of di ff erent phthalate compounds, selecting a representative set of structures is essential for practical analysis and computational modeling. Table S5 presents the eight selected phthalates for this study and their common applications in commercial products. 67,69 These representative phthalates were chosen based on their prevalence in commercial applications, structural diversity, and relevance to environmental and health concerns. 67 By focusing on a subset of commonly used phthalates, we can e ff ectively predict their properties and interactions with plastic resins and in the meantime maintain the generalizability of the findings. The chemical structures and σ -profiles showing the chemical diversity of the eight representative phthalates are presented in Fig. S1 and S2 of the SI.

In this second case study, we sought to perform both computational predictions and experiments to evaluate both distinct processes (leaching and STRAP contaminant removal) presented in Fig. 1. The primary di ff erence between these processes is that STRAP contaminant removal involves a hightemperature polymer dissolution step followed by low-temperature polymer precipitation, whereas leaching is performed a single temperature and does not involve polymer dissolution or precipitation. We note that STRAP also requires considering only the selective dissolution of a target polymer when multiple polymer components are present, although that consideration is omitted for this case study (but is included as part of Case study 4, vide infra ). To identify suitable solvents that facilitate phthalate removal via both processes, we used COSMO-RS to compute log P values (relative to PVC), phthalate miscibility in each solvent, and PVC solubility at multiple temperatures. A library of 32 common solvents was considered. Table 2 presents computational prediction results for a subset of solvent candidates; additional log P data are presented in Table S6. We placed an upper bound of 130 °C on the screening temperature for polymer solubility because higher temperatures may lead to degradation of some plastics.

We sought to identify a solvent capable of performing both leaching at room temperature and STRAP contaminant removal at a high temperature to compare contaminant removal e ffi ciencies with both processes. According to our solvent selection criteria for both leaching and STRAP, the ideal solvent should be miscible with all eight phthalate compounds considered and should promote positive log P values (with higher values preferred) at room temperature. Additionally, we also require a low PVC solubility at room temperature in the solvent, with a high solubility at elevated temperatures to enable polymer dissolution as part of STRAP. Based on past studies, 31,32,38 -40 we defined the low temperature solubility threshold as <1 wt% and the high temperature solubility threshold as >15 wt%. From the COSMO-RS calculations, nine solvents meet the log P > 0 and miscibility requirements: chloroform, tetrahydrofuran, tetrahydropyran, 2,3-dihydropyran, acetone, toluene, ethyl acetate, o -xylene, and diphenyl ether. These solvents (the first nine listed in Table 2) are thus expected to be suitable for leaching. In addition to having positive mean log P values, these solvents have positive log P values for each individual phthalate, suggesting that these solvents are capable of extracting all eight representative phthalates. This result is consistent with the structural resemblance among the eight phthalates, as illustrated by their molecular structures and σ -profiles in Fig. S1 and S2. However, not all solvents with positive mean log P values have positive log P values for all phthalates; DMSO and triethylamine are notable counterexamples, indicating the need to evaluate log P for all possible contaminants, not just individual contaminants, to ensure a high probability of removal.

text:
Table 2 COSMO-RS results for solvent screening for phthalate removal from PVC. The elevated temperature Th is de fi ned to be 1 °C lower than the boiling point (BP) of the solvent, with an upper bound of 130 °C. All log P calculations were performed at room temperature. ortho -Xylene and dodecane (bold) are used in validation experiments

Among the evaluated solvents, only one solvent -ortho -xylene ( o -xylene) - satisfies the PVC solubility requirements at both high and low temperatures. Toluene meets the low-temperature solubility threshold and is also very close to meeting the high-temperature solubility threshold with a predicted PVC solubility of 14.8 wt%, while diphenyl ether also meets the low-temperature solubility threshold and has a moderate PVC solubility of 11.5 wt% at a high temperature. These solvents are thus likely to be suitable for both leaching and STRAP contaminant removal. Of the solvents considered, o -xylene was chosen as a suitable solvent for experimental evaluation of both STRAP contaminant removal and leaching, since it exhibits a favorable mean log P value of 0.61 at room temperature, has the highest predicted PVC solubility of the three potential STRAP solvents at the maximum temperature of 130 °C, and has minimal predicted PVC solubility at room temperature.

We conducted two sets of experiments on a sample of PVC and phthalate to verify the ability of o -xylene to remove phthalates from PVC resins. The sample is a physical mixture of PVC powder and liquid butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) with a mass ratio of 2.5 : 1. This ratio was determined based on the typical concentration of phthalate additives in industrial PVC materials. 70 The mixture was extruded as filaments and cut into short pieces (Fig. 6a). Experiments used a mixture of xylene isomers (xylenes) due to their availability and the expectation that they would behave similarly to o -xylene alone for the proposed contaminant removal processes. The first set of experiments used xylenes to remove BBP from the PVC sample based on the criteria described above. The second set of experiments used dodecane as a solvent to compare to xylenes

(a) Co-extruded PVC/BBP (b) After xylene wash

Fig. 6 Experimental phthalate removal using BBP as a representative phthalate. (a) Image of the extruded PVC and BBP sample as a fi lament, which was cut into smaller pieces which are also shown. (b) PVC after BBP removal via xylene leaching; the sample changed color. (c) BBP extraction e ffi ciency at room temperature and 130 °C using a solvent that is predicted to promote contaminant removal (xylenes) and a control solvent that is not predicted to promote contaminant removal (dodecane) based on the data in Table 2. Experiments at room temperature model the leaching process because PVC does not dissolve in either solvent. Experiments at 130 °C model STRAP contaminant removal because PVC dissolves in xylenes at this temperature. Error bars indicate the standard deviation across three replicate experiments.

because Table 2 indicates that dodecane should not promote phthalate removal based on the negative log P values. We employed dodecane as a negative control solvent to test our computational predictions. Three experimental wash steps were adopted. The first wash step (wash step 1) involved immersing the sample in fresh solvent for 1 hour, after which further analysis quantified the fraction of BBP that was removed. Next, the sample after wash step 1 was dried and then immersed in a fresh solvent for another 1 hour after which the fraction of removed BBP was quantified. A similar approach was adopted for the wash step 3. Both sequences of wash steps were performed in xylenes and dodecanes at two temperatures to model the two contaminant removal processes. Experiments were performed at room temperature to model the leaching process because PVC dissolution was not expected at this temperature in either solvent. Experiments were also performed at a high temperature of 130 °C to model STRAP contaminant removal because PVC dissolution (in o -xylene) was expected at this temperature. All experiments were done in triplicate.

Fig. 6 shows the experimental measurements of phthalate mass recovered from the PVC removal experiments at room temperature and at 130 °C as well as an image of the sample after BBP removal. At room temperature, an average of 63.0 ± 5.2% (with the average and standard deviation computed across three replicate experiments) of the phthalates was removed in the 3-hour experiment ( i.e. , after the three wash steps), with decreasing percentages recovered after each wash step. We note that the predicted log P value for o -xylene is modest (with a mean value < 1 and value for BBP of 0.28; see Table S6). As shown in Table 1, similar predicted log P values led to modest extraction e ffi ciency of BFRs at room temperature ( e.g. , acetonitrile had a log P value of 0.4 and led to 71.8% extraction e ffi ciency for leaching tri-PBDE from PET). Fig. 6c shows that performing the high-temperature STRAP experiments significantly improved BBP extraction e ffi ciency to an average of 113.9 ± 6.4%, with nearly all of the contaminant removed in the first wash step. In contrast, dodecane was ine ff ective for phthalate removal as expected. At room temperature, dodecane was completely unable to extract BBP from PVC in agreement with our computational predictions, while at 130 °C the average extraction e ffi ciency of BBP from PVC was 16.7 ± 1.6%, indicating a substantially lower extraction e ffi ciency compared to o -xylene. Table 2 also indicates that at the elevated temperature BBP is miscible in dodecane, yet was still not readily removed, highlighting the utility of log P values for predicting contaminant removal. The slightly higher fraction of BBP that was removed at the high temperature is likely due to the slight dissolution of the polymer, but the low removal indicates that dissolved BBP preferentially precipitates with the PVC in dodecane.

Overall, the increased extraction e ffi ciency at 130 °C suggests that polymer dissolution as part of STRAP generally leads to higher contaminant removal than leaching. These results validate the ability of xylenes to remove phthalates from PVC resins, and more broadly serve as proof-of-concept for the computational methodology. However, Fig. 6c also shows continuous removal of BBP after each 1 hour solvent wash at room temperature, whereas the predicted room temperature log P value of 0.6 should indicate an ∼ 4× preference of BBP for the solvent vs. the polymer. Given the large amount of solvent compared to the amount of polymer sample (75 g solvent, 1 g polymer), these experimental observations indicate a lower extraction e ffi ciency than would be expected based on the predicted log P value, which is likely due to mass transfer kinetics governing contaminant migration from the polymer phase into the solvent phase. 43 Such kinetic e ff ects would be expected to be prominent at lower temperatures and in the absence of polymer dissolution and will depend on process variables such as contact time, temperature, and concentration gradients, which are not captured within the current equilibrium-based modeling approach. Therefore, we expect that operating conditions such as time and temperature could be further investigated to improve the e ffi ciency of the process for actual deployment in more realistic scenarios.

Case study 3: STRAP with PFAS removal from LDPE. Case studies 1 and 2 established that predicted log P values can be used to guide solvent selection for contaminant removal via leaching processes, with solvents exhibiting high log P values removing contaminants in experiments as expected. These promising results motivate additional case studies that integrate contaminant removal with STRAP to enable the simultaneous recovery and purification of target polymers during a recycling process. As an additional example of integrating STRAP with contaminant removal for a larger category of contaminants, we use computational predictions to assist the design of a process for removing PFAS from plastic waste. PFAS are a diverse group of synthetic fluorinated compounds known for their remarkable stability, water and oil repellency, and resistance to heat and chemical degradation. 71 These properties have made PFAS essential in applications such as nonstick cookware, waterproof fabrics, grease-resistant food packaging, and firefighting foams. 72 However, their environmental persistence and bioaccumulation pose significant health risks, including links to cancer, liver toxicity, and immune system disruption. 72 Common PFAS, including perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), both containing eight carbon atoms, as well as shorter chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), have been detected in aquatic systems, soils, and other environmental ecosystems. 73,74 Although the use of PFAS as additives in plastic manufacturing has been increasingly regulated over the past two decades, their environmental ubiquity has led to their detection in commercial products. 75 This observation suggests that these compounds can migrate into plastic waste streams from surrounding environments through pathways such as aquatic systems, landfills, material recovery facilities, municipal waste collection systems, and open dumps. Recent studies have further confirmed the presence of PFAS in postconsumer recycled polyolefins used in food-contact applications. 21 Consequently, PFAS must be removed during recycling processes to avoid their reintroduction into the plastic packaging industry, particularly via post-consumer recycled resins. 76

Although thousands of PFAS have been identified by the US EPA, 77 their detection via experimental approaches have been limited. However, the FDA have been successful at detecting 26 PFAS concentration levels in food samples purchased at grocery stores in the US. 78,79 Therefore, in this work, we apply our contaminant removal strategy to this set of PFAS. Table S7 and Fig. S3 and S4 of the SI show the PFAS compounds and chemical structures, and their σ -profiles, grouped based on their structures and primary functional groups. All 26 PFAS considered are small molecules representative of non-intentionally added substances that might be found in post-consumer waste; however, we note that fluorinated polymers such as polytetrafluoroethylene are also incorporated into plastic products as processing aids 80 as well as anti-drip additives, particularly in polycarbonates (PC) and PC/acrylonitrile butadiene styrene blends 81,82 and may potentially be removed by similar solvents selected to remove the 26 target PFAS.

We considered the same library of 32 common solvents used in previous case studies for removing PFAS from lowdensity polyethylene (LDPE) as a reference polymer. As shown in Fig. S3 of the SI, some PFAS exist as ionized compounds.

Therefore, in the case of PFAS, distribution coe ffi cients (log D values) which account for multiple ionization states are determined using COSMO-RS and used in place of their partition coe ffi cient (log P ); these quantities have similar interpretations during solvent selection. 83 We performed COSMO-RS predictions of the distribution coe ffi cients of all 26 PFAS in each solvent relative to LDPE, determined the miscibility of PFAS and each solvent, and computed LDPE solubility at multiple temperatures in the solvents. For STRAP contaminant removal, we require a high LDPE solubility at the elevated temperature and low LDPE solubility at room temperature to achieve temperature-based precipitation, with a mean log D value that is high at both temperatures to ensure preferential partitioning into the solvent of as much PFAS as possible.

We divided the 26 PFAS compounds into three di ff erent groups based on structural similarity (Fig. S3): PFAS within each group had similar chemical structures and consequently σ -profiles (Fig. S4), suggesting that they would be removed from LDPE resins using similar solvents. Fig. 7 presents the average σ -profiles and representative structures for each group, showing how the key functional groups in each PFAS group contribute to slight di ff erences in σ -profiles. For example, group 2 is distinguished by the presence of sulfonic acid groups that contribute to a unique shoulder in the average σ -profile as a distinguishing feature of this group. Table 3 shows solvent screening and property calculation results for each group. THP is identified as the best solvent to remove PFAS in groups 1 and 2 as it has excellent mean log D values while leading to low LDPE solubility at room temperatures. Toluene is the best choice for group 3, since it satisfies positive log D requirements and has a strong temperature dependence of LDPE solubility ( i.e. , able to dissolve LDPE at an elevated temperature and precipitate at room temperature), which is beneficial for STRAP.

Fig. 7 Average σ -pro fi les and representative structures for each PFAS group. The distinguishing chemical feature for each group is highlighted in red. Group 1: carboxylic acid/carboxylate groups. Group 2: sulfonic acid/sulfonate groups. Group 3: per fl uoroethers with carboxylic acid/ carboxylate groups.

In practice, the set of PFAS present in any given plastic waste may be unknown, so ideally single solvents capable of removing all PFAS would be identified. THP, toluene, and cyclohexanol were identified as e ff ective solvents capable of removing all 26 PFAS by satisfying all the solvent screening criteria via the STRAP approach. THP exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 5.1, satisfied the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.1 wt%) and high (7.3 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Similarly, toluene exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 0.7, satisfied the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.1 wt%) and high (22.6 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Lastly, cyclohexanol exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 3.8, satisfying the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.0 wt%) and high (22.1 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Owing to its high average log D value and pronounced temperature-dependent solubility behavior, cyclohexanol is identified as the preferred solvent for e ff ectively removing all 26 PFAS from LDPE. These findings further support the potential for identifying a single solvent capable of extracting groups of structurally similar contaminants. The detailed predicted miscibility and log D values of all 26 PFAS considered in this work are presented in the SI. These results can further guide the experiment of PFAS removal from LDPE resins.

text: Case study 4: STRAP with BFR, phthalates, and PFAS removal from mixed plastic waste. Having studied the removal of three di ff erent classes of contaminants in di ff erent polymer systems, in this final case study we apply the computational framework to understand the potential removal of contaminants during the separation of multicomponent plastics via STRAP. Specifically, we analyze two previously developed, experimentally tested STRAP processes for multicomponent plastic waste recycling by Sánchez-Rivera and colleagues. 31,32 The first process involved the separation of a 4-component multilayer plastic film containing LDPE, ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH), PET, and ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA). In the first step of this process, toluene was used to selectively dissolve PE from the remaining polymers at 110 °C. The dissolved PE was then cooled to 35 °C to aid its precipitation. The second process involved the separation of the same multilayer film composition with the addition of a polyurethane (PU)-based ink component. The first step of this process used dodecane instead of toluene to selectively dissolve PE at 95 °C while avoiding the dissolution of the PU-based ink, which was removed in a further processing step. The PE was then recovered by precipitation at 35 °C. Neither of these studies explicitly considered the potential for contaminants (other than the ink) to be dissolved and removed during STRAP. Therefore, in this case study, we aim to identify the contaminants that would have been removed from the first STRAP step in both processes (toluene and dodecane) based on the sets of contaminants (BFRs, phthalates, and PFAS) studied in the previous case studies.
Table 4 compares log P values (or log D values for PFAS) for the removal of contaminants from PE during the first STRAP

step using either toluene or dodecane, since the same polymer resin was removed first in both processes. Based on these values, and miscibility criteria, toluene is expected to remove all contaminants considered from PE during STRAP. This result suggests that during the recycling of the multilayer plastic via STRAP studied by Sánchez-Rivera and colleagues, 31 all four BFRs, eight phthalates, and 26 FDA-identified PFAS would have been removed, producing a recycled LDPE film with little to no traces of the studied contaminants. On the contrary, dodecane is less e ffi cient in removing any of the contaminant considered in this study, as also discussed in the negative control experiments conducted for phthalates in PVC in Case study 2. A summary of these findings, showing the flow of polymers and the extraction of these contaminants via the STRAP process using these two solvents based on an ideal, equilibrium process as predicted by our thermodynamic modeling approach is presented in Fig. 8. Since toluene was replaced by dodecane to avoid the co-dissolution of PU-based inks during the recycling of multilayer plastic film containing PU-inks, 32 this suggests that dodecane can be first used to recover PU-based ink-free LDPE and subsequently toluene can be used to further remove all the contaminants listed in this study from the residual solids if desired.

In experimentally validated STRAP processes, the target polymer typically remains swollen with solvent after precipitation ( i.e. , to form a polymer gel), which is not considered in the calculations above or Fig. 8. Retained solvent could impact the partitioning of contaminants between the solvent and (swollen) polymer by making these two phases more chemically similar, such that multiple wash steps would be required to remove this residual contaminant. Indeed, similar behavior was observed by Wagner and coworkers during the recycling of PVC waste containing phthalates via a multistep solvent-based process. 84 To assess the impact of retained solvent, we performed additional log P (or log D for PFAS) calculations to predict the room-temperature partitioning of contaminants between the solvent phase and a model swollen polymer phase. Similar to the data in Table 4, we chose two representative contaminants from each class (Tri-PBDE/HBCD as BFRs, BBP/DiNP as phthalates, and PFOA/PFOS as PFAS) and computed log P or log D in toluene and dodecane relative to a ' swollen ' PE phase. To represent the ' swollen ' PE, we note that prior STRAP studies have reported that the precipitated polymer gel retained between 70 -80 wt% solvent after separ- PE -polyethylene, Tri-PBDE -2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether, DECA -decabromodiphenylether, BBP -butyl benzyl phthalate, DiNP -di-isononyl phthalate, PFOA -perfluorooctanoic acid, PFOS -perfluorooctanesulfonic acid.

text: Table 5 shows that, as expected, predicted log P (or log D ) values substantially change for all contaminants investigated. While the signs of all values remain the same, indicating no qualitative change in partitioning preference, all values are closer to zero when compared to values computed for partitioning from a pure polymer phase. These di ff erences indicate that the presence of retained solvent would cause contaminants to distribute more evenly between the swollen PE and the solvent compared to the assumption of a dry polymer with minimal retained solvent. Consequently, in Fig. 8, retained solvent would lead to some contaminants remaining with the PE in the case of STRAP with toluene and some contaminants dissolving with the PE in the case of STRAP with dodecane. From a practical standpoint, this behavior implies that multiple washing steps following precipitation are likely required to obtain near contaminant-free PE after the STRAP process. Alternatively, additional processing steps could reduce the amount of retained solvent. For example, Yan et al. found that using a piston to mechanical compress the polymer during filtration substantially decreased the amount of retained solvent, which also reduced the amount of contaminant pigment species in agreement with this work. 33 These considerations highlight the potential of utilizing this contaminant removal framework to inform STRAP process design when considering the recovery of plastics from mixed plastic waste.

Conclusions

The removal of contaminants from plastic waste is a critical challenge for improving recycling e ffi ciency and ensuring the safety of recycled materials. We have developed computational approaches for guiding solvent selection to facilitate contaminant removal. By leveraging molecular models, it is possible to identify suitable solvents that selectively remove target smallmolecule contaminants and recover high-quality target polymer resins. We specifically consider the design of two contaminant removal methods based on leaching or on the integration of contaminant removal considerations during dissolution-based plastics recycling with the goal of achieving higher-purity recovered polymers. Two case studies leveraging either previously reported or newly collected experimental data validate the framework for the removal of brominated flame retardants and phthalates from common polymer resins. Two additional case studies then apply the computational tools to identify solvents for the removal of a broad range of PFAS from LDPE and to determine the likely contaminant removal e ffi ciency of steps in previously published plastics recycling processes.

Moving forward, further integration of computational modeling with experimental validation will enhance the predictive accuracy of solubility models and expand their applicability to a wider range of plastic waste streams. Other additive compounds in plastic products (such as stabilizers, plasticizers, modifiers, pigments, fillers, and processing aids) can also be taken into consideration with a similar approach. We note that the current methodology utilizes thermodynamic models to predict polymer solubility and contaminant removal at equilibrium and therefore neglects practical considerations, such as the kinetics of contaminant mass transfer, 43 which will be important to consider explicitly in future work. Because STRAP involves polymer-rich phases, contaminant partitioning may di ff er from the dilutepolymer limit modeled here. Our predictions therefore represent upper-bound removal e ffi ciencies; future work will incorporate polymer-rich phase behavior and experimental validation. Similarly, we found that solvent retained within polymers recovered after STRAP would a ff ect contaminant removal e ffi cacy. The case studies on STRAP presented in this work use a single solvent for contaminant removal, with the same solvent leading to both polymer dissolution and precipitation depending on the temperature. However, polymer precipitation can alternatively be induced through the addition of an antisolvent, 4,31 which then would lead to a solvent mixture that could further be used to tune contaminant removal strategies in future STRAP process designs. The computational approach also treats the partitioning of each contaminant separately, whereas interactions between contaminants may a ff ect partitioning behavior. While preliminary analysis (described in the SI) indicates minimal such interference e ff ects, further investigation of interactions between contaminants will be a subject of future work. Finally, we envision combining these methods with new computational tools, such as machine learning models, to aid in the selection of representative contaminant models in order to expand the scope of possible target contaminants considered during process design.

E-waste plastics

1. Introduction

Brominated flame retardants, commonly known as BFRs, refer to a group of chemical additives that contain organobromine. These addi tives  are  added  to  materials  like  plastics,  synthetic  resins,  textiles, electronic circuit boards, and furniture to reduce their flammability and prevent the rapid spread of fire [1]. Tetrabromobisphenol-A (TBBPA) is a common BFR found in the plastics from waste electronic and electrical equipment (WEEE). These compounds are heat and light sensitive, as well as persistent and capable of bioaccumulation [2 -4]. The adverse health and livelihood effects of various BFRs can be found elsewhere [5,6]. As per the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), the U.S. Envi ronment Protection Agency (EPA) has listed TBBPA as a chemical for risk evaluation[7]. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has not defined an occupational exposure limit for TBBPA but

A B S T R A C T

Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) is a high utility engineering thermoplastic, abundantly present in waste electronic and electrical goods. The demand for this plastic resin increases continuously with rapid industrial growth across the world. During the recycling of e-waste plastics, it is a common occurrence to find brominated flame retardants, such as Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) in the plastic. These flame retardants are intentionally added to the plastics as additives. Three processes were investigated to find the optimum solvent/antisolvent combinations, process parameters for the efficient recovery of TBBPA free plastics: microwave assisted extraction (MAE), ultrasound assisted extraction (UAE), and dissolution reprecipitation (DR). Rigorous solvent screening was carried out for both TBBPA and ABS using Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP), and their interactions with the solvents were investigated with a molecular based Conductor like Screening Model for Realistic Solvents (COSMO-RS) software platform. A 4:1 (v/v) solvent mixture of 1-propanol and heptane was found to be ideal for the solid -liquid extraction process. The optimal extraction conditions (Temperature = 110 -130 °C, time = 60 to 70  min  solid/liquid  ratio  of  0.025)  in  MAE  were  predicted  using  machine  learning  based  Support  Vector Regression (SVR) technique. MAE was found to be superior to UAE and DR processes in terms of quantity and quality of recovered plastics. The maximum extraction efficiencies for TBBPA removal were achieved with MAE, UAE, and DR processes at 95.81%, 93.92%, and 98.15%, respectively. However, the DR process had a relatively lower plastic recovery.

has  recommended  a  permissible  exposure  limit  for  Particulate  Not Otherwise Regulated (PNOR) during industrial operations [8]. Due to its extensive usage in consumer goods, the chances of human exposure of TBBPA are very high. TBBPA and its derivatives were identified as pri ority substances for screening assessment under the Canadian Environ mental  Protection  Act,  1999  due  to  their  persistence  and  inherent toxicity to non-human organisms [9]. The EU directives (2012/19/EU) on managing WEEE suggested selective treatment for the plastics con taining BFR[10]. WEEE plastics are subject to regulations which limit the presence of BFRs to 2,000 parts per million (ppm) of bromine. This is because available plastic sorting technologies are unable to differentiate between restricted and non-restricted BFRs. An operational threshold of 2,000 ppm total bromine has been set to aid in the separation of plastics containing BFRs[11]. Different BFRs and its derivatives have been found in  freshwater  fish[12],  household  dust  laundry  wastewater[13,14], P. Das et al.

indoor  air[6],  agricultural  products[15],  toys[16],  etc.  Other  studies also confirmed the presence of the bioaccumulative BFRs in different marine animals, such as predator fish [17], trout, salmon[18], bivalve [19], and sharks [20]. Thermal treatments, such as incineration or py rolysis of BFR-laden plastics, can create conditions that are favorable for the generation of highly toxic polybrominated  dibenzo-p-dioxins (PBDD)  and  polybrominated  dibenzo-furans  (PBDF)[21,22].  These compounds  are  highly  toxic  and  considered  as  persistent  pollutant, bioaccumulative[23] and can cause range of adverse health effect [24]. Other studies highlighted that these compounds affect the reproductive hormones and thyroids of laboratory animals[20,25 -27].

Heat plays a vital role in various production processes, including injection  molding,  extrusion,  3D  printing,  and  others.  However,  the presence of BFR in the plastic during heating can result in the emission of toxic fumes, posing a serious health hazard to individuals in the vi cinity[28].  Furthermore,  dumping  of  such  plastics  can  lead  to  the leaching of brominated components into the environment [29,30]. Sun, et al. [31] have argued that there is even a subtle diffusion of the BFRs from the plastic to the air through molecular matrix, and this diffusion can be significantly enhanced by abrasion tear and pulverisation of the plastics. Hence, it is essential to remove the excess BFR from the plastics before recycling.

Sun, et al. [31], Wan, et al. [32] reported the mass transfer kinetics involved in the release of BFRs such as PBDEs, TBBPA-bis-(2,3-dibromo2-methylpropyl ether) from plastics, respectively. Which implies that the interaction between the polymer, the additive, and the solvent is an important  consideration  in  the  solvent  extraction  of  additives  from plastics [33]. For efficient extraction, the solvent must diffuse into the polymer matrix by swelling/softening the polymer, followed by disso lution of the TBBPA (BFR), and diffusion back into the solvent phase with minimal loss to the polymer [34,35].

In this study, solvent-based green recycling of ABS impregnated with TBBPA from e-waste stream was performed using suitable solvents and solvent mixtures by extraction. The solvents were screened using Han sen Solubility Parameter (HSP) calculation to achieve optimal extraction efficiency. The recovery of pure polymers from contaminated plastics is important to reduce the production of virgin plastics from petroleum sources, hence decrease the carbon footprint and also fulfill the circular economic  goal  [36].  Statistically,  the  recycling  of  such  plastics  is significantly  low  due  to  process  complexity,  polymer  contamination, and limited profitability. Prior to 2020, only 10% of all plastic waste generated  had  been  recycled,  the  rest  was  either  incinerated  or  dis carded [37]. Hence, a sustainable and economical recycling of plastic will greatly reduce CO2 emissions, plastic accumulation in landfills, and environmental hazards associated with plastic.  It  was  estimated  that 30% of e-waste plastics are ABS [38,39]. ABS Plastics are made from acrylonitrile,  butadiene,  and  styrene  by  emulsion  polymerization. Acrylonitrile  is  a  synthetic  monomer  made  from  propylene  and ammonia. Butadiene is a product of hydrocracking petroleum, and sty rene is produced by dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene. All these pro cesses are highly energy intensive and carbon negative. ABS is one of the most  important  plastic  components,  used  primarily  in  electronics, electrical  equipment,  and  automotive  parts  due  to  its  high  impact strength and flexibility. The global production of ABS plastic reached 11.38 million metric tons in 2020 [40]. The cost of ABS plastic has risen sharply recently, reaching $3,305/ton (injection molding grade) in the USA[41].  Recycling  of  pristine  ABS  from  e-waste  will  increase  the availability of these plastics.

Earlier  studies  have  identified  the  problem  associated  with  BFR laden plastics and proposed various methods, such as extraction of the BFR [42 -44], thermal degradation of plastic by pyrolysis for the transfer of Br into residue products[45,46] and for direct safe reuse as recycled products[47]. Evangelopoulos, et al. [48] reported reduction of Br in the order of 10 -37% from Bromine-containing plastics using isopropanol and toluene as solvents under Soxhlet extractor, albeit no findings on recovery of plastics were reported. Vilaplana, et al. [42] reported TBBPA

removal  efficiencies  of  90.05%  and  67.64%  from  high  impact  poly styrene  (HIPS)  in  microwave  assisted  extraction  (MAE)  using  an isopropanol/n-hexane (1:1 v/v) mixture and an isopropanol/methanol (1:1 v/v) mixture as solvent, respectively. Bhaskar, et al. [49] carried out the microwave irradiation of BFR laden HIPS using aqueous organic solvents with triethylene glycol and achieved a Br removal efficiency of 85 % (w/w) at 250 °C and 30 min run time. Past studies concentrated on the separation of the BFR from the plastic, but little attention was paid to the quality of the recovered plastic. A detailed mechanism of the solvent and polymer/BFR interaction was lacking. Hence, this study focuses on the screening of appropriate solvents to improve extraction using mi crowaves  or  ultrasound  and  also  investigates  the  plausibility  of  the dissolution  and  re-precipitation  method.  Here,  we  have  reported  a computationally  guided  approach  to  rationally  select  solvents  using Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs), and demonstrated the mechanism of interaction between the solvent and the polymer/BFR [50]. This was performed using the platform combining quantum chemical and statis tical software called ' conductor-like screening model for realistic sol vents ' (COSMO-RS).  Solvent properties, including solubility and polarity, significantly impact the recovery of plastics and the extraction of specific additives during solvent extraction processes. These proper ties  are  crucial  for  determining  the  effectiveness  of  the  extraction method.  The  optimal  process  conditions  were  determined  using  the machine learning  based  Support  Vector  Regression  (SVR)  technique. The  post-process  recovered  polymers  were  analysed  intensively  and comparisons were made for all the process outcomes in terms of effi ciency and polymer recovery. The findings of this study will significantly contribute to the e-waste (plastic) recycling industry.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Sample selection and preparation

Three  real  ABS  plastic  samples  from  real  e-waste  sources  and  a customized  sample  (CS)  with  a  known  concentration  of  BFR  (Tetra bromobisphenol-A) were chosen for this study (Table 1). The prepara tion process of the real sample is explained in Text 1S in the supporting information file. The CS in granular form was obtained from Shandong Tianyi Chemical Company, China. The standard TBBPA, pure ABS as 3D printing filament (ABS3D), and all the organic solvents (Purity > 99.5%) for the screening were procured from Sigma Aldrich Singapore. The Br concentration was measured by X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (Text 2S).

2.2. Calculation of the solubility score (Si) for solvent screening

0.1 g of the solid samples (ABS3D, TBBPA) was mixed with 10 ml of the  solvent  at  40 °C  and  kept  under  ultrasound  (Qsonica  sonicator, Q125, 125 W, 20 kHz) for 30 min. Solubility was observed visually (Fig. 2S) and assigned solubility scores ( Si ) of 0, 1, and 2 for no disso lution,  partial  dissolution,  and  fully  dissolved  solutions,  respectively. The solubility score was used for the calculation of the Hansen solubility parameters  (HSP).  The  HSP  calculation  method  is  explained  in  the supporting information (Text 3S).

The framework of COSMO-RS and the simulation flow representing the TBBPA molecule and the iso lated ABS molecule with σ -surface are shown in Fig. 3(a). The corre sponding σ -profile and σ -potential/ μ ( σ ) with respect to the ABS, TBBPA and solvents are shown in Fig. 3(b) and (c), respectively.

The σ -profiles reflect the polarity comparison between the solute and the solvent. There are three regions in the sigma profile: the values of σ between 0.01 to + 0.01 e/Å 2 , ∞ to 0.01 e/Å 2 and + 0.01 to + ∞ e/ Å 2 , as the nonpolar region, hydrogen bond (H-bond) donor region and H-bond  acceptor  region,  respectively[54].  The σ -profile  peaks ' in tensities  beyond σ = -0.01  e/Å 2 and + 0.01  e/Å 2 correspond to the strength of the H-bond donor and the acceptor region on the surface. A larger peak beyond ± 0.01 e/Å 2 increases the probability of H-bond interaction, and the further the peak is from the center, the stronger the H-bond interaction. The peaks of the nonpolar segments of the surfaces are visible in the range near σ = 0 e/Å 2 . An asymmetric σ -profile can be seen for ABS and TBBPA (Fig. 3(b)). Indeed, in the case of ABS, a narrow peak beyond -0.01 and -0.02 e/Å 2 of the σ -region and the peak shifting slightly away from the center generally corresponds to the presence of H-bond donor sites. However, a slightly broad peak at 0.01 e/Å 2 rep resents  the  influence  of π -electrons  of  the C ≡ N group of the ABS molecule,  represented  by  the  slightly  red  colored σ -region  (H-bond acceptor) (Fig. 3(a)). The σ -potential ( μ ( σ )) of the ABS shows a distinct shape (Fig. 3(c)). The negative side of the σ -region ( σ > 0.01 e/Å 2 ) has more  negative  value,  indicating  its  affinity  to  interact  with  H-bond donor surfaces. On the other hand, the positive value of μ ( σ ) in the re gion ( σ > + 0.01 e/Å 2 ) reflects that ABS lacks the H-bond donor surface and has the affinity to attract H-bond acceptor surfaces. The σ -profile of the TBBPA is dominating in the non-polar region ( σ ~ 0 e/Å 2 ) with a narrow cusp near 0.01 e/Å 2 representing the π -electrons of the ring, and a small bump in the region of the σ = -0.01/Å 2 representing the elec tronegativity  around  the  oxygen  atom.  However,  the μ ( σ )  values  of TBBPA have positive values in the region of σ > -0.01 e/Å 2 and negative values in a wider range in the region σ > + 0.01 e/Å 2 , which signifies the availability  of  H-bond  acceptor  surfaces  on  the  molecule. 3.2. Extraction of TBBPA using MAE, UAE, and DR process

The microwave heat is transferred to the sample via a dual mecha nism of dipole rotation of the solvent and the sample, as well as ionic conduction [35,56,57]. Experimental outcomes of the MAE are shown in Fig. 4 for the solvent mixture 1P / Hp performed at initial experimental conditions. Fig. 4(a) and 4(b) show the % Br extraction efficiency and the plastic recovery for three mixing ratios and for all four samples, respectively. Using a 4:1 mixing ratio of 1P to Hp solvents, the maximum extraction rates were achieved for all four samples, as depicted in Fig. 4 (a).  Specifically,  the  extraction  rates  for  CS,  ReBRS1,  ReBRS2,  and ReBRS3 samples were 91.25%, 94.02%, 95.81%, and 91.03%, respec tively.  Correspondingly,  the  plastic  recovery  percentages  for  these samples  when  using  the  4:1  1P  and  Hp  solvent  mix  were  88.29%, 84.66%,  80.24%,  and  84.4%,  respectively.  Recovery  of  plastic  was consistent across all conditions, and > 80% of clean ABS plastics were recovered in each run (Fig. 4(b)). Mass loss occurred due to BFR and additive  dissolution  and  experimental  losses  during  collection.  Small particle  size  leads  to  better  extraction  efficiency  (Fig.  4(c)).  Earlier studies  have  reported  extraction  efficiencies < 85%  [42,48,49].  MAE with a suitable solvent can be a viable option for the recovery of clean plastics. High-capacity microwave ovens are used in the food, paper, timber and textile industries primarily for drying [58], with some design modifications.  A  high-capacity  microwave  oven  has  the  potential  to serve as a viable technique for the extraction of TBBPA from ABS plastic, particularly in the context of recycling e-waste plastics [59].

A  temperature in the range of 110 ---130 °C, time in the range of 60 to 70 mins, and s/l ratio of 0.025 give the maximum extraction efficiency. Hence, the predicted output in the  response  surfaces  matches  well  with  experimental  observations (Fig. 4(g)).

After MAE, a comparative evaluation of UAE and DR techniques was conducted. A 4:1 (v/v%) mixing ratio of 1P and Hp was used for UAE. Table 3 presents the Br extraction efficiencies (%) and the corresponding plastic recoveries (%) obtained from all three processes experimentally. The results obtained from the UAE technique were found to be like those obtained through MAE, though a minor decrease in plastic recoveries was observed, possibly attributed to high agitation leading to polymer dissolution.  In  contrast,  the  DR  method  resulted  in  almost  complete elimination of BFR, albeit at the expense of a substantial reduction in the amount of recovered uncontaminated plastics (Fig. 5(b)). The solution may contain a considerable amount of plastic material, particularly low molecular weight ABS, that may remain dissolved [60]. Low extraction efficiency (50 -60%) for TBBPA from HIPS was reported by Vilaplana, et al. [51] using UAE. Guo, et al. [61] used d-limonene as solvent and npropanol  as  precipitant  (anti-solvent)  to  recover  HIPS  from  e-waste plastic  sample  with  decaBDE as  BFR  and  achieved only ~  88% BFR removal efficiency in the DR process. Table 4 showcases several previ ously documented results pertaining to the extraction of bromine (Br)/ BFR  from  e-waste  plastics.  However,  most  of  these  studies  lack comprehensive data regarding plastic recovery. In contrast, the results obtained from the present study demonstrate high Br extraction effi ciency  over  the  reported  finding  and  yield  a  substantial  quantity  of recyclable ABS plastics.

text: FTIR-ATR spectra of the CS/Real samples are consistent with those of pure  ABS  (Fig.  3S(b)).  On  the  other  hand,  values  of  glass  transition temperatures ( Tg) of the BFR laden plastics are lower than the Tg values of pure ABS plastics which are around 105 -107 °C [62,63]. The Tg of the CS,  ReBRS1,  ReBRS2  and ReBRS3 are  99.7,  93.7,  92.2  and  91.8 °C, respectively. The two-step degradation profile can be seen in Fig. 7S(d) for the CS/Real samples with a peak degradation temperature at 427 °C, 443 °C, 436 °C, 443 °C for CS, ReBRS1, ReBRS2 and ReBRS3, respec tively. For post MAE recovered plastics, the FTIR-ATR, DSC, and TGA (DTG) analysis are shown in Fig. 5. Typical ABS absorption bands are distinctively present in the FTIR-ATR spectra (Fig. 5(a)) as demonstrated when compared bands from treated samples with those of pure ABS (Fig. 3S(b)). A detailed band assignment for the IR absorption bands associated  with  ABS/TBBPA  is  listed  in  Table  6S.  Precisely,  the  C-H stretches of the aliphatic and aromatic bonds are clearly visible in the range of 3200 -3000 cm 1 and 3000 -2800 cm 1 , respectively[64]. A well-defined peak at 2239 cm 1 represents the C ≡ N stretch of acrylo nitrile and the ring structure of styrene appears at absorption bands of 1602 and 1494 cm 1 . The other indicators of aromatic ring are seen at 1452 cm 1 ( -CH2 scissoring, ring C-H), 757 cm 1  and 696 cm 1 (ring P. Das et al.

bends) [65]. The bond deformation of the C-H bond adjacent to the double bond of the butadiene from ABS is seen at 967 and 910 cm 1 . The narrow peak at 1262 cm 1 corresponds to the -OH vibration due to the presence of trace amounts of leftover TBBPA[66]. Furthermore, the Tg values of the post MAE samples improve significantly and approach the Tg values of the commercial ABS (~105 °C)[67]. The thermal degrada tion characteristics of the plastics recovered after microwave-assisted extraction (MAE) demonstrated a comparable peak degradation tem perature  to  that  of  the  reference  ABS  plastics,  with  a  temperature proximity of 440 °C observed under non-isothermal heating conditions of 20 °C/min for all samples (Fig. 5(d))[68]. Therefore, the disappear ance of the peak associated with TBBPA in the DTG analysis following MAE did not significantly alter the properties of the polymer. In sum mary, all  the  properties  of  ABS,  which  was  treated  with  MAE,  were consistent with those of the reference polymer.

The characterization results of the recovered polymers after UAE and DR  processes  are  shown  in  Fig.  8S  and  Fig.  9S,  respectively.  The chemical structure of the polymer, as shown by the FTIR-ATR spectra and Tg from DSC, appears to be consistent with pure ABS. No significant changes appeared in the TGA/DTG plot of the samples recovered from UAE.

A  slight  distortion  in  the  DTG  profile  can  however  be  seen  in recovered samples of the DR process (Fig. 9S(c)). Changes in the peak degradation  temperature  can  be  seen,  particularly  for  the  ReBRS2, which changes from 436 °C to 465 °C. This could be due to the removal of the stabilizing additives during the dissolution process. The GCMS peaks  from  the  MAE  and  DR  processes  are  shown  in  Fig.  10S  and Fig. 11S, respectively, along with the likely components discovered by searching the Mass spectral library. TBBPA appeared in all the solutions. In addition to that, traces of phenolic compounds, aromatic compounds (isoquinols), and organic acids were also present in the solutions, which could be attributed to the various additives, such as dyes, antifungals, antioxidants, and anti-aging compounds mixed within the plastics. The presence of Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) in the solvents from the DR process can be attributed to the usage of THF for dissolution, as BHT is a stabilizer commonly found in THF solvents. Among the two solid -liquid extraction processes, MAE appeared to be better than UAE in terms of plastic  recovery  yields.  However,  both  processes  have  challenges  in terms of scale-up and implementation. UAE requires external heating, while MAE uses microwaves to heat the system. Management of heat and pressure is simpler in MAE compared to UAE because heat can be delivered to the target material via microwave without contact. On the other hand, the DR process can restore the purity of the polymer by reprecipitation  from  the  liquid  phase,  with  reduced  polymer yield  and abated polymer properties. A DR-like process (CreaSolv ® ) was devel oped by Unilever/Fraunhofer Institute for the separation of polymers from a mixed polymer stream of plastics (from different sources)[69,70]. Walker, et al. [71] developed a similar process called solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process to deconstruct multilayer films  and  recover  the  pure  resin  by  performing  rigorous  solvent screening using HSP and COSMO-RS calculations. Peng, et al. [43] used supercritical CO2 as an antisolvent for the separation of Deca-BDE (BFR) from HIPS obtained from e-waste. Our results show that MAE can be an excellent  method  for  removing  BFR  from  plastics  without  affecting plastic properties.
4. Conclusions and perspectives

This study reports the optimal combination of solvents that can be applied to remove the tightly bound BFR additive (TBBPA) from ABS plastics recovered from e-waste[31]. We adopted a rigorous methodol ogy  to  screen  suitable  solvent/solvent  mixtures  that  would  allow maximum extraction and minimum loss of plastic. The mixture of 1propanol and heptane was found to be suitable for the extraction of TBBPA from ABS plastics. Non-polar solvents, such as heptane mixed with alcohol, improved the extraction efficiency more significantly than their individual counterparts. COSMO-RS Calculations showed that both TBBPA and ABS have polar and nonpolar properties on their molecular surfaces  that  influence  the  extraction.  The  targeted  solvent-based extraction  for  recovery  of  BFR  (TBBPA)-free  plastics  from  contami nated e-waste ABS plastics was improved by heating with microwave/ ultrasound.  In  terms  of  extraction  rates,  MAE  was  superior  under optimal process conditions as it also preserved/improved the polymer properties of the ABS. The recovery of ABS plastics from the DR process was low compared to MAE /UAE with high extraction efficiency. Such processes could provide a common framework for developing solvent based processes for debromination of BFR laden e-waste plastics. The implementation of a selective and targeted approach is better suited for the recovery of clean plastics and achieving a closed-loop system for recycling e-waste plastics.

Abstract

Direct reuse of plastic film with printing results in a colored polymer, which is less stiff and weaker than the original plastic upon re-extrusion. There is substantial economical and environmental incentive to remove the ink (deink) from heavily printed plastic film so that it can be reused to produce clear films. In this study, a commercial polyethylene film with water-based ink printing was deinked using different surfactants under a variety of conditions. At a pH of 12, water (containing no surfactant) can achieve about 90% deinking, but less basic solutions are less effective; at a pH 10 and below, insignificant-deinking occurs. Solutions of cationic surfactant are the most effective at deinking, showing high efficiency at surfactant concentrations both above and below the critical micelle concentration (CMC) over a pH range of 5-12. Amphoteric surfactant is effective above the CMC over a wide pH range. Both anionic and nonionic surfactants are only effective at deinking above the CMC at very basic conditions, with anionic surfactant being only slightly better than just water even at these high pH levels. The cationic surfactant is most effective and the anionic surfactant is least effective, possibly because the binder is an acidic acrylate with a negative charge. © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V.
