Con fi dence scores were assigned to individual categorizations based on the information origin and outlet control of individual sources, nature of the keywords (i.e., synonym, hyponym, and hypernym), and observed error frequency (Table S4 in Supporting Information S2).

2.4. Identi fi cation of Substances of Potential Concern. Substances of potential concern were identi fi ed and assigned a level of potential concern using a simpli fi ed two-step approach, based on hazard classi fi cations and production volumes as surrogate re fl ecting potentials for causing adverse e ff ects and exposure, respectively.

In the fi rst step, substances that ful fi ll one or more of the following hazard criteria under EU REACH were identi fi ed as substances of potential concern: PBT/very persistent and very bioaccumulative (vPvB), carcinogenicity (C), mutagenicity (M), reproductive toxicity (R), endocrine disruption (ED), speci fi c target organ toxicity upon repeated exposure ( STOT-RE), and chronic aquatic toxicity (AqTox). Detailed criteria for the di ff erent hazard classi fi cations can be found in Table S5 in Supporting Information S2. Substances with insu ffi cient hazard information or without any information at all in the considered regulatory databases were categorized as ' unknown ' , whereas those with full hazard information but that did not meet any of the considered hazard criteria were categorized as the ' low level of concern ' . In the second step, depending on production volumes, identi fi ed substances of potential concern were either considered the ' medium level of concern ' (<1'000 t/yr) or ' high level of concern ' (>1'000 t/yr).

2.5. Quality Assurance and Quality Control. As stated above, data quality was assured using several procedures. For substance identi fi cation, quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) included assigning con fi dence scores to the sources and substances (Sheet S1 in Supporting Information S1), verifying the check digit of CASRNs, 45 and checking the CASRN status in SciFinder (Section 2.2). For substance type and use pattern categorization, QA/QC included iterative keyword optimization (Section 2.3) and assigning con fi dence scores to each categorization. For the identi fi cation of substances of potential concern, QA/QC included a hazard data consistency check (Figure S6 in Supporting Information S2) and manually double-checking the regulatory status. The remaining uncertainties are mostly due to misreported or missing information and are qualitatively discussed in Section 4.

3. RESULTS

3.1. Overview of Plastic Monomers, Additives, and Processing Aids. In total, substances with 10'547 unique active CASRNs are identi fi ed, mostly with high con fi dence in their use as plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids (Figure 2A, Sheet S8 in Supporting Information S1). These active CASRNs are associated with another 24'901 deleted CASRNs (i.e., replaced by the active CASRNs) and 22 alternate CASRNs (i.e., CASRNs in parallel use to the active ones). A number of these deleted or alternate CASRNs are still being used in di ff erent information sources.

All source types (scienti fi c, regulatory, and industrial) are important for substance identi fi cation (Figure 2A). A total of 4'280 CASRNs have been reported in more than one type of source, whereas over 6'267 CASRNs have only been reported in one type of source (note that they can occur in several sources, but all of these belong to the same source type).

More than 25% of the substances (2'703 CASRNs) are UVCBs, mixtures, and polymers, whereas almost all the rest (7'561) are individual compounds (Figure 2A). The majority of individual compounds are organic ones (6'513), including 232 organosilicons, 228 organophosphorus, 418 organosulfurs, 1'189 organohalogens, and 1'268 organic metal(loid) salts, metalorganics, or organometallics. For 2.5% of the identi fi ed substances (283), their substance types are currently uncategorizable (Figures 2A, 3  data availability) because they are registered by their trade or trivial names [for example, Ixol M 125 (CASRN 86675-46-9), C.I. Pigment Yellow 157 (CASRN 68610-24-2)] and lack other identi fi ers such as SMILES or molecular formulas that can re fl ect their chemical structures.

Information availability varies considerably among the 10'547 substances, with most substances having information on their use or registration status in speci fi c regions (>90%), followed by production volumes (70%), functions (69%), and any reported hazard classi fi cations (61%). For the rest, substantial information gaps persist: industrial sectors of use (40%), regulatorharmonized hazard classi fi cations (22%), and compatible polymer types (16%). Around 3% of the substances lack any information other than their chemical names and CASRNs (Figure 2B).

Overall, 55% of the substances identi fi ed are categorized as plastics additives, 39% as processing aids, and 24% as monomers, with signi fi cant overlaps between these three categories. In addition, due to a lack of information, 30% of the substances remain uncategorizable regarding their functions (Figure 2C).

Overall, more than 90% of the substances are registered for production and use in one or more of the regions or countries considered; about 55% are registered in more than 9 countries and regions, compared to 7% that are region/country-speci fi c. In individual countries or regions, 20 -80% of the substances are registered (Figure 2D). Inventories from the US, EU, and Nordic countries (Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden) contain publicly accessible use information; our analysis shows that many of the identi fi ed substances are seemingly registered for uses without direct linkages to plastics in these inventories (US: 50%, EU: 50%, and Nordic countries: 20%; Figure 2D). Reasons for this reporting di ff erence may be actual uses for other purposes, ambiguity in the reporting, or under- or misreporting. For example, tetrabromobisphenol A bis(dibromopropyl ether) (TBBPA-BDBPE; CASRN 21850-44-2; a fl ame retardant) and Tinuvin 765 (CASRN 41556-26-7; a light stabilizer) are registered in both the SPIN and REACH databases, but their use in plastics is reported in only one (Tinuvin 765 in the SPIN database and TBBPA-BDBPE in the REACH database).

3.2. Overview of the Use Patterns. Functions are identi fi ed for a majority of the substances (7'265 CASRNs, 69%), in comparison to the much lower identi fi cation of information on compatible polymer types (3'002 CASRNs, 28%) and industrial sectors of use (4'383 CASRNs, 42%). Typically, substances can ful fi ll several functions (on average, two to three functions), be used in multiple polymer types (particularly in similar polymer types such as polyole fi ns), and be used in multiple industrial sectors (Figure 3). A total of 2'263 CASRNs are reported for use in the following applications with high exposure potential: 2'109 in food-contact applications, 522 in toys, and 247 in medical items including masks (Sheet S8 in Supporting Information S1 under the ' industrial_sector ' ).

Based on the production volumes reported in the EU, the US, and the Nordic countries and the OECD HPVC list, about 4'000 substances are HPVCs (i.e., >1'000 t/yr; Figure 3); however, these represent their total production volumes for all uses and not just the fractions used in plastics. If production volumes in other regions were available, more substances might be identi fi ed as HPVCs. Furthermore, the production volumes of many substances have been reported as ' con fi dential ' ; their share was the largest for antioxidants (10%), fl ame retardants (11%), and uncategorizable substances (12%).

3.3. Substances of Potential Concern and Their Regulatory Status. In total, reported hazard classi fi cations are available for about 6'400 substances (61%), whereas about 4'100 substances (39%) lack any reported hazard classi fi cations in the considered regulatory databases (unknown level of concern). Most substances with unknown levels of concern lack information about their functions (Figure 2B), are not HPVCs in the EU or the US or in the OECD countries, and belong to UVCBs, mixtures, and polymers (Figure S19 in Supporting Information S2).

In total, 3'950 substances (37%) do not meet any of the considered hazard criteria, while their hazard classi fi cations are available; these are designated as substances of a low level of concern. Another 2'486 substances (24%) meet one or more of the hazard criteria considered and are identi fi ed as substances of potential concern; among them, 1'254 substances (12%) are also HPVCsandthus of a high level of concern. The remaining 1'232 substances (12%) are of a medium level of concern.

An overview of all substances of potential concern is provided in Table 1, and the entire substance list is provided in Sheet S9 in Supporting Information S1. In short, 22 substances are PBT and another 35 are vPvB substances. A total of 2'368 substances show toxicity of concern, including 951 CMR toxicants, 30 EDCs, 1'646 substances that can cause chronic aquatic toxicity, and 891 substances that may cause speci fi c target organ toxicity upon repeated exposure.

Around 53% of the substances of potential concern are not subject to any sort of management measures under one or more of the regulations considered in this study (Table 1). Five percent (136 CASRNs) of the substances of potential concern are regulated under the Stockholm Convention, the Rotterdam Convention, or the Montreal protocol. Additionally, 960 of the substances of potential concern are subject to national/regional restrictions (EU: 135; Republic of Korea: 46; and Japan: 16), authorizations (EU: 53; Republic of Korea: 362; and Japan: 15), or prohibitions in speci fi c areas (EU, toys: 440 and EU, electronic waste: 102). Surprisingly, despite having highly problematic hazardous properties, 901 substances of concern also appear on the regulatory positive lists for use in foodcontact plastics (EU: 225; Japan: 568; and US: 667; see columns under ' Regulation  Food-contact positive lists ' in Sheet S9 in Supporting Information S1).

The number of scienti fi c references that are linked in SciFinder varies greatly per substance (range = 0 -1'086'797 and median = 1'410; see Figures S16 and S24 in Supporting Information S2). Around 10% of the identi fi ed substances of potential concern lack any scienti fi c references in SciFinder, indicating that they may have been poorly studied (Table 1), of these 10% most are UVCBs, mixtures, and polymers.

4. DISCUSSION

4.1. Numbers of Plastic Monomers, Additives, and Processing Aids on the Market. This study has identi fi ed over 10'000 CASRNs that are or may potentially be used as plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids. This number is much higher than previous studies because of the broader scope, whereas earlier studies have focused on plastic packaging (4'000 substances) 13 and plastic additives with registered tonnages above 100 t/yr in the EU (400 substances). 12 Even so, these 10'000 identi fi ed substances might still be an underestimate of the total number of substances present in plastics, mainly due to the following three clusters of reasons:

I There is a general lack of transparency regarding substances present in plastics. 66,67 Existing practices of

national/regional chemical inventories provide limited help on this matter, due to (1) limited public accessibility of production and use information (e.g., only three of the 21 investigated inventories made use information public; much of the information reported in these three inventories is claimed to be ' con fi dential business information ' ) and (2) incompleteness (e.g., reduced reporting requirements for low production volume or ' non-hazardous ' chemicals 62 ). Currently, several initiatives targeting better communication of information on chemicals in products along supply chains have been initiated, for example, the EU Sustainable Product Policy Initiative, 67,68 the Substances of Concern In articles or Products database (SCIP database) hosted by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), 69 and the HolyGrail Project led by P&G (under the New Plastics Economy program of the Ellen MacArthur Foundation). 70 However, their e ff ective implementation is currently hindered by factors such as (claims of) complex supply chains, diverging interests and technical capacities of actors within supply chains, and data storage and transfer issues. 71,72

II Not all data in the public domain are readily machineaccessible and processable; in this study, substances for which the assigned CASRNs are not provided are excluded from the analysis, including ions for ionizable substances or structural isomers (see Section 2.2). This is largely due to a combination of the following reasons: (1) the wide use of nonmachine-readable data formats; (2) current limitations in reporting all relevant substances, including the common use of ambiguous trivial names and group names such as phenolic antioxidants without specifying relevant substances, the wide use of di ff erent names for the same substances, the underuse of unique identi fi ers such as assigned CASRNs, SMILES, and InChI(Key), 62 and common mixed reporting of neutral, ionized substances, isotopologues, and other isomers using the same identi fi ers such as CASRNs and chemical names; and (3) a lack of standardized terminology for use patterns across jurisdictions. Concerted e ff orts to address these problems are necessary to improve, harmonize, and foster nonambiguous reporting of substance identities and use patterns by all stakeholders across the world, building on existing initiatives. 3,73 -76 In addition, advances in information technologies (such as optical character recognition, natural language processing, and cheminformatics tools) to unambiguously recognize di ff erent types of chemical identi fi ers in the text and convert between them may help collect information that currently requires manual processing. 77 -81

III Besides the intentionally added substances considered in this study, also NIASs are highly relevant for plastics because (1) they have been frequently reported in measurements, (2) plastics in many applications are prone to contamination from production, processing, and use, and (3) substance transformation is an integral part of ful fi lling speci fi c functions (e.g., formation of quinones from oxidization of phenolic antioxidants). 10,41,82 -84 However, NIASs are not yet comprehensively understood, their identi fi cation remains challenging, not least because of a dearth of clarity on plastic compositions and conditions during production and use, and analytical di ffi culties of unequivocally identifying substances at low

concentrations remain. 10,11,41 To improve NIAS identifi cation and quanti fi cation, measures such as increasing product transparency through company reporting, obligatory provision of analytical standards, and standardization of sample treatment, separation, and data treatment procedures may be taken. 41

Meanwhile, for the 10'000 substances identi fi ed here, some uncertainties may remain regarding their use in plastics and their commercial relevance despite several measures for QA. For example, the keyword search in substance identi fi cation (Section 2.2) might have yielded substances that are relevant for polymers in uses other than plastics (e.g., polymeric adhesives) or substances used for plastic-related functions but appearing in other materials (e.g., fl ame retardants in fabrics and plasticizers in concrete formulations). In addition, in the analysis of regional registrations and production volumes (Section 2.2), the current commercial status is not fully covered, as some substances may no longer be in use or might only be used in materials other than plastics (see the next subsection).

4.2. Interpretation of Use Patterns and Their Uncertainties. In line with earlier research, many of the substances identi fi ed in this study can be used for di ff erent functions in multiple polymer types and industrial sectors. 12,13 Regarding substances in food-contact applications, a comparison with the recently compiled database of intentionally added food-contact chemicals (FCCdb) showed that despite identifying fewer substances, this study has a good overlap with the FCCdb (this study: 2'109 CASRNs; FCCdb: 11'609 CASRNs; overlapping substances identi fi ed by both: 2'026 CASRNs). 85

The results regarding use patterns (Section 3.2, especially Figure 3) need to be interpreted with caution, as only the number of substances potentially used for di ff erent functions (dominated by 3'663 colorants and 1'833 fi llers) and the total production volume for all uses (including uses for other functions and in other materials) is presented. A recent market study based on global production volumes shows a di ff erent picture that plasticizers, fl ame retardants, and heat stabilizers dominate the plastic additive market. 86,87 In addition, solid use data remain lacking for many of the identi fi ed substances, especially concerning relevant industrial sectors (missing for 58% of the substances) and compatible polymer types (missing for 72%). Furthermore, uncertainties may be expected for some of the identi fi ed uses for the following reasons:

I Reported uses may be incomplete, outdated, or inaccurate. For example, diethyl phthalate (DEP, CASRN 84-66-2) is still frequently reported as a plasticizer in the scienti fi c literature, 33,88 -90 while the industry has reported phase-out of its use as a plasticizer (it is now primarily used as a solvent in cosmetics and other personal care products). 91 Thus, DEP may be relevant for legacy plastic products and recycled plastics, but not for new virgin plastics. Minimizing such uncertainties requires not just gathering more information from di ff erent sources but rather more stringent monitoring of industrial activities and comprehensive QC of existing data (including verifying and updating information sources on a regular basis).

II Some of the keywords used in the identi fi cation process in this study may still be incomprehensive or inaccurate, despite e ff orts to eliminate errors using an iterative learning approach (Section 2.5). This is because a simple keyword search cannot take the whole context into

account, cannot distinguish ambiguous terms, and requires large manual e ff orts to include infrequent keywords. An example of the lack of context sensitivity is benzo[ a ]pyrene (CASRN 50-32-8). It was fi rst incorrectly identi fi ed as a cross-linking agent, a fi ller, and a lubricant; a closer look revealed that it was reported as a contaminant or byproduct in substances ful fi lling these functions. To more accurately categorize use patterns, future e ff orts need to be made both on developing advanced search algorithms (e.g., using semantic searches and natural language processing) and on standardizing use descriptors. 3,74 -76,79,80,92

III Someimportant factors concerning use reporting (such as registrants ' knowledge on the topic, information processing before reporting, and potential ulterior motives in fl uencing reporting) could not be taken into account. For example, ulterior motives may play a role in the comprehensiveness and accuracy of reporting (such as missed or wrong reporting of risk-related information and exaggeration of the number of applicable uses). 93,94

Substances of Potential Concern and Associated Uncertainties. More than 2'400 substances of potential concern used in plastics are identi fi ed in this study; it may well still be an underestimate of the number of substances of concern, as it is only based on reported hazard classi fi cation. For example, many more substances than considered in this study may be persistent and/or bioaccumulative, as only the substances with the PBT assessment outcome of ful fi lling (or not ful fi lling) all PBT or both vPvB criteria were separately listed in the REACH PBT assessment list and considered in this study. 95 Thus, substances that are registered under REACH ful fi lling the P and/or B criteria are not identi fi ed in this study, due to time and resource constraints to individually check their REACH registration dossiers.

Surprisingly, about 350 substances of potential concern appear on both negative (e.g., authorization requested for speci fi c uses and bans in certain applications) and positive (i.e., approval for use in food-contact plastics) regulatory lists. For example, while authorization is required for use of dibutyl phthalate (CASRN 84-74-2) in the EU and Republic of Korea, it is approved for use in food-contact plastics in the EU, US, and Japan. This regulatory inconsistency needs to be properly addressed, for example, through closer collaboration among regulatory domains and agencies. 96

In this study, the production volume is used as a rough surrogate to re fl ect exposure potential of a chemical. More realistic exposure estimates for a large set of chemicals are currently not possible to make due to a lack of substance- and use-speci fi c information in the public domain. 37,97 Substancespeci fi c information is particularly lacking for metal-containing organic substances (30% of the identi fi ed substances) and surfactants, as measurements or estimations of substance properties such as partition and di ff usion coe ffi cients remain di ffi cult to do or make for these substances. 98,99 Future work may focus on, for example, developing new approaches for measuring or estimating partition and di ff usion coe ffi cients of all substances and generating and releasing detailed use information such as used volumes, product contents, and release potential concerning individual uses. 100

The screening of regulations in this study reveals some gaps and inconsistencies; this e ff ort is not comprehensive. This is partially due to (1) a lack of easy information access to regulations in many parts of the world, (2) a common listing of groups of substances using generic descriptions without specifying individual substances, and (3) general challenges in identifying all relevant substances by manual list curation or manual search. An example of (2) is that the listing of PFOArelated compounds under the Stockholm Convention refers to ' any substances that degrade to PFOA, including any substances (including salts and polymers) having a linear or branched per fl uoroheptyl group with the moiety (C7F15)C as one of the structural elements ' ; the recognition of individual substances such as ' alkyl iodides, C 10 -12 , γ , ω -per fl uoro ' (CASRN 6839033-0) as PFOA-related compounds currently requires expert knowledge. Therefore, facilitating information access to regulations around the world, for example, through a global virtual knowledge base and further developing cheminformatics tools that help identify whether a substance is listed based on its molecular structure can be highly useful. Speci fi cally, data engines that are capable of identifying all related CASRNs, chemical names, and structures and of indexing them based on InChI(Keys) could prove to be bene fi cial in this work.

5. POSSIBLE WAYS FORWARD

This study identi fi es over 10'000 plastic-related substances and details several critical knowledge and data gaps, particularly in terms of substance- and use-speci fi c information. This scale of chemicals to be addressed may be much greater than previously expected according to previously published assessments. Here, we highlight the following overarching areas that warrant concerted international e ff orts, in order to address these chemicals e ffi ciently and e ff ectively. This study can also serve as a starting point of immediate action, for example, by prioritizing substances of potential concern and the critical knowledge and data gaps identi fi ed above. Furthermore, while this study focuses on plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids, many of the lessons learned may also be used to enhance the general sound management of chemicals.

5.1. Establishing a Centralized Knowledge Base. Information on chemicals is scattered throughout the public domain, resulting in numerous di ffi culties in understanding the presence of chemicals in plastics and other products and their properties and risks, as illustrated above. It may be worthwhile to consider establishing an open and transparent centralized knowledge base of chemicals in products with inputs and support from all relevant stakeholders along the supply chains (e.g., chemical and material producers, product designers, retailers, and waste managers). It can contribute to a better overview of relevant chemicals and related information and thus provide a basis for prioritization of future work, for example, based on production volumes and/or hazardous properties.

Such a knowledge base could build on this work and other existing public databases (e.g., PubChem, SciFinder, OECD eChemPortal, CAS Common Chemistry, and USEPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard) and industrial transparency initiatives [for example, Global Automotive Declarable Substance List (GADSL), the HolyGrail project led by P&G]. 70 The costs of establishing and maintaining such a large database can be perceived an impediment, as well as questions around data ownership (e.g., CASRNs are intellectual properties of the Chemical Abstracts Service and may require licensing for publication). 101 Options to navigate these barriers to access may include cofunding such an initiative through public -private partnerships, as a part of companies ' corporate social responsibility and commitments to the human right to science, and harmonizing information exchange standards across the existing major databases to allow easy retrieval and compilation of information at one central place. 102 -104 Regardless, transparency, independence, and open accessibility are crucial for such a knowledge base, and strong leadership through national and/or international governmental organizations (e.g., United Nations Environment Programme, OECD, ECHA) is needed for setting it up.

5.2. Ensuring Transition to a Safe and Sustainable Circular Plastic Economy. A vast number of diverse substances are potentially used in the manufacture of plastics, with over 20% being substances of potential concern. Meanwhile, current regulations, scienti fi c and regulatory monitoring e ff orts, and industry initiatives lag far behind the introduction of these substances to the market, to ensure clean, safe, and highquality virgin and recycled plastics. For example, the current European chemicals regulations mostly focus on single substances and/or certain industrial sectors (e.g., plastics for food-contact purposes, in toys, in electrical and electronic equipment, and in automotive applications). 105 -107 Similarly, current industrial circular economy initiatives focus primarily on the material level (e.g., using the same polymer for multilayer plastics to increase recyclability), with limited attention paid to the chemicals therein. 108 -113

To ensure the transition toward a safe and sustainable circular plastic economy, concerted e ff orts by all stakeholders are needed in at least the following areas: 114 developing standardized approaches to assessing the sustainable circularity of plastics and chemicals therein; avoiding hazardous substances and embedding sustainable circularity in the design phase of plastic polymers, additives, processing aids, and value chains; fostering greater transparency throughout value chains including waste management and broadening monitoring e ff orts; developing and sharing knowledge on creating sustainable circularity of plastics and chemicals therein; and fostering innovative and chemical management enabling business models and practices.

The information compiled in this study may help initial screenings of safer alternatives in speci fi c applications, followed by more detailed alternative assessments. 115 Note that the indispensability or ' essential ' use of a substance for a speci fi c function/performance (in a speci fi c application) may also be evaluated fi rst to phase out those uses that are nonessential and thus reduce the numbers of existing chemicals on the market and their uses to be assessed and transitioned. 114 -118

5.3. Expanding and Harmonizing Regulatory E ff orts. Current chemical regulation does not ensure global sustainable management of chemicals for several reasons: (a) not all substances of potential concern are listed under relevant international or regional regulations (Section 3.3); (b) substance-by-substance regulations may not protect against regrettable substitutions; 119,120 (c) regional regulations might lead to shifting chemical pollution elsewhere; 121 and (d) negative externalities (e.g., monitoring costs, potential cleanup costs, public health damages, and impaired ecosystem services) of chemicals throughout their life cyles are not fully addressed by current regulations. 122,123 Potential ways forward include (a) increasing the number of substances under regulatory scrutiny to cover all substances of potential concern; 124 (b) focusing on group- or class-based regulatory approaches to avoid substituting one hazardous substance with another hazardous one in the same group or class; 125,126 (c) fostering cooperation among regulators from di ff erent fi elds 96,127 and regions 128,129 to ensure consistent measures and avoid shifting pollution to countries with less stringent regulations; and (d) complementing current regulation with market-based policy instruments to internalize externalities and incentivize true innovation and pioneers. 114 Examples of market-based policy instruments include tradable use permits or a Pigouvian tax, where the raised governmental revenue is used to fi nance cleanup or chemical-related public health costs and helps to create fi nancial incentives for avoiding the use of hazardous or unnecessary chemicals. 122,123 Overall, concerted e ff orts from industry, civil society organizations, the scienti fi c community, regulatory agencies, and other policymakers are urgently needed to ensure sustainable chemicals management in the future.

H I G H L I G H T S

De-inking is an undermined pretreatment step in packaging plastic recycling.

There are concerns over the toxicity and hazards of surfactants used in de-inking.

This study critically analyses the state of the art of packaging plastic de-inking.

Developed a chemical selection tool that minimises hazards in three categories.

Bio-based and green chemicals should be explored for packaging plastic deinking.

A B S T R A C T

Achieving circularity in the plastic economy predominantly depends on sourcing higher quality recyclates. Packaging plastic poses a significant challenge as it is often not prioritised for collection or recycling initiatives. The presence of additives, such as printing ink, impedes the quality of recyclates. Considering the volume of packaging plastics and the importance of branding (aesthetics and consumer information), ink removal is a critical pre-treatment step. However, the literature is limited, with only 14 studies exploring de-inking processes. Drawing parallels with the detergent laundering process, surfactants have been widely investigated in plastic deinking, with cationic surfactants proving the most effective with a de-inking efficiency of up to 100%. However, concerns exist regarding the toxic and hazardous nature of the surfactants and chemicals. The average hazard quotient (AHQ) was developed, which compares de-inking chemicals as one of the key findings. 1. Introduction

Since the early 1900s, the annual plastic production has grown 230fold to reach 460 million tonnes in 2019 [1]. Two-thirds of the plastic waste generated in 2060 will be from ephemeral applications such as packaging, consumer products and textiles [2]. Packaging plastic accounts for 44% of polymer consumption [3] and 46% of plastic waste generation [4]. By 2060, the sector is projected to double in size, more specifically, the use of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyethylene (PE) [1]. The growth is primarily from the versatile use of PE as short-lived packaging plastic in flexible packaging applications [5]. Even with a high recycling potential, an effective recycling strategy for flexible packaging waste is lacking. This can be attributed to material properties and additives, lack of technology readiness, and inadequate material recovery strategies [6,7]. Due to this, 95% of the packaging material, valued between USD 80 -120 billion, is lost from the economy annually, and the resultant additional recoupment cost to society per annum is USD 40 billion [8].

Packaging plastics are often printed with inks as part of branding or to convey necessary consumer information. On average, 2 -4% of the total weight of packaging plastic is printed ink [9]. While these inks are essential, they are also the source of significant contamination in plastic recycling [10,11]. Printing inks are mainly composed of pigments that impart colour, binders that provide adhesion, carriers (also referred to as solvents) that hold the suspension and additives for additional characteristics (Table 1).

Based on the carrier, inks are classified as water-based, solvent-based or UV-based (Table 1) [12]. The carriers evaporate during ink drying processes (i.e. manufacturing stage) and are insignificant during recycling [13]. However different binders are used, based on the carrier type, which is problematic in packaging plastic recycling. Solvent-based inks are compatible with most surfaces on which to print. In contrast, water-based inks have limited application as water evaporates slower than solvent, making the drying process energy-intensive. These inks are preferably used in papers and boards, which promote absorption capabilities. Finally, UV-based inks use reactive resins such as acrylates that can be activated by UV irradiation [14,15].

Printing inks leads to several issues when recycling packaging plastic waste [9], and mixing plastics with different colour pigments during recycling results in black, brown or grey recyclates [16]. These are often suitable only for downcycled applications and have lower market value [17,18]. The presence of inks was also found to lower the tensile properties of recyclates [13]. Further, nitrocellulose (NC), one of the most widely used binders in flexible packaging plastic (Table 1), is vulnerable to thermal degradation between 160 -185 °C. While other ink binders do not follow similar gassing patterns, they are also susceptible to decomposition at extrusion temperatures [9,19]. This shows the importance and benefits of de-inking packaging plastic waste before conventional recycling.

Realising a circular plastics economy will significantly depend on advancements in the recycling infrastructure, especially closed-loop recycling strategies. In such cases, removing additives and contaminants becomes imperative to producing higher-quality recyclates [20]. De-inking is a critical yet undermined pre-treatment step in recycling printed plastic waste. In the past decade, a renewed focus has been on de-inking research. Studies have explored the potential of various de-inking media, specifically surfactants. The effect of surfactant concentration, pH, temperature, ink pigment composition, and other parameters in de-inking have also been experimented with. However, there is a lack of streamlined information on how the research area has developed over time and the status quo of plastic de-inking. Thus, a systematic literature survey will be conducted to collate and critically analyse the packing plastic de-inking literature. In addition, the surfactants and chemicals employed in previous de-inking studies have not been assessed for their toxic and hazardous nature. Thus, as another niche aspect, a chemical selection tool based on the average hazard quotient (AHQ) will be formulated, and it will offer new avenues for sustainable de-inking surfactant and chemical development in the future.

2. Background info on plastic waste recycling

Plastic waste can be managed through closed-loop or open-loop recycling (Fig. 1). In closed-loop recycling, plastic waste is recycled back into plastic products in the same product category, though openloop recycling produces a recyclate employed in different applications.

2.1. Mechanical recycling

Mechanical recycling (cascade recycling) is the most prevalent method employed at a large scale. This is further classified into primary and secondary recycling based on the source of waste [21]. Mechanical recycling is affected by the quality of the waste stream, as different types of plastic respond differently to treatment based on their physio-thermo-chemical properties [22,23].

Primary recycling sources plastic waste from post-industrial applications, which are of higher quality. The collected waste is often recycled back into production after shredding and blending with virgin plastic. Secondary recycling handles the post-consumer plastic waste mixed with different plastic types (i.e. lower quality feed) [24]. The key steps involve washing, shredding, melting and remoulding. In secondary recycling, the quality of the recyclates is inferior, resulting in downgraded applications. Other interferences, such as organic contaminants, labels, inks, fillers, and additives, significantly deteriorate the material and optical properties of the recycled product [25,26]. Thus, secondary recycling is not favourable for a circular plastic economy in the long run.

2.2. Waste-to-energy recycling

In this open-loop recycling process, the heat from incinerating plastic waste generates superheated steam for electricity production [27]. The lower heating values (LHVs) of PE (42.8 MJ kg 1 ) and polypropylene (PP) (46.5 MJ kg 1 ) are closely comparable to that of petroleum (42.3 MJ kg 1 ) and kerosene (46.5 MJ kg 1 ) [28]. However, post-consumer plastic waste (mixed, low-quality) is 40% less efficient, which can be improved upon segregation. It has been shown that the best fuel efficiency is obtained from the purest waste streams [27]. A comparative study by the Waste & Resources Action Programme (WRAP) showed that recycling was better than incineration, considering greenhouse gas emissions and energy balances [29]. In contrast, incineration performed better when a significant volume of recycled plastics could not be incorporated back into virgin plastic production or when there was a high washing requirement [29]. Even if waste-to-energy is prioritised higher than landfilling in the waste hierarchy, its preference is debated. This is because waste-to-energy provides an incentive to avoid other recycling strategies where the materials could be retained in use for longer life. Hence, it contradicts the principles of the circular economy.

2.3. Chemical recycling

The chemical recycling method comprises various strategies to convert plastic waste into reusable monomers or to produce fuels and feedstock for subsequent processes [21]. 'Chemical recycling ' and 'feedstock recycling ' are often used interchangeably. In reality, chemical recycling can be considered an umbrella term including both open-loop thermolysis and closed-loop solvolysis. Thermolysis, also known as 'feedstock recycling ' , produces chemicals for other purposes, including fuels, syngas or naphtha. Whereas solvolysis produces monomers that can be used in polymer production [30]. Chemical recycling is limited by economic viability, feedstock availability and feedstock quality. Often, it is hard for the recycling process (including pre-treatment and purification steps) to compete with the costs of virgin material production. Heterogenous plastic waste from post-consumer sources, contaminated with additives, colourants, impurities, moisture and dirt, severely impacts the feedstock quality. Nevertheless, extensive research is focused on chemical recycling due to the potential to recover high-quality recyclates and remove contaminants, such as halogenated flame retardants [27]. It was also found that supplementing mechanical and chemical recycling can improve the overall recycling rates [27]. Holistically, advancements in chemical recycling are needed to maximise material utilisation and further circularity in the plastic economy.

3. Methodology

To comprehensively understand the field, literature on packaging plastic de-inking was collected following the steps detailed in Sections 3.1 -3.3. A bibliometric study is conducted to analyse the evolution of the research field. This is followed by the methodology for the chemical selection tool of de-inking surfactants and chemicals in terms of the AHQ (Section 3.4).

3.1. Search strategy

The relevant publications in the field are gathered from the three major scientific databases -Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Google Scholar. The following search strings were used in each case:

Scopus: TITLE-ABS-KEY (de-inking OR deinking OR "ink removal") AND TITLE-ABS-KEY (plastic OR "plastic waste" OR "packaging waste"). WoSCC: (TS = (de-inking) OR TS = (deinking) OR TS = ("ink removal")) AND (TS = (plastic) OR TS = ("plastic waste") OR TS = ("packaging waste")).

Google Scholar: (de-inking of plastic waste).

Boolean operators (OR, AND) were used in the search string to include common usages and emphasise the relation between the key topics, such as de-inking and plastic waste. All results available until 3 rd September 2023 were collected.

3.4. Development of AHQ model

The surfactants currently used in de-inking are toxic and hazardous. However, there may be instances where such surfactants are unavoidable. The previous de-inking studies did not quantify the surfactants ' physical, environmental and health hazards. Furthermore, no specific toxicity tests were performed using standards, such as the Globally Harmonised System (GHS) and the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 (EC No 1907/2006) [33].

Traditionally, the methods of hazard classification follow a qualitative or semi-quantitative approach, which provides the necessary information but can be complex to interpret and compare chemicals directly. This presented the need for a mathematical model to categorise and rank the chemicals employed in de-inking based on their potential hazards. As such, the AHQ was introduced to simplify comparisons and decision-making on surfactant and chemical selection.

The GHS hazard classification provides baseline data to model the AHQ in this work. As of June 2023, twenty-one countries have fully adopted the GHS classifications, including Australia and Malaysia [34]. Several countries have adopted part of it as required, as well. The GHS classifications are presented as part of material safety data sheets (MSDS) or safety data sheets (SDS) for chemicals. They offer a standardised approach to presenting hazard classification and necessary precautions. However, GHS only provides qualitative data on hazards by broadly classifying them into three classes: physical, health, and environmental. There are 16 physical hazards, 10 health hazards and 2 environmental hazard classes. Based on the severity, each hazard is categorised from 1 to N (where N = 2, 3, 4, etc.) or A to G. In each case, 1 or A presents a more severe hazard, and severity reduces as the value increases. Furthermore, every SDS has a signal word, such as ' danger ' , ' warning ' , or ' nothing ' . It was observed that the signal word ' danger ' was used whenever a category 1 or 2 hazard was present in any of the classes.

This work employed the given classifications and qualitative descriptions to model the AHQ (Eq. 1). A sample AHQ calculation using SDS data for cyclohexane is shown in Appendix B.

AHQ = ∑ α r α [ 1 N α × ∑ n i = 1 1 H f i ] (1)

where α is the hazard class (physical, health or environment), N is the number of hazards in each class as shown in the SDS, H is the category of hazard (1, 2, 3, A, B etc.), f is the significance factor for categories (if H is 1 or 2, then f = 1; if H ≥ 3, then f = 2), and r is the significance factor for hazard classes (by default, r = 1 to assume equal priority for all hazard classes unless specified otherwise, and rphysical + rhealth + renvironmental = 3) .

4. Packaging plastic de-inking

4.1. De-inking methodology

Based on the literature, a generalised de-inking procedure can be summarised as follows:

Sample preparation: Commercial PE films [32,35], uni-coloured PE films [36], PP films [11], rigid high-density polyethylene (HDPE) [37,38], low-density polyethylene (LDPE) films [13], and multilayer plastic films [39] were used in previous studies. The samples are not typically derived from post-consumer plastic waste, except in Guo et al. [12] and Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39], who used post-consumer and post-industrial waste, respectively. The printed packaging plastic is cut into small pieces as feasible for the test runs. In addition, some pre-treatment operations, such as pre-soaking and abrasion, were also employed.

Surfactant preparation: The required amount of surfactant is determined based on the surfactant-specific CMC and the test condition (above, below or at CMC). The surfactant solution is freshly prepared by mixing the required surfactant with either de-ionised or distilled water. The pH level of the surfactant solution is immediately adjusted using either sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid solutions.

Experiment: The cut plastic pieces are soaked in water for the specified duration to analyse the effects of pre-soaking. The samples are then transferred to the surfactant solution in a beaker in a temperature-controlled water bath or magnetic stirrer. The experiment is allowed to run for four hours on average. Once the experiment is completed the samples are thoroughly washed and air-dried. Some researchers have employed control experiments in de-inking, for example, using water [13,32]. However, those did not result in any significant de-inking.

Image analysis and de-inking efficiency: Using CIELAB, flake sorting or scanning and pixel reading methods detailed in Appendix C, the samples are analysed before and after the experiment. The respective equations are then utilised to calculate the de-inking efficiency in each case.

4.2. De-inking mechanisms

Chotipong et al. [40] proposed the mechanisms behind de-inking after a series of tests on CMC, wettability, zeta potential, solubilisation and de-inking performance. The proposed mechanisms are explained below and shown in Fig. 5.

Step 1: Surfactant adsorption or wetting on the printed and unprinted plastic surfaces. This process lowers the surface tensions between the ink-water and plastic-water interfaces. The cationic surfactant is composed of a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail groups. At the point of zero charge (PZC), it is expected that a stoichiometric pairing occurs between the positively charged surfactant head and negatively charged ink components. Due to the heterogeneity in composition, the ink surface may not be uniformly negatively charged. This results in a tail-in arrangement of the surfactant molecule across the plastic surface

Fig. 5. Proposed four-step mechanism for surfactant-based de-inking. Adapted from Guo et al. [13].

(which is hydrophobic) and the positively charged areas on the ink surface. This tail-in arrangement is made possible by Van der Waal ' s force of interactions and results in a monolayer (hemimicelle) of surfactant molecules. A head-in tail-out arrangement of surfactant molecules is observed for the negatively charged areas on the ink surface. Progressively, this will result in a bilayer (admicelle) formation, with a second layer of surfactant molecules getting attached in a tail-in headout arrangement over the previous layer. Complete wetting is achieved when the contact angle becomes 0 ° . However, it is difficult to differentiate between hemimicelle and admicelle formations, resulting in reduced contact angle and increased zeta-potential.

Step 2: Solubilisation of binder in micelles. This is hypothesised to be due to three factors: (i) the hydrophobic components of the ink being incorporated into the micelle core, (ii) electrostatic binding of the negatively charged carboxylate groups on the binder and the positively charged surfactant head groups on the micellar surface, (iii) the iondipole interactions between π -electrons of aromatic rings and hydrophilic surfactant head groups. Step (ii) is the most dominant de-inking mechanism, especially in cases where the surfactant concentration is above its CMC [13], and it happens simultaneously with Steps (i) and (iii).

Step 3: Detachment of ink from the plastic surface. This is hypothesised due to the electrostatic repulsion between the surfactant head groups. As the edge of the ink surface detaches, more surfactant molecules can be adsorbed to the newly uncovered areas on both the ink and plastic surfaces. It increases the electrostatic repulsion, resulting in further ink detaching.

Step 4: Stabilisation and dispersion of the detached ink particles. As more surfactant molecules are adsorbed to the detached ink particles and plastic surface, electrostatic stabilisation is achieved. Further, the electrostatic repulsion between the surfactant head groups on the plastic surface and detached ink prevents the redeposition of ink.

It can be noted that plastic de-inking is a surface reaction, which means the contact between ink on the plastic surface and the surfactant is vital to facilitate de-inking. This has been validated by Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39], who used a multi-layered printed plastic film and observed no significant de-inking compared to single-layer LDPE/HDPE films employed by several authors, including Gecol et al. [32], Songsiri et al. [38] and Chotipong et al. [40]. Despite varying surfactant concentrations, reaction temperatures and pH were tested, including using a pressurised system, de-inking efficiency was poor with multi-layered printed plastic films.

Fig. 6. (a) De-inking via solubilisation in NC binder, (b) De-inking via peeling in PVB binder, and (c) De-inking via peeling in UV-crosslinked binder [13].

Guo et al. [13] noted the presence of two different de-inking behaviours on single-layer printing ink systems, including solubilisation and peeling (Fig. 6). In solubilisation, the detached ink is observed to be dispersed in the bath, resulting in a cloudy solution with homogenous pigment colour. This was observed for NC and polyurethane (PU) binder systems (Fig. 6a). Meanwhile, for polyvinyl butyral (PVB) (Fig. 6b) and UV acrylic binder systems (Fig. 6c), the detached ink was found to have ' peeled off ' in tiny flakes and sediment in the water phase.

Binder systems can be classified into two based on the bonding mechanisms -(i) resulting in only Van der Waal ' s forces and hydrogen bonds due to polar groups in binders and the activated plastic surface from corona treatment, (ii) resulting in covalent bonds in addition to Van der Waal ' s forces and hydrogen bonds due to the presence of a reactive cross-linked system [13]. The latter enhances the bonding between the binder and the plastic surface, making it harder for ink removal. In such cases, a surfactant alone cannot cleave covalent bonds. In contrast, the surfactant hinders de-inking as it forms a protective layer over the ink surface when the hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) value is too low. Furthermore, alkaline hydrolysis can be an effective de-inking mechanism, as shown in Figure D.1 in Appendix D.

Based on the above discussion, a modified de-inking mechanism was proposed by Guo et al. [13], including (i) surfactant adsorption, (ii) breaking of hydrogen bonds via solubilisation and covalent bonds via chemical reaction, (iii) detachment of ink from the plastic surface through micelle solubilisation (for non-cross-linked binders) and mechanical peel off (for cross-linked binders), and (iv) stabilisation and dispersion of pigment particles.

5. Analysis of de-inking surfactants for packaging plastics

5.1. Cationic surfactants

Cationic surfactants are characterised by nitrogen-containing functional groups, such as amines, quaternary ammonium, imidazolium and pyridinium [41]. As the amine-based surfactants can only be protonated (activated) at acidic pH, their applications are limited to this pH range. Whereas quaternary ammonium-based surfactants ('quats ' ) are not pH sensitive [42]. Cationic surfactants find major applications where surface adsorption is required (Fig. 7a), as most surfaces (including plastics) at neutral pH have a negative charge [43]. Thus, cationic surfactants are most explored for packaging plastic de-inking, even though they are the third by size in surfactant application. The various cationic surfactants employed in plastic de-inking are summarised in Table 2.

Cationic surfactants were effective in plastic de-inking above its CMC over a broad range of pH values. As cationic surfactants showed the most de-inking potential in early studies, the effect of various process parameters was explored in detail over time. Pre-soaking and mixing the samples via mechanical agitation improved de-inking efficiencies [38]. However, the design conditions are to be determined based on economic optimisations. More than 90% de-inking can be obtained with 5 h of pre-soaking and 2 h of mixing with hexadecyl trimethylammonium bromide at CMC. Conversely, if the pre-soaking time is reduced to 2 h, the mixing time increases to 4 h to obtain the same de-inking efficiency.

Fig. 7. Schematic diagrams depicting the surface adsorption of surfactants: a) cationic, b) cationic with calcium ions, c) anionic and d) anionic with calcium ions, on ink surface. Adapted from Gecol et al. [44].

Increasing the lengths of alkyl chains was found to favour de-inking, as longer hydrophobes improved the adsorption rates [44]. The longer alkyl chains produced stronger Van der Waal ' s forces between the surfactant and ink particles [37]. Significantly high to complete de-inking can be achieved at highly alkaline pH. This is hypothesised due to the opening of epoxide rings (carrying negative charges) within the epoxy resins in inks, providing additional adsorption sites for the positively charged cationic head groups [37]. On the other hand, calcium ion addition was found to impede de-inking performance due to competitive adsorption (Fig. 7b).

5.2. Anionic surfactants

Anionics are the largest surfactant class used worldwide, accounting for roughly 70% of overall consumption [46]. This popularity is attributed to the ease and low cost of manufacturing. They are characterised by carboxylate, sulfonate, sulfate or phosphate functional groups [47] and are widely employed in detergent formulations and paper de-inking processes [48]. Anionics possess the highest cleansing power and good wetting properties. Table 3 summarises the anionic surfactants used in packaging plastic de-inking.

A few early studies in plastic de-inking explored the potential of using anionic surfactants. Observations show that they are barely better than de-inking using water at respective pH. A possible explanation is the electrostatic repulsion between the negatively charged ink particles and the hydrophilic head of the surfactant, hindering adsorption (Fig. 7c). This is probably why recent studies have opted out of exploring anionic surfactants. However, adding calcium ions improved the deinking capacity by providing additional sites for co-adsorption (Fig. 7d) [44]. Nevertheless, it was only found to be practical above the CMC of the surfactant in alkaline conditions.

5.3. Non-ionic surfactants

Non-ionics are the second largest class of surfactants used worldwide [41]. They are preferred due to the ease of production, readily available and inexpensive feedstock, and wide-ranging applications. This category is characterised by either polyether or polyhydroxyl functional groups [42]. A list of non-ionic surfactants used in packaging plastic de-inking is given in Table 4.

Early studies on non-ionic surfactants were conducted as they were less expensive and more biodegradable than amphoteric and cationic surfactants [49]. Generally, non-ionic surfactants are effective in plastic de-inking above its CMC in alkaline conditions. The exception is ethoxylated amines, which is a non-ionic. Despite that, it behaves like cationic in acidic conditions with low ethylene oxide levels [50]. Consequently, ethoxylated amines exhibit similar de-inking behaviour to cationic surfactants at acidic, neutral and basic pH, which is favourable. However, Guo et al. [12] observed no notable influence from pH values on de-inking efficiencies for non-ionic surfactants.

text:
Over the years, only one amphoteric surfactant, dimethyl dodecylamine oxide, has been explored for plastic de-inking. Based on Gecol et al. [32], the amphoteric surfactant shows comparable de-inking capacities to cationic surfactant at pH 5, 7, 11 and 12 above its CMC. Whereas, below its CMC, a more consistent trend is observed with the anionic surfactant. Both the 'amphoteric ' nature and the CMC of the surfactant depend on pH, and the effects of varying CMC on de-inking at various pH levels have not yet been explored.

6. Packaging plastic de-inking: the status quo

Packaging plastic de-inking studies are summarised in detail in Appendix D, and the effects of various parameters on de-inking efficiency are illustrated in Table 6.

Gecol et al. [32], the earliest work on packaging plastic de-inking, explored the potential of various surfactants (amphoteric, anionic, cationic, and non-ionic) in removing water-based inks from commercial plastic films. A control test was also designed using water to de-ink plastic films by varying the pH at room temperature. Results showed no significant de-inking until pH 10. At pH values 11 and 12, partial de-inking of 30% and 60% was observed. Several characterisation tests were conducted to understand the effect of inks on re-extruded plastic and how it impacts recycling. It was observed that there were significant colour changes, including the clear films turning beige and the printed films turning reddish brown. The decomposition of inks during re-extrusion released gases that caused crack points and holes across the cross-section. Ink aggregates were found to act as stress concentration points, reducing the strength of the material (e.g. modulus, ultimate strength and elongation at break are reduced). It was concluded that cationic surfactants are the most effective choice functional across various CMC and pH levels. Conversely, anionic surfactants were the least effective.

Following this, extended studies were conducted to understand various facets of de-inking. Exploring potential non-ionic surfactants, it was seen that nonylphenol polyethoxylate and ethoxylated alcohols exhibited good de-inking capacity at pH 10. In contrast, ethoxylated amines (which are amphoteric and classified as non-ionic but behave as cationic in acidic media) showed de-inking capacity at acidic, neutral, and basic pH [49]. Cationic surfactants, such as n-hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide, exhibited de-inking capacity only above its CMC (complete de-inking at 5 times CMC) and high pH levels above 11.75.

In recent years, more systematic and non-conventional approaches to packaging plastic de-inking have been observed. Guo et al. [12], explored the possibility of using a new type of non-ionic surfactant oxirane, methyl-, polymer (commercial name: TEGO Surten W111) to de-ink LDPE film samples from post-consumer waste. In addition to the conventional CIELAB method for de-inking performance evaluation (Appendix C), a flake sorting method (Appendix C) is also considered to account for the heterogeneity of post-consumer plastic waste.

Guo et al. [13] explored the effects of various binders, pigments, over-print varnishes (OPV), cross-linkages in binders or OPVs and the materials ' layering. Five detergents and four test conditions were included to analyse various possible scenarios. NC binder-based inks exhibited high de-inkability, and crosslinked binder systems can impede de-inking. Based on the above, it was concluded that breaking the Van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, and covalent bonds between inks and the plastic surface are critical steps in de-inking.

Ügdüler et al. [11] conducted an interesting study to understand the effect of seven different de-inking media in liquefying and solubilising 14 chemically different polymer resins in printing inks. The basic cost assessment also determined that the price of the de-inking agent and its required volume played a crucial role in the economic feasibility of the de-inking process.

text: Only four studies attempted sustainably sourced solvents in plastic de-inking by utilising biomass-derived or valorised waste materials in surfactant production. El-Sherbiny et al. [45] developed novel cationic surfactants from recycled PET waste (GT-pyr-Br and GD-pyr-Br -Table 6), which were achieved by depolymerising PET followed by esterification and quaternization. Gd-pyr-Br resulted in a maximum de-inking efficiency of 96% at CMC. Ferreira et al. [51] performed solvent extraction using the dissolution-precipitation technique to remove blue and orange pigments from HDPE using a range of bio-solvents. 94% and 100% de-inking were observed for blue and orange pigments, respectively. In this method, a solvent is initially used to solubilise HDPE and then an anti-solvent is used to selectively precipitate the polymer. Both the solvent and anti-solvents could be recovered and reused, ensuring economic and environmental sustainability. Ye et al. [35] explored the potential of quarternary ammonium-modified waste cooking oil (soybean oil) in de-inking. This was prepared by ring-open esterification and quaternary amination reactions. De-inking efficiency of around 70% was observed through this method. Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39] reported a solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) strategy to de-ink a multilayer plastic film from post-industrial sources. It was seen that biomass-derived gamma-valerolactone (GVL) was able to de-ink all the studied colours. The techno-economic analysis also showed that the STRAP process could be economically viable for a processing capacity of 6000 tonnes per year. This shows the efficacy of bio-based and waste-based surfactants, and the de-inking efficiencies are comparable to those of synthetic ones.

Considering the potential industrial applications of packaging plastic de-inking, a few commercially available and patented technologies are listed in Table 7 for a comprehensive overview.

7. Impacts of conventional de-inking surfactants

Drawing parallels with the detergent laundry processes, surfactants are predominantly used in packaging plastic de-inking. However, the use of surfactants poses several ecotoxicological and health hazards (Fig. 8). Anionic surfactants, such as linear alkylbenzene sulfonates (LAS), cause pathological, biochemical, and physiological impacts on terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. It also interferes with marine biota ' s environmental stress, reproduction, and growth. Surfactants facilitate eutrophication by increasing the solubility of contaminants in water bodies (Fig. 8). Their toxicity increased proportionally with increasing hydrophobic properties [58].

Even wastewater treatment plants cannot properly manage the surfactants, which are incompletely degraded and discharged into water bodies. Surfactant concentrations above 0.1 mg/L in water bodies cause huge, persistent foams that prevent oxygen adsorption [59]. It also impacts the hydrological cycle by impeding evaporation. When the surfactant concentration increases beyond the CMC, higher concentrations of soluble and insoluble pollutants in the water are observed [59].

Surfactants also interfere with soil properties, primarily by reducing the capillary pressure at the air-water interface [60]. This causes an altered air and water distribution in the soil ' s pore system and reduces water retention and infiltration (Fig. 8). Irrigating soil with surfactant-rich water increased the soil salinity, electrical conductivity, sorptivity and pH, while hydraulic conductivity was reduced [61]. It was also studied that surfactants retarded microbial growth and increased microbial mutation and mortality [62].

Fig. 8. Potential environmental and human health hazards from surfactant use.

In humans, when ingested, surfactants react with proteins in the liver and serum, causing long-term metabolic effects and disrupting the endocrine system [63]. It was reported to cause skin burning, eye irritation and respiratory problems. Nonylphenol ethoxylates were studied to have estrogenic effects in mammals, Pisces, and amphibians [64] (Fig. 8). Surfactants, such as LAS, can change the cell membrane structure and impair the transpiration and translocation of water and essential nutrients [58]. Sodium dodecyl sulfate inhibits ATPase activity, damages membrane structures and initiates oxidative stress [65].

In an attempt to reduce the impacts of plastic waste, it is vital not to unintentionally cause secondary impacts through the use of hazardous and toxic chemicals and surfactants. Thus, the surfactant selection in packaging plastic de-inking applications is paramount.

8. Modelled AHQ values for chemical selection

Calculated AHQ values based on the GHS can be used for one-to-one comparison of chemical hazards (Table 8). Based on the current dataset, cyclohexane would be the most hazardous chemical (check the note in Appendix B). Cationic surfactants (e.g. hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide, cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide, hexadecylpyridinium chloride) have been extensively studied for de-inking, though possess the maximum environmental AHQ. Hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide, explored in 9 studies, has a concerning total AHQ of 1.43 out of the maximum possible 3. In this way, informed decisions can be made when selecting appropriate solvents for de-inking purposes.

All chemicals with a total AHQ less than 0.5 in this work match with the signal words ' warning ' or ' nothing ' in the SDS. The only exception is polydisperse nonylphenol polyethoxylate with the signal word ' warning ' , though the calculated AHQ is 1.0. In short, the consistent method employed in work to ascertain AHQ values is satisfactory, though improvements can be made based on the significance level of hazard classes (Eq. 1 and check the note in Appendix B).

Appropriate chemical selection tools, such as AHQ, should be utilised to minimise potential hazards and toxicities from plastic waste recycling. While AHQ is a preliminary chemical assessment tool, local sociotechno-economic factors, such as low chemical cost, desirable chemical action, low carbon footprint and local availability, should also be considered to improve the quantitative assessment of chemical and surfactant selection.

9. Future directions

Material characterisation tests should be conducted to address the conflict of opinion on whether de-inking improves recyclate quality.

Only Guo et al. [13] explored the impacts of ink pigments, binders, OPVs and cross-linking in de-inking. Future studies can characterise the most common ink types, categorise them based on application (food contact materials and others) and identify whether a specific de-inking solution is required for each application.

Carbon black was identified as one of the most challenging inks to remove [13,36]. Previously, Gecol et al. [36] demonstrated that a mixture of cationic and non-ionic surfactants can effectively de-ink carbon black. However, this was not studied further. Future studies can explore the performance of this mixture for other ink-substrate combinations and whether it can be utilised for post-consumer plastic waste.

Bioaccumulation of de-inking chemicals and their related health and environmental impacts should be thoroughly studied through pilot plants and industrial applications.

The majority of the studies have focussed on uni-coloured plastic films. In real life, printed materials utilise several colours. Thus, treatments to achieve the desired quality and output with multi coloured printed materials are required.

Mixed and contaminated plastic streams from post-consumer applications are available. Hence, the applicability of the identified surfactants in de-inking this complex post-consumer plastic waste should be thoroughly explored.

The recycling industry should investigate the feasibility of integrating conventional mechanical and chemical recycling methods and supplementing them with the studied de-inking processes.

Techno-economic and life cycle assessment (LCA) studies should also be conducted to understand the feasibility and impacts of commercialising de-inking processes in the recycling industry.

10. Conclusions

With 175 nations agreeing to develop a legally binding Global Plastics Treaty by 2024, all the aspects of plastic recycling should be thoroughly explored. Obtaining the highest quality of recyclates will be paramount in moving towards a circular plastics economy. While advancements have been made across various fronts in plastic recycling, de-inking was found to be an undermined pre-treatment step. This study provided a critical understanding of plastic de-inking ' s state of the art. While surfactants are conventionally utilised in de-inking owing to similarities with laundering processes, a general caution needs to be exercised regarding potential hazards and toxicities. The proposed AHQ model could be an effective chemical rating and selection tool. Advancements in plastic de-inking will contribute towards the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, such as Industry, innovation, and infrastructure (Goal 9), Responsible consumption and production (Goal 12), and Climate Action (Goal 13).

C. Methods used in de-inking performance evaluation

C.1. CIELAB method (by the International Commission on Illumination)

Eight of the fourteen studies in de-inking literature have employed a standardised evaluation, the CIELAB method. It was first devised by the International Commission on Illumination in 1976 based on the tristimulus values of a colour. It quantifies the red, green, and blue light required to produce that colour [66]. A spectrophotometer or a colorimeter is used to evaluate the CIELAB values (L*, a*, b*) (Figure C.1).

Figure C.1. Schematic of the three-dimensional CIELAB colour model (adapted and redrawn from [67]).

Once the averaged values for L* , a* and b* are obtained, the de-inking efficiency can be calculated as follows:

DE * = ̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅ Δ L 2 sample blank + Δ a 2 sample blank + Δ b 2 sample blank 2 √ DE * blank (C.1)

where, DE* - De-inking efficiency. DE * blank - De-inking efficiency for reference material. Δ L , Δ a , Δ b -Differences in CIELAB values between the sample and reference materials.

C.2. Flake sorting method

To account for the heterogeneity of post-consumer plastic waste, Guo et al. [12] implemented a modified approach to analysing the de-inking efficiency. The de-inked samples were manually sorted into -fully transparent, partially transparent, and opaque (non-de-inked). The weight of each of these sample groups is measured, and the de-inking efficiency is then calculated as follows:

.

DE * = ( mct + mpt × 0 . 5 ) msample (C.2)

where, DE* - De-inking efficiency. mct -The mass of fully transparent flakes (in grams). mpt -The mass of partially transparent flakes (in grams). msample -The mass of the entire selected sample (in grams).

Guo et al. [12] showed significant variations between the CIELAB and the flake sorting methods. It was determined that the CIELAB method displayed a high standard deviation (11% to 76%) and was suggested not to be the optimal choice for evaluating post-consumer plastic waste. However, CIELAB is still the most suitable method for a homogenous sample.

C.3. Scanning and pixel reading

Another approach observed in the literature is scanning the plastic specimen directly or sticking it to a white paper using transparent glue [40,37, 38]. The scanned copies were then analysed using software, such as Adobe Photoshop, to count the number of pixels (in proportion to the amount of ink) on the plastic surface. The de-inking efficiency is then calculated as follows:

DE * = ( Pixelsbefore de inking Pixelsafter de inking ) Pixelsbefore de inking × 100 (C.3)

Meanwhile, Guo et al. [13] developed a Python code to read the pixels from the scanned files and generate the L* , a* , and b* values as per the CIELAB standards. The output from running the Python can then be used in Equation C.3 to calculate the deinking efficiency. Another Python code was developed by Ügdüler et al. [11] using the Open-Source Computer Vision (OpenCV) Library. The scanned images were first grey-scaled and processed to obtain arrays with values ranging between 0 (black) to 255 (white). This represented the shades of grey and corresponded to the amount of ink remaining on the plastic film. The de-inking efficiency can then be calculated as follows:

DE * = ( dsample d min ) ( d max d min ) × 100 (C.4)

Where, dsample -the average grey value of the sample. d max -the average grey value of the fully printed plastic film. d min -the average grey value of the transparent plastic film.

Room-Temperature Material Recycling/Upcycling of Polyamide Waste Enabled by Cosolvent-Tunable Dissolution Kinetics

Jonathon Tanks* and Kenji Tamura*

Abstract: Polyamides (PAs, nylons) are a ubiquitous class of high-performance plastics used extensively in a wide range of applications. Their high resistance to many common solvents and tendency to hydrolyze in strong acids or bases creates a major hurdle to low-emissions material recycling (i.e., resource separation and recovery). In the present study, the first detailed investigation into the molecular mechanisms of polyamide dissolution, we show that introducing a weakly hydrogen-bonding cosolvent into formic acid can effectively tune the solvent-solvent and solvent-polymer interactions, drastically accelerates the room-temperature dissolution kinetics of common (short-chain) polyamides such as PA6 and PA66, as well as long-chain and semi-aromatic varieties. The recovered polymers show no change in their chemical structures or properties, and sufficient selectivity allows for fillers such as short and long fibers, inorganic nanoparticles, metals, and other mixed polymer phases to be recovered at high efficiency ( > 95%) along with recirculation of all solvents ( > 98%). This cosolvent-enabled approach has the potential to make polyamide recycling more sustainable and economical by reducing the energy input and CO2 emissions required to separate and recover the various constituent materials from automotive and electrical components, textiles, and beyond.

Introduction

Polyamides (PAs, or nylon) exhibit excellent heat resistance and mechanical properties, making them a key material in numerous industries ranging from automotive, electrical/electronics, textiles, and fishing/leisure and represent a market size of 8 Mt yr -1 valued at 40 bil $ yr -1 (Figure 1a). [1,2] The synthesis of conventional polyamides such as PA6 and PA66 uses non-renewable feedstocks and carries a large carbon footprint (6-9 kg CO2-eq kg -1 ) energy demand (3560 MJ kg -1 ). [3,4] Recycling technology for PAs has received far less attention than other plastics, e.g., PET, despite their high cost and widespread use. As a result, polyamides often end up in landfills and even the ocean. [1,3,5]

PAs are commonly used in blends and composites containing secondary materials (SM) such as fibers/microparticles,

Results and Discussion

Polyamide Dissolution in a Cosolvent System

It is well known that short-chain PAs dissolve in FA at room temperature (RT), but it can take up to 12 h for complete dissolution. As shown in Figure 2a, PA6 formed a slightly cloudy solution after 4 hr in pure FA (RT, no agitation), whereas PA66 became completely clear (Figure S2). After screening various solvents (see Supporting Information), a measurable positive effect on the dissolution rate of PA6 was only observed for chlorinated hydrocarbons like dichloromethane (DCM), chloroform (CHCl3), and dichloroethane (DCE); they have characteristic low polarity and the ability to form weak H-bonds and effectively solvate hydrocarbons. [36] Ethyl acetate (EtOAc), MEK, and THF are similar to DCM in terms of, e.g. viscosity and HSPs, but they had the opposite effect of decreasing overall solubility. H-bond titration of PA6 solutions revealed that FA is more sensitive than PA to the cosolvent and that solubility shows strong negative correlation with the cosolvent's donor number (DN) (Figure S3). This means it must act as a weak H-bond donor (HBD)

and poor H-bond acceptor (HBA) to promote polyamide dissolution. This characteristic has been demonstrated for fluorinated polar solvents such as HFIP, [37] suggesting that chlorinated hydrocarbons combined with formic acid can serve the same role.

DCM was selected as the primary cosolvent for our study due to its compatibility with FA, relatively low cost, and low boiling point. PAs do not dissolve in pure DCM at RT (Figure 2a), contrary to predictions by HSP theory and implicit solvation models which do not account for explicit H-bonding (Figure S1). PA6 dissolution in FA/DCM mixtures is accelerated by varying degrees depending on the cosolvent ratio, reaching a maximum at 1:1 w/w (i.e., DCM fraction of f DCM = 0.5) and reversing to a slower rate at f DCM = 0.7 (Figure 2b). When f DCM > 0.7, only swelling with limited dissolution is observed. Viscosity measurements of PA6 solutions at different solids concentrations and cosolvent ratios, shown in Figure 2c normalized to the molar ratio of FA to amide units, made it clear that higher f DCM correlates to lower solution viscosity with the lowest value obtained when f DCM = 0.7, which tells us that dissolution rate is not necessarily affected by viscosity of the bulk solvent or solution (Figure S2).

Considering the polyamide as a semi-crystalline solid, the dissolution of the crystalline fraction would be the ratelimiting step. Employing the Brunner-Nernst model [38,39] to analyze the mass transfer process at the polymer-solvent interface (Figure 2d; details in Supporting Information), we found that the mass transfer coefficient ( km ) for PA through a boundary layer ( Lb ) between bulk crystal and bulk solvent increases linearly with cosolvent fraction up to f DCM = 0.5 and then sharply decreases at f DCM = 0.7 (Figure 2e), and
