For their importance in industrial applications and also due to their relatively simple structure, we use polyethers as the subject of this study to demonstrate the importance of different aspects when performing COSMORS calculations for polymeric systems, including the inclusion of a combinatorial term, the description of the polymer volumetric data, the effect of conformations, and the scaling of molecular weight from the σ -profile of small oligomers. In this work, we investigate the use of MD simulations to obtain realistic conformers for COSMO-RS calculations and discuss the obtained activity coefficient results in light of the aforementioned topics.

2. METHODS

2.1. MD Simulation Details. Atomistic simulations were performed for polyether molecules (PEG400, PEG1000, and PPG400) in water, using the Gromacs 2020.6 13 software. The SPC/E model was used for water and the OPLS-AA 14 force field was used to model the polymer molecules. The equations of motion were calculated with the leapfrog algorithm, 15 using a time step of 2 fs. The forces were calculated exactly within a cutoff distance of 1.4 nm. Beyond the cutoff, the PME 16 algorithm was used to correct the electrostatic interactions and the missing pressure and energy components were added to the dispersive term. Bonds that contain H atoms were constrained using the LINCS 17 algorithm. Random initial cubic simulation boxes were generated with PACKMOL. 18 An energy minimization step was performed before an equilibration stage in the NPT ensemble, which was run at a temperature of 298.15 K for 2 ns. Following this step, production runs of 100 ns were carried out in the NpT ensemble, where the pressure (1 bar) and temperature (298.15 K) were kept constant with the Parrinello -Rahman 19 barostat and the Nose ́-Hoover 20,21 thermostat, using coupling constants of 10 and 0.5 ps, respectively. Visualization of the simulation trajectories was made with VMD 1.9.4. 22

2.2. COSMO-RS Calculations. COSMO-RS calculations were made with COSMOtherm version 21.0 software, 23 using the 'BP_TZVP_21.ctd' parametrization. The DFT quantum mechanics calculations to obtain the σ -profiles were made with Turbomole version 17 at the BP86/def-TZVP level of theory. The calculations were made with polymer geometries obtained from MD simulations. A fine mesh was used to more accurately sample the charge density inside cavities. Before the single-point calculation, a relaxation step using the BP86/ def-SV(P) method was necessary to avoid unrealistic highly polarized regions. The calculations for higher-molecular-weight polymers were made by scaling the σ -profile of the repeating units (excluding the end-groups). In addition to the residual term, the Elbro combinatorial term 24 was used to account for the asymmetry of molecular volumes to the entropy of mixing. The molar volumes used to calculate the Elbro combinatorial term were derived from experimental data and, in some cases, extrapolated to the desired temperatures when no data were available.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1. The Choice of Conformers. 3.1.1. MD Simulations. The adequate choice of conformers used for COSMO calculations is of importance, as they can have a visible impact on the quality of the inputs in the form of the σ -profiles. For polymeric systems, the conformations are inherently linked to the affinity toward the solution media and can deviate considerably from gas-phase optimized geometries; thus, the obtention of representative conformers of the polymer chains is of particular importance. Due to the size and flexibility of the polymer chains, the number of possible conformers is too large to be assessed in a deterministic way. Moreover, the use of optimized geometries or heuristic generation of conformers, such as with COSMOconf, might not be suitable to obtain realistic backbone structures of large and flexible molecules. However, atomistic MD simulations for the targeted mixtures can be a viable option to extract conformers that resemble the real molecules, as has been recently demonstrated by Zhou et al. 8,9 Nevertheless, this approach has been used with extensive sampling of several geometries to construct the input for COSMO calculations. In this work, the effect of molecular geometries is assessed for a system of poly(ethylene glycol) and water. First, the effect of polymer concentration was investigated by performing MD simulations of PEG 1000 at two different concentrations: at infinite dilution ( W PEG1000 ≈ 0) and W PEG1000 = 0.2. The radius of gyration of PEG 1000 at the two concentrations and the corresponding simulation snapshots are presented in Figure 1. The calculated average

Depending on the morphology of the MD simulation conformers, some differences are also observed regarding their calculated activity coefficients. In particular, conformers 1 and 2 , which correspond to high/low values of SASA and R g , respectively, display very similar activity coefficients for both the polymer and solvent. This is not surprising as the two conformers have very similar morphologies in an extended geometry. Certainly, more surprising is the fact that, of all of the tested conformers, these are the ones that further deviate from the results obtained for the all-trans optimized geometry. Nonetheless, the extended arrangement of the PEG molecules is likely to contribute to more accessible association centers along the molecule, which explains the low activity coefficients. The remaining conformers 3 and 4 , corresponding to the maximum probability in the SASA versus R g and the lowest value of R g/SASA, respectively, also display similar results between them. These two conformers are significantly more curled when compared to conformers 1 and 2 and, following the same reasoning, the lower accessibility of the charged ethoxy or hydroxyl groups likely contributes to slightly larger activity coefficients. Nonetheless, the differences observed between the two sets of MD conformers are not very significant, especially when compared to the optimized geometry. The small differences can be justified by the available polar regions at the surface of the molecules, which is visible in the σ -profiles (see the Supporting Information) and, in turn, in the residual contribution to the activity coefficients, but a small contribution can also be attributed to the combinatorial term, where very small differences in the calculated COSMO-RS volume can be observed. When compared with experimental data (only found for water activity coefficients), the agreement for all MD conformers is very satisfactory overall. As such, it seems like the use of a single conformer from MD simulations might be enough to get satisfactory COSMO-RS predictions and should be a better approximation than using optimized geometries.

3.2. The Combinatorial Term. A key contribution to the description of the mixing properties of polymer solutions lies in the combinatorial term, which should account for the asymmetry in space occupation between the solvent and solute. The Flory -Huggins (F-H) equation tackles the size asymmetry issue by taking into account the volume fractions of the compounds. However, due to the difference in intrinsic hard-core volume between polymer and solvent, this description can be insufficient in some situations where the free volumes of the compounds differ significantly. In order to solve this issue, Elbro et al. 24 modified the F-H equation by accounting for the inaccessible volume occupied by the hard core of the molecules, which resulted in a significant improvement over the F-H model. The estimation of the molar volume, V i , or the density of the pure compounds, is more important than it might seem at first glance, because it can have a significant impact on the calculated free volume in the Elbro equation. The use of predictive methods such as the QSPR model, while convenient, can bring significant issues into the calculation. One issue with the QSPR estimated densities is its dependence on the molecule geometry, which can lead to deviations of ∼ 5% between the highest and lowest values for the conformers of PEG400 tested in this work. An even more significant problem arises from scaling up the polymer molecular weight, which can result in densities that are unrealistically low. After some studies not detailed in this work, we realized that, whenever possible, the use of experimental data, even if extrapolated, is always preferred over any estimation method. Alternatively, the use of EoS to predict the molar volumes can be also a viable alternative. As we will show in the upcoming sections, an accurate description of the densities of both solvent and solute is essential to obtain correct trends as a function of polymer molecular weight. For now, we will focus on showcasing the impact of the density value at a constant temperature and MW.

The activity coefficients of PEG400 using the QSPR method to estimate the densities are listed in Figure 4. The curves presented also compare the impact of using (solid lines) or not using (dashed lines) the combinatorial term in the predictions of the activity coefficients, as previously shown in Figure 3. The impact is clear: when the combinatorial entropic term, which always contributes to lowering the activity coefficients, is absent, the results are unrealistic and incompatibility between the compounds (i.e., positive deviations to ideality with values that could result in phase separation) is observed. As such, the entropic contribution associated with mixing compounds must be included, in addition to the enthalpic residual term for all mixtures, in order to obtain reasonable and physically sound results.

In comparison with using experimental densities, a change in density that goes up to 6% in the worst case in relation to the experimental data will have an impact on the obtained results. The predicted densities are lower than the experimental densities, leading to an increase in the activity coefficients. The predictions deviate further from the experimental data (by excess for all conformers), and only two of the tested conformers would not display phase separation at room temperature. The results show that (i) the importance of the combinatorial term cannot be overstated and (ii) an accurate description of the densities is required.

as important as the combinatorial term to describe polymer solutions. In COSMO-RS, the residual term is calculated as the sum of energetic contributions that account for van der Waals, hydrogen bonding, and misfit interactions. The three contributions can be calculated as a function of the σ -profile, which contains the charge density information for each molecule, meaning that a correct description of the surface charge density is key to correctly model polymer solutions within COSMO-RS. We established in section section 3.1 that MD simulations can be a source of realistic conformers as input for the quantum calculations. However, certain precautions must be taken to ensure that the obtained σ -profiles correspond to reasonable screening charge densities and avoid overly polarized regions. As such, for each conformer extracted from the MD trajectory, a low-level DFT optimization should be performed before the final singlepoint calculation with a fine cavity mesh to better describe the highly charged zones (more information on the methodology used can be found under section 2.2). An example that showcases the importance of using this methodology for the quantum calculations is given in Figure 5, where the σ -profiles and activity coefficients are represented for the same conformer ( 4 ) in the cases where the optimization step and fine mesh were used or absent. As can be observed, this methodology is crucial to eliminate unreasonably high charge densities from the σ -profile (>0.02 e/Å 2 ). The σ -surface representations of the conformers further illustrate the problem that arises from performing a direct single-point calculation on the conformers extracted from atomistic simulations: highly charged cavities are observed near ether groups. The way that atomistic force fields, such as the OPLSAA used in this work, fully or partially exclude dispersion and Coulombic interactions within the same molecule up to distances of 3 bonds can contribute to some overlap between atoms that generate highly polarized locations when evaluated at a quantum level.

The occurrence of extreme charge density zones results in excessive interactions between the solute and solvent. Even though the highly charged regions might not seem prevalent in the σ -profile, they contribute significantly to the strongest hydrogen bonding interactions, which have a considerable

effect on the overall enthalpic contribution. This situation is clear when we look at the calculated activity coefficients. Performing a direct single-point calculation results in activity coefficients that are too low as a result of the enthalpic contribution being overestimated, while the entropic contribution remains unaffected.

A different, yet more obvious, situation where the σ -profile can impact the properties of the system is tweaking the structure of the polymeric chain. That is the case for PEG400 and PPG400, where, despite the structural similarity between the two polyether compounds, they behave very differently in the presence of water. Experimental observations at room temperature show that while PEG400 is fully miscible with water, PPG400 undergoes phase separation in the same solvent.

The calculated and experimental activity coefficients of PEG400 and PPG400 in water solutions are illustrated in Figure 6. It is interesting to see how COSMO-RS can differentiate between the two types of polymers, which behave very differently, despite the seemingly similar structure. The higher than unity activity coefficients for PPG400 indicate a tendency to phase separate, while the contrary is true for PEG400. The predictions are also in overall good agreement with the experimental data for the case of the water activity coefficients, following very similar trends. It is important to note that the distinction between the two polymers is seen if we isolate the residual term as well, which is indicative of the model being able to differentiate the polarities of the two compounds. The presence of an additional methyl group per monomer significantly impacts the σ -profile (see the Supporting Information), decreasing the availability of polar regions along the molecular surface, as indicated by the decrease in probability at σ > 0.01 e/Å 2 . This example demonstrates that the COSMO-RS model can be very sensitive to small changes in the structure, making it a viable option to screen polymers with various constitutions/structures.

3.4. Molecular Weight Scaling. Perhaps the most challenging task when modeling polymeric systems with the COSMO-RS model is capturing the effect of the molecular weight. For larger molecules, the quantum mechanics calculations required to obtain the σ -profiles become increasingly more demanding and, at some point, impossible to perform with readily available hardware. In order to circumvent these limitations, the σ -profiles can be upscaled from smaller oligomers by applying a weighting factor to the atoms of the repeating core of the polymer chain. This approach allows performing calculations for high-molecular-weight polymers without the need to perform computationally expensive quantum calculations. This effect can be visualized in Figure 7, where the σ -profiles for different PEG molecular weights is presented.

Figure 7. σ -profiles showing the effect of molecular weight scaling for PEG400, PEG1500, PEG4000, and PEG20000. Inset shows a closer look at the negatively charged region.

As a noteworthy observation, while the lower polarity sections of the σ -profile are proportionally increasing with the molecular weight, the most positively charged regions (negative σ ), corresponding mostly to the hydroxyl hydrogen of the terminal groups, are mostly independent of the molecular weight scaling but are, nonetheless, still present, as seen in the inset in Figure 7. The approach that we followed in

uter this work does not neglect the influence of the terminal groups, which can have an impact especially on the calculation for small molecules but whose effect is negligible for long polymers. While the σ -profile is the only required input to calculate the residual part of the chemical potential, the combinatorial term requires the molar volume. As shown above in section 3.2, an accurate volumetric description is important to accurately describe the experimental trends in the activity coefficients. Since the longer PEG compounds are solid at room temperature, densities of the liquid phase were predicted by extrapolation from the data obtained for shorter polymers.

The COSMO-RS calculations are presented in Figure 8 (lines), together with the experimental datasets (circles), as a function of the polymer mass fraction. Experimental data show that the water activity coefficients are mostly independent of the polymer molecular weight. COSMO-RS is able to quantitatively predict this observation, as the activity coefficients show no dependence of the activity coefficients in relation to the polymer molecular weight. Conceptually, for the same mass fraction of the polymer, it is logical that the effect on the water interactions is mostly irrelevant. However, the same is not true for the polymer activity coefficients, as can be seen in Figure 8 (right). An increase in molecular weight leads to significantly lower PEG activity coefficients as a function of the mass fraction. Once again, the COSMO-RS is able to correctly predict the trends that arise from changing the polymer molecular weight and, to some extent, quantitatively predict the correct PEG activity coefficients. Still, some significant deviations are observed in the case of PEG35000, where the COSMO-RS consistently underpredicts the activity coefficients. It should be noted, however, that the data points presented were obtained via indirect calculations (eq S1 in the Supporting Information) from SLE diagrams and that each experimental point corresponds to a different melting temperature. Nonetheless, the theoretical calculations obtained from scaling the σ -profiles produce very satisfactory results, following the experimental observations with the correct trends and even in quantitative agreement, demonstrating the

As a final note, despite the potential that we recognize in the COSMO-RS approach, we were unable to calculate the LLE diagrams with COSMOtherm, due to numerical limitations that result from the high-molecular-weight asymmetry between polymer and solvent, thus focusing the bulk of the discussion on the activity coefficients. Hopefully, this limitation will be addressed in future software revisions, which could allow the proliferation of COSMO-RS as a method for the prediction of thermodynamic data for polymeric systems.

4. CONCLUSIONS

In this work, we discussed the details concerning polymer solution calculations with the COSMO-RS theory using the PEG family as a case study. Several factors were evaluated, such as the influence of conformations, the description of the combinatorial/residual terms, and the upscaling with molecular weight.

The use of realistic polymer conformers, sourced from atomistic MD simulations, resulted in significant improvements over the quantum mechanics optimized geometries. Nonetheless, due to the total or partial absence of intramolecular interactions between neighboring atoms in most force fields, certain precautions must be addressed in order to avoid highly polarized regions. A low-level energy minimization optimization step followed by a single-point calculation using the fine-cavity option led to realistic σ -profiles and good agreement between the COSMO-RS predictions and experimental data. Moreover, a good description of the combinatorial term was shown to be essential to predict the activity coefficients with accuracy. In this regard, the use of experimental data is preferred over predictive methods, such as QSPR, even if some data extrapolation is necessary.

The molecular weight scaling method, applied to the repeating units of an oligomer, allows the use of the COSMO-RS model without performing computationally intensive calculations for very large molecules. This methodology proved to be accurate in predicting the activity coefficients of water + polymer mixtures, with the right trends and, to a certain extent, in quantitative agreement when compared with experimental data. Overall, COSMO-RS can be a very good predictive tool for polymeric systems as long as some details inherent to the calculations discussed in this work are correctly addressed, opening perspectives for future work to scan the phase behavior of different polymer families.

Staining

1. Introduction

Plastics are used for various applications, offering many advantages over  alternative  materials.  For  example,  they  are  easy  to  process, degrade slowly and their properties can be easily modified using addi tives  or  by  creating  composites  or  multilayers  [1,2].  This  variety  of possibilities and types of polymers makes them ideal for manufacturing diverse products, but this also results in a very complex waste stream generated at the end of life. Consequently, good waste management is crucial to reduce the environmental impact, working toward a circular economy of plastics [3 -5].

Mechanical recycling is  widely applied  in  industry,  especially  for post-industrial  plastics  [4].  During  this  process,  plastics  are  sorted,

Abstract

Several technologies for de-inking plastics have been developed, yet, most face a similar problem, namely colorant staining. This means the ink may be removed, but some colorant re-adsorbs to the plastic resulting in recyclates with a slightly colored shine after extrusion. This re-adsorption or staining of colorants occurs as they become  available  in  the  medium  during  de-inking  by  dissolution  or  solubilization,  followed  by  dynamic adsorption -desorption of the dissolved and solubilized pigments between the medium and the plastic surfaces. In this paper, staining was analyzed, and methods for reducing staining are proposed. First, it was confirmed that staining is a reversible adsorption-desorption process. Next, kinetic models were established to describe the deinking, dissolution-solubilization, and adsorption-desorption for a yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) in caustic soda with detergent. First-order models were able to describe these processes, and were implemented in Aspen Plus to examine the effect of residence time, ink load, wastewater treatment efficiency, and flow pattern. It was shown that colorant adsorption increases with residence time, and that an increase in ink load or decrease in wastewater treatment efficiency also results in an increased adsorption. Next, it was shown that crossflow results in negligible adsorption of colorants ( < 0.5 ppm), and counter-current also results in reduced adsorption (up to 85 %) compared to single reactor de-inking (around 200 ppm and higher). Washing  with  fresh  media  enables  colorant  desorption  when  its  driving  force  exceeds  that  of  adsorption. Regardless, it can be argued that it is industrially unfeasible to completely counteract staining by merely altering the process flow, and more advanced techniques are needed to prevent staining.

However, there are still problems when it  comes  to  the  mechanical  recycling  of  post-consumer  plastic waste [6]. This is due to the complexity of this waste stream, which is very  heterogeneous  and  contaminated.  One  particular  issue  is  the presence of IAS (Intentionally Added Substances) such as inks, additives, coatings, and adhesives [7,8]. Plastic, and especially flexible packaging, can be heavily printed to inform the customer and to attract the po tential customer ' s attention [9,10]. If these inks are not removed during mechanical  recycling,  this  will  result  in  a  low-quality,  dark-colored recyclate with lower stiffness, strength, and density compared to virgin plastics,  reducing its economic value [7,10]. Besides, these inks may degrade  during  re-extrusion,  resulting  in  the  formation  of  rancid odorous gases [7].

text: Several techniques have been developed to de-ink plastic waste, but not all are equally effective for the wide variety of inks. The first is the patented Nordenia Extraction and Cleaning (Norec ® ) process (DE19651571A1), performing solvent-based extraction to remove inks using  hot  ethyl  acetate  [11,12].  Furthermore,  extensive  research  has been performed on the use of surfactants as de-inking agents, such as Sodium  dodecyl  sulfate  (SDS),  Cetrimonium  bromide  (CTAB)  or Dimethyl  dodecyl  amine  oxide  (DDAO).  Research  by  Gecol  et  al. [13 -15] has shown that cationic surfactants in alkaline environments, at elevated temperatures, yield the best removal rates for both water and solvent-based  inks.  Besides,  Chotipong  et  al.  [16]  has  shown  that surfactant-based  de-inking  comprises  4  steps:  (1)  adsorption  of  the surfactant on the plastic surface, (2) solubilization of the binder in the micelles, (3) detachment of the ink particles from the surface and (4) stabilization of the free ink particles. The CADEL, or nowadays named KEYCYCLE process, is a patented surfactant-based technique originating from the University of Alicante (EP2832459B1), making use of a waterbased caustic soda solution containing detergent, and is already proven at semi-industrial scale (1200 kg.h 1 ) [17 -19]. Furthermore, mechani cal cleaning is also applied to remove surface printed inks. The ECO CLEAN process, developed by Gamma Meccanica, removes inks from the plastic surface by friction using mechanical brushes. Consequently, this process  can  only  de-ink  surface  printed  plastics  [11,20].  Another patented  process  (EP1419829A1)  makes  use  of  rotating  brushes  in combination with organic solvents and nonionic surfactants. However, the medium results in a remarkable decrease in the physicochemical properties of plastics. Consequently, this process is less known and en counters problems in upscaling [7,11,21].

All these technologies face an issue that is hardly described in the scientific  or  open  literature,  namely  the  staining  or  discoloration  of plastics during the de-inking of plastic waste in liquid media. In the past, this staining was not really noticed in a research context as most ex periments were conducted at laboratory scale or relatively low solidliquid (S/L) ratios, or the de-inked flakes were not re-extruded as the color becomes only, or at least more, visible after the extrusion to a thicker shape. However, upon scaling up these de-inking technologies, it was  observed  that  this  often  resulted  in  stained/shady  plastics.  This effect is enhanced in industrial plants that operate medium circulation and might have accumulation of colorants. Consequently, the value of these recyclates becomes substantially lower, as these colored plastics have a reduced applicability for high-value applications [22]. It was found that the staining was often attributable to the colors blue, yellow, and red, caused by organic pigments such as Pigment Blue (PB) 15:4, Pigment Yellow (PY) 13, and Pigment Red (PR) 57:1. This staining was not observed for non-dissolving or non-solubilizing colorants such as carbon black (PBk 7) or TiO2. It is thus clear that organic pigments are the main cause of this staining in water-based de-inking media. When organic pigments enter the de-inking medium because the ink binder has been  removed,  the  pigments  will  undergo  an  interplay  between  the solubilization by the aid of surfactants used in the de-inking medium or already  present  on  the  pigment,  broader  dispersion,  or  true  partial dissolution of the molecule. Indeed, pigments comprise a wide variety of molecular structures to which substances are added to stabilize/disperse them in the ink medium and in the binder of the inks. It can thus be hypothesized that depending on the properties of the pigment itself, as well  as  the  substances  added  to  stabilize  it  in  the  binder,  their  in teractions  with  the  de-inking  medium  may  vary.  Regardless  of  these exact mechanisms, the pigments are 'stabilized ' in the liquid. Although not encompassing all potential phenomena, we propose in this paper to consider this as the 'dissolution and solubilization ' of the pigments. After this, the color molecules can adsorb on the plastic and cause 'staining ' . It should be noted that the term staining was preferred because it is a phenomenon different from bleeding. Bleeding refers to the inability to remove colorants, like especially soluble dyes, from the wash medium by available (wastewater) treatment technologies, whereas staining is the uptake of colorants from the wash medium onto the plastics.

Since staining has currently been observed for organic pigments, it can be presumed that this phenomenon is similar to the re-adsorption of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during the washing of plastic waste. In previous research, it was highlighted that non-polar VOCs favor the rather  non-polar  polymer  matrix  over  the  aqueous  wash  medium [23 -26].  Consequently,  re-adsorption  of  these  VOCs  occurs  when  a contaminated polar wash medium comes in contact with relatively clean plastics [23 -25]. In addition, a more direct link can also be made to the disperse dyeing of textiles. Here, the poorly water-soluble dyes are sol ubilized using dispersing agents, being surfactants, where they contribute to the breakdown of aggregated dye particles and dispersion of the dye in the liquid [27]. In this process, the surfactants direct their nonpolar groups toward the center of the dye in the micelle and the polar group outward, stabilizing the dyes, resulting in higher apparent solubility of the dye in the polar medium [27 -29]. In this process, an equilibrium is established between the undissolved dyes, the solubilized dyes present in the micelles, and partially dissolved dyes. The dissolved and solubilized dyes are consequently readily available in the medium and are able to adsorb onto the textile fibers, resulting in a new equi librium between the dyes present in the medium and those adsorbed onto the textile fibers. Consequently, a dynamic equilibrium is estab lished  where  the  adsorption  of  dyes  is  a  reversible  process,  and desorption of the dyes can occur depending on the prevailing conditions [27,28,30].

It is hypothesized that a similar phenomenon occurs during the deinking  of  plastics,  as  shown  in  Fig.  1,  where  the  inks  are  removed from the surface, the colorants dissolve and solubilize in the de-inking medium and then, depending on the affinity, tend to adsorb on to the polymer structure. Consequently, it is presumed that this adsorption of colorants  is  a  reversible  process.  As  with  disperse  dyeing  and  the removal of VOCs, it can be presumed that the actual rate of staining depends on a wide variety of factors, including the dispersing agents or surfactants  present,  physiochemical  properties  of  the  polymers,  pH, temperature, S/L ratio, contamination of the medium, residence time and potential interdependent effects [23 -25,27].

This research aimed to gain insight into the mechanism and kinetics of the staining of plastic films during de-inking in water-based media, and to assess different process configurations by means of simulations to better  control  this  phenomenon.  For  this  purpose,  an  experimental screening was performed to assess the adsorption-desorption hypothesis described  above.  Next,  the  kinetics  of  the  various  processes,  the  deinking,  dissolution  and  solubilization,  and  adsorption-desorption  of colorants, were determined and described by commonly used kinetic models. These models were implemented in Aspen Plus to assess the effect of residence time, the amount of ink present on the plastics or socalled  ink  load,  wastewater  treatment  (WWT)  efficiency  and  flow pattern on the de-inking and potential uptake of colorants. Finally, these findings were used to assess the potential to reduce staining by means of proper  process  design  and  media  management,  Design  for  Recycling guidelines and fine-tuning of the washing medium composition.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, purity of > 99.0 %, Sigma Aldrich), hex adecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB, purity of > 98.0 %, Sigma Aldrich), sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, purity of > 99.0 %, Sigma Aldrich), nitric acid (HNO3, concentration of 65 %, Chemlab), sodium bicarbon ate (0.1 M NaHCO3  in pure water (Merck); eluent concentrate for ion chromatography (IC), Merck) and ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3, purity of > 99.0 %, Honeywell Riedel-de-Ha ¨ en) were used without prior puri fication. Pure water (Merck) was used for IC measurements, deminer alized water was used for all other analyses and experiments. To avoid contamination,  the  glasswork  was  washed  with  distilled  water  and acetone, and dried in an oven at 105 °C.

The yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1),  and  associated industrial  mono-pigment solvent-based PU-inks were  supplied  by  Siegwerk  Druckfarben  AG & Co.KGaA  (Siegburg, Germany). Pigment selection was based on input from the ink manu facturer, who identified these as commonly used pigments with diverse properties and potential risk of staining, as discussed in Section 3.2. This choice was further supported by literature and prior independent studies on plastic de-inking [31 -34]. The LDPE films had a thickness of 47 μ m and  were  also  provided  by  Siegwerk  Druckfarben  AG & Co.KGaA (Siegburg,  Germany).  The  inks  were  coated  on  LDPE  films  with  a thickness of 4 μ m using a K Control Coater (RK Print Coat Instruments). The samples were then dried for 2 days at room temperature, in open air, before being cut into 1 cm × 1 cm particles.

2.2. Analytics

Ultraviolet -Visible (UV -VIS) spectrophotometry measurements were  performed  to  monitor  the  screening  and  kinetic  experiments, analyzing  the  available  concentration  of  colorant  in  the  media.  The initial  amount  of  ink  on  the  plastics  was  determined  by  inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) in the case of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) and ion chromatography (IC) for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13).

Fig. 1. 2.2.1. Ultraviolet -visible (UV -VIS) spectrophotometry

The dissolved and solubilized concentrations of colorant in the media were determined by UV -VIS spectrophotometry measurements, using a Shimadzu  UV-1280  UV-VIS  spectrophotometer  with  a  scan  range  of 190 -1100 nm, a resolution  of ± 1  nm,  utilizing  a  semi-micro  quartz cuvette (Hellma Analytics) with an outer cell dimension of 12.5 mm × 12.5 mm × 45 mm and an optical pathlength of 10 mm. First, the op timum absorbance wavelength was determined for each colorant in the de-inking medium by a full-wavelength scan in scan mode. The optimum wavelength was considered to be the wavelength at which a distinct peak in absorbance could be observed. The output of these wavelength scans is shown in Fig. 1 of the Supplementary Materials. Thereby, it was decided to measure the absorbances for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) at 453 nm and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) at 489 nm. Calibration lines were established for each colorant; these are shown in Fig. 2 of the Supplementary Materials. In this process, the calibration lines for both colorants were established such that the maximum con centration was limited so that the absorbance did not exceed a value of 2.5. Hence, calibration lines were established in the range of 5 to 70 ppm for PR 57:1, and 4 to 58 ppm for PY 13. If the absorbance was higher than  the  maximum  absorbance  included  in  the  calibration  line,  the aliquot was diluted with fresh de-inking medium and measured again. At all times, the calibration lines and samples were measured at room temperature.

For the dissolution and solubilization kinetics, a Chromafil ® RC-45/ 25 syringe filter with 0.45 μ m pores was used to remove undissolved particles from the sample. To account for the effect of the syringe filter on the measured concentration, a correction factor was established. This was determined by analyzing solutions with a known concentration of colorant before and after filtering. This involved the same procedure as discussed above. The resulting correction factors are given in Fig. 3 of the Supplementary Materials.

2.2.2. ICP-OES

ICP-OES  was  utilized  to  determine  the  amount  of  red  azo  lake pigment (PR 57:1) on the one-side full-tone coated samples. Since PR 57:1 can be traced based on Ca 2 + , it was possible to determine the ink load  on  the  plastics  by  determining  the  Ca 2 + concentration  after destruction of the sample. Hence, microwave destruction was performed in  an  Anton  Paar  Multiwave  5000,  utilizing  Teflon  bombs  (Pressure Vessel SVT50). Therefore, 0.1 g of sample was weighed into the bombs, using an analytical balance, and 2 mL of double distilled water and 8 mL of HNO3 (65 %) were added. Similarly, a blank was prepared with un coated  plastics  to  determine  the  amount  of  Ca 2 + pre-existing  in  the plastics.  The  destructions  were  performed  by  heating  the  samples  to 200 °C, at a constant rate of 5 °C.min 1 for 40 min, maintaining the temperature for 20 min. After cooling, the samples were transferred into 25  mL  volumetric  flasks,  diluted  with  double  distilled  water,  and homogenized.

For analysis, the samples were transferred into falcon tubes with a 20 mL syringe, filtering the samples using a Chromafil ® RC-45/25 sy ringe filter (Pore size = 0.45 μ m; Membrane size = 25 mm) to remove any remaining solids. Next, ICP-OES analyzes were performed using a Thermo Scientific iCAP 7200 equipped with CETAC ASX-560 autosam pler,  and  the  data  was  interpreted  using  the  QtegraTM  Software.  A calibration line (0.5 -20 mg.L 1 ) was prepared based on a 100 mg.L 1 XVI Certipur multi-element standard, and the Ca 2 + concentration was measured in the radial direction at a wavelength of 393.366 nm.

2.2.3. IC analysis

IC was used to determine the amount of yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) on the one-side full-tone coated samples. Since PY 13 can be traced based on Cl , it was possible to determine the ink load on the plastics by determining the Cl concentration after the destruction of the sample.

Therefore, oxygen combustion was performed in an Anton Paar Multi wave 5000, utilizing quartz vessels (Pressure vessel NXQ80; Max oper ating pressure = 80 bar). First, ashless, quantitative, filter paper (MN 640 m - diameter 110 mm) was punched out in an 18 mm diameter circle and placed on the quartz sample holder and 8 mL of absorption solution (1 mM NaHCO3 and 8 mM Na2CO3 aqueous solution) was added to the quartz  vessel.  Next,  0.02  g  of  sample  was  weighed  on  an  analytical balance, placed on the filter paper, and moistened by using an automatic pipette with 50 μ L of 50 w / v % NH4NO3-solution. The sample holders were  inserted  in  the  quartz  vessels,  placed  into  the  microwave  and pressurized to 20 bars with oxygen. Destructions were performed by heating the samples at 900 W for 10 min. After cooling, the samples were transferred into 25 mL volumetric flasks, diluted with double distilled water, and homogenized. Using the same procedure, a blank, an un coated  plastic,  was  also  destructed  and  subsequently  analyzed  to determine the potential amount of Cl present in the plastics.

Before analysis, the conductivity of the samples was measured using a HACH HQ30d Flexi multimeter with a CDC 401 probe (detection limit: 10 μ S.cm 1 ). The samples were diluted with double distilled water if the conductivity was above 200 μ S.cm 1 . Next, the Cl concentration was measured by IC, using a Metrohm Eco IC system with a conductivity detector and 863 Compact Autosampler. The device was equipped with a Metrosep A Supp 19 Guard 4.0 precolumn, and a Metrosep A Supp 19 -150/4.0 column. The eluent was an 8.0 mM Na2CO3 and 0.25 mM NaHCO3  aqueous  solution.  Before  injection,  the  sample  was  filtered using a Chromafil ® RC-45/25 syringe filter. Next, 20 μ L of the sample was injected, with an eluent flow rate of 0.7 mL.min 1 . The MagIC Net software was used to interpret the results, using a calibration line of 0.5 -50 mg.L 1 prepared from a 1000 mg.L 1 Chloride standard (Merck).

2.3. Experimental procedure

The  initial  ink  or  colorant  loads  on  the  one-side  full-tone  coated LDPE  films  were  determined  in  triplicate.  The  Ca 2 + concentration, analyzed by ICP-OES, was utilized to determine the amount of red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) on the coated samples, resulting in an initial ink load of 14,320 ± 645 mg.kg 1 . The Cl content, analyzed by IC, indi cated an initial ink load of 9725 ± 450 mg.kg 1 for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13).

2.3.1. De-inking conditions

All experiments were performed in a 2 wt% caustic soda aqueous solution  containing  9.2  mmol.L 1 ( = 10  CMC)  CTAB  in  tap  water, heated to 80 °C. This study focused on the staining of flexible plastic films during the de-inking process, and thus, for simplicity, only surfacecoated samples were considered. LDPE films of approximately 1 cm × 1 cm were used throughout this study, with particle size kept constant. As demonstrated by De Somer et al. [25], particle sizes within this range have a negligible effect on VOC adsorption -desorption for plastic films. This is attributed to the inherently low thickness of films, which limits the influence of particle size on the specific surface area. In contrast, rigid plastics, due to their greater thickness, exhibit a higher sensitivity to  particle  size,  resulting  in  a  more  pronounced  impact  on  adsorp tion -desorption phenomena. Consequently, since adsorp tion -desorption phenomena are governed by specific surface area, the assumption is that staining is minimally affected in the range of indus trially relevant particle sizes of plastic films.

2.3.2. Experimental assessment of the adsorption-desorption mechanism

First, a screening was performed to verify the hypothesis that the staining of plastics is due to an adsorption-desorption mechanism. For this purpose, 5 g of coated plastics was weighed and brought into contact with 150 mL of de-inking media. The media and plastics were heated up to 80 °C in a round-bottom flask equipped with reflux cooler and mixed at 500 revolutions per minute (rpm) using an overhead stirrer, equipped with a half-moon impeller. After at least 2 days, the plastics and deinking medium were separated with a sieve, and an aliquot was taken using a syringe (10 mL) with needle (Length = 120 mm, Diameter = 0.80 mm). Next, the plastics were rinsed three times with 250 mL of water to remove residual de-inking medium from the plastics. The above procedure was then repeated with the same plastics that were already washed in the previous cycle, using fresh de-inking medium. This was repeated five times, each time collecting an aliquot of the medium after washing. The aliquots were kept in vials, wrapped in aluminum foil to avoid  UV  degradation,  and  stored  at  room  temperature.  Finally,  the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant in the aliquots was analyzed by UV -VIS.

2.3.3. Dissolution kinetics

In a three-neck flask, 200 mL of de-inking medium was preheated to 80 °C, connected to a reflux cooler, and an overhead stirrer set at 500 rpm. Once the medium reached the intended temperature, 500 mg of colorant was weighed using an analytical balance and introduced into the flask. Then, after 1.5 min, 3 min, 5 min, 10 min, 15 min, 30 min, 1 h and 2 h, a 4 mL aliquot of the de-inking medium was taken using a sy ringe with a needle. The needle was used to prevent undissolved parti cles from being collected during sampling. However, to ensure that no residual particles were present, the aliquot was transferred directly into a  vial  through  a  Chromafil ® RC-45/25 syringe filter. The vials were wrapped in aluminum foil to avoid UV degradation and stored at room temperature.  Finally,  the  dissolved  and  solubilized  concentration  of colorant in the aliquots was analyzed by UV-VIS, utilizing a correction factor for the filter ' s effect on the measured concentration.

2.3.4. Adsorption kinetics

A solution was prepared with an exact known concentration of 15 mg.L 1 of colorant in the 2 wt% caustic soda + 9.2 mmol.L 1 CTAB so lution. Next, 400 mL of the solution was preheated to 80 °C in a threeneck  flask,  coupled  with  a  reflux  cooler  and  overhead  stirrer  set  at 500 rpm. Then, 15 g of uncoated LDPE was added to the media. After 2 min, 5 min, 7.5 min, 10 min, 15 min, 20 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4 h and 5 h, a 4 mL aliquot of the liquid phase was taken, using a syringe with needle. The aliquot was transferred into a vial, wrapped in aluminum foil, and stored at room temperature. Finally, the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant in the aliquots was analyzed by UV-VIS. These experiments were conducted at an increased S/L ratio combined  with  a  relatively  low  initial  colorant  concentration  in  the medium,  as  otherwise  the  change  in  concentration  measured  would have  been  small  to  the  point  that  it  would  complicate  subsequent parameter regression.

2.3.5. De-inking kinetics

400 mL of de-inking media was preheated to 80 °C in a three-neck flask, coupled to a reflux cooler and overhead stirrer set at 500 rpm. Once  the  medium  reached  the  intended  temperature,  8  g  of  coated plastic was introduced into the flask. After 5 min, 7.5 min, 10 min, 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 h, 1.5 h and 2 h, a 4 mL aliquot of the de-inking medium  was  taken  using  a  syringe  with  needle.  Subsequently,  the aliquot was transferred into a vial, wrapped in aluminum foil, and stored at room temperature. Finally, the aliquots were analyzed by UV-VIS.

2.4. Kinetic modeling

As  discussed  in  the  introduction  and  shown  in  Fig.  1,  it  was  hy pothesized  that  the  phenomenon  of  staining  during  the  de-inking  of plastics results from three successive steps: de-inking, dissolution and solubilization, and the adsorption-desorption of colorants.

First, the de-inking of plastics takes place. For simplicity, this was considered  as  the  decomposition  of  the  binder,  independent  of  the decomposition mechanism. It was assumed that the colorants are ho mogeneously distributed throughout the ink (QInk) and are then released in the medium, in first instance undissolved (CUndissolved). Consequently, de-inking was described by first-order kinetics according to literature [35 -37].

( dQInk dt ) De inking = kDe inking * QInk (1)

where QInk is the amount of colorant present in the ink on the plastics (mg.kg 1 ), kDe-inking  is the de-inking rate constant (s 1 ) and t the time (s).  Next,  the  particles  released  during de-inking  start dissolving and solubilizing,  limited  by  the  maximum  dissolved  and  solubilized  con centration, as also observed in the disperse dyeing of textiles [28]. In literature, it is frequently opted to describe dissolution kinetics by first order kinetics (Eq. (2)), with a decelerating factor according to the de gree of saturation of the solution [38 -40]. Hence, the kinetics of this step is maximal when there is no dissolved and solubilized colorant in so lution  and  declines  to  zero  when  the  solution  becomes  saturated. However, it should be emphasized that this description comprises the various  phenomena  that  result  in  the  stabilization  of  the  pigments released  during  the  de-inking.  In  the  process,  the  actual  dissolution, solubilization or formation of a dispersion will depend on the properties of the pigment and the washing medium, among others.

( dcD & S dt ) D & S = kD & S * ( 1 cD & S [ cD & S ] max ) (2)

where cD & S  is the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant (mg.L 1 ), [cD & S]max  the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentra tion of the colorant (mg.L 1 ), and kD & S the dissolution and solubilization rate constant (mg.L 1 .s 1 ). Once dissolved and solubilized, the colorant can potentially adsorb on the plastics, with the dissolved and solubilized concentration  (cD & S)  being  the  driving  force  for  adsorption.  The screening experiments showed that the uptake of colorants, similar to the VOC removal, is a reversible process. Consequently, desorption of the colorants may occur in addition to adsorption. Both phenomena can be described simultaneously by means of the reversible first order model (Eq. (3)), consisting of an adsorption and desorption term. The de-inking conditions,  such  as  media  refreshment  and  S/L  ratio,  will  determine which of the two phenomena prevails [23 -25]:

( dqAdsorbed dt ) Re adsorption = kAdsorptioncD & S kDesorption qAdsorbed (3)

where qAdsorbed is the adsorbed concentration of colorant on the plastics (mg.kg 1 ),  kAdsorption the  adsorption  rate  constant  (L.kg 1 .s 1 )  and kDesorption the desorption rate constant (s 1 ). An overview of the various conversion steps is given in the Gujer matrix, shown in Table 1. The Gujer matrix lists in the first column the various steps, being de-inking, dissolution and solubilization, adsorption and desorption, and in the last column the corresponding equations describing the kinetics. The col umns in between show how the various variables are stoichiometrically related to the respective conversion step [41]. Hence, changes of each variable can be calculated according to its corresponding column, by multiplying each stoichiometric coefficient with the kinetic expression, and taking the sum of each row (e.g. Cundissolved = S/L * (kDe-inking * Qink) -kD & S  * (1-CD & S/[CD & S]max). Furthermore, each row of the matrix al lows to see which variables affect each process step (e.g. de-inking re lates to Qink  being removed and Cundissolved  being formed). For further details  and  illustrative  examples  on  interpreting  the  Gujer  matrix, reference is made to literature [42,43].

As discussed earlier, the various steps depend on the system prop erties, including the properties of the colorants and de-inking media, as well as the process conditions and reactor design. Therefore, this cali bration should be performed for each new combination of ink, polymer and  wash  medium,  and  will  be  process  specific  in  terms  of  process conditions and reactor design.

For each of these steps, a separate parameter regression was per formed by nonlinear regression, utilizing the FME package in R. The ModFit function was used to minimize the Sum of Square of Errors (SSE) by  means  of  the  Levenberg-Marquardt  algorithm.  During  parameter regression of the dissolution and solubilization kinetics, the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration [cD & S]max  was also considered as regression parameter. Since the de-inking kinetics were experimen tally determined in terms of the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant (cD & S) as a function of time, it was necessary first to decide on the dissolution and solubilization, and adsorption-desorption kinetics. Hence, during the parameter regression of the de-inking kinetics, these dissolution and solubilization, as well as adsorption-desorption kinetics, were taken into account to describe the dissolved and solubilized con centration of colorants. Finally, the models were validated based on the Theil ' s Inequality Coefficient (TIC), Mean Relative Error (MRE), Stan dard Error of regression (SE) and R 2 to indicate their accuracy.

It may be noted that the experiments conducted to obtain the deinking and adsorption-desorption data were performed at different S/L ratios. However, the kinetic models are expressed in terms of the con centrations  present  in  the  respective  phases.  As  shown  in  the  Gujer matrix above, the S/L ratio is taken into account to convert the described concentration change of the respective component in one phase to the other. Accordingly, the de-inking is expressed as a function of the con centration  of  ink  present  on  the  plastics,  and  the  actual  kinetics  of decline in concentration of ink on the plastics does not depend on the S/ L ratio, yet the increase in undissolved colorants attributable to the deinking step is described with respect to the S/L ratio. These conversions were applied on the one hand to determine the de-inking kinetics, but also later to implement the models in the Aspen Plus simulations.

2.5. Process simulations

The resulting  kinetic  models  were  implemented  in  Aspen  Plus  as described  using  the  Gujer  matrix,  shown  in  Table 1 .  This  made  it possible  to  assess  the  effect  of  several  process  parameters  and  flow patterns on the adsorption-desorption of the colorants during de-inking, assuming  equal  reactor  design  and  hydrodynamics.  The  Aspen  Plus simulations  serve  the  goal  to  validate  seven  hypotheses  which  are formulated in Table 2. The simulations were not intended to serve as a detailed design for washing installations. The underlying models were calibrated and validated using experimental data on mass transfer and equilibria at consistent temperature and mixing. The stirring speed was consistently maintained at 500 rpm, as this provided effective mixing without  causing  adhesion  of  the  plastic  films  to  the  glassware.  The simulations assume an idealized scenario, excluding influence and het erogeneity of temperature and mixing, as well as dead zones. While this simplification  is  deemed  suitable  for  the  hypothesis  testing  and  first insight generation aimed in this paper, in future work detailed design and hydrodynamics of washing processes for plastic waste should be included. Further investigation is warranted into the effects of temper ature  and  mixing  on  both  the  de-inking  efficiency  and  the  staining behavior of plastics. With regard to mixing, attention should not only be given to the stirring speed, but also to the type and dimensions of the impeller, as these factors may significantly influence the process out comes. Additionally, scale-up phenomena such as plastic film agglom eration  and  curling  were  not  yet  examined  and  should  be  carefully evaluated during pilot testing. Further investigation into these effects is essential  to  enable  accurate,  simulation-based  process  design.  Conse quently,  validation  at  pilot  or  industrial  scale  is  recommended  for practical implementation.

The first  three  hypotheses  are  that  a  longer  residence  time  (H1), higher ink load (H2), and worse water treatment efficiency (H3) have a positive effect on colorant adsorption, meaning more staining. For these three  hypotheses,  simulations  with  a  single  continuous  stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) are performed. All simulations were consistently per formed for both the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) in order to gain insight into the extent to which the colorant affects the degree of adsorption and desorption. Next, the influence of the flow pattern and resulting contact time between col orants and plastics on potential adsorption and desorption was assessed. This involved the simulation and comparison of different configurations, consisting of co-, counter-current, and crossflow multi-stage processes of CSTRs. In addition, based on the crossflow configuration, the extent to which a high degree of media refreshment is conducive to counteracting the  staining  of  plastics  was  investigated  (H4 -5).  For  more  details regarding  the  several  flow  patterns,  reference  is  made  to  literature [44,45]. Besides, the extent to which de-inking kinetics are crucial in process configurations with a high degree of media refreshment with respect to adsorption and potential desorption of colorants (H6) was also examined. Finally, it was also verified if applying a stand-alone second wash with de-inking media could result in the desorption of the previ ously adsorbed colorants (H7). For this purpose, a two-step wash was considered, each reactor having a separate media cycle including media treatment. A schematic representation of the several configurations is given in Fig. 2 and an overview of the main settings for the various scenarios applied during the simulations is given in Table 3.
2.5.1. Simulation methodology

The colorants were specified multiple times as conventional com ponents in the property section of Aspen Plus to describe their concen trations  in  the  different  phases,  being  colorant  present  in  ink  (QInk), undissolved colorant in the medium (CUndissolved), dissolved and solu bilized colorant (cD & S) in the medium and adsorbed colorant (qadsorbed) on the plastics. The properties and relevant parameters of the compo nents were obtained by enabling all databases integrated in Aspen Plus, and any missing parameters were determined by means of the built-in estimation  tool,  using  group-contribution  methods.  For  this  purpose, the molecular structure of the molecules was specified in the properties section. The non-random two-liquid model (NRTL) property method was applied during these simulations. The kinetic models previously estab lished in Section 2.4 were applied for the conversion from one phase to another. These equations are elaborated for each phase in the Supple mentary  Materials  (S1-S4).  The  parameters  used,  determined  by parameter regression as described in Section 2.4, are shown in Table 4. The reactions were specified in the simulation environment of Aspen Plus as General type reactions, utilizing Custom terms. In this process, the reversible first-order model to describe the adsorption - desorption was  rederived  into  the  separate  first-order  models  to  describe  the adsorption  and  desorption.  As  shown  in  the  Gujer  matrix  (Table 1 ), CUndissolved  is not included in the equations, and one might expect these reactions to continue to be calculated resulting in negative concentra tions. However, this is not the case because the solver of Aspen Plus does not continue to calculate reactions once the reagent is no longer avail able. Consequently, no negative concentrations for the different forms of the colorants can be obtained during the simulations.

The  one-side  full-tone  coated  samples  were  considered  reference scenarios during the simulations. The simulations were performed for a capacity of 1000 kg.h 1 of plastics at a S/L-ratio of 42 kg plastic.m 3 deinking media, considering the 2 wt% caustic soda + detergent solution at 80 °C as de-inking medium. A S/L ratio of 42 kg/m 3 was adopted as this study was conducted as part of the CIRCULAR FoodPack project (European Union ' s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program), in which tests were performed at this S/L ratio. Furthermore, this is within the common range of 10 to 50 kg/m 3 that is typically applied in washing processes for recycling plastic film waste. Here the S/L ratio is preferably as high as possible, in order to achieve a higher capacity on a single washing line. However, the (bulk) density and the size of the shredded plastics often lowers the actual achievable capacity on a washing line for plastics [23,46 -48].

A  residual  moisture  content  of  11.5  wt%  on  the  plastics  was considered after mechanical separation [49]. The resulting loss of the de-inking medium was compensated via a make-up flow, added to the recirculated  de-inking  medium  after  the  wastewater  treatment.  The mechanical separations were simulated using a USER2 block coupled with  an  external  Excel  script  to  separate  the  de-inking  medium, including  the  undissolved  (CUndissolved)  and  dissolved  and  solubilized colorants (cD & S), from the plastics, including the colorants in ink (QInk) and adsorbed (qadsorbed) colorants. For this purpose, the USER2 block was combined with a split and mixer block to reintroduce the residual moisture content (11.5 wt%) to the plastics and to send the remaining de-inking medium to the wastewater treatment. The standard settings of the USER2 block were retained, and the Stream Flash calculations based on temperature and pressure were activated for the outgoing streams. Since no dedicated studies were published on the wastewater treatment of such a de-inking medium, the wastewater treatment was considered a black  box  with a certain efficiency. This efficiency was  varied throughout the sensitivity analyzes to examine the effect of the waste water treatment on the process. The wastewater treatment was simu lated  similarly  to  the  mechanical  separation.  Here,  the  undissolved (CUndissolved), and dissolved and solubilized (cD & S) colorants were sepa rated from the medium by a USER2 block and then removed using a split block according to a certain defined wastewater treatment efficiency. An equal degree of removal was assumed for the undissolved, and dissolved and solubilized colorants. The remaining fraction of undissolved, and dissolved  and  solubilized  colorants  was  then  reintroduced  into  the recirculating  de-inking  medium  via  a  mixer  block.  The  recirculation flow of the washing medium was closed by implementing a Transfer block, in which all properties of the obtained flow after the WWT were transferred to the input stream of the washing process, supplemented with  fresh  medium  to  compensate  losses.  A  design  specification  was applied to regulate this compensation stream in order to maintain the S/ L ratio at 42 kg/m 3 throughout the simulations. The above methodology is demonstrated in the process scheme shown in Fig. 10 of the Supple mentary Materials.

The built-in Model Analysis Tool in Aspen Plus was used to perform the sensitivity analyses. First, the residence time varied between 10 and 120 min in increments of 5 min, and this at wastewater treatment effi ciencies ranging between 30 and 90 %, in increments of 10 %. Next, the effect of the ink load on the adsorption of the colorant was also exam ined. The reference scenario, being the one-side full-tone coated sample, referred to as a relative ink load of 1. Compared to this reference, the relative ink load varied between 0.5 and 1. It should be noted that a relative ink load of 0.5 can still be considered as high. However, it was not  possible  to  reduce  this  further  due  to  the  low  concentrations  of colorants  reaching  the  limits  of  the  solver  in  Aspen  Plus,  even  after increasing the sensitivity of the solver. Again, the wastewater treatment efficiency varied between 30 % and 90 %, in 10 % increments.

2.5.3. Flow pattern

As mentioned above, the effect of the flow pattern on the potential adsorption  and  desorption  of  colorants  was  subsequently  examined. Hereby, a comparison was made between the already obtained findings for  a  single  reactor  and  several  configurations  consisting  of  multiple reactors, each with a residence time of 30 min unless stated otherwise.

2.5.3.1. Co-  and  counter-current. Several  multi-stage  process  simula tions of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 reactors were performed, each simulating the medium ' s co- and counter-current profiles relative to the plastics. During these simulations, a total residence time of 30 min was main tained,  equally  distributed  among  the  reactors,  and  the  wastewater treatment efficiency was considered to be 90 %. Next, for the multi-stage processes consisting of 4 CSTRs, the WWT efficiency was varied between 20 and 90 %, in increments of 10 %, to get insight on the difference in effect of the WWT efficiency on the adsorption of colorants in the case of co-current and counter-current configuration. A schematic representa tion of these co- and counter-current simulations is shown in Fig. 2(b) and (c), respectively.

2.5.3.2. Crossflow. A crossflow scenario was simulated consisting of a multi-stage process of 30 reactors, each with a residence time of 1 min and a S/L-ratio of 42 kg.m 3 , considering a 100 % wastewater treatment efficiency. Consequently, the plastics were repeatedly washed with un contaminated de-inking medium. Only the 11.5 wt% residual moisture content after mechanical separation and the colorants present as ink (QInk), and these already adsorbed on the plastics (qAdsorbed) were cotransferred  to  the  subsequent  reactor.  This  made  it  possible  to  gain insight into the effect of short contact times and high levels of media refreshment on the adsorption and if it is possible to desorb the adsorbed colorants by contacting the plastics with uncontaminated media. Also, the de-inking rate constant was varied during these simulations with ratios of 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 relative to the experimentally determined de-inking rate constant to obtain some understanding of the effect  of  de-inking  kinetics  on  the  uptake  of  colorants.  A  schematic representation of the simulated crossflow process is shown in Fig. 2(d).

2.5.3.3. Stand-alone  second  wash. Last,  a  simulation  was  conducted with 2 reactors in series. In this process, de-inking was performed in the first reactor, with a residence time of 30 min. In a second reactor, the plastics were subjected to a second wash with a residence time of 15 or 30 min. In this process, each reactor had a separate medium cycle with associated wastewater treatment. The wastewater treatment efficiency of the first cycle was maintained at 90 %. In comparison, the wastewater treatment efficiency of the second cycle varied between 10 and 99 %, in 10 % increments (except for the point of 99 % efficiency). A schematic representation of the simulated process is shown in Fig. 2(e).

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Experimental assessment of the adsorption-desorption mechanism

First, the staining was screened by de-inking coated LDPE films at a high solid-liquid ratio. After de-inking, the medium was refreshed five consecutive times. In each case, the plastics were washed with fresh medium for at least two days, to establish an equilibrium between the medium and the plastics. It should be noted that such extended contact time is not representative of industrial conditions, where typical total residence  times  along  the  whole  washing  chain  are  around  30  min. However, this timing was intentionally applied to demonstrate potential adsorption -desorption effects resulting from media replacement. In the subsequent simulations, a contact time of 30 min was consistently used, unless explicitly stated otherwise.

As shown in Fig. 3, it can be observed that after de-inking of both, the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), a concentration of 194 mg.L 1 and 319 mg.L 1 of dissolved and solubi lized  colorant  (cD & S)  was  present  in  the  medium,  respectively.  The higher  red  azo  lake  pigment  concentration  in  the  medium  can  be assigned to the higher concentration of PR 57:1 in the ink. For subse quent cycles with fresh de-inking media, logically, the dissolved and solubilized concentration was the highest after the second cycle. Still, somehow surprisingly, it became more or less constant from the third wash onwards. A One-Sample t -test was performed to confirm that for both  screening  experiments  with  PY  13  and  PR  57:1,  the  measured concentration  of  colorant  in  the  medium  at  the  second  cycle  was significantly different from subsequent cycles. Here, the null hypothesis, stating that the average concentration in the medium in the third and subsequent wash cycles was equal to the concentration in the medium obtained after the second cycle, was rejected for both colorants with a p -value ( α = 0.05) of 1.53*10 5 and 4.64*10 2 for PY 13 and PR 57:1, respectively. It can be observed that in the fifth wash cycle, both PY 13 and  PR  57:1  exhibit  lower  values  compared  to  the  preceding  and following cycles.  However, these measurements fall below the lower limit of the calibration curves. Therefore, this deviation is not consid ered  substantial  and  does  not  impact  the  overall  findings  of  this screening. This indicates that the majority of colorants were released during the second cycle, being the first post-wash. Thereby, it can also be noted that the release of colorants to the medium in this first post-wash was considerably lower in the case of PR 57:1 (1 mg.L 1 ) compared to PY 13 (6 mg.L 1 ), which can be related to the lower uptake of colorant and  corresponding  staining  during  the  de-inking  process.  This  lower degree  of  staining  can  be  observed  in  the  images  in  Table  2  of  the Supplementary Materials. In the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), the plastics had a yellow appearance after de-inking, and there was a noticeable release of colorants during the first post-wash. This resulted in the disappearance of the yellow staining of the plastics.

Furthermore,  cross-sectional  images  of  the  stained  LDPE  films, initially coated on one side with PY 13 and PR 57:1 inks, were obtained using microscopy, as shown in Fig. 4. A 20 μ m cross-section was pre pared using a Leica RM 2155 microtome and subsequently visualized with a Nicolet ™ iN10 infrared microscope via Omnic Picta software. Imaging was performed in transmission mode under cooled conditions (liquid nitrogen), with a collection time of 3 s. Here, it can be observed that the colorants are adsorbed to the surface of the LDPE films, indi cating that these are not able to diffuse into the polymer structure in the applied water-based de-inking medium. Similar observations were ob tained when examining cross sections of virgin, unprinted plastic films that were added to the de-inking media to confirm the occurrence of staining and no residual ink was observed. These observations, com bined  with  the  preceding  discussion  in  the  introduction  on  the adsorption-desorption of VOCs during the washing of plastic waste and the disperse dyeing of textiles, support the hypothesis that the staining of plastics is due to the reversible adsorption-desorption of the colorants released during the de-inking process.

3.2. Kinetic modeling

The three process steps, represented by the models shown in Fig. 1, were implemented in Aspen Plus. An overview of the regression pa rameters and resulting statistics of these models is shown in Table 4.

Fig. 4. Microscopic images of cross-sections from stained LDPE films coated with solvent-based ink containing (a) PY 13 and (b) PR 57:1. The adsorbed colorant is visible on the outer surfaces of the LDPE films. In each image, the staining appears more pronounced on one side of the plastic, which is attributed to the focal point of the microscope. Upon adjusting the focus, it was confirmed that the staining is present on both sides of the plastic films.

Thereby, the TIC values are consistently lower than the threshold value of 0.3, indicating that the models are capable of accurately describing the various steps [50]. This is also represented by the MRE and R 2 values for the models. It may be noted that the description of these steps for the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is systematically better compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13). Still, nevertheless, it is confirmed that the models are able to accurately describe the kinetics for both color ants. It should be noted, however, that at present no extensive testing and validation of the model has been conducted, as this is a first model that  does  not  yet  include  detailed  effects.  Therefore,  subsequent research should focus on further developing the model based on the insights  gained  to  include  several  effects,  such  as  ink  and  media composition, and process parameters, such as temperature and stirring rate,  on  the  staining  of  plastics  during  de-inking,  and  subsequent exhaustive  testing  of  the  applicability  and  validation  of  the  model should be conducted. However, it can be asserted that current models enable the description of the observed phenomena, thereby facilitating the  acquisition  of  insights,  through  subsequent  simulations,  into  the influence of the considered process parameters and flow configurations on the staining of plastics. It should be noted that the exact values of the regression  parameters  will  vary  depending  on  the  specific  process applied. Moreover, these values are also influenced by factors such as the  composition of the ink and the type of plastic. It can further be estimated that these factors may exert a more substantial influence on the regression parameters. As a result, minor errors in parameter esti mation obtained through regression are unlikely to have a significant impact on the conclusions drawn from the simulations.

As shown in Fig. 5(a), it can be observed that the rate of adsorption of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is substantially lower compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13). This is also reflected by the rate constants for adsorption shown in Table 4, here the rate constant for adsorption of PY 13 is about 5 times higher than for PR 57:1. For the yellow diarylide pigment, the adsorption-desorption equilibrium of the colorant  in  the  medium  relative  to  the  plastic  was  reached  rather quickly. Here, over the last 4 measurements (180 -330 min), an adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of 44 ± 3 mg.kg 1 was determined at a dis solved  and  solubilized  concentration  (cD & S)  of  16.6 ± 0.1  mg.L 1 . However, in the case of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), this equi librium was not yet observed after the intended run time of the exper iment. Hence, it was decided to continue the experiment overnight. In doing so, there was a further increase in adsorbed concentration from 28 mg.kg 1 to 76 mg.kg 1 , with the dissolved and solubilized concen tration  in  the  medium  decreasing  from  16  mg.L 1 to  14  mg.L 1 .  As shown in the zoom of Fig. 5(a), a more or less linear decrease in the dissolved and solubilized concentration of the red azo lake pigment was observed  in  the  first  stage.  However,  based  on  the  extra  data  point overnight and with the aid of the reversible first-order model, it can be estimated that these sorption kinetics tend to level off and approach an equilibrium.

On the other hand, as shown in Fig. 5(b), it can be observed that the rate of dissolution and solubilization of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is substantially faster, and this is with higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), being 1921 ± 52 mg.L 1 and 663 ± 26 mg.L 1 , respectively. The lower extent of adsorption combined with faster dissolution and solubilization kinetics,  and higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration indicates a higher affinity of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) for the de-inking medium, making it less likely to adsorb on the polymer. This was also observed during the screening experiments. This can be attributed to the chemical structure of both colorants, shown in Figs.  4  and  5  of  the  Supplementary  Materials.  The  yellow  diarylide pigment is a symmetric molecule, resulting in a more non-polar nature, while the red azo lake pigment will be ionized and is, therefore, a more polar molecule. The above is supported based on the Hansen solubility parameter distance [51], Dipole Moment and LogP values of PY 13 and PR 57:1, being 43.30 MPa 0.5 ,  1.29 Debye and 1.8, and 42.86 MPa 0.5 , 3.75 Debye and 0.7, respectively. This is also reflected in the red azo lake pigment ' s  dissolution  and  solubilization  rate  constant,  which  is  1.7 times higher than the yellow diarylide pigment. The dipole moments were extracted from calculations based on the density functional theory (DFT)  performed  with  Gaussian  16  [52].  The  calculations  used  the B3LYP hybrid functional [53], along with the 6 -311 ++ G(d,p) basis set, which has a proven record for organic molecules [54]. The LogP values of both pigments were determined using ChemDraw Professional v19.1 and the optimized mol files.

The rate constant of de-inking of both colorants was determined by taking into account the dissolution and solubilization, and adsorptiondesorption  kinetics.  The  resulting  rate  constants  of  de-inking  fall within two times the standard deviation on the regression coefficients of both  colorants,  being  2.6*10 3 ± 0.7*10 3 s 1 and  3.6*10 3 ± 0.4*10 3 s 1 for PY 13 and PR 57:1 respectively. The similarity of the rate constants for de-inking for both colorants can be attributed to the fact that de-inking kinetics are not related to the colorant but rather to the binder and additives, and the applied printing process. These aspects were similar for the two pigments considered in this study. However, this was not the case for the rate of dissolution and solubilization, and adsorption-desorption, as these processes are related to the respective colorants. Thereby, the plastics were 99.0 % and 99.9 % de-inked after 30 min for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), respectively. However, Fig. 5(d) indicates a faster decrease in the absolute concentration of the red azo lake pigment on the plastics than the yellow diarylide pigment. This can be related to the higher content of colorant present in this ink (QInk). Consequently, this results  in  a  higher  available  amount  of  PR  57:1  in  the  medium  and higher dissolved and solubilized concentration (cD & S) as shown in Fig. 5 (c).  Nevertheless,  the  de-inking  kinetics  are  described  based  on  the concentration  of  ink  present  on  the  plastics,  and  consequently  this higher  initial  Qink was  taken  into  account  during  the  parameter
