Besides,  this higher dissolved and solubilized concentration can also be related to the faster dissolution kinetics of PR 57:1 compared to the yellow diarylide pigment. However, as shown in Fig. 5(e), the extent of adsorption of PR 57:1 is much lower than for PY 13, and that at a higher driving force for adsorption.  For  example,  after  30  min,  the  adsorbed  concentration (qAdsorbed) was already 7 mg.kg 1 in the case of PY 13, while it was only 2 mg.kg 1 for the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1). On the other hand, at that moment 193 mg.L 1 of the yellow diarylide pigment was dissolved and solubilized in the medium, while this was 286 mg.L 1 in the case of the red azo lake pigment. For both colorants, a lag time in an increase of adsorbed concentration can be observed at the initial stage. This can be attributed to the initial absence of dissolved and solubilized colorant in the medium. Once the dissolved and solubilized concentration increases, the  driving  force  for  adsorption  increases,  and  so  does  the  adsorbed concentration on the plastics.

In addition to molecular structure, several other factors such as the presence  of  coatings,  dispersants,  as  well  as  the  particle  size  of  the pigments can affect the staining of plastics. Based on input from the ink producer, it can be assessed that the coatings and dispersants present on the pigments used in solvent-based inks will not affect the staining of plastics in water-based de-inking media. Maleic resin and gum resin are used  as  coatings  for  PY  13  and  PR  57:1,  respectively.  Both  coatings dissolve in the alkaline de-inking medium and consequently will not affect the adsorption-desorption of the colorants. Also, it can be assumed that the dispersants introduced on the pigments will not substantially affect  the  staining  process.  Since  solvent-based  inks  were  used,  the pigments contain dispersants which are insoluble in water. Hence, it can be assumed that staining will be more pronounced when water-based inks  are  introduced  into  water-based  de-inking  media,  as  the  disper sants in these inks are designed to stabilize the pigments in aqueous media,  contributing  to  the  availability  of  the  pigments  [55,56].  In addition,  it  can  be  assumed  that  the  effect  of  particle  size  is  rather limited as this is typically around 75 -200 nm for most of the pigments, including PY 13 and PR 57:1 [33,57 -59]. This particle size is consis tently employed as it yields optimal ink properties, given that both light scattering and absorption by pigments are strongly dependent on par ticle size, and that the total ink layer is only a few μ m thick [60]. Here, the smaller particle size will favor the dissolution-solubilization kinetics due to the larger specific surface area. An exception is PW 6 or TiO2 where this is around 500 nm, which can be considered non-dissolving in the considered de-inking medium, consequently not staining the plas tics. Nevertheless, the use of commercially available particle sizes, as presented in this study, is considered most representative of real-world industrial  practice.  Therefore,  it  was  deemed  of  limited  relevance  to explicitly incorporate particle size effects into the models.

Furthermore,  the  washing  medium  also  substantially  affects  the dissolution-solubilization of the colorants. This has been demonstrated by a screening in which PY 13 and PR 57:1 were dissolved in bi-distilled water, a 10 CMC CTAB solution, 2 wt% NaOH solution and a 2 wt% NaOH + 10 CMC CTAB solution. The results obtained for PY 13 and PR 57:1  are  shown  in  Figs.  6  and  7  of  the  Supplementary  Materials, respectively. In the case of PY 13, it can be observed that it does not solubilize in water and the NaOH solution, while adding CTAB, whether in the presence of NaOH or not, results in an increase in color intensity. Here, CTAB will act as a dispersant in the aqueous de-inking medium and thus induce the solubilization of the pigments. On the other hand, for PR 57:1, a slight color was already observed in water, attributable to the  dissociation  of  the  colorant.  Moreover,  the  addition  of  NaOH resulted in a substantial further increase in color intensity of the solu tion. Indeed, PR 57:1 is a laking pigment, made by the addition of acids, thereby  shifting  from  a  molecule  behaving  as  a  dye  to  a  pigment. Consequently, the addition of NaOH will result in the opposite effect, resulting in an increase in solubility of PR 57:1. Furthermore, a further increase in color intensity was observed with PR 57:1 by the addition of CTAB, which again acted as a stabilizer, promoting the solubilization of the pigment in the de-inking medium. Additionally, by measuring the absorbance of the liquids before and after filtering with syringe filters with pore sizes of 0.1 and 0.7 μ m, it was shown that both medium and colorant affect the particle size of colorants in the media. The decrease in absorbance for PY 13 and PR 57:1 in the several media is shown in Figs. 8 and 9 of the Supplementary Materials, respectively. Likewise, this can be visually observed in Figs. 6 and 7 of the Supplementary Materials, where the first vial is the initial solution, the second is the solution after filtering with a 0.7 μ m syringe filter and the third vial is this one after filtering with a 0.1 μ m syringe filter. Here it can be observed that the very  limited  color  present  in  water  of  both  colorants  is  almost completely removed by filtering with a pore size of 0.7 μ m, indicating poor dispersion of the colorants in water. On the other hand, it was found that the removal of PR 57:1 is considerably lower by adding CTAB and/or NaOH to the medium, indicating the formation of better dis persions with small particle sizes or dissolution of the colorant as dis cussed earlier. In the case of PY 13, it can be observed that the removal with the 0.1 μ m filter is about 20 % lower with the addition of NaOH compared to the CTAB solution, indicating better dispersion and thus lower particle size or better dissolution of the colorant in the medium.

Consequently, it can be postulated that the de-inking medium has a substantial influence on the dissolution and solubilization of the pig ments, and hence the degree of staining of the plastics. This will result in synergistic and antagonistic effects between the properties of the pig ments,  binder,  plastics,  de-inking  medium  and  potentially  also  the process  parameters.  It  is  essential  that  future  research  focuses  on acquiring  more  fundamental  insights  into  the  staining  of  plastics, particularly regarding the influence of surface characteristics of poly mers such as zeta potential and hydrophobicity/wettability, as well as investigating more types of pigment and the role of pigment properties and the washing medium. Preliminary findings from ongoing research suggest  that  pigment  solubilization  in  aqueous  media  is  a  timedependent process, characterized by a gradual decrease in particle size distribution (PSD). Accordingly, this explains the observed lag phase between the de-inking and staining. More in-depth research is needed to identify  and  examine  these  effects  and  to  incorporate  these  into  the model to describe the de-inking and staining of plastics. Acquiring this knowledge  will  contribute  to  a  more  detailed  understanding  of  the staining mechanisms and support the development of effective strategies to mitigate staining in recycled plastics.

3.3. Process simulations

3.3.1. Effect of residence time and wastewater treatment efficiency

First, the effect of residence time (H1) and the wastewater treatment efficiency (H3) on the adsorption of colorants was examined; these re sults are shown in Fig. 6. For both colorants, a de-inking of about 99.5 % was obtained at a residence time of 25 min. As mentioned above, the comparable degree of de-inking of both colorants can be attributed to the similar ink composition. Fig. 6(a) represents the adsorption of the yellow  diarylide  pigment  (PY  13)  against  the  residence  time  in  the reactor. It can be noticed that the degree of adsorption starts to level off once the residence time exceeds 60 min, but it continues to increase slightly, and no equilibrium is reached within 2 h of residence time. For example, at a WWT efficiency of 90 %, 494 mg.kg 1 the yellow diarylide pigment is adsorbed at a residence time of one hour, while it further increases to 662 mg.kg 1 when the residence time is extended to 2 h. This leveling off can be assigned to the relative decrease in the domi nance  of  adsorption  over  desorption,  attributable  to  the  increasing driving force for desorption due to the increase of adsorbed colorant (qadsorbed) in the plastics. Nevertheless, the first hypothesis, which states that  increasing  residence  time  results  in  higher  adsorption,  can  be considered valid.

However, as stated by the third hypothesis, the adsorbed amount of colorant  (qAdsorbed)  also  increases  along  with  a  decrease  in  WWT

efficiency,  which  can  be  attributed  to  an  increased  concentration  of dissolved and solubilized colorants in the reactor (cD & S). For example, at a residence time of 1 h and a WWT efficiency of 90 %, there is a dissolved and solubilized concentration PY 13 of 432 mg.L 1 in the reactor, while this increases to 545 mg.L 1 at a WWT efficiency of 70 % and even to 660 mg.L 1 at a WWT efficiency of 30 %. Thereby, as shown in Fig. 6(c), the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration of PY 13 in the medium is reached once the WWT efficiency is ≤ 50  %,  resulting  in consistently maximal driving forces for adsorption and uptake of the colorant into the plastics. Consequently, at a WWT efficiency of 30 %, an adsorbed concentration (qadsorbed) PY 13 of 509 mg.kg 1 , 799 mg.kg 1 , and 1111 mg.kg 1 is reached after a residence time of 30, 60, and 120 min, respectively. However, due to the adsorption of colorants, a phase shift occurs, ultimately resulting in a decrease in undissolved colorants (CUndissolved) due to the dissolution and solubilization, and subsequent adsorption of these colorants. In this regard, the scenario with a WWT efficiency of 60 % is at the tipping point. At a residence time of 35 min or less, the adsorbed concentration at a WWT efficiency of 60 % coincides with the curves of a WWT efficiency of ≤ 50 %. Once the residence time increases, all colorants are dissolved and solubilized, and cD & S decreases because of the further uptake of colorants on the plastics. For the sce narios with a higher WWT efficiency, virtually no undissolved particles

(CUndissolved) are present due to the fast dissolution and solubilization kinetics. Consequently, a decrease in dissolved and solubilized concen tration as a function of residence time is consistently observed, again attributable to the adsorption of colorants.

The adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) with respect to the residence time is shown in Fig. 6(b). In contrast to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), no distinct leveling off in an increase in adsorbed concentration can be observed with an in crease in residence time. This can be attributed to the rate constants for adsorption  and  desorption  being  substantially  lower  for  PR  57:1 compared to PY 13, resulting in lower adsorption kinetics and a slower increase in driving force for desorption. A similar trend, as discussed for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), is observed with respect to the influence of the wastewater treatment efficiency. Yet, no overlap of the curves  is  observed  with  a  decrease  in  WWT  efficiency.  This  can  be attributed to the higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration of the red azo lake pigment (1921 mg.L 1 ) compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (663 mg.L 1 ), as shown in Fig. 6(c and d). Consequently,  due  to  the  higher  Qink combined  with  the  higher maximum solubility, a higher driving force for adsorption can be ach ieved in the case of PR 57:1. However, the rate of adsorption of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is consistently lower than for the yellow diarylide  pigment  (PY  13),  attributable  to  the  lower  adsorption  rate constant.  For  example,  at  a  WWT  efficiency  of  90  %,  the  adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of PY 13 is about 494 mg.kg 1 at a residence time of 60 min, whereas this is only 227 mg.kg 1 in the case of PR 57:1. Moreover, at a WWT efficiency of 30 %, the dissolved and solubilized concentration (cD & S) PR 57:1 increases to 1881 mg.L 1 , while the cD & S of PY 13 is limited by the [cD & S]max and will be about 660 mg.L 1 . Even in this situation, the adsorbed concentration of PY 13 at a residence time of  60  min  is  higher,  being  799  mg.kg 1 ,  compared  to  the  adsorbed concentration PR 57:1 of 732 mg.kg 1 .

3.3.2. Effect of ink load

All simulations are based on one-side full-tone coated plastics, cor responding to an ink load of 14,320 ± 645 mg.kg 1 and 9725 ± 450 mg. kg 1 for the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) and the yellow diarylide pigment  (PY  13)  on  the  plastic  films,  respectively.  In  the  following simulations, this amount was varied to better understand the influence of the degree of printing of the plastics on the adsorption of colorants during the de-inking process. For this purpose, the relative amount of ink on the plastics was varied by means of a sensitivity analysis using a single CSTR with a residence time of 30 min. The relative ink load is the ratio of the initial amount of ink present on the plastics to the amount present on the one-side full-tone coated plastics. The results of these sensitivity analyzes are shown in Fig. 7.

As  stated  in  the  second  hypothesis,  the  adsorbed  concentration (qAdsorbed) increases as the degree of printing of the plastics increases. As more ink is present on plastics, more colorant will be available in the medium, resulting in a higher driving force for adsorption. For example, at a WWT efficiency of 90 %, the adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of PY 13 increases from 116 mg.kg 1 at a relative ink load of 0.5 to 328 mg. kg 1 at  a  relative  ink  load  of  1,  being  the  full-tone  coated  plastics, attributable to an increase in dissolved and solubilized concentration (cD & S) from 216 mg.L 1 to 439 mg.L 1 . This effect continues to increase as the ink load increases to the point where the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration is reached. Once achieved, there is no further increase in dissolved and solubilized amount of colorant in the reactor, and consequently, the driving force for adsorption will be constant. A similar pattern can be observed for both colorants. However, it is more pronounced in the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) due to its lower  maximal  dissolved  and  solubilized  concentration  and  stronger adsorption compared to the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1).

Lastly, it can be postulated that the effect of S/L ratio will be similar to the ink load. A decrease in S/L ratio results in a reduction in the concentration of available colorants due to the increase in the volume of de-inking media at a constant quantity of particles and ink in the system, thereby reducing the driving force for adsorption.

3.3.3. Flow pattern

3.3.3.1. Effect  of  contact  time  and  media  refreshment. First,  several multi-stage process simulations were performed with 2 to 10 CSTRs in co- and counter-current configuration, each with a total residence time of 30 min equally distributed among the reactors, as 30 min is a typical residence time in existing washing plants (including float-sinking, etc.). In first instance, the WWT efficiency was maintained at 90 %, and the number of CSTRs in the co- and counter-current multi-stage processes was varied. The output of these simulations is shown in Fig. 8 (a). As in previous simulations, the uptake of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is systematically lower than the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), but a similar pattern is noticed for both. It was observed that a counter-current multi-stage process results in a lower uptake compared to single CSTR de-inking. This can be explained by the shorter contact time between the plastics and colorants released during de-inking. This shorter contact time can be attributed to the total residence time distributed over the multiple reactors, with the medium flowing through the system in the opposite  direction,  taking  the  released  colorants  with  it.  Here  the maximum contact time depends on the number of CSTRs that must be passed through before complete de-inking is obtained. Thereby, there was a 43 % decrease in adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of the yellow diarylide  pigment  when  switching  from  a  single  CSTR  to  a  countercurrent  configuration  consisting  of  2  CSTRs,  and  an  85  %  reduction when applying a counter-current consisting of 10 CSTRs. A similar trend could be observed for PR 57:1, with a 42 % decrease when applying a counter-current  configuration  comprised  of  2  CSTRs,  and  an  80  % decrease when using a counter-current consisting of 10 CSTRs.

In the case of a co-current multi-stage process, the released colorants move together with the medium and plastics throughout the multi-stage process and, therefore, also have a contact time of 30 min. Consequently, this results in a higher adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) than countercurrent simulations. Furthermore, an increase in the adsorbed amount of colorant is observed by splitting the single CSTR into a co-current multistage process of CSTRs. This relative increase is the greatest when going from the single CSTR to 2 CSTRs in series, but also a limited further increase in adsorbed concentration is observed as the multi-stage pro cess is split into more CSTRs. For instance, an increase of 12 % and 8 % is observed for PY 13 and PR 57:1 when moving from a single CSTR to 2 CSTRs in co-current, and an increase of 23 % and 13 % when further dividing into 10 CSTRs in co-current configuration. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that the de-inking media coming from the WWT arrives  only  in  the  first  reactor,  where  a  certain  equilibrium concentration of dissolved and solubilized colorants (cD & S) in the me dium is set in relation to the concentration of colorants in the medium provided to this reactor. With the formation of a co-current process, the following  CSTRs  receive  a  de-inking  medium  that  already  contains colorants,  causing  this  equilibrium  to  be  established  at  a  higher  dis solved and solubilized concentration. Consequently, the driving force for  adsorption  in  the  following  reactors  increases,  and  the  adsorbed concentration of colorants in the plastics leaving the process is higher.

Next, to better understand the influence of the contamination level of the medium on the adsorption of the colorants in a multi-stage process, the WWT efficiency was varied for the co- and counter-current config urations consisting of 4 CSTRs. The results are shown in Fig. 8(b). Sys tematically,  it  can  be  concluded  that  a  decrease  in  WWT  efficiency results in an increase in adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of colorants, which can be related to the higher concentration of dissolved and sol ubilized  colorant  (cColorant)  in  the  medium.  Regarding  the  adsorbed concentration of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) in the co-current simulations, a clear flattening can be observed from a WWT efficiency of 70 % and below. This can be attributed to an increased adsorbed con centration and, consequently, more pronounced desorption. In the case of the counter-current simulations, this flattening cannot be observed, and the increase in adsorbed concentration with a decrease in WWT

efficiency is rather linear. This difference in trend can be related to the flow pattern throughout the reactors. At co-current, the process will tend more toward plugflow as it is split into more CSTRs and some equilib rium arises between the plastics and colorants as they flow together in the  same  direction  through  the  multi-stage  process.  In  the  case  of counter-current, on the other hand, this flattening is not observed due to the opposite flow, preventing the establishment of such an equilibrium between the two phases.

In  addition  to  the  co-  and  counter-current  configurations  already discussed, a crossflow configuration can also be utilized. Characteristic to crossflow, plastics and media were separated after each reactor, and the  plastics  encountered  fresh  de-inking  medium  in  the  subsequent reactor. A multi-stage process of 30 CSTRs, each with a residence time of 1 min, was simulated in Aspen Plus. A solid-liquid ratio of 42 kg plastics. m 3 media was maintained in each reactor, and a wastewater treatment efficiency  of  100  %  was  considered.  The  residual  ink  content  and adsorbed colorant concentrations (qAdsorbed) in the output of the reactors are shown in Fig. 9(a) and (b), and Fig. 9(c) and (d), for the yellow diarylide  pigment  (PY  13)  and  the  red  azo  lake  pigment  (PR  57:1), respectively.  Thereby, the simulations were performed for the actual experimentally  determined  de-inking  rate  constant  and  relative  rate constants of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 with respect to the experi mentally determined rate constants of de-inking. These simulations at lower de-inking kinetics were performed to demonstrate the effect of slower de-inking on the degree of adsorption, given a longer contact time of the plastics with the colorants. These simulations were consid ered relevant as the inks used during this study were relatively easy and fast to de-ink. Due to the large number of units and short residence time in each, there was a high degree of media refreshment and short contact time between the plastics and colorants. As a result, the slower the deinking, the longer the contact time between plastics and dissolved and solubilized colorants, and the associated degree of adsorption. Accord ingly, at a relative de-inking rate constant of 1, the maximum adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) PY 13 of 0.08 mg.kg 1 was obtained in reactor 3. In contrast, the maximum concentration at a relative de-inking rate constant of 1/32 was obtained in reactor 14, about 0.40 mg.kg 1 . In the subsequent reactors, the plastics were no longer in contact with dis solved  and  solubilized  colorants,  enabling  potential  desorption.  As observed in Fig. 9, the extent of desorption is negligible. In the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), at a relative de-inking rate con stant of 1, there was a decrease of 0.01 % in adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) between the third reactor and the plastics finally leaving the process.

However, as can be observed in Fig. 9, the adsorbed concentrations in these crossflow configurations were substantially lower compared to the concentrations obtained by the co- and counter-current configura tions or the single CSTR. Due to this low adsorbed concentration ( < 0.5 mg.kg 1 ),  the  driving  force  for  desorption  is  rather  limited  once  the plastics  are  de-inked.  Consequently,  almost  no  decrease  in  adsorbed concentration (qadsorbed) is observed across the several washes with fresh medium in the subsequent  reactors,  and  the  fifth  hypothesis  is  only partially confirmed (H5: A high degree of medium refreshment and short contact  time  with  contaminated  media  followed  by  a  considerable contact time with uncontaminated medium results in a lower degree of adsorption  and  subsequent  desorption  of  colorants).  Fig.  11  of  the Supplementary Materials compares the dissolved and solubilized, and adsorbed concentration of PR 57:1 obtained with a crossflow configu ration consisting of 15 against 30 CSTRs, each with a total residence time of 30 min. As the residence time in the units increases, the degree of medium refreshment in the reactors decreases, which results in an in crease in the dissolved equilibrium concentration and, thus, in a higher final adsorbed concentration.

The above findings reveal that a shorter contact time between the plastics and colorants is conducive to reduce the staining of plastics, which also affirms the fourth hypothesis. Consequently, counter-current and crossflow configurations are superior to de-inking in a single CSTR.

Also, as shown for crossflow, and stated by the sixth hypothesis, rapid de-inking  of  the  plastics  is  advantageous  to  reduce  the  contact  time between the plastics and colorants. Since the colorants are removed with the medium in opposite directions in a counter-current configuration, rapid de-inking is also beneficial in such configuration to reduce the degree  of  adsorption.  Slower  de-inking  entails  deeper  penetration  of colorants  into  the  counter-current  configuration,  resulting  in  longer contact time with the plastics and increased adsorption. On the other hand,  it  was  also  found  that  a  co-current  configuration  results  in increased adsorption due to a displacement of the equilibrium concen tration throughout the reactors and, consequently, a higher driving force for adsorption to which the plastics are exposed. Consequently, at cocurrent,  slower  de-inking  is  beneficial  because  it  lowers  the  exposed concentration in the first stage of the reactor section and, thus, the de gree of adsorption. Therefore, it can be presumed that the degree of adsorption will be higher at counter-current than at co-current if the deinking kinetics are such that the plastics are just de-inked when leaving the reactor section. However, in the case of fast de-inking, it should be stated that a co-current process configuration is not favorable for deinking plastics.

3.3.3.2. Stand-alone second wash. Since it was already shown that the adsorption of colorants is a reversible process depending on the driving force,  it  was  hypothesized  that  the  desorption  of  adsorbed  colorants (qadsorbed) is possible. However, the crossflow simulations revealed this is not feasible at low adsorbed concentrations due to a low driving force. However, it is not unusual in industrial settings to have a longer contact time between the plastics and the colorants in the media due to a lower degree of media refreshment and lower WWT efficiency, resulting in an increased  adsorbed  concentrations  of  colorants.  Therefore,  it  was examined if it is feasible to desorb adsorbed colorants after initial deinking in a single CSTR. For this purpose, a configuration consisting of two CSTRs in series, each with a separate media cycle, was simulated. The first CSTR acts as a de-inking reactor, in which de-inking, dissolu tion and solubilization, and adsorption of colorants take place, while the second reactor is used for the second wash. In the first reactor, a resi dence time of 30 min and a WWT efficiency of 90 % were consistently maintained. After mechanical separation, the plastics were transferred to the second reactor, where the plastics underwent a second washing. Since the actual de-inking already took place in the first reactor, the plastics in the second reactor only encountered the adsorbed colorants (qAdsorbed) and the colorants that were co-transferred via the residual moisture content (11.5 wt%) after mechanical separation.

The results of these simulations for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) are shown in Fig. 10(a) and (b), respectively. Here the adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) after the first reactor is shown by the dashed line, which is considerably higher in the case of PY 13 (328 mg.kg 1 ) than for PR 57:1 (118 mg.kg 1 ). At a residence time of 30 min compared to 15 min in the second reactor, the degree of desorption was systematically higher in the case of PY 13, where a maximum removal of 25 % was obtained at a residence time of 30 min, while it was only 15 % at a residence time of 15 min. Here the desorption  rate  decreased  as  the  wastewater  treatment  efficiency decreased, but a decrease in the adsorbed concentration of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) was consistently observed. For example, at a residence time of 30 min, there was a colorant removal of 25 % at a WWT of 99 %, while it decreased to 15 % at a WWT efficiency of 10 %. In contrast, the second wash did not always result in a decrease in adsorbed concentration for PR 57:1. Once the wastewater treatment efficiency of the second media cycle became less than 30 %, there was no removal, but  an  increase  in  adsorbed  concentration  of  PR  57:1  was  observed during the second wash. In this case, a longer residence time resulted in a stronger increase in adsorbed concentration. For example, at a resi dence time of 30 min and WWT efficiency of 99 %, there was a decrease of 2.6 % in adsorbed amount (qAdsorbed) of PR 57:1, while there was an increase of 3.3 % when the WWT efficiency decreased to 10 %. This increase indicates that adsorption dominates over desorption, which can be explained by the relatively lower concentrations of already adsorbed red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), and the increase in dissolved and sol ubilized concentration (cD & S) present in the medium due to the reduced decontamination of the de-inking medium. In the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), a decrease in adsorbed concentration was consistently observed, which can be assigned to the higher adsorbed concentration and associated driving force for desorption after the first wash. Consequently, the seventh hypothesis was only partially confirmed (H7: A second wash having its own media cycle promotes the desorption of colorants.). It was shown that a second wash can indeed result in a reduction in adsorbed concentration, but as with previous simulations, the WWT efficiency is decisive.

3.4. Potential pathways to prevent the staining of plastics during de-inking

Staining of plastics due to the adsorption of colorants is a reversible process that only occurs when colorants are released in the medium after liberating them from the resin. As staining is a reversible process driven by the available concentrations in the liquid phase and plastics, it is, in principle,  possible  to  (partially)  counteract  the  staining  of  plastics. However,  simulations  have  shown  that  the  complete  desorption  of already adsorbed colorants is probably not industrially feasible by me dium refreshment when utilizing caustic soda and detergent as a deinking medium. Consequently, it is critical to counteract the adsorp tion of colorants preventively. A non-exhaustive overview of potential measures to counteract the uptake of colorants is given in Table 5.

First, it was shown that the residence time in the reactor is a deter mining factor in the degree of adsorption. By changing the de-inking conditions such that the de-inking rate increases, the residence time in the reactor can decrease, potentially reducing the degree of adsorption. Accordingly, the composition of the de-inking medium can be modified, and various surfactants may be employed. As a result, the de-inking kinetics can potentially be enhanced, but this can equally contribute to the dissolution and solubilization of the colorants and consequently to the staining of the plastics. For example, it is possible that certain col orants  that  are  not  freely  available  in  the  tested  aqueous  de-inking medium, and thus not result in staining,  may  become dissolved and solubilized  in  alternative  de-inking  media  and  result  in  an  increased staining of the plastics. Consequently, targeted research into the use of detergents and alternative de-inking media is a crucial aspect in mini mizing the dissolution and solubilization of pigments, thereby reducing the staining of plastics.

The freely dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant in the medium is the driving force for adsorption, hence it is crucial to keep this low. This can be achieved in various manners, a first being the appli cation of proper wastewater treatment. As shown by the simulations, a higher wastewater treatment efficiency results in lower concentrations of colorants in the recirculated medium and consequently in a lower extent of adsorption. These findings are consistent with Roosen et al. [19] on removing VOCs from plastic waste by washing. Further research into the effective treatment of wastewater from de-inking processes is therefore essential, including techniques such as adsorption, membrane filtration, and the application of oxidizing agents like ozone or perox ides. Economic feasibility will be a key consideration, as profit margins in plastic recycling are typically narrow. Consequently, consumption of chemicals must be minimized. Besides, it can also be expected that a contaminated  washing  medium  may  contribute  to  an  increase  in contamination, and thus staining, of relatively clean input plastics. This can potentially be overcome by an alternative approach, where a prior sorting  step  takes  place  in  which  colored  and  uncolored  plastics  are separated and thus washed separately. Such approach would result in a waste stream that is much less, if at all, loaded with ink and would thus reduce  the  amount  of  colorants  in  the  washing  cycle,  potentially reducing  the  degree  of  staining  and  resulting  in higher  quality recyclates.

text: Table 5 Overview of potential pathways to prevent the staining of plastics during de-inking.

Ideally,  dissolution  and  solubilization  of  the  colorants  should  be prevented.  This  can  potentially  be  obtained  by  the  use  of  primers. Primers are an additional layer between the substrate and the printed ink, applied during the production of multilayers, that is designed in a way that  it  does  not  degrade  during  ordinary  use  but  can  be  easily removed in the mechanical recycling process [61 -63]. By targeting this primer instead of the ink or by altering the de-inking conditions such that the primer degrades much faster than the binder of the ink, no, or at least  to  a  much  lower  extent,  colorant  will  become  available  in  the medium, suppressing the adsorption of colorants. Additionally, the ink composition will influence both the de-inking and the associated stain ing of plastics. From producer to producer, this composition can alter, affecting the properties of the inks. Further research should therefore include the influence of the ink composition on de-inking and staining. Modifying the ink formulation may help reduce staining, for instance by using alternative pigments that inherently exhibit lower tendencies for staining and bleeding, or by encapsulating pigments to prevent their release during de-inking. These insights can contribute to the formula tion of design-for-recycling guidelines for inks. Indeed, it is crucial to have a detailed understanding of the composition of inks, to gain deeper insight  into  synergistic  or  antagonistic  effects  that  occur  between various process parameters and material properties, and to implement these effects in a further elaboration of the model. Yet, ink compositions are often confidential, which complicates such developments.

De-inking  in  a  single  CSTR  with  high  dissolved  and  solubilized colorant concentrations will result in high staining. Here, applying a dedicated second wash with a clean medium will potentially result in a decrease  in  adsorbed  concentration.  However,  this  wash  will  only remove the first part of the adsorbed colorants, and a residual amount will  remain  on  the  plastics  due  to  the  decrease  in  driving  force  for desorption.  Preventing  staining  is,  therefore,  better  than  subsequent removal. This is possible by applying a crossflow configuration with very low residence time in each unit and a high degree of media refreshment. In contrast, applying a counter-current process also reduces adsorption due  to  the  reduced  contact  time  between  the  plastics  and  colorants. However, the degree of media refreshment and contact time reduction is substantially lower than crossflow, resulting in a non-negligible amount of adsorbed colorants. Since the considered crossflow configuration can be regarded as economically unfeasible and staining is only limitedly reduced by means of countercurrent flow, it can be argued that it is industrially  unfeasible  to  completely  counteract  staining  by  merely altering the process flow, and other measures are needed to mitigate staining.

Roosen  et  al.  [20]  demonstrated  that  VOCs  desorb  better  from polyolefins in non-polar media than in a caustic soda with a detergent solution. Consequently, it is supposed that changing the de-inking me dium will be necessary to resolve the staining issue and achieve highquality transparent recyclates. Accordingly, this might introduce addi tional process steps, such as separating plastics and washing media, and rinsing the plastics with water in a post-wash to remove the new deinking  medium,  resulting  in  an  increase  in  Capital  Expenditures (CAPEX) and Operating Expenditures (OPEX). However, similar to the potential options previously discussed for counteracting adsorption or promoting  the  desorption  of  colorants,  this  cost  increase  must  be weighed against the increase in the economic value of the obtained highquality recyclates. Furthermore, it is also crucial to consider the envi ronmental impact of using alternative media. For example, it has already been reported that the use of surfactants, such as cationic surfactants with  tertiary  amine  groups,  can  be  potentially  hazardous  and  may induce toxicological concerns [64].

In  addition  to  the  potential  environmental  exposure  to  de-inking media,  the  release  of  pigments  into  the  environment  must  also  be avoided. As demonstrated by Guo et al. [34], solubilized pigments are not  completely  removed  through  flocculation  followed  by  filtration. When released in this manner, pigments may enter the environment as nanoparticles, exhibiting a wide range of physicochemical properties. The risks associated with the use of pigments in nanoparticulate form have been extensively discussed in a report by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) [65], which noted, however, that data on the nano toxicology  of  organic  pigments  remains  scarce.  Several  studies  have investigated the discharge of synthetic dyes into wastewater, particu larly from the textile, paper, and leather industries. These sectors are known to release large volumes of colored effluents into aquatic envi ronments, although precise numbers are lacking [66]. The presence of synthetic  dyes  in  wastewater  has  become  a  major  environmental concern due to their toxic effects and ecological consequences [66,67]. Their presence in water reduces light penetration, thereby impairing photosynthesis  and  disrupting  aquatic  food  chains.  Moreover,  many synthetic dyes exhibit carcinogenic, mutagenic, and teratogenic prop erties,  adversely  affecting  plants,  animals,  and  humans  [67].  Conse quently, it can be surmised that the release of pigments during the deinking process of plastic waste must be strictly avoided and recycling plants have to foresee suitable water treatment procedures.

However, in the context of plastic recycling, it is common practice for recyclers to minimize water discharge by maximizing the reuse of wash water [23,49]. This approach reduces the discharge of contaminated wastewater and consequently the pollutants entering the environment. However, the reuse of wash media might lead to the accumulation and recirculation of pigments within the washing process, thereby increasing the staining of the recycled plastics. Such presence of adsorbed pigments can limit the suitability of these recyclates for contact sensitive appli cations, such as food contact materials. In Europe, Regulation (EU) No. 10/2011 and its  amendment  2020/1245  establish  specific  migration limits  for  substances  migrating  from  packaging  into  food,  based  on standardized migration testing. If these limits are exceeded, the recy clates cannot be used for food contact applications, thereby protecting consumers from potential harmful exposures.

Above  discussion  underscores  the  importance  of  proper  media management in washing processes within plastic recycling. It highlights the need for advanced research to optimize wastewater treatment and sludge handling, thereby minimizing environmental losses and exposure.

4. Conclusion

While scaling up the de-inking processes, it was observed that the plastics were stained after de-inking, although they were effectively deinked. This staining of plastics yields discolored recyclates, resulting in a decrease  in  quality  and  economic  value.  Staining  was  found  to  be  a reversible process due to the adsorption and desorption of the colorants released, dissolved and solubilized during the de-inking process. Next, the de-inking, dissolution and solubilization, and adsorption-desorption of colorants PY 13 and PR 57:1 were successfully described by using first-order  kinetics,  where  the  dissolution  and  solubilization  kinetics were limited by the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration, and the adsorption-desorption was described using the reversible firstorder model.

Simulations revealed that the absorbed concentration of colorants continues to increase during the de-inking process, and no equilibrium was reached within 2 h for both PY 13 and PR 57:1. Consequently, deinking should be fast to limit the residence time in the reactors. It was also shown that a higher ink load and lower wastewater treatment ef ficiency  results  in  more  colorants  in  the  media  and,  consequently,  a higher  driving  force  for  adsorption.  The  application  of  a  co-current multistage process results in an increase (up to 23 % within range of simulations)  in  adsorbed  concentration,  while  counter-current  and crossflow configurations, on the other hand, result in a shorter contact time and less uptake of colorants, this being most pronounced in the case of crossflow. As such, within the range of simulations, a decrease up to 85 % was obtained by countercurrent and an adsorbed concentration < 0.5  ppm  was  consistently  achieved  with  crossflow  configuration. Furthermore, it was shown that adsorption is dominant over desorption, making desorption only feasible  when the adsorbed  concentration is high  while  the  dissolved  concentration  in  the  medium  remains  low. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that unit and process design should minimize contact time between plastics and colorants, and the wastewater treatment should be optimized to prevent the adsorption of colorants. On the other hand, Design for Recycling guidelines may also contribute to the reduction of staining. The use of primers, optimizing ink compositions and decreasing ink densities in printing are considered measures to reduce staining and thus improve the quality of recyclates.

1. Introduction

Polyolefins, produced from olefin (alkene) monomers, are the most widely used commercial polymers [1]. Ethylene-based polyolefins can be  classified  as  low-density  polyethylene  (LDPE),  linear  low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), and ultralow-density polyethylene (ULDPE). Polyolefins are widely used due to their unique properties, such as durability, barrier performance, op tical  clarity,  versatility,  processability,  and  cost-effectiveness  [2,3]. LDPE and LLDPE are utilized in the manufacture of reusable bags, trays and  containers,  agricultural  films,  industrial  wrappings,  and  food packaging films. HDPE is mostly used in the production of toys, milk

A B S T R A C T

Increased use of plastics and corresponding generation of plastic waste leads to growing pressure for recycling technologies that are both economically viable and environmentally sound. For plastic films, widely used in packaging  and  comprising  mostly  polyolefins,  mechanical  recycling  is  not  practical,  hence  the  interest  in chemical recycling. Dissolution/precipitation recycling can recover polyolefins for re-use, with energy needs and emissions much lower than pyrolysis. The dissolution of polyolefins is key to this recycling process, however, the underlying phenomena which govern the dissolution of semicrystalline polymers are little studied. To address this  gap  in  knowledge,  the  swelling  and  dissolution  kinetics  of  high-density  polyethylene  (HDPE)  films  are investigated here. Experiments are designed to obtain the time evolution of HDPE dissolved mass and degree of crystallinity.  A  mathematical  model  is  developed  to  describe  the  swelling  and  dissolution  of  semicrystalline HDPE based on the transport phenomena and thermodynamics governing the process. Experimental data are used to validate the model and to obtain values for the two key fitted parameters, decrystallization constant and disentanglement rate. The detailed information provided by the model, spatial and temporal composition and solvent diffusion, reveals the molecular mechanism of HDPE dissolution. A parametric analysis is performed using the validated model to simulate dissolution phenomena at varying conditions, including initial degree of crystallinity and film thickness. These insights on polyethylene dissolution facilitate the design of more energy efficient and environment-friendly dissolution-precipitation recycling processes. The model can be extended to probe the dissolution of other semicrystalline polymers.

Global  plastic  production  grew  at  a  compound  annual  growth  rate (CAGR) of 8.3%, increasing from 1.7 Mt in 1950 to 348 Mt in 2017 [4]. From 2017 to 2023, growth slowed to ~2.9% CAGR, reaching 413.8 Mt in 2023 [6]. Polyethylene (PE) is the largest single contributor to this output, accounting for 26.2% of total global plastic production in 2023 [6]. In 2017, over three-quarters of end-of-life plastic in the US was sent to landfill [7]. It has been reported that PE accounts for more than 33% of microplastics in landfill leachate [8]. According to a 2019 Department of Energy (DOE) study, the US landfilled 82% of HDPE, while only 10% was recycled [9], highlighting that much remains to be done to improve HDPE recycling. Mechanical recycling alone is insufficient for PE due to a  range  of  material  and  process  limitations  [10,11].  Many  PE-based products, particularly in packaging, are multilayer films that incorpo rate  incompatible  polymers,  and  even  metal  layers  (e.g.,  in  aseptic packaging).  These  material  combinations  compromise  the  recycled output [12 -14]. Additionally, PE waste is often contaminated with food residues,  labels,  inks,  pigments,  and  odors  that  are  difficult  to  fully remove through  mechanical  processes,  further  degrading  the  quality and usability of the recycled product [15,16]. Addition of compatibil izers could help improve mechanical recycling rates [17,18], but their application  remains  limited  due  to  high  costs.  In  general,  PE-based products, especially packaging, tend to be difficult to recycle through primary and secondary (mechanical) recycling methods [13,15].

A solution for managing such plastic waste is tertiary recycling, also known  as  advanced  or  chemical  recycling,  which  converts  polymer chains into feedstock for the production of fuels [19], chemical building blocks [20], or specialty chemicals [5,19], through depolymerization [19],  pyrolysis  [19],  hydrocracking  [21],  or  gasification  [22].  These methods  involve  high  energy  consumption  and  CO2  and  toxic  gases emissions,  and  limited  sustainability  [23].  Consequently,  chemical recycling is viewed as an environmental health risk and attracts negative publicity [23]. In addition, the presence of additives in plastic waste complicates  chemical  recycling  processes  [24].  Some  of  these  disad vantages  can  be  mitigated  using  dissolution-precipitation  recycling [25 -28].  In  dissolution-precipitation  recycling,  plastic  waste  is  first processed in a selective solvent to dissolve the target polymer. Immis cible solids are then removed via filtration. The target polymer is next precipitated from its solution using an anti-solvent, temperature drop, or both [29]. This method can unlock the potential for utilizing polyolefins that are currently landfilled or incinerated. Compared to other chemical recycling methods, dissolution-precipitation can be considered as true recycling,  as  it  recovers  polymers,  and  involves  lower  energy  re quirements and CO2 emissions [30]. The potential of dissolution-precipitation  for  recycling  PE  in  an  industrial  scale  is demonstrated by APK ' s Newcycling facility in Merseburg, Germany that recovers  primarily  PE,  and  in  some  cases  polypropylene  (PP),  from multilayer  film  waste  [31,32].  This  platform  is  being  scaled  under LyondellBasell ' s new  ownership, signaling continued commercial development  [33,34].  In  addition,  through  pilot  and  demonstration plants [31], such as a Unilever project in Indonesia and a unit at L ¨ OMI in Germany,  the  Fraunhofer  Institute  IVV ' s  CreaSolv  process  recovers quality PE from multilayer flexible packaging [35,36].

Central to dissolution-precipitation recycling of polyethylene is its dissolution. Despite PE being produced in high volumes for decades, there is  no  published information on PE dissolution kinetics and the underlying mechanisms. Few solvents are capable of dissolving poly ethylene, typically at high temperatures and low polymer concentra tions.  No  experimental  studies  of  PE  dissolution  are  available,  and relevant reports that focus on PP date from the 1970s [37]. Models of semicrystalline-polymer dissolution efforts are also scarce; the earliest study from 1997 was for poly(vinyl alcohol) in water [38]. In a more recent study, a phenomenological model was developed to analyze the dissolution of micrometer-sized semicrystalline cellulose fibers in ionic liquids [39 -41].

This  study  addresses  the  following  open  questions:  What  are  the underlying  phenomena  governing  the  dissolution  of  semicrystalline polyethylene? What are the key parameters governing the dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline polyethylene, and how do variations in these parameters influence the overall dissolution behavior? An integrated experimental and modeling effort was deployed to this end. Two types of time-resolved experimental data were generated in this work, crystal linity  of  undissolved  polymer  and  mass  loss  due  to  dissolution.  A comprehensive mathematical model, incorporating relevant transport phenomena  and  thermodynamic  principles,  described  the  coupled swelling and dissolution behavior of polyethylene. Experimental data were used to validate the model and extract key fitted parameters that carry  physical  meaning.  The  validated  model  was  used  to  perform parametric analyses across a range of conditions, enabling assessment of how key parameters influence dissolution behavior.

The novelty of this work includes: (i) integration of experiments and modeling to understand the mechanism underlying the dissolution of semicrystalline polyethylene; (ii) model-predicted information at experimental conditions that are difficult or expensive to access exper imentally;  and  (iii)  parametric  analysis  on  dissolution  kinetics  that benefit large-scale recycling applications. The experimentally-validated dissolution model developed here provides a predictive basis for largescale processing and reveals operating windows for the efficient disso lution  and  recovery  of  polyethylene  and  other  polyolefins  during dissolution-precipitation recycling.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Polymer and solvent

High density polyethylene copolymer 1-butene with density of 0.94 0.97 g/cm 3 , melting range 125 - 140 °C, and auto-ignition temperature 350 °C, produced by Braskem S.A. and supplied by Braskem America, Inc. (Philadelphia, PA), is used in this study. The solvent used for dis solving HDPE is p -xylene (99 + %, extra pure, Fisher Scientific Company LLC, Boston, MA), with 0.8660 g/mL density, 106.17 g/mol molecular weight, 13.0 °C melting point, and 138.0 °C boiling point. Dissolution experiments  were carried  out  at  101 °C  and  104 °C  with  temperature fluctuation within 0.5 °C. These temperatures were selected based on the dissolution temperatures of low weight fractions (0.0149 to 0.42) HDPE in xylene at 1 bar, reported in the range 97 °C - 107 °C [42]. The selected temperatures were below both the p -xylene boiling point and the HDPE melting temperature.

2.2. Experiments on dissolution and decrystallization kinetics

2.2.1. Dissolved mass over time

HDPE films were prepared by placing approximately 60 HDPE pellets into  two  custom-made  brass  ring  molds.  Two  mold  geometries  were used: one with a thickness of 0.1 mm and an inner diameter of 5 mm, and the other with a thickness of 0.6 mm and an inner diameter of 2.5 mm, each of which was wrapped in a Teflon PTFE film (McMaster-Carr, P/N: 8569K36). The sample mold was then transferred to a pre-heated hy draulic press (Carver Inc.) set to 180 °C. A force of 4000 pounds was applied for 5 min to produce HDPE films with uniform thicknesses of 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm. Electronic calipers (McMaster-Carr, P/N: 4996A51, increment: 0.01 mm) were used to confirm the thickness of the polymer films. Individual samples were cut using a scalpel from the bulk mold to achieve the desired dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 0.1 mm and 10 mm × 10 mm × 0.6 mm, respectively. A cage-shaped holder made of 304 stainless steel wire mesh (1 mm square holes, 0.4 mm wire diam eter) was used to contain the polymer fully surrounded by solvent and avoid contact with the container.

First,  10  mL  solvent  was  poured  into  a  pre-weighed  30  mL  glass container. The container was then placed in a preheated silicone oil bath (Sigma-Aldrich),  with  temperature  controlled  by  a  hotplate-stirrer (VWR). The system was left for approximately 30 min to equilibrate with the oil bath temperature. Then the pre-weighed wire mesh con taining the polymer sample whose weight is known was put in the sol vent. At certain time intervals, the dissolution process was stopped by pulling out the wire mesh and putting it in a pre-weighed 20 mL vial. Immediately after that,  the  glass  containing  the  solvent  and  the  dis solved polymer was removed from the oil bath, and the outer wall of the glass was cleaned completely from oil droplets using tissue paper.

Afterward, the vial containing wire mesh with undissolved polymer was placed in an oven at 60 °C for 12 h to completely evaporate the solvent. The glass containing the dissolved polymer was dried at 130 °C for  12  h.  The  amounts  of  undissolved  and  dissolved  polymer  were determined by weighing the dried vial (including wire mesh and un dissolved polymer) and the glass (containing dissolved polymer), and subtracting their respective initial weights. At each time interval, the reported  results  and  corresponding  error  bars  are  obtained  by  mean average of at least five experimental data sets.

2.2.2. Time evolution of crystallinity

A temperature-controlled FT-IR liquid flow cell (Harrick Scientific TFC-S25) for real-time in-situ experiments and peak-fitting procedure described  elsewhere  [43],  was  used  to  quantify  the  HDPE  degree  of crystallinity in real time (See Fig. 1). A VERTEX 70 FT-IR spectrometer (Bruker,  Billerica,  MA,  USA),  operating  at  2  cm 1 resolution,  1  mm aperture, 1 sample scan, and 64 background scans was used. A repeated scan  measurement  method  (OPUS  7.5  software)  captured  the  time evolution spectra between 700-750 cm 1 [43]. The procedure reported by Stavinski et al. [43] was used to quantify the crystallinity (xc) of HDPE:

xc = I crystalline I crystalline + α I amorphous ) × 100% (1)

where I crystalline and Iamorphous are the integrated areas of the crystalline and  amorphous  bands,  respectively.  The  coefficient α accounts  for intrinsic  IR  band  intensity  variations  between  the  crystalline  and amorphous  bands  [43].  Electronic  calipers  (McMaster-Carr,  0 ' -4 ' ± 0.001 ' ) determined HDPE film dimensions to be 5 × 5 × 0.05 mm. This geometry was chosen because, in the FT-IR liquid flow cell setup, the  HDPE film is adhered to a ZnSe optical window and exposed to solvent from only one side (proportional to thickness direction) (Fig. 1), unlike in the dissolution experiments where films are fully immersed and in contact with solvent on both sides. The film dimensions were scaled to maintain comparable solvent diffusion path lengths, ensuring consistent solvent exposure conditions across both experimental setups. After  solvent  filling,  the  liquid  cell  maintained  static  conditions  (no flow) throughout the data acquisition. Four trials per temperature were performed in order to account for experimental  variability;  standard deviation is calculated according to Eq. S1.

Since the FT-IR liquid flow cell is limited to rather thin films ( ≤ 0.05 mm), visual inspection was used to determine the time for full decrys tallization of thicker (0.6 mm) HDPE films. To initiate the decrystalli zation process, HDPE films (10 mm × 10 mm × 0.6 mm) were placed inside a stainless steel wire mesh that was then fully immersed in a 10 mL vial containing solvent at the target temperature. The progress of decrystallization was monitored visually, with the film ' s transition to complete transparency serving as the indicator of complete decrystallization.

2.3. Modeling of semicrystalline polyolefin film dissolution kinetics

Although the mechanism of semicrystalline polymer dissolution is still under investigation [39,44,45], previous studies have proposed a multi-step process involving solvent diffusion into the polymer struc ture,  disruption  of  crystalline  domains  (decrystallization),  polymer swelling due to solvent, disentanglement of polymer chains, and even tual diffusion of these disentangled chains into the surrounding solvent [46]. In this study, a model for dissolution of semicrystalline polymer fiber [39] was modified to describe the swelling and dissolution of a semi-infinite semicrystalline slab. A key modification was to account for temperature-  and  composition-dependent  variations  of  the  solvent diffusion coefficient in the polymer, through the incorporation of free volume theory.

The  model  captures  each  step  of  polyolefin  dissolution  using appropriate  transport  phenomena  and  thermodynamics  equations,  as depicted in Fig. 2: solvent diffusion into the polymer, specimen swelling coupled with decrystallization of crystalline domains, chain disentan glement, and diffusion of disentangled chains into a gel-like boundary layer, followed by gradual specimen shrinkage as the dissolution pro gresses. In the following, the governing equations used to model the dissolution kinetics of polyolefin films are presented.

Chain disentangle ment and dissolution may proceed only after this interfacial decrystal lization is complete. At this point, disentangled polymer chains diffuse into the surrounding solvent through a thin, gel-like boundary layer; defined  as  the  interface  between  the  polymer  and  solvent;  with  a thickness ( δ ), assumed to be 5% of the initial film thickness, i.e., δ = 0.05 × L(t = 0) [39,52]. 2.4.1. Model inputs, parameters, and predictions

The  experimental  inputs  for  the  model  include  temperature  (T), initial film thickness (2L0), initial degree of crystallinity (dc, determined via DSC), and polymer molecular weight (M).

Parameters taken from the literature include solvent viscosity ( ƞ s ), Flory-Huggins interaction parameter ( χ a), and thickness of the gel-like boundary  layer  ( δ ).  The  solvent  volume  fraction  at  the  polymersolvent interface ( ∅ s,i) and the diffusion coefficient of polymer chains in solvent (Dp), were calculated from the Flory-Rehner theory, Eq. (S6), and Stokes-Einstein equation, Eq. (12).

The key fitted parameters, decrystallization rate constant (Kdec) and polymer chain disentanglement rate (rdis), were determined by mini mizing the deviation between model predictions and experimental data.

The model predicts film thickness (L(t)); also, volume fractions of crystalline polymer ( ∅ p,c), amorphous polymer ( ∅ p,a), and solvent ( ∅ s) in the film, and solvent volume fraction in the amorphous phase ( ∅ sa), which  all  vary  with  both  time  and  position  within  the  film  during dissolution. Additionally, the model predicts the solvent diffusivity into the  polymer  (Ds)  and  the  self-diffusion  coefficient  of  solvent  in  the amorphous polymer phase (Dsa), both of which change with time and position  due  to  their  dependence  on  the  local  volume  fractions.  The induction time (tind) is determined within the model: dissolution begins once the crystalline fraction at the polymer-solvent interface reaches zero, which depends on Kdec, a fitted parameter.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Polyethylene decrystallization and dissolution kinetics: Experimental data

Experimental data on decrystallization and dissolution kinetics of HDPE films in p -xylene are discussed here, with a focus on the effects of film thickness and temperature. Dissolution progresses approximately linearly with time for both 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm HDPE films, indicating a steady dissolution rate once the process begins (Fig. 3). This is consistent with  observations  in  semicrystalline  polymer  systems  such  as  poly ( α -methylstyrene) (PAMS) films dissolving in binary solvents [58], and poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) crystals dissolving in various solvents [45].

The polymer crystallinity drops rapidly upon solvent contact, with the film becoming fully amorphous before dissolution is completed. The shorter  decrystallization  time  compared  to  the  total  dissolution  time confirms  that  chain  disentanglement  and  diffusion  out  of  the  solid polymer film are the slower, rate-limiting processes [39]. This separa tion of timescales supports the model ' s assumption that decrystalliza tion precedes dissolution. In all cases, a short, initial delay is observed

(a)

Fig. 3. Experimental results (dots) and model fits (solid lines) to experimental data for (a) undissolved polymer fraction, and (b) time evolution of crystallinity, for 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm thick HDPE films in p -xylene at 101 °C.

before the start of dissolution, corresponding to the induction time [39, 49 -51]. During this period, solvent diffusion, swelling, and decrystalli zation begin at the polymer-solvent interface.

Film thickness strongly influences the extent and duration of diffu sion, swelling, decrystallization, and dissolution. 0.1 mm films decrys tallize  and  dissolve  faster  than  0.6  mm  films,  consistent  with  prior studies examining the influence of film thickness on polymer dissolution rates [59].

Even a small increase in temperature (from 101 °C, shown in Fig. 3, to 104 °C,  data  provided  in  the  Supplementary  document  (Figure  S4)) significantly decreases the decrystallization time in HDPE films: by 55% for 0.1 mm films and 37% for 0.6 mm films, while the overall dissolution time decreases modestly, 6.7% and 5.5%, respectively. These observa tions  suggest  that  decrystallization  is  far  more  temperature-sensitive than  chain  disentanglement.  Therefore,  optimizing  temperature  is particularly  effective  in  accelerating  both  the  decrystallization  phase preceding dissolution and the overall dissolution process.

These  experimental  results,  in  conjunction  with  the  results  from modeling discussed next, support the quantitative understanding of the HDPE dissolution process.

3.2. Validation of model that describes polyethylene dissolution kinetics

To  validate  the  dissolution  model,  its  predictions  were  fitted  to experimental data on HDPE decrystallization and dissolution kinetics. Fig. 3 shows the model fits well experimental results for both the un dissolved polymer fraction and crystallinity time evolution for two film thicknesses at 101 °C, while the corresponding agreement at 104 °C is provided in the Supplementary document (Figure S4). This validates the molecular-level  mechanisms  described  in  the  model,  and  provides values for key fitting parameters and insights regarding  HDPE dissolution.

The key fitting parameters, disentanglement rate (rdis) and decrys tallization constant (Kdec), were determined from the fits to the validated model: rdis = 2.2 × 10 8 m/s ( ± 6.89%) and Kdec = 12.8 × 10 3 1/s ( ± 6.0%) at 101 °C, and as rdis = 2.4 × 10 8 m/s ( ± 2.8%) and Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s ( ± 7.13%) at 104 °C. As expected, both Kdec and rdis were found to be independent of film thickness. The increase in Kdec  with temper ature (~161%) is substantially greater than that of rdis  (~9%). This is consistent with findings on cellulose decrystallization [40], and with kinetic theory indicating that structural transformations of crystalline domains are governed by temperature-dependent rate constants [38,39, 60 -62]. Indeed, polymer melting and crystallization kinetics in semi crystalline polymers often follow Arrhenius-type behavior [63], indicating  that  even  modest  temperature  increases  can  substantially enhance  crystalline domain  mobility  [64], and, correspondingly, accelerate structural disruption (decrystallization).

The induction time (tind) for both 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm thick HDPE films is approximately 48 seconds at 101 °C, decreasing to 30 seconds at 104 °C in p -xylene. This reduction is attributed to enhanced molecular mobility  at  elevated  temperatures,  which  accelerates  the  start  of dissolution.

3.3. Model-derived insights into polyethylene dissolution

With the mechanism described in the model validated, we can now use results from the model to gain deeper insights into the HDPE film composition and structural evolution during dissolution. The knowledge on  how  swelling,  decrystallization, and  solvent transport evolve temporally  and  spatially  across  the  film  thickness  can  be  useful  for optimizing  polymer  dissolution  in  applications  such  as  dissolutionprecipitation recycling.

Fig. 4 shows the dimensionless thickness of 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm thick HDPE films over time at 101 °C and 104 °C. The film thickness initially increases due to solvent diffusion, followed by a reduction caused by decrystallization, disentanglement, and start of dissolution (Eq. 10).

To clarify the temperature-dependent differences in swelling behavior between thin and thick films, the model was used to examine the spatial distributions of solvent and crystalline domains across the film thickness. Fig. 5a and 5b present the volume fractions of solvent

3.4. Parametric analysis

The validated model is now applied to perform parametric analysis, generating  results  under  various  simulated  conditions  to  assess  the impact  on  polyethylene  swelling  and  dissolution  kinetics  of  experi mental  parameters  such  as  polymer  degree  of  crystallinity  and  film thickness, and key dissolution parameters, such as decrystallization rate constant  and  disentanglement  rate,  thereby  extending  the  analysis beyond the specific polymer and solvent systems studied experimentally.

3.4.1. Effect of polymer initial crystallinity

While  typical  commercial  HDPE  exhibits  high  crystallinity,  pro cessing modifications such as copolymerization or rapid quenching can reduce crystallinity to 30% in order to tailor mechanical properties. The degree of crystallinity of the solid HDPE specimen significantly affects its  dissolution behavior. Fig. 6 illustrates how varying initial crystal linity (in the range 30% to 70%) influences the time-dependent behavior of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film in p -xylene at 104 °C. The Kdec  and rdis values used in these simulations are specific to this temperature. High initial crystallinity results in a modest reduction (~10%) in the degree of swelling (Fig. 6a), which in the model is reflected by a lower solvent volume fraction within the film (Fig. 6c). Fig. 6d further highlights that higher  initial  crystallinity  (70%)  sustains  a  larger  crystalline  volume fraction deeper within the film compared to lower crystallinity (30%), thereby delaying decrystallization and dissolution. However, as shown in Fig. 6c, the film approaches solvent saturation in the intermediate to late stages of dissolution. This suggests that the initial polymer crystal linity  primarily  affects  the  early-stage  dissolution,  with  its  influence diminishing over time, and having little impact on the overall dissolu tion time or late-stage solvent diffusion in the film. We note that this relatively  minor  effect  of  initial  crystallinity  on  the  time  for  full decrystallization and dissolution is applicable to the experimental con ditions where Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s (reported in Fig. 6). However, a sensitivity  analysis  revealed  that  the  effect  of  initial  crystallinity  is strongly modulated by the value of Kdec. When Kdec  was reduced by about half to 15 × 10 3 1/s, which can be the result of a few degrees temperature decrease, a much stronger dependence on initial

3.4.2. Effect of film thickness

The dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline polymers such as poly olefins are not only of fundamental scientific interest but also critically important  in  practical  applications  such  as  plastics  processing  and recycling [46,66]. A key parameter influencing dissolution kinetics is the thickness of the polymer material, such as plastic films. Film thick ness  affects  durability,  mechanical  strength,  and  protective  perfor mance, and is commonly expressed in ' mil ' , where 1 mil = 0.001 inch = 0.0254 mm. Plastic films are produced in a wide range of thicknesses, from lightweight protective covers (~1-2 mil or 0.025-0.05 mm) and retail shopping bags (~3 mil or 0.08 mm), to heavy-duty construction barriers (6-20 mil or 0.15-0.5 mm) and robust containment liners used in agriculture and landfilling (20-40 + mil or 0.5-1 + mm) [67,68]. This wide range of applications highlights the need for a fundamental un derstanding of  how  film thickness influences processes such as dissolution.

To address this, the impact of thickness, in the range from 0.03 mm ( ≈ 1.18 mil) to 3 mm ( ≈ 118 mil), on the dissolution kinetics of HDPE films in p -xylene at 104 °C was investigated. This range spans commer cially  relevant  thin  films  to  thick  structural  sheets.  The  simulations across this range used the Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s and rdis = 2.4 × 10 8 m/s values obtained from experimental results for HDPE dissolution at the same solvent and temperature. We note that the film thickness re ported here corresponds to the full, initial thickness (in the model, the initial film thickness equals 2L0).

Both  full  decrystallization  time  and  complete  dissolution  time increase with film thickness, but their scaling behaviors differ (Fig. 7). Time for complete dissolution increases linearly with thickness, while time  for  full  decrystallization  shows  a  weaker  dependence  on  film thickness, as it is primarily controlled by solvent disrupting the crys talline order. Dissolution involves the additional, slower step of polymer chain disentanglement and diffusion out of the solvent-swollen polymer matrix, which becomes the dominant rate-limiting step in thicker films.

For thin films (0.03-0.1 mm), short diffusion pathways enable rapid solvent diffusion, leading to swift decrystallization throughout the film (Fig. 8b, and 8d). Consequently, a large fraction of polymer chains is simultaneously disentangled and dissolved, allowing complete dissolu tion within minutes (Fig. 8a). In contrast, for thicker films (0.6-3 mm), significantly  longer  diffusion  paths  create  a  pronounced  solvent  con centration gradient, leading to the observed reduction in the polymer swelling  degree  (Fig.  8c)  and  delayed  decrystallization  of  the  film ' s center.  Thus,  the  dissolution  process  in  thicker  films  proceeds  more gradually,  becoming  sequentially  limited  by  solvent  diffusion  -> decrystallization -> chain disentanglement.

3.4.3. Effect of the decrystallization rate constant (Kdec)

The decrystallization rate constant (Kdec) significantly influences the overall dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline HDPE films. Fig. 9 illus trates the impact of Kdec  on the time-dependent behavior of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film exposed to p -xylene at 104 °C. The 5 × 10 3 to 1 × 10 1 1/s  Kdec  range  was  chosen  based  on  values  obtained  through  model fitting to experimental data (Kdec = 12.8 × 10 3 1/s at 101 °C and 33.5 × 10 3 1/s at 104 °C). This Kdec  range captures decrystallization kinetics both slower and faster relative to the experimentally derived values, enabling the model to explore conditions that are physically plausible and relevant across a broader range of processing scenarios. Addition ally, values outside this range were found to either produce negligible changes in dissolution behavior (due to other rate-limiting steps such as disentanglement, for example, the results for 1 × 10 1 1/s are nearly identical to those at 5 × 10 2 1/s), or to yield physically unrealistic results, even though the model remained numerically stable. Therefore, the  chosen  Kdec  interval  keeps  the  parametric  analysis  reported  here grounded in experimentally-validated behavior, while capturing effec tively the system ' s sensitivity to variations in Kdec.

As  Kdec increases,  the  time  required  for  complete  dissolution  de creases due to faster unfolding of crystalline domains, allowing for faster dissolution. However, beyond Kdec = 3 × 10 2 1/s, increasing Kdec  has little additional impact, as the rate of disentanglement (rdis) becomes the controlling factor. In fact, the dissolution of semicrystalline polymers depends  on  both  decrystallization  and  chain  disentanglement;  the slower of the two ultimately governs the overall process. An increase in Kdec  also shortens the induction time (tind) and reduces the degree of swelling (Fig. 9a and 9b), due to faster unfolding of crystalline domains. The plateau in dimensionless thickness at lower Kdec  values (Fig. 9a) indicates a delay in the conversion of crystalline to amorphous domains. During this period, the polymer may become saturated with solvent, limiting  further  solvent  diffusion.  Fig.  9c  shows  that  increasing  Kdec accelerates  the  conversion  of  crystalline  domains  at  any  given  time, consistent with the direct relationship described in Eq. 3. In Fig. 9d, solvent diffusion toward the center of the slab ( ξ 1 = 0) decreases with increasing Kdec up to approximately 2 × 10 2 1/s. Beyond this point, the polymer  dissolves  more  rapidly,  so  the  time  corresponding  to  20% progress toward full dissolution occurs earlier in the process, resulting in a higher solvent volume fraction in the polymer at that stage.

While decrystallization controls the unfolding of crystalline domains, the overall dissolution process is also strongly influenced by the polymer chain disentanglement rate. The following section investigates the role of rdis  in polymer dissolution kinetics.

3.4.4. Effect of disentanglement rate (rdis)

The disentanglement rate (rdis) directly affects polymer dissolution kinetics by controlling the availability of disentangled polymer chains to diffuse into the solvent. The selected range for rdis, 1 × 10 10 m/s to 5 × 10 8 m/s,  was  informed  by  values  derived  through  model  fitting  to experimental data (rdis = 2.2 × 10 8 m/s at 101 °C and 2.4 × 10 8 m/s at 104 °C). These fitted values fall near the upper end of the rdis range, but rdis values  were  also  considered  to  capture  conditions  where  chain disentanglement becomes the primary limiting factor. rdis values above 5 × 10 8 m/s were found to have minimal influence on dissolution ki netics  due  to  the  increasing  dominance  of  decrystallization  as  ratecontrolling  mechanism.  The  1 × 10 10 m/s  -  5 × 10 8 m/s  range therefore enables the model to capture both kinetically restricted and transport-limited regimes, while remaining consistent with experimen tally observed behavior. Fig. 10 illustrates the effect of the rdis  on the dissolution process of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film in p -xylene at 104 °C. Increasing rdis reduces the time required for full dissolution and results in more dissolved polymer at any given time. This is because a higher rdis value leads to more disentangled polymer chains available to diffuse into the solvent. Fig. 10a shows that higher rdis values lead to a reduced degree of polymer film swelling.
